reports.program: Home safety, accessibility and critical repairs

what: Rebuilding Together Metro Chicago repairs homes for low-income residents, with priority for older and disabled homeowners.
Its safety and accessibility work includes handrails, grab bars and other critical repairs.
Volunteer teams, skilled trades, sponsors and public partners help residents remain in their homes.
strengths: Home hazards and accessibility barriers are concrete, actionable needs.
Local repair delivery and completed county projects demonstrate an operating mechanism.
Targeted repairs can protect both safety and household resources.
reservations: Completed repairs do not establish additional falls or serious injuries prevented.
Recognized in-kind costs and public funding complicate the return to an ordinary gift.
Actual avoided spending, disruptions, displacement and full portfolio effects remain uncertain.

sections.what: Rebuilding Together Metro Chicago, EIN 36-3803312, is the independent recipient for free repairs and accessibility improvements in Chicago and Cook County. Safe at Home includes grab bars, handrails and smoke detectors; other programs provide larger home repairs and nonprofit facility work. The official donation page identifies a registered nonprofit and current giving route, but no transaction was tested. Native delivery is repaired homes, not volunteer attendance or headquarters location.
sections.monitoring: The county confirms 30 veteran-owned homes repaired with $1.25 million of previously allocated ARPA funding, completed by May 2025. Those homes are baseline, not a new gift's entire output. Cumulative homes since 1991 and claimed service-value multipliers do not establish current incremental health or cash. Track completed additional homes, selected high-risk residents, actual hazard removal, falls, injuries, repair disruptions, money otherwise spent and alternative programs. Observe durability and maintenance rather than assuming permanent benefit.
sections.qualitative: The 2023 Cochrane review finds high-certainty fall-rate reductions from targeted home hazard interventions in higher-risk older adults; the .62 rate ratio is external, not a local RTMC effect. It searched through January 2021, usually followed people for one year and provides little evidence on serious injury prevention. Independence-focused modifications are not automatically the same tested intervention. The model therefore uses explicit high-risk selection and .5 local transport attenuation. Average acute QALY area per avoided fall is a separate weak judgment, not a claim that every fall causes a fracture or death. No mortality or ordinary survivor earnings are priced. The review does not clearly establish reductions in fractures, hospitalization or medically attended falls, and finds little important quality-of-life change. Thus .01 QALY per avoided fall remains a weak acute-area hypothesis under uncertain/null injury endpoints; the fall-rate evidence alone cannot validate that area.
sections.cost:
FY2025 tax expense is $2,993,738. Original Schedule D removes $278,560 donated services/use of facilities from audited expenses; adding that recognized in-kind expense gives $3,272,298 full annual cost. Direct event expense is zero and no rental addback was identified. Comparable full FY2024 and FY2023 costs are $2,248,873 and $2,085,610 after adding $243,542 and $290,830 donated-service expense. Mean full recognized annual cost is $2,535,593.67. This consistent accounting basis includes recognized in-kind resources; additional unrecognized volunteer opportunity costs remain unknown and are not arbitrarily valued by a retail service multiplier.

A judged 100 local household repair opportunities and .5 additional annual-work response imply 50 exposed households. Thirty contain one modeled higher-risk older resident. A judged one fall per person-year, external .62 fall-rate ratio and .5 local transport factor imply 5.7 avoided falls over one finite year. The .01 expected acute QALY per avoided fall averages across minor and serious outcomes, including falls with no injury; it is a judgment, not a proven fracture reduction. After a half-year delay at 3%, the result is .056164 clinical QALYs. No additional accessibility utility is stacked on the same residents.

Twenty households have a judged $500 one-year net energy/care-resource gain and $1,000 one-time spending they would actually otherwise pay within that year. Each positive component retains .5 for health overlap before the full $100 disruption/time/care burden is subtracted, leaving $650. Thirty other households lose $100. All gains exclude taxes, benefit withdrawal, new maintenance costs, replacement resources and displaced earnings; the separate $100 is temporary repair disruption rather than repeated maintenance. Retail donated repair value, property appreciation and gross salary are excluded. Actual alternative spending is a required conditional premise, not an observed household fact.

At $25,000 annual resources, one welfareperson per household and one finite year, a joint log gives .5 × [20 log(1 + 650/25,000) + 30 log(1 − 100/25,000)] / 1.03^.5 = .193674 equivalents. Together .249837 implies $130.977170 million per ten combined equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs. Clinical residents are a subset of all resource-exposed repair households; changed and unchanged financial branches are disjoint, with a 50-household union for full harm stress. Resource exposure and disruption remain when health fails.

Positive overlap never shrinks negative components or costs. Distinct local contractor/payer losses and external care burdens are explicit stresses; recognized donated expense is not counted again as a household opportunity burden. Central counterparty incidence is unknown-neutral, not factual zero or complete-world benefit. Public opportunity costs, nonlocal incidence, displacement and the broader portfolio remain unknown.
sections.funding: FY2025 original government grants are $1,865,647. Current repairs rely on public programs, sponsors and volunteer resources; completed ARPA-funded work and available alternatives stay in the counterfactual. Large repair amounts are not automatically household income gains, and operating recipient costs are not a marginal cash need. The .5 response prior judges additional annual funded work while retaining the full annual denominator; b=1 shows full response. No specific unfunded donor expansion or funding replacement rate was established. A secondary audit-control lead is not asserted as an original verified finding in this bounded phase.

Direct event expense is zero and no rental addback was identified. Comparable full FY2024 and FY2023 costs are $2,248,873 and $2,085,610 after adding $243,542 and $290,830 donated-service expense. model.geographicAttribution: Chicago/Cook repair households; one high-risk clinical resident within resource-exposed household subset.
model.formula: exposed=N*b; clinicalPeople=exposed*highRisk; avoidedFalls=clinicalPeople*fallRate*(1−externalRR)*transport. Q=avoidedFalls*qPerFall*discounted finite years−full union harm. Signed energy/care and one-time actual spending components preserve full negatives, then net household costs before one log. Price=10*C/(health+resources).
model.counterfactual: Existing county-funded repairs, alternative providers, owner spending and sponsor/volunteer resources continue.
model.attribution: Additional annual response, household throughput, high-risk selection, transport, injury area and resource changes are distinct conditional judgments.
model.uncertainty: Full portfolio, serious-injury causality, actual household spending, unrecognized social costs and marginal gift effects unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional completed repaired homes, targeted avoided falls, finite expected acute injury burden and signed net household resources; no donated-value-as-income.

reports.program: Birth and postpartum support, doula development and perinatal advocacy

what: Chicago Volunteer Doulas connects families with pregnancy, birth, postpartum and pregnancy-loss support.
Its doulas provide practical, emotional and advocacy support, including for families facing barriers to care.
The organization also supports doula training, compensation and community partnerships.
strengths: Continuous labor support has a plausible evidence-backed route to better birth experiences.
Local access and postpartum help may reduce burdens on under-resourced families.
Training and compensation can strengthen the available doula workforce.
reservations: Local unique births and incremental outcomes were not verified.
Older low-certainty trials do not establish local mortality or long-term infant effects.
Coverage alternatives, household costs, provider opportunity costs and finances require further diligence.

sections.what: Chicago Volunteer Doulas Inc, EIN 27-3636022, supports labor, postpartum and pregnancy-loss care and doula workforce development. Official sources identify Chicago South and West Side beneficiaries despite a Springfield mailing address. The current giving page supports fair compensation, training and under-resourced family care. Services are not uniformly free: the current matching page describes a $25 nonrefundable contribution for traditional labor support, paid professionals and postpartum support options. No donation transaction was tested.
sections.monitoring: The current impact introduction covers October 1, 2025 through September 1, 2026, an eleven-month service period, not a verified annual unique birth cohort. Its full linked report was inaccessible in this bounded check. Observe completed distinct local births and postpartum care, coverage alternatives, actual delivery mode, adverse events, family time and out-of-pocket costs, doula payment after opportunity costs and collected reimbursements. Training targets do not establish new doulas' net earnings or incremental births served.
sections.qualitative: Cochrane's 2017 review, searched mainly through October 2016, pools 26 usable trials and finds possible reductions in cesarean birth and negative birth experiences. Evidence quality is low and settings differ. The .75 pooled cesarean risk ratio is an external observation; applying it locally requires explicit transport and coverage judgments. No apparent special-care nursery or breastfeeding benefit was established. Low Apgar scores are not infant lifetime QALYs or deaths prevented. This reference gives no maternal or infant mortality credit and no additional ordinary survivor wages. Infant health is unknown-neutral centrally, with signed acute stresses rather than a factual zero claim.
sections.cost:
FY2024 original recognized annual cost is $708,622. Direct event and reviewed rental fields are zero; no netted addback was identified. FY2023 cost is $493,603 and FY2022 $479,599, giving a comparable October–September annual mean of $560,608. Donated-service fields are zero in the latest two returns; this does not establish zero unpaid social cost. The whole recipient denominator includes training and nonclinical work while the numerator prices a limited conditional birth-support channel, not a verified marginal expansion.

A judged 300 local birth-household opportunities and .5 additional annual-work response give 150 exposed households; .8 delivery uptake gives 120 supported births. A judged .32 cesarean baseline, external .75 risk ratio and .5 local transport attenuation imply 4.8 avoided cesareans. A .02 integrated acute physical-recovery QALY per avoided cesarean and .002 integrated emotional birth-experience QALY per supported birth are judgments, truncated within the first postpartum year, not permanent utilities. The experience area explicitly excludes physical surgical recovery and is not a depression effect; an additional conservative overlap adjustment guards residual shared welfare. Retaining .8 of positive components for overlap and discounting a quarter-year delay at 3% gives .266821 clinical QALYs. Negative clinical components remain full. Maternal and infant health are distinct persons; no mortality, Apgar conversion or infant lifelong outcome is added.

Resource exposure does not depend on clinical effect. Forty-five parent households have a judged $200 net care/work-resource gain, retain .5 for health overlap, then incur the full $50 burden: $50 net. The other 105 lose $50. The $50 includes the observed $25 traditional-support contribution plus a judged $25 travel, care or time burden; applying this uniformly is a conditional service-mix assumption, not a statement that every family pays it. Gains are after taxes, benefits, replacement earnings and new costs; no retail doula fee is counted as income.

Ten distinct provider households incur a judged $200 net unpaid-time/foregone-resource burden at a $40,000 baseline. Net provider compensation is unknown-neutral centrally, not observed zero; a $1,000 net-gain sensitivity excludes taxes and alternative earnings. Parent baseline is $30,000, one welfareperson per household and one finite year. Joint household resources before a single log give −.074614 equivalents including providers; combined .192207 yields $36.867559 million per ten combined equivalents. This signed ledger is not ten clinical QALYs.

Clinical parent households are a subset of all parent resource exposure. Provider households are assumed disjoint, giving a 160-household union for general harm stress; their time burdens remain even when birth benefits fail. Positive overlap never shrinks negative resources or unavoidable costs. Matched local payer and external care cost stresses are explicit. Central counterparty neutrality is unknown, not complete-world benefit; public and insurer opportunity costs, nonlocal incidence and the full portfolio remain unpriced.
sections.funding: Illinois Medicaid coverage for certified enrolled doulas is an existing alternative, effective February 2024 under the December 2024 notice, not a new donation's entire benefit. CVD's training toward reimbursement eligibility supplies a mechanism but does not establish collected additional income or net new service. Original FY2024 government grants are zero; net assets are −$59,881. Negative reported assets and liabilities warrant accounting and liquidity diligence, not a conclusion that services have stopped. The cost return predates the new impact period. No priced unfunded expansion or donor replacement rate was verified. The .5 response prior represents additional annual funded work against existing coverage and providers; b=1 is exposed separately.

model.geographicAttribution: Chicago birth households and assumed local distinct provider households; postal location not beneficiary attribution.
model.formula: births=N*b*uptake; avoided cesareans=births*baselineRisk*(1−externalRR)*transport. Q=positiveOnly(avoided*acuteQ,k)+positiveOnly(births*experienceQ,k)+positiveOnly(births*infantQ,k)−full union harm, discounted once. Household net precedes .5*people*log(1+net/baseline). Price=10*C/(clinical+resources).
model.counterfactual: Covered Medicaid doulas, family companions, paid providers and alternative community programs continue.
model.attribution: Local cohort, annual response, delivery, transport, utility and resource changes are conditional judgments; external risk ratio is not a local causal observation.
model.uncertainty: Complete portfolio, local birth and infant outcomes, net compensation, payer incidence and marginal funding unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: Completed supported births, finite avoided cesarean and birth-experience burdens, signed parent care/work resources and provider opportunity costs; no mortality credit.

reports.program: Sexual assault counseling, advocacy and prevention education

what: ZCenter provides free, confidential support to sexual assault survivors and their families in Lake and northern Cook counties.
Its services include counseling in English and Spanish, a support line and referrals.
Advocacy and prevention education complement counseling at its Gurnee location, while Skokie currently provides counseling only.
strengths: Free bilingual services reduce barriers to specialist support.
Individual and group counseling offer a plausible route to short-term trauma recovery.
Local referrals and advocacy can help survivors navigate additional needs.
reservations: The reported 447 counseled conflicts with adult 384 plus child 213, so unique throughput remains uncertain.
Adult trials do not establish local QALYs, child effects or durable earnings.
Household net gains, volunteer opportunity costs and marginal donor response are unmeasured.

sections.what: Zacharias Sexual Abuse Center, EIN 36-3314976, provides free individual and group counseling to adults and children, a confidential English/Spanish support line and referrals. Gurnee in Lake County also provides advocacy and outreach; Skokie in Cook County currently provides counseling only. Both locations fall within the Chicago metro boundary. The official giving page identifies the independent recipient, but no donation transaction was tested. [Services](https://zcenter.org/survivor-services/services/)
sections.monitoring: The fiscal 2025 Year in Review covers July 2024–June 2025. Its first page reports 447 counseled, 384 adults and 213 children, whose sum is 597. We use 384 as a reported category only, with a judged uniqueness share of 0.8, not confirmed unique or completed therapy. Calls, advocacy clients and students may overlap and are not added. The CEO describes a lower waiting list without establishing marginal funding need. Obtain reconciled unique adults, treatment dose, symptom outcomes and household resource burdens before treating this as calibrated EV.
sections.qualitative: Free bilingual counseling offers a plausible trauma-recovery mechanism. Cochrane supports low-certainty short-term adult symptom improvement across heterogeneous interventions; high attrition and limited harms reporting weaken local transfer. No QALY conversion or durable recipient effect was measured. Child counseling, advocacy and prevention are outside this narrow priced channel, with their benefits and burdens unknown. Public funding and alternative free providers remain the counterfactual.
sections.cost: The conditional center is $16.855 million per ten combined equivalents: 1.37222 clinical QALYs plus 0.12319 signed household-resource equivalents. Cost is full annual economic recognized resources: $2,454,250 Form 990 expense + $61,260 netted event costs + $5,000 Schedule D donated services = $2,520,510. Against this full denominator, adult category 384 × judged uniqueness 0.8 × annual-work response 0.5 gives 153.6 exposed household units, with one welfare-equivalent person per unit. Clinical completion 0.6, utility 0.03 and duration 0.5 year after 0.25-year delay are unsupported conditional priors, not measured local effect. Independent resource success 0.2 gives 30.72 households a hypothetical finite one-year $1,500 net access/work gain after taxes, benefits, replacement earnings and new costs; retain half for positive overlap then subtract full $100 participation burden, leaving $650. The other 122.88 households lose $100. One joint log per household is counted, with no retail counseling price or ordinary survivor wages. Clinical null retains all resource costs. Harm applies to the full exposed union; clinical recipients are its subset. Central external/provider/payer losses are unknown-neutral, not observed zero or complete world incidence. Matched payer and volunteer-resource stresses retain full losses. Gain exposure is at most one year; zero resource duration removes all signed gains but not attendance burden. Longer clinical durations are discounted year by year, including negative symptoms; union harm is charged once.
sections.funding: Gross comparable FY2023–2025 recognized costs are $1,900,276, $2,156,058 and $2,520,510; mean $2,192,281.33. Schedule D omitted donated services and netted event costs are added once. The FY2024 audit independently confirms prior gross functional totals and notes substantial unrecognized volunteer services. Its $7,069,345 net assets include property and restrictions, not all spendable cash. FY2025 government grants $1,236,493 imply potential funding replacement. Annual response 0.5 is a conditional annual-work counterfactual, not measured next-gift capacity or a separate donor haircut. Donation website and recipient are verified; no checkout transaction was completed.

model.costScope: Conditional narrow adult counseling channel against whole annual cost; not complete recipient EV or marginal gift efficiency.
model.geographicAttribution: Lake and Cook county adult counseling household opportunities; all modeled local. Other programs unpriced.
model.formula: exposed=N*unique*b; clinical=positiveOnly(exposed*completion*q,clinicalOverlap)*discountedYears(T,delay,r) minus full once-only exposed*harm at delay, then geography once. Resource success share jointly nets positiveOnly(gain,overlap)*resourceYears-cost, with resourceYears in [0,1]; others=-cost. CG .5*people*discountedYears*log(1+net/householdConsumption). Matched payer losses scale resourceYears; external costs remain full.
model.counterfactual: Existing free services and publicly funded care continue; not all reported care is additional. Child, advocacy and prevention effects unknown.
model.attribution: Judged annual response beyond existing public funding and alternative providers; clinical subset of financial exposure union. Independent resource success does not depend on clinical completion.
model.uncertainty: Conditional reference, not calibrated expected value: uniqueness, completion, utility, duration, resources and donor response unmeasured.
model.nativeOutcomes: Reported adult counseling category; additional completed adult therapy, finite trauma utility and signed net household access/work resources.

reports.program: Violence intervention, trauma support, education and employment

what: Chicago CRED combines outreach, trauma therapy and life coaching for people at high risk of gun violence.
It helps participants pursue education, paid work experience and employment.
CRED also funds community partners and supports Chicago’s violence-intervention network.
strengths: A sustained local service model reaches people facing severe violence and employment barriers.
Original evaluations examine participants, service dosage and neighborhood outcomes.
Therapy and supported employment offer plausible complementary health and resource mechanisms.
reservations: Participant victimization was null in the original evaluation, and completers are selected.
Current causal net earnings, trauma utility and additional annual cohorts remain unverified.
Whole-recipient grant costs, overlapping public CVI and marginal donor replacement complicate attribution.

sections.what: Chicago CRED Inc, EIN 81-3130448, is the legal recipient. Its official site now links a current Give Lively donation page, replacing the closed historical Network for Good campaign. The linked page was accessible, but no transaction or fulfillment was verified. South and West Side service delivery establishes Chicago beneficiaries despite the tax filing's California address. [Current services](https://www.chicagocred.org/)
sections.monitoring: The 2025 impact report separates direct services from grants and ecosystem work but does not establish causal avoided injury or net household resources. Its cumulative grants and multi-organization historical shooting estimates are not current annual CRED-only outcomes. Current employment services include paid internships and a year of coaching after placement. The official donation link reaches Give Lively; no transaction was performed. Follow-up needs current unique entrants, phase completion, clinical dose, validated trauma scores, victimization and net earnings, not only placements or gross pay.
sections.qualitative: The original 2023 PNAS paper is a quasi-experimental comparison of 324 recruited men and 2,500 matched peers, including 111 alumni. It cannot identify randomized intent-to-treat effects. No phase showed a discernible victimization improvement. The alumni arrest association is not an injury coefficient: remaining long enough to graduate excludes fatalities and some high-risk departures, while police records introduce measurement bias. The May 2026 CORNERS summary adds updated comparisons and neighborhood findings, but acknowledges overlapping CVI coverage; survey changes do not supply a causal dollar or utility effect. These sources strengthen mechanism and counterfactual assessment, not the numerical injury, trauma or earnings priors. Completion, injury-null and unknown cases retain this uncertainty.
sections.cost:
Calendar 2024 original Form 990-PF reports $36,314,414 total book expenses. Its $37,047,914 charitable cash disbursements are a different accounting measure, not an addback. The whole recognized annual recipient cost includes direct work, grants, administration and other activities; it is not a restricted participant-program denominator. No equivalent Form 990 netted event/rental addback was identified. Outside implementation and social costs remain separate.

A judged 400 local household opportunities and .5 annual-package response imply 200 exposed households, with 100 clinical participants. A .05 annual victimization risk and .05 causal reduction imply .25 avoided physical victimizations. One integrated injury QALY per event is truncated within three years and excludes trauma. The remaining 99.75 people receive .03 trauma utility for half a year. Positive clinical components retain .8 for overlap; harms remain full. A one-year delay and 3% discount produce 1.356311 clinical QALYs.

The clinical cohort is a subset of the 200 resource-exposed households; one participant household carries one modeled welfare-equivalent person, with other family welfare unpriced. Resource exposure remains when clinical benefit fails. Fifty households have judged net job resources of $1,500 and net stipends of $300. Positive components each retain .5, then full attendance costs of $300 are subtracted: $600 net. The other 150 households net −$150. Negative components are never attenuated by overlap. A single joint household log gives .5 × [50 log(1.04) + 150 log(.99)] / 1.03 = .220138 equivalent healthy years at a $15,000 household baseline for one finite year. Combined 1.576449 yields $230.355757 million per ten combined equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs.

Job gains are after taxes, benefit withdrawal, replacement earnings and new-job commuting or care costs; stipends are after taxes and benefits. Class attendance, early foregone work and travel are separate full burdens. These amounts are hypotheses, not observed gains. No ordinary survivor wages are added. Central payer and external care incidence is unknown-neutral, not factual zero. Matched stipend-payer losses, external costs, negative resource changes, adverse trauma and mixed-sign cases are explicit. Household gains and losses combine before one log; distinct payer households are modeled separately. Whole portfolio and nonlocal incidence remain unknown.

This deep review retains the initial conditional center unchanged, not an empirically calibrated complete-portfolio estimate. Fiscal 2024 grants of $10,552,266 are already in $36,314,414 book expenses. A direct-service numerator is deliberately incomplete against the whole-recipient denominator; unknown grant and neighborhood benefits and burdens are not asserted zero. The 0.5 funded-work response is a conditional annual counterfactual, not a measured next-gift effect. A 111/324 uptake sensitivity uses historical completer selection only as a throughput hypothesis, not current efficacy.

Finite job-duration cases distinguish one-off stipends and attendance disruption from recurring net job resources. When employment starts in the same year, first-year stipend, net jobs and full process costs enter one joint household log. Later years contain only net job resources, including taxes, benefit withdrawal and new-work commuting or care; no stipend or attendance cost repeats. Delayed employment must start after the first-year window, avoiding overlapping same-household logs. Zero job duration keeps the stipend and full process burden. Added tax/care inputs are incremental stresses beyond the already-net central $1,500, not claims about observed component amounts. Matching payer cases represent distinct displaced beneficiaries or outside providers, not charging the donating household twice for expenditure already in annual cost. Complete world incidence remains unknown.
sections.funding: Comparable calendar 2022, 2023 and 2024 book expenses are $34,196,858, $33,370,210 and $36,314,414, mean $34,627,160.67. Contributions in 2024 are $26,010,890 and net assets $16,146,226. The current impact report describes CRED as privately funded while partners increasingly receive public support. This is not evidence that an additional gift expands services rather than replacing another donor. The .5 response prior judges additional annual funded work against alternatives; b=1 shows full response. No specific marginal expansion cost was verified. Existing coalition appropriations and historical projects are not credited anew. [Original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202522209349101107/IRS990PF)

model.geographicAttribution: Chicago South and West Side household cohort; clinical participants are a subset of resource exposure.
model.formula: Clinical health is discounted integrated injury benefit plus time-sliced finite trauma utility, positive-only clinical overlap, minus full exposed-union harm. For each disjoint household group and nonoverlapping year, net positive-only-overlap job/stipend components minus full negative resources and burdens enter 0.5 × households × discounted years × log(1 + net / annual consumption baseline). Headline counts signed resources once alongside health and full annual book expenses plus separately identified external cost.
model.counterfactual: Existing public CVI, alternative employment, therapy, other donors and partner grants continue. Annual additional funded work is conditional; neither all grant outcomes nor next-gift expansion is identified.
model.attribution: All population, risk, uptake, response, efficacy and resource success coefficients are conditional judgments, not recipient causal observations.
model.uncertainty: Conditional reference retains prior judgments. Original individual victimization null, completer selection and overlapping neighborhood interventions do not calibrate injury/PTSD or employment coefficients. Current unique households, actual dose and net income, outside incidence, portfolio effects and marginal funding remain unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional completed services, prevented gunshot victimization and finite trauma relief, plus actual net household earnings and stipend resources; not arrests, graduation counts, placement salaries, cumulative grants or ecosystem totals converted directly to welfare.

reports.program: Violence interruption, trauma support and paid workforce preparation

what: Institute for Nonviolence Chicago supports people at high risk of violence in Austin, West Garfield Park and Back of the Yards.
Outreach staff mediate conflicts, support victims and connect participants with trauma-informed care.
Paid workforce preparation combines job readiness, mentorship and nonviolence training.
strengths: Local outreach can reach people underserved by conventional services.
Trauma support and job preparation address connected barriers to safety and stability.
Paid participation may make sustained attendance more feasible.
reservations: Service counts and neighborhood trends do not establish additional shootings prevented.
Evidence from longer, different interventions does not identify this recipient's clinical effect.
Government replacement, attendance burdens and transfer-payer costs materially affect donor value.

sections.what: Institute for Nonviolence Chicago, EIN 81-1098722, is the independent donation recipient. Current services include violence interruption, victim support, reentry, behavioral supports and paid workforce preparation. Official program locations establish Chicago delivery rather than relying on headquarters alone. [Programs](https://www.nonviolencechicago.org/pathwaystopeace)
sections.monitoring: The 2025 aggregate of 1,307 unique participants spans service types; it is not a workforce cohort. The reported 197 mediations and 25% neighborhood decline do not measure counterfactual violence reduction. Pathways describes twelve weeks, weekly stipends and ten in-person hours Monday through Thursday plus remote Friday work. Its 4,070 participants since 2016 are cumulative. Track distinct participants, attendance, exposure-adjusted injuries, validated trauma measures, collected net earnings and services available without the Institute.
sections.qualitative: The READI lottery evaluated an eighteen-month subsidized job and cognitive behavioral intervention, not this twelve-week program. Its primary composite violence result was not significant. Shooting victimization was 18% lower but statistically uncertain; a larger arrest reduction did not survive adjustment for multiple outcomes. Neither arrests nor neighborhood trends become QALYs here. Injury risk, causal reduction and trauma utility are explicit weak priors. Physical injury and trauma cohorts are partitioned to avoid stacking both benefits for one person. No ordinary survivor earnings are credited.
sections.cost:
FY2025 original recognized expense is $15,749,475. No direct event or rental expense group was identified in the reviewed return. The annual whole-recipient denominator prices a limited conditional channel, not the complete portfolio or a verified marginal expansion. The .5 response prior represents annual work additional to continuing public and nonprofit alternatives; b=1 is reported separately, not another donation haircut on realized outcomes.

A judged 500 local household opportunities yield 250 additional exposed households and 125 clinical participants. A .05 injury risk and .1 causal reduction imply .625 avoided victimizations. One integrated physical QALY per event is truncated within three years, excludes trauma and is not repeated annually. The other 124.375 people receive .03 utility for half a year. Retaining .8 of positive health components and applying a one-year delay at 3% gives 1.934466 clinical QALYs.

Resource exposure is independent of clinical success. One participant household carries one modeled welfareperson; other family welfare is unpriced. For 62.5 households, judged net job resources of $1,500 and net stipends of $300 each retain .5 of positive components, while the full $300 attendance burden remains: $600 net. The other 187.5 households net −$150. Negative job changes and stipends retain their full sign separately before household netting and a single log. At $15,000 annual household resources for one finite year, .5 × [62.5 log(1.04) + 187.5 log(.99)] / 1.03 = .275173 equivalent healthy years. Combined 2.209639 yields $71.276232 million per ten combined equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs.

Job resources are after taxes, benefit withdrawal, replacement earnings and new-job commuting or care costs. Stipends are after taxes and benefits; attendance costs separately cover class time, early foregone work and travel. All dollar amounts are hypotheses, not observed collected gains. Costs remain when clinical effects fail. Central payer and outside care costs are unknown-neutral references, not factual zeros. Matched stipend losses and external care burdens are explicit stresses. Government opportunity costs, nonlocal incidence, displacement and full portfolio effects remain unknown.
sections.funding: FY2025 government grants are $13,950,007 and grants to domestic individuals $942,369; neither establishes net new household income. Annual recognized expenses for FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 are $10,268,003, $12,274,566 and $15,749,475, mean $12,764,014.67. Funding replacement and a specific unfunded donor expansion were not established. A secondary index flags a possible FY2025 control finding; the original audit was not verified in this bounded phase, so this is a follow-up lead rather than a factual audit conclusion.

The .5 response prior represents annual work additional to continuing public and nonprofit alternatives; b=1 is reported separately, not another donation haircut on realized outcomes.
model.geographicAttribution: Chicago neighborhoods; all modeled participants local, not a national result.
model.formula: Q = positiveOnly(events × integrated injury Q, .8) + positiveOnly((treated − events) × trauma utility × .5 years, .8), discounted one year. Resources = sum .5 × people × log(1 + jointly net household change/baseline) / 1.03. Headline = 10 × cost/(clinical Q + resource equivalent).
model.counterfactual: Existing public violence prevention, employment and trauma services continue; alternative jobs, benefit offsets and funding replacement matter.
model.attribution: All population, risk, uptake, response, efficacy and resource success coefficients are conditional judgments, not recipient causal observations.
model.uncertainty: Complete portfolio and marginal-gift EV unknown; reference priors are not calibrated posterior estimates.
model.nativeOutcomes: Distinct local participants, avoided physical victimizations, finite trauma improvement and net household resources; no arrest-to-QALY conversion.

reports.program: Walking, bicycling, transit advocacy and community engagement

what: Active Transportation Alliance works with Chicago-area residents and public agencies to improve walking, bicycling and transit.
Its advocacy supports safer streets, connected routes and more accessible transportation.
Community organizing, education and events help residents participate in those changes.
strengths: Safer routes can reduce injuries while making regular activity easier.
Better transport access can protect household resources and access to work.
Current local organizing and a clear independent recipient make the delivery mechanism inspectable.
reservations: Announced funding and projects do not establish additional users, injuries prevented or net household gains.
Public agencies and coalition partners provide much of the implementation, limiting charity attribution.
Travel burdens, construction costs, displacement and counterparty losses may offset benefits.

sections.what: Active Transportation Alliance, EIN 36-3385886, is an independent nonprofit recipient for advocacy, events, education and suburban work. Its current official pages describe Chicagoland walking, cycling and transit improvements, with local street-safety organizing and regional transit implementation. The modeled branch is local to the Chicago metro; headquarters alone is not the beneficiary evidence. [Current work](https://activetransportation.org/) [Official giving](https://activetransportation.org/about-us/get-involved/donation/)
sections.monitoring: The current homepage describes recent Portage Park safety work, calls for stronger city safety staffing and the new regional transit authority. Existing 2025 capital funding and transit legislation are in the baseline; neither is a new gift's entire output. Observe completed improvements, distinct local users, actual physical activity, exposure-adjusted crashes and the transport options users would otherwise have. Event participants, project miles and appropriations are not causal clinical QALYs.
sections.qualitative:
Safer walking and cycling infrastructure can reduce injury risk and support activity, while better transit can improve access to work and essential services. These channels overlap: activity gains must not be added to the same wellbeing improvement already priced through safety or money. The model retains 80% of each positive clinical component for overlap, but retains full negative injury or exercise effects.

A hypothetical 1,000 local household opportunities, .2 additional implementation/behavior probability, .25 coalition share and .5 annual-package response imply 25 expected additional clinical trajectories. Annual net utility priors are .005 for activity and .002 for injury risk, for three finite years after a two-year delay. No local clinical causal estimate was identified in this bounded review; these are explicit planning judgments, not a transferred mortality coefficient. No lifetime survivor earnings or historical-project replay is credited.
sections.cost:
Calendar 2024 original expense is $2,526,835 plus $53,646 direct event cost netted against revenue: $2,580,481 full recognized recipient cost. September 2023 and September 2022 annual totals are $2,969,440 and $2,743,142. The descriptive mean is $2,764,354.33. A separate October–December 2023 transition return totals $464,363 over three months and is excluded from the annual mean. No rental expense group was identified in reviewed returns. Different fiscal year ends and recipient-only accounting limit comparability; public project capital and outside contributed resources are not verified marginal costs. [Latest original](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202533189349305038/IRS990)

The conditional clinical result is 0.384471 QALYs. Resources use a separate judged 200 unique household opportunities, .5 funding response and .25 additional resource success: 100 exposed households, 25 with a changed outcome. Their $300 one-time net access or commuting gain is halved for health overlap, then the full $20 time/work burden is subtracted before log, yielding $130. The other 75 households lose $20. At $40,000 annual household resources, one welfare person per household, one finite year and a two-year delay, .5 × [25 log(1 + 130/40,000) + 75 log(1 − 20/40,000)] / 1.03² = 0.0205528 equivalent healthy years. Combined 0.405024 implies $63.7118 million per ten combined equivalents, not a measured marginal donation return.

Full negative costs remain when clinical benefits fail. Positive gains alone receive overlap adjustment, and household changes are netted before log. Gross salaries and ordinary survivor earnings are excluded. Central counterparty and external implementation costs are unknown-neutral, not observed zeros; matched local losses and external cost stresses are explicit. Broader construction, nonlocal incidence, displacement and full portfolio effects remain unpriced. The full annual recipient denominator is retained while b represents conditional response against continuing alternatives; b=1 exposes that judgment.

The separate resource branch represents additional commuting or route-planning and engagement outcomes, not implementation of the same infrastructure policy. Its .25 success prior already judges additional net access beyond alternatives; clinical implementation and coalition factors are not applied again to that different branch. This distinction is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated program yield. Central clinical households are assumed to be a subset of resource households. Full harms use the union of both cohorts; if a sensitivity has more clinical households, excess people are included. There is no hidden exemption for clinical-only households. The direct bike-to-work guidance supplies a concrete mechanism for the separate behavior branch, but proves neither incremental households nor dollars. No-policy-success therefore can retain direct behavior resources conditional on their own judged success. [Commute guidance](https://activetransportation.org/resources/bike-to-work/get-ready-to-ride/)
sections.funding: The 2024 original reports government grants of $477,691. The official giving page identifies the recipient and describes coalition-backed 2025 transit and capital funding. Public implementation and previously enacted legislation continue in the counterfactual; their full benefits are not assigned to a new ordinary gift. No priced unfunded expansion tranche or verified donor replacement rate was found. Audit issue dates are not used as publication dates. [Giving scope](https://activetransportation.org/about-us/get-involved/donation/)

model.costScope: Whole EIN recipient annual gross recognized expense; finite local clinical and resource component, not project capital, full world return or verified marginal cash-gift yield.
model.geographicAttribution: Hypothetical local Chicago metro branch; statewide transit and shared coalition benefits are not assigned wholesale.
model.formula: changed=N*implementation*credit*b. Clinical=g*changed*sum finite discounted[positiveOnly(exercise,k)+positiveOnly(safety,k)] minus full harms. Resources=.5*people*finite discounted log(1+joint signed net/baseline). Combined=health+resources; price10=10*C/known positive combined.
model.counterfactual: Existing public capital, 2025 transit legislation, existing routes, other advocates, alternative jobs and transport options continue.
model.attribution: Implementation, coalition contribution and annual-funded response are distinct priors, not repeated discounts on already-measured incremental outcomes. Resource exposure independent of clinical success. Resource success is an independent annual engagement/commuting branch, not raw implementation of the same policy. Central clinical25 is nested in resource100 by judgment; union population determines full harms.
model.uncertainty: Observed financials and current program mechanisms; all local population, causal effect, resource and marginal response conversions are judgments. Full portfolio unknown is explicit.
model.nativeOutcomes: Conditional planning reference: 25 expected clinical trajectories, 100 resource-exposed households and 25 additional resource changes. None is an observed current causal count.

what: LVEJO organizes Little Village residents around pollution, land use, food access and environmental justice.
Current campaigns seek stronger industrial review and remediation of contaminated places.
Its farm and community garden also distribute food and provide places for residents to grow culturally meaningful produce.
strengths: Resident organizing addresses pollution and land-use decisions close to affected households.
Active growing spaces provide a concrete food-resource mechanism beyond policy advocacy.
Current campaign descriptions distinguish proposed protections from completed historical wins.
reservations: Proposed ordinances and pending remediation petitions do not establish additional exposure reductions.
Local clinical benefits, net food resources and the response to another gift are judgment-led.
Coalition overlap, industrial relocation, worker losses and housing costs could offset benefits.

sections.what: LVEJO, EIN 36-4259477, is the direct general-support recipient for organizing, food justice, youth leadership and administration. Its Little Village service sites and campaigns lie in Cook County, within the Chicago metro. Headquarters alone is not the geographic evidence: the farm, garden and Collateral Channel work provide local anchors. [Current organization](https://lvejo.org/)
sections.monitoring: Current campaign descriptions identify a proposed cumulative-impact zoning ordinance and a Collateral Channel remediation petition whose status is pending. These are mechanisms and implementation questions, not observed pollution reductions. The food page reports weekly deliveries to over 50 families, garden plots for over 60 families and 2025 production, but not deduplicated annual household use or net resource value. Request implementation dates, exposed population, measured air or water changes, unique households, food substitution and actual participant burdens. [Campaigns](https://lvejo.org/our-work/campaigns/) [Food justice](https://lvejo.org/our-work/food-justice/)
sections.qualitative:
Historical coal closures, cleanup and park conversion demonstrate organizing experience, but are already in the baseline and are not credited again each year or to a new gift. Current prospective protections could improve clinical health only if they actually change exposure beyond existing rules and other coalition work. The model uses separate judgments for implementation probability, LVEJO's coalition contribution and annual funding response. Pollution relocation, unsafe redevelopment, worker losses and displacement remain possible.

The 1,000 local policy-household reference is hypothetical, not a reported cohort. It produces 12.5 expected attributable clinical trajectories after .1 implementation, .25 coalition share and .5 annual response. A .001 annual clinical utility gain for three years after a two-year delay is a finite judgment, not an observed local QALY effect. No permanent coal-closure benefit, citywide mortality reduction or survivor earnings is assumed. Food health effects are not separately stacked on the same cash-equivalent benefit.
sections.cost:
Original 2024 recognized expense is $4,269,375; comparable 2023 and 2022 expenses are $4,090,659 and $3,195,698. Their descriptive mean is $3,851,910.67. The reviewed originals did not identify separate event, rental, gaming or inventory expense groups requiring a revenue addback. This is the whole recipient's recognized accounting boundary; unrecognized volunteer, partner and external compliance resources remain unknown. [2024 original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202543189349305014/IRS990)

Conditional clinical health is 0.0343278 QALYs from 12.5 expected trajectories, three finite years and a two-year delay. Food exposure uses 50 delivery families plus 60 garden families minus 30 judged overlapping households: 80 units. Annual response .5 leaves 40 incremental household units. A judged one-time $300 net resource benefit is halved for health overlap, then the full $50 participant labor/work/travel burden is subtracted in the same household before log. At $20,000 annual household resources and one welfare person per household, .5 × 40 × log(1 + 100/20,000) / 1.03 = 0.0968455 healthy-year welfare equivalents. Combined 0.1311733 implies $325.476 million per ten combined equivalents. No gross salary or pounds of food is directly treated as QALYs.

Only positive gains receive the overlap adjustment; losses remain full. Clinical-null retains food resources and costs, while zero funding response removes incremental effects. Central policy and payer burden fields are unknown-neutral references, not observed zeros. Worker, rent, compliance and matched producer losses are explicit signed stresses. The joint food-policy case nets same-year household changes before log, or separates different-year household time slices. The headline is a conditional partial-world comparison, not a complete portfolio return or a verified next-dollar donation price.
sections.funding: The 2024 original reports government grants of $196,034. Existing grant support, coalition partners, food distribution and public rules remain in the counterfactual. Ordinary support funds the full LVEJO recipient, not a ring-fenced new ordinance or another historical closure. A priced unfunded staffing or campaign tranche, donor replacement risk and real partner costs were not verified. The official homepage links the 2026 general-support route; its giving-page extractor was unavailable in this review. [Official giving lead](https://lvejo.networkforgood.com/projects/287421-lvejo-2026-general-support)

model.costScope: Whole annual recipient recognized expense; prospective local policy-health and food-resource component. External resources and marginal gift conversion unknown.
model.geographicAttribution: Little Village direct local branch inside Chicago–Naperville–Elgin; statewide or displaced pollution benefits are not assigned automatically.
model.formula: Policy=N*implementation*credit*b; clinical=g*Policy*q*sum finite discount(delay+y) minus full distinct-household harms. Food=(delivery+garden−min(delivery,garden)*overlap)*b. Resources=.5*people*finite discounted log(1+joint signed net/baseline). Combined=clinical+resources; price10=10*C/known positive combined.
model.counterfactual: Historical closures and cleanup, existing rules, food aid, markets, already-funded farms and other coalition efforts continue. No wholesale new-gift credit for completed victories.
model.attribution: Separate enactment/exposure probability, coalition share and annual-package response. Direct food households deduplicated by judgment; one clinical person and one welfareperson per household reference, no family or lifetime multiplier.
model.uncertainty: Observed recipient cost and approximate food scale; clinical conversion, net food dollars and causal funding response are judgments. Full portfolio and outside incidence unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: Conditional reference: 12.5 policy clinical trajectories and 40 incremental food household units. These are judged expectations, not measured protected population or causal food outcomes.

inputs.name: q

reports.program: Lung health education, school asthma response, research and policy

what: Respiratory Health Association provides lung-health education and works on asthma, COPD, tobacco and air quality.
Its school asthma work helps staff prepare for respiratory emergencies with training, equipment and rescue medication.
Research, caregiver support and policy advocacy complement those practical services.
strengths: Prompt asthma response offers a concrete acute health mechanism.
School staff training and stocked medication can reach students before emergency escalation.
Current institutional reporting and original returns make implementation scale and costs inspectable.
reservations: Cumulative medication uses and reported avoided ER visits are not a causal annual outcome estimate.
State funding, school nurses and existing inhalers materially constrain donor additionality.
Local household resources, outside payer costs and marginal funding capacity are unknown.

sections.what: Respiratory Health Association, EIN 36-2222687, is the whole recipient for education, research, policy and events. RESCUE Illinois Schools supplies medication, equipment and training with state support; statewide eligibility intersects Chicago counties but does not prove their actual caseload. This model uses a hypothetical Chicago local branch, not all Illinois outcomes. [Current asthma programs](https://resphealth.org/asthma-programs/)
sections.monitoring: RHA reports cumulative medication use and alleged avoided ER visits, not a verified annual causal outcome for unique Chicago students. Request local student and household counts, severity, access to alternative inhalers, repeated events, emergency care and parent work/care outcomes. Current state funding requires health and economic evaluation; required reporting is not itself evidence of realized benefits.
sections.qualitative: Prepared staff and prompt rescue medication may prevent acute asthma escalation. The model uses 500 hypothetical local households, a 25% annual-package response and a separate 20% incremental acute improvement rate; these are judgments, not observed causal rates. Each avoided event receives 0.003 QALY—about 1.1 healthy days, once—not lifelong asthma recovery, mortality prevention or survivor wages. Existing state funding, school nurses and personal inhalers remain alternatives. Other lung, research and policy effects remain unpriced.
sections.cost:
The original FY2025 return records $3,564,916 in Part IX expenses, plus $368,911 of fundraising costs and $64,394 of rental costs netted separately against revenue: $3,998,221 in gross recognized costs. The comparable 2023–2025 mean is $3,923,552.33. Donated resources outside recognized accounting remain unknown. [Original FY2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202631359349305888/IRS990)

The conditional model exposes 125 of 500 hypothetical local households to additional work. A separate 20% clinical improvement rate gives 25 acute events avoided, valued at 0.003 QALY each after one year's delay: 0.0728155 clinical QALYs. Separately, 25 households receive a judged $400 one-time net work/care resource gain. Halving positive gains for possible health overlap, then subtracting a full $20 process burden, gives $180 per changed household; the other 100 households lose $20. One welfare person per household and a $40,000 resource baseline give 0.0302112 signed resource equivalents using the logarithmic bridge.

Combined impact is 0.1030268 equivalents, implying about $388.1M per better life. These are initial planning assumptions, not measured donation returns. Whole-recipient annual cost covers more than this local acute pathway. Null, adverse, full-response, matched-payer and three-year-cost sensitivities remain inspectable. Negative changes receive no positive-overlap discount; burdens remain when clinical benefit fails. Wider portfolio effects, nonlocal payer losses and marginal donor capacity remain unknown.
sections.funding:
The FY2025 return reports $1,337,733 of government grants and $1,661,969 of net assets. The current Illinois listing names a $535,000 award for July2026–June2027 and requires health and economic evaluation. This is an existing funded baseline, not evidence of additional donor capacity. [Illinois grant listing](https://omb.illinois.gov/public/gata/csfa/Program.aspx?csfa=2343)

RHA's July2025–June2026 report describes education and advocacy, including an inhaler copay cap effective January2026. Those existing policy benefits are not assigned to this acute branch or automatically attributed to new gifts. An unrestricted gift supports the whole recipient; request an incremental work plan, local coverage and funding substitutions. [Official annual report](https://resphealth.org/about-us/annual-report/) [Giving](https://resphealth.org/support-us/)

reports.program: Disability rights, protection and advocacy, and community integration

what: Equip for Equality protects the civil rights of people with disabilities through legal advocacy, investigation and education.
Its Cook County community-integration litigation seeks appropriate supports so nursing-home residents can live safely in the community.
The statewide recipient also works on education, employment and access to services.
strengths: Rights enforcement can connect people with safer care and practical supports.
Cook County litigation provides a concrete local implementation mechanism.
Original audited accounts identify government funding and contributed resources.
reservations: No verified local incremental health or net household-resource cohort was identified.
Existing decrees, public care and other counsel prevent assigning all transitions to a donation.
Unrecognized pro bono resources, unsafe transitions and caregiver/payer costs may materially change the comparison.

sections.what: Equip for Equality, EIN 36-3361312, is Illinois's designated protection and advocacy organization. Its Colbert work concerns Medicaid-eligible disabled nursing-home residents in Cook County, within the Chicago metro; other statewide work is not assigned wholesale to Chicago. [Official systemic work](https://www.equipforequality.org/systemic-litigation/)
sections.monitoring: The FY2025 court-filed plan requires outreach, assessment, service planning, transition and quality reporting. It explicitly notes that some new compliance data had not yet been reliability-validated. Commitments are not verified completed transitions, additional safe placements or measured QALYs. Request unique local clients, safe retained placements, health changes, resources, burdens and actual alternative help. [Primary implementation plan](https://www.equipforequality.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Colbert-IP-FY-2025.pdf)
sections.qualitative: Safer community support, prevented neglect and appropriate access can improve health, but transition without sufficient care can cause harm. Autonomy and legal rights have value beyond clinical utility; this initial model does not turn every legal victory into health. Existing decree obligations, public Medicaid care and other plaintiff counsel remain in the counterfactual; shared transitions are not credited in full to each organization. No clinically calibrated local effect was identified in this bounded review. The 100-household reference, .2 clinical additionality, .5 annual-work response, .1 annual utility and two-year duration are transparent planning judgments, not observed causal rates. No lifetime survivor earnings or automatic family multiplier is used.
sections.cost:
FY2024 audited recognized expense is $9,770,963, including $117,984 contributed nonfinancial assets. Revenue is $9,408,652 and government funding $7,442,120. Central recognized-cost accounting does not include approximately $1.8 million additional unrecognized professional services noted in the audit; the explicit $11,570,963 sensitivity adds that approximate external resource value without duplicating recognized donations. It is not evidence that all volunteer time sacrifices billable household income. [Original audit](https://www.equipforequality.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/EFE-Single-Audit-9.30.24-FINAL.pdf)

A hypothetical 100 local households × .5 annual-funded-work response yields50 incremental resource-exposed households. Clinical additionality .2 gives10 changed clinical trajectories, .1 utility for two discounted years:1.913470 clinical QALYs. Financial .2 implies10 resource-changing households. Their judged one-time $1500 net resource gain is halved for health overlap and netted against full $100 process/work/care burden BEFORE log, yielding$650;40 otherHH lose$100. One modeled welfare person per household and$20k annual household baseline produce .5×[10 × log1.0325+40 × log.995]/1.03=.0579266 welfare-equivalent healthy years. All negative changes remain full and clinical-null retains resources.

Combined1.971396 equivalents imply $49.563667 million per ten combined equivalents, not a measured marginal donation return. Full statewide annual recipient expense remains the denominator while only this finite Cook branch is priced. b=1 sensitivity exposes annual-response assumptions. Central payer neutrality is UNKNOWN, not factual zero; matched transfer and adverse cases price signed local payer loss. Nonlocal costs, additional caregiver/provider burdens and wider portfolio effects remain unpriced, so this is not complete world EV.
sections.funding: The 2024 audit reports net assets$2,977,296, unrestricted$2,633,895 and restricted$343,401. Heavy government support complicates donor additionality; there is no verified marginal general-support expansion tranche. Ordinary gifts support the statewide recipient, not a ring-fenced Colbert project. [Official giving](https://www.equipforequality.org/give/) The audit opinion is dated May 29, 2025; this is not verified publication time. Root independently read official FY2023 and FY2022 audits with expenses $9,358,418 and $8,102,494. Together with 2024, the descriptive annual mean is $9,077,291.67, not a forecast.

model.costScope: Whole statewide annual recognized recipient expense; conditional finite Cook health/resource component, unrecognized professional costs separate stress, not measured marginal-gift yield.
model.geographicAttribution: Cook County branch within Chicago–Naperville–Elgin current OMB boundary; no statewide outcomes silently assigned local.
model.formula: Clinical=g*N*a*b*q*sum(y=0..T-1)(1+d)^-(delay+y)-g*N*b*harm/(1+d)^delay. Household resource=.5*people*discountedlog(1+signedjointnet/baseline), positive-only recipient overlap. Combined=clinical+resource;price10=10*C/Combined only if known andpositive.
model.counterfactual: Existing public P&A support, decree implementation, Medicaid/community services and alternative counsel continue. b is conditional annual-package response not an extra donor haircut on measured effects.
model.attribution: Hypothetical distinct local household cohort; one clinical person/one welfareperson per household. Different clinical/resource resolutions are not inferred from raw litigation output. No repeated lifetime or gross salary credit.
model.uncertainty: All effect and resource conversions are judgments; source evidence establishes scope and cost, not causal QALYs. Full portfolio unknown is explicitly null.
model.nativeOutcomes: Planning reference100 distinct local households,50 annual-response exposedHH,10 incremental clinical trajectories and10 resource-changingHH; no observed completion counts claimed.

what: NHeLP uses litigation, policy analysis and legal-aid support to protect access to health care.
Its California team works on Medi-Cal and consumer access, while national implementation cases can also benefit Californians.
Our weak-confidence estimate is about $35.5 million per 10 California QALYs for a Medicaid-rule pathway, with other portfolio health unquantified.
strengths: A direct rights-to-effective-care mechanism can affect many people at once.
Current original audits distinguish recipient costs, restricted funding and donated legal labor.
California expertise connects policy work to local health-access problems.
reservations: Court filings and policy participation do not identify marginal donation credit.
California's share of this policy pathway is modeled; its share of all recipient benefit remains unknown.
Substantial existing funding and reserves complicate claims that a new gift buys an extra lawyer or changes a case outcome.

sections.what:
This report covers the entire charitable recipient, National Health Law Program, EIN 95-3080947, rather than only its California office. The dedicated California program combines policy advocacy, litigation and a Health Consumer Alliance support-center role. National federal work can also affect California residents. [California advocacy and support-center role](https://healthlaw.org/california-advocacy/) [Strategic framework 2023–2027](https://healthlaw.org/strategic-framework/)

The current docket includes lead or co-counsel cases and amicus participation; those are different causal roles. September 2026 appellate briefs, Medicaid disputes in other states and California-related federal challenges demonstrate an active mixed geographic portfolio, not an aggregate California benefit estimate. [Current litigation portfolio](https://healthlaw.org/our-cases/)
sections.monitoring:
The health endpoint is effective care obtained or delay avoided, not a lawsuit filed, insured person named in a rule, or bill canceled. Health Consumer Alliance accounts include both restored access and debt disputes after treatment; those cannot all be valued as newly delivered care. Local legal-aid representation must be separated from NHeLP's support-center contribution. [Health Consumer Alliance services and client accounts](https://healthconsumer.org/)

Oregon's randomized Medicaid evidence supports increased utilization and improved self-reported health/depression, but did not show significant measured physical-health or mortality effects over the initial follow-up. A later economic analysis maps self-rated health to QALYs; its population and coverage contrast are not a direct estimate for legal-policy work in California. [The Value of Medicaid: Interpreting Results from the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8081392/)

Request a case-level chain from incremental funded capacity to changed policy implementation, distinct affected people, effective uptake, finite duration and health outcomes, including unsuccessful and displaced work.

The forecast describes enrollment at a point within each year, not integrated insured person-years. Our central calculation assumes that difference persists for a full benefit year; a half-year average reduces modeled health by half. Replacement coverage and the scope a legal remedy could actually change are discounted separately.
sections.qualitative:
A concrete current pathway is enforcing timely behavioral-health access. NHeLP's June 2026 review identifies repeated commercial-plan failures and calls for follow-up and implementation accountability. These investigations concern a specified commercial-plan domain, not all Medi-Cal beneficiaries. [California commercial-plan behavioral-health investigation analysis](https://healthlaw.org/regulatory-investigations-reveal-systemic-failures-among-commercial-california-health-plans-in-delivering-timely-behavioral-health-care/)

The original regulator schedule shows a publicly financed investigation program underway across multiple phases, with additional 2026 reviews and some reviews postponed because other enforcement or plan changes were already in progress. A donation therefore cannot receive credit for the entire regulatory program; its plausible contribution is improving implementation or timing beyond that baseline. [Behavioral health investigation phases and plan changes](https://www.dmhc.ca.gov/Portals/0/Docs/OPM/HealthPlanChanges.pdf)

Policy health benefits may be substantial, but a small direct-assistance proxy would omit the recipient's primary strategic value. Fiscal transfers and rights protection also have value outside QALYs; this report does not silently monetize them as health.
sections.cost:
A weak-confidence estimate for the Medicaid-rule implementation pathway is about $35.5 million per 10 California QALYs. It retains three years of the entire recipient's latest audited cost, $39,107,481, while modeling about 11.0 California QALYs over two benefit years. This is a policy-pathway estimate with other portfolio net health provisionally zero, not a measured whole-portfolio return or proven lower bound.

The national model starts from Manatt's 1.9 million annual difference between statutory-language and CMS-rule enrollment forecasts for2028–29. It applies .5 for realized/remediable scope, .5 for genuinely avoiding uninsurance, .02 QALYs per insured year, .1 incremental coalition influence, .1 NHeLP attribution and .25 financial additionality. Those are explicit subjective judgments; the current amicus role identifies neither a ten-percent causal share nor an unfunded staffing elasticity. Benefits are discounted3% in years2 and3 and then stop.

For California, the original state table gives a 2028 forecast difference of474,000 (2,147,000 minus1,673,000), versus1,900,000 nationally. Applying g=474/1900 to the shared national model gives11.007095 California QALYs. Carrying the2028share into2029 and assuming comparable conditional remedy, insurance replacement and health yield are transfer judgments. This is not California's share of all NHeLP work. [Original Manatt state forecast](https://assets-us-01.kc-usercontent.com/9fd8e81d-74db-00ef-d0b1-5d17c12fdda9/23b961e2-a654-4fd1-9358-1e3d42205358/Vital%20Signs%2050-State%20Tracking_CMS%20Medicaid%20Work%20Requirements%20Rule.pdf)

The brief addresses medically-frail exemptions and self-attestation, narrower than eliminating the federal law. Current legal work and public administrators remain in the counterfactual. Zero policy change, zero health benefit or complete financing substitution removes the modeled benefit; adverse public-resource or other-portfolio effects may make net health negative. Public treatment expenditures are outside the recipient numerator, so this is not full social cost-effectiveness. [Original September10 amicus](https://healthlaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Mass.-v.-Oz.Amici-Brief-1.pdf)
sections.funding:
Audited calendar-year expenses are $11,023,768 in 2023, $11,725,264 in 2024 and $13,035,827 in 2025: a comparable mean of $11,928,286.33. [2024 audited financial statements with 2023 comparative](https://healthlaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/National-Health-Law-Program-2024-Audit-Final.pdf) [2025 audited financial statements](https://healthlaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/20251231-National-Health-Law-Program-Inc.pdf)

The 2025 audit records $20,349,524 revenue and $33,596,890 ending net assets, including $21,527,078 without donor restrictions and $12,069,812 restricted. Its $339,667 donated professional services are noncash legal labor, not additional cash treatment spending. Large grant concentration and restrictions matter; the surplus does not establish either unlimited capacity or a particular unfunded opportunity. The audit opinion is dated March 27, 2026; that is not asserted as its publication date. [2025 audited financial statements](https://healthlaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/20251231-National-Health-Law-Program-Inc.pdf)

The careers page shows no specific current opening in its displayed opportunities section. This is not proof of no staffing need, but historical advertisements cannot establish a present cash bottleneck. An ordinary donation route is verified; no restricted California allocation or recipient commitment was assumed. [Current job opportunities](https://healthlaw.org/careers/) [Official donation route](https://healthlaw.org/?form=together)

model.costScope: Three years of all recipient programs/support at FY2025 audited resource cost including donated legal labor. One national implementation pathway quantified; other portfolio net health set zero, not a proven lower bound. Public treatment and wider social costs excluded.
model.geographicAttribution: Specific Medicaid-rule pathway only, not whole-recipient share. Manatt Table2's 2028 CA difference=(2147−1673)*1000=474000; national=(8606−6706)*1000=1900000. g=474/1900=.2494736842. Applying this share to 2029 and other scenario years, and assuming equal conditional remedy, replacement coverage, utility and advocacy yield across states, are explicit judgments. Table1's 2027–34 average451/1808=.2494469 is a consistency check, not the chosen temporal denominator.
model.formula: A=sum(t=start..start+T-1)(1+discount)^(-t); V=N*r*u*A; H=V*q; Q_all=b*(p*a*H-h); Q_CA=g*Q_all; Cost=C*Y; Price10=10*Cost/Q_CA when positive. Central g=(2147-1673)/(8606-6706)=474/1900. National enrollment snapshots are assumed sustained over each credited year; q is a sustained annual utility judgment. All-population outcomes match the national view; California and USA are not additive donations.
model.counterfactual: Existing state litigation, other amici, public administrators, grants and clinical care continue. Only further work's change in strict versus less restrictive administration counts, not repeal or all losses. r removes forecast/remedy overreach, u removes replacement coverage, b removes financial substitution.
model.attribution: p=.1 incremental coalition contribution, a=.1 NHeLP share and b=.25 funding additionality are separate subjective factors. Current amicus and strategy show a live role but identify none of them. Existing work receives no automatic future-donation credit.
model.uncertainty: Weak-confidence, explicitly subjective policy-pathway best estimate. Finite central is useful conditional on the shared USA judgments; it is not a measured portfolio return or rigorous lower bound. Clinical, policy and financial priors dominate the source-observed geographic ratio. Root may reject numerical acceptance. Other California and national portfolio health is set net zero, not proven absent.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional Medicaid enrollment, then genuinely additional insured person-years with effective access; finite QALY utility differences. Filings, fiscal transfers and legal wins are not health units.
