what: National Health Law Program protects access to care through litigation, policy analysis and support for legal-aid advocates.
A current national opportunity is preserving meaningful medical-frailty exemptions as statutory Medicaid work requirements are implemented.
Our weak-confidence best estimate is about $8.9 million per 10 USA QALYs; policy influence and marginal capacity—not filings—drive the result.
strengths: National implementation changes can preserve effective care for many people.
A current amicus and detailed external enrollment model identify a concrete, narrower policy difference.
Randomized Medicaid evidence supplies a health bridge; current audits reveal full recipient costs.
reservations: Neither NHeLP's incremental policy influence nor its funding additionality is measured.
Enrollment forecasts are not uninsured person-years; replacement coverage and effective access need discounts.
Existing grants and reserves weaken demonstrated next-dollar urgency; zero and adverse health remain possible.

sections.what: NHeLP's [national strategy](https://healthlaw.org/prepare/) combines litigation, regulatory analysis and state partnerships. It also works on disability services, reproductive health, eligibility and California access. All recipient functions remain charged. Its [September 2026 amicus](https://healthlaw.org/resource/amicus-massachusetts-v-oz-district-court-of-massachusetts/) supports state plaintiffs challenging medical-frailty and self-attestation restrictions. Being an amicus differs from leading the states' lawsuit, and neither establishes new-donation impact.
sections.monitoring:
[Manatt's original forecast](https://www.manatt.com/insights/white-papers/2026/cms-medicaid-work-requirements-rule-a-50-state-analysis-of-additional-coverage-losses-ffy-2027-2034) projects 1.9 million more Medicaid enrollment losses under strict implementation than its statute-only scenario in each of 2028 and 2029. It assumes 40% versus 30% disenrollment among affected people, informed by earlier state experience. This is a forecast, not an experiment on the new rule. We halve the difference for forecast/remedy uncertainty and halve it again for enrollment that genuinely prevents uninsurance. Track effective coverage-person-years, not filings or the entire enrollment population.

The forecast describes enrollment at a point within each year, not integrated insured person-years. Our central calculation assumes that difference persists for a full benefit year; a half-year average reduces modeled health by half. Replacement coverage and the scope a legal remedy could actually change are discounted separately.
sections.qualitative:
The [CMS announcement](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/press-releases/cms-launches-nationwide-framework-implement-medicaid-work-requirements) confirms statutory work requirements and public implementation support. The opportunity modeled is narrower administration and enforcement, not repeal. States and other counsel continue without NHeLP, and existing work is not caused by future donations.

The [Oregon experiment analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8081392/) maps the self-rated health difference at approximately one year to about .05 utility units; early physical-health and mortality effects were not statistically significant. We assume a .02 utility gain sustained for each credited insured year, allowing different patients, provider access and mapping uncertainty. Depression, mortality and financial protection are not added again. Rights and financial relief also have value outside this health measure.
sections.cost:
Three years at the latest recipient cost yields a modeled 2,206 discounted, attributable insured person-years and about 44 USA QALYs over two benefit years: roughly $8.9 million per 10 QALYs. Favorable assumptions yield about $53,000; very weak influence and access about $218 billion. These are judgment scenarios, not confidence limits.

Central policy attribution is .1 incremental coalition probability/intensity improvement multiplied by .1 NHeLP share, followed by .25 funding additionality. These deliberately modest but subjective values recognize specialist capacity alongside strong substitutes. This is not the cost of a single brief. Other portfolio health is set net zero, not proven absent or a rigorous lower bound.

Public treatment expenditures and displaced uses of government resources are outside the recipient numerator. Insurance can finance previously uncompensated care as well as induce new treatment, so this is not a full social cost-effectiveness estimate.
sections.funding:
Shared original-audit review verifies [2025 expenses of $13,035,827](https://healthlaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/20251231-National-Health-Law-Program-Inc.pdf), including $339,667 donated professional services. Revenue was $20,349,524; unrestricted net assets $21,527,078 within $33,596,890 total. These balances do not identify an unfunded opportunity. The 25% marginal-capacity assumption allows existing grants, reserves and donor substitution.

Audited expenses were $11,023,768 in 2023, $11,725,264 in 2024 and $13,035,827 in 2025, averaging $11,928,286.33. [2024 audit with comparative](https://healthlaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/National-Health-Law-Program-2024-Audit-Final.pdf) Historical job advertisements are not current evidence of a cash bottleneck. A costed incremental implementation workplan and committed-grant restrictions are important beta inputs.

model.formula: A=sum(t=start..start+T−1)1/(1+discount)^t; V=N*r*u*A; H=V*q; Q_all=b*(p*a*H−h); Q_USA=g*Q_all; Cost=C*Y; Price10=10*Cost/Q_USA if positive. Central start=2,T=2. Local marginal rate assumes proportional capacity adjusted by b.
model.counterfactual: Existing state litigation, other amici, public administrators, grants and clinical care continue. Only further work's change in strict versus less restrictive administration counts, not repeal or all losses. r removes forecast/remedy overreach, u removes replacement coverage, b removes financial substitution.
model.attribution: p=.1 incremental coalition contribution, a=.1 NHeLP share and b=.25 funding additionality are separate subjective factors. Current amicus and strategy show a live role but identify none of them. Existing work receives no automatic future-donation credit.
model.uncertainty: Weak-confidence best-estimate opinion, not measured return or statistical interval. Root may reject numeric acceptance if these judgments are insufficiently supported. Policy influence and funding additionality dominate; zero/harm explicitly retained.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional Medicaid enrollment, then genuinely additional insured person-years with effective access; finite QALY utility differences. Filings, fiscal transfers and legal wins are not health units.

what: The Institute for Safer Trucking advocates for safer heavy vehicles and supports people affected by truck crashes.
Its work includes technical policy submissions, legislative engagement and informed survivor participation.
Our model examines whether one additional advocacy work packet could modestly increase the chance of earlier automatic-emergency-braking deployment.
strengths: Automatic emergency braking addresses a substantial, technically studied source of fatal and nonfatal road injuries.
The organization brings policy experience and survivor perspectives to a concrete national safety issue.
Original accounts and current public activity support an identifiable, continuing organization.
reservations: The effect of an extra advocacy packet on national policy timing is a declared judgment, not an observed probability.
Manufacturers, agencies and other advocates would continue working without the gift.
Fleet adoption, injury severity, household costs and technology harms remain uncertain; the model covers only one pathway.

sections.what:
IST works on heavy-vehicle safety policy and provides survivor resources. Its public team, Advocacy Days and hearing statement support a technical-policy and survivor-engagement mechanism, not a truck-installation program. Road Safe America merged with IST in 2023, so older organizational boundaries require care.

The forecast considers one next-year automatic-emergency-braking work packet: review technical evidence, prepare a rulemaking submission and policy briefs, organize informed survivor input, and follow up on a defined implementation issue. Existing guides and events are evidence of activity, not measured additional clinical care or policy wins.
sections.monitoring:
The decisive outcome is a change in compliant deployment timing, not the number of meetings or briefs. A useful evaluation would record the specific policy issue, counterfactual agency/manufacturer plans, a funded versus unfunded workplan, submissions and responses, and the organization’s actual role relative to other advocates. No current source identifies that causal effect.

The regulatory proposal estimates AEB-only annual effects of 106 fatalities and 8,058 nonfatal injuries at fully equipped residual-fleet scale. Its pre-proposal voluntary uptake and reduced dark/weather performance are already accounted for. The combined Class 7–8 row also includes electronic stability control, so it is not an AEB-only class estimate. Fleet replacement makes benefits gradual. National forecasts must not be described as observed IST-caused outcomes.
sections.qualitative:
We are interested in an organization addressing a large safety problem through technically informed advocacy. Current public work and original returns support continuing operation, while manufacturer development and other advocacy demonstrate a substantial alternative pathway. The small direct probability shift in this model is therefore explicitly conditional, not a claim that IST owns the rule’s benefits.

Survivor engagement may improve the quality of policy discussions, but its separate support benefits are unpriced. Earlier deployment may also create false activations, equipment costs or freight-price effects; neither a legacy complaint nor regulatory monetized benefits identifies future household incidence. Funding flexibility, current staffing and an actual incremental work packet need confirmation.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter sees truck-safety advocacy as a potentially high-leverage way to reduce road injuries. Our conditional estimate is approximately $1.74M per better life, combining health and net household-resource effects. The initial estimate was $1.65M. Their proximity is not evidence that the original assumptions were validated: the revised forecast changes the cost period, policy contrast, finite mortality value and injury/resource channels. This is not a quoted donation purchase or a complete-portfolio return.

An exploratory $100,000 normalizer pays for one year’s advocacy packet: a judged 400 fully loaded hours at $150, $20,000 external review, $10,000 travel/participant support and $10,000 publication/administration/fundraising. These are budget priors, not IST’s quoted costs or a recommended gift size. The old numerator charged five annual organizational budgets.

Without the packet, the declared joint forecast is 10% earlier deployment, 40% later deployment and 50% no modeled rollout; with the packet it is 10.1%, 39.9% and 50%. The .1-percentage-point shift incorporates gift replacement and all other actors in one direct contrast, rather than multiplying another rule-pass probability, funding haircut or coalition share. It is not empirically estimated. Six-versus-seven-year deployment starts and 7% risk-weighted annual turnover are finite transport priors; both fleet paths converge within the 25-year event horizon.

After a separate subsequent-adoption/transport adjustment and USA-resident share, the forecast represents .05247 avoided fatalities and 3.98871 nonfatal injuries before event discount, not all 106 deaths and 8,058 injuries in the rule forecast. Each death receives twenty finite remaining years at .9 utility, discounted from death onward: 13.589 health years, rather than the old q=20. Nonfatal injuries receive a judged .12 average utility improvement for a quarter-year, without a permanent-disability tail. An exposure-linked technology-harm prior is subtracted independently of gross clinical utility. Net health is .570013 years per normalizer.

Only the nonfatal-injury branch receives household cash benefits. A judged .8 distinct households per injured person and 30% actual cash incidence receive a once-only $500 net saving: illustrative actual copays and short-recovery lost pay after insurance, sick-pay, employer and benefit offsets. This is not medical charges, claims, shadow time or saved lives’ baseline future wages. A $50,000 annual household-consumption reference and separate one-year window convert the savings through the Coefficient Giving .5 log-resource crosswalk. Resource welfare adds .00325287 years, making .573266 combined years.

Positive-only injury overlap, zero/negative probability shifts, finite survival and recovery ranges, signed technology/independent harms, unknown components and independent cash horizons are tested. Fatal-family finances, long-term earnings, property damage, survivor support and complete equipment/pass-through costs remain unpriced, not proven zero. Complete donor return and societal cost-effectiveness remain unknown.
sections.funding:
Original same-entity returns report expenses of $336,891 in 2022, $286,009 in 2023 and $365,248 in 2024: an average of $329,383. Latest functional expenses reconcile to $311,588 program, $39,396 administration and $14,264 fundraising. The latest displayed return is FY2024, filed September 4, 2025; this does not prove that no subsequent return has been filed.

FY2024 revenue was $303,964; salary/benefit/payroll expense was $246,183 with three employees. Unrestricted net assets of $635,726 and traded investments of $598,138 do not establish spare staffing, unused commitments or an unfunded work packet. The 2023 merger affects portfolio comparability but all three rows describe the same legal recipient. No separately netted event/gaming/inventory costs were reported for the chosen gross expense boundary.

Current public sources still describe proposed AEB rulemaking, rather than a final mandate. The exact-RIN publication search located no newer final AEB rule in this bounded review; unpublished agency action is not excluded. The declared next-year packet is about 27% of latest annual expense, a scale check rather than evidence that it buys policy change. A current restricted budget and clear incremental staffing plan could replace these cost and additionality priors.

model.costScope: Full one-year exploratory donor packet charged to a partial AEB advocacy forecast; equipment/provider/coalition social costs and household freight pass-through remain unknown.
model.geographicAttribution: USA-resident share .99 is a declared domestic road-user prior; no foreign policy or territory credit.
model.formula: Expected extra coverage=(with−without joint early-rollout probability)*[earlier fleet path−later fleet path], after one-packet capacity. For each year, apply remaining opportunity, resident share, disjoint mortality/nonfatal forecasts, finite clinical utility and exposure-linked technology harms. Net household resources=.5*distinct affected households*independent window*log1p(one-off net cash/(window*annual baseline))*event/resource discount. Price=10*full donor packet/(health+resources) when known and positive.
model.counterfactual: Public mandates/agencies, other advocates, manufacturers, reserves and donors continue. Direct with-versus-without probability shift moves mass from later to earlier deployment, not from impossible-to-guaranteed success; no extra policy-pass/funding/coalition multiplier.
model.attribution: One declared .001 unconditional joint probability shift for one advocacy packet; no repeated independent national policy chances or whole-rule credit.
model.uncertainty: Numerical conditional partial forecast. Work costs, probability shift, residual uptake, fleet turnover, remaining survival, injury severity, net cash incidence and technology harm are explicit priors, not identified IST outcomes.
model.nativeOutcomes: Forecast .05247 avoided fatalities and3.98871 nonfatal injuries before event discount per exploratory100K; actual observed native activities are submissions, advocacy and survivor resources, not these outcomes.

reports.priceScope: Conditional AEB advocacy, finite road-safety health and net household resources; partial forecast, not a quoted donation purchase.

historicalModel.costScope: All recipient program, management and fundraising expenses; five-year constant-FY2024 cost cohort. Only prospective AEB mortality health is quantified. Not restricted AEB efficiency, not total social cost.
historicalModel.geographicAttribution: Domestic heavy-vehicle crash prevention. Central 99% of modeled health is assigned to residents of 50 states plus DC, allowing 1% nonresident road users. This is a judgment, not a measured residence share; foreign/territorial policy effects excluded.
historicalModel.formula: Fj(t)=min(cap, rate*max(0,t-Lj+1)); A=sum(t=1..T)[F1(t)-F0(t)]/(1.03^t). H=D*r*q*A. Q_all=b*(p*a*H-h); Q_USA=g*Q_all. Cost=C*Y; price=10*Cost/Q_USA when positive. For normalized support G, multiply both cohort cost and Q by G/(C*Y); no linear scaling claim beyond small marginal support.
historicalModel.counterfactual: Public agencies, manufacturers and other advocates continue. Both deployment paths ultimately converge; only acceleration is counted. D already removes pre-NPRM voluntary adoption; r allows subsequent erosion and transport. Existing donor/reserve/public substitution is represented by b.
historicalModel.attribution: Congress, agencies, manufacturers and multiple advocates continue absent the gift. Historical Road Safe America participation does not identify IST's future marginal role; do not double count merger entities or coalition effects. Alpha p=.15, a=.10 and b=.50 lack calibration and are diagnostic only.
historicalModel.uncertainty: Central withdrawn; no calibrated gift-sensitive policy acceleration, IST-specific contribution or funding capacity. Unknown is not zero. Retained alpha numerical inputs and scenarios are conditional diagnostics, not recommendation or confidence bounds.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: Reports, survivor resources and advocacy engagements are observed service categories, not health units. Model bridge uses residual risk-weighted fleet deployment, additional crash fatalities prevented, then discounted QALYs; no policy-win-to-QALY shortcut.

inputs.name: C
inputs.rationale: FY2024 total functional expenses; no separately netted direct-event, rental, gaming or inventory costs reported. All programs and overhead charged.

inputs.name: Y
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Five-year policy-support cohort priced at constant FY2024 annual scale; not a restricted AEB budget.

inputs.name: D
inputs.unit: annual fatalities prevented at completed AEB deployment
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Sourced regulatory forecast of 106 AEB fatalities prevented annually at full residual-fleet deployment; not observed deaths. Based on four test vehicles; baseline adoption/dark/weather already adjusted.

inputs.name: r
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Halve the 2023 AEB opportunity for subsequent voluntary uptake, narrower eventual rule, real-world transport and execution. Does not reapply all historical uptake already removed from D.

inputs.name: q
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Rounded mixed-age adult road-user expectation; approximately decades of future survival adjusted for quality and 3% discounting at time of death. Range 10–25; not the regulator's monetary fatal-equivalent metric.

inputs.name: L1
inputs.unit: first deployment year with successful acceleration
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Accounts for regulatory finalization plus new-vehicle compliance lead time; not a claim of a currently effective mandate.

inputs.name: L0
inputs.unit: first deployment year absent accelerated coalition effort
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Same eventual adoption but two years later; public agencies, manufacturers and other advocates continue in the counterfactual.

inputs.name: rate
inputs.unit: fraction of residual opportunity deployed / year
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Risk-weighted fleet replacement approximation; slower than immediate installation. Not observed current vehicle penetration.

inputs.name: cap
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Coverage is of the remaining D*r opportunity, not all trucks.

inputs.name: T
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Central deployment paths converge before year 25. The poor scenario converges in years 32–33, so its 25-year truncation omits later positive acceleration benefit; it is not a complete-duration lower bound.

inputs.name: discount
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Discount event-year benefits; q is separately discounted from event onward, not double discounting the same interval.

inputs.name: p
inputs.unit: probability of acceleration due to incremental coalition work
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Fifteen percent over five years recognizes pending statutory process and adverse policy climate. Not probability any rule ever passes. This is a subjective expected-value estimate, not identified causal likelihood.

inputs.name: a
inputs.unit: IST contribution conditional on coalition-enabled acceleration
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Ten percent recognizes experienced staff, survivor engagement and stated participation while reserving 90% for agencies, manufacturers and other advocates. No historical rule credited wholesale.

inputs.name: b
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Half allows reserves, donor substitution and staff capacity; current public evidence does not identify a funded-versus-unfunded workplan.

inputs.name: g
inputs.unit: share of modeled road-user QALYs accruing to 50-state/DC residents
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Domestic crash mechanism, with 1% allowance for nonresident road users. Not measured residence; test .95–1. No territorial or foreign regulatory effects credited.

inputs.name: h
inputs.unit: other net health harm over five-year cohort, before b and g
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Other portfolio branches and technology-induced harm set net zero centrally; not proven zero or a lower bound. Negative outcomes included in sensitivity.

inputs.name: deploymentPaths
inputs.rationale: Retained alpha diagnostic, not beta central. Inspectable central paths, F1/F0. Multiplication by D*r yields averted-death opportunity; neither advocacy contacts nor report downloads enter health arithmetic.

reports.program: Alcohol-policy research translation, state coordination and public education

what: US Alcohol Policy Alliance convenes advocates and researchers, develops public education and helps state networks advance policies intended to reduce alcohol harm.
Its current work includes a national prevention strategy, policy conferences, warning-label advocacy and discussion of state alcohol taxes.

Our best estimate is about $4.4 million per 10 USA QALYs, using a deliberately small, uncertain contribution to one state-sized tax opportunity rather than crediting the organization with national drinking trends.
strengths: Alcohol pricing has a plausible and empirically supported pathway to lower consumption and some alcohol-related disease mortality.
The organization has moved beyond a volunteer conference model by hiring executive leadership and preparing an explicit national policy strategy.
State networks can create policy scale without treating every resident as a directly served client; all recipient costs are retained in our calculation.
reservations: No public evidence identifies the next dollar's effect on a specific state's tax, implementation date or population exposure.
Tax studies differ substantially, and some well-controlled analyses find little lasting crash benefit; mortality effects cannot be read directly from sales or meeting attendance.
The most recent located accounts predate the new CEO and larger agenda; the current operating budget, donor restrictions and funding gap remain unverified.

sections.what: USAPA translates research into public-health advocacy rather than providing addiction treatment. Its [public portfolio](https://www.alcoholpolicy.org/) includes labeling, alcohol availability and taxation. Its [2024 leadership plan](https://www.alcoholpolicy.org/latest/usapa-executive-director) described 15 state alliances, and [Mike Marshall's appointment](https://www.alcoholpolicy.org/latest/usapa-taps-veteran-political-strategist-as-ceo) followed in January 2025. The planned [September 2026 Advocates Institute](https://www.alcoholpolicyconference.org/advocate-institute) is intended to refine a national prevention strategy. At the research date the event was still in the future; attendance and a strategy document are not yet policy implementation or health gains.
sections.monitoring: The [current podcast index](https://www.alcoholpolicy.org/podcasts) includes a May 2026 discussion of New Mexico's alcohol-tax effort. This demonstrates engagement, not USAPA-caused legislation. The public record supports a live coordination role but not a verified marginal tax opportunity. Beta monitoring should connect staff time and technical assistance to specific policy texts, votes, implementation, beverage prices, cross-border purchases and resident mortality. It should distinguish proposals, defensive victories and enacted changes from policies that would have occurred anyway. Historic state changes listed on the website cannot all be attributed to USAPA.
sections.qualitative:
Alcohol taxation is more promising than awareness alone, but the causal effect is not uniform. A [New York quasi-experimental study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22436591/) found a 7% decline in alcohol-related disease mortality after a combined beer/spirits increase, while a spirits-only change and small beer-tax reductions had no significant effect. The public abstract was reviewed; the blocked full text was not used to claim a precise transferable coefficient. A [Maryland study](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/77031/cdc_77031_DS1.pdf) estimated 3.8% lower alcohol sales after its tax change in an adjusted model, but the unadjusted per-capita ethanol comparison was unchanged and estimates depended on macroeconomic controls. Sales are not QALYs. An [Illinois synthetic-control reanalysis](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ecin.12811) found little sustained reduction in alcohol-related fatal crashes, with a temporary interior-county effect consistent with cross-border avoidance. We therefore exclude injury benefits and use a modest, explicitly subjective disease-mortality response.

The central policy package raises actual retail prices by 5% across beverage types. That is not the same as raising an excise-tax rate by 5%; the website's loose tax/consumption claim is not our coefficient. Ten QALYs per avoided disease death allows substantial chronic illness and competing mortality. Abrupt unsupported withdrawal, unsafe substitution, financial hardship and stigmatizing communication are potential harms, not automatically offset by tax revenue.
sections.cost:
Our central cost is $350,000 a year for five years, the upper end of the organization's published operating-budget plan. This is a judgment for present scale, not an observed 2026 expenditure. The model prices every program and overhead dollar while quantifying only a state tax pathway. A hypothetical policy package covers five million residents; a 5% retail-price rise and mortality elasticity of 0.4 imply 2% fewer alcohol-induced deaths before a 25% leakage/erosion adjustment. A 20% incremental coalition policy probability, 5% USAPA contribution and 50% funding additionality yield about 4.0 expected USA QALYs over the cost cohort—roughly $4.4 million per 10 QALYs.

This is an expected value over uncertain outcomes, not a forecast that USAPA will visibly save four QALYs. Favorable combined assumptions produce about $18,000 per 10 QALYs; a deliberately weak scenario exceeds $1 trillion, with explicit zero and negative cases. These are judgments, not confidence intervals. The 2026 training ticket is $145 with conference registration or $190 without, but that fee is neither a full service cost nor a health-effect price. No verified beneficiaries per donor dollar can be inferred from it. State administrative costs, partner effort and household economic burdens are excluded from the donor-cost numerator and remain relevant to social value. Tax receipts are transfers, not health gains; no treatment funded by the proceeds is counted.
sections.funding:
The original [FY2024 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202512589349301026/IRS990) reports $208,012 expenses, including $65,531 travel, $60,168 equipment rental and $56,425 contract services. It reports zero employees, $204,294 program-service revenue—largely registrations—and $45,196 contributions. Year-end cash was $199,877 and net assets without donor restrictions $202,477; liabilities were $2,500. These figures predate the CEO hire. Independent review and audit were both marked no. The fiscal year is a full 12 months, not a partial startup period.

Original [FY2023](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202402889349302035/IRS990) and [FY2022](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202333199349304513/IRS990) accrual expenses were $26,948 and $200,361. All three have no reported netted direct-event, rental, gaming or merchandise cost to restore; their mean is $145,107. This conference-cycle average is not the current recurring budget. The [recruitment plan](https://www.alcoholpolicy.org/latest/usapa-executive-director) specified a $115,000–130,000 salary range and $200,000–350,000 annual operating budget. Current conference receipts, project grants, staffing commitments and unrestricted reserves need reconciliation before recommending a gift. None of the three returns reports government grants, but national coordination may still replace work paid for by public, academic or partner budgets. The model's 50% additionality is an opinion about that risk, not documented funding room.

model.costScope: All recipient costs at a judged $350,000 annual current scale for five years, informed by the published $200,000–350,000 operating plan. Historical IRS expenses are separately disclosed. Tax-only health quantified; not a restricted-program price or full social cost.
model.geographicAttribution: The modeled policy population N consists only of residents of 50 states plus DC, so g=1 by construction. N is a subjective successful-policy scale, not measured reach or a headquarters/population-share allocation. Foreign attendees and territorial effects are excluded from credited health while all recipient costs remain.
model.formula: A=sum(t=1..T)1/(1.03^(L+t)); annual avoided disease deaths=N*d/100000*x*e*k; H=annual avoided deaths*q*A. Q_all=b*(p*a*H-h); Q_USA=g*Q_all. Cost=C*Y; price=10*Cost/Q_USA if positive. Central A=7.8063439787, annual deaths=10.275, H=802.1018438079 before policy/funding attribution. Small support normalization G multiplies both by G/(C*Y), not a scalable guarantee.
model.counterfactual: State advocates, legislators, researchers and fiscal pressures operate without USAPA. Only an incremental coalition-enabled policy chance is counted, with small USAPA contribution and donor/reserve substitution. No nationwide federal tax victory, historic state victory, concurrent treatment revenue or injury effect is credited. Ten years is a judged differential duration, which falls if baseline adoption catches up.
model.attribution: p=.20 is incremental coalition policy probability, a=.05 is USAPA's conditional share, and b=.50 is donor additionality. Effective pre-funding policy contribution is 1% of one five-million-resident package. These are explicit opinions supported by network activity, not measured causal rates. Do not sum overlapping state/charity credit.
model.uncertainty: Exploratory expected-value best estimate with very broad scenarios. It can fail at policy influence, price pass-through, heavy-drinker response, survival or funding additionality. Unknown other portfolio effects mean this is not a proven lower bound. Central number is not donor-ready endorsement.
model.nativeOutcomes: Conferences, technical assistance, newsletters and policy discussion are services. A funded-to-policy-to-retail-price-to-disease-mortality bridge is required before QALYs. The modeled mortality subset excludes accidents, homicides and most partly attributable disease; no conversion from awareness or tax dollars to health.

inputs.name: C
inputs.rationale: Upper end of publicly described $200,000–350,000 annual operating plan, not an observed 2026 expense. Includes new executive leadership, communications, convening and overhead; current accounts missing. Test $250,000–700,000.

inputs.rationale: One medium-state-equivalent package across the network, not actual wins or all 15 states. Public plan described 15 state alliances; national/state advocacy could support this scale, but the next target docket is unverified.

inputs.name: d
inputs.rationale: CDC2024 crude national alcohol-induced rate, excluding accidents and homicides. Applying it to a future policy population is a transfer judgment, not observed state mortality. No 178,000 broader-attributable-death numerator.

inputs.name: x
inputs.rationale: A reasonably material all-beverage policy package. Five percent RETAIL PRICE, not five percent increase in excise-tax rate; tax design and pass-through required to attain it remain unknown.

inputs.name: e
inputs.unit: absolute disease-mortality elasticity to retail price
inputs.rationale: A 5% retail-price rise is assumed to reduce targeted alcohol-induced mortality 2% before leakage. Intentionally modest relative to some historical disease studies, allowing weak heavy-drinker response, confounding and modern transport. Not fitted from the NY study or the charity's website.

inputs.name: k
inputs.rationale: Post-price avoidance, cross-border/beverage substitution and subsequent real-value erosion only. Initial pass-through is already included in the actual retail-price increase x and is not discounted again.

inputs.name: q
inputs.unit: discounted QALYs per averted alcohol-induced death
inputs.rationale: Approximately 20 additional life-years at .65 quality discounted 3% gives about 9.7 QALYs, rounded to 10; chronic comorbidity and mortality displacement could make it much lower. Test 3–15.

inputs.name: L
inputs.rationale: Legislation, implementation and disease-response lag; first counted outcome year is year4.

inputs.name: T
inputs.rationale: Finite window after lag; no lifetime policy permanence or benefits after year13. Public/state baseline adoption and reversal may shorten this window.

inputs.name: p
inputs.rationale: Twenty percent extra chance of a material package within five years because of the wider coalition's added effort, not probability that any state ever changes a tax. Current political opposition and small central staffing justify wide uncertainty.

inputs.name: a
inputs.unit: USAPA contribution within additional coalition effect
inputs.rationale: Five percent reserves most credit for state/local organizations, elected officials, voters and fiscal pressures. National coordination, convening and communications provide a plausible but unmeasured enabling role.

inputs.name: b
inputs.rationale: Half of incremental donor support creates otherwise absent capacity; the balance substitutes conference income, other donors, reserves or public/academic support. No restricted tax-only pathway assumed.

inputs.name: g
inputs.unit: USA resident share of modeled health
inputs.rationale: N is explicitly defined as residents of 50 states plus DC covered by state policy. Thus all modeled outcomes qualify; foreign delegates and territories have no credited health. This does not assert all recipient spending is domestic.

inputs.name: h
inputs.unit: other net health harm over five-year cohort, before b
inputs.rationale: No other portfolio health credited centrally. Financial hardship, stigma, unsafe substitution or abrupt unassisted withdrawal could create harm; central zero is a judgment and not a proven lower bound.

inputs.rationale: Event-year discount; q already discounts life-years after that event.

reports.program: Violence prevention, hospital intervention and trauma healing

what: Youth ALIVE! works with people affected by violence in Oakland and Alameda County.
Its programs combine hospital-based support, employment and education assistance, trauma counseling, and violence prevention.
Staff help participants recover, navigate services, and pursue safer, more stable lives.
strengths: Hospital-based outreach offers a practical route to reach injured people at a vulnerable moment.
Counseling, employment support, and compensation navigation offer distinct pathways to improved health and household resources.
Recent original financial returns and program-specific output reports allow costs and activities to be examined together.
reservations: Local outcome reports do not establish how much reinjury, clinical recovery, or income would change without these services.
The conditional estimate covers only selected clinical and resource pathways; prevention, interruption, family, and policy effects remain unquantified.
Current program denominators conflict, and no costed plan establishes how additional donations would expand services beyond existing public and private funding.

sections.what: [Caught in the Crossfire](https://www.youthalive.org/programs/intervention/caught-in-the-crossfire/) sends community intervention specialists to survivors' hospital bedsides and provides ongoing practical support. [Pathways](https://www.youthalive.org/programs/intervention/pathways/) combines mentoring with employment and education assistance. [Counseling Services](https://www.youthalive.org/programs/healing/counseling-services/) provides free community-based trauma care. Youth ALIVE!'s broader portfolio also includes violence interruption, Teens on Target, homicide-family support and advocacy. The quantified direct-service footprint is Oakland/Alameda; statewide policy, national replication and other unquantified effects are discussed separately rather than assigned a population multiplier.
sections.monitoring:
[Current results](https://www.youthalive.org/results/) report 118 CiC clients in 2025 and 96% without reported reinjury, alongside overlapping program activity. Neither figure is a causal injury reduction; citywide homicide trends cannot be assigned to this recipient. The [2020 CalVIP local evaluation](https://www.bscc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Healing-to-Scale-in-Oakland-Final-CalVIP-Local-Evaluation-Report-August-2020.pdf) documents missing data and loss to follow-up; only 24 people had initial trauma-symptom assessments and 17 follow-up responses. The larger [Mathematica Oakland evaluation](https://cao-94612.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/documents/SSOC-Agenda-and-Materials-10-26-20.pdf) explicitly lacks an untreated comparison, so its often-repeated post-program victimization change is not a causal clinical effect. [Urban's 2025 multi-provider school evaluation](https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2025-12/A_Process_and_Outcome_Evaluation_of_Oakland%E2%80%99s_Measure_Z_Funded_School_Violence_Intervention_and_Prevention_Program.pdf) had too few shooting/homicide outcomes to estimate that effect reliably. The next monitoring step is a residence-linked referral-to-completion ledger with comparable injury severity and validated utility follow-up, including people not served.

The current Pathways program page reports 74 participants, while the results page reports 72; both report 16 new jobs. Counseling reports 91 client/family units. The model reserves 31 CiC and 18 Pathways counseling overlaps, leaving 42 analytical units before funding scale; this is not an observed count of unique independent clients. Compensation reporting describes applications, not verified incremental awards. These conflicts and causal gaps are retained explicitly.
sections.qualitative:
The local [Becker 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14967340/) and [Shibru 2007](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17964444/) matched retrospective studies did not detect a significant reinjury or death reduction; Shibru's juvenile-justice finding and detention savings are not health QALYs. These small studies do not prove no effect. A [2026 systematic review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42611686/) pooled ten studies and favored hospital violence intervention for violent reinjury (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.38–0.94), but evidence quality was low and heterogeneity substantial. That supports a plausible mechanism, not transfer to every current Oakland participant or a new unrestricted gift.

The old health anchor is [Chong's Markov model](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25728889/), evaluated in [NICE's evidence table](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK579689/bin/niceng211er5-apph-et1.pdf). Its 4.64 versus 4.62 five-year QALYs are modeled, not observed participant utility, and rounded to only two decimals. NICE rated the analysis partially applicable with potentially serious limitations and no apparent probabilistic sensitivity analysis. Published payer-cost and ICER figures conflict across records. The retained scenarios are historical diagnostics; neither the short horizon nor a subjective transfer discount turns them into a current donor-effect estimate.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter estimates approximately **$476.4M per better life** for the clinical and household-resource pathways quantified here. This is a conditional, partial-portfolio comparison, not a complete valuation of Youth ALIVE!'s work or a quoted expansion opportunity. A better life means ten health or income-equivalent years; income-equivalent years are a welfare comparison, not measured clinical QALYs.

**What does additional funding support?** The model scales current outputs against FY2025 gross expenses of $7,831,321, allowing 35% of proportional funding to produce additional activity. An illustrative $100,000 therefore corresponds to about 0.53 additional CiC client-equivalents, 0.33 Pathways participant-equivalents, and 0.19 analytically independent counseling units. These are planning quantities, not an available purchase or unique people who can be summed. Prevention, interruption and other unquantified work remain charged in the cost base.

**How could these services improve lives?** CiC support may reduce recurrent violence; trauma counseling may improve clinical recovery; Pathways may help participants obtain jobs; compensation navigation may release household resources. The historical local Markov model used a 4% untreated one-year reinjury risk. We use that as a transferred input and judge a net relative risk of 0.8, rather than treating the observed 96% non-reinjury rate as a causal effect. Nonfatal loss, fatal survival and counseling benefits have separate finite trajectories. The resulting health estimate is 0.0014316240 California QALYs per illustrative budget.

**Income and overlap.** The 16 reported jobs are descriptive. We attribute a quarter of scaled placements to the added services, with a $3,000 annual net household gain lasting half a year. Compensation uses the 60 reported applications, not assumed awards; success, navigation incrementality and a $500 one-off net resource gain are judgments. After timing, household allocation and positive-benefit overlap exclusions, these pathways contribute 0.0006674205 income-equivalent years. Baseline resources are assumed to be $25,000 per household. Benefits, taxes, work costs and payer offsets belong in net gains; gross wages, public spending and baseline survivor earnings are not added.

**Why the estimate changed.** The historical illustration was **$27,335,578** per ten health years. It combined subjective scenario weights with a partial historical contract cost and a rounded five-year QALY difference from a model. The current calculation uses matched current recipient expenses/output and reconstructs clinical effects explicitly, while adding income once. The narrower quantified benefit relative to the full cost base makes this estimate substantially less favorable. Targeted expansion could be cheaper, and omitted effects could be important; neither can be priced confidently from current evidence.

The current scenarios test funding and capacity nulls, alternative injury/counseling effects, finite job durations, household baselines, and signed resource harms. They are unweighted judgment cases, not a confidence interval. Full historical scenarios remain preserved separately.
sections.funding:
The [current CalVIP award list](https://www.bscc.ca.gov/s_cpgpcalvipgrant/) grants Youth ALIVE! $5 million for the 2026–29 cohort, overlapping CiC, violence interruption and family response. [DHCS](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/community-health-workers/) allows eligible violence-prevention community-health-worker services, but Youth ALIVE!'s actual billing and uncovered caseload are unverified. Both public pathways belong in the no-gift baseline; neither proves that all needs are funded.

The [2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202642239349300149/IRS990) reports $5,634,909 contract revenue and $428,802 service fees, but does not identify actual Medi-Cal collections. Cash was $3,957,649 plus $210,161 savings at year-end; $1,208,418 net assets were donor-restricted and $4,478,159 were without donor restrictions. Those balances do not by themselves establish spare deployable cash or an unfunded expansion. Reopen a donor price only with a dated staffing and waitlist plan reconciled to CalVIP, county contracts and payer claims, plus comparable injury and utility follow-up.

Historical expense reference: the original FY2022 return reported $5,360,166 on the gross recipient expense basis. It is preserved here as context, not included in the latest comparable FY2023–2025 three-year mean of $7,208,761.33.

The latest model uses the same funding-response judgment across current program outputs, not a separate donor budget per program. The existing $5M 2026–2029 CalVIP award remains part of the baseline. No costed private-donor expansion tranche or additional staffing capacity has been verified.

model.costScope: Proportional additional funding of the recipient's current portfolio using FY2025 gross expenses. All portfolio costs remain in the denominator; only specified clinical and household-resource pathways are quantified. An illustrative budget normalizes the calculation and is not a verified donation tranche.
model.geographicAttribution: Quantified direct-service benefits occur in Oakland/Alameda, so central California health and income shares are each 1. These shares are independently varied. No headquarters/population multiplier or unmodeled statewide policy benefit is credited.
model.formula: Shared scale=min(gift/expense*funding,capacityScale). Clinical effects integrate finite nonfatal injury, fatal survival, and allocated independent counseling trajectories. Income uses 0.5*people*log(1+net gain/baseline) with finite timing, causal, geography and overlap shares. Price=10*donor cost/(California health+income equivalent years+signed independent burdens), only if total is positive.
model.counterfactual: Existing hospital referrals, counseling, jobs, compensation navigation and county/state/payer support continue. Funding additionality and causal pathway shares are distinct judgments; grants, descriptive outputs and public compensation are not automatically additional donor-caused benefits.
model.attribution: One shared portfolio scale funds CiC, Pathways and counseling outputs once. Counseling reserves 31 CiC and 18 Pathways overlaps before allocating one index person per residual unit. Job income is conditional-alive benefit among existing Pathways recipients, not wages for lives newly saved. Compensation excludes 25% of positive resource credit for potential job-household overlap; negative resources are not overlap-discounted. Independent induced harms persist outside positive-benefit assignment.
model.uncertainty: Conditional partial-portfolio estimate, not complete organizational EV, a lower bound, a confidence interval, or a verified marginal offer. Current cost/output normalization replaces a partial historical contract. what: Vision To Learn brings vision care to students at school without charging their families.
California is a substantial part of a national organization, so an ordinary gift also supports activity elsewhere.
School-based delivery helps children obtain usable glasses without requiring families to arrange a separate clinic visit.
strengths: A direct, understandable pathway removes logistical barriers to correctable vision care.
Randomized school-program evidence supports some educational benefits, and measured refraction supports immediate acuity improvement.
Recent original financial returns and a California public-funding route make the delivery and cost pathways inspectable.
reservations: California's marginal gift allocation is unknown; historical reach is not the next-dollar share.
The child health-utility gain and sustained counterfactual correction period are judgments, not measured QALYs.
Public reimbursement, restricted gifts and donated inputs can alter cash leverage; replacement needs require a current California course budget, and the latest audit download remains inaccessible.

sections.what:
The recipient is the national nonprofit Vision To Learn, EIN 45-3457853. Mobile clinics supply screenings, examinations and glasses in low-income school communities. The current site advertises $150 for a child's screening, exam and glasses; that is not verified marginal full-recipient cost. [Current program and advertised contribution](https://visiontolearn.org/) [Ordinary donation route](https://visiontolearn.org/donate/)

The 2024–25 annual report's cumulative map shows 262,821 California children provided glasses out of 601,741 nationally (the report also labels the national total as pairs elsewhere), about 44%. This is historical reach, not a fiscal-year or marginal allocation. The report also describes new Dallas work and a two-year grant expanding services in Maryland, DC and New Jersey. Those outside-state benefits remain outside this edition's numerator. [2024–2025 Annual Report](https://visiontolearn.org/wp-content/uploads/VTL_AnnualReport_2025_20-ocr.pdf)
sections.monitoring:
In a Baltimore cross-sectional study of 4,972 children prescribed glasses, 70% improved at least two lines in their better-seeing eye with refraction. Only 46% met the study's clinically significant refractive-error definition. Immediate best-corrected acuity is not sustained wear, utility or an untreated comparison. [Visual acuity and refractive findings in children prescribed glasses](https://eye.hms.harvard.edu/publications/visual-acuity-and-refractive-findings-children-prescribed-glasses-school-based)

The Baltimore cluster randomized school intervention improved some reading outcomes after one year, but sustained achievement effects were not observed at two years. This supports a real intervention pathway while arguing against automatically crediting lifetime educational gains. Test scores are not converted into QALYs here. [Cluster randomized school vision program academic outcomes](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaophthalmology/fullarticle/2783867)

A Chinese cluster trial tested free glasses with teacher incentives against prescriptions alone, showing that dispensing and adherence interventions are distinct. Its setting and package do not measure California wear. [Free glasses and teacher-incentive cluster randomized trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26275472/)

Request unique children with a correction gap, delivered courses rather than pairs, observed wear over time, replacement costs, presenting/best-corrected acuity and alternative care. Avoid counting replacements or two pairs as two independently benefited children.

Follow-up evidence review: [Huang et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31112777/) observed glasses use in 87% of 197 year-one completers, but fewer than two-thirds reported prescribed use; 66% required replacements. The study supplied two pairs and replacements. Point observation is not fraction of time worn, and selected completers are not all eligible children. The model retains effective use at 60% as a judgment, not a direct estimate. [Mudie et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33745874/) found improved presenting acuity into the next school year, supporting continued correction with follow-up but not identifying child utility or a donor counterfactual.
sections.qualitative:
School delivery can reduce transportation, scheduling and caregiver barriers. Clearer vision can improve daily functioning even when an educational benefit is not captured by a health metric. Children needing specialist care also require a completed referral pathway rather than only screening.

The current model explicitly assesses household resources and later education-related earnings. It credits small, separately modeled purchase savings, but no central future earnings because the available trial measured reading rather than wages. Its one-year central correction window is a finite advantage over alternative care, not a claim that glasses work for only a year. The two-year favorable case requires continued effective correction and replacement resources within its assumed costs.

For a California-focused donor, the decisive question is the next funded route, staffing capacity and beneficiary mix. A national organization's California history alone cannot establish that an unrestricted gift stays in California.

The small average presenting-acuity deficit in the Baltimore follow-up makes adult blindness utilities an unsuitable shortcut. Child preference-weighted health gain remains unknown. Teasing and inappropriate prescriptions are possible burdens; the small health allowance is not a measured upper bound. No mortality benefit or additional lifetime survival is credited. A finite correction horizon already bounds duration; wear decay is tested independently from alternative care.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter estimates about **$4.28 million per better life in California**, including modeled child health and household resources. School delivery provides examinations, prescribed glasses and supported use at a moderate course cost; the benefit depends on changing timely correction and using the glasses. The following independent reassessment replaces, rather than preserves, the earlier health-only central estimate.

## Decision and independent anchor

The current provisional central California price is **$4,280,415.60703891 per ten combined health/income-equivalent years**, versus historical $2,003,590.9323512588. For $100,000: California health .2322944218698827; household-resource equivalent .0013277521908684907; total .23362217406075114. All-region health .5807360546747067, income .0033193804771712264: do not apply California attribution twice. This is a judgmental estimate, not measured local QALYs or validated marginal donation response. The change follows a new smaller generic-child-utility judgment and a coherent all-in course cost; neither is derived by subtracting cash from the old total or selected to target a price.

The Baltimore randomized school program found a small one-year iReady reading effect (.09 SD, P=.02), no PARCC reading effect, and no sustained two-year effect. It measured no earnings. This supports an educational native outcome, not a lifetime earnings or generic-utility conversion. Original JAMA: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaophthalmology/fullarticle/2783867 . School follow-up found mean presenting distance acuity .14 to .05 logMAR. The utility bridge remains much less secure than the visual-acuity bridge.

Mannava's original child EQ-5D-Y study (DOI 10.1186/s13561-024-00552-0) is uncontrolled, hospital-based, includes mixed pathologies/treatments, and uses foreign value sets/proxies in younger children. Its mild best-corrected impairment subgroup median change .02 is neither a refractive-only causal effect nor a mean individual spectacle gain. Baltimore children had substantially milder presenting impairment. We use **.01 utility while effectively corrected** as a small positive generic-health prior reflecting severity, setting and measurement uncertainty. It is not an empirical half-effect. Alternatives .005/.02/zero/negative remain decisive. The original .02 may remain a sensitivity, not the independently preferred point. Native acuity/reading benefits may persist even if generic utility is zero.

## Exact central inputs and equations

G=100000; C=300 cash/all-in per unique completed one-year supported course; financial additionality a=.5; California share g=.4; portfolio assignment k=1; unmet timely adequate correction p=.6; time-average wear w=.6; u=.01; T=1 year; delay d=.125; r=.03; acute adaptation/teasing harm h=.00005 health-years per additional completed course at dispensing. Household-distinct fraction z=.8; counterfactual purchaser fraction b=.05; net one-off household saving S=50; annual household resource baseline Y=50000. Caregiver/future earnings central zero; induced failed applicants central zero; donor fees central zero.

N=G*a/C=166.66666666666666 additional unique supported courses. Financial replacement a is separate from recipient access p: a asks whether the donation expands provision, p asks whether an additional course changes the child's timely correction. They must not be collapsed or repeated. Cost300 is already all-in: do **not** multiply budget by historical f=.8 again. A transparent working allocation is175 examination/device,50 outreach/clinic,50 support,25 replacement; these are analyst allowances, not reported invoices. The denominator is a course, not a pair or every exam.

Let L=(1+r)^(-d), A=L*[1-exp(-ln(1+r)*T)]/ln(1+r), with A=T when r=0. All-region H=k*N*(p*w*u*A-h*L). California health=g*H. The harm begins at dispensing like benefit; it is not multiplied by unmet status/wear. A=.9817310906700654. One-year exposure is an incremental supported/catch-up window, not a claim glasses stop working at a year. The warranty supports that finite window. A two-year case doubles C to600 rather than receiving a free unsupported second course.

Distinct households N*z=133.33333333333334. Purchaser households N*z*b=6.666666666666667. Income-equivalent I=k*.5*N*z*b*log(1+S/Y)*L. It is a **single receipt**, normalized to a one-year household resource change, not a recurrent annual50-dollar gain. The inspectable economic inputs are people=N*z, causalShare=b, years=1, annualIncomeBeforeUSD=Y, annualIncomeGainUSD=S, delayYears=d, discountRate=r, editionShare=g, independentShare=k. Do not apply savings to every family member. California total=g*(H+I+B); price=10*G*(1+fee)/total if total>0, otherwise null. `editionQalys` records health only; economic effects are added separately once.

## Counterfactual, overlap and resources

Central .6 unmet and .05 purchasers are disjoint. The remaining .35 already obtains adequate timely correction, uses another route or has no incremental benefit. Purchasers get the same correction in the counterfactual, so no additional clinical credit; unmet children cannot save a purchase they would never make. The .05 purchaser incidence and $50 net saving are explicit low-income school-catchment judgments: Medicaid/CHIP/free alternatives make full retail-price savings inappropriate, while incomplete coverage and family purchase routes make literal zero savings too strong as a general prior. Net saving excludes insurer payment and fundraising sticker prices. z=.8 recognizes siblings/repeated household courses; it is unmeasured locally and should be tested .5–1. Y is a whole-household annual-resource reference, not per-person earnings; $25K/$100K cases expose uncertainty.

Caregiver time is a real potential benefit but not automatically realized cash. Central excludes it. A disjoint covered-clinic stratum .2 with net20 one-off household resources is conditional on avoided travel expenses or actual paid-work realization; ordinary time saved remains native time, not income. Central education earnings0 means unidentified cash effect, not proof no eventual benefit. Conditional future case: .05 of unmet children receive an incremental500 annual resources on baseline50K for **one year at year10**; no link from .09 SD to500 is established. It is an explicit stress case, not empirical education-to-wage evidence. Future income is temporally/outcome-distinct from first-year visual health, so no automatic overlap subtraction; any broad psychosocial utility overlap remains a sensitivity judgment.

Negative purchaser resources (-50) retain sign. Induced failed-access case a=0,20 new households lose10 each at d produces CA burden -.0007971292894102223 and null price. This is only additional exposure caused by the gift, never unchanged baseline pickup effort. Literal no change a=0 and exposure0 gives zero. Portfolio assignment applies once to all attributed program effects, including induced burden; no subjective scenario probabilities. Recipient costs are not charged again to donor budget.

## Fresh finances, operations and feasibility

Original national EIN45-3457853 returns: FY2023 expense19,589,987; FY2024 24,131,355; FY2025 25,497,887. Comparable three-year mean **23,073,076.333333332**. FY2025 program20,761,273, admin3,314,355, fundraising1,422,259; revenue28,180,734. Restricted net assets15,354,367 and unrestricted3,651,603 are June2025 balances, not current available cash. Government grants3,778,592; Medicaid fees2,576,632; CHIP751,020. Noncash contribution revenue of1,359,892 has not been independently reconciled with expense recognition or cash outlay; it is not an extra verified cash margin. FY25 national93,225 pairs,107,520 exams and273,618 screens are different outputs, not unique additional CA children. Whole expense/pair273.5091 is an annual expense sanity check. Expense less noncash contribution revenue per pair258.9219 is an unreconciled arithmetic proxy, not verified cash expense, measured course cost or marginal capacity. This supports a300 all-in judgment with250/400 alternatives, not a precise new quote.

Current official site and annual-report links establish continued operation; $150 fundraising pitch is not an all-in incremental quote. The annual-report page lists a new 2025 PDF but latest openly listed audit link2022; no fresh FY25 audit opinion verified. Current glasses page describes6–8week delivery and one-year repair/replacement; how-it-works says about2weeks. Delay.125 is a conservative shared prior, with2/8week cases, not a measured donation-to-service lag. Huang2019 follow-up:87% observed wearing among197 completers but fewer than two-thirds reported prescribed use;66% required replacement and two pairs were initially supplied. Consequently use .6 time-average wear, not observed87% multiplied again or a second device-survival filter.

DHCS currently names VTL as an eligible California MOS provider. Historic2018 evaluation66% Medicaid-eligible examinees lacked Medicaid-funded eye care over prior4years; it is not the current unmet fraction. MOS requires certification/contract and approved donor arrangements; CHIP may require private funding, but no automatic marginal match is verified. CA .4 is a conditional national-donation allocation prior close to cumulative historical44%, not a measured next-gift share. A CA-restricted gift may use1 only with verified scope; national gift may be0. No current $100K tranche or long-run capacity is confirmed. Gross external Medicaid, donated goods and school time remain separate from household income and donor cash; no hypothetical match centrally.



The historical $2.00 million estimate is retained below for comparison, not used for current ranking. The current price is a conditional analyst scenario, not a measured California return or a verified next-dollar offer. Source receipts and an executable calculator accompany the independent review.
sections.funding:
Accrual Form 990 total expenses were $19,589,987, $24,131,355 and $25,497,887 for June-ending fiscal years 2023–2025; the comparable mean is $23,073,076.33. The 2024 filing supplies 2023's comparative. [Original FY June 2024 Form 990 and 2023 comparative](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/453457853/202511289349304146/full)

The 2025 return reports $20,761,273 program expense, $3,314,355 administration and $1,422,259 fundraising. It records 93,225 pairs and 107,520 examinations, outputs rather than health gains. Revenue is $28,180,734; net assets $19,005,970 include $15,354,367 restricted and $3,651,603 unrestricted. Government grants are $3,778,592; Medicaid/Medi-Cal fees $2,576,632 and CHIP fees $751,020. This mix requires funding-substitution analysis rather than assuming each donated dollar purchases otherwise absent care. [Original FY June 2025 Form 990](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/453457853/202621359349308582/full)

The annual report uses a different funding summary from the tax return; those totals are not silently mixed. Donated optical inputs support delivery but are real resources, not evidence that all additional cash is unconstrained. [2024–2025 Annual Report](https://visiontolearn.org/wp-content/uploads/VTL_AnnualReport_2025_20-ocr.pdf)

DHCS lists Vision To Learn as a MOS provider. Its cited 2018 evaluation found 66% of Medicaid-eligible examined children lacked Medicaid-funded vision care in the prior four years. This is not proof that they had no glasses from any source or a current 66% treatment gap. [Mobile Optometric Services program](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/services/medi-cal-resources/medi-cal-eligibility-division/mobile-optometric-services-mos-program/)

MOS combines private donations and federal funds, without State General Fund support. Provider qualification and contractual processes matter. [MOS funding and provider requirements](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/services/medi-cal-resources/medi-cal-eligibility-division/frequently-asked-questions-mos-faqs/) Donors must undergo DHCS conflict review and receive approval instructions, so the central model assumes no automatic extra public match. [MOS donor approval process](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/services/medi-cal-resources/medi-cal-eligibility-division/how-do-i-become-a-donor/)

The historical model included a hypothetical public-payment diagnostic. The current estimate assumes no new public match; a verified payment would require its own additional funded-course ledger rather than doubling the revised central automatically. Confirm eligible spending, approved donor status, reimbursement timing and whether those payments would occur without the gift.

The financial review re-read all three original returns, including the [FY2023 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/453457853/202401359349308510/full), and reconciled each Part IX total. Program/management/fundraising were $17,107,898/$1,754,929/$727,160 in FY2023; $21,216,025/$1,927,587/$987,743 in FY2024; and $20,761,273/$3,314,355/$1,422,259 in FY2025. The latest return includes $1,359,892 noncash contributions. Donated resources may already be recognized in accounting expenses: do not add them again to those totals. Cash plus temporary investments of $5,130,190 and pledges/grants receivable of $11,529,330 show why unrestricted net assets are not cash runway.

The [regional program document](https://visiontolearn.org/wp-content/uploads/California_RegionalPages_10.pdf) is explicitly 2022–2023, not a current marginal roster. It establishes historical service in multiple California regions, including San Diego and the Sierras, beyond the Bay Area. The current DHCS provider listing confirms ongoing California operations; neither it nor the cumulative map measures the next-dollar share. The [FY2025 audit listing](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/display_audit/2025-06-GSAFAC-0000420841) was located, but its download returned security content; audit opinion and remediation remain unverified. Request the audit, a California gift-specific course budget, supported wear and replacement plan, and approved reimbursement terms before a recommendation. No contact, gift or matching approval has been made.

model.costScope: Entire ordinary national gift at all-in supported-course cash cost; gross external inputs separate.
model.geographicAttribution: California health and each economic channel receive marginal geographic attribution once.
model.formula: N=G*a/C; L=(1+r)^(-d); A=L*integral_0^T exp(-ln(1+r)*t)dt; H=k*N*(p*w*u*A-h*L); purchaserI=.5*k*N*z*b*ln(1+S/Y)*L. Add separately timed signed resource channels once. CA=(H+I)*g; Price10=10*G*(1+fee)/CA if positive.
model.counterfactual: Separate new funded courses, unmet timely correction and families otherwise purchasing adequate glasses. Induced unsuccessful-applicant burden persists with zero additional completed delivery.
model.attribution: Marginal national funding/California allocation are judgments; no automatic public match, no accounting output-to-health shortcut.
model.uncertainty: Utility, marginal costs, resources, households and allocation remain judgmental. No lifetime wage tail; scenarios are not confidence intervals.
model.nativeOutcomes: Mobile examinations, prescribed glasses, supported correction and some first-year reading benefit. Normalization yields about 66.67 additional California courses, approximately 40 changing timely correction and 2.67 purchaser households saving an assumed net $50 once. These are modeled incremental outcomes, not reported current delivery.

inputs.name: cost

inputs.name: additionality
inputs.rationale: Incremental delivery after funding substitution, separate from timely correction.

inputs.name: ca
inputs.rationale: Marginal national benefit fraction, not historical reach.

inputs.name: unmet
inputs.rationale: Timely-correction gap; disjoint from purchaser/caregiver strata.

inputs.name: wear

inputs.name: utility

inputs.name: years
inputs.rationale: Finite supported incremental correction window; two-year case doubles cost.

inputs.name: delay
inputs.rationale: Dispensing delay for benefits, burdens and one-off receipts.

inputs.name: discount
inputs.rationale: Annual rate with exact finite clinical integral.

inputs.name: harm
inputs.rationale: Acute burden per additional course at dispensing; not filtered by wear/unmet.

inputs.name: households
inputs.rationale: Distinct household fraction; siblings do not create several income baselines.

inputs.name: purchasers
inputs.rationale: Disjoint families otherwise purchasing adequate correction.

inputs.name: saving
inputs.rationale: Net household saving once, not insurer payment or annual repeated cash.

inputs.name: baseline
inputs.rationale: Whole-household annual resource reference, not measured income.

inputs.name: caregiverShare
inputs.rationale: Disjoint conditional cash-realization stratum; zero centrally.

inputs.name: caregiverGain
inputs.rationale: Actual net cash/paid-work benefit; hours saved are not automatically income.

inputs.name: educationShare
inputs.rationale: Future resource responders among unmet children; zero centrally.

inputs.name: educationGain
inputs.rationale: Conditional net annual resources, not empirical reading-to-wage conversion.

inputs.name: educationYears
inputs.rationale: Finite income window, not lifetime stream.

inputs.name: educationDelay
inputs.rationale: Positive future income starts after clinical window.

inputs.name: inducedApplicants
inputs.rationale: Additional unsuccessful households caused by gift, not baseline effort.

inputs.name: applicantLoss
inputs.rationale: Signed one-off resource loss; persists when delivery additionality zero.

inputs.name: assignment
inputs.rationale: Program credit applied once to attributable effects.

inputs.name: fee
inputs.rationale: Additional donor fee fraction, zero centrally.

inputs.name: externalPerCourse
inputs.rationale: Gross associated resources absent from cash cost, not household income; zero centrally.
