reports.program: Street safety implementation advocacy, school access and crash-survivor support

what: Walk San Francisco advocates for safer streets and supports people affected by traffic crashes.
Its campaigns seek more protective street designs, safer school routes, and stronger public safety policy.
Community organizing and Families for Safe Streets connect residents and survivors with the city's decision-making process.
strengths: Physical traffic calming has credible external injury evidence and a direct route to improving health.
A focused local advocacy program can help prioritize high-risk streets and connect community concerns to agency decisions.
Original recent financial returns and current agency plans make costs and the public baseline inspectable.
reservations: No named project and costed additional workplan establish how an extra donation changes implementation.
Advocacy influence, future casualty exposure, victim prognosis, and net household-resource gains remain uncertain.
The conditional estimate quantifies only selected street-safety pathways; school, survivor, accessibility, and wider policy effects remain unquantified.

sections.what:
The recipient is Walk San Francisco Foundation, EIN 47-2000881, not the city agency constructing streets. Its portfolio includes street-design/policy advocacy, school walking programs, community organizing and Families for Safe Streets. The official impact page provides giving links and original returns; the third-party checkout could not be opened in this review. [Current portfolio and financial source index](https://walksf.org/about-us/our-impact/)

Current Slow Our Streets work seeks traffic-calming designs, safer limits and enforcement. Thirty-three speed-camera locations are already operating. Their historical implementation and observed speeding changes are not benefits created anew by today's ordinary gift. [Current Slow Our Streets campaign](https://walksf.org/slow-our-streets/)

The 2025 report describes continued work on city implementation and potential expansion of camera authority, along with survivor support. These are plausible distinct pathways; only a hypothetical physical traffic-calming acceleration is quantified here. No restricted-best-program donation is assumed. [2025 Impact Report, published June 2026](https://walksf.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/walksf-impact-report-2026_digital_v2.pdf)
sections.monitoring:
SFMTA reports 25 traffic deaths in 2025, compared with 43 in 2024. This citywide change is not a causal estimate for Walk SF or for a new gift. [2025 traffic fatality count](https://www.sfmta.com/press-releases/press-release-san-francisco-traffic-fatalities-drop-nearly-half-2025) SFDPH's assessment describes roughly 550 severe traffic injuries per year historically since 2014; it is not a 2025 injury count. The model's paired 25/550 baseline is deliberately labeled constructed. [2024 Community Health Assessment, historical severe-injury context](https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/San_Francisco_Population_Health_CHA_2024_2025-04.cleaned.pdf)

Grundy and colleagues analyzed London 20 mph zones with physical traffic-calming using a controlled interrupted time series. Overall casualties fell about 42%; restricting analysis to 2000–06 yielded smaller estimates, including about 28% for killed/seriously injured. Death-specific precision was weak. The study adjusted underlying trends and examined nearby roads; it was not randomized and does not prove the same effect for modern San Francisco, speed-limit signs or education alone. [Controlled interrupted time series of London 20 mph zones](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2791801/)

Meaningful monitoring links a named street package to baseline casualty exposure, a with-gift and without-gift opening date, implemented design, displaced traffic and actual casualties. Meetings, supporters, surveys and adopted resolutions are not substitute health outcomes. Check independent agency plans and co-advocate accounts before assigning contribution.

The current recalibration uses the original London full-text XML obtained through Europe PMC. It supports physical engineering, not an empirical advocacy coefficient. Neither before/after camera speeding nor citywide fatality changes establish the effect of new donations.
sections.qualitative:
Current agency evidence supports a real participation role without establishing sole credit. September 2026's draft Safe School Connections plan names Walk SF among multiple partners, describes public capital and existing Safe Routes resources, and seeks final approval in late 2026/early 2027. Its long-term reach requires additional staff and finance. This is a live implementation context, not a verified Walk SF funding gap or the model's identified package. [Safe School Connections draft approach, September 2026](https://www.sfmta.com/ja/node/45746)

Survivor support and a more accessible walking environment can be valuable beyond counted physical injuries. They remain unquantified rather than assumed absent. Conversely, street changes require review of emergency access, disability access, diverted traffic, enforcement burdens and opportunity cost; a successful advocacy campaign is not automatically a net health gain.

California includes San Francisco and the rest of the state. People injured on San Francisco streets can live elsewhere, so the model assumes 98% California benefit rather than equating crash location with residence. This is an explicit prior, not measured victim geography; no statewide camera-policy spillover is added.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter estimates approximately **$878.4M per better life** for the physical street-safety health and household-resource pathways quantified here. This conditional calculation is not a verified donation opportunity or a complete valuation of Walk SF's portfolio. A better life means ten health or income-equivalent years; income equivalence compares welfare, not measured clinical QALYs.

**What does funding support?** Donations support advocacy, organizing and survivor-related work rather than directly buying city construction. The model normalizes additional funding against FY2025 gross recipient expenses of $992,695, judges that half produces additional activity and half of that activity concerns physical-safety advocacy. It then assigns a conditional influence factor of 0.25 to that annual-effort unit. None of these fractions is measured marginal influence. An illustrative $100,000 corresponds to about 2.52% of an annual advocacy-effort unit before influence; it is not a quoted staffing tranche.

**What could that work achieve?** A hypothetical disjoint package covering 1% of city casualty risk opens half a year earlier, after a 1.5-year preparation delay. Only the earlier exposure window counts; baseline public work subsequently catches up. Physical design is assigned 10% net fatality reduction and 20% severe-injury reduction, below several external engineering estimates but still judgment-dependent. The historical city baseline of 25 fatalities and roughly 500 severe nonfatal injuries is not a project-specific forecast. The model implies about 0.0000787 fatal events and 0.003148 severe nonfatal events avoided per illustrative budget.

**Health and income.** Fatal injury prevention uses a finite 30-year survival trajectory, utility 0.8, annual competing mortality 2%, and a 3% discount rate. The duration is retained as an unvalidated continuity judgment, not measured victim prognosis; shorter-horizon cases remain. Nonfatal impairment is valued at 0.1 utility for one year. A fixed 30% positive clinical-overlap allocation remains unchanged when resource gains switch sign or become zero; a coexistence case shows both outcomes without that exclusion. These assumptions produce 0.001116993681986368 California health years.

For 30% of avoided severe nonfatal injuries, the resource model assumes one baseline-alive household preserves $2,500 net resources once, against $50,000 annual baseline resources. This covers plausible work loss or private costs after taxes, sick pay, insurance and benefit offsets—not baseline earnings for extra survivors or public spending. Timing and the separate California share give 0.000021439697733860847 income-equivalent years.

**Why the estimate changed.** The historical illustration was **$4,437,877** per better life. It assumed a $100,000 gift had a 10% chance of moving a package covering 2% of city casualty risk two years earlier. Those package assumptions were not established. The current model scales influence to recipient-wide annual advocacy effort and uses a smaller, shorter acceleration window, while adding household resources explicitly. This changes the model's unit and judgments, not observed organizational effectiveness. Marginal influence remains the decisive uncertainty; the approximately 198-fold difference should not be read as a measured deterioration.

Current city plans and already-operating cameras remain the counterfactual, not benefits purchased anew. Associated construction/maintenance resources are separate from donor cost. Source-vetted project schedules, casualty exposure, a costed additional workplan and recipient outcome data are needed before treating this as donor-ready. Other school, survivor, accessibility and policy pathways are unquantified and may matter materially.
sections.funding:
Original accrual Form 990 functional expenses were $863,052, $921,193 and $981,449 for June-ending fiscal years 2023–2025. Separately netted event costs are added to the gross spending comparison below. [Original FY 2023–24 Form 990 with prior-year comparative](https://walksf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/walk-san-francisco-2324-form-990.pdf)

The 2025 return allocates $513,353 to programs, $252,527 to management/general and $215,569 to fundraising. Revenue is $894,475, including $198,441 government grants. Net assets are $885,931, with $50,000 restricted. These original figures do not establish present spare capacity or an unfunded advocacy tranche. The return indicates compiled/reviewed statements, not an independent financial audit. [Original FY 2024–25 Form 990](https://walksf.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/wsff-24-25-taxfinal-990.public.pdf)

The public construction counterfactual is substantial. SFMTA's May 2026 capital update says its planned improvements reach 62% of the High Injury Network. It already has funded quick-build and other safety projects. A donation could change timing/design, but cannot claim all existing planned benefits. [Current planned street-safety capital projects](https://www.sfmta.com/blog/investing-san-francisco-streets-together-new-safety-connectivity-and-community-benefit-projects)

The June 2026 Safety Zone initiative also includes an already-approved Community Corners program. Its existence updates older descriptions of pending daylighting commitments; do not treat an approved agency initiative as a new philanthropic purchase. [Safety Zone program and Community Corners approval](https://www.sfmta.com/press-releases/sfmta-gives-daylighted-curbs-new-purpose-safety-zone-initiative)

Before relying on the estimate, ask for a costed staffing or organizing increment, the exact agency bottleneck, project risk exposure, capital availability and expected opening date without the new work. Financial deficit alone does not answer those questions.

For a consistent gross-spending comparison, the annual figures add direct event costs netted against revenue: $39,957 in FY 2023, $26,021 in FY 2024 and $11,246 in FY 2025. Gross totals are therefore $903,009, $947,214 and $992,695; their mean is $947,639.33. These organizational size figures do not change the separate gift-based health calculation.

model.costScope: Entire recipient donor budget, proportionally normalized to latest gross annual expenses. Half the additional portfolio effort is assigned to physical-safety advocacy; all other costs remain charged. Associated public capital is a separate resource sensitivity, never donor cash or household income.
model.geographicAttribution: Central health and household-resource shares are independently 98% California, allowing for visitors. The share is a residence judgment, not observed casualty geography. No duplication across SF/Bay/California donations or population/headquarters multiplier.
model.formula: scale=gift/expense*funding*advocacyShare; additional risk exposure-years=scale*influence*riskShare*acceleration. Fatal and nonfatal events avoided feed separate finite health trajectories discounted from the acceleration-window midpoint. Distinct net nonfatal household receipts use 0.5*people*log(1+receipt/baseline). Price=10*donor cost/(California health+income equivalent years+signed independent burden), only for positive total.
model.counterfactual: Existing capital, already-operating cameras, agency staff and other advocates continue. Credit only net physical protection delivered earlier or improved by the added work. Positive annual exposure ends when baseline implementation catches up; injuries already avoided retain finite later health.
model.attribution: Funding response, advocacy allocation and conditional influence are distinct planning judgments applied once. A disjoint hypothetical package represents 1% of city casualty risk, not 1% of street length. Fatal and nonfatal cases are separate. Household resources concern baseline-alive nonfatal victims; no extra-survivor wage stream. Fixed positive clinical overlap allocation is independent of income sign, with coexistence sensitivity; negative health and independent induced burdens are retained.
model.uncertainty: Conditional partial physical-safety portfolio estimate, not complete organizational EV, a lower bound, an empirical confidence interval or a verified donor tranche. The old hypothetical package did not establish donor influence; tying expense to annual advocacy effort changes the unit but does not identify causality. Missing project-specific evidence can materially change either sign or magnitude.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional early exposure to physical street-safety design; fatal and severe nonfatal injuries avoided; finite survival and impairment benefit; one-off preserved net household resources among baseline-alive nonfatal victims. Meetings, total city crash changes, public construction budgets and camera speeding counts are not new gift outcomes.

reports.program: Nutrition and food-safety research, consumer education, and policy advocacy

what: CSPI researches food and health risks, informs consumers and advocates for stronger public protections.
Its sodium work includes scientific submissions, monitoring proposals and public accountability for industry reformulation.
We examine whether additional charitable work could improve eventual sodium reductions or bring an otherwise similar reform forward.
strengths: Sodium reduction has a well-supported blood-pressure mechanism and a finite US cardiovascular model.
Technical submissions and requests for better monitoring identify a concrete prospective advocacy pathway.
Three original charitable-recipient returns and a separate affiliate audit support a consistent financial boundary.
reservations: The effect of additional work on compliance or implementation timing is an explicit judgment, not measured charity attribution.
Government monitoring, manufacturers, other advocates and replacement funding would continue without this donation.
Clinical transport, household savings and broad food-price pass-through remain uncertain; the quantified sodium pathway is not the full portfolio.

sections.what:
CSPI researches nutrition and food safety, informs consumers, and advocates for public protections. An ordinary charitable donation supports the 501(c)(3) recipient, EIN 23-7122879, rather than the separate CSPI Action Fund. Its current strategy and impact report cover labeling, school meals, chemicals, dietary guidance and scientific communication. Historical policy achievements do not automatically become benefits of new funding.

The prospective sodium-accountability mechanism is sales-weighted packaged-food and restaurant monitoring, technical FDA submissions, and public reporting on industry compliance. Its January 2025 comment asks for stronger targets and better data. These are identifiable activities, not observed charity-caused reductions in cardiovascular disease. Our calculation charges the full annual charitable portfolio while quantifying only this branch; other programs may have benefits or harms not yet priced.
sections.monitoring:
As checked October 2, FDA’s sodium page still calls PhaseII draft and voluntary, with three-year targets across 163 categories and about 2,750 mg/day if achieved. This page check does not establish that no newer agency action exists elsewhere. The published2010–2022 comparison largely precedes final2021 guidance; the share of categories near targets cannot establish sales-weighted consumption changes or the causal effect of the guidance.

Useful measures would include a funded-versus-unfunded technical workplan, original submissions and agency responses, public data that the work changes, sales-weighted consumed sodium, compliance persistence and a credible counterfactual for industry/agency action. Meetings, comments and publicity alone are not health outcomes. No current uncovered sodium staff position or data contract was verified.

The randomized meta-analysis supports sodium lowering blood pressure, but trial reductions are much larger than the modeled125 mg/day. This review used indexed primary abstract material after native full-text access failed; it does not claim a refreshed full-text read. Potassium substitution evidence is not treated as an identical US food-reformulation trial.
sections.qualitative:
We are interested in technically informed advocacy addressing a large cardiovascular risk. Current submissions and requests for monitoring support a plausible contribution, while an existing FDA proposal, public agency duties, industry reformulation and other advocates provide strong alternative explanations. Neither alignment with a final decision nor an old legal victory identifies a new donation’s effect.

The revised forecast uses a direct with-versus-without probability difference for one additional annual charitable work portfolio: .255 versus .250 for a defined further125 mg/day consumed-sodium opportunity. The half-percentage-point increment includes replacement funding, reserves, agency/industry work and charity-affiliate limits once. It is a declared small-leverage prior, not an observed frequency. Small donations scale linearly up to one work-year; no extra coalition or funding multiplier is applied.

The preferred judgment assigns25% to additional lasting reform and75% to two-year acceleration of an otherwise identical finite stream. Existing draft guidance and monitoring plans weaken the old all-durable interpretation, but they do not prove timing-only influence. All-durable and timing-only alternatives are approximately$330K and$5.75M per better life—not confidence limits.

Potential harms include food-price changes, adverse substitutions and microbiological effects. Marketable investments do not prove either spare capacity or no funding need. This is a conditional research estimate, not a qualified donor-ready recommendation or a verified marginal work purchase.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter sees sodium-accountability advocacy as a potentially cost-effective route to better cardiovascular health. Our revised conditional estimate is about $1.13M per better life, combining health and net household-resource effects; the initial health-only estimate was$484K. The change is principally a revised clinical comparison and reform counterfactual, not simply adding income to the old model.

The donor denominator is one full annual charitable-recipient expense of $17,926,322. A plausible technical module might use3,000 fully loaded expert hours at $120, $100Kdata procurement, $20K external review and$20K publication/support: $500K total. Those allocations are illustrative priors, not a quote or observed sodium-only cost. Charging the full annual portfolio and then applying another sodium-budget share would double-charge allocation. The old model charged five annual budgets.

The source US simulation covers adults30–84 over2017–2036. The nearer modest-minus-pessimistic comparison gives400K discounted QALYs,100K cardiovascular cases and a265 mg/day endpoint difference. These are rounded scenario projections with different exposure ramps, not measured outcomes or a new paired uncertainty interval. We scale to a judged125 mg/day consumption opportunity and a .7future clinical-transport factor. This is approximate endpoint interpolation, not a rerun. Its original finite health horizon and competing mortality are already included; only a separate five-year implementation delay is added.

The direct probability contrast and25% lasting / 75% two-year-acceleration mixture yield .0921927 gross health years per $10K. A separately judged policy/substitution harm allowance leaves .0914946 net health years. Independent harms remain evaluable even with no extra policy influence. Health effects are not supplemented with saved lives’ baseline earnings or another lifetime utility tail.

Only baseline-alive nonfatal cases enter the household savings branch. A judged 90% nonfatal share, .8distinct household episodes per case and 30% actual cash incidence identify the modeled affected households. Half avoid$500 net medical out-of-pocket cost; half avoid$2000 including$1500 unreplaced after-tax short-recovery earnings. Insurance, public coverage, paid leave, disability benefits, employer payments and work costs are assumed offset first. These are explicit incidence/amount priors, not the paper’s gross economic savings. Retired patients do not automatically receive wages.

Case cash occurs once per episode, with a judged uniform 20-year event profile and independent one-year consumption window. The Coefficient Giving logarithmic resource crosswalk uses a $50K annual household baseline. The actual primary annual incidence profile was not reconstructed, so timing alternatives are tested. Case resources contribute .000045524 equivalent years per $10K.

Food-price costs apply separately to a judged130M exposed household episodes, not only avoided-CVD households: a once-only $3 net pass-through burden per conditional reform, after assumed retail/competition/public offsets. This is not an observed price increase or the manufacturer’s gross reformulation cost. It contributes−.00268246 resource years, making net resources−.00263694 and combined benefit .08885769 years per $10K. The food loss is not repeated 20 times. The source paper’s$41B societal savings mix medical spending, productivity and informal care and cannot be credited wholesale as household income.

Food costs and policy harms remain if clinical benefit is zero. The zero-consumption diagnostic means costly physical reformulation without improved consumed intake, not no physical reform; zero policy contrast is a different case. Positive-health overlap alternatives never erase negative resources or independent harms. Other programs, recurrent medication savings, long-run disability earnings and full public/industry social costs remain unpriced, not zero. The numerical partial pathway is neither complete EV nor a proven lower bound.
sections.funding:
Original FY2023/24/25 charitable-recipient expenses are $18,005,982/$17,289,504/$17,926,322, exact mean$17,740,602.67 (about $17.7M). Fiscal years end June30. Latest functional costs reconcile to $15,140,797 program,$569,181 management and$2,216,344 fundraising; salary/benefit/payroll costs were$8,999,433 with 94 employees. No reported direct event/gaming/inventory expense addback changes the chosen gross boundary. These accounts establish size and continuing activity, not an available sodium work package.

The charity-only audit expense is$17,916,541, versus the higher tax expense used in the model. The unresolved$9,781 classification difference is paired with a revenue difference after investment adjustments, leaving the same$2,805,236 netasset decrease. Consolidated affiliate expense is not recipient cost. Charity net assets of $31,412,665 and marketable investments do not by themselves identify unrestricted cash availability, marginal staffing or unused commitments.

A stronger funding assessment needs current charitable-versus-affiliate allocations, a costed uncovered sodium workplan and evidence of what changes with new support. The direct probability prior already includes reserves/replacement, so no extra 50% funding-response factor is added. The illustrative technical module is not a restricted gift offer; no donation, contact or form submission was performed.

model.costScope: One full annual charitable-recipient portfolio cost; only the sodium-accountability pathway quantified. Illustrative500K module is not a quote or extra allocation multiplier.
model.geographicAttribution: USA share .99 is a declared resident/coverage prior; original clinical reference is adults30–84, not all ages.
model.formula: Work fraction=min(one-year capacity,gift/annual recipient expense). Probability delta=work fraction*(with−without opportunity probability). Apply a lasting-versus-complete finite shifted-stream mixture separately to discounted clinical health and cash ledgers. Price=10*gift/(net health+net resources) only when known and positive.
model.counterfactual: FDA guidance/monitoring, manufacturers, other advocates and reserves/replacement continue; direct joint contrast includes these once. Existing outcomes receive no retroactive credit.
model.attribution: Judged .005 response per additional charitable work-year; preferred25% lasting extra reform/75%two-year acceleration, not observed causal estimates.
model.uncertainty: Partial conditional forecast; clinical endpoint interpolation, policy response, mix, incidence, pass-through and timing are explicit priors. Full donor and social returns unidentified.
model.nativeOutcomes: Technical submissions, sales-weighted monitoring and public compliance reporting are native activities. National consumed sodium and finite cardiovascular cases are projected intermediate/final outcomes, not observed CSPI-caused effects.

reports.priceScope: Conditional sodium-accountability health and household resources; full annual charitable-recipient cost, partial forecast.

historicalModel.costScope: Whole ordinary charitable-recipient gift. Five years of full FY2025 recipient expense at constant real scale; sodium is the only quantified health pathway. No restricted-project price, no affiliate double count, no historical victory credit. Additional external social costs remain unquantified.
historicalModel.geographicAttribution: USA 50 states plus DC. g=.99 remains a judgmental national-coverage allowance, not a measured territorial allocation. The underlying clinical model covers ages30–84, so the discounted scale is not all-age measured health; no population multiplier fills missing age groups.
historicalModel.formula: H=(2100000-700000)*(dm/565)*e*t/(1.03^L); S=fDurable+(1-fDurable)*(1-1.03^(-accelerationYears)); Qall(G)=G/(C*Y)*b*(p*a*H*S-h); Qusa=Qall*g; price10=10*G/Qusa only when Qusa>0. Central C=17926322,Y=5,dm=250,e=.5,t=.7,L=5,p=.2,a=.1,b=.5,g=.99,h=0,fDurable=1. Existing alpha values reproduced; additional timing scenarios vary S.
historicalModel.counterfactual: Phase I-scale progress, government activity, private reformulation, and other advocates continue without this funding. Only a further 250 mg/day opportunity is considered; p is an incremental probability change attributable to the broader campaign rather than the unconditional chance FDA acts. b removes expenditure that would occur from reserves or replacement funding anyway.
historicalModel.attribution: p=.2 is a subjective campaign-induced probability increment over five years; a=.1 allocates a tenth of that increment to charitable CSPI, excluding credit owed to its Action Fund, other advocates, researchers, officials, and manufacturers. The resulting p*a=.02 is not measured. Because all portfolio costs are charged, no additional sodium budget fraction is multiplied in; doing both would double-charge portfolio allocation.
historicalModel.uncertainty: Retained judgmental sodium partial-health best guess, not a measured portfolio return. Durable change, policy acceleration, clinical transport and funding replacement are separate uncertainties. Central other-portfolio net health=0 is a judgment, not a proven lower bound. Missing observed marginal inputs alone do not force null.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: Prospective policy response -> otherwise-unavailable sustained sodium reformulation -> consumed sodium -> blood pressure -> finite cardiovascular health. Success-case consumed change=250*.5=125mg/day; probability-weighted full-scale national change=125*.2*.1*.5=1.25mg/day before clinical transport. These are model expectations, not monitored outputs. No comments-to-QALYs shortcut.

inputs.name: C
inputs.rationale: FY2025 Form 990 Part I/IX, all functional expenses; Part VIII direct-cost lines empty.

inputs.name: Y
inputs.rationale: Sustained advocacy horizon; not one annual budget assigned a full national reform.

inputs.name: Qopt
inputs.rationale: Published simulated optimal scenario, not measured outcomes.

inputs.name: Qshort
inputs.rationale: Published short-term-only scenario.

inputs.name: Sshort-minus-Sopt
inputs.rationale: Reported 2036 medians 2789 and 2224; difference is an interpolation reference, not current intake.

inputs.name: deltaS
inputs.rationale: Phase I target3000 minus Phase II2750; achievable further reduction is uncertain and the current baseline is not assumed empirically known.

inputs.name: e
inputs.unit: fraction of incremental sodium opportunity implemented
inputs.rationale: Discounts voluntary noncompliance, purchasing substitutions, and incomplete persistence; not fraction of food categories with any decrease.

inputs.name: t
inputs.rationale: Old population, treatment trends, nonlinearity, different reformulation ramp, and rebasing to future benefits justify a broad discount.

inputs.name: L
inputs.rationale: Five-year delay before the rebased already-discounted health stream; no claim of a final Phase II date. Original modeled clinical lag is not reapplied.

inputs.name: p
inputs.unit: incremental campaign probability of achieving modeled opportunity
inputs.rationale: Subjective 20-percentage-point coalition contribution over five years relative to government/industry background action; broad 0–.5 scenarios.

inputs.name: a
inputs.unit: charitable CSPI share of coalition increment
inputs.rationale: A tenth is a cautious opinion given sustained technical/legal work and many other actors; not a causal audit. Tested .01–.2.

inputs.name: b
inputs.rationale: Allows half to replace reserves, donors, or otherwise-funded work over five years; reserves and loss are observed, this response is not.

inputs.name: h
inputs.unit: net other-pathway QALYs lost per five-year effort
inputs.rationale: Central assigns zero net non-sodium benefit or harm. Negative-outcome stress tests retain loss even if policy influence is zero.

inputs.name: g
inputs.unit: USA share of credited sodium health
inputs.rationale: Near-national US pathway with small geographic/coverage allowance; not an audited outcome-weighted share.

inputs.name: marginal-resource-cost
inputs.rationale: Required for a current social-cost model; historical external implementation/savings estimates are not added as donor savings.

inputs.name: fDurable
inputs.unit: fraction of credited influence producing additional finite reform rather than timing only
inputs.rationale: Central preserves alpha durable-change interpretation; timing-only and50:50 cases reveal dependence on that judgment.

inputs.name: accelerationYears
inputs.unit: years earlier identical finite health stream in timing sensitivity
inputs.rationale: Simple present-value shift approximation, not a rerun of population survival. Both streams have finite20-year duration; later counterfactual ends3years later.

reports.program: Vehicle-injury prevention, incident research, education, and safer-design advocacy

acceptance.evidence: docs/geography-discovery/kacs-usa-independent-acceptance-2026-10-02.md — signed partial planning model; final report integration/publication gates separate

what: Kids and Car Safety documents vehicle-related injuries, educates caregivers and supports affected families.
It advocates vehicle designs that can detect an unattended child and alert someone able to provide a timely rescue.
Its national work also covers backovers, frontovers, entrapment and submersion.
strengths: Detecting a child and enabling timely rescue offers a clear route to preventing avoidable deaths.
Incident evidence and family testimony can inform a still-developing technical standard.
The organization is small and publicly active, making a focused advocacy contribution plausible.
reservations: The change in adoption caused by additional support is a forecast assumption, not an identified organization-specific effect.
Field effectiveness, fleet coverage and rescue behavior are not established by selected laboratory scenarios.
Net technology prices across many purchasing households can outweigh benefits; original financial re-verification and current funding capacity remain unresolved.

sections.what:
[Kids and Car Safety](https://www.kidsandcars.org/hot-cars/hot-cars-federal-legislation-technology) gathers incident evidence, brings affected families into policy discussions and presses for better detection and escalating alerts. Its [2026 public activity](https://www.kidsandcars.org/media/press-releases) supports continued operation. This review prices one prospective advanced-detection timing pathway, not every program or all future vehicle-safety improvements. Existing manufacturer systems, statutory obligations, other advocates and public education continue without another donation.

The illustrative work is maintaining evidence, recruiting survivor testimony, preparing technical comments and engaging manufacturers. A capacity sketch of 500 fully loaded expert hours at $150/hour plus $25,000 specialist/communications support is a judgment, not a quoted unfunded package. We normalize to the latest $256,454 annual recipient expense and charge that full cost scale, without multiplying by another program-allocation fraction.
sections.monitoring:
[NHTSA](https://www.nhtsa.gov/campaign/heatstroke), checked October 2, reports 31 child vehicular heatstroke deaths in completed 2025. Surveillance counts are not charity outcomes; year-to-date counts and weather-confounded trends do not identify impact. The [current OIRA record](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/eAgendaViewRule?pubId=202510&RIN=2127-AM49) remains at prereule stage. Its statutory deadline and ANPRM timetable do not prove a final rule, compliance or actual deployment.

Useful monitoring would connect a funded work plan to a specific specification or timing change, then risk-weighted installed coverage, reliable detection, alert recipients and timely rescue. Model counts, media mentions, brochures and hearings are activities, not prevented deaths. Funding substitution, staff/consultant capacity, false alarms and household price incidence need separate observation. Existing reminders and radar deployments belong in the counterfactual.
sections.qualitative:
[NHTSA’s original door-logic tests](https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/79012/dot_79012_DS1.pdf) found gaps in selected scenarios, including no gained-access alert. They explicitly do not estimate field mortality prevention. The [primary author-institution abstract](https://researchdiscovery.drexel.edu/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/Preventing-Real-World-Pediatric-Vehicular-Heatstroke-Events/991022197403204721) evaluates representative fatal-event scenarios, not a randomized deployment trial. [Transport Canada’s public abstract](https://tc.canada.ca/en/road-transportation/dangers-hot-vehicles-children/technical-report-testing-occupant-monitoring-systems) favors advanced radar/strong alerts; the email-only full report was not obtained. We import no unseen field coefficient.

The [industry reminder commitment](https://www.autosinnovate.org/posts/press-release/2024-industry-heatstroke-report) and [Toyota’s existing radar system](https://pressroom.toyota.com/2025-toyota-sienna-introduces-advanced-rear-seat-reminder-system-to-help-identify-rear-seat-occupants-via-in-cabin-millimeter-wave-radar/) are active alternatives, not evidence that all cars have effective child detection. Connectivity, opt-in alerts, older vehicles and actual rescue limit reach. Sustained advocacy supports a plausible mechanism but does not independently calibrate a donation-to-adoption probability.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter sees a plausible mortality-prevention mechanism, but the preferred conditional forecast has a negative combined result: per $10,000, 0.05351 health QALYs and −0.07927 household-resource-equivalent years, totaling −0.02576. No positive cost per better life applies to that signed total. The original roughly $920K health-only estimate remains historical, not the result of this reassessment. The revised health-only calculation is about $1.87M per ten health years.

The model asks whether one additional annual work portfolio raises the probability of one-year-earlier advanced detection from 25% to 25.5%. That 0.5-percentage-point difference is a standardized elicitation prior—not a source-estimated KACS effect. The $10,000 illustration represents 0.03899 annual work portfolios, capped at one. Replacement funding, regulator/manufacturer effort and other advocates are inside this direct comparison, not multiplied again.

Protection begins in year five rather than six, expands by five percentage points annually to 80% and eventually converges. Coverage, timing and 60% incremental mortality reduction relative to current reminders are judgments. The finite child-survival prior is 60 years at 0.95 utility with 3% discounting, about 26.29 health years at the event date. Avoided nonfatal episodes, short symptom benefit and rescue harm are separate uncertain priors; clinical timing and later survival are each discounted once.

Household costs matter because advanced protection reaches many more purchasers than the number of children saved. A stylized 100-million-household cohort maps the same coverage fraction to risk and once-only acquisitions; at 80% it implies 80 million systems, not 100 million purchases every year. That homogeneous risk/purchaser mapping is a strong assumption, not observed targeting. The preferred $25 net incremental household price is after existing reminders, shared hardware value, manufacturer absorption and insurer offsets. It is not an observed radar price. The earlier purchase loss and later identical counterfactual loss are both credited at their actual dates, so undiscounted acquisitions cancel rather than charging a permanent extra device stream.

Avoided nonfatal episodes receive one $1,000 net medical/unreplaced after-tax caregiver-pay benefit; rescued otherwise-deceased children incur one $2,500 acute household bill. These are judgments after insurance, paid leave and benefit offsets, not societal savings, shadow time or saved children’s lifetime wages. Each uses a one-year consumption window, independently of the long health tail. Coefficient Giving’s [income-to-health welfare comparison](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/) is used; resource equivalents are not observed clinical QALYs.

At a $15 net technology price, the conditional combined estimate becomes positive at about $16.85M per better life; at $25 it is negative. We do not select the cheaper assumption to preserve a favorable ranking. Zero price, changed risk concentration, weaker/stronger influence, clinical null, adverse policy delay and independent harms are separate diagnostics—not confidence limits. Clinical overlap removes only potentially overlapping positive nonfatal symptom credit, never prevented-death benefit or negative costs. The complete portfolio and a verified ordinary-gift return remain unidentified.
sections.funding:
The prior original-return review recorded gross annual expenses of $265,887, $262,881 and $256,454 for FY2022–24, a mean of about $261,741. In this reassessment the original Form 990, XML and PDF retrieval routes were inaccessible; they were not freshly original-audited. The [fresh IRS-derived index](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/200024715) reports FY2023 functional expense $258,364, $4,517 below the historical gross figure. The prior review attributed the difference to direct event costs; this phase cannot re-verify that reconciliation, so both means remain sensitivity cases and historical annual rows are preserved.

FY2024 $256,454 is the conditional annual cost normalizer. The index’s historical revenue and assets do not establish current unrestricted liquidity, an uncovered funding gap, staff capacity or an additional match. No newer original accounts were verified here; inaccessible retrieval is not evidence that no filing exists. A priced incremental work plan, reserve/restriction reconciliation and influence milestone would materially improve donor assessment. Hypothetical work fractions are not purchasable outcomes, and the negative partial forecast does not establish the value of every other program.

model.costScope: Full annual recipient expense normalizes a conditional partial advocacy pathway, not five recurring budgets or a priced funding offer. Public/manufacturer implementation resources are not fully priced.
model.geographicAttribution: National USA burden and acquisition cohort; domestic outcome share1, no foreign benefits.
model.formula: work=min(gift/annualRecipientCost,capacity<=1); delta=(pWith-pWithout)*work; finite discounted health from early-versus-late protection plus separately signed acquisition and episode consumption logs. combined=health+resources; positive price only if combined>0.
model.counterfactual: Same eventual advanced-system acquisition occurs later; current reminders/radar, public duties, manufacturers and other advocates continue. Actual price losses reverse only as accounting comparisons at later receipt dates.
model.attribution: The .005 direct probability change is explicitly a standardized elicitation prior, not independently calibrated KACS causal influence. Other actors/reserves/replacement are included in this contrast once.
model.uncertainty: Partial conditional planning model dominated by unmeasured influence, effectiveness, homogeneous purchaser/risk mapping, net device price and morbidity/household cash incidence. No empirical scenario weights, complete-portfolio EV or donor readiness.
model.nativeOutcomes: Earlier effective detection and rescue may prevent child deaths and nonfatal heat injury. The preferred modeled acquisition-cost timing outweighs those clinical benefits; cheaper net devices reverse the sign. Historical $920K is preserved separately, not confirmed.

historicalModel.formula: Diagnostic only: F1(t)=min(cap,rate*max(0,t-L1+1)); F0(t)=min(cap,rate*max(0,t-L0+1)); A=sum(t=1..T)[F1-F0]/1.03^t; H=D*d*r*k*q*A; Q_USA(G)=G/(Y*C)*b*(p*a*H-h)*g; price=10*G/Q for positive Q. Current central null: additional effort, recipient influence and incremental adoption are unidentified. Inputs/scenarios retain alpha for reproduction only.
historicalModel.counterfactual: Industry reminders/radar, regulatory work, other advocacy, public education and fleet turnover continue without the next gift. Past mandate and advocacy wins are not credited again. Same adoption, funding substitution and possible delay remain.
historicalModel.attribution: Participation is documented, but alpha p=.2,a=.2,b=.5 are unsupported causal judgments. Beta does not turn an assumed small influence into a measured conservative central estimate. Recipient-specific marginal contribution and gift response remain unknown.
historicalModel.uncertainty: Structural uncertainty dominates: revised counts, engineering-to-mortality transport, risk-weighted uptake, disablement/rescue, lumpy policy and correlated other actors. Scenarios are unweighted diagnostics, not confidence bounds; null does not mean proven zero.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: Additional domestic child deaths prevented; intermediate adoption/alerts/rescues are not deaths. Diagnostic 27 discounted QALYs/death (20–30 sensitivity) is judgment; no observed marginal gift-to-death coefficient, nonfatal disability or family-health estimate.

reports.program: Independent living services, assistive technology and accessibility

what: The Berkeley Center for Independent Living helps people with disabilities live in their communities.
It lends and repairs mobility equipment, helps make homes accessible, and offers benefits counseling, peer support and other independent-living services.
These services can restore daily function and reduce out-of-pocket costs for Northern Alameda County residents.
strengths: Equipment repair and loaners address a concrete barrier to everyday mobility.
Free services and home-access support can help people who cannot obtain equivalent assistance elsewhere.
Original annual accounts and primary studies allow us to examine costs, alternative services and plausible benefits separately.
reservations: Current additional repair capacity, unique completed cases and functional days restored are not measured in the public evidence.
The repair estimate depends on judgmental utility and household-savings assumptions; other CIL programs could materially change the overall result.
The original FY2025 audit remained inaccessible, so the exact prior control findings and their remediation are not verified.

sections.what:
CIL serves Northern Alameda County residents through a broad independent-living portfolio. It is the Berkeley charity with EIN 23-7175191, not the similarly named Corporation for Independent Living at cil.org. Its current service pages offer loans of wheelchairs, ramps and other equipment as inventory permits, with a repair-request route. This is evidence of delivery capability, not an assured inventory or turnaround time. [Current programs and Northern Alameda County service area](https://thecil.org/) [Assistive technology loaners and repairs](https://thecil.org/assistive-technology/at-loaners-and-repairs/)

Home-access work includes modifications such as ramps and grab bars. Berkeley's publicly funded program is distinct from nearby cities, where CIL says lack of funding limits it to consultations. A gift might enable otherwise-unfunded modifications, but no priced expansion plan establishes that an unrestricted gift would go there. [Residential access and geographic funding gap](https://thecil.org/residential-access/)

CIL offers free demonstrations and is also a licensed Whill vendor. Separate purchased powerchairs from donated devices and free loaners; sales capability does not establish sales volume or donated-service outcomes. [Whill sales and demonstrations](https://thecil.org/assistive-technology/whill-sales/)
sections.monitoring:
The most useful repair measure is additional person-days with a safely functioning device compared with the actual alternative: vendor repair, insurance, another loaner, self-repair or going without. Record request and completion dates, device fit and use, recurrent failures, outside repair availability and resulting health/function. Repeat repairs for one person must not each receive an entire lifetime benefit. [Assistive technology loaners and repairs](https://thecil.org/assistive-technology/at-loaners-and-repairs/)

The attendant registry prioritizes high-risk people when provider supply is scarce. Matching information is not itself paid care, filled hours or prevented institutionalization. CIL should measure additional sustained care hours and health outcomes, including cases where the limiting resource is a worker rather than coordination money. [Personal attendant services and limited provider registry](https://thecil.org/core-services/personal-attendant-services/)

Original returns provide financial detail but broad, partly historical program descriptions rather than current cohort outcome data. The audit index flags FY2023/FY2024 internal-control weaknesses. The underlying audit download was unavailable in this review, so neither the exact finding nor its resolution is independently established here; this is a follow-up item, not a finding of fraud. [Filing and audit index](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/237175191)

The [city’s draft FY2025 CAPER](https://berkeleyca.gov/sites/default/files/documents/DRAFT_COB_PY24%20CAPER_SAGE_0.pdf) reports seven CIL-supported rental accessibility projects. These are publicly supported outputs, not additional donor-caused health.

September 30 update: a [FY2025 audit is indexed](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/display_audit/2025-06-GSAFAC-0000413595), but the original auditor report remained inaccessible. No exact finding, audit opinion or remediation is newly verified. Absence of an index warning does not establish resolution of prior control weaknesses.

October 2 reassessment rechecked the three original returns and current service pages. The original FY2025 auditor download returned an access error; no new audit opinion or remediation finding was established. A month to respond is not completion time. A useful additional ledger would pair unique completed repairs with counterfactual function-days and net household payments, while separating publicly funded or otherwise available services.
sections.qualitative:
A multicenter observational wheelchair study found frequent repairs and adverse consequences, including being confined at home; another reported median repair time of 14 days. These document a meaningful problem, but they do not estimate the causal effect of CIL repair or a health-utility decrement. Vendor users may differ in severity, device complexity and resources. [Factors influencing wheelchair repairs and consequences](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8501145/) [Wheelchair repairs: delays, causes and associated outcomes](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39427781/)

Other branches have credible external evidence. The HIPI randomized home-modification trial estimated an adjusted reduction in home fall injuries, with a crude estimate whose interval included no effect. Its New Zealand households and modification package are not interchangeable with CIL's client mix or every ramp installation. [HIPI home modification cluster-randomized trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25255696/)

Living Well was evaluated with a randomized wait-list design in 246 consumers across independent-living centers. Results support some improvement in secondary conditions and health-related outcomes. The investigators' later synthesis says symptom days returned to baseline by twelve months and health costs by two months; neither perpetual savings nor lifelong QALYs are justified. CIL currently offers the curriculum, but delivery fidelity, additional enrollment and local results remain unknown. [Health promotion: evaluation of Living Well with a Disability](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17032708/) [Living Well with a Disability: intervention and follow-up synthesis](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/65/su/su6501a10.htm) [Living Well Senior Program](https://thecil.org/core-services/living-well-senior-program/)

Independence, access and dignity are important even when incompletely measured by QALYs. Disability status is not a discount on a person's worth; any quantitative benefit should be a change in their experienced health or function, not an assumption that disability makes a life less valuable.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter estimates approximately **$146.4 million per better life** for a conditional repair-and-household-savings pathway. A better life here means ten combined health and income-equivalent years in California. This is a partial planning estimate, not a price for a confirmed donation opportunity or a complete assessment of CIL's work.

**What does money buy?** The illustrative calculation allocates 10% of ordinary additional funding to repair and loaner services. A support-loaded attempted episode costs about **$450**, based on assumed staff time, employment costs, materials and organization support. After allowing for funding replacement, completion and equivalent alternatives, each $100,000 of ordinary funding corresponds to about **4.44 additional restored-function episodes**, totaling **62.17 otherwise-lost functional days**, plus **0.89 separate households avoiding a $100 payment**. These are modeled yields, not CIL-reported output counts or a $100,000 funding request. The full gift remains in the cost calculation, including the 90% supporting services not quantified here.

We think the repair mechanism matters because a functioning wheelchair, walker or temporary loaner can let someone move around and participate in daily life while another device is unavailable. But CIL's month-long response queue is not evidence of a month of function restored. The external survey's fourteen-day median among completed repairs is only a time-scale anchor; the actual gain must be measured against vendor, insured, public loaner and backup options. [CIL repair and loaner services](https://thecil.org/assistive-technology/at-loaners-and-repairs/) [Primary repair survey](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39427781/)

**Health and household resources.** The central calculation gives **0.005069201 health years** and **0.001759633 income-equivalent years** per illustrative $100,000. Unmet-access recipients receive the temporary health credit; people who would otherwise purchase timely equivalent service receive only net household savings, not duplicate health credit. The $100 one-off saving, 10% purchaser share and $25,000 household-resource baseline are explicit assumptions, not observed invoices or client income. They are distinct from the $100 materials allowance. Additional paid work and caregiver resources are examined in signed scenarios, with no positive central earnings assumption. Public/insurer expenditure and unpaid time are not automatically household income. [Income-to-health comparison](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/)

**What changed?** The historical repair illustration was **$59,187,952.33** per better life. The revised central is **$146,437,882.12**: the temporary utility judgment falls from 0.10 to 0.03 to align with the mixed adult-mobility mechanism, while separately adding household savings. Neither utility is a measured CIL effect. The shared 0.03 prior is a consistency judgment, not independent confirmation; severe-dependence cases may warrant more. The new calculator uses a 3% annual discount convention and preserves the old continuous-3% calculation separately.

Removing savings gives about **$197.3M**; retaining 0.10 utility with the new savings gives about **$53.6M**. Household-resource baselines, function-days, allocation, completion, funding replacement, utility, burdens and original-audit follow-up remain decisive uncertainties. The scenarios are not confidence intervals.

**Other pathways.** Home access, benefits navigation, Living Well, institutional transitions, peer support and advocacy are not assigned zero value. An outside-Berkeley modification scenario tests a separate budget and nonoverlapping cohort, but the stated funding gap does not establish a priced additional project. Original studies support some home-safety and independent-living mechanisms, not CIL-specific effect sizes. Donated equipment, volunteers and public shipping also have resource costs not fully priced here. [Residential access](https://thecil.org/residential-access/)
sections.funding:
Original returns report full-recipient expenses of $2,986,495 (FY2023), $3,662,458 (FY2024) and $4,370,584 (FY2025), all June-ending twelve-month periods. The three-year mean is $3,673,179. FY2024 functions were $3,017,406 program, $644,978 management and $74 fundraising. [Original FY2024 Form 990 with FY2023 comparative totals](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/237175191/202521359349306602/full)

FY2025 expenses split into $2,752,037 program, $1,362,449 management and $256,098 fundraising. Revenue was $3,996,267, including $3,223,822 government grants and $349,468 other contributions. Compensation and benefits totaled $3,219,987. The operating deficit was $374,317; net assets were $7,809,089, of which $2,385,204 carried donor restrictions. Net assets are not all immediately available cash. Functional allocations changed substantially; they are accounting categories, not measures of effectiveness. [Original FY2025 Form 990, IRS electronic filing](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/237175191/202641359349312384/full)

CIL says services are free and supported by government, foundations and individuals. Publicly funded Berkeley modifications, insured equipment alternatives and other donors all matter to substitution. A reported funding gap outside Berkeley is promising but does not price the ordinary-gift margin. The general donation page supports the broad portfolio and includes optional designated routes; this report assumes no designation and records no actual donation. [Eligibility, free services and funding](https://thecil.org/about-us/faq/) [General donation route](https://thecil.org/donate/)

CIL's [current careers page](https://thecil.org/job-listings/) posts a $28/hour starting-pay floor and benefits, while the [AT page](https://thecil.org/assistive-technology/) seeks skilled repair and preparation volunteers. These support a labor-capacity pathway but do not prove that cash is the binding constraint or that a donation funds a new position.

September 30 review checked all three original returns and confirmed the $3,673,179 mean. [Original FY2023 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202401369349313445/IRS990) reports $2,132,657 program, $757,676 management and $96,162 fundraising. Total/program ratios are 1.400, 1.214 and 1.588 for FY2023–2025. FY2024's miscellaneous/indirect line allocates $325,124 to program and negative $302,724 to management. These accounting allocations require explanation before treating the ratio as a marginal repair cost; they are not evidence of misconduct. Included noncash contributions were $67,154, $68,766 and $67,668: avoid counting recognized resources twice. Full incremental donated-device, volunteer and partner costs remain unknown.

model.costScope: Ordinary unrestricted gift, C=$100,000 analytical normalization. Full gift remains charged even though this model quantifies only a repair/loaner health pathway. f is an explicit marginal portfolio allocation, not a restricted donation. Unit cost k includes wages, employment loading, materials and allocated recipient support. This is donor-dollar cost, not a societal-cost estimate; donated device and partner resource opportunity costs remain unknown.
model.geographicAttribution: g_CA=1 for the short-duration direct-service scenario, based on Northern Alameda County eligibility. National advocacy benefits are not counted. This is an inference about weeks of local client benefit, not location of headquarters.
model.formula: calculate() in lib/cil-ca-calibrated-model.mjs. Support-loaded cost → funding/completion/deduplicated episodes → disjoint unmet-function and counterfactual-purchaser cohorts. Finite health and paid-work integrals use log1p(annual discount); one-off savings use the Coefficient Giving log-resource crosswalk. Separate clinical, income, burden and geography components are added once. The original continuous-discount illustration is frozen separately.
model.counterfactual: CIL's existing grants, payroll and inventory, insured/vendor service, publicly financed device loan centers, Easy Does It emergency repair and individual backups continue. A donor-funded slot must actually accelerate restoration relative to these options. CIL's current month-long response queue is NOT itself the number of functional days lost or saved.
model.attribution: m discounts replacement of grant/reserve funding or staffing constraints; a separately discounts equivalent alternative repair/loaner service and usable backups. s accounts for failed or unsuitable delivery. Do not count one disability-related utility improvement separately as avoided injury, isolation and mobility restoration. No attribution of all recipient work to the repair branch.
model.uncertainty: Conditional partial planning estimate, not measured CIL outcomes, a comprehensive organization estimate, a lower bound or a verified donor capacity offer. Revised temporary utility .03, purchaser share .1, net cash100 and resource baseline25000 are explicit judgments. Original auditor findings/remediation are still unverified. Other independent-living benefits and third-party costs may materially change the total.
model.nativeOutcomes: Illustrative $100,000 ordinary funding: support-loaded episode $450.39; 4.440568 additional unmet-function episodes; 62.167958 function-days; 0.888114 separate counterfactual-purchaser households. Central health 0.005069201 + resources 0.001759633 California equivalent years. These are modeled, not observed outputs.

inputs.name: gift
inputs.rationale: Calculation normalization; not a verified funding request.

inputs.name: repairAllocation
inputs.unit: ordinary gift share supporting repair/loaner capacity
inputs.rationale: A modest share within a broad portfolio. Core consumer services includes AT along with housing, home modification and transitions; repair-only allocation is not reported. Stress 0.02–0.25. The allocated share includes its corresponding support costs; k is therefore support-loaded, not a second charge to the total gift.

inputs.name: wage
inputs.rationale: Rounded proxy from current $33.99/hour community independent-living specialist vacancy; not a verified repair technician wage. General CIL careers page states starting pay $28/hour. Stress $28–40.

inputs.name: benefitLoad
inputs.rationale: 35% benefits/payroll/paid-leave loading; CIL advertises extensive benefits but actual marginal load is unreported. Stress 1.2–1.5.

inputs.name: hours
inputs.rationale: Intake, handling, repair or loaner preparation, fitting and closeout combined. No local time-motion study; stress 2–8 hours.

inputs.name: materials
inputs.rationale: Average repair/cleaning/component allowance, not device retail price or CIL observed invoice. Stress $50–500; actual case mix could exceed this.

inputs.name: supportLoad
inputs.rationale: Central proxy equals observed total/program expense ratio 1.5881269; applying average support loading to marginal service cost is a judgment. Stress 1.3–2, not an accounting confidence bound.

inputs.name: funding
inputs.rationale: Half the modeled allocation adds usable service capacity after grant/reserve replacement and staffing constraints. Public grants are large, while requests and volunteer needs suggest unmet demand. Stress 0.1–0.8 plus zero.

inputs.name: completion
inputs.rationale: Repair/loaner can fail or be unsuitable. External SCI repair survey's completion data motivate uncertainty, not a measured CIL success rate. Stress 0.5–0.95.

inputs.name: dedup
inputs.rationale: One modeled unique household per episode; repeated function-days and repeated savings require deduplication. No observed deduplication rate.

inputs.name: unmetShare
inputs.rationale: Half successful episodes deliver function otherwise lost after allowing insurance/vendors, state loan centers, EDI and backups. Stress 0.1–0.9.

inputs.name: purchaserShare
inputs.rationale: 0.10 judgmental counterfactual purchaser stratum, disjoint from the 0.50 unmet-function stratum. No observed purchase incidence.

inputs.name: functionDays
inputs.unit: functional days gained per truly additional episode
inputs.rationale: Finite acceleration prior, not observed days saved. External survey median repair duration was 14 days; CIL reports roughly one month before responding, so its current service is not automatically faster. Stress 2–60 days.

inputs.name: utility
inputs.rationale: 0.03 mixed adult-mobility family prior replaces 0.10. Neither is measured CIL utility; the cross-sectional repair survey does not identify a generic decrement.

inputs.name: delay
inputs.rationale: Central quarter-year implementation/queue delay; stress 0.05–0.5.

inputs.name: discount
inputs.rationale: 3% annual convention; continuous-time finite benefits use log1p(rate). Historical continuous3% remains frozen.

inputs.name: netCash
inputs.rationale: Avoided repair/copay/rental payment after offsets, not materials cost or measured invoice. Zero and negative cases retained.

inputs.name: baseline
inputs.rationale: 25,000 planning judgment, not measured client income; 50,000 and100,000 tested separately.

inputs.name: earnerShare
inputs.rationale: Zero central paid-work incidence; optional20% judgment does not create an observed employment effect.

inputs.name: annualNetWork
inputs.rationale: Optional signed work/caregiver resource scenario; only finite function-days counted, no positive central work incidence.

inputs.name: clinicalOverlapShare
inputs.rationale: Zero central overlap because purchasers are disjoint. Optional work cases reserve20% independently of earnings sign; adverse utility is not reduced.

what: Comité Cívico del Valle works on health and environmental conditions in Imperial Valley.
Its portfolio includes asthma home visits, air monitoring, heat work, community relief and energy-related advocacy.
A conditional air-implementation health estimate uses full recipient cost and explicit judgment assumptions; asthma and other portfolio pathways remain unpriced.
strengths: Direct home visiting and local exposure work offer identifiable routes to better health.
The organization participated in a local comparative study, providing unusually relevant evidence to challenge generic claims.
Original accounts and an identified public asthma grant clarify recipient scale and funding substitution.
reservations: The local study found no statistically detected effect of the randomized family intervention at twelve months.
Asthma was a small reported expense category; the unrestricted portfolio is much broader.
Monitoring, environmental review and education require additional implementation before they yield measurable health benefits.

sections.what:
CCV's current site describes seven initiatives spanning public health, environmental justice and energy transition. The asthma program offers bilingual home education, trigger identification and self-management support; it identifies CalEPA funding. This is not a clinic that independently supplies all medication and medical care. [Current initiatives and organization](https://ccvhealth.org/) [Current asthma intervention and management](https://ccvhealth.org/asthma-intervention)

The same recipient operates air monitoring and broader community programs. Its air-quality page describes California work alongside collaborations in Canada and Mexico, so an unrestricted gift's California benefit share cannot simply be assumed to be 100%. Direct Imperial Valley care is California-scoped; cross-border and national effects require separate attribution. [Air-quality network and monitoring initiatives](https://ccvhealth.org/air-quality)
sections.monitoring:
For home visiting, useful measures are additional completed patient courses beyond public funding, changed medication/trigger management, and symptom-free days measured against usual care. Track baseline severity, actual visit dose, dropout, seasonal change and recurrence. For monitoring, the key bridge is how information changes exposure: implemented controls or protective behavior, duration, uptake and alternative data sources. A monitor reading alone is not avoided illness. [Current asthma intervention and management](https://ccvhealth.org/asthma-intervention) [Air-quality network and monitoring initiatives](https://ccvhealth.org/air-quality)

Current heat work is described as a community research and mitigation initiative with San Diego State University. The reviewed page does not supply a completed counterfactual evaluation or a priced unfunded intervention. General community relief may reduce hardship, but distributed items cannot be converted directly into health gain. [Taking on the Heat initiative](https://ccvhealth.org/extreme-heat) [Share and Care](https://ccvhealth.org/share-and-care)
sections.qualitative:
The most directly relevant evidence is Respira Sano, conducted with CCV in 400 Imperial County youth. Assignment to family home visiting was randomized; clinic exposure depended on where children received care. The investigators found no statistically detected effect of the family intervention at twelve months. Fewer unplanned visits in the clinic comparison cannot be credited to CCV home visits, and clinic selection was not randomized. All groups received community intervention, so its independent effect was not identified. Missing process data and imperfect lung tests limit interpretation. This does not prove today's program has zero benefit, but it is substantial counterevidence to an automatic positive transfer. [Respira Sano primary comparative-effectiveness report, April 2021](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK599376/)

A separate Seattle randomized trial found 2.10 more symptom-free days per two weeks after CHW home visits versus usual care, with a 95% interval of 1.17–3.05. Different targeting, service dose and existing care may explain differing results. The trial's symptom-day outcome is not a QALY measure; caregiver quality-of-life scores and avoided visits cannot simply be added as QALYs. [Randomized home visits for Medicaid-enrolled children with asthma](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26270287/) [CDC Medicaid Asthma Home Visit Project registry](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02258308)

CCV's August 2026 account reports an appellate decision requiring further environmental review of a lithium/geothermal project, particularly water and Salton Sea air-quality issues. I verified the organization's statement, not the original opinion's full contents. Improved review is not yet a measured reduction in dust exposure. Any health model must compare actual mitigation with the project and energy alternatives that would otherwise occur, including harms from delay or substitution. Coalition work with Earthworks cannot all be assigned to a marginal CCV gift. [CCV reports lithium-project environmental review appeal](https://ccvhealth.org/news/california-court-of-appeal-orders-imperial-county-to-correct-major-environmental-deficiencies-in-hells-kitchen-lithium-project-approval)

The central decision scenario now models three years of monitoring, organizing and implementation support producing a 20% chance of an additional 0.2 microgram-per-cubic-meter PM2.5 reduction for a modeled 20,000 older adults over five years. This is an unverified scale hypothesis, not a measured result of the court decision or the monitor network. CCV's current air page explicitly covers both PM2.5 and PM10; the PM2.5 mortality bridge is not applied to all dust or metals. A 25% CCV coalition contribution, 25% ordinary-gift funding response and 90% California benefit share are subjective priors.

A [large Medicare study](https://xiaowu.io/publication/wu2020evaluating/wu2020evaluating.pdf) supplies an exposure–mortality anchor, not CCV's implementation effect. The model integrates the difference between closed-cohort survival curves for ten years, with lower hazard only for five years. No repeated lifetime is assigned to annual avoided deaths. Asthma, heat, relief, clean-energy benefits and potential energy-delay harms remain outside the positive priced branch, with separate zero/adverse scenarios. This component is not a whole-portfolio ranking.
sections.cost:
The conditional air-implementation central uses three years of full recorded recipient expense: 3 × $6,458,632 = $19,375,896. It yields 0.241461 modeled California QALY, about $802.44 million per 10. A favorable joint case is about $3.73 million per 10; a weak case exceeds $78 trillion per 10. These are explicit judgment stress cases, not confidence limits or an empirical estimate of campaign effectiveness.

The full expense denominator includes all programs and support, not only the $341,076 air-monitoring category. It preserves recorded depreciation and grants. Additional outside mitigation, public administration and partner resources must be added for a social-cost estimate. The model assumes a marginal implementation improvement using existing planned resources, not that all new control equipment is free.

An explicit finite clinical sensitivity gives a useful hurdle. If the Seattle endpoint difference of 2.10 symptom-free days per fourteen days held throughout one full year, and each gained symptom-free day improved health utility by an illustrative 0.10, q = (2.10/14) × 0.10 = 0.015 QALYs per additional patient-year. Full-year persistence is optimistic relative to an endpoint measurement; the 0.10 mapping is judgment, not trial data. A linear rise from zero to that effect over the year halves q. No mortality, second year or separate urgent-care benefit is added. [Randomized home visits for Medicaid-enrolled children with asthma](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26270287/)

At q = 0.015, reaching $1 million per 10 QALYs requires 66.667 additional California patient-years per $100,000, or at most $1,500 of whole-recipient gift cost per effective patient-year. A $100,000 threshold requires 666.667 patient-years, or $150 each. Those are break-even requirements, not predictions. Under a purely diagnostic assumption that the gift follows the FY2024 asthma expense share (1.928%), allowable asthma-branch cost per effective patient-year falls to $28.93 or $2.89 respectively. Historical share is not a measured marginal allocation; the calculation demonstrates why restricted-program efficiency cannot stand in for recipient efficiency.

Other branches could add substantial benefit, but require independent finite models of implemented exposure changes, incremental public action or delivered care. Overlapping respiratory benefits must be combined at person level, not counted once for asthma visits and again for air-quality work.
