what: Help America Hear coordinates donated prescription hearing aids and professional fitting for financially constrained people nationwide.
Its standard program offers two hearing aids, custom molds and one year of limited service, helping recipients communicate and participate in everyday life.
It also supports students through scholarships and assistive devices; those additional benefits are not priced in this hearing-access estimate.
strengths: A manufacturer-confirmed donation partnership offers a concrete route to prescription hearing aids for people who cannot otherwise afford them.
Randomized studies support meaningful hearing-related benefits, although broader generic health effects are less certain.
Published eligibility and follow-up terms help identify both the service provided and the patient costs that should enter the estimate.
reservations: Donated aids, annual service recipients and unique completed new fittings are different counts, and the linked delivery records remain unavailable.
The forecast of additional completed care and lasting benefit relies on explicit judgments rather than measured results for Help America Hear.
Patient costs, earnings effects, current donation capacity and legal-payee verification need further evidence before a donor-ready recommendation.

sections.what:
Help America Hear Inc., EIN 20-0878279, coordinates nationwide prescription hearing-aid access and scholarships. Its [current program](https://helpamericahear.org/help-america-hear-program) provides two aids, molds and one year of limited service. A $250 deposit is applied to fitting or refundable when the provider donates services; patients pay for evaluation, clearance, batteries, accessories and extended warranties. The [FAQ](https://helpamericahear.org/faq) gives two-to-six-month provider matching and possible travel up to 50 miles. Current page and FAQ fee/eligibility language still conflict. No application or payment was submitted.

A [June 2026 golf event](https://helpamericahear.org/the-john-thomas-golf-classic) and [2025–26 scholarship page](https://helpamericahear.org/scholarship-program) support current activity, though the home page retains older copy and inconsistent scholarship numbers. Current activity does not establish legal payee verification or an additional funded tranche.

The modeled opportunity is coordination of existing donated-device allocations: application review, provider matching and follow-up that could turn an otherwise stalled opportunity into a completed fitting. It is not an assumption that a cash donation purchases more manufacturer devices. The manufacturer describes 100–150 aids annually, while the standard program supplies two aids per person. Our midpoint of 125 aids therefore represents 62.5 potential paired opportunities, not 125 patients or an observed annual completion count.
sections.monitoring:
All three original returns repeat an explicitly annual claim: over 120 individuals received hearing aids and services during the year. Repetition does not prove a cumulative count or inaccuracy. However, services may include adjustments, replacements or repeat recipients; there is no linked new-completed-fitting cohort. [ReSound](https://pro.resound.com/en-us/marketing/resound-gives-sound) separately describes 100–150 hearing aids annually plus scholarship devices. These are aids, not people. Schedules M record hearing-aid contribution/item counts 178, 164 and 164, valued at $133,500, $124,500 and $123,000. The column permits contributions or items and supplemental unit clarification is blank. Neither count should be silently converted into completed bilateral patients. Inventory movement, dates and scholarship overlap remain unreconciled.

No HAH longitudinal use, hearing-function or utility cohort was located. FAQ support is three to five visits or up to one year according to provider policy. Five-year reapplication eligibility is not evidence of five-year adherence.

A useful delivery ledger would connect each allocated device pair to inventory, scholarship or standard-program designation, a unique applicant, provider appointment, completed fitting and follow-up. It would also identify which opportunities were unused without additional coordination. Until that exists, the 62.5-pair benchmark and completion probabilities in our forecast remain planning assumptions. A device count or active partnership alone cannot establish the output caused by another donation.

Our fresh October 2 check retrieved the program, FAQ, manufacturer partnership and clinical sources. Original annual returns could not be retrieved through either attempted access route; the prior original-return receipts remain the basis for the gross financial figures. The fresh IRS-derived index corroborates functional-expense fields, not all schedules or restored fundraising-event costs. This limitation is not evidence that filings do not exist.
sections.qualitative:
Prescription hearing access is a promising mechanism because hearing aids can improve communication, participation and hearing-specific quality of life. The [Singapore delayed-start trial](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12913-020-05977-x) found an approximately 0.12 HUI-3 difference at three months, but used modified scoring for nonusers and studied volunteers willing to adopt aids. Its longer cost-utility horizon was extrapolated, not a controlled observation of five years of benefit.

The [ACHIEVE generic-quality analysis](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2826555) found no statistically significant physical or mental composite advantage over three years. Its hearing-communication analysis supports a narrower benefit, but HHIE scores cannot simply be read as QALYs. These studies do not measure Help America Hear’s local effectiveness, adherence, earnings, dementia prevention or mortality. Generic-null and short-duration alternatives are therefore important parts of the forecast.

We use a judged annual hearing-utility profile of 0.06, 0.04 and 0.02 over three years following a four-month fitting delay. These are already adjusted cohort utility assumptions, not trial-measured annual values. No additional adherence multiplier is applied to health. Later decline represents benefit and use uncertainty within the newly accessed-care cohort; it does not repeat the separate subtraction for people who would obtain equivalent care elsewhere.

Program matching friction makes additional coordination plausible, but does not establish unused inventory or available clinician slots. A direct completion contrast of 80% with versus 60% without one additional annual work portfolio is an elicited planning judgment, not a source-calibrated effect. Replacement funding, reserves, provider capacity and manufacturer constraints belong inside that contrast, rather than being multiplied in again. A fixed, fully used allocation can produce no additional service.

We count ordinary fitting and acclimation burdens only for newly accessed care. People who would receive equivalent care elsewhere have no central health increment or duplicate generic fitting burden. A separate stress test considers additional HAH-specific burdens relative to that alternative. Independent donation-induced harms are tested even when service response is zero. These distinctions matter more than presenting a falsely precise headline.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter considers prescription hearing access a promising way to improve lives. Our conditional forecast for this program is approximately **$3.07 million per better life**, combining health with net household resources. It is less favorable than the historical $689,124 estimate mainly because we no longer treat an annual aid-and-service count as completed new patients or assume the same gift-induced fitting yield.

**What a donation could provide.** The forecast charges the full annual recipient accounting proxy of $303,522 against a partial hearing-access pathway. That is restored gross expense of $426,522 less $123,000 of donated-aid book expense, not verified cash flow or a marginal quote. An illustrative coordination workload of 62.5 opportunities times five hours at $80 fully loaded per hour is $25,000; these hours and rate are judgments, and the remaining annual cost still includes other programs, events, administration and fundraising. We do not discount those costs away to improve the estimate.

A $10,000 normalization supplies 0.03295 annual work-years, capped at one annual cohort. The 62.5 potential pairs and judged 20-percentage-point completion difference imply about 0.412 additional HAH fittings. Of these, an assumed 75%, or 0.309 people, would otherwise lack equivalent care for the modeled period; the remaining 25% receive no additional hearing benefit. These are modeled increments, not reported outputs or an offered donation package.

**Health benefit.** We apply the finite 0.06/0.04/0.02 annual cohort utility profile after the fitting delay, a judged 2% competing annual mortality risk and 3% discounting at year midpoints. Ordinary fitting harm is 0.001 health years per newly accessed recipient. No dementia-prevention, mortality benefit or lifetime wage gain is added. The resulting health benefit is approximately 0.03435 years per normalized $10,000.

**Household resources.** Newly accessed-care households face a judged net initial cost of $320: an expected $150 fitting charge, $50 evaluation expense after insurance, $80 travel and $40 unreplaced after-tax patient or caregiver pay. The $150 is a judgment about a $250 charge incurred by 60% of recipients, not a reported average. A refunded deposit is not a permanent cost, and no second application fee or optional donation is stacked on it. Costs can be higher or lower; fee and refund terms remain partly inconsistent.

We assume $50 annual maintenance while devices are used, with independent resource-use exposure of 70%, 60% and 50% over three years. A judged 25% working subgroup receives $120 net additional pay per year for two years, after taxes, benefit withdrawal and work costs. This modest positive prior is not inferred from shadow prices for unpaid time or from an employment association. Nonworking recipients receive no assumed wage gain. Otherwise-equivalent-care households receive a separate judged $250 net copay saving once; that is actual payer incidence, not the retail or book value of donated devices.

Net cash is combined within each household before applying Coefficient Giving’s income-equivalence comparison: 0.5 times the logarithm of the resource ratio, using a judged $25,000 annual resource baseline. Clinical utility and these income-equivalent welfare years are different quantities. The model does not count each family member as another identical income recipient, repeat an upfront payment as annual wages, or credit insurer spending as household cash. Cash pathways use their own dates and finite exposure.

Household resources contribute approximately **−0.00175 equivalent years** per $10,000: modeled patient costs outweigh the small earnings and copay benefits. Together with health, the forecast gives approximately **0.03260 combined equivalent years**. Health-only cost is approximately $2.91 million per ten health years. The complete organization’s expected value and a verified next-gift return remain unidentified, not zero. Scholarships and other pathways may add benefits or costs not covered here.

**Sensitivity and history.** Test shorter or null clinical benefit, manufacturer allocations of 100 or 150 aids, nearly replaced or zero completion response, refunded or fully charged deposits, no earnings or negative earnings, maintenance costs, alternative care, household resource baselines and signed additional harms. These are unweighted judgment scenarios, not a confidence interval. The original $689,124 alpha and prior unknown beta center are retained separately. A forecast is useful for comparison but cannot establish that this recipient currently has additional funding room.
sections.funding:
Original fiscal-year-ending-February returns show gross expenses $386,116 (2023), $436,995 (2024) and $426,522 (2025), mean $416,544.33. These restore Part VIII direct event costs to Part IX functional expenses. FY2025 buckets: $123,000 aids/miscellaneous (matching recorded donated-aid value), $74,027 other hearing/awareness program expense, $40,000 scholarships, $36,534 management/general, $5,215 functional fundraising, $147,746 direct events. They sum to $426,522. Removing aid fair value gives $303,522, an accounting proxy including depreciation, not cash flow or a marginal quote. Donated clinician labor and patient costs remain incomplete; aid fair value is not manufacturer opportunity cost.

FY2025 event receipts $239,440 include $194,060 contributions. Less $147,746 direct costs leaves $91,694 before other fundraising expense; the −$102,366 net-event line alone is not a loss. FY2024 gross receipts minus direct costs are −$2,018. FY2023 also has $73,572 special-event costs in Part IX in addition to $50,600 direct costs in Part VIII. Filed classifications are retained without inventing corrections or claiming a forensic accounting audit.

FY2025 net assets without restrictions are $71,754, versus $82,110 and $96,836 previously. Cash is $12,298 and other investments $57,713. Donor-restricted net assets are blank in all returns; year-end unrestricted balances do not mean all receipts were unrestricted. [SNF's 2024 grant](https://www.snf.org/en/work/grants/grants-database/help-america-hear-1-program-2024/) supports ten scholarships and hearing/assistive devices. Current remaining restrictions, matching balances and next-gift allocation are unknown.

Schedule L Part IV discloses Mitchell Shapiro: FY2023 $7,750 ($6,000 rent/$1,750 utilities), FY2024 $7,200 ($5,800/$1,400), FY2025 description rent $2,500 with amount column blank and former founder/chairman/CEO relationship. Each says no revenue sharing; Parts I–III disclose no excess-benefit transactions, loans or assistance. Related-party disclosure is not proof of wrongdoing. FY2025 Part VI reports a written conflict policy and annual disclosures but no regular monitoring/enforcement. Lease comparability, disinterested approval and implementation remain unknown. The earlier secondary California registration flag remains unresolved against an original registry; no national closure is inferred. Independently verified payee and additional capacity are required before recommending a donation.

The October 2 index check lists functional expenses of $335,516, $298,757 and $278,776 for the same three fiscal years. These differ from the restored gross figures above because direct event costs are separately reported. Prior original receipts, not this fresh index, support those restorations and the schedule details. Fresh original retrieval failed, so this is not a new audit.

Before moving from a research estimate to a source-vetted giving choice, verify the legal payee, current registry status, unused device allocations, provider slots, matched funding and restrictions, and an uncovered coordination plan. Related-party disclosures warrant verification rather than allegations. Existing balances, an active event or a donation partnership do not themselves establish a donor-sensitive work tranche.

model.costScope: Full annual non-in-kind accounting proxy against a partial hearing-access pathway; donated-resource opportunity cost and actual marginal package unidentified.
model.geographicAttribution: Domestic resident benefits centrally1; .98 diagnostic. Geography applied once to health and household cohorts.
model.formula: Incremental completions=min(G/annualCost,capacity) × aids/2 × (completionWith−completionWithout). Newly accessed fraction receives finite cohort utility; otherwise equivalent care receives no central incremental health. Independently timed signed household log resource differences are added once.
model.counterfactual: Direct completion contrast includes donor replacement and provider/manufacturer capacity. Separate patient split distinguishes newly accessed from otherwise-equivalent care; generic fitting burdens cancel in the latter.
model.attribution: One household per recipient is a judgment. Clinical profile already incorporates use/transport; resource-use exposure is independent. No device book/retail value, mortality wages, dementia or unpaid shadow-time income.
model.uncertainty: Completion lift, potential pairs, duration and net household costs/pay are declared planning priors. Complete portfolio and verified next-gift price remain unknown; sensitivity is unweighted, not a confidence interval.
model.nativeOutcomes: Manufacturer100–150 aids/year; paired midpoint62.5 is potential opportunity, not observed completed new recipients. Repeated annual service claims are not a linked fitting ledger.

historicalModel.costScope: Whole unrestricted recipient support. Gross historical costs retained; identifiable aid value removed only for non-in-kind accounting proxy, not cash flow. Donated clinician and patient resources incomplete. Scholarships remain costed and non-health benefit unquantified.
historicalModel.geographicAttribution: Official program and return describe nationwide domestic services and no foreign operations. Conditional g=.99 allows incidental nonresident benefit; range.98–1. USA includes residents of50states and DC. Headquarters location and citizenship are not allocation keys.
historicalModel.formula: D=sum[t=1..T]((1−m)/1.03)^t. N=(G/c)×b. Q_all=N×(s×u×p×D−h). Q_USA=Q_all×g. Price per10=10G/Q_USA only if positive. b is financing/provider/manufacturer additionality; s is benefit not otherwise obtained; p is sustained effective use; u is utility gain while using devices. h is an adverse-burden allowance retained for all additional fittings even when s=0. Numerical inputs are retained alpha diagnostic judgments; no beta central inputs are established.
historicalModel.counterfactual: The financial screen makes otherwise-unmet need plausible but does not prove no alternative care. s allows Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, veterans' programs, other charities, family purchase or suitable OTC options. b separately discounts existing sponsorship, fixed donated-device quotas, provider slots and reserves. The alpha c attempted to include failed applications and administration through a whole-recipient cost anchor, but its completed-fitting denominator is unverified. p discounts post-fitting use rather than counting completion twice.
historicalModel.attribution: No extra hearing gain is credited to both scholarship and standard-program recipients. Scholarship cash and awareness receive no assumed health benefit but remain in cost; their separate benefits are unquantified. Each recipient is counted once, not once per device. Clinical priors transfer from external trials with better follow-up, not from device retail values. The main uncertainty is donation-sensitive completed care, so numerical cases are conditional and do not establish a favorable bound.
historicalModel.uncertainty: Central withdrawn: both completed-care denominator supporting c and donation-induced device/provider capacity supporting b lack calibration. This is unknown, not zero. Clinical priors support diagnostics only.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: Annual services claim >120 people; completed new fittings unknown. Schedule M aid contribution/item counts 178/164/164; manufacturer says 100–150 aids annually plus scholarship aids. No linked completion or inventory ledger.

acceptance.evidence: docs/geography-access-batch-five-acceptance.md; independent Medium audit plus root review; research only.; docs/geography-central-estimates-acceptance.md

what: Rx Outreach operates a nonprofit mail-order pharmacy with low cash prices and free standard delivery.
It also provides separately funded medication assistance, including Fill the Gap for eligible older adults around St. Louis.
Its promising health mechanism is preventing clinically important treatment gaps, not simply selling more prescriptions.
strengths: Existing pharmacy infrastructure can reach patients and clinics without a general income application or insurance requirement.
Randomized free-medicine studies support a real adherence mechanism, especially when cost prevents necessary treatment.
Original financial schedules separate purchased medicines from donated inventory, making financial claims inspectable.
reservations: Additional human patient-years caused by an unrestricted donation, rather than earned revenue or partner funding, are not measured.
Medication class, patient risk, sustained use and realistic alternatives determine health yield; shipment totals cannot establish a QALY estimate.
Territorial and pet prescriptions are outside this human USA boundary, while current finances lag a changing pharmacy model.

sections.what: The [current general pharmacy](https://rxoutreach.org/patients/) requires an available medication and valid prescription, not an income application, membership or insurance. Its [clinic service](https://rxoutreach.org/why_clinics/) supports patient-pay, clinic-pay and hybrid arrangements and can ship to a clinic for people without secure housing. [Fill the Gap](https://rxoutreach.org/fill-the-gap/) separately offers covered medicines free to eligible adults aged 55 or older, at or below 300% of the federal poverty level, in the St. Louis region; meeting eligibility does not guarantee enrollment. Current criteria allow insured patients and should not be replaced with older launch restrictions. Other [assistance pathways](https://rxoutreach.org/patient-assistance-programs/) include disaster relief and a Blue Circle Health partnership. An ordinary donation supports this mixed recipient, not exclusively the strongest free-medication pathway.
sections.monitoring: A [dated 2024 overview](https://rxoutreach.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Printable-RxO-Two-Pager-2.18.25.pdf) reports 34,740 unique patients, 188,993 shipped prescriptions and 2,534 facilities/clinics. Its geographic statement includes all 50 states, DC, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands. These are delivery outputs, not additional treatment or health outcomes. The [current donor page](https://rxoutreach.org/donors-supporters/) instead gives a loose 120,000-plus annual prescription claim without a reporting year; it is not a like-for-like trend. No usable recipient-level comparison of medication persistence, disease control, admissions or utility was found in this bounded review. A next evaluation should link human recipient-years, drug class, baseline cost-related nonadherence, alternative coverage, fills, actual use, harms and outcomes. [Pet prescriptions](https://rxoutreach.org/pets/) need a separate denominator.
sections.qualitative: [CLEAN Meds](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8139488/) randomized 786 Canadian primary-care patients reporting cost-related nonadherence. Free essential medicines improved appropriate adherence by 10.1 percentage points at two years, but available diabetes, blood-pressure and lipid outcomes were not statistically different; missing clinical measurements limit interpretation. Its [one-year findings](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6784757/) included better blood pressure, illustrating why a short-term surrogate should not be assumed permanent. The US [MI-FREEE trial](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1107913) improved adherence by 4–6 points after myocardial infarction; the primary vascular-event/revascularization outcome was not significantly reduced, although a secondary first-major-vascular-event rate was 11.0 versus 12.8 per 100 person-years. [ARTEMIS](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2720024) likewise improved medication persistence without a significant one-year cardiovascular-event reduction. These studies support plausibility, not a universal shipment-to-health multiplier. Our judgment is that targeted prevention of high-risk treatment interruption merits further diligence; the unrestricted recipient is not yet demonstrated to have unusually high health yield.
sections.cost: Our best estimate: About $6.3 million per 10 USA QALYs through cardiovascular medication access. A $10,000 normalization supports about 12.5 additional patient-years after the funding discount. With 10% at post-MI-equivalent risk, half the trial event reduction and two discounted QALYs per event prevented, net benefit is about 0.0013 QALY per patient-year before geography. We adopt $400 per supported patient-year, anchored to $401 gross expense per unique patient, and 50% funding response. Our best-judgment post-MI-equivalent risk share is 10%, below the earlier 25% probe: the formulary spans broader cardiovascular, diabetes and respiratory conditions. Patient counts are not matched patient-years, so this remains a rough planning cost. Other clinical benefits remain unpriced. Favorable, zero and adverse cases remain in the transparent model; positive scenarios are not confidence bounds or verified funding offers.
sections.funding: Original Form 990-PF book expenses were [$12,368,983 in 2022](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202331939349100408/IRS990PF), [$21,535,029 in 2023](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202402299349100110/IRS990PF) and [$13,936,912 in 2024](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202531989349100408/IRS990PF), averaging about $15.95 million. The [2024 expense schedule](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202531989349100408/OtherExpensesSchedule) already includes $3,132,063 of purchased drug costs, $2,610,784 of in-kind inventory and $79,473 of other in-kind expense; do not add drug costs again. Removing only identified in-kind expenses leaves a $11,246,655 non-in-kind expense proxy, not cash flow. The corresponding proxies rose from $7.12 million in 2022 and $9.05 million in 2023: the gross decline does not show improved efficiency. In 2024, prescription revenue was $10,516,967, contributions $2,892,140 and the book deficit $516,395. Year-end unrestricted net assets were $1,640,703, with $437,272 in savings/temporary cash investments; these are dated figures, not a current runway forecast. The 2026 [clinic page](https://rxoutreach.org/why_clinics/) says nearly all inventory is now purchased directly, so prior donated-drug shares may be obsolete. [Deaconess's December 2025 award](https://deaconess.org/dec-2025-deaconess-awards-organizations-dedicated-to-youth-older-adults/) supports Fill the Gap expansion but does not establish an unfunded patient quota or matching leverage. A current budget, program-specific subsidy schedule, committed grants and waitlist are needed.

model.costScope: Unrestricted support to Rx Outreach Inc., EIN35-2378788. Recipient expenses include pharmacy procurement, dispensing, staff, systems, overhead and fundraising. Gross book expenses include in-kind inventory; c is judgmental net recipient support needed per newly supported human patient-year, not retail drug value. Patient/clinic payments and sponsors can finance services without a new donation. Unmodeled pet services and other activities cannot be silently removed from the donation numerator. The cost of medication access borne by patients, providers or other funders is not free in a societal model; the reported donation skeleton does not claim total economic cost-effectiveness.
model.geographicAttribution: Human health of residents of 50 states plus DC. Observed 2024 service includes Puerto Rico and Virgin Islands, which are excluded. Current pet prescriptions are not human QALYs and require separate allocation before human patient-years. No outcome-weighted territorial share is available. g=.98 is the central geographic judgment; current St. Louis Fill the Gap human patients would be within boundary, but unrestricted allocations are not all Fill the Gap.
model.formula: General skeleton: Q_USA = G × (b/c) × theta × g, where theta is net cumulative QALYs produced by one additional human patient-year of medication access, including later consequences discounted once. Inspectable post-MI test only: theta = f × e × t × q + z − h. f=share with trial-like high-risk post-MI prevention; e=0.018 fewer first major vascular events per patient-year (secondary MI-FREEE rate difference); t=transport/implementation attenuation; q=discounted net QALYs per event prevented; z=net health from other mechanisms; h=incremental adverse-treatment/access burden per supported human patient-year. Price = 10c/[b theta g] for positive theta. G=10000 merely normalizes disclosure arithmetic. No extra adherence multiplier is applied to e, which already measures intention-to-treat access effects.
model.counterfactual: Compare to the medication access patients would actually obtain through existing Rx Outreach sales, clinic subsidies, insurance, Medicare/Medicaid, manufacturer assistance or other cash pharmacies. [Current Medicare Part D](https://www.medicare.gov/health-drug-plans/part-d/basics/costs) has a $2,100 2026 covered-drug out-of-pocket cap, while [Cost Plus Drugs](https://www.markcubancostplusdrugcompany.com/) supplies an alternative cash/mail-order channel. These do not eliminate all barriers, but old retail sticker-price savings are not the counterfactual. An unrestricted gift could subsidize already-paid fills, replace renewed grant support, finance marketing or sustain operations rather than add patient-years. b includes that financing additionality; t captures clinical transport, not the same funding discount.
model.attribution: Do not attribute all efficacy of a prescribed drug to the dispensing charity. Prescribers, patients, manufacturers, clinics and public/private payers contribute. The trial event contrast incorporates access-induced uptake/adherence rather than treatment efficacy in fully adherent patients. Pharmacy-specific clinical mix and the share of services actually expanded by philanthropy remain unknown; no claim of zero alternative care.
model.uncertainty: We adopt $400 per supported patient-year, anchored to $401 gross expense per unique patient, and 50% funding response. Our best-judgment post-MI-equivalent risk share is 10%, below the earlier 25% probe: the formulary spans broader cardiovascular, diabetes and respiratory conditions. Patient counts are not matched patient-years, so this remains a rough planning cost. Other clinical benefits remain unpriced. Zero and adverse outcomes remain possible; the quantified pathway is not a complete portfolio valuation.
model.nativeOutcomes: Observed 2024: 34,740 unique patients; 188,993 shipments; gross recipient expense $401.18 per unique patient or $73.74 per shipment. Identified non-in-kind expense proxy $323.74 per unique patient or $59.51 per shipment. Unique people are not full patient-years, shipments have varying days supply and polypharmacy, and donated inventory fair values distort resource prices. Desired causal unit is additional appropriately treated human patient-year, separated by drug/risk class and alternative care.

reports.program: California clean-air policy, community monitoring and education

what: Coalition for Clean Air works to reduce pollution from transportation and other sources across California.
It advocates for clean-air protections and helps communities monitor air quality.
Our estimate examines one part of its work: advocacy that could preserve controls on emissions from ships while they are at berth.
strengths: Cleaner air can prevent premature deaths and reduce illness, and CARB has modeled the benefits of this specific regulation.
The organization is actively working on the policy issue rather than relying solely on a historical campaign.
Three original annual returns make the organization’s operating scale and spending inspectable.
reservations: The advocacy allocation, donor additionality and change in legal-enforceability probability are judgments, not measured donation effects.
The historical regulatory projection is not a measured remaining-year trajectory; physical rollback, current legal status and survival prognosis remain uncertain.
Private savings, work effects and compliance costs have unknown net incidence; regional splits and other organizational pathways remain unquantified.

sections.what:
Coalition for Clean Air is a California nonprofit, EIN 23-7120567, working on air-quality policy, transportation pollution, community monitoring and education. Its official donation form identifies the same legal recipient. [Current work](https://www.ccair.org/) [Donation form](https://ccair.app.neoncrm.com/forms/donate)

This estimate focuses on advocacy to preserve enforceable emissions controls for ships at berth. Shore power and other controls reduce pollution while ships are in port; preserving the rule could protect the benefit of those controls. CCA’s participation does not establish that its work changes the legal outcome. The comparison is additional CCA work versus existing advocacy, litigation, infrastructure and earlier controls continuing without a new donation.

The estimate does not credit a new gift with already installed YMCA filters, previously signed laws or historical emissions reductions. Other CCA programs may matter, but their effects are not quantified in this partial model.
sections.monitoring: AirAware is an existing EPA-funded partnership with TD Enviro, IQAir and three Los Angeles-area YMCA sites, not three donor-created sites. Monitoring and installed filtration support a mechanism but do not establish occupied person-hours or a causal clinical effect. [Project reports](https://www.ccair.org/projects/airaware-ymcas/) Already funded installations and adopted policy remain in the baseline. Future maintenance may be valuable, but no priced unfunded schedule is established. Source receipts and the full clock-anomaly exclusion are preserved in the dated evidence packet.
sections.qualitative:
We see a plausible connection between the organization’s policy work and a meaningful health outcome: reducing exposure to pollution from ships. CCA’s September 24, 2026 campaign describes defending California’s at-berth waiver after House action. The subsequent legislative disposition was not freshly confirmed in this review; the model is conditional on a remaining legal and implementation margin. [CCA campaign](https://www.ccair.org/oped-dirty-tricks-why-is-congress-voting-to-scrap-californias-clean-air-protections/)

CARB’s original final response projects 230 fewer premature deaths, 72 hospital admissions and 116 emergency visits statewide during 2021–2032 from the expanded rule. These are modeled regulatory outcomes, not observed CCA outcomes. We use the projected totals as a scale anchor, not as proof of the remaining benefit in 2026. The complete PDF was retrieved and hashed; the decisive passage was read through primary-domain indexed extraction, not a new full-document numerical audit. [CARB final response](https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/barcu/regact/2019/ogvatberth2019/ogvfsorapp1.pdf)

The key unanswered question is how much an additional donation changes the outcome beyond other advocates and existing funding. Neither an op-ed nor a deficit answers it. We also lack a remaining-year emissions profile and beneficiary age distribution. Those gaps make this an exploratory comparison, not a source-vetted giving recommendation or complete estimate of the organization’s expected value.
sections.cost:
Our conditional estimate is approximately **$10.2 million per better life**: ten combined California health and income-equivalent years. It prices a small change in the likelihood of preserving at-berth emissions controls—not the purchase of a guaranteed health outcome.

We think this pathway could be valuable because preserving a regulation can affect many ships and nearby residents. CARB projects fewer premature deaths and nonfatal illnesses from the expanded rule. The economic question is whether a modest amount of additional advocacy changes enforceability enough to justify its cost. Our estimate explicitly includes donor additionality and the physical benefit that would remain even if legal protections were lost.

For an illustrative $10,000 normalization, we allocate 40% to this policy margin and divide by the full FY2025 gross recipient expense of $2,494,912. We assume 50% funding additionality and a five-percentage-point net legal response per whole-annual-budget-equivalent of added policy effort. The resulting probability increment is 0.00004008, or about 0.004 percentage points—not a 5% success probability for this donation. These are judgments, not measured staffing costs or causal policy influence. The cost includes the recipient’s shared administration, fundraising and event expenses once.

Conditional on a legal change, we assume half the projected physical benefit is at stake: existing shore-power infrastructure, earlier controls and voluntary compliance may preserve some reductions. That physical-realization assumption is separate from the legal probability, which already accounts for other actors and litigation. We assume a five-year future benefit window beginning after three months. The historical 230/12 death-event profile is reused as a flat future planning assumption; no 2021–2026 benefit is credited retrospectively.

Each prevented premature death receives a finite survival valuation: utility 0.75, annual competing mortality hazard 0.035 and a ten-year tail, discounted at 3%. This produces about 5.53 health years per event before the event-date discount. These prognosis assumptions are unvalidated, not ten guaranteed years or a CARB-derived life table. We do not multiply CARB’s mortality projection by another pollutant risk estimate. The central yields **0.0097926 health years** per $10,000.

**Income and household resources:** the central resource contribution is zero because the net household incidence and sign are not established. That is not evidence of no economic benefit. The model separately tests baseline-alive households’ avoided private payments, net work gains and compliance costs. It excludes gross insurer/public medical savings, construction spending and baseline earnings of extra survivors. Positive and negative resource cases leave the health cohort unchanged.

In nonfatal-event scenarios, a judgmental 25% of admissions or emergency visits become distinct household resource units, with net receipts of $100 per admission and $25 per emergency visit—or signed losses. These are not observed bills or wages. Repeated households must be combined before logarithmic valuation; event receipts occur once rather than repeating over the mortality survival tail. Other diagnostic cases test annual productivity gains and consumer compliance costs only during the policy-active window. Gift-induced engagement costs remain possible even if advocacy fails, but unchanged baseline activity is not charged. [Income comparison method](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/)

The historical **$3.34 million** illustration used a generic population and pollution change rather than this named regulatory pathway. It remains preserved for comparison; the new calculation is not a residual obtained by subtracting income from the old total. The exact current price is $10,211,794.84 versus $3,343,794.81 historically. This change is a model revision, not measured organizational deterioration. See the expandable model for all 29 scenarios, including different policy responses, time windows, survival tails, signed resources, nulls and adverse mortality.

Public and private implementation costs are not fully priced here. The result is a partial donor comparison, not a complete societal cost-effectiveness ratio or a lower bound.
sections.funding:
The latest three original returns reconcile comparable gross expenses of $1,472,176 in FY2023, $2,162,329 in FY2024 and $2,494,912 in FY2025, averaging **$2,043,139**. This includes Part IX, separately netted event costs and applicable donated services without adding those services twice to Schedule D totals. [FY2023](https://www.ccair.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CCA-Form-990-2022-23.pdf) [FY2024](https://www.ccair.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/2023-CCA-Form-990.pdf) [FY2025](https://www.ccair.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/2024-2025-CCA-Form-990.pdf)

FY2025 Part IX reports $1,479,082 for programs, $647,639 for management and $326,174 for fundraising. Revenue was $2,149,048, with a $303,847 deficit. Assets of $1,518,894, liabilities of $405,280 and net assets of $1,113,614 are June 30, 2025 balances, not current available cash or evidence of a funding gap. Schedule D financial reconciliation is available; an independent CPA opinion and control findings were not separately verified.

The organization’s current campaign and donation route support ongoing operations, but no priced marginal staffing or consultant tranche was established. The model’s $100,000 exploratory gift cap is a numerical domain, not verified funding room. A funding decision needs a current work plan, alternative funding, staff availability and an explanation of what changes without the gift. The existing EPA-funded AirAware project is baseline activity, not new donor-created capacity.

model.costScope: Whole FY2025 gross recipient expense normalizer; full gift cost and fees once,40% policy allocation; no verified donor tranche. Public/private implementation resources unpriced.
model.geographicAttribution: CARB projected statewide California health; CA1 only once. No measured Bay/LA split. Resource geography separate; independent gift-induced engagement cost assigned California.
model.formula: effort=G*policyShare/E; deltaP=effort*funding*response<=1; w=deltaP*realization*assignment; q=u*(1-exp(-(hazard+ln(1+r))*tail))/(hazard+ln(1+r)); H_CA=w*annualDeaths*q*sum(y/(1+r)^(delay+t+y/2))*healthCA. Separate incomePathways sum .5*households*log1p(net/Y) at event/annual midpoints; independent gift-induced exposure is outside policy funding/assignment. Price=10*G*(1+fee)/(health+income) only when positive.
model.counterfactual: Legal enforceability with/without incremental CCA advocacy, net of other actors/litigation. Conditional physical exposure realization separately includes installed infrastructure, earlier controls and voluntary operation. Already realized/adopted benefits remain baseline.
model.attribution: Funding additionality .5, policyShare .4 and response .05 are distinct judgments. response is absolute net legal probability per whole-annual-budget effort, not measured outcome; realization .5 is physical exposure, not second legal probability. Shared portfolio assignment applies once to policy benefits/resources, not independently induced harms.
model.uncertainty: Conditional partial planning central, not measured donor EV or complete portfolio/lower bound. No empirical scenario weights. Current legal status, donor tranche, remaining exposure, prognosis and private-resource incidence uncertain.
model.nativeOutcomes: Prospective prevented premature-death event equivalents from regulatory projections; separate nonfatal baseline-alive household cash/work and consumer-cost diagnostics. No baseline survivor wages or public payer savings.

what: Disability Rights California provides legal advocacy and representation across California.
Its work spans health care, community living, benefits, education and other disability rights.
This report evaluates the California health benefit of an ordinary donation, not a restricted mental-health project.
strengths: Enforceable agreements and access rights offer mechanisms beyond education or awareness alone.
Original agreement terms permit checking implementation, financing and already-existing services.
Statewide California remit makes geographic scope substantially clearer than marginal health impact.
reservations: Additional legal capacity per donated dollar and the outcomes it changes are not disclosed.
Public contracts, county financing and already-planned services substantially shape the counterfactual.
Clinical evidence supports possible benefit but does not supply a transferable QALY value for every legal win or housing placement.

sections.what:
DRC's current annual report describes a broad statewide rights organization, not solely a behavioral-health provider. Individual representation and systemic litigation can change access to appropriate care or community living; informational contacts and monetary awards are not themselves health outcomes. The reported assistance and outreach totals lack a comparison group and cannot be used as additional people helped by a new gift. [2025 Annual Report](https://www.disabilityrightsca.org/2025-annual-report) [2025 reported impact](https://www.disabilityrightsca.org/2025-annual-report/impact)

A concrete pathway is enforcing Tulare County's 2025 settlement so that otherwise unavailable services actually reach eligible residents. That is an example within the recipient, not a promise that an unrestricted donation buys this specific project. [Tulare County mental health settlement implementation account](https://www.disabilityrightsca.org/2025-annual-report/tulare-county-mental-health-settlement-agreement)
sections.monitoring:
The original agreement requires funding 20 new permanent supportive housing units within five years and applying for 100 vouchers; applying is not obtaining or occupying 100 additional homes. Existing ACT service already reached more than 200 people at a time. Additional capacity depends on needs assessment and funding. The instrument includes expert monitoring, with the county paying up to $680,000, and $337,750 in DRC legal fees. These are relevant to implementation and substitution, not costs that can automatically be charged again to donors. [Tulare County settlement agreement, original instrument](https://www.disabilityrightsca.org/system/files/file-attachments/Tulare_Settlement_0.pdf)

The 2026 annual-report account describes crisis-service contracting and work toward a peer-respite property, not a completed outcome evaluation. I did not locate a current public expert report during this review; that is an evidence gap, not a finding of noncompliance. A useful follow-up would link implementation milestones to unique additional service users, baseline alternatives, repeated validated health measures, and funded versus unfunded DRC enforcement work. [Tulare County mental health settlement implementation account](https://www.disabilityrightsca.org/2025-annual-report/tulare-county-mental-health-settlement-agreement)

Current OCRA reporting provides a more concrete casework pathway: 6,406 clients versus 10,475 issues, with 4,899 issues closed at the information/referral level. The accompanying selected cases describe restored protective supervision, nursing hours and usable Medi-Cal access. They demonstrate what advocacy can change, not a representative success rate or new-donor attribution. [Director report](https://www.disabilityrightsca.org/system/files/file-attachments/Directors%20Report.FINAL__0.pdf) [Selected advocacy cases](https://www.disabilityrightsca.org/system/files/file-attachments/Exhibit%20C%20-%20Advocacy%20Report.FINAL__0.pdf)
sections.qualitative:
External causal evidence is mixed in a way that matters here. A 152-person US randomized trial found ACT improved symptoms, perceived health and stable housing relative to usual services over twelve months. It supports a plausible pathway, not a measured DRC effect. [Randomized trial of ACT for homeless persons with severe mental illness, 1997](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9366661/) The 251-person London REACT trial found better engagement and satisfaction but no corresponding clinical or inpatient-use advantage over well-developed community teams. Existing service quality changes the incremental effect. [REACT randomized trial of ACT versus community mental health teams](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/166247/1/Bebbington_REACT.pdf)

A randomized Housing First economic analysis measured housing stability and costs; it did not establish a significant between-group EQ-5 D improvement that could justify assigning a fixed positive QALY value to each home. Housing, autonomy and legal rights remain valuable even when their effects are incompletely captured by this metric. Disability status is not a discount on a person's worth; the model would measure changes in health within each person's trajectory. [Cost-effectiveness of Housing First with intensive case management](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2748596)

County accounts say several initiatives were already underway. DRC's contribution may accelerate, broaden or enforce them, but neither the county narrative nor a successful settlement identifies what an additional donation changes. [County describes community behavioral health expansion](https://tularecounty.ca.gov/tulare-county-behavioral-health-expands-services-with-commitment-to-community-salud-conductual-del-condado-de-tulare-amplia-sus-servicios-con-un-compromiso-a-la-comunidad)

As an additional causal anchor, the Oregon insurance lottery study found a 9.15-percentage-point reduction in positive depression screens after approximately two years, without statistically significant improvements in the measured physical-health outcomes. It is evidence that usable insurance can affect health, not a DRC QALY conversion: population, baseline coverage, care type and counterfactual differ. The model’s 0.02 utility prior remains subjective. [Oregon experiment](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1212321)
sections.cost:
A conditional estimate for individual care-access advocacy is about $65 million per 10 California QALYs. This is a partial health price with all recipient costs charged, not DRC’s comprehensive portfolio return or an empirically measured donation effect. Systemic policy and litigation, other programs and non-health rights benefits remain unquantified. The positive channel is not a proven lower bound.

The model starts with the primary annual table’s $46,894,183 expenses and 22,297 requests for assistance. It assumes 60% represent distinct effective client opportunities, 15% concern a modeled care-access pathway, marginal funding produces 50% of historical-scale capacity, and 25% of these opportunities change actual care beyond existing alternatives. Only the costs and request count are observed. The deduplication prior is loosely anchored to OCRA’s separate client-versus-issue counts; it is not a success rate. [Annual financials](https://www.disabilityrightsca.org/2025-annual-report/financials-and-employment) [Reported impact](https://www.disabilityrightsca.org/2025-annual-report/impact)

For each otherwise unrealized care trajectory, the analyst prior is 0.02 average health-utility improvement in the first year, half that incremental benefit in the second, then zero, discounted 3%. This is a finite within-person health change, not a discount on the worth of disabled people. It is not measured in DRC clients. External insurance and community-care studies support possible benefit but also meaningful null effects; neither legal success nor authorized service hours guarantees health improvement.

Favorable and low-yield stress tests give roughly $506,000 and $361 billion per 10 QALYs, with explicit zero and negative cases. These are not confidence bounds. The useful next evidence is marginal funded capacity, additional implemented services, and actual beneficiary health change. Incremental public nursing, personal assistance and medical resources would be added in a social-cost analysis.
sections.funding:
The FY 2024 consolidated audit reports $42,828,773 in FY 2023 expenses and $46,138,125 in FY 2024 expenses. Consolidation includes the wholly owned property entity; it is not a program-only denominator. Restricted cash and investments mean gross liquidity should not be described as freely deployable reserves. [FY 2024 consolidated financial statements and single audit, with FY 2023 comparative accounts](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/download-audit?download=true&filename=2024-09-GSAFAC-0000360163)

DRC's primary FY 2025 annual table reports $46,894,183 in expenses, including $40,196,305 program, $6,587,357 administration and $110,521 fundraising, against reported revenue of $47,407,629. Federal, state and State Bar funding sum to $43,156,717, about 91% of that revenue; donations are $127,238. These figures establish scale but do not establish a marginal funding gap. [2025 annual financials and employment](https://www.disabilityrightsca.org/2025-annual-report/financials-and-employment)

The original FY 2025 Form 990 is now retrievable. Part IX reports $46,787,232 expenses; adding $110,521 direct event costs netted from Part VIII gives $46,897,753 gross, still $3,570 above the annual table. The original resolves the earlier return-access blocker, but the remaining difference and consolidation boundary are not fully reconciled. Retain FY 2025 as non-comparable and do not assert a three-year mean. [Original FY 2025 Form 990](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202641769349300314/IRS990)

DHCS confirms a statutory patients' rights contract currently held by DRC. An ordinary gift might support work beyond contract restrictions, but replacing public or other private funding would reduce additionality. There is no verified donor-sensitive staffing, litigation or monitoring backlog priced in the reviewed material. [Patients' rights: state contract and responsibilities](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/services/patients-rights/) The general donation route is verified; this is not an endorsement or claim that a donation has occurred. [DRC donation page](https://www.disabilityrightsca.org/drc-donation)

model.costScope: Full ordinary-recipient donation, all functions. The historical annual-report expense denominator is $46,894,183; $100,000 is an analytical normalization, not a suggested gift. Only the individual access-to-care health pathway is quantified. Systemic litigation, policy, income, autonomy and other benefits are omitted, not assumed zero. Public care and other actors' incremental resources are excluded from the donor price but required for a social-cost estimate.
model.geographicAttribution: Count California residents' modeled two-year benefit time only, g=1 after this filter. National precedent spillovers excluded.
model.formula: N_CA = (C/E) × R × d × h × m × a; Q_CA = N_CA × du × sum(t=1..T, s^(t−1)/(1+r)^t) − H. Central E=46894183, R=22297, d=0.6, h=0.15, m=0.5, a=0.25, du=0.02, s=0.5, T=2, r=0.03, H=0. N means unique additional implemented care-access trajectories, not requests or legal wins. Price = 10 × C / Q_CA for positive Q_CA. All recipient costs are retained while counting only the individual health-access channel.
model.counterfactual: Existing publicly contracted rights work, county plans and treatment, fee-funded enforcement, other advocates and alternative care continue. Count acceleration only for the time genuinely gained. A legal settlement or award does not imply all associated services disappear without a new gift. A case must change actual usable care or personal support, not merely legal eligibility; self-advocacy, existing staff/contracts and alternative provider/family support remain. Unfunded need does not prove an ordinary donation changes it.
model.attribution: d deduplicates requests; h isolates potentially health-relevant care/support requests; m discounts marginal spending productivity for public contracts, reserves, alternative finance and differing marginal allocation; a is the joint chance that added advocacy changes actual care beyond existing family/agency/other-advocate action. No historical settlement percentage or equal coalition share assigned. du and persistence are within-person health differences, not disability weights or valuations of persons. Overlapping nursing/IHSS/insurance gains count one trajectory.
model.uncertainty: Very-low-confidence conditional central for a partial health pathway, not comprehensive portfolio return. Organization counts and costs observed; all key marginal conversions and health effects are explicitly subjective priors. External trials establish possible and null incremental care effects but do not estimate DRC casework QALYs. Scenario endpoints are not empirical confidence bounds; zero, harms and omitted positive systemic benefits remain possible.
model.nativeOutcomes: Unique additional California residents receiving usable appropriate health care, nursing or personal assistance; duration gained relative to services that would otherwise occur; finite within-person health-utility improvement. Requests, training, dollars awarded, hours authorized and placements are intermediate and cannot be treated as QALYs.

sensitivity: Price varies inversely with d, h, m, a and du; the data do not identify their joint product. Changing du from 0.02 to 0.002 alone raises the price tenfold.

At central q=0.0288434 QALYs per trajectory, $1 million per 10 QALYs requires 34.66998 additional trajectories per $100,000, versus the central 0.53491. The $100,000 target requires 346.6998. These benchmarks do not bound systemic policy effects.
OCRA's unique-client fraction is only a deduplication proxy, not a clinical success rate. All DRC requests may have a different mix.
Replacing annual expenses of $46,894,183 with the gross Form 990 figure of $46,897,753 changes the price by only 0.0076%, negligible beside model uncertainty.
At zero additional care or zero health improvement, there is no finite favorable price. Improved autonomy, housing or income may remain valuable outside the QALY measure.

A future case-level cohort should jointly track baseline alternative care, actual funded service hours, uptake, unique people, health utility and counterfactual catch-up time. Do not add this model to Tulare housing or ACT benefits without deduplication.

reports.program: Safe-sleep equipment distribution, caregiver education and hospital/partner training

what: Cribs for Kids provides portable infant sleep spaces and caregiver education through local partners across the United States.
Its partners purchase and distribute products, while the national charity also donates equipment and supports hospital and professional safe-sleep programs.
We are interested in whether additional equipment and education help families replace otherwise unsafe sleeping arrangements and prevent sleep-related infant deaths.
strengths: A portable sleep space can address a practical barrier for families who lack a suitable place for their baby to sleep.
Studies document supplied-crib use and changes in reported practices, providing a basis for investigating the equipment-and-education pathway.
Three original financial returns document donated cribs separately from product sales, making the organization’s scale and business model inspectable.
reservations: Distribution is not sustained safer sleep: many recipients have another safe option, and some continue bed-sharing or other unsafe practices.
Our estimates of additional provision, recipient risk and mortality reduction remain judgments rather than measured effects of a new donation.
Current package prices, partner costs and household cash effects are unverified, while hospital and broader education benefits are not yet quantified.

sections.what:
Cribs for Kids Inc. (EIN 25-1442806) provides portable play yards and related safe-sleep supplies, caregiver education, partner support, and hospital and professional programs. Its [partner FAQ](https://cribsforkids.org/faq/) describes a network that buys discounted products and distributes them locally with education. Sales proceeds also support national programs; a product shipped to a paying partner is therefore not necessarily an additional household reached because of a new donation.

The original returns report 1,456 local and 1,641 partner-associated donated cribs in FY2023; 1,375 and 2,638 in FY2024; and 1,421 local cribs plus 1,600 through 40 Building Blocks awardees in FY2025. The local program serves Southwestern Pennsylvania. These are reported distribution counts, not a linked cohort with measured changes in sleep practices. The [Building Blocks launch](https://cribsforkids.org/building-blocks-launch-press-release/) planned 20 awards of 20 kits funded by JPMA Cares. That 400-kit launch does not reconcile the later 1,600 figure, and existing funded awards belong in the baseline.

The pathway we quantify is equipment plus the education embedded in its delivery. A suitable crib matters most when an infant would otherwise sleep in an unsafe place and the caregiver uses it consistently, early enough to cover the relevant risk period. A crib replacing another suitable surface may still save a household money, but it does not receive an additional mortality benefit in this model. Hospital certification and stand-alone education are separate pathways whose incremental benefits remain unquantified.
sections.monitoring:
The [partner FAQ](https://cribsforkids.org/faq/) does not require annual partner reports. The [July 2026 impact statement](https://cribsforkids.org/cribs-for-kids-impact-statement/) describes reach and utilization tracking, with expanded knowledge and intended/reported behavior evaluation planned for 2027. We checked official indexed text where direct retrieval failed; this is not a measured mortality evaluation.

The [Georgia multisite study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34209643/) had 615 paired surveys but only 66 follow-ups. Among respondents, 66.1% reported a recommended alternative sleep location without the supplied crib. That self-reported counterfactual is useful context, not an unbiased national estimate of actual alternative purchases. The [75-family home-visit study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29472971/) found 70 supplied cribs in use and 67 without unsafe items, but only 42 caregivers had renounced bed-sharing. One observation is not exclusive safe sleep through infancy. An [11-family qualitative study](https://journals.ku.edu/kjm/article/view/25004) likewise documents mixed sleep arrangements.

To improve this estimate, we would want unique recipients linked to delivery age, pre-existing sleep arrangements, actual alternative sources, repeated sleep-practice checks, and household expenses. Current national distribution and hospital reach do not supply that chain. Program counts, fiscal periods and grant expansions also need reconciliation before they become a denominator for donor impact.
sections.qualitative:
We think the equipment-and-education mechanism is credible, but its benefit depends on the circumstances it changes. A separate, suitable infant sleep surface is recommended by the [AAP evidence review](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article-abstract/150/1/e2022057991/188305). Observational [pooled risk evidence](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23793691/) and a [context-specific analysis](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0107799) show that risks vary substantially with smoking, alcohol, infant age and other hazards. An odds ratio for bed-sharing is not the causal effect of distributing a crib to every family.

A [randomized mobile-education trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28742913/) improved several reported practices, including room sharing without bed-sharing. Its timed messages are not automatically equivalent to the education delivered with these packages. An uncontrolled [Bedtime Basics evaluation](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25331608/) also reports practice changes, but cannot identify a national marginal effect. The [2025 Pennsylvania PRAMS analysis](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/155/2/e2024067659/200623/A-Hospital-Based-Initiative-for-Infant-Safe-Sleep) separately modeled a state hospital initiative and Cribs for Kids designation; all four designation confidence intervals crossed a null association. This limits a separate certification claim without proving there is no benefit.

We retain a conditional research estimate, not a confirmed donation offer. The organization has an inspectable operating model and documented distribution, but the current gift-to-additional-safe-sleep bridge remains unmeasured. We have not verified a costed available tranche or promoted this model to a source-vetted giving recommendation. Inventory, sales margins and assets neither prove no funding need nor establish that a donation would expand the modeled pathway.
sections.cost:
Our current conditional estimate is approximately **$6.1 million in donation dollars per better life**, including health and household-resource effects. It replaces the initial $3.74 million health-only estimate. The change comes mainly from reconsidering how much of a national gift supports additional provision and how many packages produce sustained, otherwise-unavailable safer sleep—not from adding a deeper-review label.

To make the estimate concrete, the $10,000 normalization models about **5.44 additional supported packages**, or roughly $1,837 of the whole donation per extra package. A judged 35% of the donation supports this material pathway; the estimated national cash package cost is $225 ($125 equipment, $25 freight, $75 coordination and education), with a 50% response probability and 70% conditional provision additionality. These are separate judgments about allocation and funded expansion, not quoted costs or measured funding elasticities. The entire donation stays in the numerator, including support for pathways whose benefit we cannot quantify.

We estimate 0.98 full-risk-period-equivalent safer-sleep transitions across those packages. The central transition share is 18% of all additional packages, already accounting for alternatives, incomplete use and timing; it is not multiplied again by the share without purchase savings. A remaining sleep-related mortality risk of 1.5 per 1,000 changed infants and a 40% risk reduction imply 0.000588 modeled prevented deaths before USA attribution. Neither coefficient is a measured Cribs for Kids effect. We do not substitute the high observed supplied-crib use rate for this causal transition share or treat all national SUID deaths as preventable by cribs.

For each modeled prevented death, we use the [NCHS 2024 life table](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Publications/NVSR/75-05/Table01.xlsx), 0.9 utility and 3% health discounting. A judged prevented-death age of three months removes credit for earlier life. We approximate the remaining first year and then borrow general-population survival conditional on age one, giving 26.497 discounted QALYs. This is a survival proxy, not beneficiary-specific prognosis: it assumes remaining first-year survival and does not identify high-risk infant competing mortality. Saved-age and 30%-lower lifetime-value scenarios test that limitation. With a judged 99.5% USA share, health contributes 0.0155024 QALYs per normalization.

Household resources are modeled separately. In the central judgment, 20% of additional households would actually spend $100 on another safe sleep space and avoid that purchase; all households incur $10 of additional cash expenses such as travel, data or childcare. These amounts are not measured financial outcomes, and the burden is not a shadow wage for leisure. Purchasers have a net $90 gain; the other 80% have a $10 loss. At a judged $30,000 annual disposable-resource baseline, separate household log changes yield 0.0009003 income-equivalent healthy years, rather than taking the log of an average cash gain. Expected net household cash is about $54 across the modeled USA recipients. Purchase savers are in the safe-alternative group, disjoint from the health-changing group. No donated-device retail value, child lifetime earnings, bereavement earnings or extra medical savings are credited.

Combining the two streams gives 0.0164027 equivalent healthy years and approximately $6.1 million per ten. Income equivalents are welfare comparisons, not observed clinical QALYs or DALYs. Removing all household cash effects produces a health-only donor price of approximately $6.45 million. A companion calculation adds a judged $125 of local partner resources per extra package, giving $10,680.56 institutional resources and roughly $6.51 million per better life; this is not a comprehensive societal cost and is not the donation-dollar headline. Household losses already enter welfare and are not charged again to the numerator.

Favorable, downside, zero, adverse and unknown cases remain separate. The downside has negative combined benefit after household expenses; zero funded expansion produces no additional packages; unknown response is not zero. A low-hazard risk difference, no purchase savings, delayed cash receipt, different utility and discount rates, and lower beneficiary survival each have inspectable scenarios. The 93% crib-use diagnostic intentionally shows why using observed utilization as causal change would be misleading. These cases are not confidence bounds or a probability-weighted posterior. The calculation is restricted to a modest normalization of at most $10,000; it does not imply unlimited scalable capacity. Hospital, wider education, nonfatal injury and caregiver effects remain unknown rather than proven zero.

The complete earlier model is preserved with its initial $3.74 million illustration and later unidentified central. The current price is an independently reviewed conditional judgment, not evidence that a donor can purchase these outcomes at a fixed rate.
sections.funding:
The latest three available original returns cover fiscal years ending June 30, 2023–2025. We freshly rechecked all three. Part IX functional expenses were $2.264M, $2.429M and $2.634M; consistently restoring cost of goods sold and direct fundraising-event expenses gives annual gross accounting costs of $8.033M, $9.187M and $11.915M. These totals establish accounting scale, not a marginal cost per newly helped household. Fiscal-year evidence and source links are retained in the financial appendix.

The [FY2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202641339349303909/IRS990) reports $12.620M inventory sales and $9.232M cost of goods sold, leaving a $3.388M margin. Contributions of $181,536 include $70,560 noncash. Reported surplus was $925,012. Reported assets included $3.740M inventory, $1.526M receivables and $514,451 cash; net assets were $5.438M. Assets are not all immediately spendable. [Schedule R](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202641339349303909/IRS990ScheduleR) identifies wholly owned taxable retailer Ette Cetera Inc. and intercompany transactions; [Schedule O](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202641339349303909/IRS990ScheduleO) includes a negative $145,455 subsidiary-investment adjustment. Subsidiary turnover and transfers cannot be added without consolidation eliminations.

A public [current product price list](https://cribsforkids.org/partner-product-catalog/) is unavailable because of tariffs and supply-chain increases. We did not request a quote or contact the organization. The model’s $225 national cash package and $125 partner resources are explicit estimates, not procurement offers. Existing sales-funded provision, inventory and JPMA-funded grants belong in the without-gift baseline. A useful next funding check would identify a current unfunded budget, extra timely deliveries, local capacity and ongoing practice monitoring before treating the estimate as an available giving opportunity.

model.costScope: Whole donor gift stays in numerator; judged225 national cash package separately estimates provision. Companion institutional resource cost adds125 local resources per extra package; not comprehensive social cost. No household loss charged twice.
model.geographicAttribution: USA50states/DC material-pathway share.995 judgment; nonresident stress.98. Overseas hospital reach and military affiliation do not establish domestic residence.
model.formula: N=G×allocation/cashPackage×responseProbability×conditionalAdditionality; deaths=N×saferSleepShare×mortalityRisk×riskRemoved; health=deaths×finite2024 age1-survivor life-value proxy×geography−independent health harm. Resources=sum household .5×log1p(netcash/baseline)×timing×geography, separate purchaser/nonpurchaser cohorts. Donation price=10G/(health+resources) when positive and known.
model.counterfactual: Partner sales, inventory, funded grants and alternative support belong in baseline. Allocation selects material path; response and conditional additionality describe funded expansion. Safer-sleep share already excludes alternative safe arrangements and partial/late use, not discounted again by purchaser share.
model.attribution: All causal and donor-response coefficients are explicit judgments, not measured marginal elasticity or available donor tranche. Safe-alternative purchase savers and unsafe-sleep health transitions are disjoint. No hospital/system reach converted to mortality, donated retail value converted to income, or lifetime child wages.
model.uncertainty: Conditional partial pathway, not identified portfolio expected value. Joint stresses are not bounds/confidence intervals. Unknown response or income remains null; adverse outcomes stay signed. Restricted to modest donor normalizations<=10000 with no verified scalable capacity.
model.nativeOutcomes: FY2025 reported1421 local cribs plus1600 through40awardees. Central forecast5.444 extra packages,.98 risk-period transitions,.000588 prevented deaths before geography; these are judgments not observed cohorts. Exact2024 native Lx and age1survivors retained separately.

historicalModel.costScope: Whole ordinary unrestricted national-recipient support. G is only normalization. Historical gross accounting costs restore COGS and direct event expenses but do not represent consolidated all-resource costs. Diagnostic c is a full-support allowance, not an audited cost per unique donated recipient. Partner staff, volunteer/caregiver time and donated freight remain unmeasured; subsidiary transactions require consolidation eliminations. No retail-sales or medical-savings offset is credited.
historicalModel.geographicAttribution: Local donated cribs are reported in Pennsylvania and national grants target US communities. Hospital certification also reaches overseas sites. US military affiliation is not USA-50-states-DC residence. Retained g=.99 (.95–1 stress range) is an unmeasured outcome-weighted assumption and not a beta central.
historicalModel.formula: N = (G×a/c)×b. Δdeaths = N×u×r×e. Q_all = Δdeaths×L. Q_USA = Q_all×g. Price per10 =10G/Q_USA. u is the incremental full-risk-period-equivalent transition to safer sleep, already discounting alternative crib access, partial use and delayed provision; r is the remaining sleep-related mortality risk of infants whose behavior changes, and e is the causal fraction removed by that change. L is discounted QALYs per prevented infant death. No separate education effect is added to the same infant.
historicalModel.counterfactual: b discounts for sales-funded provision, reserves, other donors and partner capacity. u separately discounts households that would obtain a crib anyway, follow safe sleep without the intervention, continue unsafe practices or receive equipment after much of the risk period. r is not the mortality risk of every child reached; it applies to the higher-risk behavior-changing subgroup. A crib that replaces another safe surface has no modeled mortality benefit.
historicalModel.attribution: All numeric causal inputs are retained alpha diagnostic judgments. New money's allocation and additional capacity are unresolved; partner purchases, existing stock, funded grants and public/hospital campaigns are baseline activities. Education embodied in a package must not be credited twice. A restricted local grant or retail purchase is a separate decision from the ordinary national donation.
historicalModel.uncertainty: Central withdrawn: a,c,b,u,r,e and outcome-weighted geography are not calibrated for the next ordinary unrestricted gift. The six numerical alpha cases are diagnostics only, not a posterior, confidence interval, favorable bound or whole-recipient estimate. Unknown is distinct from zero. Unmeasured education/system benefits and adverse sleep substitution remain possible.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: Return-reported donated cribs: FY2023 1456 local +1641 partner-associated; FY2024 1375+2638; FY2025 1421 local +1600 via 40 Building Blocks awardees. These are not a reconciled gift-funded unique cohort. The launch planned 400 kits; delivery timing and expansion to the return's count are unverified.
