what: Operation Access connects uninsured Californians with donated surgery and specialty care.
Staff coordinate referrals, appointments, language support and practical help while volunteer clinicians and facilities provide treatment.
The network provides outpatient treatment across ten specialties, from cataracts and hernias to gynecological and orthopedic conditions.
strengths: Its clinical network turns coordination spending into tangible completed care for patients facing access barriers.
Current eligibility requires Northern California or Central Valley residence, giving a clear California benefit boundary.
Public budgets, annual reporting and audited accounts support a concrete cost and activity assessment.
reservations: Reported encounters and people are documented, but within-specialty diagnoses, transferable health gains and net household cash effects remain judgments.
A former public funder declined renewal after questioning expansion impact and cost; replacement donations and substantial year-end reserves complicate the funding-gap story.
No current additional-slot offer is verified. Fast alternative care, limited capacity and procedural harms can erase the conditional positive estimate.

sections.what: Operation Access coordinates volunteer outpatient specialty care for low-income uninsured people in Northern California and the Central Valley. The actual 501(c)(3) recipient is Ambulatory Surgery Access Coalition dba Operation Access, EIN 94-3180356; its [donation page](https://www.operationaccess.org/donate) names that tax identity. The estimate concerns additional care supported by ordinary donations, rather than a quoted price for an earmarked operation. Staff handle referral matching, language/travel support and follow-up. The [audit](https://www.operationaccess.org/s/2025-Audited-Financial-Statements.pdf) also discloses fiscal sponsorship of Western Farm Workers Association in Yuba City, without a separate amount in the material reviewed. We retain the whole financial denominator and add no unverified sponsorship benefit.
sections.monitoring:
The [2025 Form 990](https://www.operationaccess.org/s/2025Form990.pdf), page 2, reports 1,529 services to 1,130 unduplicated residents. The [annual report](https://www.operationaccess.org/s/Operation-Access-Annual-Report-2025.pdf) splits those services across ten specialties, records 627 people who volunteered that year, and reports a 72-day median wait to a specialty appointment—not necessarily definitive treatment or days of delay prevented. Its approximately 1,000-person network is a roster, not the same volunteer count. Services rose 15.8% from 2024; reported referrals rose 28%, but neither gives available slots for a new donor. Patient-reported improvement lacks an untreated comparator and cannot become QALYs directly.

Our model uses the old repeat-service priors with 1,529/1,130 across a disjoint diagnosis ledger. Applying that aggregate ratio uniformly to marginal cases is a judgment. Diagnosis-specific people, baseline severity, treatment completion, validated utility, adverse events and alternative-care waits are still needed. An annual-report story requiring two operations illustrates why a procedure is not automatically a new beneficiary. The 1,130 count is verified as an original filed organizational report, not as independently audited patient-level data. Using one aggregate ratio and mutually exclusive diagnosis allocations enforces arithmetic nonoverlap, but does not demonstrate that the marginal clinical mix has the same repeat-care pattern.
sections.qualitative:
Operation Access makes a clinically plausible connection between scarce donated specialty capacity and patients who face financial or coverage barriers. The importance of a service depends on the diagnosis, severity, alternative treatment and wait it replaces—not simply whether surgery occurs. We assess symptom relief and preventive care separately, use finite horizons, and retain procedure harms. Reported satisfaction or a larger number of encounters does not by itself demonstrate an incremental health effect.

The [cataract randomized economic evaluation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2095519/) found an integrated first-year incremental gain of 0.056 QALYs for expedited treatment versus ordinary waiting in women over 70. We use a 0.75 transport judgment and stop after that first-year endpoint: it is not a permanent annual utility gain. Existing procedural harm remains a separate conservative assumption, not an additional risk measured in that trial. OA's mixed-age uninsured cohort and its eye-case selection may differ substantially. Routine later treatment is the comparator, not lifetime absence of care.

The [Medicine or Surgery trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15039411/) supports earlier relief for selected women with refractory abnormal uterine bleeding. Its SF-36 improvement does not directly establish QALYs. We now use a 0.07 utility judgment rather than 0.10 and retain zero and 0.10 sensitivity cases; later comparator surgery limits the duration of advantage. For uncomplicated symptomatic gallstones, [C-GALL](https://www.bmj.com/content/383/bmj-2023-075383) found no clear overall quality-of-life superiority over conservative treatment during 18 months. That selected subgroup receives zero central gross benefit while surgical harms remain; urgent or complicated cases are not covered by that conclusion.

[Minimally symptomatic hernia evidence](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16418463/) and [sham-controlled degenerative-knee evidence](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24369076/) challenge indiscriminate treatment value. Positive-FIT follow-up survival evidence is observational and vulnerable to selection into colonoscopy. The other diagnosis-specific utility, completion, catch-up and mortality parameters remain externally informed judgments, not newly validated local effects. We would place more weight on OA diagnosis-level follow-up with a credible alternative-care comparison than on added numerical precision.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter estimates approximately **$3.32 million per better life** for this conditional California portfolio, including health and net household resources. The mechanism is concrete: staff coordinate donated appointments and operations, interpretation and practical support; selected care relieves symptoms or prevents later disease. Our estimate is not a verified offer of additional treatment slots.

Original [2023](https://www.operationaccess.org/s/2023Form990.pdf), [2024](https://www.operationaccess.org/s/2024Form990.pdf) and [2025](https://www.operationaccess.org/s/2025Form990.pdf) returns show total expenses of $2,658,742, $2,678,152 and $2,261,505, averaging $2,532,799.67. Matching 2025 expense to its 1,529 specialty encounters gives approximately **$1,479 per service** including organizational support and fundraising. This is an average cash-like coordination cost, not a measured marginal operation price. We do not treat an appointment as a distinct surgery or remove overhead from donor cost.

Under the declared 0.3 funding-additionality judgment, each $1,000 supports about 0.203 additional service-equivalents or 0.150 patient/household-equivalents. That corresponds to roughly $4,930 per additional encounter and $6,671 per patient-equivalent. We use the observed specialty mix and 1,529/1,130 encounters per unique person, while assuming that ratio applies within each diagnosis. Neither the marginal mix nor one affected household per patient is measured. A 100-service capacity cap is a diagnostic assumption, not a provider commitment.

For the model's normalized donor budget, gross clinical benefit is 0.35670 health years and procedural harm is 0.05430, leaving 0.30239 health years. First-year household resource effects subtract 0.00092 equivalent years; the combined denominator is 0.30148. Health and consumption are distinct contributions: we do not add a survivor's ordinary lifetime earnings or call income-equivalent years measured clinical QALYs. The [income comparison method](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/) values a proportional net consumption change using a logarithmic conversion.

The household branch combines savings, paid work and extra cash costs before applying that conversion, using a $30,000 annual household-consumption reference. Selected symptomatic conditions receive a declared $60 net first-year medicine-saving amount, adjusted for treatment success; it is assumed already net of alternative-care catch-up and payer offsets, not twelve months of measured purchase avoidance. A native recovery story informs the direction of the cyst pathway, but five net recovered paid days, $100 after-tax daily pay and 50% wage-loss incidence are judgments. Other pathways receive no assigned earnings gain because its magnitude is unresolved, not proven absent.

The [carpal-tunnel economic trial](https://research.vu.nl/ws/files/2213413/195347.pdf) separates improved clinical success from uncertain utility and recovery-related absence. We model a one-off 0.3-day paid-work loss for that pathway as a transport judgment, not its shadow productivity cost. All households incur a $25-per-service net travel/appointment cash assumption after assistance and avoided alternative visits. Each household's combined first-year amount is discounted at delivery delay plus half a year; clinical survival and catch-up tails are not reused for recurring wages. Costs can outweigh these modest savings, as in the center.

The previous estimate was **$1.88 million**, retained as a historical comparison. The revision uses matched-year expenses, observed specialty allocation, a finite cataract endpoint, lower bleeding-utility mapping, zero uncomplicated-gallstone gross benefit, and a revised donation-response judgment. Keeping the old 0.5 funding response produces about $1.99 million: the new price is not solely a clinical evidence downgrade. Funding response 0.1/0.8 gives about $9.95 million/$1.24 million; five added slots gives $13.46 million; rapid alternative care gives $42.29 million. These are judgment tests, not confidence limits.

The [audit](https://www.operationaccess.org/s/2025-Audited-Financial-Statements.pdf) records $22,876,888 expenses including $20,530,000 waived clinical charges and $89,922 other donated services. Removing those leaves $2,256,966; $4,539 donated materials explains the remaining tax-expense difference. Waived charges are neither household cash savings nor measured opportunity costs. A complete societal estimate needs the actual additional clinician, facility and public resources. Null health, unknown income, complete replacement and signed harm are evaluated separately rather than converted into favorable prices.
sections.funding:
The [CMSP May 2025 minutes](https://cmspcounties.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/II_Correspondence.pdf), pages 2 and 14, record refusal of renewed funding after the five-year $5.7M grant. The board questioned expansion reach, rising per-person costs and changing public coverage. OA reported stronger referrals and restructured staffing. This is a genuine adverse funder assessment—not proof of no clinical benefit, and not proof a new gift restores lost care.

The [audited year-end accounts](https://www.operationaccess.org/s/2025-Audited-Financial-Statements.pdf) show cash down $246,920 but total net assets up $177,249: receivables and restricted support changed. There were $913,650 restricted net assets and $2,531,766 financial assets available within twelve months; OA reported 16 months of operating cash against an eight-month target. These are December 2025 balances, not current bank balances. The [2025 budget-versus-actual statement](https://www.operationaccess.org/s/2025OperationAccessFinancialStatements.pdf) reports a $222,752 operating deficit before future-pledge timing adjustments; it is not the GAAP surplus or cashflow. The [2026 budget](https://www.operationaccess.org/s/2026Budget-8pz4.pdf) plans $1.9M revenue and expense after restructuring, including $1.628M personnel. Replacement donations and reserves mean grant loss cannot be equated with present funding room.

[DHCS current rules](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/medi-cal/updates/medi-cal-changes/) freeze new full-scope enrollment for some adults from January 2026, while existing eligible enrollees can retain coverage by renewal and exceptions remain. Later scheduled changes are not already realized OA demand. Current English intake wording and OA's earlier bridge-care description differ; publicly eligible but unenrolled patients may obtain care later. We use a 0.3 funding-additionality judgment and separately test 0, 0.1, 0.5 and 0.8. Dated reserves, an approved smaller budget, layoffs and replacement fundraising challenge automatic 0.5 additionality, but do not identify 0.3 or establish present funding room. The next decisive evidence is funded versus unfunded approved cases, current slots, enrollment alternatives and 2026 unrestricted commitments. The CMSP minutes quantify the expansion concern: 91% of grant-period people served came from the original four counties and 9% from the eighteen expansion counties. This describes the grant evaluation, not California-wide clinical ineffectiveness. Current English intake explicitly says uninsured and ineligible for full-scope Medi-Cal, Medicare or CMSP; the Spanish version says uninsured without the same eligibility qualification. That inconsistency and historical bridge-care language require clarification before assuming all current participants are excluded from public alternatives.

model.costScope: 2025 total same-entity tax expense/service forecasts next-year coordination costs, including support and fundraising; donated clinical opportunity costs excluded. Donation paid at time zero.
model.geographicAttribution: Direct California residents; share1 is assumed retained through the finite modeled effects.
model.formula: 10 × donor cost / (credited California clinical health years + net first-year household-consumption-equivalent years). Funding scales added encounters once; overlap excludes only positive individual clinical credits, not signed harms.
model.counterfactual: Already funded activity and alternative public/charity care; each clinical diagnosis has finite catch-up, treatment failure, mortality and procedure risk.
model.attribution: Funding response0.3 and cap100 are declared judgments; annual count and dated reserves do not identify new donor-sensitive slots. One unique patient/household assumed; specialty diagnosis shares remain priors.
model.uncertainty: Conditional central, not empirical expected value; no scenario weights. Net household incidence, clinical transport, case selection and marginal capacity unresolved. Unknown components are not zero.
model.nativeOutcomes: 1529 specialty encounters /1130 reported unduplicated people in2025 across ten specialties. Services are not unique surgeries; observed mix informs a partial health/resource portfolio.

missingInputs: Current approved but unfunded unique cases and volunteer/facility capacity
Diagnosis-specific repeats, validated utility, alternative-care waits and outcome follow-up
Net household medicine, wages, benefits, travel and paid-leave incidence
Marginal unrestricted budget and additional provider/public opportunity costs

historicalModel.costScope: Full ordinary gift in donor numerator. All ten specialty allocations sum to one and include recipient program, management, fundraising and failed-referral work. Separate gross associated resource sensitivity includes all nominal services, not merely health-credited cases; no waived-charge multiplier. Prospective cash per-service costs are judgments anchored to 2025 recipient cash-like scale. Whole legal-recipient finance also includes disclosed fiscal sponsorship of Western Farm Workers Association; its amount is not separately established. We retain the full gift and whole-recipient spending calibration, add no unverified sponsorship health, and test a ten-percent loss of clinical activity. The sponsorship is not silently removed from costs. Gross associated resources include nominal activity even when a gift adds none and therefore are not net marginal social costs.
historicalModel.geographicAttribution: Current patient eligibility requires residence in Northern California or the Central Valley. Accordingly all modeled direct patient benefit is assigned to California: Q_CA=Q_all. This is a service-eligibility inference, not headquarters/population allocation; no Bay=0.6 or SF=0.08 factor is reused. Migration or secondary spillovers are unmodeled. Geographic nesting means these QALYs must not be summed with the same services' Bay/USA benefits.
historicalModel.formula: Let F(r,H)=(1-exp(-r*H))/r with F(0,H)=H. For specialty k: nominal S_k=C*a_k/c_k; S=sum S_k; activity A=min(S*f,K)/S. For disjoint diagnosis path j within k: P_j=S_k*s_j*A*d_j/r_j, where s=case share,d=nonoverlap fraction,r=services/person. Symptom Q_j=P_j*[success_j*utility_j*(1+discount)^(-delay_j)*F(catchup_j+loss_j+mortality_j+ln(1+discount),horizon_j)-harm_j]. For CRC let z(t)=delta_hazard*exp(-catchup*latency)*F(catchup,min(max(t-latency,0),active_years)); Δsurvival(t)=exp(-baseline_mortality*t)*(exp(z(t))-1). CRC Q=P_crc*[linkage*surviving_utility*(1+discount)^(-delay)*integral_0^H Δsurvival(t)*(1+discount)^(-t)dt - harm]. Sum CRC, cataract, hernia and all named symptom paths, subtract independent harm once. Q_CA=Q_all; donor_price_10=10*C/Q_CA for positive Q_CA. Full exact parameter vectors and scenario overrides are below. Numeric reproduction uses existing lib/oa-portfolio-model.mjs and lib/oa-portfolio-foundation.mjs; its regions.us.q equals CA here solely because eligibility was independently verified. The modeled service and patient equivalents represent completed care at the procedure date. The pre-procedure delay is discounted financially in time; no separate survival/catch-up attrition before completion is applied because it is assumed included in additional completed activity. If nominal activity instead means referrals, an additional completion/dropout factor is required. Procedural harm is conservatively charged without a favorable delay discount.
historicalModel.counterfactual: Without a new gift, existing funded OA care and other providers continue. f represents the fraction of nominal activity that is maintained/expanded because of new funds, K capacity; catch-up hazards separately represent patients obtaining equivalent care later. Modern medical management and spontaneous remission remain alternatives. Uninsured at intake does not mean no lifetime access. Current English eligibility says uninsured/ineligible for full-scope public coverage, while OA's March 2025 funder presentation describes bridge care for some people who may qualify. Actual current intake implementation remains unverified. Neither uninsured status nor grant loss establishes lifelong absence of care. Current coverage restrictions can increase need but do not quantify donor-sensitive appointments.
historicalModel.attribution: Within each specialty, diagnosis shares sum to one. Every modeled path uses r=1,529/1,130 and d=1: the aggregate unduplicated count already absorbs repeats/overlap, so no additional blanket patient discount is added. Applying one aggregate conversion uniformly to unknown diagnosis-specific and marginal activity is a judgment; the alpha conversion remains a sensitivity. This accounting partitions patient-equivalents without claiming actual unique-person linkage. Provider capacity and funding replacement enter f and K once; later equivalent care enters the separate catch-up hazard. There is no extra navigation multiplier on completed services, provider credit multiplier, productivity benefit, or duplicate all-cancer survival benefit.
historicalModel.uncertainty: Conditional scenario model dominated by diagnostic mix, baseline utility, funding additionality and later-care assumptions. Favorable, rapid-catch-up, null and adverse states are deliberately wide stress tests, not probability intervals or empirical bounds. The central input set is a transparent judgment, not an observed expectation. Twenty-one supplementary named paths plus CRC/cataract/hernia cover the full specialty allocation; the small other-assessment path has no central benefit and retains burden.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: 2025 Form 990 Part III reports 1,529 surgical/diagnostic services for 1,130 unduplicated residents: 1.353097 services per person. Specialty service counts sum to 1,529, but patient-linked diagnosis frequencies remain unavailable. Beta uses the observed aggregate ratio across all diagnosis paths as a judgment transfer to marginal activity, replacing the older repeat/overlap priors. The output is disjoint patient-equivalents, not 24 independently observed patient cohorts. The 2025 whole-recipient cash-like average is $1,476 per service, not a marginal quote. At the $100,000 gift normalization, the central has 66.727 nominal mixed services, 33.364 additional service equivalents and 24.657 patient equivalents. Gift cost is $2,997.27 per additional service and $4,055.60 per patient equivalent before diagnosis-specific utility, timing and harms. These are conditional marginal equivalents, not actual quoted slots or a new observed treatment cohort.

inputs.rationale: Two-year assumed lag from procedure to differential fatal risk. Not observed OA survival timing; existing alternative care can catch up during this lag.

inputs.name: crc_active_years
inputs.rationale: Five years of possibly different fatal hazard after latency, not five avoided deaths or a life expectancy.

inputs.name: crc_horizon_years
inputs.rationale: Ten-year finite survival observation from procedure; both arms return to common mortality after the hazard-effect window. No lifetime tail.

inputs.name: crc_delay_years
inputs.rationale: Quarter-year procedure delay; cohort already conditioned alive at service start, so delay discounts only.

sensitivity: Central 0.531150 California QALYs per $100,000, or $1,882,706 per ten QALYs. This is a conditional judgment, not measured OA effectiveness or a recommendation.

The observed aggregate patient conversion changes central health by only 3.40% from alpha; its diagnosis-specific transfer remains unknown. Reverting fully to alpha conversion reproduces 0.513674 QALYs.

Central nominal activity is 66.727 services; f=0.5 gives 33.364 additional service-equivalents and 24.657 disjoint patient-equivalents. The K=100 cap does not bind. Five available slots instead yields 0.079600 QALYs ($12.56M per ten); f=0.1 yields 0.106230 ($9.41M). Neither slot count is observed.

Supplementary pathways without relief yield -0.014544 QALYs; all gross benefits null yields -0.087362. Zero clinical activity gives zero; adding one independent QALY of harm gives -1. Negative or zero health has no favorable price.

Rapid later care yields 0.048612 QALYs ($20.57M per ten); favorable combined assumptions yield 2.212014 ($452,077). One-year symptom horizons give 0.297722, whereas limiting CRC as well gives 0.293068. CRC latency prevents survival gain before year two.

AUB contributes 0.125349 net QALYs, the largest single path. Setting only AUB relief to zero, retaining harm, lowers total to 0.379380. Its 65% gynecology share, 0.10 utility and 0.8 success are priors, not trial estimates in OA patients.

Gross associated resources are $369,105.29, giving $6.95M per ten California QALYs. This includes nominal clinical, patient and downstream costs; it is neither waived hospital charges nor net incremental societal spending.
At this donor margin, meeting $1M per ten QALYs requires 1 QALY per $100,000 (1.88 times central), and $100k requires 10 (18.83 times). These are arithmetic thresholds, not benchmark endorsements.

what: Legal Action Center uses legal services, litigation and policy advocacy to reduce discrimination against people with substance use disorders, HIV/AIDS, or arrest and conviction records.
It works on access to health care alongside employment, housing, education, privacy and other civil rights.
A finite judgment model estimates MOUD-access health from individual and prospective targeted policy work, with other civil-rights and health pathways unpriced.
strengths: Removing an actual treatment barrier offers a concrete route to better health, and methadone and buprenorphine have substantial mortality evidence.
Recent litigation produced enforceable institutional changes with admission-denial monitoring, rather than only awareness or recommendations.
National policy work could reach many more people than direct representation, while the charity also reports a substantial New York legal-service caseload.
reservations: No public model links additional unrestricted funding to extra treatment initiation, retention or health outcomes after other actors' contributions.
Much of the portfolio produces important non-health benefits that cannot simply be relabeled QALYs.
Current financial publications disagree on revenue and net assets; expense totals can be reconciled, but a marginal funding plan and reserve restrictions still need clarification.

sections.what: LAC combines individual representation, institutional litigation, national and state policy work, coalitions and professional training. The [2025 annual report](https://www.lac.org/assets/files/LAC-2025-Annual-Report.pdf) describes insurance assistance, health-care discrimination cases, criminal-record remedies and alternatives to incarceration. Its [January 2026 Medicare comments](https://www.lac.org/assets/images/CY27-MAPD-Comments-LAC.pdf) seek lower treatment barriers and better network oversight. These show an active health-policy portfolio, not evidence that the requested reforms were adopted or caused additional care.
sections.monitoring: The [FY2025 Form 990](https://www.lac.org/assets/files/LEGAL-ACTION-CENTER-OF-THE-CITY-OF-NEW-YORK-INC-990-Public-Copy.pdf) reports 869 New Yorkers helped with 1,770 civil cases: 808 clients had conviction-record issues, 37 substance-use-disorder issues and 24 HIV/AIDS issues. The 2025 annual report instead reports calendar-year activity, including 999 clients and 1,980 cases; these periods should not be mixed in a cost-per-case calculation. Neither series identifies additional medication treatment or survival. In the [2025 nursing-facility settlement](https://disabilityrightsnc.org/news/press-release/groundbreaking-settlement-in-lawsuit-about-right-to-nursing-care-for-individual-with-substance-use-disorder/), two facilities agreed to nondiscrimination policies, training and one year of admission-denial reporting. Actual additional admissions and patient outcomes are the decisive next measures.
sections.qualitative:
The best-judgment model prices one credible health pathway—additional retained MOUD access—while leaving much of this civil-rights institution’s value unpriced. A [Massachusetts cohort study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29913516/) followed 17,568 overdose survivors; methadone and buprenorphine were associated with adjusted all-cause mortality hazard ratios of 0.47 and 0.63 respectively. This is observational evidence, not a trial of LAC. A [2024 Medicare study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38884975/) also associated greater medication exposure with lower fatal-overdose risk, but its older population differs from many legal clients. Treatment access only matters clinically if patients initiate and retain effective care. The nursing-facility settlement is jointly produced with Disability Rights North Carolina and applies directly to two facilities; it should not be priced as a nationwide change in admissions. Employment, dignity, privacy and avoided incarceration can be valuable without forcing them into an unsupported health conversion.

A [difference-in-differences study of the 2014 small-group insurance parity expansion](https://www.nber.org/papers/w29001) found more residential treatment but less agonist medication. That is not an evaluation of LAC or every parity reform. It does show why coverage, spending and total admissions are inadequate substitutes for the mix and duration of effective treatment.
sections.cost:
The central cost excludes donated legal services; including recognized donated resources raises the estimate from $239.9 million to $283.5 million per 10 USA QALYs.

The consistent Form 990 expense series is $8.19 million for FY2023, $8.65 million for FY2024 and $8.98 million for FY2025, years ending March 31. The [FY2025 return](https://www.lac.org/assets/files/LEGAL-ACTION-CENTER-OF-THE-CITY-OF-NEW-YORK-INC-990-Public-Copy.pdf) assigns $2.71 million to legal services. Dividing by its matched 869-client count gives about $3,100 per legal client, before allocating shared support and donated services; this is an average workload measure, not a price for an additional successful case. Audited expenses reported in the annual report are $10.61 million, including $1.63 million donated services excluded from the 990. We do not combine those accounting bases in the three-year average.

A conditional mortality bridge is possible: 0.005–0.020 fewer deaths per additional retained treatment-year, multiplied by 5–15 discounted quality-adjusted years per death prevented, gives 0.025–0.30 QALYs per net treatment-year. Both ranges are explicit judgments informed by clinical evidence, not measured LAC effects or statistical confidence limits. To meet $100,000 per ten USA QALYs, LAC's enabling contribution would need to cost roughly $250–$3,000 per additional attributable USA treatment-year; the $1 million threshold permits $2,500–$30,000. Clinical provision also uses public or private resources. The missing quantity is how many such years LAC actually causes at the margin; an insurance approval, favorable policy or legal client is not automatically a retained treatment-year.

For scale, [NIDA's historical 2018 report](https://nida.nih.gov/sites/default/files/21349-medications-to-treat-opioid-use-disorder_0.pdf) cites preliminary delivery costs of $5,980 per buprenorphine patient-year and $6,552 for methadone with associated services. These are not current quotes. Even these historical prices imply about $6,000 in downstream delivery resources per treatment-year, additional to legal or advocacy spending and before medical cost offsets.

The finite judgment central is $239.95 million per 10 USA QALYs, with 0.37431 QALYs per annual full-recipient support cost. The37 reported SUD clients are reduced for OUD relevance, access changed beyond alternatives, uptake, retention and funding response; they are not37successful treatment restorations. The separate prospective policy branch assumes four opportunities, each involving100 eligible people, a .15 attributable implementation probability change, .4 uptake and .5 retained years. This is a planning prior informed by an active legal-policy portfolio and a concrete two-facility precedent, not a replay of the completed settlement. No overlap with direct clients is allowed.

This estimate charges all Form990 recipient spending, not only legal-service expense. Using the annual report’s rounded $10.61 million including pro bono resources increases the price by 1.181 times; source reconciliation remains as previously disclosed. Clinical provision and outside partner resources add further social cost. A finite price does not establish an available funding gap or endorsement.
sections.funding:
The [FY2025 return](https://www.lac.org/assets/files/LEGAL-ACTION-CENTER-OF-THE-CITY-OF-NEW-YORK-INC-990-Public-Copy.pdf) records $6.47 million revenue against $8.98 million expenses and $11.94 million ending net assets. Net assets are not freely spendable cash or proof that new donations are unnecessary. The annual report gives different revenue and net-asset figures for the same stated period; without reconciliation, we rely on the return for those quantities and do not infer runway. Government contracts, foundations, individual support and donated professional work all matter. A costed current funding gap, restrictions and the next unfunded hires or cases were not found.

LAC's [October 2025 opioid-settlement recommendations](https://www.lac.org/assets/files/October-2025-LAC-Recommendations-OSFAB-FINAL.pdf) explicitly identify missing baseline funding, outcome and other-funder information in public spending reports. That is also central to evaluating the charity: protecting or redirecting appropriations can help, but only incremental effective services count after replacement by other government, insurer or private funding. Published historical achievements cannot be attributed to a new gift.

model.costScope: Ordinary unrestricted gift across legal, policy, other programs and shared support. annual recipient spending uses Form990 expenses excluding donated services; full economic resource use additionally includes pro bono services and clinical/public implementation costs. An unrestricted gift is not assumed restricted to MOUD litigation.
model.geographicAttribution: Count residents of the 50 states plus DC. Individual New York clients and the North Carolina case lie inside this boundary. National insurance and policy work may extend to territories; no resident-weighted marginal share was found. A 100% USA share applies only to explicitly identified in-boundary clients, not automatically to the full portfolio.
model.formula: At full annual recipient cost C=8981593: Ydirect=S*o*v*u*t*b; Ypolicy=K*dp*N*up*tp*b; L=sum(y=1..T) U*((1-m)/1.03)^y; Qall=(Ydirect+Ypolicy)*d*L; QUSA=Qall*g. Direct and prospective policy recipients are disjoint. b funding responsiveness appears once. dp is net LAC contribution versus other counsel, so no extra coalition multiplier. Retained treatment exposure at most one year; post-averted-death survival finite, no extra lifetime term.
model.counterfactual: No-gift world includes existing staff, funded cases, other counsel, federal enforcement, advocacy coalitions, insurers and clinical providers. A change caused earlier counts only the additional benefit during acceleration. Successful historical cases are not repeatable units automatically purchased by a new donor. Public funding may be shifted rather than increased; measure net effective care, not budget totals.
model.attribution: Use probability difference with versus without the incremental LAC work, not all beneficiaries of a coalition win. Partners and clients are necessary contributors. Keep individual-case and policy-spillover beneficiaries separate to avoid duplicate credit. Count patient residence, not LAC headquarters. Do not count legal damages, insurance savings, employment income and medical savings as QALYs. Changes in treatment mix can be harmful as well as helpful; subtract displaced effective medication treatment rather than assuming every coverage expansion has a positive sign.
model.uncertainty: Genuine best-judgment partial-health estimate. Legal-to-treatment implementation parameters are weak priors, not measured client outcomes or bounded probabilities from source data. Broad joint scenarios, zero and adverse cases remain. Other HIV, incarceration, civil-rights and economic value is not assumed worthless.
model.nativeOutcomes: Central direct pathway yields 1.734375 donor-responsive retained treatment-years; separate future targeted-policy pathway yields 6. L=4.938368555103658 discounted QALYs per avoided near-term death over10years, already adjusting utility and competing mortality.

As a deliberately narrow direct-case test, all37SUD-issue clients receiving one extra attributable retained MOUDyear would yield0.925–11.1QALYs. Against the fullFY2025budget this is roughly$8.1m–$97m per10. This is not a whole-organization estimate or upper bound: SUD cases may not restoreMOUD, and policy spillovers, HIVcare and other health gains are omitted.

At fullFY2025budget, annual USAhealth hurdles are about898QALYs for$100k per10 and90QALYs for$1m per10. Full societal costing raises the numerator by additional clinical care and partner resources; medical savings are not health gains.

Halving retention, counterfactual additionality or clinical benefit doubles the price; zero additional benefit leaves no finite positive price. Older, medically complex patients may have lower remainingQALYs and higher immediate risks, so one universal treatment-year value is inappropriate.

Repeated treatment-years need survival weighting; do not count the same averted death multiple times or assume lifetime treatment retention. The mortality-only bridge omits morbidity and infection effects, which require separate estimates and overlap checks.

The parity study found no statistically significant overall clinical-outcome or spending effect; its null result is not proof that all targeted access reforms fail. It argues for case-specific implementation assumptions rather than importing a generic positive policy multiplier.

what: End Overdose teaches people to recognize opioid overdose and respond with naloxone, rescue breathing and emergency assistance.
It distributes prevention supplies through online certification, schools, college chapters, music events and community partners, including rural outreach in Arkansas.
The main health benefit occurs when its work equips an otherwise unprotected witness to provide effective help early enough to change a person's outcome.
strengths: Naloxone has a direct clinical mechanism, and the organization delivers tangible training and supplies rather than reporting awareness alone.
The original quarterly report and independent public-health partners document substantial real activity, including publicly supplied medication distributed through End Overdose.
The current giving page identifies the nonprofit and offers both a general fund and program designations, making a future, specifically costed community-delivery proposal practical to investigate.
reservations: No public evidence identifies how many additional high-risk recipients an ordinary gift would reach with usable medication, or how often they would add a rescue beyond existing protection.

Manufacturer donations, public supplies and funded partnerships may complement private delivery spending, but their inventory, restrictions, remaining funding and substitution effects are not reconciled.
Follow-up and financial reconciliations are incomplete, and recipient shipping can reduce household resources; our estimate remains sensitive to targeting, other rescuers and delivery costs.

sections.what:
End Overdose combines education, direct supply distribution and outreach. Its [2026 campaign](https://endoverdose.net/campaign/) supports digital instruction, instructor certification, chapters and state operations as well as naloxone. Ordinary unrestricted support therefore cannot be modeled as a purchase of medication alone. This review counts health accruing to residents of the 50 states and DC; attendance at a US event does not by itself establish residence.

A [July 2026 Arkansas announcement](https://endoverdose.net/news/blog/end-overdose-distributes-free-naloxone-boxes-throughout-arkansas/) describes 12 grant-funded rural cabinets and reports 89,000 doses distributed in that state to date. Claims that cabinets were rapidly claimed show demand for placement, not independently confirmed installation, continuing restocking or extra rescues. The [Arkansas bulk form](https://endoverdose.net/bulk-order/) offers free shipping and asks applicants how supplies will be used. This is a different delivery channel from the national store, where certified recipients are asked to pay shipping.

The [official donation checkout](https://donate.endoverdose.net/give/546264) identifies END OVERDOSE as a 501(c)(3). Its default is General Fund Project; other designations include Community Organizations & Treatment Facilities, Middle & High Schools, and Nightlife & Music Festivals. The receiving organization's [original tax return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202530849349300213/IRS990) identifies EIN 83-0696963 and endoverdose.net. This review remains a general-fund analysis: a menu designation alone does not establish an enforceable restriction or an unfunded delivery opportunity.
sections.monitoring:
The [original July–September 2024 report](https://cdn.sanity.io/files/03xshhuu/production/fc944226581fe8e9a80cd6d39aa74f59574d954e.pdf) reports 44,952 people trained and 71,733 naloxone doses distributed. It separately describes a school pilot with 1,797 kits; those kits are not added to the quarter's doses or treated as unique rescues. The [2024 filing](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202530849349300213/IRS990) reports over 230,000 trainees for the year. These measures have different periods and units and do not establish a matched cohort of trained people receiving and retaining kits.

Public partners corroborate distribution activity. The [Overdose Response Strategy account](https://orsprogram.org/nevada-ors-team-facilitates-partnership-for-naloxone-distribution/) says Southern Nevada Health District supplied 30,000 doses for EDC 2025. [Los Angeles County's announcement](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/los-angeles-county-department-of-public-health-partners-with-end-overdose-to-address-fentanyl-crisis-859515770.html) describes joint festival outreach. Neither provides an experimental estimate of End Overdose's incremental mortality impact.

The report index still exposed the original summer PDF; the displayed annual-report label did not yield a separately retrievable 2024 annual document in this review. Public totals lack a reconciled stock-flow ledger, channel-specific costs, unique recipient follow-up, and linked rescue and survival records. Necessary monitoring would track certification, dispatch, receipt, usable carriage or access, witnessed overdose, other available rescuers, timely administration, three-day survival and subsequent mortality. Repeated trainees, shared scenes and repeat rescues of the same person require linked, privacy-preserving accounting.

Information quality also affects usable supply. The [bulk-order page](https://endoverdose.net/bulk-order/) broadly says doses can remain effective 30 years after expiration. The [study behind that familiar claim](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30596290/) tested expired injectable solutions, not clinical effectiveness of this organization's intranasal inventory over 30 years. [FDA guidance](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-alerts-and-statements/fda-announces-shelf-life-extension-naloxone-nasal-spray) advises observing the printed expiry for the relevant product. This does not establish that End Overdose ships expired medicine; it means current product, storage and expiration records are needed before treating all stock as equally usable.

The current kit page remains internally ambiguous about stock and certification-gated purchasing. Neither the badge nor structured product metadata identifies additional funded slots. Recipient shipping amounts and the counterfactual cost of obtaining equivalent supplies elsewhere are not observed. A fiscal deficit is not a measured funding-response coefficient.
sections.qualitative:
The strongest case is for funding otherwise unavailable, reliable delivery to people likely to witness an overdose. Naloxone's clinical action is well established, but a drug's efficacy does not identify the value of another general-fund dollar. The [Rhode Island simulation](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2819204) emphasizes saturation, targeting and witnessing; it is neither an End Overdose evaluation nor an estimate that transfers automatically to other states. The [HEALing Communities randomized trial](https://vivo.weill.cornell.edu/display/pubid38884347) found no statistically significant primary mortality difference for its broader intervention bundle: adjusted rate ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.76–1.09. Only 38% of implemented strategies had begun by the comparison year's start, so this is a caution about achieved implementation and timing, not a clean test of naloxone alone.

A [Colorado festival survey](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41430526/) found that 55.5% of 227 participants carried naloxone in some context and 8.4% had ever administered it. The selected, cross-sectional sample suggests both relevant exposure and substantial existing protection; its lifetime reports cannot be divided into an annual rescue rate. A [Rikers visitor cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29175025/) reached 226 of 283 enrollees at six months; 40 respondents witnessed 70 overdoses. It supports the plausibility of higher-risk channels while illustrating repeated events and loss to follow-up. It is not a rate for the organization's students or event attendees.

Rescue also does not confer normal remaining life expectancy. In a [Massachusetts EMS cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32242763/), 7.5% of those alive three days after treatment died by one year. The related [ED cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31229387/) found 5.5% one-year mortality, and a [King County study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10842336/) reported 5.2 all-cause deaths per 100 person-years. These are different cohorts, endpoints and periods, not interchangeable exact hazards. They justify explicit continuing mortality and finite health horizons. Future mortality and utility in End Overdose's additional survivors remain unknown; [patient-reported OUD utility research](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11452457/) also cautions against assigning low quality of life solely from general-public stereotypes.

Our assessment is therefore conditional rather than an endorsement. Community and rural distribution could be worthwhile, especially where free stock does not reach likely witnesses. Broad awareness, reduced stigma, fentanyl-test use, care referrals and family effects may also matter, but are not valued here. Their omission is not evidence that they are zero, nor does it make the quantified pathway a proven lower bound on the whole organization's value.

The October 2026 revision independently reconsiders the clinical pathway and signed household resources. Its central price is a conditional, partial comparison, not an identified expected unrestricted-gift return. Carriage surveys and selected high-risk cohorts support plausible pathways but do not calibrate the marginal recipient mix. We therefore retain explicit one-way challenges to the revised cost, opportunity, deduplication and survival judgments rather than treating refreshed citations as validation of them.
sections.cost:
Our conditional estimate is about **$2.7 million per better life in the USA**, counting ten combined health and household-resource equivalents. The model charges the full donation, including work whose benefits are not quantified. Its best case is timely delivery to people likely to witness an overdose who would otherwise lack effective protection; donated medication can make that last-mile work relatively inexpensive. The numbers are analyst judgments, not measured services per dollar or an available delivery offer.

**What does a dollar enable?** A modeled $10,000 supports 162.5 nominal training-and-kit offers. After allowing for replacement funding and incomplete fulfillment, it adds 54.84 delivered two-dose kits, or about $182 per additional kit. The $40 cash budget per nominal offer assumes $15 paid equipment and $25 paid fulfillment, education, administration and fundraising, including failed offers. Another $15 of equipment is contributed. This half-contributed equipment hypothesis is not an audited unit cost or a national procurement quote. Sixty-five percent of the gift enters this pathway; the entire gift remains in the price numerator.

**How do kits become health benefits?** We exclude the 5% assumed to purchase equivalent naloxone without the gift. Among remaining recipients, the model assumes a 0.7% one-year relevant overdose opportunity, 55% timely usable access, 35% help additional to equivalent timely rescue by others, and 60% unique-patient credit. This yields 0.0421 additional timely administrations per $10,000. The separate 12-percentage-point three-day survival advantage applies only to those genuinely additional administrations: spontaneous recovery, incomplete reversal and subsequent acute care can still limit their effect. Other naloxone or EMS replacement is handled in the 35% factor, not discounted again here. These fractions are not End Overdose measurements.

The resulting 0.00505 added three-day survivors receive a finite 20-year survival proxy: 8% first-year mortality, 5% later annual mortality, utility 0.8 and 3% discounting. It gives 7.58 discounted clinical QALYs per added survivor at the gift date, rather than normal remaining life expectancy. With a judged 99.5% USA-resident share, clinical benefit is **0.03813 QALYs per $10,000**, or **$2.62M per ten health QALYs**. The [historical Massachusetts EMS study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32242763/) informs prognosis after three-day survival; it does not identify the causal survival advantage or the prognosis of End Overdose's otherwise-fatal beneficiaries.

**What happens to household resources?** Five percent of delivered-kit recipients are assumed to avoid an actual $20 purchase; 40% incur $6 incremental shipping compared with their without-gift alternative. The [official kit page](https://store.endoverdose.net/products/nasal-nalonxone-kit) asks for shipping payment but supplies no verified dollar amount. Both amounts, recipient shares and $30,000 baseline annual disposable resources are judgments. Four buyer/nonbuyer × mailed/unmailed groups receive separate signed logarithmic welfare calculations: +$14, +$20, −$6 or $0. This avoids logging an average cash change. Purchase savings total $54.57 and shipping expense $130.97 in the USA, a net −$76.40. Their **−0.001255 household-resource equivalents** reduce total benefit to **0.03687 combined equivalents per $10,000**, giving **$2.71M per better life**. The [Coefficient Giving crosswalk](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/) compares resources with health; these equivalents are not observed clinical QALYs.

People who would already buy the medicine do not also receive full added-access health credit. Ordinary earnings of newly surviving people are not added to survival value. Separate signed cash scenarios for people alive under either treatment remain unmeasured, with explicit independence and nonoverlap assumptions. Equal alternative postage makes incremental shipping zero, producing $2.56M with clinical benefit unchanged. No actual purchase savings, adverse cash burdens and unknown income are separately inspectable.

**Why did the estimate change?** The preserved earlier USA health-only estimate was **$1.76M per ten QALYs**. The revision reconsiders cash cost, program allocation, funding replacement, completion, targeting, other rescuers, deduplication and survival. New clinical benefit is about 67% of the old normalized benefit; household costs worsen the combined price slightly further. None of the revised coefficients is presented as a newly measured organizational effect. Restoring the earlier $50 cost, 0.5% opportunity and 50% unique-patient credit together yields **$5.83M**, while halving the causal survival advantage yields **$5.62M**. These are assumption challenges, not confidence intervals.

The gross institutional-resource companion is $13,758.56 per modeled gift, or **$3.73M per ten combined equivalents**. It adds $15 contributed stock and $8 unpaid support per nominal offer plus $500 emergency response per credited administration. It intentionally covers nominal commitments, including unsuccessful/nonadditional offers, not measured induced delivery or net societal expenditure. Recipient shipping is a separate household burden rather than charged again. Future care, travel, work effects and other program benefits remain unknown.

Favorable targeting, weak targeting, clinical null, funding/allocation/completion zero, independent harm and unknown-component cases are retained in the calculator. Negative net benefit has no positive price; unknown benefit is not zero. The $10,000 normalization and $100,000 mathematical ceiling do not demonstrate current capacity or unlimited linear scaling.
sections.funding:
The current campaign reports a manufacturer contribution of 25,000 naloxone units, but does not define that unit or reconcile receipts, inventory, dispatches, returns and expirations. It must not be combined automatically with the older public donation or converted into 25,000 two-dose kits. The [national kit page](https://store.endoverdose.net/products/nasal-nalonxone-kit) says two intranasal doses, recipient-paid shipping and a 7–14-day shipping notice. Its extracted HTML contains a generic Sold out badge, but its product structured data says InStock and the purchasing control is restricted by certification. We therefore retract the initial report's implication that this text demonstrated a stockout. Neither the badge nor the structured data verifies a fulfillable donor-funded queue.

Public supply is a concrete alternative and potential complement. [California's NDP](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/individuals/naloxone-distribution-project/ndp-frequently-asked-questions/) provides free medication and shipping to eligible organizations; it does not distribute directly to individuals. This can leave real last-mile work for private support. The Nevada partner's donation and Arkansas' funded cabinets similarly do not prove that a new private gift adds inventory or capacity. A useful next proposal would specify the intended higher-risk channel, committed stock and other funds, unmet orders, additional paid hours, completed-delivery target and follow-up plan. No current costed, unfunded proposal meeting those conditions was located. An old match announcement in the 2024 report is not treated as a current match.

Annual spending appendix: the original [2022](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202340609349300739/IRS990), [2023](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202411169349302221/IRS990) and [2024](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202530849349300213/IRS990) returns are all 12-month calendar-year, cash-basis filings for EIN 83-0696963. Part IX reports total spending of $516,362, $942,519 and $970,440, averaging $809,774. The respective program / management / fundraising splits are $464,735 / $51,627 / $0; $786,575 / $155,944 / $0; and $730,276 / $207,274 / $32,890. These are consistent total-cost accounting figures, not a marginal allocation to high-risk naloxone delivery or full values of contributed medicines and labor.

There are unresolved financial discrepancies. Part III program totals are $272,610, $1,199,424 and $980,427, respectively, and disagree with Part IX. The 2022 and 2023 Part XI net-asset roll-forwards miss $3,277 and $9,081; the latter [Schedule O](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202411169349302221/IRS990ScheduleO) does not explain the difference. These discrepancies do not prove wrongdoing, but require reconciliation before relying on reserve or program-efficiency claims. At year-end 2024 the return reports $20,042 cash, $36,709 liabilities and negative $16,572 net assets; the 2024 roll-forward does reconcile. The [filing index](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/830696963) and targeted search yielded no newer original return. These historical figures cannot establish October 2026 runway, restrictions or funding room. The 2023–24 returns report compiled or reviewed statements, not audited statements.

model.costScope: Full donor gift in numerator; judged $40 comprehensive cash per nominal offer. Separate gross institutional companion values contributed stock/unpaid inputs per nominal offer and emergency response per credited administration, not measured induced net societal cost. Signed recipient shipping enters welfare, not twice into the companion.
model.geographicAttribution: USA means residents of the 50 states and DC. Domestic program and partner records support a predominantly domestic footprint but do not measure patient residence. All scenario shares g, including reference 0.99, are analyst judgments. Territorial and international attendee benefits fall outside edition QALYs and are not separately identified. No California, Bay Area or population-share allocation is inherited. Do not sum this report with nested state or metro benefits.
model.formula: N=G*a/c; A=N*b; D=A*q; R=D*(1-purchaseShare)*e*k*t*d; Z=R*f; L=sum finite trapezoidal survival after day3, discounted at year-.5+delay; H=g*(Z*L-R*h-donorHarm). Separate buyer×shipping cohorts each add .5*people*log1p(net cash/baseline)*g/(1+discount)^delay. Combined=H+signed resource equivalents; price=10*G/combined when positive. Unknown is not zero.
model.counterfactual: Without the gift, existing End Overdose funding, already funded cabinets, manufacturer and public stock, other distributors, trained witnesses and EMS remain. b represents the share of nominal offers made additional by the gift, after replacement funding. q represents actual completed delivery; k usable access at the opportunity; t clinical timing beyond other available response. These are distinct counterfactual steps. Public stock may enable donor-funded last-mile work rather than make it redundant, but the current overlap is unmeasured.
model.attribution: Would-be actual purchasers are excluded before t. t excludes equivalent timely other rescue in the remaining pool; f is residual absolute extra three-day survival conditional on genuinely additional administrations, not a second EMS/other-naloxone discount. Repeat-event d and funding b are separate judgments. Ordinary survivor earnings excluded. Always-alive cash pool share<=1-abs(f), with explicit independence.
model.uncertainty: The central naloxone-pathway estimate is a subjective best guess, not a whole-portfolio expected return. Its inputs and joint stress tests are not probability-weighted estimates, confidence intervals or bounds. Older EMS and ED survivor cohorts do not identify the survival of otherwise-fatal cases rescued by this organization in 2026; future hazards and utility are explicit judgments. Endpoints, cohort composition and annual rates versus risks differ. Capacity constraints may make the linear gift model fail. Unpriced portfolio effects can be positive or negative, so the naloxone pathway is not a proven lower bound on the whole organization's value.

scenarios.label: Historical USA clinical-only estimate, retained for comparison

sensitivity: Current conditional donor combined price$2,712,178; health-only$2,622,897 versus historical clinical-only$1,759,485. Crosswalk equivalents are not measured clinical QALYs.
Restoring old cost/opportunity/dedup together produces$5,830,531; fhalved$5,615,504. These expose judgment dependence, not posterior confidence intervals.
Zero incremental shipping yields$2,562,681 with unchanged health. Positive/negative cash, survival and independent harms remain separately inspectable.
Unknown health/income/response nulls combined price; true no-additionality is zero. Mathematical ceiling is not verified donor capacity.
missingInputs: Costed, currently unfunded capacity and the share of unrestricted next dollars allocated to added high-risk delivery.
Manufacturer/public/purchased inventory reconciliation by dose, package, expiry, remaining stock, restrictions and distribution channel.
Actual fulfillment completion, recipient shipping receipts, paid and unpaid labor, and current workload constraints.
Marginal recipient exposure, usable access and other available witnesses or EMS; linked unique scene and patient follow-up.
Additional survival probability versus no added response, subsequent mortality, utility, adverse effects and future net costs.
USA-resident outcomes separated from territorial and foreign attendee spillovers.
Reconciled 2022–24 program totals and 2022–23 net-asset roll-forwards; current management accounts, debt, restrictions and funding commitments.
Effects of education, test strips, stigma, referrals and other portfolio activity, including possible harms; no whole-organization lower bound is established.
Actual counterfactual household purchase, incremental shipping, disposable resources, always-alive cash changes and independence; finite judgments are not measurements.

Cash cost c includes paid staff, overhead, fundraising allocation, training, stock where purchased, and fulfillment. No restriction or current $100,000 capacity is assumed. Nominal-activity resource envelopes separately add contributed medicines, unpaid support, recipient cash and emergency response. Future medical care, recipient time, exact postage receipts, opportunity costs and unpriced portfolio effects remain unknown; no full societal return is claimed.
historicalModel.geographicAttribution: USA means residents of the 50 states and DC. Domestic program and partner records support a predominantly domestic footprint but do not measure patient residence. All scenario shares g, including reference 0.99, are analyst judgments. Territorial and international attendee benefits fall outside edition QALYs and are not separately identified. No California, Bay Area or population-share allocation is inherited. Do not sum this report with nested state or metro benefits.
historicalModel.formula: N=G*a/c nominal offered packages. A=N*b additional offers after funding replacement. D=A*q additional completed delivered two-dose kits; doses=2*D. R=D*e*k*t*d additional timely administrations with unique-patient credit. Z=R*f additional three-day survivors. S(0)=1; S(1)=1-m1; S(y)=S(y-1)*(1-m) thereafter. L=sum(y=1..T)[u*(S(y-1)+S(y))/2/(1.03^(y-0.5+delay))]. Q_all=Z*L-R*h; Q_USA=g*Q_all. Donor price for ten USA QALYs=10*G/Q_USA only when Q_USA>0. Resource envelope=G+N*(stock+unpaid+recipientCash)+R*ems, with omitted future net care and time explicitly unknown.
historicalModel.counterfactual: Without the gift, existing End Overdose funding, already funded cabinets, manufacturer and public stock, other distributors, trained witnesses and EMS remain. b represents the share of nominal offers made additional by the gift, after replacement funding. q represents actual completed delivery; k usable access at the opportunity; t clinical timing beyond other available response. These are distinct counterfactual steps. Public stock may enable donor-funded last-mile work rather than make it redundant, but the current overlap is unmeasured.
historicalModel.attribution: Doses, packages, trainees, witnessed events, administrations and unique patients are separate units. d is only a scenario proxy for shared-scene and repeat-patient overlap, not a substitute for linked records. f is an absolute three-day survival advantage from an added credited administration, never the observed fraction surviving after naloxone. m1 applies after the modeled three-day endpoint, avoiding inclusion of early deaths in both f and later survival. Repeat rescues cannot each earn an independent lifetime gain; subsequent rescue and competing mortality are reflected in the finite survival schedule. No intervention-caused treatment retention or normal lifespan is assumed.
historicalModel.uncertainty: The central naloxone-pathway estimate is a subjective best guess, not a whole-portfolio expected return. Its inputs and joint stress tests are not probability-weighted estimates, confidence intervals or bounds. Older EMS and ED survivor cohorts do not identify the survival of otherwise-fatal cases rescued by this organization in 2026; future hazards and utility are explicit judgments. Endpoints, cohort composition and annual rates versus risks differ. Capacity constraints may make the linear gift model fail. Unpriced portfolio effects can be positive or negative, so the naloxone pathway is not a proven lower bound on the whole organization's value.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: Nominal training-and-kit offers; additional offers; completed delivered two-dose kits; doses; timely usable access; unique witnessed overdose opportunities; additional timely administrations with unique-patient credit; additional three-day survivors; finite retained health. Reference per $1,000 of total gift: 15 nominal offers, 6 additional delivered kits, 12 doses and 0.00375 additional credited administrations. These are conditional model outputs, not measured services per dollar.

scenarios.assumptions: Education, referrals, test strips and other program effects are not identified. The central calculation values only the modeled naloxone pathway while charging full donation cost; it is not a proven lower bound.

sensitivity: Conditional naloxone-pathway best guess: $1,759,485 per ten USA QALYs. Holding the reference assumptions fixed, a $1 million price requires annual opportunity e=0.8797%; a $100,000 price requires e=8.7974%. No source establishes either threshold for marginal recipients.
Changing e from 0.5% to 5% reduces the reference price tenfold. Halving b, q, k, t, d or f separately doubles it; these are not six independent empirically estimated effects.
The donated-stock scenario lowers the donor-cash price to $1,090,880 per ten, but adds the medicine to the resource envelope. A historical donation does not establish recurring free inventory.

With all other reference inputs fixed, horizon, health utility and first-year mortality alter retained health; the accompanying calculation artifact reports the exact one-way sensitivities. A 30-year horizon is a scenario rather than normal life expectancy.
The joint higher-risk scenario changes e to 5%, t to 75%, b to 80% and q to 90%, producing $65,166 per ten. It requires a different implemented delivery channel; no probability is attached.

Zero added delivery or zero added clinical help produces zero quantified benefit. A negative net health scenario has no positive cost-effectiveness price. Very large finite downside prices are an arithmetic warning about approaching zero benefit, not an upper confidence bound.
USA share 95% rather than 99% changes a positive price by about 4.2%; geographic uncertainty is smaller than unmeasured targeting, completed delivery and rescue additionality in these examples.

reports.program: Overdose response training, naloxone access and community outreach

what: End Overdose trains people to recognize and respond to overdoses and distributes naloxone through online and community channels.
Its national operations include California chapters and a California-resident kit offer.
Participants learn overdose recognition and response before requesting medication.
strengths: Timely naloxone can avert fatal opioid overdoses when no adequate alternative response is available.
California-specific fulfillment and local chapters establish a real in-state delivery pathway.
Current campaign reporting distinguishes donated medication from cash-supported training and operations.
reservations: Chapter counts and mailing eligibility do not establish California's share of additional health.
Free public supply, other rescuers and later overdose risks substantially reduce attribution relative to doses distributed.
National conditional estimates rely on wide judgments about risk, additional timely rescue and gift-sensitive expansion.

sections.what: [End Overdose](https://endoverdose.net/about/solution/) combines overdose education, naloxone access, test strips and youth-oriented outreach. Its [chapter directory](https://endoverdose.net/about/chapters/) includes California communities and campuses, while the [California kit page](https://store.endoverdose.net/products/narcan-kit-ca-residents) offers a two-dose intranasal kit after training, with shipping charged. The page displayed 'Sold out' when reviewed; its stated shipping delay is not proof that more donations would resolve the constraint.
sections.monitoring:
The [July–September 2024 impact report](https://cdn.sanity.io/files/03xshhuu/production/fc944226581fe8e9a80cd6d39aa74f59574d954e.pdf) reports aggregate training and distribution. These are outputs, not independently measured unique lives saved. The [August 2026 campaign](https://endoverdose.net/campaign/) is newer and documents national chapter growth and operations beyond California. No state-by-state unique-recipient, additional rescue or funding allocation dataset was located. A useful evaluation would link kit exposure, actual emergency use, alternative rescue availability and unique-person follow-up without counting repeat reversals as repeated lifetimes.

A focused geographic audit counted 16 California cards among 62 in the current directory, which is not reconciled with the campaign's 80-plus chapter claim. Four named California event highlights in the 2024 report sum to 5,280 of 71,733 reported quarterly doses (7.36%). This is a subset of historical delivery, not a floor for current California health, and the venue does not establish patient residence. These observations inform a weak scenario only; no chapter or dose ratio is mechanically substituted for QALYs.
sections.qualitative:
My central judgment is that broad-reach delivery probably has positive health value, but an ordinary gift is not yet a compelling high-confidence health bargain. [Walley's community study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23372174/) associated greater overdose-education/naloxone implementation with lower mortality; it was not randomized and did not evaluate End Overdose. [Zang's 2024 Rhode Island simulation](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2819204) highlights targeting and whether somebody actually witnesses an overdose. It is a model, not an observed charity effect. Importantly, the [HEALing Communities cluster trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38884347/) found no statistically significant primary mortality reduction for a broader intervention bundle: rate ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.76–1.09. This does not negate naloxone's clinical action, but warns that increasing activities does not guarantee population benefit.

The model therefore discounts broad-audience exposure, unusable or unavailable kits, other rescuers, repeated scenes and replacement funding. Nonfatal morbidity and test-strip effects are omitted rather than invented.

A [2025 festival survey](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41430526/) found 55.5% of 227 respondents already carried naloxone in some context and 8.4% had ever used it on someone. This small, selected cross-section cannot supply an annual End Overdose rescue rate; it supports both relevance and substantial existing protection. In a more targeted [Rikers visitor cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29175025/), 40 of 226 follow-up respondents witnessed an overdose in six months. That high-risk result is not transferable wholesale to students or festival audiences.

For California, residence at delivery is insufficient if rescue or subsequent health occurs elsewhere. California chapter share is not an outcome-weighted marginal allocation.
sections.cost:
Our revised conditional scenario is about **$13 million per ten California QALYs**. It retains the national model's naloxone-mortality calculation and all recipient costs, then makes the geographic assumptions explicit. This is a weak, judgment-based allocation—not a measured California return or a comprehensive estimate of every End Overdose program.

The central geographic prior assigns 15% of marginal exposure/person-time to California before allowing for relative effectiveness. It then assumes California's incremental yield is 75% of that elsewhere because existing supply and alternative rescue may substitute more; normalizing those weights assigns about 11.7% of national modeled health to California. Neither fraction is observed. The [original 2024 report](https://cdn.sanity.io/files/03xshhuu/production/fc944226581fe8e9a80cd6d39aa74f59574d954e.pdf), current chapters, a California kit offer and [event footprint](https://endoverdose.net/events/) support meaningful California presence, but not an exact health share. National online delivery and out-of-state expansion prevent assuming that an ordinary gift stays here.

Holding clinical assumptions fixed, a 1% California health share gives roughly $152 million per ten QALYs, while 50% gives $3.0 million. Combining geographic and clinical stress assumptions expands the range from roughly $17,000 to $1.46 trillion; these are not confidence bounds or donation offers. A gift could produce national benefit and no additional California benefit. The direct-delivery mechanism supports an inspectable scenario, but a state-by-channel marginal delivery and unique-patient dataset is needed to replace these priors.

The [2024 Form 990](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202530849349300213/IRS990) records $970,440 total expenses: $730,276 program, $207,274 management and $32,890 fundraising in Part IX. Its Part III program total is inconsistent with those figures, so it is not used to allocate the model. Dividing total spending by reported trainees gives roughly $4.20 per training, but does not price a completed training-plus-kit package or an extra rescue.
sections.funding:
The [August 2026 campaign](https://endoverdose.net/campaign/) reports 25,000 naloxone units donated by Amneal, alongside training, chapter growth and state operations. Units are not explicitly two-dose kits, and remaining inventory is unknown; a gift must not automatically be modeled as purchasing medication. [California DHCS](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/individuals/naloxone-distribution-project/ndp-frequently-asked-questions/) offers naloxone to eligible entities and identifies other free community sources and a $19 consumer two-pack alternative. Individuals cannot apply directly to NDP, and NDP stock must remain in-state. We did not verify that End Overdose receives NDP stock. Public supply can complement outreach while also making replacement of another source more likely.

The original 2024 filing reports $20,042 cash and negative $16,572 net assets; these historical figures do not establish a current cash emergency. The independently checked 2022–24 expense series averages $809,773.67.

model.costScope: Full ordinary recipient gift across all functions. National model conservatively quantifies the naloxone pathway while costing unquantified activities; C=100000 is normalization only.
model.geographicAttribution: An explicit subjective geographic allocation replaces the null: p=0.15 is the share of marginal exposure/person-time provisionally assigned to California before relative yield; rho=0.75 is California's incremental health yield relative to elsewhere. g_CA=p*rho/(1-p+p*rho)=0.1168831169. p accounts for patient location and later mobility once; rho accounts for relative incremental yield after local alternatives. Neither is an observed resident, chapter or dose share. Normalization calibrates the two regional yields to the fixed national mean: it reallocates, rather than reduces, national benefit. CA and USA totals must not be added. The unchanged all-population health total is divided between CA and elsewhere consistently. This is a weak prior, not a geographic finding.
model.formula: Offers=G*a/c. Unique additional deaths prevented=Offers*e*d*r*f*b. L=sum(k=1..T)[u*(1-m)^k/(1.03)^k]. All-populationQALYs=deaths*L/1.03 for rescue at end ofyear1. CaliforniaQALYs=allQALYs*g_CA. DonorUSD/10CaliforniaQALYs=10G/CaliforniaQALYs. Gross resources=G+Offers*(unpaid labor+donated stock value). Central parameters: a=.75,c=50,e=.005,d=.5,r=.2,f=.2,b=.5,u=.75,m=.04,T=30. Geographic extension only: g_CA=p*rho/(1-p+p*rho), Q_CA=Q_all*g_CA. Central p=.15,rho=.75; favorable p=.5,rho=1.5; pessimistic p=.02,rho=.25. National clinical parameters and Q_all remain unchanged. p is a modeled marginal exposure/person-time allocation, not a chapter-count ratio; rho reallocates relative local effectiveness without applying a second blanket discount to national benefit.
model.counterfactual: Other free distribution, public stock, purchase and emergency responders remain available; only changes in timely rescue and subsequent survival beyond those alternatives count. Ordinary gifts may replace funding or support national expansion outside California. Geographic p may be zero if the marginal gift supports only out-of-state work. rho distinguishes local alternatives from the already included nationwide average rescue and budget additionality; it is not another medication-stock replacement factor.
model.attribution: Funding additionality is distinct from incremental rescue; donated stock is a complement with no assumed cash purchase cost. Public/partner contributions and repeated rescues cannot each receive full causal health credit.
model.uncertainty: The original California share remains empirically unidentified. This version provides a deliberately subjective conditional central rather than pretending lack of measurement requires no scenario. Historic event doses, current California chapters and a CA-specific offer establish substantial delivery presence, but no calibrated distribution for p or rho. The central is not a statistical expectation, and finite stress scenarios are not bounds. A California-only null can coexist with positive national health. This quantifies the naloxone mortality pathway while retaining all recipient costs; unmodeled morbidity/test-strip/education effects are not demonstrated zero.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional two-dose kit opportunities; unique otherwise unprotected overdose situations; additional timely rescues; unique-person survival and quality-adjusted life-years, not gross doses or training completions. New geographic bridge distinguishes venue/delivery outputs from where additional patient health occurs; no observed dose or chapter is mechanically converted to a California QALY.

sensitivity: Conditional central Q_CA=0.0769425918759858 per $100,000 gives $12996702.80943714 per ten California QALYs. This is the naloxone mortality pathway with all recipient costs, not a comprehensive portfolio estimate.
Geography alone, holding clinical yield central, gives roughly $3.04 million at g=50% and $151.91 million at g=1%. No evidence establishes either as a bound.
At p=.15, changing rho from .75 to1 removes the relative CA-yield adjustment: g=.15, price about $10.13 million. Public alternatives do not automatically erase the value of last-mile outreach.

Combined favorable and pessimistic clinical/geographic cases inherit the national stress assumptions and should not be advertised as alternative donation offers. Zero California benefit is possible even with positive national benefit.

With all clinical inputs central, even g=1 costs about $1.52 million per ten QALYs. Geographic concentration alone cannot reach the $1 million benchmark; better targeting or delivery yield is required.

Venue, shipping address, chapter count and eventual California patient health are distinct. A state-by-channel fulfilled-kit and unique-patient follow-up dataset should replace p/rho before the point estimate is treated as decision-grade.

Channel shares of marginal delivery, geographic exposure and relative state-level incremental rescue; no weights were observed.
No probability distribution supports a statistical best estimate for geographic allocation. This model is a disclosed weak prior, to be updated rather than presented as measurement.
