what: Surgery on Sunday is the Lexington, Kentucky charity coordinating free outpatient surgery and associated assessment for eligible uninsured or underinsured people, not the separate Louisville organization.

Its volunteer surgeons, anesthesia teams and donated facilities support procedures ranging from cataracts and hernias to gallbladder, tonsil and orthopedic surgery; a donation pays the recipient’s support costs rather than buying a standardized operation.
The modeled benefit is additional relief of pain, impaired vision and functional limitations over a finite period, after allowing for alternative treatment, operating constraints and surgical harm.
strengths: The service has a direct clinical pathway and screens patients for medical necessity; clinicians may choose less invasive care rather than operate.
Original returns now provide all recipient expenses, including separately netted fundraising-event costs, and a matched FY2023 benchmark of $2,943 per surgical patient.

A December 2025 medical-society account corroborates continuing volunteer-based operations; donated professional and facility inputs can make modest cash support useful when both patient need and clinical capacity are available.
reservations: Our working estimate is about $1.2M per better life, combining health and household-resource equivalents; clinical persistence, targeting, cash costs and donation-driven surgery remain judgments.
No current procedure mix, severity distribution, complication series or donation-funded case queue was found; newer filings change patient counts while retaining an old narrative date.

Substantial historical unrestricted assets and volunteer bottlenecks leave the next gift’s effect uncertain. Cash costs omit donated and external resources, and the fiscal transition prevents a comparable consecutive three-year expense mean.

sections.what: The recipient is Surgery on Sunday, EIN 20-3187452, in Lexington. The [official donation route](https://surgeryonsunday.org/donate/) leads to a [Charityproud form](https://surgeryonsunday.charityproud.org/Donate) naming this charity and offering general giving; no transaction was made. Its [clinical menu](https://surgeryonsunday.org/types-surgeries/) covers several outpatient specialties, not only unusually cost-effective cataract surgery. The [FAQ](https://surgeryonsunday.org/frequently-asked-questions/) describes monthly volunteer operating lists, eligibility near Lexington, low income and lack of usable insurance. Residence within 250 miles, with limited exceptions, supports attribution to the USA’s 50 states and DC regardless of citizenship. Dental care is currently excluded despite the broader wording in the tax-return mission. Patients needing overnight admission are outside the routine service. The separate Louisville program’s research and outputs are not attributed to this recipient.
sections.monitoring:
The [FY2022 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202340389349300129/IRS990) reports 78 surgical patients in its dated year and the [FY2023 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202303499349300825/IRS990) reports 86. Recipient costs per such patient are $2,845 and $2,943 after event-cost addbacks; these are average support benchmarks, not marginal operation prices. One person may have multiple procedures, while assessment and nonsurgical care also consume resources. The [transition filing](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202423189349301977/IRS990) and [2024 filing](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202543189349301704/IRS990) retain a June 2023 narrative date beside changing counts of 46 and 93, so neither supplies a reliable matched current denominator. A [December 2025 partner account](https://www.lexingtondoctors.org/2025/12/04/supported-by-the-lms-foundation-surgery-on-sunday-2/) supports continued operations, not a 2026 volume estimate. The public surgery-date page still lists 2024 dates. Priority monitoring is dated unique patients and procedures, clinical indications and baseline severity, complications, follow-up utility, alternative-care waiting time, cancellations and cash-funded extra slots. Testimonials are not a controlled health-outcome series. A [May 2026 partner fundraising notice](https://www.lexingtondoctors.org/event/36th-annual-lexington-medical-society-golf-tournament-may-20th-2026/) again names the charity among supported services; it reports no new grant amount or completed-case count.

The October 2026 source check still finds calendar 2024 as the latest original filing, with the same stale June 2023 narrative beside93 patients. Current FAQ timing is30–60days after approval, conditional on surgeon availability, not a measured gift-to-surgery latency. The May 2026 nonclinical-volunteer capacity banner does not measure surgeon or operating-room slots. Actual recipient purchases, unpaid leave, net travel after assistance, recovery earnings and volunteer expenses remain unobserved.
sections.qualitative:
Trials establish that benefits depend on clinical selection, not that every free operation creates the same QALYs. [Earlier first-eye cataract surgery](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2095519/) added 0.056 QALYs over one year in older women compared with a waiting-list strategy; that is a timing comparison, not evidence of perpetual untreated blindness. [Minimally symptomatic hernia repair](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17000388/) added 0.031 QALYs over two years. The [24-month C-GALL analysis](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK604689/) found a small, statistically uncertain 0.019 QALY advantage for cholecystectomy over conservative management in uncomplicated symptomatic disease. [NATTINA](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK599279/) found an adjusted, multiple-imputation 0.118 QALY advantage over two years for tonsillectomy in adults meeting UK recurrent-tonsillitis thresholds; its [safety report](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK599275/) also recorded 52 postoperative bleeding episodes among 231 operated participants and 47 readmissions. Those risks must not be assigned to every outpatient specialty. Trial QALYs already reflect their trial comparators and measured treatment burden: we do not add them together or deduct a second harm allowance from them. Instead, our independent utility-duration prior is discounted for alternative care and charged an explicit perioperative loss. There is no measured Surgery on Sunday case mix with which to transport these effects. Selection of more impaired patients could support greater relief; mild disease and eventual access elsewhere could produce much less.

The current estimate separates purchaser replacement from clinical additionality, considers signed economic effects and retains both the historical clinical model and independent sensitivity cases. One- to two-year trial findings do not identify the current three-year utility prior or local procedure mix. Scientific acceptance verifies the declared conditional arithmetic and boundaries, not measured marginal effectiveness or a current funding offer.
sections.cost:
Our working estimate is about **$1.2 million per better life in the USA**, counting ten combined health and household-resource equivalents. Surgery on Sunday can turn donated professional and facility capacity into relief of impaired vision, pain and functional limitations at relatively modest recipient cash cost. We charge the full gift, including assessment and other work whose separate benefits are not quantified. This is a conditional research comparison, not a quoted surgical slot or measured donation return.

**What does a donation enable?** A $10,000 normalization funds 3.33 nominal patient-treatment equivalents at $3,000 comprehensive recipient support cost each. That allowance includes administration, fundraising, assessment and unsuccessful referrals; it is anchored to the matched FY2023 average of $2,943 per surgical patient, not the narrower, undated $1,000–$1,500 public illustrations. A judged 50% funding and operating response produces **1.67 additional patient equivalents**, or $6,000 donor cash per added equivalent. Clinician schedules, facilities, other donors and reserves may limit that response. Neither the normalization nor the five-patient mathematical cap verifies current capacity.

**Why should surgery improve health?** We model 10% of added patients as otherwise buying equivalent care: their matching surgical benefit and burden occur in both worlds, so they receive no added clinical credit. For the other 1.5 patient equivalents, a separately judged annual utility improvement of 0.04 lasts three years, adjusted for 1% annual mortality, a quarter-year intervention delay and 3% discounting. After retaining 60% of relief relative to alternative free care, later treatment or conservative management, and subtracting a full 0.01 QALY treatment burden, each nonbuyer gains 0.05613 QALYs. Total health is **0.08420 USA QALYs per $10,000**, or **$1.19M per ten clinical QALYs**. These are not measured Surgery on Sunday outcomes. Trials described below show why indication and severity matter; their net QALYs are not inserted as gross utility and charged harm again.

**What happens to household resources?** Ten percent are assumed to avoid an actual $600 own payment for equivalent care, less $30 incremental travel. This is not a waived hospital bill or insurance payment. Nonbuyers incur $30 residual travel, $150 actual lost disposable pay and $20 medication cost beyond their without-gift alternative, after any support or paid leave. Together these one-off recipient flows are **−$205**. All purchase probabilities, cash amounts and the $30,000 household-resource baseline are judgments; eligibility is not measured disposable income.

Functional recovery may improve work. Among nonbuyers, 25% are assumed to be work-limited in a way that can improve, with the same 60% clinical additionality discount. The resulting 0.225 patient equivalents earn a judged $500 of extra disposable income per year for two years. These are patients alive in both counterfactual worlds, not ordinary earnings of newly surviving people. Applying yearly mortality gives $221.64 expected raw earnings. Only 25% of its welfare-equivalent score is credited independently of health utility, which can already reflect role limitations and worry; this overlap adjustment does not erase real cash.

Restored earnings are survival-adjusted year-end flows. The first annual log increment uses resources after the contemporaneous $200 burden; the next uses the unburdened baseline. One-off costs and avoided payments are valued at the quarter-year delay. Five volunteer-person equivalents per added patient each incur a judged $10 actual unreimbursed cash cost, or −$83.33 per gift; unpaid leisure is not lost wages. These signed pathways, using the [Coefficient Giving resource-to-health crosswalk](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/), yield **−0.003239 household-resource equivalents**. Health plus resources is **0.08096 combined equivalents per $10,000**, giving **$1.24M per better life**. Resource equivalents are welfare comparisons, not observed clinical QALYs.

**Why did the estimate change?** The preserved earlier health-only price was **$405K**. The new model shortens assumed relief from five to three years, lowers annual gross utility from 0.05 to 0.04, lowers funding response from 60% to 50%, and explicitly separates purchasers and intervention timing. These are reconsidered priors, not newly measured effects. Restoring the old clinical assumptions reproduces the old health result; cash and timing alternatives are inspectable separately. One- and two-year relief, zero funding, absent capacity, greater harms, negative earnings, no purchase savings and unknown components challenge the central. No scenario range is a confidence interval.

The institutional gross-resource companion adds a judged $5,000 of donated labor/facility/supply opportunity cost and $200 expected external complication resources per added patient, making $18,666.67 per gift and **$2.31M per ten combined equivalents**. It is not a net societal estimate: displaced alternative care and other institutional effects are unknown. Recipient and volunteer cash losses already in welfare are not charged again, and donated professional time is not credited as household income. Screening, referral, survival and other unquantified effects remain unknown rather than observed zero. Gifts above the model's $25,000 domain cannot be linearly extrapolated into a delivery promise.
sections.funding:
The [2024 original filing](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202543189349301704/IRS990) reports $250,740 in Part IX expenses and $12,073 of event costs netted against revenue. Reconstructing gross recipient spending gives $262,813: $186,178 program, $50,794 administration and $25,841 fundraising including the addback. Gross receipts similarly rise from $250,470 to $262,543, leaving the same $270 deficit. Payroll, benefits and payroll taxes total $119,697; patient care is $70,833 and interpreter/credentialing costs $16,570. Cash and savings were $352,026, with $108,363 securities and $459,108 unrestricted net assets at year end—not a current cash-shortfall finding. The [FY2022](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202340389349300129/IRS990) and [FY2023 returns](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202303499349300825/IRS990) classify $21,218 and $95,407 as government grants. Their programs are unidentified, but these entries contradict an unqualified claim of no government assistance. A [2023 founder appeal](https://www.lexingtondoctors.org/2023/06/14/surgery-on-sunday-needs-volunteers/) identified volunteers as the greatest need; it is not evidence of today’s bottleneck. A [2022 direct account](https://www.chausa.org/news-and-publications/publications/health-progress/archives/fall-2022/the-power-of-teamwork-nonprofit-changes-lives-through-free-surgery-model) describes nominal facility rent, per-patient supplies, donated ancillary care and some travel support. Public evidence does not show what extra cash now unlocks. The 50% response factor is a judgment covering donor replacement, reserves and operating constraints once, not a measured expansion promise. Appendix: corrected full-period expenses are $221,875 for July 2021–June 2022, $253,116 for July 2022–June 2023, and $262,813 for calendar 2024. These are not consecutive periods. Adding the intervening six-month $125,061 return produces $862,865 over 42 months, an annualized historical rate of $246,533—not the standard consecutive three-year mean, which remains unavailable.

The October 2026 original-source refresh reproduces all four expense/event-cost reconciliations. The latest three contiguous filings span 30 months and $640,990 gross expense, annualized $256,396; this is a separate historical rate, not a consecutive three-year mean. Current unrestricted cash-funded surgical capacity remains unresolved.

model.costScope: Full donor gift retained with judged $3000 comprehensive recipient cost per nominal patient-equivalent. Separate gross institutional resources per added case. Household and volunteer cash affect welfare, not a repeated donor charge.
model.geographicAttribution: Routine 250-mile Lexington residency eligibility supports USA residents. Central g=1; pessimistic .99 allows exceptional nonresident cases. Citizenship is not residency. Independent affiliates are excluded. Actual residence extract is not available.
model.formula: N=min(G/cashCase*funding,capacity); nonbuyer=N*(1-purchaseShare); health=g*[nonbuyer*(clinicalAdditionality*du*sum finite survival/discount minus acute h)-donorHarm]. Signed recipient, survival-adjusted year-end restored earnings, and volunteer cash each use separate logarithmic crosswalks. Price=10*G/(health+resources) only when positive.
model.counterfactual: Purchased equivalent care has matching benefits and surgical burden in both worlds; no additional clinical or restored-wage credit. Other clinical relief discount is conditional on nonbuyers. Common-alive patients may regain function, not ordinary wages of newly surviving people. Actual cash after support and paid leave, not retail bills.
model.attribution: No procedure-mix weights inferred from menu or stale counts; all dose/cost/funding/capacity/clinical/economic parameters explicit judgments. Recovered wage cohort includes annual mortality and year-end receipts; full one-off burdens retained regardless earnings overlap discount.
model.uncertainty: Conditional partial judgment comparison, not identified expected unrestricted return or verified capacity; typed unknowns remain different from zero, and negative welfare has no favorable price. Year3 relief and all income parameters are unmeasured.
model.nativeOutcomes: Per $10,000: 3.33 nominal patient equivalents, 1.67 additional equivalents, 1.5 nonbuyer clinical equivalents, 0.084202 health years, −0.003239 resource equivalents and 0.080963 combined equivalents. These are conditional model outputs, not observed services per dollar.

model.priceScope: Working judgment estimate of incremental USA surgical health from an ordinary unrestricted gift, charging all recipient support costs. It excludes unquantified assessment/referral benefits and unpriced external resources; it is neither a measured whole-portfolio return nor a full societal resource-cost estimate.

annualExpenses.accountingBasis: Original cash-basis Form 990, 2021-07-01 through 2022-06-30; Part IX plus separately netted event costs. Reported depreciation retained. Full-year windows are not consecutive across the transition; no standard three-year mean.

reports.priceScope: Conditional partial donation-dollar comparison including signed household resources; no verified marginal surgery offer.

historicalModel.costScope: Whole ordinary recipient gift including program, administration, fundraising and separately netted event costs. Full reported cash-basis accounting expenses retain reported depreciation; this is not a pure bank-cash-flow measure. The $3,000 case-equivalent is calibrated to $2,943 per FY2023 surgical patient, not a contracted per-operation rate. No restricted best-procedure allocation, retail-bill savings, earnings or public-cost offsets.
historicalModel.geographicAttribution: Routine 250-mile Lexington residency eligibility supports USA residents. Central g=1; pessimistic .99 allows exceptional nonresident cases. Citizenship is not residency. Independent affiliates are excluded. Actual residence extract is not available.
historicalModel.formula: q_gross = Δu × sum[t=1..T]((1−m)^t/(1.03)^t). N_add = (G/c)×b. q_net = s×q_gross−h. Q_all = N_add×q_net. Q_USA = Q_all×g. Price per 10 = 10 × scenario costUSD / Q_USA only when Q_USA>0. Scenario costUSD=G for recipient-cash scenarios; the two resource-cost stresses explicitly add their opportunity-cost allowance. b is funding-driven operating/capacity additionality; s discounts gross benefit for equivalent counterfactual care. Perioperative loss h applies to every added patient-treatment equivalent, including s=0, and is not multiplied by s.
historicalModel.counterfactual: Without the gift some care may still occur using reserves or other donors (b), and some patients may obtain equivalent care through other charities, insurance, public eligibility or later treatment (s). s is a fractional health-benefit discount, not necessarily a literal permanently untreated patient fraction. Conservative nonoperative care may be sufficient for some cases. No assumption that every billed procedure creates benefit. Even where equivalent benefit occurs elsewhere, this conservative formulation retains the full incremental perioperative burden h for every donation-enabled patient-treatment equivalent; it does not assume that alternative care perfectly offsets that harm.
historicalModel.attribution: The $3,000 benchmark is per surgical-patient treatment equivalent because the original denominator counts patients, not operations. Repeated procedures per patient are implicitly averaged into the utility and harm assumptions; there is no extra credit for each procedure. Volunteer/facility cooperation complements cash; b discounts its operating response, reserve use and donor replacement once. s separately discounts health relative to alternative care, including later access. No independently measured case mix or funding response is claimed.
historicalModel.uncertainty: A genuine working best judgment, not a probability-weighted measurement or endorsement. The $3,000 cash benchmark survives the cost correction, while the clinical persistence and marginal capacity assumptions remain weak. Five years extrapolates beyond the one- to two-year trials. Gross utility is a new independent prior, not trial net QALYs with duplicate harm deductions. There is no survival benefit or lifetime expansion. Positive, zero and adverse scenarios are judgment stresses, not confidence limits.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: Observed FY2023: 86 surgical patients and $253,116 gross recipient expenses, including $13,847 of event costs outside Part IX. Derived average $2,943.21 per surgical patient includes assessment and referral overhead. The model uses 3.33 nominal patient-treatment equivalents per $10,000 and 2 additional equivalents after funding response. Patient-treatment equivalents are an approximation, not an observed count of distinct operations. Gross 0.22234 QALY and net 0.12340 QALY per added equivalent yield 0.24681 USA QALY.

inputs.name: G
inputs.rationale: Small normalization relative to annual spending; no verified room-for-more-funding tranche.

inputs.name: FY2023 surgical patients
inputs.rationale: Matched year-ending June 2023 original filing; do not use later stale-date counts.

inputs.name: FY2023 full expense
inputs.rationale: Original Part IX $239,269 plus Part VIII event direct expense $13,847. All reported recipient expenses; reported depreciation retained.

inputs.name: Historical expense per surgical patient
inputs.rationale: Derived arithmetic from observed gross recipient expense divided by 86 surgical patients in the matched year; not a procedure count or observed marginal price.

inputs.name: c
inputs.rationale: Rounded from corrected matched $2,943 recipient cost per surgical patient. Stress $1,500–$5,000; no inflation update or binding current price is observed.

inputs.name: b
inputs.rationale: Discount for reserves, replacement donors and volunteer/OR constraints; stress .2–.9 and zero.

inputs.name: s
inputs.rationale: Discount for alternative access, later treatment and conservative management; not a measured untreated share.

inputs.name: Δu
inputs.rationale: Independent annual utility prior for selected heterogeneous surgical patients, not a weighted trial estimate. Trial net QALYs anchor plausibility but are not plugged into the gross-utility formula.

inputs.name: T
inputs.rationale: Explicit five-year judgment about relief persistence, not observed trial follow-up. No benefit after year five; stress one to ten years.

inputs.name: m
inputs.rationale: Simplified survival adjustment, not recipient age-specific life table; pessimistic .02.

inputs.name: h
inputs.rationale: Judgment allowance for pain, complications and rare fatal harm across a treatment episode, including repeated procedures; not an observed adverse-event rate. Retained even when s=0.

inputs.name: discount rate
inputs.rationale: Conventional analyst discount choice.

inputs.name: g
inputs.rationale: Residency eligibility strongly supports domestic boundary; pessimistic .99.

inputs.name: Donated resource addition
inputs.rationale: Illustrative opportunity cost, not hospital retail charges; actual shadow cost unknown.

inputs.name: 2023 transition expense
inputs.rationale: Original July–December 2023 six-month period, separately shown. Used only in the explicit 42-month bridge, not as a full year.

inputs.name: Current procedure mix and marginal funded queue
inputs.rationale: Exact key diligence gap; no inferred mix from the service menu.

The adverse low-additionality scenario is net harmful. s=0 with b=.6 retains -.02 QALY of perioperative loss; b=0 gives zero operations and zero harm. Neither has a finite favorable price.

An illustrative $5,000 opportunity cost per added treatment equivalent gives about $810,000 per 10. Charging the same allowance to every nominal equivalent gives about $1.08 million. Both omit unresolved external costs and are sensitivities, not measured social returns.

reports.program: Trauma-focused outpatient mental health treatment for veterans, service members and connected family members

what: Headstrong pays a network of clinicians to provide trauma-focused outpatient care to veterans, service members and family members connected to their care.
It offers therapist matching, in-person and telehealth treatment, with the first 30 sessions provided without a client charge.
The intended health benefit is relief of persistent trauma-related distress and functional impairment through treatment that would otherwise be delayed, inaccessible or unsuitable.
strengths: The intervention is direct clinical treatment supported by randomized evidence and VA recommendations, not awareness activity counted as health.
Current disclosures provide treatment-session volume, client counts, treatment fees and access time, enabling a transparent service-cost benchmark.
Nationwide telehealth and private clinician matching plausibly address barriers that remain even when veterans have insurance or VA eligibility.
reservations: Headline outcome percentages rely on selected treatment-duration/completer samples and do not establish incremental health effects for all clients.
A complete treatment episode can cost much more than one session; current episode length, attrition, durability and alternative-care use remain uncertain.
Public and private care can substitute, and unrestricted reserves can finance services without the next donation; our central does not indicate exceptional cost-effectiveness.

sections.what: [Headstrong's current pathway](https://theheadstrongproject.org/get-help/) includes intake, therapist matching and trauma-focused care such as CPT, EMDR and prolonged exposure. The first 30 sessions have no client charge; extended treatment includes a copay paid to the therapist. These are paid clinicians, not a volunteer-surgery model. Its [2025 report](https://theheadstrongproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/2025AnnualReport_FINAL.pdf) records 52,000 sessions, 2,947 clients, 12 days on average to care and in-person coverage in 20 states plus DC, alongside telehealth nationwide. Sessions delivered to continuing clients are not completed new treatment courses.
sections.monitoring: The [public outcome page](https://theheadstrongproject.org/about/) qualifies its improvement statistics as applying to clients with at least 15–20 sessions or completed treatment. The annual report's chart shows a newer 61% PTSD-symptom-reduction metric without a sufficient denominator or definition to use as a causal effect. An [earlier program description](https://www.traumacenternyc.org/projects/utilizing-emdr-as-the-primary-modality-to-treat-veteran-ptsd-in-a-community-based-program) provides paired PCL-5 scores for only 89 clients: 73 initially above its PTSD cutoff and 54 afterward. This is encouraging but uncontrolled and selectively observed. We need entry-cohort follow-up including early exits, completed episode length, diagnosis mix, utility outcomes and use of alternative care. Satisfaction, symptom-score changes and historical suicide counts are not directly converted into QALYs.
sections.qualitative: The [VA recommends](https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/txessentials/overview_therapy.asp) CPT, EMDR and prolonged exposure. A [60-veteran wait-list trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17032094/) supports CPT's causal symptom benefit. However, a [larger veteran trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8771295/) comparing two active therapies found substantial dropout—about 47% for CPT and 56% for prolonged exposure—so completer success is not a safe population effect. A [randomized US cost-utility trial](https://www.psychiatrist.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/12214_cost-effectiveness-prolonged-exposure-therapy-versus.pdf) found an intention-to-treat advantage of 0.056 QALYs over one year for prolonged exposure versus sertraline. It largely enrolled civilian women and is an anchor, not a directly transferable Headstrong effect. No suicide-prevention benefit or separate depression benefit is added.
sections.cost: Total [2025 Form 990 expenses](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202621319349302162/IRS990) divided by reported sessions imply roughly $269 per session, including organizational overhead; treatment fees alone imply about $157. Our model uses $275 per session and 30 sessions per treatment-entry equivalent, or $8,250 before additionality adjustments. Its cautious judgment central is about $2.0 million per 10 USA QALYs. The favorable and pessimistic scenarios are about $82,000 and $474 million, with a separate zero-additionality case; these are stress tests, not confidence bounds. The model discounts clinical transfer, relapse/counterfactual catch-up and care available elsewhere. Current data do not justify calling Headstrong a high-confidence bargain. The decisive upside would be shorter equally effective courses reaching genuinely unserved clients.
sections.funding: The [2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202621319349302162/IRS990) reports $13.964 million expense, including $11.933 million program, $0.771 million management and $1.259 million fundraising; treatment fees are $8.172 million. Revenue is $13.637 million, including $0.991 million service fees. Net assets total $10.220 million, of which $5.362 million is unrestricted. The [2024 audit](https://docs.candid.org/efiles/9218143/d01eb21e-d83c-43de-935c-f44b59e37424.pdf) describes a minimum four-month operating reserve policy and a longer-term goal of eight to twelve months or more. A [June 2026 funder account](https://nyhealthfoundation.org/grant-outcome/maintaining-and-maximizing-veterans-access-to-mental-health-care/) supports continuing access work but pools Headstrong with NYU services; it is not an isolated cost-per-patient experiment. No current marginal funding commitment was identified. Annual-report and filing totals differ slightly, and 2023 audited expenses differ from the tax return; the financial series below consistently uses Form 990 rather than silently mixing bases.

model.costScope: Ordinary unrestricted recipient donation, with all accounting overhead included in session cost; no cherry-picked trauma modality. G=$10,000 is arithmetic normalization only. Donor cost is gross, with no fee-for-service leverage or avoided medical-cost deduction assumed. Paid clinicians already enter the cost. Patient time, extended-care copays and incremental downstream care are excluded from donor cost and tested separately where possible.
model.geographicAttribution: Reported domestic in-person network and all-50-state telehealth support predominantly 50-states/DC resident benefits. Central g=.99, favorable1 and pessimistic.95 are residence-share judgments allowing overseas/territorial service-member spillover; client military status is not residence. A verified residence extract is missing.
model.formula: Episode-equivalents = G/(c×n). q = q1 × sum[t=1..T](p^(t−1)/(1.03^t)). Q_all = G/(c×n) × q × f × b × s. Q_USA = Q_all×g. Price per10 =10G/Q_USA. q1 is a net intention-to-treat first-year increment, already including trial attrition/treatment burden; no additional completer multiplier is applied.
model.counterfactual: q1 compares an effective trauma-treatment offer with insufficient/less-effective care, not with perfect health. s discounts for an equivalent health trajectory through VA, military, insurer or other charity treatment; delayed treatment can yield partial additionality. b separately discounts for reserves, replacement funding and capacity not expanded by a gift. Annual persistence p includes relapse and untreated/comparator catch-up. No suicide mortality reduction is inferred from symptoms.
model.attribution: f discounts transfer from researched modalities/populations to the actual mixture of adult trauma, family care and routine delivery. It is not the accounting program-expense share and does not remove overhead twice. Full-portfolio dollars remain in c. Clinical improvements and funding access are separate links.
model.uncertainty: The central is a deliberately cautious judgment informed by observed costs and external causal evidence, not a fitted organizational effect. First-year utility, long-term persistence, treatment episode length and counterfactual access dominate. Scenarios span plausible favorable and poor execution rather than statistical percentiles; zero health additionality remains possible.
model.nativeOutcomes: 2025 reported 52,000 sessions and 2,947 clients; 70% of sessions via telehealth per Form990. These are annual services, not incident treatment courses. At central c=$275 and n=30, the normalization buys 36.36 nominal sessions or1.212 episode-equivalents before the funding and counterfactual discounts.

sensitivity: At central inputs, halving episode length from30 to15 sessions halves the price only if net clinical efficacy is preserved; more sessions are not automatically more QALYs.
With30 sessions at$275 and f×b×s×g=.3564, meeting$100,000 per10 requires q≥2.3148 per entry; meeting$1 million requires q≥.23148. Central q=.11553 meets neither.
Holding central efficacy and other factors fixed, the$1 million threshold requires n≤14.97 sessions; the$100,000 threshold requires n≤1.50, which is inconsistent with a full clinical course.

Using2025 annual-report instead of tax expense changes the gross session benchmark by less than1%, much less than uncertainty in episode length or counterfactual care.

reports.program: Coordinated donated dental treatment for financially vulnerable older, disabled and medically fragile adults

acceptance.evidence: docs/geography-discovery/dln-usa-independent-acceptance-2026-10-02.md — independently reconsidered health and signed resources; negative wages fully charged and finite-domain/timing controls corrected. Conditional comparative estimate, not verified donor capacity.

what: Dental Lifeline Network connects financially vulnerable older adults, people with disabilities and medically fragile patients with volunteer dentists and dental laboratories.
Its coordinators assess eligibility, match patients and organize comprehensive donated treatment such as restorations, extractions and dentures.
The intended health benefit is relief of oral pain and impaired eating or daily function when effective dental care would otherwise remain unavailable or delayed.
strengths: Volunteer dentists and laboratories create plausible leverage for donated coordination dollars, with a direct treatment mechanism rather than awareness alone.
Current eligibility requires patients to exhaust available dental benefits, reducing some public/private insurance substitution.
A randomized denture trial supports oral-health benefit for a relevant older population, and current program examples demonstrate substantive restorative care.
reservations: Reported patients served can include untreated volunteer matches, and licensee patients do not share the national recipient’s exact financial boundary; neither count proves a completed donor-caused treatment.

Our estimate is approximately $1.3M per better life, but clinical utility, eventual completion, funding response and net household effects remain uncertain judgments rather than measured DLN outcomes.

Existing government and private grants, Medicare-covered medically linked care, volunteer availability, and restricted reserves all affect additionality; neither donated retail value nor a medical-clearance label proves exceptional cost-effectiveness.

sections.what: [DDS eligibility](https://dentallifeline.org/help/) requires financial need plus age 65 or older, permanent disability or medically necessary dental care. Volunteers provide comprehensive non-cosmetic treatment at no patient charge. The [2025 annual report](https://dentallifeline.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/2025-Annual-Report-v10.8.pdf) distinguishes 4,367 DDS individuals served from 6,038 people reached across programs; the latter is not a clinical-treatment denominator. The DDS total includes licensee states. Dentists and labs contribute treatment in their own practices; coordination, matching and support still require paid resources. A [June 2026 example](https://dentallifeline.org/blog/veterans-oral-health-restored-through-the-dds-program/) describes restorations and a partial denture for a patient with extensive decay and pain, illustrating the mechanism rather than its average effect. The [current FAQ](https://dentallifeline.org/help/faq/) says the program is not emergency treatment, ordinarily excludes implants, and depends on volunteer availability. An official national gift goes to EIN 84-6129064, not automatically to a particular separately funded state or licensee. DDS is the strongest direct health pathway; nonclinical education and outreach costs are retained in the support-cost prior but receive no separate QALY credit. An [August 2026 Rhode Island update](https://dentallifeline.org/blog/dln-ri-donated-dental-services-achieves-milestone-of-9m-in-donated-treatment/) reports 88 people served in the past year and points to the national donation route, confirming ongoing activity without establishing completed-care or marginal-gift outcomes.
sections.monitoring:
A critical distinction appears in DLN’s [Florida report](https://www.floridadental.org/docs/stateflfloridalibraries/default-document-library/dln-florida-dds-report-11-2024.pdf?sfvrsn=de3fbb3b_1): patients served includes completed care, incomplete treatment and volunteer matches that have not yet received treatment. The [Indiana report](https://dentallifeline.org/success-stories/indiana-state-highlight-report-for-june-2020/) uses the same convention. The national annual total therefore cannot safely be read as completed treatments without a separate reconciliation. These state definitions are not a measured national completion rate. Historical [Massachusetts reporting](https://www.massdental.org/~/media/MassDental/Foundation/GRANTS/GRANT-RECIPIENTS/Massachusetts-DDS-Program-SemiAnnual-Report.ashx?la=en), available as indexed primary text but now a broken live URL, described five completions among 28 served during a half-year and longer treatment plans; this is a stock/flow snapshot, not evidence that only 18% ever finish. Our 0.65 eventual completed-care-equivalent yield per candidate is a testable judgment, not an estimate calculated from that snapshot. Needed monitoring is unique entry cohorts followed through eventual completion, time to relief, abandoned or partial care, pain/eating and generic utility, adverse events, residence and alternative treatment. Repeated-year cases must not become new donor-caused completions twice.

The October 2026 source check confirms that these counts still do not establish a completed national treatment cohort. The application collects work ability, income, benefits and possible family assistance, but publishes no resulting representative household-income, wage-effect or travel-cost distribution. Disability, older-age and medical-need categories overlap; adding them cannot identify a worker share. Outcome monitoring should distinguish otherwise private purchasers, people with an equivalent free alternative, and patients gaining treatment they would not otherwise receive. Those cohorts have different health and household-cash effects.
sections.qualitative:
The [randomized denture trial](https://www.nature.com/articles/bdj.2007.569) assigned 133 housebound older adults to immediate dentures or waiting and found improved oral daily function at three months. We freshly checked its abstract/preview, not a full accessible trial dataset. This supports selected denture relief; it does not identify DLN's national procedure mix, a generic QALY mapping, or three-year persistence. The [original caries study XML](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC6698006/fullTextXML), read in targeted abstract/results excerpts, reports non-significant generic utility differences between active and inactive caries groups. That observational Swedish comparison is not evidence that DDS has zero effect: generic instruments may miss important eating and pain outcomes. It does prevent treating dental-specific improvement as an automatically validated generic health gain.

Our annual gross utility increment is therefore a stated 0.025 judgment, about nine full-health-equivalent days of relief per additional completion-year, rather than the previous 0.03. The three-year clinical valuation window, mortality, loss of useful treatment and later alternative access are explicitly separate assumptions. Three years is accounting truncation, not a claim that every restoration or every associated income effect stops abruptly then. Selected short follow-up, uncertain case mix and unmeasured symptom persistence warrant near-null, shorter-window and faster-catch-up stresses. The episodic harm allowance is also a judgment, not a trial complication probability or a second deduction from an imported trial net QALY effect.

The [original rehabilitation abstract](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:16373686&format=json&resultType=core) concerns 377 welfare recipients and associates completed care with favorable or neutral employment outcomes. Selection into completion and the absence of random untreated comparison prevent converting its odds ratio into a DLN wage coefficient. We nevertheless model a modest, explicitly judged earnings pathway separately, instead of declaring all earnings zero. Most DDS patients are older, disabled or medically fragile, so only a small share is assumed to have additional earnings responsiveness. Actual disposable pay, net of tax and benefit offsets, differs from nominal salary, leisure time or volunteer dentistry retail value.

We do not price unestablished systemic disease, mortality-prevention or medical-clearance effects. [CMS coverage](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coverage/dental) can pay for qualifying medically linked care; a clearance label alone does not establish an otherwise blocked life-saving treatment. A separate medical-access model would need the exact blocked procedure, timing, alternatives, prognosis and downstream resource costs. Current evidence supports a promising oral-function mechanism, not an identified unrestricted-donation return. The documented volunteer network and current grants confirm continuing activity, while independently checked original filings identify the national payee and affiliate accounting boundaries.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter sees volunteer-supported dental treatment as a promising way to relieve pain and restore eating and daily function. We estimate approximately **$1.3M per better life** from the DDS pathway, combining clinical health with signed household-resource welfare. The benefit unit is ten health/income-equivalent years; the economic component is not a measured clinical QALY. This is a conditional national-gift comparison, not an offer to buy a specified treatment package.

**What does the money support?** At the $10,000 modeling scale, our $1,500 full-support allowance and 50% funding response imply **3.33 additional candidate equivalents** and **2.17 eventual completed-care equivalents**. That is approximately $3,000 per additional candidate and $4,615 per completed equivalent after the response assumption. Support includes national and affiliate coordination, administration, fundraising, nonclinical work and unsuccessful matching; it is not merely the dentist's bill. Volunteer dentists and labs supply much of the treatment. The completion factor does not turn annual patients served into measured completed donor-caused patients.

**Why might treatment help?** We separate 0.108 otherwise-purchasing completions, 0.515 completions with equivalent same-time free alternatives, and 1.544 genuinely additional completed-care equivalents. Equivalent alternative care cancels both matching clinical benefit and matching treatment harm. Additional-care patients receive a judged 0.025 annual gross utility gain over a three-year clinical valuation window, discounted for mortality, loss of benefit and later alternative access; episodic harm and extra application burden are charged separately. The result is **0.081029 clinical QALYs** at the modeling scale. The clinical-only donor price is about $1.23M per ten. The denture trial makes the relief mechanism plausible, but neither that selected population nor dental scores establish the national utility coefficient.

**Income, savings and costs.** We use the [Coefficient Giving reference framework](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/) to compare signed changes in household disposable resources with healthy-year equivalents. The $22,000 household-resource baseline is a judgment, not measured DLN average income. One candidate maps to one representative household, with no household-size multiplier. Additional application/transport cash is $20 per candidate. Otherwise purchasers avoid a judged $300 actual care payment minus $20 incremental travel; this is not the donated retail value of treatment, and those buyers receive no added clinical-access or earnings credit. Patients with equivalent free care incur only the assumed $20 additional travel difference. Newly treated households incur $80 additional travel and $30 actual missed net pay, not a leisure shadow wage.

Maintenance adds $40 in each of two subsequent years for newly treated households, weighted for survival. This is explicitly a persistent **net incremental cash obligation** associated with receiving treatment, including after benefit loss or later alternative care; it is not inferred from a published invoice. If maintenance only exists while treatment remains causally additional, that alternative needs a different population rule. The allowance represents one possible scenario because ongoing donated maintenance is not guaranteed. Volunteers have no actual lost-pay/cash deduction centrally; a separate burden stress is shown. Clinical opportunity resources are a different ledger.

The earnings pathway assumes that 10% of genuinely additional-care completions gain $300 annual net pay for two years. Those are bounded judgments, not the employment study's measured effect. Receipts are at years 1.5 and 2.5, following assumed care at year one; mortality, loss and alternative-care catch-up attenuate the common-alive working cohort. We do not credit ordinary earnings of newly surviving people. The clinical valuation window is separate from earnings receipt timing. Only 25% of positive earnings welfare is retained to avoid overlap with oral-role and financial-stress benefits; **negative wage effects and direct cash burdens are fully charged**, even when positive-benefit independence is zero. The after-burden earnings baseline is a marginal annual-consumption convention, not a second cash saving.

Direct household cash welfare is **−0.007271 equivalent years** and independent earnings contribute **+0.000422**. Net resources are **−0.006849**, so combined health/resource benefit is **0.074181 equivalents** and the exact donor comparison is $1,348,058 per ten. Undiscounted expected direct cash falls about $333 across the modeled cohort; expected common-alive net pay rises about $79 before the overlap adjustment. These money amounts are not the welfare score itself.

**What changed from the earlier estimate?** The historical $818K clinical-only result remains available below. We independently increased the support allowance from $1,300 to $1,500, reduced annual utility from 0.03 to 0.025, lengthened modeled time to relief from nine to twelve months, and increased episodic harm from 0.001 to 0.0025. We revisited but retained completion, funding response, mortality and benefit-loss assumptions because current evidence does not identify a precise replacement. Explicit purchaser/free-alternative partitions and signed household effects replace a single clinical calculation; the old total was not preserved by subtracting cash from an inherited envelope.

**Uncertainty and associated resources.** Favorable, short clinical-window, fast-catch-up, negative wage and burden cases are judgment stresses, not confidence intervals. A failed-completion scenario still incurs application losses; zero funding or no gift are genuine zero effects; unknown clinical or resource components produce unknown combined benefit. Purchasers cannot also receive added access benefits. The model's $25,000 software gift limit and eight-candidate capacity assumption are not verified fundraising room or a promise that larger gifts scale linearly.

The selected gross institutional companion adds $2,000 per completion and $200 per incomplete candidate, net of clinical materials already in support. At the central scale its numerator is $14,567 and its price is about $1.96M per better life. These are opportunity-resource judgments, not retail bills, a second charge for household cash loss, or a reconciled net societal cost. The main list continues to use donor dollars.

**Financial appendix.** The national payee's original FY2023–25 expenses are $1,758,119, $2,172,269 and $2,090,255: mean $2,006,881. Corrected affiliate-group support, including netted event/gaming costs, is $2,588,442, $2,879,656 and $3,095,483. Adding the national return gives a two-return support bridge of $4,346,561, $5,051,925 and $5,185,738, not a consolidated audit or matched completed-patient price. The national negative $1,007,229 staff-reimbursement credit is already netted; the group bears that expense, so adding the credit again would double count it. Donated clinical valuations stay outside this bridge. Annual scale, restricted assets and new borrowing do not establish incremental volunteer capacity. Original forms and source-access boundaries are listed in Sources.
sections.funding:
The FY2025 [national return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202630589349300233/IRS990) reports $386,734 program, $1,202,072 management and $501,449 fundraising after the shared-staff credit; the [group return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202620589349301627/IRS990) reports $2,621,544 program, $399,622 management and $69,707 fundraising before $4,610 of netted event/gaming costs. The allocation is not a clinical efficiency score. Part III discloses $103,782 national and $12,471,071 group donated clinical services, outside this support-cost bridge; these valuations must not be counted as both free leverage and health benefit. National FY2025 revenue is $1,767,467 versus $2,090,255 expense, but unrealized investment gains offset the operating deficit in net assets. Of $5,126,614 net assets, $2,622,593 has donor restrictions; $334,358 is cash, and an $875,000 unsecured borrowing is newly reported. Neither all net assets nor the accounting deficit is an available cash runway or a proven funding gap.

Current counterfactual funding is concrete: [Maine’s amended contract](https://www.maine.gov/dafs/bbm/procurementservices/sites/maine.gov.dafs.bbm.procurementservices/files/noi-docs/NOI%200320260179.pdf) adds $36,463 and verifies coordinator support through June 2027, for $72,926 across two years; its earlier concern about June 2026 expiration has been superseded. A [2026 Massachusetts grant](https://www.massdental.org/news/mds-foundation-awards-2026-access-to-care-grants/) provides $7,500 to help 30 people, a $250 partial funding projection, not a national all-in price. These commitments belong in the no-new-gift baseline. The national gift’s 50% funding response is a judgment that some extra support still buys coordinator and matching capacity while some replaces grants, reserves or cannot attract additional volunteer slots.

[CMS](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coverage/dental) generally excludes routine dental care but covers qualifying medically linked services around specified transplants, cardiac procedures, cancer treatment and dialysis, subject to coordination and documentation. Exhausting benefits is helpful targeting, not proof that every medically fragile patient has zero coverage. Baseline alternative access and subsequent catch-up are modeled separately. No current unrestricted expansion budget or unfunded number of completed cases was located. The next donor-relevant request is a dated budget linking unrestricted incremental dollars to added completed cohorts and volunteer capacity, net of committed state/private support. The current review is not confirmation of additional funded treatment capacity.

The October 2026 source check directly reread the six original national/group returns and relevant reciprocal accounting schedules. Return audit-Yes boxes are not a substitute for obtaining a consolidated audited statement. The national three-year revenue series is $863,744, $936,784 and $1,767,467, distinct from expenses and net-asset changes. The $875,000 borrowing requires terms and a cash forecast before interpreting liquidity. Current grant announcements belong in the no-new-gift baseline; partial state grants do not reveal the all-in national cost or unrestricted donor response.

model.costScope: Main price charges the full ordinary national gift to an explicit partial DDS comparison, not a measured unrestricted-portfolio return. Gross institutional opportunity resources are a separate diagnostic; household cash losses stay in welfare, not the numerator.
model.geographicAttribution: USA residents only; g applies once independently to clinical and each household resource stream. National/affiliate accounting differences are cost/additionality issues, not fabricated foreign benefit.
model.formula: N=min(G*b/c,capacity), C=N*r; buyers=C*p, free=C*(1-p)*(1-s), A=C*(1-p)*s. Clinical=g*[A*(u*exp(-ln(1+d)*L)*integral_0^T exp(-(ln(1+d)+m+loss+catchup)*t)dt-h*exp(-ln(1+d)*L))-N*ha]. Resources sum signed per-household logarithmic receipt flows. Positive wages use independence; negative wages and direct cash burdens are charged fully. Combined=clinical+resources; donor price=10*G/combined only if positive and known.
model.counterfactual: No-new-gift includes committed public/private support, existing volunteer slots, insurance exhaustion, medically linked Medicare, other free providers and delayed private care. Otherwise purchasers and equivalent same-time free care have no incremental clinical benefit or matched treatment harm. Additional application burdens remain.
model.attribution: Funding response, completion, otherwise purchasing, same-time alternatives and later catchup are separate judged pathways. Common-alive earnings are not survival-created pay. One candidate-equivalent is one representative household; no hidden household-size or patient-repeat multiplier.
model.uncertainty: All causal, marginal-support and household monetary coefficients are independently reconsidered judgments, not identified local estimates. T is a clinical valuation window, not abrupt termination of every economic benefit. Maintenance is a persistent net incremental obligation despite treatment loss or alternative care; its value/persistence is unknown empirically. Fixed software bounds do not verify donor capacity. Negative/zero/unknown cases stay distinct; selected stresses are not probability distributions or confidence limits.
model.nativeOutcomes: The reported 4,367 DDS people are not a national completed marginal cohort. At the central $10K scale: 3.33 added candidate equivalents, 2.17 completions and 1.54 genuinely additional-care equivalents. Clinical .0810294138082641 plus signed household resources −.006848613292933911 yields .07418080051533019 combined equivalents, not all clinical QALYs. Donor price $1,348,058 per ten.

Licensee scope is an organizational attribution issue, not foreign health: it is addressed by conservative c and b, not by pretending those US patients live elsewhere. No overseas outcomes are credited.
historicalModel.formula: discount=ln(1+d_input), with d_input=.03; k=discount+m+loss+catchup; q=u*exp(-discount*L)*(1-exp(-k*T))/k. N=(G/c)*b extra candidate cases; C=N*r eventual completed-care equivalents. Q_all=C*(s*q-h*exp(-discount*L))-N*ha; Q_USA=g*Q_all. Cost=G+N*(r*resource+(1-r)*unfinishedResource+patientResource). Price per 10=10*Cost/Q_USA only if Q_USA>0. All gains stop at T after completion; no terminal value. r includes pre-completion death/dropout, so mortality is applied only after completion and not again through the lag.
historicalModel.counterfactual: The no-new-gift world includes continued state contracts, private grants, insurance and Medicare medically linked dental care, existing volunteers and assets. b=.5 concerns extra supported candidates from the national gift rather than displaced funders or spare fixed costs. s=.75 concerns immediate clinical access additionality conditional on added completed care, and catchup=.06/year later alternative access. Maintenance failure is separate loss=.0625/year; competing mortality m=.04/year is an explicit population judgment, not a DLN survival estimate. National-to-licensee production is not credited automatically.
historicalModel.attribution: c=$1,300 per candidate and r=.65 jointly replace alpha c=$2,000 completion-adjusted case prior. They are an explicit decomposition, not newly observed productivity. No further clinical success discount is applied: u averages case mix and incomplete symptom relief among completed-care equivalents. r also allows incomplete cases to contribute less than a whole completed package; it is not inferred from a half-year completion snapshot. b discounts the national gift response once. s handles benefit already achievable at completion; catchup is the later hazard that a remaining health gap closes. h and ha are excess burdens versus the comparator, not all pain from treatment that would also occur elsewhere. Here r is an eventual completed-care-equivalent yield, which may include weighted partial relief; it must not be reported as an observed probability of all-or-nothing completion. Candidate and completed counts in the model are additional equivalents, not national annual patients. Any completion status measured later should replace both this yield and the associated resource mix consistently.
historicalModel.uncertainty: All causal conversion parameters are broad analyst judgments. Finite outcome accounting does not create clinical identification. The external denture trial supports selected oral function outcomes; it does not validate generic utility, national completion, mortality or marginal funding response. Medical-treatment access, systemic health, employment and nonclinical education remain unpriced, so the estimate is a partial health pathway with the whole gift charged. Unmeasured positive mechanisms are not automatically zero, but no unsupported survival bonus is added. Adverse and no-capacity cases remain explicit.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: Reused FY2024–25 annual report: 4,367 DDS people served including licensees, not established completions; 6,038 across programs is not the clinical denominator. New primary state definitions show untreated matches can be included. Central $10,000 supports 3.8461538461538463 additional candidate cases and 2.5 completed-care equivalents after the funding and completion judgments, at $2,600 per added candidate and $4,000 per additional completion. Those completed cases yield 0.12224162318811595 modeled finite USA QALYs after utility, alternatives and excess harm.

reports.program: Street health, overdose response, behavioral care and housing support

what: Homeless Health Care Los Angeles provides street outreach, overdose response, behavioral health, hygiene and housing support.
Its Los Angeles teams reach people facing unusually high risks and barriers to conventional services.
Teams combine emergency response with ongoing services for people experiencing homelessness.
strengths: Direct street response can add urgent treatment when nobody else would intervene in time.
Organization-specific research and current county reporting provide more substance than activity totals alone.
Original audits disclose service costs, substantial public funding and liquid resources.
reservations: Most revenue is government-linked, and unrestricted gifts have no verified marginal allocation or unfunded response queue.
Reported reversals are not unique lives saved; other rescuers and continued mortality risk matter.
The portfolio includes many services whose marginal health is not quantified, and an older HHCLA-delivered randomized brief-intervention trial found no significant outcome benefit.

sections.what: [HHCLA's current service portfolio](https://www.hhcla.org/services) spans outreach, behavioral health, community engagement, employment and housing navigation. Its [homepage](https://www.hhcla.org/) also identifies wound care, psychiatric care, acupuncture and hygiene facilities. We assess the ordinary recipient rather than treating a donation as restricted to its most promising clinical work. The [street-team account](https://www.hhcla.org/post/letters-from-skid-row) describes opportunistic encounters using naloxone, oxygen, an AED and subsequent paramedic support; this is a concrete mechanism, not an independent estimate of effectiveness.
sections.monitoring: [Los Angeles County's provider page](https://publichealth.lacounty.gov/sapc/providers/provider-advisory-committee.htm) credits HHCLA outreach teams with more than 360 overdose reversals during 2024. We use 360 only as a historical benchmark, not a current annual count or an estimate of deaths prevented. The [2006–08 Skid Row program evaluation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4291458/) enrolled 66 participants and followed 47 at three months; 22 reported responding to 35 overdoses. Knowledge and appropriate response practices improved, but there was no randomized comparison and reported scene mortality did not fall. This establishes a high-exposure delivery setting, not a donation-sensitive mortality effect. Current unique-patient counts, repeat episodes, alternative rescue and longer follow-up remain decisive.
sections.qualitative: The case for the quantified pathway is additional timely rescue, not the proposition that all harm-reduction activity has identical value. [HHCLA staff delivered an SBIRT trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5312829/) involving 732 jail participants; after baseline adjustment, the groups did not differ significantly on substance use, treatment engagement, HIV-risk behavior or quality of life at follow-up. That older intervention is not the current street-response program, but cautions against assigning broad counseling or referral counts automatic health credit. A [Massachusetts overdose-survivor cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29913516/) observed 4.7 deaths per 100 person-years and associations between medication treatment and lower mortality. It supports continuing-risk and treatment-retention concerns, not a causal estimate for HHCLA. Our finite survival model uses explicit transfer judgments and does not award multiple lifetimes to repeat rescues.
sections.cost: The [FY 2025 audit](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/display_audit/2025-06-GSAFAC-0000413586) reports $25,876,205 in full expenses, including $4,168,667 directly assigned to the harm-reduction center before allocated indirect costs. The model deliberately uses full recipient spending, not that attractive program denominator. It combines a historical 360-event benchmark with explicit judgments about current marginal event density, duplicate patients, additional timely rescue, mortality reduction and funding substitution. Its cautious central implies about $9.6 million per ten California QALYs. Joint stress tests range from roughly $160,000 to $12.8 billion per ten, with zero or adverse health possible outside the finite range. These are conditional planning scenarios, not a confidence interval or empirically measured return. Other service benefits receive zero quantified credit, not a finding that they are worthless. Full care, housing and future medical resource costs are not a net societal-cost estimate.
sections.funding: The [FY 2025 audit](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/display_audit/2025-06-GSAFAC-0000413586) reports approximately 90% of revenue from state/federal grants or contracts, directly or indirectly. It also shows $7.42 million cash and $14.05 million financial assets available within one year, largely including contract receivables, against a goal of 90 days' operating expenses. These balances are not all uncommitted spending money. Costs reimbursed by contracts may continue without private gifts; gifts might fill genuine uncovered staffing needs or mainly replace other support. The [current executive article](https://www.hhcla.org/post/radical-thinking-is-solving-homelessness) describes a $40 million budget, newer and larger than FY 2025 audited spending, but provides no detailed budget or response-specific expansion plan. We therefore stress-test rather than assume historical productivity persists. The original FY 2024 and FY 2025 audits establish a consistent three-year expense series; audit figures are gross of event expenses and differ from netted IRS extracts.

model.costScope: Full recipient ordinary-gift cost. E is audited all-function annual expense, not harm-reduction program expense. C=100000 normalization only. Benefits of other portfolio functions are unquantified and assigned zero in the conditional numerical model, with costs retained; not a claim of zero actual health.
model.geographicAttribution: Current direct service and historical rescues are in Los Angeles. Quantified pathway assumes all modeled health remains in California; migration is unmeasured, so a lower geographic fraction is a sensitivity rather than invented precision. Training spillovers are not quantified.
model.formula: Candidate future response episodes N=C/E*R*lambda. Unique additional deaths prevented D=N*unique*rescue*delta*funding. L=sum(t=1..T)[utility*(1-m)^t/(1.03)^t]/1.03, finite years of health following an event at end of year 1. Q_CA=D*L*g. price10=10*C/Q_CA. This approximation requires unique-person accounting: all repeated rescues of one person share one survival/utility trajectory. More generally Q=sum_person integral_0^T[(S1*u1)-(S0*u0)]/(1.03)^t dt, with later alternative rescue and treatment in S0. Do not add separate lifetime credit for later repeat rescues.
model.counterfactual: Existing government contracts, other witnesses, paramedics and other naloxone programs continue. funding discounts whether a gift changes services; rescue discounts whether an otherwise similar episode receives additional timely care. delta is the causal fatality-risk difference conditional on that extra timely care, not the observed proportion surviving.
model.attribution: No distinct naloxone, oxygen, CPR, outreach and paramedic lifetime claims for the same event. Unique-person adjustment is an explicit prior, not proof that registry deduplication was done. Public funding and other services are complements but not all attributable to private gifts.
model.uncertainty: Numerical model is judgment-based partial health accounting over full recipient cost. Calendar2024 reversal reporting and FY2025 expense periods are not matched; their ratio is a deliberately conservative benchmark, not observed cost per event. lambda explicitly captures current scale, program mix and marginal-versus-average productivity. No scenario is a probability-weighted expected value or a validated bound.
model.nativeOutcomes: Staff response/reversal episodes; unique patients; additional timely administrations/resuscitations; unique-person survival and health utility. Historical event count is neither drug doses nor deaths prevented.

sensitivity: Central roughly$9.57m per ten California QALYs; favorable$160k; pessimistic$12.84bn. Extremes are joint stress tests approaching zero, not credible interval endpoints.
At central L=5.958, $1M per ten requires0.16784 unique additional deaths prevented per$100k; $100k requires1.67841. Central0.01753 is below both.

At other central assumptions, lambda must rise9.5747-fold to reach$1M per ten, or95.747-fold for$100k. Such improvements require evidence of a genuinely more productive marginal channel, not re-labeling the whole gift as harm-reduction restricted.
Replacing auditedFY2025 cost with a$40m current budget while holding absolute response count constant lowers health by25.876205/40; actual new response volume could offset this, but is unknown.
If half modeled health occurs outside California after migration, price doubles. No arbitrary geography discount is embedded.

Other clinical or housing pathways could improve overall value. At central modeled0.10444Q/$100k, unquantified branches need an additional0.89556Q to reach$1M per ten or9.89556Q to reach$100k, without double-counting the same survival or disability.
The entire portfolio is costed, but donated labor, partner resources, downstream care and medical savings are not comprehensively priced. A donor-cost estimate is not a societal-cost estimate.
