reports.program: Free medical, dental, vision and surgical care

acceptance.evidence: docs/geography-discovery/lestonnac-la-independent-acceptance-2026-10-02.md — scientific conditional acceptance; integration/publication checks separately required.

what: Lestonnac Free Clinic provides medical, dental, vision and surgical care to low-income uninsured people across Southern California.
Its clinics and mobile services connect patients with volunteer clinicians, glasses and treatment for painful or disabling conditions.
This report models health and household-resource benefits reaching Los Angeles and Orange County residents.
strengths: Free clinical care can relieve symptoms, improve vision and restore everyday function.
Volunteer clinicians and donated services help provide treatment alongside paid clinic operations.
Three consecutive original returns disclose operating expenses and donated services, supporting a transparent financial comparison.
reservations: Current unique patients, clinical mix and outcomes are not measured in the available records; the estimate relies on explicit planning judgments.
Patient prescriptions, travel and follow-up costs can offset savings and earnings benefits; household-level effects remain unmeasured.
Volunteer staffing, alternative care and already-funded partnerships may limit what additional ordinary donations accomplish.

sections.what: The [medical program](https://www.lestonnacfreeclinic.org/medical) includes primary care and many specialties; dental treatment, glasses and retinal care add distinct clinical pathways. The [Orange surgery center](https://www.lestonnacfreeclinic.org/surgery-days) opened in May 2025. [Hoag’s July 2026 update](https://www.hoaghospitalfoundation.org/hoag-and-lestonnac-free-clinic-expand-free-surgical-care-in-orange-county.html) describes support for equipment, supplies and operations, including cataract and selected general, urologic, gynecologic and orthopedic procedures. Opening, credentialing and a waiting list are not completed surgeries or incremental health outcomes. The official [giving page](https://www.lestonnacfreeclinic.org/donate) names Lestonnac Free Clinic as check payee at its Orange address; the filed entity is St Jeanne De Lestonnac Free Clinic, EIN 95-3499011. No gift is assumed restricted to the highest-benefit procedure.
sections.monitoring:
The 2024 return reports over 10,000 patients and 20,000 visits; definitions and deduplication are not supplied. The model carries 10,000 forward as a judgment scale, not observed 2026 activity. [Dental care](https://www.lestonnacfreeclinic.org/dental-programs) reports 3,843 visits in 2024, mixing prevention and treatment. The [vision page](https://www.lestonnacfreeclinic.org/vision-programs) reports 2,374 glasses, 780 retinal exams and 629 ophthalmology visits in 2023. These overlapping and differently dated counts are not added together. The 2026 second-unit goal of 2,000 exams/glasses is prospective, not realized output. Before a stronger recommendation, obtain current distinct patients by residence and primary treatment, completed surgery types, pre/post symptoms or vision, complications, alternative-care wait times and an incremental budget tied to staffed appointments.

The October 2 source review rechecked the original 2022–24 return and donated-service bridges. Current eligibility identifies possible patient-paid labs, imaging and prescriptions, but does not quantify household costs or earnings. Clinical papers were retrieved as indexed primary abstracts only; the Oregon employment result is the investigators’ summary, not a full-paper review. Current outcome/capacity claims remain unverified.
sections.qualitative:
The historical clinical review replaced an opaque 0.02-QALY average with four explicit, mutually exclusive primary-benefit packages. Their weights and utilities are judgments, not a reconstruction of observed patient mix. Medical care can improve symptoms and access, but the [Oregon randomized insurance study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3701298/) did not show short-term improvement in several physical biomarkers; insurance is also not a free-clinic treatment package. An [expedited cataract trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17585002/) in older UK women found a 0.056 one-year QALY difference versus routine waiting, supporting finite benefit from earlier treatment but not a transferable clinic-wide gain or lifetime cure. A [glasses trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17998508/) supports improved vision-related function over a two-month delay in nursing homes, not our generic utility value in community patients. A [dental trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39325552/) compares two active treatments, so it does not identify the effect versus no care. The model accordingly discounts alternative access separately, caps benefits at three years, allows decay and competing mortality, subtracts a burden for every added package and awards no separate avoided-death, cancer-detection or screening credit.

Current recalibration replaces the earlier four-package response assumptions with disjoint purchasers, equivalent-free alternatives and otherwise-unmet patients. Current health, signed money and finite recovery pay are independent judgments rather than an old welfare envelope minus cash. The original clinical narrative above describes the historical model; the cost section and current parameters govern the revised comparison.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter estimates about $8.02 million per better life from Lestonnac’s clinical portfolio in the LA metro area, including household-resource effects. Free treatment can improve symptoms and vision, while avoiding some otherwise-paid care. It can also create prescription, testing and access costs. The estimate combines those signed effects rather than assuming all medical care improves income.

For a hypothetical $10,000 donation, the model offers 3.90 medical, 1.15 dental, 1.28 vision and 0.064 surgery package-equivalents. Completion leaves 3.12, 0.86, 1.15 and 0.042 packages respectively. Half of completed packages represent otherwise-unmet care; 20% replace purchased care and 30% replace equivalent free care. These disjoint groups prevent adding clinical benefit when the same treatment would occur anyway. Modelled responders among the unmet group are 0.31 medical, 0.22 dental, 0.40 vision and 0.012 surgery cases. These are hypothetical planning units, not observed additional patients.

The four exclusive primary-benefit branches carry independently reconsidered utility, response, finite duration and decay judgments. Medical symptoms receive 0.03 utility for one year; dental symptoms 0.08 for three months; vision 0.025 for one year; surgery 0.06 for two years, before decay, response, survival and discounting. The cataract and glasses evidence concerns specific older populations, not this clinic-wide mix. It motivates plausible mechanisms without supplying transferable coefficients. No separate mortality, screening or lifetime-cure benefit is added. Treatment and attempt harms are retained even without a successful clinical response.

Health gains begin after a three-month delay and are survival-adjusted through that delay and the finite benefit course. The result is 0.0125191 local healthy years per $10,000. Earnings represent short recovery gains among workers alive under either counterfactual, not baseline wages created by saving a life. Each short earnings period receives common-alive survival exposure once.

Household resources are valued separately using signed changes in actual disposable resources. Otherwise-buyers can avoid assumed medical/dental/vision/surgery outlays of $150/$200/$60/$500. Unmet patients do not save a purchase they would never have made. Thirty percent of offered households face incremental acquisition costs of $50/$50/$20/$100, including unsuccessful access. Thirty percent of unmet completed cases face new maintenance costs of $150/$40/$20/$200, such as prescriptions or labs. These amounts and incidences are judgments, not measured bills. Each primary package represents one household-equivalent; neither family members nor overlapping program visits are multiplied.

Discrete purchaser/free/unmet, completion and cost states are evaluated before the log-income welfare conversion at a $25,000 annual household baseline. Cash comes first; recovery pay uses the cash-adjusted baseline. Positive earnings receive a 50% overlap allowance, while adverse earnings and induced costs remain fully debited. At the current center, local discounted cash is −$12.38 and recovery pay +$21.12 per $10,000; their welfare equivalents sum to −0.0000464462 years. Combined health and resources are 0.0124727 equivalent years, producing $8,017,528 per ten. The Coefficient Giving crosswalk is a welfare comparison, not evidence that income is a measured clinical QALY.

The donor normalization uses $4,695,553 of narrower 2024 accrual expenses; gross institutional resources are $7,283,853 after separately disclosed donated services. Narrower accrual is not actual cashflow or a marginal appointment quote. Fixed patient scale of 10,000 and 30% funding response are independently stated assumptions, not extra patients manufactured by removing donated services. The matching gross envelope is $15,512 per $10,000, or $12.44M per better life. Gross-only accounting stresses hold physical benefits fixed; stricter donor-support costs are a separate financing stress. External partner resources are incompletely valued.

LA-plus-Orange health and resource shares are each 65% judgments because services also reach Riverside and San Bernardino. Residence data—not clinic addresses—would be needed to validate attribution. Current output, household finances and staffed marginal capacity are still missing. Positive, negative, zero and unknown cases are unweighted diagnostics, not confidence intervals or empirical expected values.

Historical comparison and expense appendix. The prior clinical-only augmented-resource estimate was $4,369,540.65 per ten local QALYs. Its complete 18 scenarios remain frozen; the new center changes counterfactual groups, completion, benefit course and financing scope, rather than allocating income inside an inherited total. The following original cost analysis is historical; its accounting disclosures remain useful.

The best judgment is $4,369,541 per ten local QALYs. At the $7,283,853 annual resource normalization, 35% funding response gives 3,500 added patient-package equivalents; 35% effective additional care leaves 1,225 all-population packages, or 796.25 local packages. Full resources per added package are $2,081; per effective package $5,946; per local effective package $9,148. These are modeled marginal units, not observed treatment costs. Finite conditional health averages 0.02236 QALY per effective package before a 0.0005-QALY burden per added package, yielding 25.646 all-population and 16.670 local QALYs. This resource-normalized price conservatively charges donated services as well as the recipient’s other expenses; it is not a literal claim about cash buying volunteer time. The gross-accounting diagnostic excluding separately disclosed donated services is approximately $2,816,835 per ten, but omits those resources. Joint stress scenarios range widely and include zero and net harm, not statistical confidence bounds. No clinical package receives overlapping medical, dental, glasses and surgery credit.

Expense appendix. Three original calendar-year returns support a consistent resource bridge: 2022 Part IX $3,378,797 + separately netted events $50,553 + Schedule O donated-service expense $2,922,330 = $6,351,680; 2023 $4,165,218 + $35,118 + $3,369,000 = $7,569,336; 2024 $4,655,295 + $40,258 + $2,588,300 = $7,283,853. The three-year mean is $7,068,289.67. Each Schedule O discloses equal donated-service income and expense with zero net effect; a blank Schedule D is not evidence that services were absent. This is an original-return-derived resource bridge, not an independently audited GAAP series; the 2024 return answers no to audit/review questions. The previous gross-accounting series, excluding these services, remains $3,429,350 / $4,200,336 / $4,695,553, averaging $4,108,413. In 2024 Part IX allocates $3,698,845 to program and $956,450 to management; separately netted events add $40,258. Donated services are shown separately because their functional allocation is not supplied. Expense types include $2,364,715 compensation/benefits/payroll tax, $531,382 other contractor services, $486,771 medical supplies, $193,151 labs and $368,093 depreciation. Those components are already in Part IX and are not added again. Gross asset purchases are not stacked onto depreciation. The 2022 other-net-assets note mentioning $3,474,709 services/supplies and 2023 donated-inventory changes are not added without proof of annual consumption. Part III service revenue versus Part VIII and unusual payroll classification remain unresolved. Partner-paid resources outside the return and patient time/travel have no reliable dollar valuation, so the model is not a full societal cost estimate.

Independent accounting check: [IRS Form 990 instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i990) exclude donated services from Parts VIII and IX. Each original Schedule O separately discloses the annual donated-service amount; the detailed 2024 Part IX rows sum to the filed total without a matching donated-service addition. Adding the disclosed value once is defensible as a filer-valued resource proxy, not independent proof of economic opportunity cost. Part IX already includes depreciation and potentially noncash goods, so its narrower series is not pure cash spending. Schedule O's contractor components sum to $531,381 versus the filed $531,382; we retain the filed total and do not turn the $1 discrepancy into another expense.
sections.funding:
The 2024 return reports $6,388,245 revenue, $802,500 government grants, $6,452,219 cash and $9,587,829 unrestricted net assets. These are historical balance-sheet amounts, not a current spendable runway or a verified funding gap. Government grants also appear in 2022 and 2023; general fundraising language should not be read as absence of public funding. Hoag already supports the new center. The [2026 room campaign](https://www.lestonnacfreeclinic.org/aar2026) says 75% of a second vision unit is funded and directs campaign contributions toward the remainder, but does not establish its total price, unrestricted-gift deployment, a fourfold match or an achievable incremental treatment rate. [Volunteer credentialing](https://www.lestonnacfreeclinic.org/surgerycenter), clinician availability and patient follow-through may bind before cash. The historical 35% cash response was a discount, not measured leverage. The next donor-useful request is a current operating budget showing the last unfunded inputs and committed clinical hours, with additional completed treatment compared with the no-gift plan.

Public baseline. Other clinics, insurance, emergency care and existing public/partner support continue without the gift. [DHCS](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/medi-cal/updates/medi-cal-changes/) reports an enrollment freeze affecting some adults from January 2026, not termination of every existing enrollee’s coverage. Its [current dental notice](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/services/medi-cal-dental-benefit-changes/) delays the relevant adult dental change until July 1, 2027; emergency dental benefits continue and several groups are exempt. We do not infer patients’ immigration status or treat all dental care as newly uncovered. Increased need does not by itself establish cash-responsive capacity.

For the current conditional comparison, funding response is 30%, not measured leverage. The $25,000 calculator ceiling is a comparison-domain limit, not verified donation capacity. A gross accounting adjustment alone changes no physical patient outcome.

model.costScope: Donor narrower accrual normalization and separate gross institutional envelope; neither measured marginal cash productivity nor complete societal cost.
model.geographicAttribution: LA and Orange County residence shares: health .65 and household resources .65 independently declared judgments.
model.formula: offers=D/cashCost*N*funding*branchWeight; completed=offers*completion; unmet=completed*(1-buyer-free); responders=unmet*response. Health uses finite utility/survival/decay integral and latency survival, less unmet treatment and all-offer attempt harms. Signed discrete cash states plus common-alive finite recovery earnings pass through the shared log-income welfare bridge; positive overlaps only discounted, negative fully debited. Price=10*gift/(local health+local resource equivalent) only for a positive known denominator.
model.counterfactual: Disjoint purchaser, equivalent-free and otherwise-unmet treatment; no clinical benefit for equivalent alternative care, no saved nonexistent purchases, signed induced household costs.
model.attribution: Exclusive primary-package household equivalents and local shares once; no additive program visit, family-member, mortality wage or duplicate cash credit.
model.uncertainty: Unweighted conditional judgments, not identified donation return, posterior or verified capacity.
model.nativeOutcomes: Offered/completed/unmet/responder packages by branch, finite health, signed cash/pay equivalents and actual dollar flows.

reports.priceScope: Conditional LA/Orange health and signed household-resource comparison; donor narrower accrual normalization versus separate gross institutional resource envelope. No measured marginal cash return, empirical expected value or verified donation capacity.

historicalModel.costScope: Whole recipient resource-cost denominator, including separately disclosed donated services; low-confidence judgment of its combined clinical health portfolio for LA and Orange County residents. Not measured patient outcomes, a cash-only donation return, a surgery-only price, or a complete societal analysis. Non-health benefits and unmeasured partner/patient costs are not valued.
historicalModel.geographicAttribution: LA MSA comprises Los Angeles and Orange counties, not Riverside or San Bernardino. Listed fixed-clinic schedules imply approximately 99 local weekly hours and 42.4 outside; the medical page additionally lists 12 Riverside mobile hours, lowering the proxy to about 64%. g=.65 is a rounded judgment, not observed residence or current throughput: the medical page mixes historical statistics, surgery is concentrated in Orange, and cross-county patients and variable staffing remain unknown. No population-share shortcut.
historicalModel.formula: For branch j, q_j = u_j * (1-exp(-(ln(1+d)+m+rho_j)*T_j))/(ln(1+d)+m+rho_j). q=sum(w_j*q_j). At annual full-resource normalization E: delivered=N*b, effective=N*b*e; Q_all=N*b*(e*q-h); Q_LA=g*Q_all. Price=10*E/Q_LA only if Q_LA>0. Benefits begin at completed treatment t=0, with continuous discounting equivalent to annual d, continuous mortality hazard m and decay rho. A delayed start requires an additional discount/survival factor and is not silently credited.
historicalModel.counterfactual: Existing insurance/emergency/other clinic access and Hoag/public grants continue. e is the fraction of added packages with consequential effective care beyond that alternative, not funding leverage. b is the separate net funding-to-throughput response after substitution, reserves and volunteer bottlenecks, applied once. Finite T concerns how long the successful package differs from its alternative; shorter alternative waits are stressed.
historicalModel.attribution: One patient-equivalent receives one primary clinical package; weights sum to one. Repeated visits, screenings, glasses and surgeries are not added as separate people or outcomes. No avoided mortality is separately credited. The generic harm/access burden is applied to all added packages, including those without benefit. Cash response is a conservative judgment on a full-resource cost normalization, not a measured grant production function.
historicalModel.uncertainty: Very low confidence in the clinical and marginal parameters. Mix weights, utility changes, duration, decay, mortality, burden, local share and cash response are explicit subjective priors; trials establish plausibility and counterfactual dependence rather than calibrating these values. Costs are original-return-derived, but service valuations and the post-opening cost trajectory are uncertain. Non-health benefits are omitted; externally paid and patient resources are incompletely priced.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: At normalization: 3500 added packages; 1225 effective packages; 796.25 local effective packages. Cost per delivered/effective/local effective package is 2081.100857142857/5946.0024489795915/9147.696075353218 USD. These prospective equivalents are not an observed surgery yield or an additional count on top of the reported patients.

reports.program: Road-safety advocacy, collision-survivor support, education and community programs

acceptance.evidence: Independent source/model review and corrected release checks: docs/la-first-six-acceptance.md

what: SAFE works on road-safety policy, local street improvements, survivor support and education.
Its camera-implementation work offers a concrete route from advocacy to fewer serious crashes.
The quantified estimate below prices only that pathway against all recipient costs—not SAFE's entire portfolio.
strengths: Direct participation in implementation coalitions, not only general awareness campaigning.
Independent studies support a camera-to-injury pathway, with current LA plans providing a concrete deployment scale.
Original accounts permit a full-recipient denominator including fundraising costs netted from revenue.
reservations: Ordinary-gift additionality is especially uncertain: the 2023 return describes vendor-directed advocacy and current city plans are publicly financed.
The $65 million per 10 LA QALYs central scenario is a subjective camera slice, not an overall rank or measured portfolio return.
LA beneficiary residence, residual camera-days changed by SAFE, and local casualty yield remain unobserved; zero and downside are plausible.

sections.what: SAFE combines policy advocacy, local street projects, survivor navigation and public education. Its [current policy agenda](https://www.streetsareforeveryone.org/blog/california-road-safety-legislation-2026) spans DUI, e-bikes, speeding and other road-safety issues; support or sponsorship is not evidence that a bill has become law. [Survivor services](https://www.streetsareforeveryone.org/safe-support) include emotional support, insurance and medical navigation, and help finding legal services. Those outcomes, community representation, and the wider policy portfolio remain unpriced here. The camera model covers LA City locations only, not the other California pilot cities or SAFE's work outside the MSA.
sections.monitoring: SAFE describes [implementation checklists and coordination with local coalitions](https://www.streetsareforeveryone.org/blog/update-speed-camera-implementation-in-so-cal), followed by a [December 2025 city report card](https://www.streetsareforeveryone.org/blog/speed-safety-systems-report). These establish participation, not causal acceleration. Current [LADOT information](https://ladot.lacity.gov/speed-safety-system) and its [August 2026 update](https://ladot.lacity.gov/dotnews/weekly-update-august-13-2026) anticipate a fall launch; the old report-card grades are not used as current deployment status. The decisive monitoring would be dated camera activation/interruption records, documented changes attributable to SAFE rather than staff/vendor/other advocates, matched crash outcomes, beneficiary residence, and the unrestricted staffing or contracting gap.
sections.qualitative: Camera effectiveness is better supported than advocacy additionality. [NHTSA's synthesis](https://www.nhtsa.gov/book/countermeasures-that-work/speeding-and-speed-management/countermeasures/enforcement/speed) finds meaningful site-specific injury reductions but notes context dependence. Tang's [2017 quasi-experimental study](https://eprints.lse.ac.uk/86567/1/sercdp0221.pdf) supplies projected native annual yields of up to 190 fatalities and 330 serious injuries prevented per 1,000 additional cameras, with rebound away from cameras; it is not an LA estimate. A [2025 NYC study](https://knowledge.uchicago.edu/record/16690/files/stagoff-belfort-et-al-2025-can-speed-cameras-make-streets-safer-quasi-experimental-evidence-from-new-york-city%20%281%29.pdf) finds injury reductions during the first seven months, not a perpetual compounding monthly effect. We retain only 10% of the UK native yield and apply an additional displacement adjustment as explicit judgments. Fines, mistaken citations, privacy risks and financial distress can reduce welfare; statutory safeguards are not proof that harms disappear.
sections.cost: The [2024 original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/473036490/202533519349300828/full) reports $396,681 expenses, split $236,640 program, $116,901 management and $43,140 fundraising. Adding $53,282 direct event costs netted against revenue gives a $449,963 full-recipient cash denominator. The similarly grossed-up 2022-24 costs are $224,206, $324,459 and $449,963 (mean $332,876); all three returns mark cash accounting. Program narratives contain allocation inconsistencies, so no program-cost bargain is inferred. The conditional camera slice produces 0.3125 additional attributable camera-years, 0.00475 deaths and 0.00825 serious nonfatal injuries avoided before geographic allocation, or 0.06917 LA QALYs per annual cost normalization. Its price is about $65.1 million per 10 LA QALYs. This is not a whole-portfolio estimate: unpriced programs may be valuable or harmful, and no confidence interval or overall ranking follows from the extreme stress scenarios.
sections.funding: The [2023 original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/473036490/202433209349328313/full) describes advocacy priorities and direction from Verra Mobility, alongside $81,781 program revenue. This documents a commercial relationship, not improper conduct or the amount of current vendor support. In 2024, program revenue was $290,088 and net assets $149,829; the payers and restrictions are not sufficiently disaggregated to establish a gift-sensitive gap. [LADOT's Council report](https://ladot.lacity.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/speed-safety-program-report-and-policy.pdf) already plans procurement, staff and public outreach, while its [Impact Report](https://ladot.lacity.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/speed-safety-program-attachment-a-impact-report.pdf) estimates $7.95 million annual public costs plus $0.5 million one-time services, initially financed by sales-tax funds with citation cost recovery. Ordinary donations do not buy these cameras or merit all rollout benefits. The model discounts substitution and includes only a residual delay/interruption equivalent within one year; no five-year enactment credit, donated-asset multiplier, or claimed funding match is applied.

model.costScope: All recipient cash costs, including netted direct fundraising costs, for an ordinary unrestricted funding normalization. Numerical benefits cover only residual LA City camera implementation; not whole-portfolio return and not a restricted gift to cameras. Public resource costs excluded from donor price but disclosed and sensitized.
model.geographicAttribution: Only the 125 LA City locations enter N. g=.90 is an explicit resident-benefit prior for LA+Orange counties, not LA County population share, office location, event attendance or percentage of SAFE operations. Non-MSA visitors/commuters excluded; other cities and statewide policy benefits unpriced.
model.formula: For ordinary incremental D: K=(D/C)*N*t*p*a*b additional camera-years. Deaths=K*fd*z*s; serious nonfatal injuries=K*fi*z*s. L=u*(1-exp(-(mu+ln(1+d))*T))/(mu+ln(1+d)). Q_all=(Deaths*L+injuries*qi)/(1+d). Q_LA=g*Q_all. Price=10*D/Q_LA. Displayed normalization D=C=449963; never claim one gift alone changes all cameras. qi is a discounted-at-injury lifetime decrement over a finite ten-year injury horizon.
model.counterfactual: Without marginal ordinary funding, AB 645 remains enacted, city funding, vendor installation, paid outreach and other advocates continue. Only a probabilistic residual three-month-equivalent delay/interruption avoided within the next year is modeled. No causal claim about future bill passage; no indefinite pilot renewal, no annual re-crediting of the same survivor.
model.attribution: p=.20 is coalition incremental implementation probability; a=.20 allocates its effect to SAFE; b=.25 is response to marginal ordinary funding after sponsors, reserves and replacement. These separate conditional judgments are not empirical probabilities. The evidence establishes participation but does not calibrate any of them. Their product can be zero.
model.uncertainty: Structural and prior-dominated. Central numerical result is a camera-only decision scenario, not an identified portfolio best estimate or statistical expected value. Poor/favorable combinations are stress tests, not credible bounds. Nonhealth fines/privacy harms and benefits of other programs are not assigned invented QALYs. Zero and negative net-health scenarios retained; a whole-portfolio ranking would be misleading without additional causal work.
model.nativeOutcomes: At D=C: 0.3125 additional attributable camera-years; 0.00475 deaths and 0.00825 serious nonfatal injuries avoided before resident allocation. No event participants, PSA views, bills supported, citations, speed reductions or locations treated are themselves counted as QALYs.

inputs.rationale: 2024 Part IX $396,681 plus $53,282 event costs netted against revenue in Part VIII; no event income subtraction or program-only denominator.

inputs.name: t
inputs.unit: camera-years per location conditional on successful intervention
inputs.rationale: A residual three-month delay/interruption equivalent within the next year, not five years of credit for the already-authorized pilot. Can represent partial network delays with the same sum of camera-days.

inputs.rationale: Multiple advocacy organizations, officials, consultants and vendor participate. Co-sponsor status does not measure causal share.

inputs.name: b

inputs.name: fd

inputs.rationale: Tang's projection of up to 190 lives saved per 1,000 additional cameras annually; upper projected external yield, not measured LA yield. Paper dated September 2017; exact publication day unknown.

inputs.name: fi

inputs.rationale: Tang's separate projection of up to 330 serious injuries prevented per 1,000 additional cameras annually. This projected external upper yield is not measured LA impact; fatalities and nonfatal serious injuries kept separate.

inputs.name: z
inputs.rationale: 90% haircut for older UK sites, high historical casualty risk, local baseline uncertainty, two-direction system differences, and short implementation horizon; not empirical calibration.

inputs.name: s

inputs.rationale: 20% further reduction for rebound beyond sites; newer NYC evidence is more reassuring but does not identify LA spillovers.

inputs.name: g

inputs.rationale: Only LA City locations modeled; 10% excluded for visitors and commuters resident outside the MSA. Road location does not establish residence. Stress .70-.98, not an observed bound.

inputs.name: u
inputs.rationale: Average counterfactual health utility; no local survivor age/health mix.

inputs.name: T
inputs.unit: maximum remaining life-years per death avoided
inputs.rationale: Finite horizon; not an indefinite value for every crash avoided.

inputs.name: mu
inputs.rationale: Simple age-mix proxy; uncertainty in remaining lifetime is explicit.

inputs.name: d
inputs.rationale: Continuous equivalent log(1.03) for survival, one-year event delay.

inputs.unit: discounted-at-injury QALY loss avoided per serious nonfatal injury
inputs.rationale: Judgment for discounted-at-injury lifetime loss over at most ten years; no validated local severity distribution. Stress .1-3 QALYs; separate from death outcomes.

inputs.rationale: Impact Report Table 1 includes $1.2 million staffing plus $6.75 million equipment/vendor; Council narrative gives $6.675 million vendor estimate, a $75 thousand discrepancy. Estimates, not final outturn.

sensitivity: Price scales inversely with additional camera-years, external transfer and resident share. g=.70 vs .90 increases price by 28.6%; .98 lowers it by 8.2%.

At central clinical/transfer assumptions, each attributable camera-year yields 0.22134841887494536 LA QALYs. Reaching $1 million/10 requires 20.328268089152893 attributable camera-years per annual recipient cost; $100 thousand/10 needs ten times that.
Camera technology's effect is not SAFE's effect. Replacing p*a*b with 1 would wrongly give an ordinary gift all coalition, public and vendor credit.
Removing the priced injury term leaves the finite survival integral; no separate lifetime credit for repeated crashes or recurring injury-years.
Using the three-year gross cash-cost mean $332,876 reduces the price by the cost ratio, but understates current expense growth; central uses latest year.

City memorandum vendor estimate $6.675 million differs from Impact Report $6.75 million. Use total Table 1 $7.95 million only in public-cost sensitivity; no false precision about executed public contract.

what: Breathe Southern California provides asthma support, clean-air education and advocacy, and has expanded local purifier distribution following the Boyle Heights warehouse fire.
BEAM serves Los Angeles and San Bernardino counties, so its California scope cannot be copied into this edition.
A judgment best estimate prices BEAM asthma-support health against full recipient costs, with broad ranges; purifier and policy effects remain separately unpriced.
strengths: A current insured asthma pathway and original accounts establish real operations and recipient-scale costs.
Home-asthma randomized evidence supplies a finite symptom-day bridge instead of equating visits with health.
Named LA purifier distribution locations and public-agency response documents make geography and substitution questions concrete.
reservations: Insurer-covered asthma and a separate public purifier program may replace services credited to private gifts.
The priced BEAM pathway omits potentially important purifier and policy effects, so it is not a complete portfolio ranking.
Annual marginal patients, county mix, effective purifier use and health-relevant exposure reductions are unknown; past matching claims are not current offers.

sections.what:
Breathe Southern California (EIN 95-1641451) is distinct from similarly named Northern California organizations. The [BEAM page](https://www.breathesocal.org/beam) currently limits eligibility to Los Angeles and San Bernardino counties. LA County is within this edition; San Bernardino is outside, and Orange County patients are not listed as eligible. The [current homepage](https://www.breathesocal.org/) reports over 300 patients during 2024–2026, not an annual or gift-induced caseload.

The [official events list](https://www.breathesocal.org/events) also describes August 2026 purifier distributions to named neighborhoods and cities entirely in LA County. [BlueSky LA](https://www.breathesocal.org/bluesky-la) and [building-decarbonization outreach](https://www.breathesocal.org/buildings) have different mechanisms; workshops, maps and equipment counts are not themselves health outcomes. No donation, processor transaction or endorsement was made.
sections.monitoring:
A randomized King County study of 373 Medicaid-enrolled children found an additional 2.10 symptom-free days per two weeks (95% CI 1.17–3.05) and 1.31 fewer urgent-care events over 12 months. Its structured multi-contact intervention differs from a visit with optional follow-up. Outcomes included self-report, and caregiver questionnaire points are not preference-based QALYs. [Randomized Medicaid childhood-asthma home-visit outcomes and costs](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4605150/)

The adult HomeBASE trial similarly improved symptom-free days and asthma-related quality of life but did not improve unscheduled health-care use. This supports a morbidity pathway while cautioning against automatically assigning hospitalization savings or childhood effects to every adult. [HomeBASE randomized adult asthma trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25419871/)

For BEAM, request unique-patient baseline severity, completed visits and supplies, symptom days or validated utility at follow-up, hospital claims, retention and alternative-provider availability. Compare against contemporaneous usual care and avoid selecting only high-utilization patients at a temporary peak. The public workshop page describes instruction, not controlled follow-up demonstrating fewer exacerbations. [Lung Power education workshops](https://www.breathesocal.org/lungpower)

For the new purifier response, obtain unique households, public-program eligibility, already-owned equipment, distribution dates, room size, effective clean-air delivery, actual use, replacement filters, baseline particulate exposure and symptom outcomes. A [randomized HEPA trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21149427) found fewer unscheduled asthma visits but no significant symptom difference among smoke-exposed asthmatic children; it does not validate assigning the multi-contact BEAM trial benefit to each purifier. Warehouse-smoke, odor and later background pollution exposures are distinct.
sections.qualitative:
The clinical and environmental pathways are plausible, but their marginal funding mechanisms differ. A new gift might support navigation for otherwise unserved patients, effective filter use or people outside a public program's footprint. That hypothesis needs a costed queue and comparison against services already available.

The [public Palos response](https://www.aqmd.gov/palos) distinguishes the June smoke episode from ongoing cleanup monitoring and odors. It reports up to $5 million additional purifier funding, direct shipment and three years of replacement filters for eligible residents. This is an alternative-provider counterfactual—not funding received by Breathe. It makes gross distribution counts a particularly weak proxy for private-donation impact.

The [organization's LinkedIn account](https://www.linkedin.com/company/breathesocal) reports thousands of purifiers and a matching appeal ending September 4; the exact post date and subsequent fulfillment are unverified. That deadline has passed, so no active match or remaining donor gap is assumed. [AAFA's partner account](https://asthmaandallergyfriendly.com/USA/aafas-2026-asthma-capitals-report-highlights-certified-partners-driving-community-impact/) documents an order of 300 upgraded Rabbit Air units, not that the entire shipment was donated. The policy portfolio needs its own finite exposure and coalition-attribution model.
sections.cost:
The donor-facing judgment best estimate is approximately $428.3 million per 10 LA QALYs for the BEAM asthma-support pathway, charging the full recipient annual cost. It is a partial-health estimate, not an expected return for all purifier, advocacy and other activities. Missing measurements widen uncertainty; they do not by themselves invalidate a transparent finite estimate.

The central BEAM judgment uses full recipient annual expenses of $2,923,727, 100 annual courses (a judgment from the 300-plus cumulative count across three calendar-year labels), 25% marginal funding responsiveness, and a 50% LA-resident share. The latter is an explicit neutral scenario over the two named counties, not observed caseload or population weighting. Transferring half the childhood trial's symptom-day effect, retaining 75% for within-year timing, and assigning utility difference 0.10 gives about 0.00546 discounted QALYs per additional course over one year. The scenario yields about 0.0683 LA QALYs, or about $428.3 million per 10 LA QALYs. It is a priced component, not a whole-portfolio estimate or recommendation. The annual course count is weakly anchored to a cumulative count, not measured throughput; the utility and funding inputs are explicit subjective priors.

At that clinical bridge, a $1 million price per 10 QALYs would require 5353.7 additional LA patient-years per annual recipient-cost normalization, compared with 12.5 in the conditional scenario. The corresponding maximum full-recipient cost is $546.12 per additional LA course; for a $100,000 target it is ten times tighter. These are exact break-even quantities, not forecast patient demand. No mortality, lifetime cure or overlapping hospitalization QALYs are added.
sections.funding:
Original accrual returns for fiscal years ending June report expenses of $2,075,948 in 2023, $2,305,383 in 2024 and $2,923,727 in 2025: a three-year mean of $2,435,019.33. The 2024 return supplies the 2023 comparative. Its $4,719,274 revenue included $2,441,575 miscellaneous income; that unusually large category should not be assumed recurring clinical revenue. [Original Form 990, fiscal year ending June 2024 with 2023 comparative totals](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/951641451/202501359349311575/full)

For 2025, revenue was $2,573,083, including $1,527,260 contributions and $814,003 rent. The return classifies every expense as program, with zero management/fundraising allocation; this does not establish zero overhead. It reports no independent financial-statement audit. Net assets were $10,700,896, including $4,612,972 restricted; Schedule O labels a $1,092,063 reconciliation addition only as a book/tax difference. Those facts merit clarification rather than interpreting the $350,644 revenue-expense deficit as proof that every gift funds additional care. [Original Form 990, fiscal year ending June 2025](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/951641451/202611359349315411/full)

Government-grant and program-fee rows on that historical return do not negate the current contracts on the BEAM page. Detailed payer receipts, current BEAM cost centers and contract reimbursement margins are needed before allocating ordinary donations. [BEAM services, eligibility, counties and managed-care contracts](https://www.breathesocal.org/beam)

DHCS's finalized update removes assessment and self-management education from the Asthma Remediation Community Support beginning January 2026 because the Asthma Preventive Services benefit covers them; physical supplies and modifications remain complementary remediation services. This is a separation to avoid duplication, not elimination of all asthma support. The old all-in-one description should not be used to infer a new donor gap or a flat payment received for each patient. [Final asthma-remediation definitions and January 2026 benefit separation](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/Documents/MCQMD/Community-Supports-February-2025-Service-Definition-Updates.pdf)

Current DHCS resources describe a provider enrollment pathway for community organizations delivering asthma preventive services. A gift might improve access, pay unreimbursed navigation or serve people otherwise excluded, but a costed unmet queue and the alternative plan/provider response were not found. [Current CHW and asthma provider enrollment resources](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/community-health-workers/)

Fresh LA review checked the retained original FY 2024/FY 2025 returns against the current index: FY 2025 remains the latest listed return. Parts VIII report no separate netted rental or event costs to add; reported zero expense allocations are not evidence of genuinely zero overhead. These accounts predate the 2026 warehouse response. A current response budget, grants and in-kind inventory are therefore needed before treating historical cost as current capacity. No active matching multiplier is used.

The original FY2023 return was independently reopened for this revision. Part IX confirms $2,075,948; the accrual checkbox is selected and Part VIII reports no separately netted rental, event, gaming or inventory costs. The comparable three-year reported-gross mean is therefore $2,435,019.33. Blank addback rows do not prove that volunteer resources or economic overhead are zero. [Original FY2023 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202401369349317700/IRS990)

model.costScope: Ordinary gift/full recipient annual cost normalization, not a restricted BEAM or emergency-purifier gift. Latest annual cost is historical and predates 2026 response; insurer/public resources not subtracted.
model.geographicAttribution: BEAM LA+San Bernardino county eligibility requires exclusion of San Bernardino; g_LA=.5 is only a judgment scenario, varied .2-.9. Named 2026 purifier-event neighborhoods lie within LA County, so g_LA=1 can apply to those specifically verified households, not to all recipient activity or effects.
model.formula: Q_LA(D)=(D/C)*N*b*(deltaSFD14/14)*deltaU*r*w*T*g/(1+d) + Q_filter_LA(D)+Q_policy_other_LA(D)-H_LA(D). C=2923727; central judgment N=100, b=.25, deltaSFD14=2.1, deltaU=.1, r=.5, w=.75, T=1, g=.5, d=.03. Filter skeleton: effective additional occupied-room person-days * health gain per reduced exposure-day; both unknown after alternative provision. Price=10*D/Q only for identified positive scope.
model.counterfactual: Medi-Cal asthma preventive services/Community Supports, alternative providers, existing purifiers, AQMD funded distribution, donors and partner resources continue absent a new gift. A gift cannot retroactively change June smoke exposure, past distributions or an expired match.
model.attribution: b is a subjective marginal responsiveness factor combining recipient allocation/capacity and substitution; clinical r and within-year w are separate. Do not apply both BEAM multimodal symptom gains and filtration gains to the same patient's same symptoms. Policy benefits need coalition counterfactual and geographic exposure allocation.
model.uncertainty: Finite judgment best estimate with broad joint scenarios, zero and harm. Unknown observed marginal inputs do not require suppressing the priced asthma pathway. The central is partial health at full gift cost, not a measured unrestricted-portfolio expectation.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional LA asthma-support patient-years and symptom-free patient-days; additional effective occupied-room exposure-days from purifier use; implementation-induced exposure reduction. Patients, devices, screenings, maps and public grants are not health outcomes.

what: NLSLA provides free civil legal help to low-income LA County residents.
Housing representation, health-care access and public benefits offer concrete health pathways, alongside self-help, domestic violence, disaster and systemic advocacy work.
The numerical estimate prices only a modeled health component using the whole organization's costs; it is not the value of all legal rights or policy outcomes.
strengths: Current original audited accounts, detailed case categories and explicit 2026 priorities make costs and mechanisms auditable.
California's Shriver evaluation includes Los Angeles and supports improved legal outcomes, with important design limitations.
LA County eligibility provides direct geographic attribution without assigning all statewide litigation effects to LA.
reservations: No measured marginal case yield or recipient-specific QALY conversion; most model links are subjective judgments.
Public contracts, other legal aid, substantial reserves and in-kind attorneys complicate ordinary-gift additionality.
The partial health price must not be displayed as a complete portfolio return; unpriced rights, safety and systemic effects may dominate.

sections.what:
NLSLA (EIN 95-2408642) represents low-income LA County residents in housing, health care, public benefits and other civil matters, and operates self-help and medical-legal partnerships. Its [health service description](https://nlsla.org/services/healthcare/) includes coverage and treatment denials, equipment, in-home support and medical debt. Debt relief for care already received is not automatically new treatment or health. [Medical-legal partnerships](https://nlsla.org/services/medical-legal-partnerships/) connect legal help with clinical settings; a developing partnership is not counted as operational capacity.

The original 2024 return reports 8,531 attorney/advocate assisted legal and case-management cases, including 2,483 housing, 1,893 health and 1,162 public-benefit closed cases. These are activities, not proven additional resolutions. Its 61,350 self-help users and online traffic are excluded from the numerical model because service intensity and overlap are unresolved. [Original 2024 Form 990](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/952408642/202533179349306253/full)
sections.monitoring:
The [July 2017 Judicial Council evaluation](https://courts.ca.gov/sites/default/files/courts/default/2024-12/lr-2017-jc-shriver-civil-right-to-counsel.pdf) randomized 424 tenants across oversubscribed Kern, LA and San Diego programs for one month. Crucially, its reported analysis excluded 31 assigned clients who did not receive full representation and 10 comparison clients who obtained other counsel. It is therefore not a clean intention-to-treat estimate. Section 8 tenants were excluded from randomization, and all participants sought help. The analyzed groups had positive credit-related outcomes in 45% versus 17% of cases, but landlords obtained possession in roughly three quarters of cases in both groups. This is evidence for a less damaging transition, not a 94% eviction-prevention rate. Selected one-year interview results are not used as a causal housing-retention estimate.

The [Oregon Medicaid randomized experiment](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1212321) supports a coverage-to-mental-health pathway while finding no significant improvement in measured physical health at two years. Its mental-health score is not a QALY. The model's 0.02 utility-year per meaningful health-access improvement is explicitly judgment, not a trial estimate.

Request unique clients across case categories, representation intensity, net coverage/treatment months, actual stable housing following resolution, benefit receipt rather than awards, and validated health utility. Compare against alternative counsel and ordinary public-service appeal routes. Track delayed cases and lost opportunities, not only favorable closures.
sections.qualitative:
Legal protection has intrinsic and economic value beyond health. The numerical component includes three concrete pathways but does not price domestic-violence safety, disaster recovery, education, family rights, self-help or statewide litigation. Their omission is not evidence of zero value and makes the component unsuitable for an unqualified cross-charity portfolio ranking.

The [2025 review of priorities](https://nlsla.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/December-2025-Review-of-Priorities.pdf) sets 2026 resource priorities: housing 40%, health 25%, economic security 10%, domestic violence/family 7%, self-help 15%, community advancement 2% and disaster 1%. These board priorities establish broad scope, not how an extra unrestricted dollar will be allocated. Public agencies and coalition partners remain in the counterfactual. No statewide settlement or proposed policy is assigned wholly to NLSLA or wholly to LA.
sections.cost:
The illustrative central health component is about $193.5 million per 10 LA QALYs, using all $41,529,139 of audited annual recipient expenses. This is a partial health price, not the whole portfolio's return. Full costs are retained rather than selecting a cheap restricted program. No claim is made that this expenditure level can be purchased again at the same marginal productivity.

The housing bridge starts with 2,483 closed cases, the external 28-percentage-point credit-outcome difference, 50% transfer to mixed NLSLA cases, a 25% judgment probability that the incremental legal improvement produces a meaningful one-year health-relevant housing improvement, and 0.02 utility-years for that improvement. Health uses 1,893 cases × 20% additional meaningful access × 0.02 utility-years. Benefits use 1,162 cases × 15% additional receipt × 0.01 utility-years. A 25% ordinary-funding responsiveness factor and 80% overlap retention apply to the sum, then a one-year 3% discount. The result is about 2.15 LA QALYs per annual cost normalization.

None of the probabilities or utility weights after the external legal benchmark is empirically calibrated for NLSLA. All effects end after one year; no repeated-case lifetime benefit, household multiplier, mortality or face-value debt conversion is added. Conservative and favorable judgments are stress tests, not statistical bounds; full substitution gives zero. A harmful net outcome remains possible but lacks a defensible numerical bound.
sections.funding:
[Audited 2025 accounts](https://nlsla.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/NLSLA-25-FS.pdf), with 2024 comparatives, report expenses of $41,529,139 and $38,289,241. The [2023 audit](https://nlsla.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/NLSLA-2023-Audited-Financial-Statements.pdf) reports $31,413,744. These comparable calendar-year accrual totals include imputed donated services; the three-year mean is $37,077,374.67. The 2025 financial-statement opinion is unmodified, dated April 27, 2026; this is not claimed as the publication date or as proof of every grant-compliance issue being clear.

2025 revenue was $45,369,370, including $29,829,464 government contracts and $8,674,897 donated materials/services. Expenses were $36,691,117 program, $4,038,649 management and $799,373 fundraising. Removing imputed donations gives a $32,854,242 cash-resource proxy, not a verified marginal cash budget. Using it alone lowers the same modeled health price by about 21%; it assumes volunteer capacity remains available and is a sensitivity, not the central cost definition. Program subgrants of $5,736,120 are included once, not credited again as independently caused partner outputs.

Year-end net assets were $22,164,478, including $3,352,752 donor-restricted and $10,018,955 board-designated. The liquidity note reports $20,614,098 financial assets available within a year after specified deductions; this includes receivables/investments and is not bank cash. Client trust deposits are not spendable charity resources. Refundable public advances cannot be treated as unrestricted cash. LSC basic-field advances of $3,921,034 include resources reserved for 2026; approved carryover is part of the continuation counterfactual. These facts do not prove a funding gap or that every donation immediately adds a lawyer.

The newer costs are combined conservatively with the latest detailed 2024 case counts: no proportional caseload increase is assumed from expense growth, which partly reflects additional imputed legal services. A current costed intake queue, reimbursement conditions, hiring capacity and use of unrestricted reserves would materially improve the marginal model.

model.formula: Q_LA(D)=(D/C)*b*k*g*[Nh*deltaCredit*rH*pH*uH + Nm*pM*uM + Np*pP*uP]/(1+d). model.counterfactual: Public contracts, approved LSC carryover, existing legal aid/self-help, non-Shriver counsel, public appeals, partners and reserves continue. b reflects how ordinary funds change total case capacity versus those alternatives; legal probabilities then reflect substantive resolution beyond no additional NLSLA case.
model.attribution: Housing external comparison already incorporates alternative self-help; rH reduces transfer to mixed case intensity and post-randomization selection. pH is subsequent health-relevant improvement, not an additional legal success rate. k handles cross-case health overlap. model.uncertainty: Explicit subjective central for priced component. Not a full-portfolio ranking estimate. No posterior confidence claim: public finance, service mix, marginal capacity and health bridge could move return greatly; zero and unquantified downside retained.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional health-relevant stable-housing years, effective health-access years and benefit-receipt years among LA clients; legal closures and favorable credit orders are intermediate outputs.

reports.program: Heat resilience, local cooling and climate policy

what: Climate Resolve works on local climate policy, neighborhood cooling and technical assistance in Los Angeles.
It supports indoor-heat protections and installs cool roofs with partners in neighborhoods including Pacoima, Watts and Wilmington.
Its broader work includes transportation, wildfire resilience, planning and international cool-surface initiatives.
strengths: Cool roofs and effective indoor cooling offer a plausible way to reduce heat exposure in vulnerable neighborhoods, and the organization reports specific installations.
Implementation work could help tenants obtain useful protection beyond an adopted rule, while local partnerships connect policy with projects.
The current local projects and complete recipient accounts make additional funding, exposure and household costs concrete questions for donors.
reservations: Additional compliance, occupied cooling exposure, utility gains and marginal gift responsiveness remain unmeasured judgments.
Energy bills, rent, landlord capital, displacement and roof savings can offset health benefits; household incidence and donor room are unknown.
The estimate prices a partial local cooling pathway; broader organizational and nonlocal effects remain unestimated.

sections.what:
Climate Resolve (EIN 46-4736278) combines policy, implementation, technical assistance and community engagement. Its [2025 year-end account](https://climateresolve.org/winds-of-change/) reports more than 40 cool roofs in Pacoima, Watts and Wilmington and local public-space cooling projects. These named places are within LA County. [Shine On](https://climateresolve.org/shine-on-initiative/) also works internationally, whose global climate benefits cannot simply be assigned to LA residents.

The original FY 2025 return describes heat standards, county plans, resilience funding, wildfire recovery and neighborhood work. An ordinary gift supports that recipient, not an assumed restricted roof project. The donation route was verified without making a transaction. [Original FY 2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/464736278/202620709349301592/full)
sections.monitoring:
An [original county report dated July 14, 2025](https://file.lacounty.gov/SDSInter/bos/bc/1188278_EstablishingaSafeMaximumTemperatureThresholdforResidentialUnitsDirective1Jan23.2024Item47.14.pdf) supplies a 97,124-unit unincorporated rental inventory in Table 1. It is an estimated inventory, not homes needing cooling. The same report says retrofit needs cannot be quantified from assessor data and notes enforcement, grid and tenant-cost concerns. Its countywide 75% air-conditioning survey is not an observed fraction for those rental units.

A [randomized crossover experiment](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38329752/) exposed 16 older adults to four eight-hour indoor temperatures. It found greater core-temperature and cardiovascular strain at 31°C and 36°C, with much less change at 26°C. This establishes physiological plausibility, not a QALY effect or mortality rate for an 82°F ordinance. The [Pacoima field study](https://doi.org/10.1088/2515-7620/ad2a8e) concerns thermal conditions around reflective pavement, not randomized clinical outcomes; surface-temperature reductions are not equivalent to residents' whole-day exposure reductions.

Monitor effective cooling during occupied heat-hours, electricity affordability and actual use, resident symptoms and utility, complaint resolution, landlord compliance and displacement. Compare supported buildings with otherwise-similar buildings already receiving county or utility help. For roofs, verify replacement timing, preexisting code/rebate obligations, occupancy, exposure change and coating durability.
sections.qualitative:
The county rule applies to unincorporated rentals. Enforcement starts in January 2027, with small-landlord room exceptions and possible extensions. Existing rebates, public assistance and landlord obligations belong in the baseline. The city's amended motion does not establish a final citywide ordinance, so no citywide rental cohort is priced.

The physiological crossover study supports heat-strain plausibility but does not measure the model's clinical utility weights. Roof and solar projections, or pavement surface changes, cannot establish occupied personal exposure or causal household savings. The reported $300,000 savings projection mixes installations without a verified horizon or breakdown and is not assigned to annual roof savings. Additional jobs and broader climate or resilience effects remain unmeasured.
sections.cost:
The conditional central is **$22.87 million per better life**, meaning ten combined healthy-year equivalents. A $10,000 normalization yields 0.00708457 clinical QALYs and −0.00271146 consumption-equivalent years, totaling 0.00437311. The initial $14.12 million health-only illustration is preserved and reproduces when financial effects are excluded. The change follows signed resource assumptions, not measured clinical deterioration.

The denominator is the full gross annual recipient expense of $3,745,093, including support, fundraising and events once. One year's organizational work is assumed to improve additional implementation beyond existing funding and accelerate protection for three years before the baseline catches up; roofs receive five finite years. The first benefit occurs one year after an October 2026 gift. There is no perpetual law benefit or retrospective purchase of laws or installed roofs.

Clinical inputs retain the initial assumptions: 97,124 inventory units, 25% with meaningful unmet cooling need, 2.5 residents per unit, a ten-point additional coalition implementation effect, 10% recipient causal share and 50% funding responsiveness. Each effective resident receives 20 equivalent relieved days at a utility gain of 0.05. The roof illustration uses 40 units, 50% additionality, three residents, 20 days and utility 0.02. These are priors. More than 40 reported installations in 2025 do not verify a future annual cohort or unrestricted donor queue.

The financial ledger counts households rather than every resident. Unincorporated tenants have a judged $30,000 resource baseline and $100 annual net productivity gain after taxes, benefits and work costs. A positive overlap adjustment halves this to $50. Full annual costs of $120 for energy, $60 for rent and $20 for user participation are jointly deducted before logarithmic valuation, leaving −$150.

Separate landlord households are assumed to own two units each, live locally and have a $60,000 baseline. Per unit, the $60 rent transfer is offset by $120 in annual net capital-service or financing costs from accelerated implementation and $10 maintenance: −$70 per unit, or −$140 per owner. These incidence and residency assumptions are unverified. The $120 is a provisional acceleration opportunity/service cost, not a full retrofit purchase repeatedly charged. An upfront stress replaces it with a one-time $1,000 per unit cost, jointly netted in the first year, yielding $38.06 million per better life. A separate case adds one-time counterfactual expenditure relief when the baseline catches up at year four, yielding $20.05 million. Neither amount is an observed cost or refund.

Owner-occupied roof homes in incorporated Pacoima, Watts and Wilmington are geographically separate from the unincorporated policy cohort. Judged annual bill savings of $150 are halved for positive overlap, then full recurring maintenance and operating user costs of $40 are deducted, leaving $35 on a $30,000 baseline. The $40 is not a repeated upfront payment. These figures do not come from the solar savings projection. A separate utility/counterparty ledger judges $20 of net margin or displacement loss per roof across ten owner units with a $60,000 baseline, half local. It does not treat all electricity revenue as profit. All negative costs remain full.

The production income method nets each household's dollars before the logarithm and counts resource equivalents once; clinical QALYs stay separate. [Comparison method](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/) Clinical-null and failed-thermal cases retain the entire negative financial ledger and have no beneficial price. No additional installation gives true zero unless a gift induces participation costs, which can persist after failure. Unknown incidence retains a health diagnostic with no combined price. Adverse rent, energy or capital costs can outweigh health gains. Other sensitivities test owner concentration, overlap, delay, duration, baseline resources, clinical effects and funding; they are scenarios, not confidence bounds.

Public and partner capital, enforcement, nonlocal counterparty burdens and broader portfolio effects remain unpriced. Donor expense and household welfare losses are distinct; the same capital must not be added twice. This is a partial local comparison, not complete world welfare, a full societal ratio, a lower bound or a donor-ready recommendation.

The counterparty ledger prices the illustrative utility margin loss from roof savings. Additional tenant electricity payments could also create utility margin gains; their net household incidence is unknown and unpriced here, rather than established as zero. A complete resource ledger would net policy-energy gains and roof losses for overlapping utility households in each year before logarithmic valuation. This partial central therefore cannot be described as total household resources or complete world benefit.
sections.funding:
Fresh original returns for FY 2023–2025 reconcile gross expenses of $3,311,328, $3,626,028 and $3,745,093, averaging $3,560,816.33: Part IX plus separately netted event costs once. Latest Part IX expense is $3,582,432 and event costs $162,661. Programs were $2,538,921, management $663,918 and fundraising $379,593 before event costs. Net assets of $906,954 include $603,069 restricted and $303,885 unrestricted. The return indicates an independent audit; its actual opinion and control findings were not obtained. These dated figures do not identify a current priced marginal funding gap.

Request current unrestricted staff and contract allocations, additional compliant buildings beyond the 2027 baseline, roof replacement timing, partner finance, a costed donor tranche and monitoring of household bills, capital costs and displacement. Existing rebates, county enforcement and developer or utility-funded installations remain alternatives. No restricted best-program donation or fundraising outreach is implied.

what: Coalition for Clean Air advocates for cleaner transportation and freight, community air monitoring and public education.
Its EPA-funded AirAware partnership operates at two YMCA facilities within Los Angeles County, alongside a Corona-Norco site outside this edition.
Its ports work seeks stronger emissions controls and implementation for residents exposed to freight pollution.
strengths: Local reports identify concrete filtration and operating constraints rather than counting publicity as health outcomes.
Current agency plans establish which infrastructure and incentive commitments already exist, allowing an explicit additional-work comparison.
Original recipient returns and a large older-adult pollution study make cost and health assumptions inspectable.
reservations: The additional policy probability, local exposed cohort, pollution reduction and gift response remain unmeasured judgments.
No priced next-dollar work plan or signed household resource incidence establishes donor room or a complete welfare estimate.
Port pollution crosses the metro boundary; local projects and statewide CARB projections cannot establish the LA beneficiary share.

sections.what:
Coalition for Clean Air (EIN 23-7120567) is the California recipient, not the international Climate and Clean Air Coalition. General donations support policy, education, community projects and overhead. The [current organization page](https://www.ccair.org/) identifies statewide clean-transportation and air-protection work; many historical achievements already belong in the counterfactual.

The [AirAware project](https://www.ccair.org/projects/airaware-ymcas/) is EPA-funded with TD Enviro and IQAir. Its 'Los Angeles area' description includes Corona-Norco, which is outside this LA-plus-Orange-county boundary. The other two facilities are verified within LA County: [Southeast-Rio Vista in Maywood](https://www.ymcala.org/locations/southeast-rio-vista-ymca/) and [Weingart East Los Angeles](https://www.ymcala.org/locations/weingart-east-los-angeles-ymca/). No equal one-third project weighting is used.
sections.monitoring:
The [current Southeast-Rio Vista report](https://www.ccair.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/2026.07.01_Southeast-Rio-Vista-YMCA-Y2Q2-Report.pdf) documents eight purifiers installed in March 2026 versus a room-sizing target of fifteen. Funds, available outlets and wall space constrained placement. The large gym received three units where roughly six were indicated. Higher fan speeds did not materially resolve the large-room filtration problem; the report also identifies doors and indoor sources. Thus seven units is a sizing shortfall, not a verified cash-only waiting list.

The [Weingart report](https://www.ccair.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/2026.07.01_Weingart-YMCA-Y2Q2-Report.pdf) reports six units against an eight-unit target. It records an apparently user-changed low setting in one multipurpose room from May 7 until correction on July 16, and possible HVAC problems. Device purchase is only one route: operating settings and source control may be cheaper, but partners may already do them. The report's exact initial installation dates vary internally, so only March 2026 is asserted here.

Both reports are labeled April–June but include July observations or actions. Publication dates are left unknown rather than inferred from the July 1 filenames. Indoor-versus-outdoor reductions, changes in outside pollution and overnight fireworks when buildings may be closed cannot establish additional occupied personal exposure. The next data request is room-level occupied person-hours, age mix, observed concentrations with and without additional devices/settings, lifecycle costs and what EPA/YMCA/IQAir resources will already cover.
sections.qualitative:
A [large Medicare analysis](https://xiaowu.io/publication/wu2020evaluating/wu2020evaluating.pdf) provides the external PM2.5 mortality benchmark used in the diagnostic: its most conservative full-cohort hazard ratio was 1.06 per 10 micrograms/m³. Causal interpretation still depends on confounder control and transfer across ages and pollutant mixtures. It is not a clinical result for YMCA children or a few hours of indoor exercise. Clinical morbidity, mortality and black-carbon pathways should not be added independently when they describe overlapping exposure or outcomes.

The [current ports agreement](https://www.aqmd.gov/home/air-quality/air-quality-management-plans/air-quality-mgt-plan/facility-based-mobile-source-measures/comm-ports-wkng-grp/potential-cooperative-agreement-with-the-ports-of-long-beach-and-los-angeles) and [September 2026 addendum](https://www.aqmd.gov/docs/default-source/ports-ca/addendum-to-ports-ca_final-approved-sept-2026.pdf?sfvrsn=a4db637e_2) are already part of the baseline. They establish infrastructure planning and ship/truck incentive design, including a $40 million off-port infrastructure commitment. That is not a CCA grant or measured emissions reduction. The addendum explicitly leaves participation outside ports' control and requires future budgets, targets and tracking metrics.

CCA could improve incentive design, uptake or accountability. But the source does not identify a current extra-dollar work package, its effect on the number of additional cleaner trips, the dirty trips actually displaced, or LA/Orange exposure under competing designs. Transported pollution and truck routes extend into the Inland Empire and beyond; a port address cannot set the beneficiary share to one. A model multiplying an invented small advocacy probability by an invented large health total would hide, rather than resolve, the decisive uncertainty.
sections.cost:
The conditional central remains approximately **$10.0 million per better life**: ten combined healthy-year welfare equivalents in LA/Orange. A $10,000 ordinary-gift normalization yields 0.0099687 clinical QALYs and zero central resource equivalents by neutral-sign judgment. It is a partial planning illustration, not observed charity effectiveness. Clinical QALYs remain separate from consumption equivalents.

The model charges five full FY2025 budgets of $2,494,912, including shared administration, fundraising and event expenses once. Additional technical/policy effort is judged to change the probability of a local freight-pollution increment by 10 percentage points over that five-year effort, beyond existing rules, partner action and funded infrastructure. A 50% marginal funding response separately addresses replacement funding and capacity; coalition attribution is already inside that 10-point probability. For $10,000, donor-attributable probability is 0.0000400816. No priced marginal staff tranche verifies this linear response.

Conditional on implementation after three years, 500,000 older residents alive then experience 0.2µg/m³ lower annual ambient PM2.5. These local exposure figures are judgments. The external HR 1.06/10µg/m³ is multiplied on log-risk by 0.7; annual competing mortality 0.035, survivor utility 0.75 and finite ten-year horizon are unvalidated prognosis priors. Half the effect is durable; half accelerates the same reform by three years. The latter credits the finite survival difference against later implementation, not permanent prevention. [Primary study](https://xiaowu.io/publication/wu2020evaluating/wu2020evaluating.pdf)

Current adopted controls, the executed ports agreement/addendum and its $40 million commitment are baseline. The gift cannot buy existing YMCA devices or past corrections. CCA-specific additional uptake, enforcement, design or accountability must exceed those commitments. California CARB's 230 statewide projected premature deaths are not transplanted to LA; regional exposure evidence is missing.

**Signed resources:** the central zero is a judgment about unresolved net sign, not proof of no household benefit. A transparent diagnostic considers 1,000 baseline-alive households with $100 annual private-care/work gains after tax, benefits and work-cost offsets; a 50% positive overlap adjustment leaves $50, then full $20 compliance costs produce net $30 before log. A disjoint 1,000 counterparty households lose $10 annually. No extra-survivor earnings or gross public/insurance savings are counted. These counts/dollars are illustrative, not measured. Resource years follow the 10-year durable/three-year acceleration branches with delay and discounting. [Comparison method](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/)

That positive-ledger case contributes 0.000042893 equivalent years, yielding $9.99million per better life. Holding the identical financial ledger while making clinical benefit null yields $2.33billion. A signed loss ledger contributes−0.000429923 years and yields $10.48million with unchanged health. Adverse exposure yields negative health and resources; a gift-induced household loss persists when policy/funding response is zero. True-zero has no beneficial price. Unknown-resource incidence has a null combined price, retaining the health diagnostic rather than treating missing dollars as zero.

Sensitivity tests retain the complete initial 11 cases and add local exposure, survival, delay, signed finance, clinical-null, financial-only, adverse, failed-policy burden and unknown cases. The numerical central is unchanged apart from rounding because sources do not identify a better LA point estimate. The three-year cost mean is corrected, not used to force a favorable headline. Original alpha is frozen as a complete diagnostic.

Public/partner capital, compliance resources, donated effort and displaced activity beyond household incidence are additional unpriced external social costs. The donor denominator is complete recipient operating cost; this is not a complete societal ratio or a lower bound.

The financial scenarios count one representative adult per modeled household, not every family member. Their $50,000 baseline is the resource reference for that representative unit; the same-household percentage change is applied once. The recurrent household-year forecast is distinct from the fixed older-adult clinical cohort: only people who would be alive without the cleaner-air change enter the financial roster. No extra survivors' earnings are credited. Neither the number of households, their resource baseline nor the incidence values have been measured for this intervention.
sections.funding:
Corrected full gross recipient resources are $1,472,176 (FY2023),$2,162,329 (FY2024) and $2,494,912 (FY2025), mean $2,043,139. The earlier LA display omitted $10,170 and $11,407 of donated services in the first two years; California deep review reconciled these original returns. Part IX plus event costs plus applicable donated resources are included once; Schedule D audited totals are not increased again. Latest annual expense is unchanged, so this correction does not change the central denominator.

FY 2025 revenue was $2,149,048 after event netting, $303,847 below Part IX expense. It included $373,769 government contributions and $321,468 fee-for-service contracts. Program, management and fundraising expenses were $1,479,082, $647,639 and $326,174 before direct event costs. Net assets were $1,113,614, including $1,036,114 without donor restrictions. Consultants accounted for $974,336; a consultant total does not reveal which incremental policy work is unfunded.

The new reports narrow an actionable question: can an ordinary gift fund technically feasible extra filtration or sustained correct operation beyond existing EPA and YMCA partner plans, and for how many occupied dose-hours? A funder would need the costed plan and subsequent exposure monitoring. An unrestricted donation is not automatically allocated to this gap, and no restricted offer, matching multiplier, transaction or endorsement is implied. For policy, request the specific additional staff/consultant work, alternative funding and measurable implementation target.
