model.formula: h1=h0*exp(-ln(HR)/10*transport*pm); rho=ln(1.03); F(a,t)=(1-exp(-a*t))/a. qD=u*(F(h1+rho,T)-F(h0+rho,T)). a=min(A,T). qT=u*(F(h1+rho,a)-F(h0+rho,a)+(1-exp(-(h0-h1)*a))*(exp(-(h1+rho)*a)-exp(-(h1+rho)*T))/(h1+rho)). q=(f*qD+(1-f)*qT)/1.03^L. Qgift=10000/(E*Y)*b*(p*N*q-harm). Price=100000/Qgift if positive. N is cohort alive at implementation; no extra survival-to-implementation multiplier. Costs are constant-real full budgets; no cost discount haircut. Signed resources: each disjoint baseline-alive household group nets positiveUSD*positiveOverlapShare+negativeUSD before logarithm; negatives remain full. CG equivalent=.5*people*discountedYears*log1p(net/baseline)*gift/(E*Y)*b*p*branchShare. Durable branch lasts T, timing branch only min(A,T). Independent gift-induced burdens bypass policy/funding probability. Shared production income calculator and reportPrice count income once.
model.counterfactual: Existing EPA, IQAir and YMCA devices, already-corrected fan settings, partner HVAC investigation, public plans, current ports agreement and clean-truck rules continue. A new gift cannot retroactively buy March installations or July corrections. The policy alternative must exceed the current baseline. Policy/technical capacity changes the probability of additional transport/freight emissions controls or implementation beyond adopted rules, the current ports agreement and already-agreed public funding. Current activities establish a live mechanism, not the assumed probability or PM reduction. YMCA device gaps and indoor/outdoor percentages do not determine this ambient older-adult model.
model.attribution: p is the incremental recipient-specific probability effect of a five-year whole-organization effort versus partner/regulator action without it. b models donation-sensitive capacity after replacement funding, distinct from coalition p. Local linear extrapolation to a small gift is judgment and can fail at lumpy capacity thresholds. Financial people are unvalidated recurrent baseline-alive household-year exposure forecasts, allowing replacement households as rosters turn over; no additional-survivor earnings or guaranteed fixed cohort survival.
model.uncertainty: Explicit judgment central, not identified causal charity effectiveness. Wide scenarios include clinical-null, no-policy-effect and harm. This is not a complete portfolio estimate or a reason to override donor diligence.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional annual ambient PM2.5 exposure reduction among an explicitly modeled older cohort; finite discounted all-cause survival differences, without adding overlapping mortality/morbidity or lead/IQ units. Signed additional household consumption: private care/work gains after taxes/benefit withdrawal/work costs, compliance losses and separate counterparty/displacement losses. No survivor wages, gross medical savings or construction spending.

historicalAlphaModel.costScope: Five full latest-year gross reported recipient budgets, across all programs and support, normalized linearly to a $10,000 ordinary gift. No policy-only cost carveout. External social resources unpriced.
historicalAlphaModel.geographicAttribution: Only health within Los Angeles and Orange counties (FIPS 06037, 06059) is counted. The 500,000 older adults are an analyst-selected conditional exposure cohort, not an office-count allocation or observed participant total. Riverside and San Bernardino outcomes are excluded. CA and LA are nested views of the same recipient; never add them. The statewide 1.5m and local 0.5m central cohorts are separate judgment exposure denominators, not measured shares. allPopulationQalys includes the modeled California branch only.
historicalAlphaModel.formula: h1=h0*exp(-ln(HR)/10*transport*pm); rho=ln(1.03); F(a,t)=(1-exp(-a*t))/a. qD=u*(F(h1+rho,T)-F(h0+rho,T)). a=min(A,T). qT=u*(F(h1+rho,a)-F(h0+rho,a)+(1-exp(-(h0-h1)*a))*(exp(-(h1+rho)*a)-exp(-(h1+rho)*T))/(h1+rho)). q=(f*qD+(1-f)*qT)/1.03^L. Qgift=10000/(E*Y)*b*(p*N*q-harm). Price=100000/Qgift if positive. N is cohort alive at implementation; no extra survival-to-implementation multiplier. Costs are constant-real full budgets; no cost discount haircut.
historicalAlphaModel.counterfactual: Existing EPA, IQAir and YMCA devices, already-corrected fan settings, partner HVAC investigation, public plans, current ports agreement and clean-truck rules continue. A new gift cannot retroactively buy March installations or July corrections. The policy alternative must exceed the current baseline. Policy/technical capacity changes the probability of additional transport/freight emissions controls or implementation beyond adopted rules, the current ports agreement and already-agreed public funding. Current activities establish a live mechanism, not the assumed probability or PM reduction. YMCA device gaps and indoor/outdoor percentages do not determine this ambient older-adult model.
historicalAlphaModel.attribution: p is the incremental recipient-specific probability effect of a five-year whole-organization effort versus partner/regulator action without it. b models donation-sensitive capacity after replacement funding, distinct from coalition p. Local linear extrapolation to a small gift is judgment and can fail at lumpy capacity thresholds.
historicalAlphaModel.uncertainty: Explicit judgment central, not identified causal charity effectiveness. Wide scenarios include clinical-null, no-policy-effect and harm. This is not a complete portfolio estimate or a reason to override donor diligence.
historicalAlphaModel.nativeOutcomes: Additional annual ambient PM2.5 exposure reduction among an explicitly modeled older cohort; finite discounted all-cause survival differences, without adding overlapping mortality/morbidity or lead/IQ units.

what: Shatterproof works to improve addiction prevention, treatment access and quality through navigation, provider education, stigma campaigns and policy.
Treatment Atlas is an information service, not a treatment provider; reaching a website does not mean receiving effective care.
Our weak-confidence best estimate is about $45 million per 10 USA QALYs on full reported resource costs; the estimate is highly sensitive to unmeasured treatment conversion.
strengths: Navigation toward effective opioid treatment has a plausible, clinically consequential mechanism.
Public monitoring defines engagement metrics, making it possible to distinguish activity from verified treatment.
Current reports and audited accounts reveal the broader portfolio and unusually large donated-media component.
reservations: No comparative evidence located establishes how many additional treatment-years Atlas causes.
A favorable scenario is about $185,000 per 10 QALYs, but weak conversion produces negligible benefit; zero and harm remain possible.
Public contracts, available financial assets and an unspecified next-dollar workplan make marginal capacity uncertain.

sections.what: Shatterproof combines treatment navigation, quality improvement, prevention and advocacy. Its [2025 report](https://www.shatterproof.org/sites/default/files/2026-05/Impact_report_25_05_16_26.pdf) describes 1.2 million Atlas users, 1.6 million sessions and 6,700 provider learners. These are different denominators, not treatment starts. The report also describes stigma campaigns and policy activity; those branches are not assigned automatic health credit.
sections.monitoring: The strongest inspectable monitoring is a [Florida quarterly report](https://development.myflfamilies.com/external/documents/66691.pdf): 29,613 users and 1,961 referrals, with referral explicitly defined as a facility-profile view. It does not verify patient contact, enrollment, medication, retention or survival. National reporting says 63% of facilities contacted ranked in the top fifth for science-based care; this is not evidence of the counterfactual provider choice. A useful beta evaluation would link consented user referrals to treatment records and compare against otherwise similar users of existing referral routes.
sections.qualitative: [Provider resources](https://treatmentatlas.org/resources-providers) encourage established treatment principles. The clinical bridge is plausible: [Sordo et al.](https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1550) found lower mortality during methadone or buprenorphine treatment in 19 observational cohorts, while induction and the period after stopping carried extra risk. Historical cohort differences are not randomized Atlas effects and may not transport to current fentanyl exposure or its user mix. The model uses a smaller net mortality benefit and short retained treatment duration. Prevention restrictions may shift substance use rather than eliminate it; stigma and policy effects may help or harm and remain explicitly unpriced.
sections.cost:
The central model yields about 119 additional treatment-years before funding substitution, 60 after it, and 11.8 USA QALYs per annual activity cohort. At full recipient resource costs this is about $45 million per 10 QALYs; excluding recognized donated resources gives about $18 million. Neither is a provider treatment price. Clinical care paid by insurers, public programs and patients is additional to recipient costs and is not a social cost-effectiveness numerator. The favorable scenario requires much stronger conversion and retention; its roughly $185,000 price is not an evidence-based confidence limit. All other portfolio health is set net zero centrally, not asserted to be zero or used to claim a rigorous lower bound.

Pairing 2024 resource costs with 2025 reach is a stationary-scale approximation, not an observed same-year cost-per-output ratio. The alternative denominator excludes recognized donated resources from accrual expense; it is not cash flow. Additional treatment starts are net of alternative care in e; t is retained exposure conditional on those additional starts, not a second subtraction of the same start.
sections.funding: The [2024 audit](https://www.shatterproof.org/sites/default/files/2025-10/2024%20Shatterproof%20Financial%20Audit_0.pdf) reports $52,747,632 expense; restoring $61,441 direct event benefits gives $52,809,073. Recognized donated media/services total $31,286,172, leaving a $21,522,901 cash-like accrual numerator—not cash-flow expenditure. Available financial assets were $14,073,387; some contracts reimburse eligible costs. A donation can substitute for reserves or public/private support, so the model halves expected marginal activity. The [2023 audit](https://www.shatterproof.org/sites/default/files/2024-12/FINAL%202023%20Shatterproof%20Financial%20Statements.pdf) gives gross comparable 2023/2022 costs of $25,439,567/$16,796,216; controlled affiliates had no activity. Three-year mean $31,681,619 is distorted by donated-media valuation and is not a current cash budget. No current quantified unfunded capacity plan was located.

model.formula: PY=U*f*o*e*t; Q_all=b*(PY*(d*q+w)-h); Q_USA=g*Q_all; price=10*C/Q_USA for positive Q. One annual activity cohort, short treatment exposure, discounted remaining-life QALYs in q. No repeated lifetime cohort credit.
model.counterfactual: e is additional treatment net of alternative directories, clinicians, existing care and unavailable slots; b separately adjusts the effect of incremental support on recipient activity. Zero conversion or no funding additionality gives zero health absent other effects.
model.attribution: Atlas receives only the net change in effective treatment, not all health among visitors. National transport of Florida engagement ratio and treatment conversion are explicit subjective judgments. Other provider/payer inputs are necessary complements, not free social resources.
model.uncertainty: Weak-confidence judgment model, not a measured causal return or probability interval. Scenarios span strong conversion, negligible yield, zero and negative health. No source identifies the marginal conversion parameter; root should treat price as provisional.
model.nativeOutcomes: Users, sessions, profile views, additional treatment starts and retained treatment-years. Health counted only after the explicit treatment conversion and clinical bridge.

inputs.name: C
inputs.unit: USD annual full recipient resource cost
inputs.rationale: Audited gross 2024 expense, restoring direct donor benefits; includes recognized donated media and services. The 2024 costs and 2025 reach are paired as a stationary-scale approximation, not a same-year measured unit cost.

inputs.name: U
inputs.rationale: 2025 report says more than 1.2 million people; use rounded floor, not unique patients or starts.

inputs.name: f
inputs.rationale: Florida quarter 1,961 profile views / 29,613 users = .06622. Transport to national annual population is subjective; repeat views and national mix could differ.

inputs.name: o
inputs.rationale: 20% reserves most engagements for alcohol/other disorders, caregivers or irrelevant contacts; not measured Atlas case mix.

inputs.name: e
inputs.unit: net additional effective treatment starts per OUD engagement
inputs.rationale: 3% after non-enrollment, inappropriate capacity, alternative locators and treatment that would happen anyway. A weak prior, not a measured Atlas effect; test zero.

inputs.name: t
inputs.unit: additional retained treatment years per start
inputs.rationale: Quarter-year retained treatment exposure conditional on an additional start already adjusted for alternative care in e; no second subtraction of the same otherwise-received start and no lifelong adherence assumed.

inputs.name: b
inputs.rationale: 50% allows replacement of other donations, reserves and public contracts. This is separate from patients finding care anyway in e.

inputs.name: d
inputs.unit: net deaths prevented per additional treatment-year
inputs.rationale: 1% between historical buprenorphine and methadone cohort rate gaps; discounts confounding and modern transport, includes induction/discontinuation risks rather than using peak untreated risk.

inputs.name: q
inputs.unit: discounted QALYs per premature death prevented
inputs.rationale: 15, broadly about 30 remaining years at .77 utility and 3% discount; not patient-level survival evidence. Test 10–20.

inputs.name: w
inputs.rationale: Small .05 utility improvement while retained, separately from mortality. Could be zero/negative; no long-term recovery dividend.

inputs.name: g
inputs.rationale: 99% for domestic navigation, allowing nonresident use. Not inferred from headquarters or a claim all online users are residents.

inputs.name: h
inputs.unit: other net health harm per annual activity cohort before funding additionality
inputs.rationale: Net zero centrally for unpriced prevention, stigma, policy and adverse effects; not established zero or a proven lower bound.

scenarios.label: Much stronger treatment conversion and retention
Excludes recognized donated resources from numerator
No treatment benefit plus 10 QALYs other harm

sensitivity: Central effective treatment yield before funding substitution is about 0.0000993 treatment-years per user. This is a judgment, not an observed conversion rate.

At other central inputs, e must be 1.3425 to beat $1 million per 10 USA QALYs, or 13.4254 to beat $100,000: impossible as a probability without stronger case mix, retention or other beneficial pathways.
At full resource costs, thresholds are about 2,667 / 26,671 additional treatment-years after funding substitution for $1 million / $100,000 per 10 QALYs, using .2 QALY per year and g=.99.
Net other harm above 23.84 QALYs before funding additionality erases the central benefit; harm is not multiplied by the treatment-conversion probability.
The cash-like denominator lowers price by 59.2%, but donated advertising fair value is not necessarily its opportunity cost. A social model must add care costs and account for media displacement.
If geographic share is .95 rather than .99, price rises 4.2%; treatment conversion and funding additionality dominate.

what: FRAC works to improve access to federal nutrition assistance through policy research, advocacy, technical assistance and grants.
Its portfolio includes WIC, SNAP, school meals and local anti-hunger projects.
A provisional SNAP-continuity model suggests about $69 million per 10 USA QALYs, but leaves major WIC and school-meal pathways unpriced and is not a measured return.
strengths: Federal nutrition programs reach populations whose health can improve when assistance becomes more reliable.
Research, implementation support and regranting provide several plausible routes beyond simply publishing advocacy materials.
Original accounts permit recipient-only cost reconciliation, and current policy work identifies a concrete administrative-funding decision.
reservations: The central result depends on subjective avoidable-churn, coalition-leverage and funding-additionality assumptions.
Historical lifetime health effects may transfer poorly to short interruptions in today's SNAP; zero health gain remains plausible.
Federal WIC regrants dominate recent costs, but the reviewed evidence does not identify their additional enrollment or the next unrestricted dollar's destination.

sections.what:
FRAC is a national nutrition-policy and implementation charity, not a food bank. It supports access to WIC, SNAP, child nutrition and related programs, including DC Hunger Solutions and Maryland Hunger Solutions. The 2024 recipient return reports $13.76 million for early-childhood nutrition, of which $11.99 million was grants, and $1.80 million for child nutrition. These are spending categories, not health results. The separate FRAC Action Council is outside this recipient estimate. [Recipient return](https://frac.org/wp-content/uploads/FRAC-2024-Form-990-PDC.pdf)

WIC CIAO awarded $14.8 million in its second and final subgrant round in January 2025, backed by USDA and implemented with partner organizations. The award announcement does not establish additional enrollment, retention or health. It also does not establish that an ordinary donation will expand the already awarded federal project. [WIC CIAO](https://www.hellowic.org/wic-ciao-round-2-subgrants/)
sections.monitoring:
The useful outcomes are additional benefit-receipt months, reduced administrative churn, successful enrollment and redemption, with appropriate comparison groups—not the number of policy reports, eligible people or schools offering meals. USDA's 2023 table counts 4.464 million preschool-age SNAP participants nationally, defining preschool as younger than five; the table includes territories. This anchors scale, not FRAC attribution. [USDA](https://fns-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/resource-files/snap-FY23-Characteristics-Report.pdf)

For the modeled branch, monitor whether administrative relief changes state staffing and timeliness, whether eligible families actually retain benefits, and whether FRAC changes the outcome relative to other advocates and public agencies. For WIC, request project-level enrollment and retention effects against a credible comparator, unique participants, age/pregnancy mix and cost, separated from general WIC participation trends. The reviewed sources did not supply those decisive marginal results.
sections.qualitative:
The clinical bridge is promising but indirect. A large historical rollout study links earlier Food Stamps access to later survival; its preferred treated estimate is about 1.2 additional life-years for exposure from conception to age five. That is model-based life expectancy, not observed completed lifespans, and the design observes early access alongside later access. Modern short gaps may behave differently. [Study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11395512/)

A contemporary pre-pregnancy SNAP analysis finds that some favorable conventional estimates do not survive its event-study checks. This discourages simply assigning a fixed infant-health dividend to every benefit month. [Contemporary study](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1468-0009.70097) WIC has a separate evidence base, but associations and program effectiveness alone do not identify FRAC-induced enrollment or QALYs. [AHRQ review](https://effectivehealthcare.ahrq.gov/products/outcomes-nutrition/research)

The current SNAP administrative-cost decision supplies a concrete prospective route. FRAC argues for relief while USDA's June 2026 proposed rule reflects a 25% federal administrative share from FY 2027. Preventing administrative disruption is not the same as reversing every statutory eligibility cut. State spending could replace federal funding anyway; relief could also redirect public resources from other valuable services. [FRAC](https://frac.org/blog/why-the-snap-administrative-cost-shift-threatens-state-budgets-and-program-operations) [USDA proposal](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/24/2026-12696/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-changes-in-federal-state-administrative-cost-sharing)
sections.cost:
The recipient's 2024 expense is $21,497,588 after restoring $14,674 of event costs netted against revenue; do not use the larger consolidated affiliate total. Two annual budgets, $42,995,176, fund the normalization used below. This includes all recipient programs and overhead, not only SNAP advocacy. [2024 return](https://frac.org/wp-content/uploads/FRAC-2024-Form-990-PDC.pdf) Comparable gross-expense figures are $14,821,886 in 2023 and $9,720,220 in 2022; the three-year mean is $15,346,565. [2023 return](https://frac.org/wp-content/uploads/FRAC-990-2023-Public-Disclosure-Copy.pdf) [2022 return](https://frac.org/wp-content/uploads/PDC-Food-Research-and-Action-Center-2022-990-Tax-Return_signed.pdf)

My weak-confidence central judgment uses four million early-child SNAP participants, 5% additional annual benefit continuity for two years conditional on effective relief, a 10% coalition-induced change probability, 5% FRAC attribution and 50% funding additionality. That yields 1,000 expected additional child-years, about $42,995 per child-year. A deliberately attenuated and discounted lifetime bridge gives about 0.0062 QALYs per child-year, then a 99.8% USA resident share: roughly 6.2 USA QALYs, or $69 million per 10. These probabilities and effects are opinions, not measured program performance.

This is a partial-pathway estimate charged full recipient costs, not a proven lower bound or a complete valuation. WIC, school meals, adult nutrition and other policy benefits are centrally net zero solely because they are unpriced; adverse effects can reverse the result. Federal food benefits, state administration and the opportunity cost of taxes or displaced spending are outside the charity-cost numerator. Thus this is not a social cost-effectiveness estimate.

The joint favorable scenario is about $668,000 per 10 USA QALYs; the poor positive scenario is about $584 billion. These are stress tests, not confidence bounds. Zero and negative scenarios are retained. On this narrow branch alone, the central case is not especially compelling; a stronger recommendation would need evidence for additional WIC/school-meal yield or substantially better policy leverage.
sections.funding:
Recent financial scale is heavily influenced by federal regranting. The recipient return shows $14.27 million in government grants in 2024; year-end unrestricted net assets were about $0.81 million, while most net assets were restricted. Receivables and cash cannot be treated as unrestricted room for more funding. [Return](https://frac.org/wp-content/uploads/FRAC-2024-Form-990-PDC.pdf) The consolidated audit describes a roughly $1.6 million reserve draw during 2024 and substantial grants payable; these are group context, not recipient-only free-cash figures. [Audit](https://frac.org/wp-content/uploads/FRAC-2024-audit.pdf)

The latest disclosed finance year on the current index is 2024. No verified 2026 marginal hiring, implementation or matching-funds plan was found in the reviewed material. A donation could support urgent flexible policy work, replace other contributions, rebuild reserves, or support restricted-project overhead. The 50% additionality judgment is intentionally revisable and does not claim a specific unfunded opportunity. [Finance index](https://frac.org/financials)

The final application FAQ anticipated a January 2025–December 2026 project period and explicitly no further rounds. That is evidence of a planned end, not proof that current work has stopped or that federal support was terminated. Sustaining effective methods afterward could be valuable, but requires evaluation and a funded-versus-unfunded continuation plan. [Round 2 FAQ](https://www.hellowic.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/WIC-CIAO-Round-2-RFA-FAQ.pdf)

The verified official giving page names Food Research & Action Center as the recipient and links its EveryAction form. Use the general fund for this recipient-wide assessment, not a restricted initiative or the separate Action Council. The processor page identifies FRAC, but its JavaScript checkout and tax details were not independently inspected; the donation link therefore goes to FRAC's official giving page. [Ways to donate](https://frac.org/ways-to-donate)

model.costScope: Two years of full recipient-only gross operating expense, including regrants and overhead, excluding separate active Action Council. Accrual Form 990 basis restores event costs. Public benefits and public administrative/social opportunity costs are outside numerator. This is a local scaling approximation for ordinary marginal support, not a claim one donor must finance two budgets or that effects scale linearly indefinitely.
model.geographicAttribution: g=.998 is an explicit judgment allowing territorial/nonresident effects, informed by USDA participant geography but not equal to an observed outcome-weighted share. 50 states plus DC residents only; noncitizen residents count. No headquarters-based apportionment.
model.formula: q=(life/exposure)*utility*transport/(1+discount)^lag; PY=N*z*T*p*a*b; Q_all=PY*q-b*h; Q_USA=g*Q_all; price=10*C/Q_USA when Q_USA>0. C is two annual budgets; only one two-year continuity cohort, no perpetual policy credit. lag includes the delay to realized lifetime gains.
model.counterfactual: z is additional continuity conditional on relief relative to states replacing funds or fixing administration anyway; p is advocacy coalition-induced relief/implementation probability increment, not total enactment probability. a apportions that increment to FRAC; b separately discounts donor replacement/reserve substitution. Only additional early-child receipt counted.
model.attribution: Subjective policy branch tied to current administrative-funding advocacy, not credit for all national SNAP spending or all historic wins. FRAC's WIC and other portfolio effects are net zero centrally but unestimated, not established absent. Other coalition/public inputs remain necessary.
model.uncertainty: Very weak-confidence best estimate, not calibrated probabilities or confidence interval. Core policy and marginal enrollment quantities are judgments; historical clinical transport can be zero. Favorable/poor scenarios deliberately vary several parameters together. Full costs do not prove this partial model conservative if excluded effects are harmful.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional preschool child-years of SNAP receipt; WIC enrollment/retention and school-meal access tracked separately but not converted to health without causal bridges.

inputs.name: C
inputs.rationale: Judgment extrapolation to two years at the observed annual recipient expense: 2 × (2024 Form 990 Part IX 21,482,914 + event direct costs 14,674); continuation at this scale is a model judgment.

inputs.name: N
inputs.rationale: Round down 2023 4.464 million preschool count to 4 million prospective scale; not a forecast of 2027 enrollment or number at risk.

inputs.name: z
inputs.unit: additional benefit-year fraction conditional on relief
inputs.rationale: 5% annual continuity equivalent: e.g. 20% avoid a three-month gap. Net of state replacement and other causes; no observed FRAC-specific estimate.

inputs.name: T
inputs.rationale: Two years; no permanent repeal or lifelong benefit eligibility assumed.

inputs.name: p
inputs.rationale: 10 percentage points for useful relief/implementation due to advocacy rather than political forces alone; weak prior, test zero.

inputs.name: a
inputs.unit: FRAC share of incremental coalition contribution
inputs.rationale: 5% allows many national/state advocates and officials; not an empirical pivotality estimate.

inputs.name: b
inputs.rationale: Half of normalized activity additional after other donations, public funds and reserve substitution. Separate from policy counterfactual.

inputs.name: life
inputs.rationale: Study's modeled treated life-expectancy estimate, not measured FRAC outcome or observed complete lifespans.

inputs.name: exposure
inputs.unit: years from conception to age five
inputs.rationale: 5.75-year exposure window; linear division is an additional model assumption, not demonstrated effect of isolated gaps.

inputs.name: utility
inputs.rationale: 0.7 for later-life health, not study-measured utility.

inputs.name: transport
inputs.unit: fraction of historical per-year effect retained
inputs.rationale: 25% discounts modern nutrition, short discontinuities, selection and lifetime extrapolation. Zero remains credible.

inputs.name: discount
inputs.rationale: 3% standard modeling choice, not empirical finding.

inputs.name: lag
inputs.rationale: 60-year lumped approximation including prospective program delay; test 40–70 years rather than claim age-specific survival curve.

inputs.name: g
inputs.rationale: 99.8% permits territorial effects; uncertainty in relative health yield remains.

inputs.name: h
inputs.unit: other net QALY harm before funding additionality
inputs.rationale: Zero for unpriced portfolio centrally; positive h captures displacement, implementation harm or other downside independent of policy success.

inputs.name: WIC marginal enrollment
inputs.unit: additional retained participants per unrestricted dollar
inputs.rationale: Awards and participation totals do not identify causal incremental uptake or next-dollar allocation.

sensitivity: Central q=0.006198947635382195; about 1,000 expected additional child-years before geographic apportionment, not 400,000 FRAC-attributable child-years.

At q=0.006198947635382195 and g=.998, beating $1 million/$100 thousand per 10 USA QALYs requires 69497.82642372415 / 694978.2642372416 additional child-years after all attribution and funding adjustments.

Holding other central inputs, p*a must exceed 0.34748913211862076 for $1 million per 10 or 3.4748913211862074 for $100 thousand per 10, versus .005 central; the latter exceeds one. Stronger health/continuity or other pathways are needed.
Other net harm h above 12.39789527076439 QALYs before b erases central benefit. Harm is not multiplied by policy-success probability.
Every halving of z, p, a, b or transport doubles price absent other effects. Reducing the 60-year lag to 40 raises the present health value about 1.81-fold.
Using the historical mean reduces cost by about 29%, but the federal regrant portfolio is changing and neither historical cost base identifies next-dollar efficiency.

WIC could materially improve the assessment: require retained additional pregnancy/child episodes × causal QALYs per episode, net of alternative outreach, alongside a specific unrestricted-funding pathway. Do not divide national WIC health by FRAC's grant dollars.

what: CEH tests products, pursues chemical-law enforcement and helps institutions buy safer alternatives.
Its work can change manufacturers' behavior beyond California, and recent receipt-paper agreements address several potentially harmful substitutes together.
An extremely uncertain judgment estimate prices prospective receipt-exposure acceleration at full recipient cost; the clinical health prior is explicit and other prevention pathways remain unpriced.
strengths: Product testing and detailed settlement terms provide more inspectable mechanisms than general awareness campaigns.
Class-wide restrictions on receipt additives can reduce the risk of replacing one concerning chemical with another.
There are plausible nationwide manufacturing spillovers and complementary local pollution-remediation pathways.
reservations: A settlement count or chemical-content exceedance does not establish absorbed dose, disease reduction or QALYs.
Already committed reformulation and existing legal obligations weaken the link from a new donation to future changes.
The strongest recent numerical claims describe market reach, while geographical, clinical and funding additionality remain unresolved.

sections.what:
CEH combines litigation, product testing, safer purchasing and community pollution work. Its 2024 return allocates about $1.06 million to consumer-product litigation, $0.64 million to green chemistry, $0.31 million to industrial-pollution work, and the remainder to other programs and support. The return describes soil screening and safe-gardening/landscaping help around a battery-recycling facility, as well as product and industrial cases. [Original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/943251981/202542259349303204/full)

The annual report records 315-plus products tested and 33 companies with legal agreements. These are concrete activities but heterogeneous units: a small product reformulation and a major manufacturing change do not have equal health value. Safer foodware and institutional-purchasing support are additional branches, not automatic QALYs from waste avoided. [Annual report](https://ceh.org/about/ceh-2024-annual-report/)
sections.monitoring:
The August 2026 receipt announcement reports agreements with 163 companies representing 7% of the US retail market. Market share is not the share of residents, cashiers, receipts or health risk affected. [Announcement](https://ceh.org/receipts-are-about-to-get-safer-how-ceh-got-one-toxic-phenol-after-another-out-of-receipts/)

The court-filed amended Domtar judgment, entered August 11, 2026, is more informative: its operative reformulation clause covers products for use in California; the recitals describe an expected nationwide transition. The filing stamp and clerk's service certificate verify entry, not actual compliance. Compliance monitoring should establish dates, sales destinations, chemical migration and worker/customer exposures—not merely signed agreements. [Entered judgment](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/prop65/judgments/2025-01392J5988.pdf) [DOJ registry](https://oag.ca.gov/node/602156)

The next useful evidence is a product-by-product panel of pre/post formulation, use frequency, geography and biomarkers, with a comparator and actual implementation date. For local remediation, measure contaminated areas made inaccessible, sustained blood-lead/exposure changes and health-relevant follow-up. Repeat tests should distinguish enforcement success from changes already required or planned.
sections.qualitative:
Human studies support a receipt-exposure route, but do not identify a QALY return. In one study, urinary BPS rose after shifts among 33 cashiers handling BPS receipts; it was an exposure study, not a disease-prevention trial. [Thayer et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26309242/) A separate small controlled/observational project found no statistically clear shift-related signal and emphasized measurement and sample limitations, not proof of safety. [NIOSH research](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/218609/cdc_218609_DS1.pdf)

A 2024 NHANES analysis found broad exposure declines and substitution patterns: BPA decreased while BPS increased. Similar trends inside and outside California and concurrent scientific/regulatory attention complicate causal attribution to Proposition 65, let alone CEH. It supports the plausibility of national formulation effects, not a measured CEH share of national disease burden. [Primary analysis](https://escholarship.org/content/qt3r4691xq/qt3r4691xq.pdf)

I also tested a more direct chromium/contact-dermatitis route. A recent Danish study of 4,830 patch-tested patients found stable chromium-allergy trends after the EU leather limit; clinic prevalence is not general-population incidence. That does not invalidate CEH's specific agreements, but it prevents assuming every compliant leather product removes a predictable dermatitis burden. [Clinical study](https://doi.org/10.1111/cod.70045)

My judgment favors a small positive but extremely uncertain prospective exposure-acceleration health yield. I assign a20percent probability to clinically meaningful benefit and a small conditional health area, while retaining an expected substitution burden. These are transparent priors, not evidence that chemical warning exceedances cause a known quantity of disease. Effects differ by dose, route, age and replacement material; a warning threshold is not an estimated probability of disease. Regulatory burden, regrettable substitutions, unnecessary avoidance and diverted resources are possible downsides.
sections.cost:
Full recipient expense was $4,045,100 in 2024, including management, fundraising and investment-management fees. The original return does not show event or inventory costs to restore. [2024 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/943251981/202542259349303204/full) The comparable 2023 and 2022 totals are $5,130,659 and $5,438,516, giving a $4,871,425 mean. The higher IRS totals relative to audited operating expense reconcile to $22,661 and $27,923 investment fees, respectively. [2023 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/943251981/202423199349315237/full) [2022 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/943251981/202313199349312596/full) [Audit](https://ceh.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/CtrEnviroHealth-23-FinalFS.pdf)

For scale only, dividing all 2024 costs by 33 agreements is about $123,000 per agreement, or by 315 tested products about $12,800 per product. Neither is a marginal service price or a clinical outcome. The latest 163-company settlement cohort covers different timing and must not be divided into a single historical budget as though it were annual throughput.

At $4.05 million annual expense, a price of $1 million per 10 USA QALYs requires 40.45 net attributable USA QALYs; $100,000 requires 404.51. If a verified additional exposure reduction benefited 100,000 USA worker-years after all counterfactual and funding adjustments, those thresholds would require 0.000405 or 0.004045 QALYs per worker-year—about 3.5 or 35.5 quality-adjusted hours. Those are break-even requirements, not claimed benefits. A valid estimate needs both the additional exposure-years and a causal dose-to-health function.

The finite best-judgment receipt-acceleration branch yields 0.018447 USA QALYs per full $4,045,100 recipient cost, or about $2.19 billion per 10. The100000-worker planning cohort is reduced by .1 chance of acceleration, .25 CEH contribution, .5 funding response, .8 compliance and .25 year of earlier exposure reduction. The seven-percent retail-market claim is not used to infer population reach. A20 percent clinical-benefit prior times .0005 conditional QALY per exposure-reduced worker-year, less .00002 expected burden, is the weakest link. These choices were not solved backward from a favorable price. Only the remaining transition-period acceleration is credited; completed legal wins and future recurring monitoring effects are not automatically credited. Other product, lead, industrial-pollution and purchasing pathways remain unpriced. Outside counsel and corporate compliance resources add social cost beyond the recipient denominator.
sections.funding:
The 2024 return reports $3.82 million revenue, including $1.71 million in awards and settlements; net assets were $3.47 million, with $2.20 million unrestricted. Cash was $1.38 million and investments $2.59 million, but liabilities and restrictions prevent treating all assets as available expansion funding. [Return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/943251981/202542259349303204/full) Operating scale fell relative to 2022–2023. The official finance page still lists 2023 as its newest audit, while the IRS provides the newer 2024 return. [Financials](https://ceh.org/about/financials/)

Legal recoveries can help fund enforcement but can also replace donations. Payments to outside attorneys and corporate compliance expenditures are not all included in CEH's own expense, so this is not a full social-resource model. A current case-development or compliance-monitoring plan with unfunded costs would improve next-dollar assessment.

The Domtar document records the defendant's assertion that reformulation efforts began in early 2024, before it was added to the case in July 2025, and an expectation of nationwide phenol-free offerings by December 2026. These are assertions and commitments, not a proven no-CEH counterfactual; nevertheless, new donations cannot simply receive credit for all of that transition. Incremental enforcement, acceleration or future cases must be specified. [Primary settlement text](https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/prop65/judgments/2025-01392J5988.pdf)

model.costScope: Full annual recipient expense on comparable accrual Form990 basis, all programs and support including investment fees; no subtraction of settlement revenue. External legal, corporate compliance and public enforcement resources require separate social-cost analysis.
model.geographicAttribution: USA50states+DC resident outcomes only. California legal scope can generate nationwide manufacturing spillovers but does not establish their realized extent. Each product/site pathway needs outcome-weighted resident allocation; 7% retail market is not g.
model.formula: C=4045100 full annual recipient cost. E=N*dp*a*b*e*t additional exposure-reduced worker-years; Qall=E*(p*k-h)/1.03; QUSA=Qall*g. N prospective handling-worker cohort, dp probability of earlier actual reformulation/uptake versus existing commitments, a CEH contribution conditional on coalition change, b funding response, e actual compliance/use, t acceleration years. p probability of clinically meaningful dose-related benefit; k conditional one-year QALY area per reduced worker-year; h expected replacement/disruption burden. No benefits after modeled acceleration; no lifetime disease multiplier or credit for historic agreements.
model.counterfactual: d0 is exposure with existing laws, supplier plans, competitors, consumer pressure and other enforcement but without the incremental supported CEH work. N is unique users/worker-years, not market share times population. Already committed reformulation receives no automatic marginal credit.
model.attribution: a separates CEH's contribution from public agencies, partner groups, litigation counsel and manufacturers; b adjusts donation replacement by legal recoveries, reserves, grants and other donors. Court settlement may be strong evidence of a mechanism without identifying the incremental donor effect.
model.uncertainty: This is an extremely uncertain but genuine best-judgment partial-health estimate. No primary study identifies a BPS-to-QALY slope: p and k explicitly encode a small clinical-benefit prior, and harm can dominate. Wider or zero priors are reasonable. The estimate is not a statistically calibrated expectation, safety certification or measured CEH effect.
model.nativeOutcomes: The prospective cohort and counterfactual factors imply 250 additional exposure-reduced worker-years before geography, not100000beneficiaries directly credited. Expected net health-area prior p*k-h=.00008 QALY per worker-year before3percent discount; no lifetime extension.

sensitivity: At 10,000 / 100,000 / 1,000,000 net additional USA worker-years, k required for $1 million per 10 is .0040451 / .00040451 / .000040451; multiply by ten for $100 thousand per 10.
If only 10% of a gross exposure cohort is additional after donor, manufacturer and partner counterfactuals, required per-worker health gain rises tenfold.
Using 2022–24 mean expense instead of latest annual expense raises both frontier requirements by about 20.4%.
Any positive net harm H adds one-for-one to required USA QALYs. Substitution is not assumed harmless merely because a listed chemical disappears.

Illustrative dermatitis branch: at .02 QALY per prevented episode (judgment, not measured here), 2,023 / 20,226 net additional USA episodes would be needed for $1 million / $100 thousand per 10; chromium-regulation evidence does not establish those episode counts.

Receipt transition expected by Dec2026 limits the defensible acceleration horizon; post-transition monitoring must show prevented relapse/noncompliance or new cases rather than reuse the original historic win.

Outcome-weighted USA share, repeated users and cross-chemical/outcome double counting; net replacement and social-resource harms.
Current compliance and post-reformulation exposure evidence. Court entry on August 11, 2026 is verified; implementation and actual nationwide spillovers are not.

what: Toxic-Free Future combines product research, retailer pressure, Washington policy and national chemical-safety advocacy.
Its current work includes defending federal protections and helping states and companies choose safer chemicals.
A partial model of federal TCE and PFAS protections gives roughly $126 million per 10 USA QALYs, with very wide uncertainty and other recipient pathways still unpriced.
strengths: A long-running mix of technical research, market campaigns and policy coordination can influence the same exposure pathway at several points.
Federal risk models provide explicit clinical outcomes, allowing a cautious numerical assessment beyond chemical quantities or campaign reach.
Current coalition activity and original recipient financial disclosures make scope and costs inspectable.
reservations: The numerical estimate covers two narrow branches; the remaining portfolio is unestimated, so this is not a reliable ranking of the entire recipient.
Future influence on implementation or rollback is subjective; existing laws, firms and many other advocates are important counterfactuals.
Chemical detection does not establish disease risk, and two corrections to a high-profile exposure example warrant careful quantitative review.

sections.what:
TFF runs Mind the Store, Washington's Toxic-Free Legacy work, the fiscally sponsored Safer States alliance and federal advocacy. The 2024 return records $0.52 million, $0.53 million, $0.90 million and $0.30 million of respective program expenses. The assessment includes all of them and support costs—not just the federal branch used in the numerical model. [Original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/911214158/202523179349310762/full)

Retailer grading, product testing and technical comments are mechanisms for changing exposure, not health outcomes themselves. State product restrictions can influence national supply chains, but a Washington prohibition does not automatically cover every American. [Retailer project](https://toxicfreefuture.org/retailer-report-card/) [State implementation](https://toxicfreefuture.org/key-project/safer-products-for-washington/)
sections.monitoring:
In July 2026, TFF publicized a 250-organization letter organized by an alliance of more than 85 groups defending TSCA. This verifies active work and substantial partners, not a measured policy effect or an equal share of the result. [Current coalition](https://toxicfreefuture.org/press-room/250-organizations-urge-senate-put-americans-health-before-chemical-industry-profits/)

The TCE rule is already in force. EPA describes postponed exemption conditions pending judicial review and specific extended deadlines, including nuclear-fuel processing and wastewater disposal; it also discusses enforcement priorities. A donor cannot receive credit for the entire original ban. [Current EPA status](https://www.epa.gov/assessing-and-managing-chemicals-under-tsca/risk-management-trichloroethylene-tce)

Track specific decisions at risk, alternative policy text, compliance dates, affected worker exposures and TFF's documented contribution. For market campaigns, verify actual formulations and sales, not simply promises or report-card scores. A prospective unfunded work plan is missing.

The higher-impact alternative is PFAS drinking-water implementation. EPA's May 2026 proposal would let eligible systems request two extra years, to 2031, while retaining PFOA/PFOS limits. It includes interim measures above 12 ppt; comments closed July 20. TFF and Safer States publicly opposed the proposal. Avoiding all long-term PFAS mortality is not the relevant counterfactual. [EPA proposal status](https://www.epa.gov/sdwa/proposed-pfoa-and-pfos-compliance-extension-rule) [TFF response](https://toxicfreefuture.org/press-room/epa-announces-rollback-of-protections-for-toxic-pfas-forever-chemicals-in-drinking-water/)
sections.qualitative:
The TCE pathway has a real causal toxicology/risk-assessment bridge: the federal rule models avoided cancers. It is not an organization trial and remains sensitive to exposure estimates and future implementation. It does not quantify all non-cancer outcomes. The model below deliberately leaves other chemical benefits unpriced rather than assigning a health value to pounds removed. [Final rule](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-12-17/pdf/2024-29274.pdf)

Cancer survival varies substantially: current five-year relative survival is about 79% for kidney/renal-pelvis cancer, 74% for non-Hodgkin lymphoma and 22% for liver/intrahepatic-bile-duct cancer. These are not TCE-attributable case-mix estimates and are not lifetime fatality probabilities. They support a broad QALY judgment rather than treating every cancer as a death. [Kidney](https://seer.cancer.gov/statfacts/html/kidrp.html) [Lymphoma](https://seer.cancer.gov/statfacts/html/nhl.html) [Liver](https://seer.cancer.gov/statfacts/html/livibd.html)

TFF also has a concrete history campaigning against methylene-chloride paint strippers; EPA documents fatal acute poisonings. That is another credible pathway, but past fatalities and bans cannot simply be credited to a new donation. [Campaign](https://toxicfreefuture.org/federal-policy/epa-ban-toxic-methylene-chloride/) [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/biden-harris-administration-finalizes-ban-most-uses-methylene-chloride-protecting)

Scientific disclosure is a mixed signal. TFF acknowledged corrections in December 2024 and July 2025 to the exposure example in its black-plastics study, with the second lowering estimated utensil exposure. Product-contamination findings may remain meaningful, but the errors reinforce the need to check dose and clinical consequences independently. No black-plastic health benefit is counted here. [Corrections](https://toxicfreefuture.org/update-study-correction-does-not-impact-conclusion/)

For PFAS, EPA models serum exposure, birth-weight effects, cardiovascular risk factors and renal cancer. Its summaries give approximately 1,300 developmental deaths, 3,700 cardiovascular deaths and 2,000 kidney-cancer deaths prevented over the long model horizon—not per year. I exclude bladder-cancer co-removal and nonfatal illness here. The original analysis spans 2024–2105; the delay proposal extends its comparison to 84 years. I halve the transported clinical yield and explicitly discount future timing; these are judgments, not EPA estimates. [Native outcomes](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-04/pfas-npdwr_fact-sheet_cost-and-benefits_4.8.24.pdf) [Clinical model](https://nepis.epa.gov/Exe/ZyPURL.cgi?Dockey=P101DTYY.TXT)
sections.cost:
Full 2024 expense is $2,689,041, including $209,491 management and $221,723 fundraising. The original return shows no netted fundraising-event or inventory expense requiring restoration. Comparable 2023 and 2022 totals are $2,790,134 and $2,298,941: a $2,592,705 mean. [2024](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/911214158/202523179349310762/full) [2023](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/911214158/202423199349313782/full) [2022](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/911214158/202343189349306929/full)

For a two-year support horizon, cost is $5.38 million. EPA's published rule figures imply about 4.16 potential cancer cases avoided per full-equivalent year of reduced exposure, averaged across its analytical period. The TCE-only central is 0.036 expected USA QALYs. Adding a separate PFAS timing branch gives 0.428 expected USA QALYs, or roughly $126 million per 10. The joint favorable scenario is about $581,000; zero benefit and net harm are also possible. These are judgment scenarios, not statistical confidence limits.

This is not a comprehensive valuation of TFF. Other chemicals, state policy, market effects and PFAS benefits beyond the specific delay branch could dominate; they are not adequately quantified. At this cost, $1 million or $100,000 per 10 would require 53.78 or 537.81 net USA QALYs across the portfolio. The combined partial model does not meet those thresholds centrally.

The PFAS calculation credits only the present-value difference between an earlier and a two-year-later health stream, not the entire regulation. Its central contribution is about 0.392 USA QALYs, dominated by subjective policy influence, actual delay avoided and clinical transport. Neither EPA's monetized benefits nor an arbitrary dollar-to-QALY conversion enters the calculation.

The rigid two-year shift of the entire modeled health stream is a structural approximation, not EPA's estimate of the extension's health effect. The parameter u accounts for exemption uptake, independent early treatment, state rules and interim mitigation; actual delay and health accrual may differ across systems and years.
sections.funding:
Revenue was $3.59 million in 2024, mostly contributions. Net assets were $4.88 million, including $3.18 million without donor restrictions. Cash and savings totaled $1.41 million, alongside $2.90 million publicly traded investments. These balances suggest financial resilience but do not establish additional hiring or unfunded implementation capacity. [Return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/911214158/202523179349310762/full)

The official finance index lists older returns and says audited statements are available on request; no outreach was undertaken. The newer original 2024 IRS return supplies the comparable recipient figures. [Financials](https://toxicfreefuture.org/financial-reports/)

Flexible donations may replace other donors or finance reserves, while advocacy partners and agencies provide complementary resources. The model discounts funding additionality rather than assuming every dollar expands effective work. Corporate compliance and public enforcement costs are outside the recipient budget; the analysis is not a social cost-benefit calculation. Essential-use and replacement-material risks may create health downsides, which must not be erased by calling all regulation beneficial.

EPA itself flags that assuming all systems use the PFAS exemption can overstate delay: some will treat early because of state rules, customer demand or existing plans. Interim filters, real construction bottlenecks, affordability and public technical assistance also matter. The model includes a further 50% effective-delay allowance, with zero-effect and harm scenarios. [Proposal analysis](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/20/2026-10086/extending-the-compliance-deadline-for-the-pfoa-and-pfos-maximum-contaminant-levels)

model.costScope: Two years of full recipient expense at 2024 scale, including all programs, regrants and support; no best-program denominator. Only TCE cancer and PFAS mortality-timing branches quantified. Public and corporate implementation resources excluded from recipient cost, disclosed separately.
model.geographicAttribution: USA50states+DC residents. Federal occupational model is predominantly domestic; g=.995 is a judgment excluding territorial/nonresident exposure. No global supply-chain benefits or Washington-to-USA population multiplier. PFAS includes Tribal residents of the 50states; territories excluded through the small judgment allocation allowance.
model.formula: C=2*2,689,041. TCE=F*m*Y(T)*e*a*b*q, with F=64.1/15.4 and Y=sum(t=1..T)1/1.03^t. PFAS: B=(1300*qi+5700*qa)*d*mp; P=B*(1-1/1.03^2)*u*pp*ap*b. Q_all=TCE+P-H; Q_USA=g*Q_all; price=10*C/Q_USA if positive. PFAS qi/qa are lifetime QALYs discounted to the avoided death date; d discounts those dates to2026. Two-year shift factor prices timing, not a permanent loss of the full regulation. TCE q includes latency to each exposure year, Y discounts exposure timing.
model.counterfactual: Existing rule, committed company transitions, enforcement and other advocates remain. e is the expected fraction of full-rule health protection retained by additional coalition defense: central .025 represents a 10-percentage-point difference in probability of preserving25% of modeled exposure benefit, not a 25%chance the whole ban survives. Five full-equivalent years are a judgment, not observed2027–31 exposures. For PFAS, compare earlier treatment with the proposed two-year delayed stream, retain the MCLs, and discount by u for actual delay/mitigation/independent action. pp is the incremental coalition probability of preventing the modeled delay; ap is TFF's distinct PFAS causal share.
model.attribution: a=.05 is TFF's subjective share of the incremental coalition contribution, recognizing coordination but many partners. b=.5 discounts replacement by reserves, other donors and institutional funding. Neither comes from a measured causal attribution study; scenario variation is deliberately wide. PFAS uses pp=.1, ap=.03 and shared b=.5; its public opposition is observed but this particular influence is not measured. No equal allocation among signatories.
model.uncertainty: Very-low-confidence two-branch partial central. EPA risk forecasts are not observed donor outcomes. Mortality timing, QALYs, clinical transport, effective delay and political influence are judgments. Broad scenarios include near-zero, zero and harm, not confidence intervals. Other programs remain unpriced, so this is neither an aggregate estimate nor a lower bound. The rigid two-year shift of the entire modeled health stream is a structural approximation, not EPA's estimate of the extension's health effect. The parameter u accounts for exemption uptake, independent early treatment, state rules and interim mitigation; actual delay and health accrual may differ across systems and years.
model.nativeOutcomes: Specific policy protections retained, unique workers with lower exposure, full-equivalent protected exposure years, potential cancer cases prevented, clinical QALYs. Bills, letters, products tested, pounds of chemicals and retailer scores are not QALYs. PFAS branch counts timing of modeled developmental, cardiovascular and kidney-cancer mortality only; excludes bladder co-removal and all nonfatal events.

what: Farmworker Justice combines healthcare-access assistance, occupational safety, policy advocacy and litigation for farmworkers.
It develops multilingual resources and works with public agencies and other advocates on heat and pesticide protections.
A partial heat-mortality model gives about $97 million per 10 USA QALYs; favorable assumptions give about $147,000, while zero or harmful effects remain possible.
strengths: Heat prevention has a credible clinical mechanism and a live implementation problem, beyond awareness alone.
Current partner evidence verifies technical and coalition work, including a 2026 clinician guide.
Original financial records allow full recipient costs and public funding to be distinguished.
reservations: Policy influence, genuinely additional funding and future enforcement are subjective and dominate the estimate.
Existing state rules, employer duties and other organizations would protect some workers without additional support.
The numerical result excludes substantial recipient pathways and should not be treated as an overall ranking.

sections.what:
Farmworker Justice is a national 501(c)(3), EIN 52-1196708, combining health access, occupational safety, immigration/labor advocacy and legal work. Its stated farmworker population is a constituency, not a count of people whose health it changed. [Organization](https://www.farmworkerjustice.org/en)

The 2024 audit assigns about $1.01 million to health projects, alongside labor/immigration and other programs. Health work includes technical assistance to health centers and community organizations; the organization is not itself a nationwide direct-care clinic. All programs and support expenses remain in the cost denominator. [Audit](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/download-audit?download=true&filename=2024-12-GSAFAC-0000379518)
sections.monitoring:
Current pages describe heat policy and multilingual training. Partner sources independently verify an August 2025 coalition webinar, a December 2025 state-rule analysis and a clinician guide updated in 2026. These establish activity, not prevented illness. [Policy](https://www.farmworkerjustice.org/en/policy/occupational-safety) [Webinar](https://nfwm.org/news/webinar-too-hot-to-work-farmworker-heat-protections/) [State review](https://cafs.vermontlaw.edu/cafs-report-reviews-state-standards-to-prevent-heat-illness-among-farmworkers) [Guide](https://www.migrantclinician.org/resources/350%2B467/%2A/index.html)

Track actual policy text, enforcement resources, workers newly receiving water/rest/shade/acclimatization, retaliation protections and clinical outcomes. A published toolkit is not evidence of employer adherence. Request an unfunded work plan and de-duplicated health-center implementation results before increasing confidence.
sections.qualitative:
Heat protection has a plausible physiological pathway. A 2019 retrospective study of 604 municipal workers found fewer heat illnesses after a multi-component program; it lacked a concurrent control and cannot isolate training. [Study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31274674/)

The 2025 California study reports larger mortality reductions after enforcement and revisions, but period estimates were individually imprecise; only their joint test was significant. It is observational, covers four states and includes vehicle-death codes not necessarily caused by heat. It therefore supports plausibility and the importance of enforcement, not a precise causal 33% effect for farmworkers. [Original study](https://doi.org/10.1377/hlthaff.2025.00096)

Federal law already imposes a general duty concerning recognized hazards. Small farms with ten or fewer nonfamily employees and no temporary labor camp in the prior year face a federal enforcement funding limitation. State protection and employer action also exist. These are important counterfactuals, not grounds to count all national heat deaths as preventable by FJ. [Current OSHA resources](https://www.osha.gov/heat-exposure/) [Small-farm policy](https://www.osha.gov/memos/2014-07-29/policy-clarification-oshas-enforcement-authority-small-farms)

Pesticide protection, healthcare access and legal rights can matter substantially but have no recovered marginal service-to-health bridge here. Lost pay, retaliation, policy displacement and ineffective implementation could offset benefits; non-health dignity and income gains are not silently converted into QALYs.
sections.cost:
Full recipient expense was $2,255,738 in 2024, restoring $53,661 of event costs netted out of Form 990 expense. The audit confirms that total. Comparable 2023 expense is $2,236,619 after restoring $31,296, and 2022 is $2,349,230: a three-year mean of $2,280,529. [2024](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/521196708/202542739349300309/full) [2023](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/521196708/202422899349302067/full) [2022](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/521196708/202312869349301981/full)

A two-year support horizon costs $4.51 million at the latest scale. The partial agricultural heat-mortality model yields 0.464 expected USA QALYs centrally, or about $97 million per 10. Its favorable joint scenario reaches 307 QALYs, about $147,000 per 10. These scenarios are not confidence bounds; a weak-influence case is effectively negligible, and zero/harm remain explicit.

OSHA's proposal forecasts 531 annual deaths prevented across industries, not observed lives saved. Its 14-fold fatality undercount adjustment is transported from general-population evidence. This model instead starts from 52 reported/imputed natural-resources deaths over 12 years, narrows to farmworkers, uses a 3-fold undercount and then discounts reach, effectiveness and causal contribution. [Original regulatory model, pp.70963–70969](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-08-30/pdf/2024-14824.pdf)

Employer compliance and public enforcement costs are real but outside the recipient expenditure denominator. No monetary value of a statistical life is converted into QALYs. This partial result is neither a total recipient estimate nor a guaranteed lower bound.
sections.funding:
The 2024 return records $758,068 of government grants, down from $1,052,974 in 2023. Private support could sustain complementary work or replace public funding; neither its additionality nor a current funding cliff is established. Year-end 2024 unrestricted net assets were $629,075 and restricted net assets $521,427. Cash and savings totaled $871,519. [Original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/521196708/202542739349300309/full)

The 2024 audit issued unmodified financial and federal-compliance opinions with no current findings. Prior-year award-reporting and procurement documentation issues were addressed in its corrective-action record; they should not be presented as new 2024 findings. The audit was signed August 4, 2025 and does not establish 2026 liquidity. [Audit](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/download-audit?download=true&filename=2024-12-GSAFAC-0000379518)

model.costScope: Two full annual recipient budgets at 2024 expense, all programs and support including netted event costs. Employer/public implementation costs excluded and disclosed; only agricultural heat mortality quantified.
model.geographicAttribution: USA 50 states plus DC resident health; g=.9 judgment, .7–.98 sensitivity. National headquarters does not determine attribution. H-2A status alone is not a residence classification. No overseas or other-industry spillover credit.
model.formula: C=2*2255738. F=52/12. Y(T)=sum(t=1..T)1/1.03^t. Q_all=F*f*u*k*e*q*Y(T)*p*a*b-H. Q_USA=g*Q_all. Price=10*C/Q_USA when positive. q discounts lifetime health after each averted death; Y discounts when that death would occur. Two-year spending buys a subjective five-year effective protection stream, not five years of spending.
model.counterfactual: Without additional work, federal deliberation, state standards, employer duties, public enforcement and other advocates continue. k limits the baseline burden newly reachable beyond these protections and jurisdictional gaps; e is reduction among that reachable burden under real implementation. p is incremental coalition effect on securing the modeled protective stream, not the raw chance a rule passes.
model.attribution: a=.1 assigns a modest share of farmworker-specific coalition influence to FJ's technical and advocacy role. b=.5 discounts reserves, other grants and donor replacement. Neither is measured. No sole credit for OSHA, no equal division of signatories, no separate toolkit benefit added to the same protection.
model.uncertainty: Very-low-confidence partial expected-value judgment. Numerical assumptions are revisable opinions, not measured organization effectiveness or a confidence interval. Mortality data, occupational undercount, farmworker share, enforcement, timing and marginal advocacy all matter. Other recipient work unpriced; net harm possible.
model.nativeOutcomes: Newly protected workers, effective protected years, heat deaths prevented and discounted lifetime health. Clinical training contacts, guides, comments and policy wins are intermediate outputs. Nonfatal heat illness and indirect injuries deliberately excluded.

inputs.name: F
inputs.unit: reported/imputed natural-resources heat fatalities per year
inputs.rationale: 52 over 2011–22; includes mining, forestry and fishing, not exclusively farmworkers.

inputs.name: f
inputs.rationale: Exclude other industries; .5–.9 scenarios. A selected farmworker-specific series would improve this approximation.

inputs.name: u
inputs.rationale: Use 3 rather than OSHA central 14; the 14-fold transport comes from general-population excess mortality, not a measured occupational undercount.

inputs.name: k
inputs.unit: baseline farmworker burden newly reachable by protection
inputs.rationale: Excludes small-farm enforcement gaps, existing state/employer protection and independent improvements. .2–.8 scenarios; not a measured workforce fraction.

inputs.name: e
inputs.rationale: Clinical-mechanistic judgment, not direct transplantation of the California point estimate. .1–.7 positive scenarios, zero possible; includes imperfect real-world adherence.

inputs.name: q
inputs.unit: discounted lifetime QALYs per prevented heat death
inputs.rationale: Working-age population; roughly 27 remaining years at 3% and .82 health quality gives 15. Not observed decedent age/utility data. 8–25 scenarios.

inputs.name: T
inputs.rationale: Bounded 2027–31 equivalent horizon, not a claim that finalization occurs in 2027. Delay or nonfinalization reduces this value.

inputs.name: p
inputs.unit: incremental coalition probability of securing modeled protection
inputs.rationale: Ten percentage points is a subjective policy forecast, not baseline passage probability. Covers adoption and survival to implementation; .01–.3 scenarios with zero possible.

inputs.name: a
inputs.unit: FJ share of incremental coalition contribution
inputs.rationale: Farmworker-specific expertise and ongoing work, but government, labor groups, MCN, Public Citizen and others matter; .02–.2 scenarios, not equal signatory allocation.

inputs.name: b
inputs.rationale: Discount reserves, existing grants and replacement donors; .1–.8 scenarios. No verified next-dollar work plan.

inputs.name: g
inputs.unit: USA 50 states and DC resident health share
inputs.rationale: Domestic work focus; .7–.98 sensitivity for temporary nonresident workers, territorial work and follow-on health outside the resident boundary. Immigration status alone does not decide residency.

inputs.name: r
inputs.rationale: Future effective protection years discounted separately from lifetime health after each death.

inputs.name: H
inputs.rationale: Provisional zero, not demonstrated absence of harm; adverse scenario subtracts 1 for retaliation, lost income or displaced care.

inputs.name: otherPathways
inputs.rationale: Healthcare-access assistance, pesticides, immigration/labor litigation, nonfatal heat injury and spillovers to other industries unpriced.

sensitivity: At $4,511,476 cost, $1 million/$100 thousand per 10 requires 45.11476/451.1476 net USA QALYs. With q=15 and g=.9, that is 3.34183/33.41834 fully additional discounted deaths prevented, compared with central .03438 before QALY conversion.
Price scales inversely with each positive multiplicative input. A political contribution of zero or complete donor replacement eliminates quantified benefit.
Using OSHA's 14-fold undercount alone instead of 3 improves the central price by 14/3, not enough to reach $1 million per 10. The favorable result requires multiple favorable assumptions together.
Using the three-year expense mean increases cost about 1.1%. Restricting the denominator to the heat project would not represent ordinary recipient support.
Any all-population harm above .51573 QALYs erases the central partial benefit. Nonfatal benefits and other pathways might add value, but are not established offsets.
Implementation delay matters: shifting the same stream five years later reduces it by 1/1.03^5. A paper rule without protection is zero, regardless of advocacy success.

what: Earthjustice provides free environmental legal representation alongside policy, scientific and public-information work.
Its portfolio includes clean air and water, toxic chemicals, energy, climate, wildlife and public lands across and beyond the United States.
A partial model of additional national soot-standard implementation gives about $35 million per 10 USA QALYs, with a favorable scenario around $279,000 and zero/harm possible.
strengths: A large specialist legal team can make binding public-health duties enforceable when agencies fail to act.
Current court records provide concrete evidence of implementation work rather than only claimed campaign victories.
Primary regulatory models and epidemiology connect cleaner air to clinical outcomes, allowing a numerical partial estimate.
reservations: Most recipient pathways remain unpriced, so the partial number is not an overall ranking.
Recent court victories already belong in the counterfactual; a new donor cannot claim the entire regulation.
Other litigators, state governments, reserves and existing gifts may replace the marginal contribution.

sections.what:
Earthjustice, EIN 94-1730465, supplies legal representation without charging public-interest clients. Litigation is supported by policy and public information; work spans health, energy and climate, public lands and wildlife. The ordinary recipient scope includes all these activities, not just the clean-air case modeled below. [Portfolio](https://earthjustice.org/feature/trump-environment-lawsuits)

The current financial report says staffing reached 600 and describes accelerated staffing growth. This indicates organizational capacity and demand, not 600 health-producing positions. Earthjustice Action is a separate 501(c)(4); the audit describes a reimbursement agreement, not consolidated inclusion of that organization's political work. [Financial report](https://earthjustice.org/about/financial-statements) [Audit](https://earthjustice.org/document/2025-audited-financials)
sections.monitoring:
The July 17, 2026 district-court order requires EPA to promulgate final PM2.5 area designations by February 6, 2027 and retains jurisdiction. It follows June's ruling upholding the strengthened standard. The order is a real implementation milestone, but designation is not attainment or a measured reduction in deaths. [Actual order](https://earthjustice.org/document/ruling-court-orders-epa-to-implement-national-soot-standard) [June result](https://earthjustice.org/press/2026/court-upholds-life-saving-national-soot-air-quality-standard)

Earthjustice, Clean Air Task Force and Southern Environmental Law Center represented coalition groups, while state/local plaintiffs brought parallel claims. Future monitoring should distinguish designation, enforceable plans, actual controls and exposure changes; investigate which would be delayed without added legal capacity. [Counsel and partners](https://earthjustice.org/press/2026/court-orders-epa-to-implement-national-soot-standard)

The active MATS case challenges repeal of 2024 amendments. It does not justify credit for all health gains from the original 2012 standards. The 2026 repeal and current legal challenge are separate from already-achieved historic reductions. [Challenge](https://earthjustice.org/press/2026/coalition-sues-trump-epa-over-illegal-repeal-of-mercury-and-air-toxics-standards) [EPA status](https://www.epa.gov/stationary-sources-air-pollution/mercury-and-air-toxics-standards)
sections.qualitative:
The PM pathway has strong evidence beyond policy outputs. Wu and colleagues analyzed 68.5 million Medicare enrollees with five approaches and found broadly consistent mortality effects. Causal interpretation still requires confounding assumptions; predicted residential exposure has measurement error. This supports a causal health mechanism, not a measured Earthjustice effect. [Original study](https://xiaowu.io/publication/wu2020evaluating/wu2020evaluating.pdf)

EPA's native table provides alternative adult mortality estimates of 2,100 and 4,500 for identified controls under the revised annual standard in 2032. They must not be added. The model uses their midpoint as a judgment, then applies a transport haircut. It excludes infant and nonfatal outcomes, including asthma, to avoid case/utility overlap. Mortality occurs with a cessation lag; the QALY assumption includes that timing. [RIA, Table 5-5 and methods](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-02/naaqs_pm_reconsideration_ria_final.pdf)

Habitat, climate and legal-access benefits may be important independently of USA health. They are not converted from acres, tonnes, case counts or economic damages. Litigation can also delay projects with benefits; implementation costs or energy access may harm health. No empirical estimate of those offsets was recovered, so zero and adverse scenarios remain.
sections.cost:
Audited full recipient expense is $183,685,874 for FY 2025, $165,760,409 for FY 2024 and $158,385,625 for FY 2023; the comparable mean is $169,277,303. Fiscal years end June 30. Latest expense includes $16,809,973 of donated legal and public-information services; these are retained as resources, not mistaken for cash spending. [FY 2025 audit](https://earthjustice.org/document/2025-audited-financials) [FY 2024 audit](https://earthjustice.org/document/2024-audited-financials)

Two annual budgets cost $367.4 million. The partial PM model produces 103.64 expected USA QALYs centrally, approximately $35.4 million per 10. The favorable joint scenario produces about 13,176 QALYs and costs about $279,000 per 10; a low-influence scenario is vastly worse. This is a partial pathway estimate, not a total recipient effectiveness claim or a guaranteed lower bound.

The model counts one conditional full-equivalent year of additional exposure protection at 2032 scale, with only a 10% incremental coalition probability, a 20% Earthjustice contribution and 50% funding additionality. It gives no new credit for the already-issued court order. Public regulators and pollution sources bear substantial implementation costs outside the recipient denominator; those resources are not free.
sections.funding:
The audit reports $56,995,368 of financial assets available for general expenditure within one year and a $201,282,311 board-designated reserve. The latter can be redesignated and is distinct from donor-restricted endowment assets. Those reserves support long-term legal obligations, but they also make complete next-dollar additionality implausible without a specific work plan. [Liquidity and reserve notes](https://earthjustice.org/document/2025-audited-financials)

FY 2025 revenue was $207,196,608 and net assets rose $23,510,734. Court-awarded fees and costs contributed $5,787,062; these can recycle resources after successful cases, but are not assured. The marginal funding question is whether support expands otherwise-unfunded legal work or mainly replenishes reserves. The staffing-growth statement is promising capacity evidence, not a quantified funding gap. [Current plans](https://earthjustice.org/about/financial-statements)
