what: Garment Worker Center organizes low-wage garment workers and operates a wage-theft and retaliation clinic in Los Angeles.
It provides rights education, self-help, referrals and representation in Labor Commissioner hearings alongside worker leadership and member support.
It is developing a Justice Campus and advocating for stronger enforcement and garment-sector job quality.
strengths: Original return narrative reports wages and penalties collected rather than pricing outreach as completed outcomes.
Trusted representation can help workers turn existing legal rights into payments; current clinic hours establish ongoing access.
Original finances and the capital campaign expose costs, public funding and the distinction between operations and future expansion.
reservations: Paid household count, net recovery, alternative enforcement, baseline resources and payer incidence remain unmeasured.
Unrestricted gifts may replace other funding or support capital and organizing rather than additional wage collection.
Retaliation, displacement, transfer losses and unresolved audit/capital evidence can offset gains; this is a conditional partial comparison.

sections.what:
This report covers Garment Worker Center, EIN 81-0622327. Its [clinic](https://garmentworkercenter.org/wage-clinic/) provides consultations, self-help and representation for wage theft and retaliation. Worker organizing, youth leadership, member support and industry development are substantive parts of the recipient, not overhead to be discarded.

The [current industry campaign](https://garmentworkercenter.org/lagfip/) seeks implementation and resources for LA garment-sector development. Its [recent report](https://garmentworkercenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Building-a-Sustainable-and-Equitable-Garment-Industry-in-California-RBG.pdf) describes continued noncompliance and economic vulnerability. The report's 18,408 apparel-manufacturing employees and the homepage's broader 45,000-worker figure have different coverage and are not treated as current beneficiaries caused by a gift.
sections.monitoring:
The [2024 return narrative](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202513159349306456/IRS990ScheduleO) reports 194 workers assisted with wage claims and approximately $878,000 of wages and penalties collected. It separately reports 135 workers/youth in training, 6,250 outreach contacts and 191 support cases. These categories may overlap; no contact or workshop automatically earns health credit.

Collections are a realized financial outcome, but still do not reveal which dollars would have arrived without GWC, whether recipients lost benefits or earnings, or how a new gift changes capacity. Future measurement should follow net household resources, timing, retaliation, worker residence and non-overlapping injury outcomes. Policy wins should be assessed against already funded implementation.
sections.qualitative: Existing SB62 and DIR wage enforcement remain the baseline. Additional trusted representation may improve collections, but the sources do not identify next-dollar causal recovery. We replace the initial 0.01-QALY-per-$6,000 shortcut with direct signed consumption welfare and a central judgment of zero separately counted clinical QALYs. This avoids adding the same material-hardship or stress outcome twice; it does not establish that health effects are absent. Safety, organizing, deterrence, jobs and campus effects remain unquantified. The independent clinical sensitivity is hypothetical, not derived from income.
sections.cost:
The conditional central estimate is **$23.36 million per better life**: ten combined healthy-year welfare equivalents. A $10,000 gift normalization produces zero separately counted clinical QALYs and 0.00428138 signed consumption-equivalent years. The initial $88.14 million health-only illustration remains a diagnostic. The change reflects direct income accounting and full claimant/counterparty costs, not measured improvement in the organization.

Full recognized annual recipient resources are $2,974,158: $2,820,655 in Part IX plus $153,503 of rental expenses separately netted from revenue. All programs and support remain charged; there is no favorable campaign carveout. The state-funded campus acquisition is already in the baseline, not wholly a one-year operating expense or permanently free capital. Public enforcement, capital services and unrecognized donated work remain additional unpriced social costs. [Original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202513159349306456/IRS990)

The reported $878,000 in collected wages and penalties anchors 100 judged receipt-household units, not 194 confirmed paid households. Equal $8,780 gross awards, a $30,000 disposable-resource baseline and 75% retention after taxes/benefit losses are assumptions, not measured household data. The resulting $6,585 receipt is netted jointly with $300 of claimant time, travel, forgone earnings and retaliation costs before log valuation. One representative adult-equivalent is counted per modeled household; additional family members are not multiplied in. A one-time award supports one consumption year after a one-year delay. [Original program narrative](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202513159349306456/IRS990ScheduleO)

Half the recoveries are judged additional to public enforcement, other representation and employer payment. In the other outcome no additional receipt arrives, but claimant costs remain. The other 94 assisted-equivalent units also incur full costs without a credited payment, independently of recovery probability. Treating the reported 194 assisted workers as distinct resource units is a judgment tested against household overlap. A separate 50% funding response accounts for replacement funding and operating/capital allocation. No priced staff tranche verifies a linear ordinary-gift response.

Restitution transfers resources from payers. The model charges the full incremental gross transfer to 50 disjoint counterparty units with a judged $100,000 resource baseline and 50% local incidence. Worker residence is judged 95% local. Payer incidence, tax offsets and household baselines are unknown; legal liability does not erase their signed welfare loss. Positive overlap discounts apply only to worker gains, not costs. Out-of-boundary payer losses are not included in the LA headline, so it is not a complete global welfare estimate. [Comparison method](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/)

The 27 scenarios retain the same financial ledger when clinical benefit is null. Concentrating the same award total among ten recipients raises the reference price to $95.41 million; counting only 100 claimant units gives $19.94 million. Lower collection additionality, poorer fully local payers or large retaliation/displacement costs can make net welfare negative. Complete funding replacement gives zero; independent gift-induced engagement costs can survive that failure. An unknown-incidence scenario has no combined price. Two-year smoothing spreads the same award and costs instead of repeating annual collections. These are judgment sensitivities, not confidence bounds. Neither the current reference nor the frozen initial model is a complete portfolio valuation or a verified donation offer.
sections.funding:
The latest return records $9,257,935 in government grants and $10,060,845 total revenue. Net assets were $7,653,173, but cash was only $204,063 and net land/buildings/equipment were $10,468,795; net assets are not an unrestricted cash runway. The return does not separate donor restrictions using the usual FASB categories.

The [Justice Campus page](https://garmentworkercenter.org/justice-campus/) confirms a state-funded 2024 property purchase and describes renovations in stages. These are plans, not completed additional clinic capacity. [Schedule O](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202513159349306456/IRS990ScheduleO) also says the emergency hardship fund closed after reduced donations and grants. The [2023 narrative](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202433189349310008/IRS990ScheduleO) identifies the DIR wage-claim pilot partnership. These details show both public support and real allocation tradeoffs.

The central 50% funding response is a judgment that a proportional resource increment produces half the corresponding collection capacity after replacement and delays. New unrestricted gifts could instead fund capital, worker leadership or support services, so this operating scenario is conditional. No restricted best-program donation, outreach or payment is assumed.

sections.what:
This report covers Southern California Housing Rights Center, EIN 95-2572642, doing business as Housing Rights Center. Its [current services](https://www.housingrightscenter.org/services) include counseling, investigations and education. The recipient also administered rental-related public programs in the latest fiscal year; it is not simply an accommodation clinic.

The [coverage page](https://www.housingrightscenter.org/about) explicitly includes both LA and Ventura Counties. Ventura is outside the LA/Orange metropolitan boundary. The model estimates the share of fair-housing case outcomes accruing to LA residents rather than attributing all benefits to its LA headquarters. No separate Orange County caseload is established.
sections.monitoring:
The [FY2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202621349349300637/IRS990) identifies 188 City of LA and 45 LA County investigations, against far larger inquiry and potential-discrimination counts. These 233 investigations are not 233 successful remedies or prevented evictions. Counts from the city and county contracts may overlap, so a deduplication prior is applied.

The [2026 newsletter](https://www.housingrightscenter.org/newsletters/fair-housing-in-action-june-edition-2026) gives concrete examples involving assistance animals and threatened displacement. They show a mechanism but are selected successes, not a success rate. A [summer-2024 newsletter](https://www.housingrightscenter.org/_files/ugd/55e2fa_461d4fe5b3884f118087832b988e0908.pdf) also describes accessible-unit transfers and mobility modifications. The needed next data are all closed cases, failures, implemented remedies, residence and finite health follow-up.
sections.qualitative:
A successful accommodation can remove a daily barrier or preserve a home that supports a person's disability needs. The model assigns health only to a subset of investigations and only when the resolution differs from what would happen through the landlord, HUD, California enforcement or another advocate. It adds no automatic life-years for every housing case.

External evidence supports caution as well as plausibility. [CAPABLE](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/2720136) combined home changes with nursing and occupational therapy and reduced disability in selected older adults. HRC does not deliver that clinical package. Conversely, the [OTIS randomized trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34254934/) found no beneficial average fall or QALY result from its home-assessment intervention. Neither trial supplies HRC's effect size. The central 0.03 utility-year gain for two years is an explicit judgment about health-relevant, successfully changed accommodations—not a measured HRC effect or a CAPABLE transfer estimate.

The priced branch covers accommodation-related health within fair housing. Counseling outside investigations, discrimination litigation, deterrence, rental processing and dignity can matter. Their value is not zero merely because it is not quantified. A reported [Ventura settlement](https://www.housingrightscenter.org/press-release/housing-rights-center-secures-landmark-settlement-in-section-8-housing-discrimination-case?lang=es) is not counted as an LA outcome. These boundaries prevent a complete-portfolio ranking.
sections.cost:
Original gross accrual expenses were [FY2025 $4,696,526](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202621349349300637/IRS990), [FY2024 $4,465,598](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202531359349308813/IRS990) and [FY2023 $8,670,376](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202421359349312677/IRS990). No separately netted rental, fundraising-event, gaming or inventory costs were shown. Their mean is $5,944,166.67. FY2023 includes $4,397,050 of emergency rent relief in other expenses, explaining much of the change; it is retained as recipient expenditure, not erased to make the mean smaller.

The latest return divides program expenses into $1,059,837 for City of LA fair housing, $939,491 for county fair housing, $930,449 for other-city contracts and $1,612,552 for rental-program activity. Part III includes inconsistent 'including grants' values, sometimes greater than the expense field; those values are not used as separate costs or grants delivered. The expense fields sum to Part IX program cost. Full recipient cost includes $154,197 reported administration and is not replaced with a selected clinic budget.

Schedule D reports matching statement and return expenses, with no donated-service exclusion. However, Schedule O says the records were undergoing a mandatory audit, and the reviewed index supplied no recent completed audit. These remain return-based figures, not an independently verified current audit. Unrecognized volunteer/legal resources are unknown. The conditional component is about $94.67 million per 10 LA QALYs, with positive joint stress cases from $1.97 million to $115.66 billion; these are not confidence limits.
sections.funding:
FY2025 government contributions were $2,652,295, and municipal pass-through contracts are central to delivery. Total revenue was $4,896,330, including $150,000 classified as operating support in other income. Unrestricted net assets were $5,216,333 and cash was $4,447,781, but liabilities and contract obligations limit how much is freely deployable. A $501,720 prior-period net-asset adjustment is not explained by the reviewed supplemental narrative; it is not current operating income.

Existing [fair-housing law and public complaint channels](https://www.hud.gov/stat/fheo/rights-obligations) belong in the counterfactual. Private gifts may fund cases beyond contract rules, earlier intervention or improvements in implementation; they may also replace reserves or other funding. The central 25% proportional funding response is a judgment, not evidence of an uncovered staffing gap. Rental-program continuation in a tax narrative is not proof of a current open cash-aid program: the public service site directs people seeking rental assistance to 211.

The full-portfolio break-even requirements are 46.96526 net LA QALYs annually for $1 million per 10, and 469.6526 for $100,000 per 10. Landlord modifications, outside legal enforcement and participant time are additional social costs. No outreach or donation was made.

sections.what:
This report covers Downtown Women's Center, EIN 31-1597223, and its consolidated housing entity—not the similarly named organization in Texas. Its [2025 impact report](https://downtownwomenscenter.org/2025annualreport/) describes 4,499 women and survivors served through housing, wellness, employment and advocacy. The webpage title refers to 2026, but its reported activity year is 2025. The report models the dominant housing-and-support health pathway at full recipient cost; it does not treat the CAPABLE pilot as the entire charity.

Housing and community services are concentrated in Los Angeles. The central LA/Orange benefit share is 98%, an explicit allowance for residence changes and boundary uncertainty rather than a measured client-address percentage. No benefit is assigned merely because the headquarters is local.
sections.monitoring:
The current report records 700 housed residents: 163 in permanent supportive housing and 537 in community-based housing, including 176 new residents. These are people served, not measured person-years or 700 newly prevented episodes of homelessness. The model applies an assumed average exposure of three-quarters of a year. Reported 97% retention is an annual organizational measure, not lifetime housing security or a randomized counterfactual.

CAPABLE began in April 2025, and 92% of its reported participants had stable or improved daily functioning. The denominator, comparison group and separate improvement rate are not supplied. This combined measure is not added as a second health benefit. Reported meals, appointments, therapy and case-management contacts are likewise not counted as independent QALYs. Future evaluation should link unique residents to housing exposure, alternative placements, utilities and outcomes after exit.
sections.qualitative:
A [five-city randomized Housing First trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26620289/) found 71% versus 29% of time stably housed, with small improvements in quality of life and functioning. That supports a causal housing mechanism, but the Canadian serious-mental-illness population and treatment package are not identical to DWC. The quality-of-life standardized effect is not a QALY gain. The central 30% incremental exposure assumption is deliberately below that trial's 42-percentage-point difference, but is still a transfer judgment—not an estimated DWC effect.

The health bridge is less secure. A [2026 observational analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41758416/) found that adjustment for comorbidity and other factors explained much of the health-related quality-of-life association with homelessness. A [2021 preference survey](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34629422/) valued a hypothetical homelessness state, not the causal health effect of housing. Its large utility loss is not imported. The central 0.05 utility gain for one additional housed person-year is a subjective, survival-adjusted health prior, tested from zero to 0.15; it includes mental and functional health once.

A [2026 housing microsimulation](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2847326) projects 1.89 discounted lifetime QALYs for older adults, alongside continuing housing costs. Applying that lifetime benefit to a single DWC budget year would mismatch costs and benefits. This model instead stops after one year and adds no separate mortality gain. The dominant housing branch is useful for understanding the donation mechanism, but day-center health, employment, advocacy and future housing development remain unpriced.
sections.cost:
The original consolidated audits give recognized gross expenses of [2023 $27,250,997](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/display_audit/2023-12-GSAFAC-0000057330), [2024 $29,047,316](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/display_audit/2024-12-GSAFAC-0000381204) and [2025 $30,530,472](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/display_audit/2025-12-GSAFAC-0000419329), averaging $28,942,928.33. Each restores direct event costs netted from revenue: $109,610, $135,652 and $281,365 respectively. The figures use one consistent consolidated accrual perimeter, not a mixture of parent-only returns and audits.

For 2025, $30,249,107 of reported expense plus $281,365 of event costs equals recognized gross cost. The audit separately values 9,700 hours of unrecognized volunteer services at approximately $405,000. Adding that resource produces the central $30,935,472 denominator. Recognized in-kind contributions of $905,043 and depreciation/amortization of $861,496 are already included and are not added again. Corresponding unrecognized volunteer valuations were $284,673 in 2024 and $237,106 in 2023; they are disclosed separately rather than silently mixed into the annual accounting series.

Housing program expense was $17,494,065, against $5,824,263 for health and wellness and $3,559,078 for other programs. The model retains all fundraising, administration and other program cost. It assigns 39.375 donor-responsive additional housing-and-support person-years before geographic adjustment, yielding 1.87318 LA QALYs and about $165.15 million per 10. Positive joint stress cases span about $6.74 million to $40.46 billion per 10, not confidence limits. Capital acquisitions and outside public/health resources require separate cohort accounting; this is not a full social-cost estimate.
sections.funding:
The 2025 audit reports $20,163,690 of grant income; this is not identified as entirely governmental. Financial assets available within one year were $11,184,101, with substantial restricted assets excluded. Conditional government awards of roughly $11.055 million through June 2027 were unrecognized because performance conditions remained; they are not unrestricted cash or a verified private-funding gap. The current impact report says government funding for new placements decreased in 2025, without quantifying the marginal effect of a private gift.

An ordinary gift could preserve staffing or placements beyond contract coverage, or substitute for reserves, grants or another donor. The central 25% proportional funding response is a judgment about that margin. The 97-unit development is future capacity and is not credited as already occupied. No automatic leverage is assigned to the capital campaign.

The model requires 309.35472 net LA QALYs per annual resource denominator to reach $1 million per 10, or 3,093.5472 for $100,000 per 10. Its priced branch does not approach those thresholds centrally, but omitted pathways are unknown rather than zero. No outreach, donation or endorsement was made.

what: Radiant Health Centers provides HIV care, prevention, counseling and social services in Orange County.
A conditional estimate prices selected clinical health benefits against the full recipient's gross expense.
It is not a complete portfolio return, and the treatment mix, additionality and transfer assumptions are explicitly subjective.

sections.what:
This report covers AIDS Services Foundation Orange County, EIN 33-0126481, doing business as Radiant Health Centers. Its [current site](https://www.radianthealthcenters.org/) offers medical care, HIV prevention and treatment, counseling, case management, housing, food and transport. The recipient is not a single Rapid ART program. Orange County belongs inside the LA/Orange metropolitan edition; the central 98% local benefit share is a residence assumption, not a measured address distribution.

The model uses the full recipient budget while pricing three selected health branches: HIV treatment continuity, PrEP and counseling. Housing stability, non-HIV primary care, reproductive care, nutrition, youth support and broader wellbeing remain unpriced. The result must not be presented as a complete portfolio ranking.
sections.monitoring:
The [latest published impact report](https://www.radianthealthcenters.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Radiant-Health-Centers-Annual-Report-2023-2024.pdf) covers FY2024 and reports 1,872 clinic patients and 322 unduplicated counseling clients. Its broader supportive-service totals are not added to the clinical cohort because overlap and exposure are unclear. The FY2025 return describes integrated care but does not supply updated unique clinical counts. The central model holds the older counts constant rather than converting spending growth into proven patient growth; a half-to-one-and-a-half capacity factor tests this mismatch.

[Current Rapid ART delivery](https://www.radianthealthcenters.org/lgbtq-medical-clinic/rapid-art-hiv-treatment) includes same-day starter medication and follow-up for newly diagnosed or disengaged patients. [PrEP](https://www.radianthealthcenters.org/lgbtq-medical-clinic/prep) is also offered, but neither page establishes annual treatment person-years or the share who would otherwise lack medication. The model's assumed 40% ART and 15% PrEP clinic shares are not reported facts. These groups are mutually exclusive for the modeled year; they are not all 1,872 patients counted twice.
sections.qualitative:
The [SMART randomized trial](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa062360) found approximately two fewer opportunistic-disease-or-death events per 100 randomized-strategy follow-up years with continuous rather than episodic ART. This is not an effect per pill or per extra ART year, nor a same-day versus five-day initiation effect. The model applies it only to a judged subset whose alternative involves meaningful interruption, reduces transfer by half, and values a prevented composite event with a finite one-year health area. It assigns no full remaining lifetime to every medication start.

The [PROUD trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26364263/) found 86% lower HIV incidence with immediate PrEP in a high-risk British population. The model uses a subjective 1% annual untreated risk, below that trial's high-risk setting, and only additional PrEP exposure. Prevented infections receive an explicitly assumed 0.1 annual survival-adjusted health difference for 20 years, discounted and then stopped. No secondary transmission or separate lifetime mortality term is added.

The [CoBalT trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24824481/) found 0.057 additional QALYs over one year from CBT added to usual care for treatment-resistant depression. Radiant's [current counseling page](https://www.radianthealthcenters.org/lgbtq-counseling) primarily describes group counseling over Zoom, with limited in-person groups and individual care case by case. That is not CoBalT's clinical package. Only half of counseling clients are assumed clinically compatible, and a 25% transfer factor jointly accounts for treatment content, intensity and alternative counseling. These are judgments, not measured eligibility or response rates. A further 10% overlap adjustment reduces the sum of the three branches.
sections.cost:
Gross accrual expenses were [FY2023 $11,405,310](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/display_audit/2023-02-GSAFAC-0000402587), [FY2024 $13,167,555](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202500159349302735/IRS990) and [FY2025 $13,825,994](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202630849349300343/IRS990), averaging $12,799,619.67. The gross figures restore event costs of $112,402, $262,104 and $240,092 respectively. For FY2025, the audited $13,585,902 expense plus the original return's $240,092 netted event cost gives the model denominator. No inventory-cost addback is shown separately.

The [latest audit](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/display_audit/2025-02-GSAFAC-0000401968) includes $3,903,594 for the 340B program, $2,650,906 case management, $1,819,615 clinical services, $535,478 Rapid ART and $630,206 mental health. Drug-program revenue of $5,072,290 is not subtracted from resource cost. Donated materials of $58,439 are already recognized; the audit describes gift cards, event tickets, trips and other goods, not a verified donated ART stockpile. Unrecognized volunteer time is not valued in the reviewed current statements, so a full social-resource denominator remains incomplete.

The conditional clinical component yields 0.78564 LA QALYs at $13,825,994 of recipient gross cost, or about $175.98 million per 10. Positive joint stress cases run from about $2.77 million to $48.88 billion per 10; these are not confidence limits. The FY2024 public annual report has internally inconsistent program-detail and net-asset presentations, so original audits and returns control the financial model.
sections.funding:
FY2025 public grants and contracts were $6,176,734. The audit describes 340B margins supporting other programs and FQHC Look-Alike status awarded in September 2024. The [current payment policy](https://www.radianthealthcenters.org/lgbtq-medical-clinic/payment-billing) accepts public and private insurance and offers sliding fees. These existing financing routes and alternative clinics belong in the counterfactual; private giving does not automatically create the entire medication benefit.

The latest audit, dated January 31, 2026, reports unrestricted net assets of $306,241, cash of $313,185 and current liabilities exceeding current assets. It discusses management's plans to address negative operating cash flow through billing, reimbursement rates and systems. Two short-term loans totaling $300,000 were paid off in July 2025. The audit opinion is unmodified, current reportable control findings are absent, and prior listed findings are marked corrected. The older going-concern/control flags should not be repeated as unchanged current findings, but liquidity risk remains relevant.

An ordinary gift might preserve service access during a reimbursement gap, fund care beyond payer rules or substitute for later collections and other support. The central 25% proportional funding response is a judgment, not a demonstrated uncovered gap. Full-portfolio thresholds are 138.25994 net LA QALYs for $1 million per 10 or 1,382.5994 for $100,000 per 10 at the annual denominator. These cannot be assessed from the selected clinical branches alone. No outreach or donation was made.

sections.what:
HALA, EIN 20-5142259, combines direct service with education and organizing. Its [current website](https://www.hungeractionla.org/) includes Market Match, food delivery, CalFresh support and advocacy. The recipient scope includes all of these activities. The model prices the selected Market Match nutrition-health and signed household-resource pathways against the entire recipient expense; other pathways are unknown rather than worthless.

The original return identifies LA-area markets and county support. A 98% LA/Orange benefit share allows for shoppers living outside the boundary; it is not an address-based measurement. Benefits to farmers elsewhere in California are not added as local health gains.
sections.monitoring:
Current measurement boundary: the October 2 review freshly checked three original returns, 2024 Schedules M/L, 2022 Schedule D and current CDFA CNIP passages. Redeemed matching is an observed physical scale anchor; recipient-equivalent years are an assumed incidence normalization, not unique households or transactions. No 2025–26 HALA redemption/residence series or gift-sized expansion capacity was identified. The current cost section and calibrated parameters govern the comparison. The following earlier monitoring analysis is preserved as historical context.

The [2024 original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349320717/IRS990) reports $1,224,579 redeemed Market Match incentives at 39 markets across 67,183 transactions, or $18.23 per transaction. The 2,978 new customers are not all unique annual households, and customer CalFresh spending of $1,631,637 is not new benefit created by HALA. WIC/Senior coupons and delivery are separate unpriced pathways with unresolved overlap.

Dividing redemptions by a hypothetical $240 annual dose yields 5,102.4 standardized incentive-equivalent years, not people observed receiving a year of treatment. The model really depends on q/u, the assumed health yield per incremental incentive dollar. Doubling both u and q leaves results unchanged. Holding q fixed while changing u is a substantive dose-response assumption, not a harmless change of units. Current HALA market instructions conflict between $20 and $15 caps, and no 2025–26 HALA redemption/unique-client series was located.

The live delivery page says 120 households but has undated COVID-era prose; the 2024 return says roughly 200 regularly. Neither establishes current 2026 throughput. Recent volunteer activity does not date the service count, so no contraction or growth is inferred.
sections.qualitative:
Current evidence boundary: HIP, CNIP and the produce-prescription clinical trial were read as indexed original abstracts, not full papers or freshly read audit opinions. The current healthPerUnit=.001 prior is independently judged; the historical q=.005 and alpha-comparable discussion below are not current assumptions. Signed restricted-consumption resources and actual costs are separate from clinical utility and from any farmer/program revenue. Earlier source discussion follows as historical context.

The [HIP randomized evaluation](https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165%2822%2904555-5/fulltext) supports an increase of about 0.24 cups of targeted produce daily, not a measured QALY effect. Its [original final report](https://www.abtassociates.com/sites/default/files/migrated_files/7bc6854f-0067-457c-ae93-235711e1764a.pdf) reports average incentives of $3.65 per household-month during steady operation; that does not validate HALA's $240 exposure assumption or dollars-to-health linearity. Different subsidy ratios, household composition, access and repeat uptake limit transfer.

The [2026 Drake trial](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/article-abstract/2844658) randomized 2,155 adults with diabetes and food-insecurity risk to $80 monthly produce support for a year or usual care. It found no clinical advantage; the HbA1c difference favored usual care. This is not proof of HALA harm, but directly cautions against equating food subsidies with clinical improvement. The [2026 Kane dose trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42745148/) supports dose sensitivity for some diet/food-security outcomes but has no untreated arm or QALY endpoint. [California CNIP cross-sectional evidence](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35807882/) found no quantitatively measured consumption association and cannot isolate causal effects.

The central q=0.005 is retained solely as an alpha-comparable judgment, not an empirically calibrated expected value. It is finite net first-year health area, including competing mortality, burdens and within-year fade. A lower q=0.001 case is judgment sensitivity, not a numerical inference from the trial. Zero remains plausible. Long-horizon national microsimulations are not imported: their sustained program exposure, disease-risk equations, cost offsets and population differ from a marginal HALA gift. Policy, enrollment and food delivery may matter but remain unpriced, not worthless.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter estimates about $10.05 million per better life for a conditional Market Match pathway including nutrition health and signed household-resource effects. This is a ten-healthy-year-equivalent welfare comparison, not measured clinical QALYs alone, a whole-portfolio return or a verified donor offer. Food benefits can improve restricted consumption or free an existing food budget; the model counts that resource value once and never treats it as both food and the same cash.

A hypothetical $10,000 gift supports $1,032.46 of redeemed matching under a proportional annual-support assumption. Of this, $309.74 is assumed to replace equivalent incentives available anyway, leaving $722.72 of incremental matching: $289.09 in a substitution cohort and $433.63 in a diet-expansion cohort. These are fractional modeled expectations, not observed current extra recipients. Dividing by an assumed $240 annual household dose gives 4.302 recipient-equivalent years; 67,183 transactions and 2,978 new customers are not annual unique households.

The underlying anchors are $1,224,579 of 2024 redeemed matching and $2,965,205 of whole-recipient accrual expense. Both remain fixed independently of accounting adjustments. The 25% funding response is a judgment: public reimbursement, other donors and alternative incentives continue without an ordinary gift. Public Ecology Center and county ARPA funding already account for $805,512 and $419,067 of that historical redemption; these are not a new private-donation multiplier. Other current awards and statewide solicitations do not identify HALA’s unrestricted marginal capacity.

Household counterfactuals are disjoint. Thirty percent would receive equivalent free incentives anyway and obtain no incremental transfer or diet credit. Among the remaining 70%, 40% substitute matching produce for purchases they would otherwise make, freeing their existing food budget once but receiving no extra diet-quality health credit. The other 60% obtain incremental restricted food consumption, valued at 80% of matching face value as a planning judgment. No donated delivery stock, farmer revenue, government payment or charity payroll is stacked as household cash income.

Qualifying CalFresh or own-food purchases are assumed to occur anyway centrally. The model does not silently charge a new copay, nor credit existing CalFresh spending as a new HALA benefit. A separate qualifying-cost stress debits net additional restriction, price premium or budget cost after accounting for the ordinary food acquired; it does not subtract all EBT spending while discarding the food bought with it. These counterfactual shares and valuations are unmeasured judgments.

Nutrition health is credited only to the diet-expansion cohort. The current prior is 0.001 finite first-year healthy years per $240 of diet-expansion matching, not the historical 0.005 prior. HIP’s randomized trial increased targeted produce intake by about 0.24 cups per day but measured no QALYs. The California CNIP cross-sectional study found no quantitatively measured consumption association. A fresh indexed abstract of the 2,155-person produce-prescription trial found no 12-month cardiometabolic or utilization improvement; its HbA1c difference favored usual care. These results motivate a small conditional prior and null/negative alternatives, not a measured HALA utility or a mechanically inferred harm coefficient. No lifetime disease microsimulation or household-member multiplier is imported.

HealthUnit is purely a normalization: doubling both healthUnit and healthPerUnit preserves health, resources and native incidence. HouseholdDose is different—it is the assumed actual dispersion of annual matching among household-equivalents and therefore changes the nonlinear household-resource calculation. Neither number is an observed unique annual exposure. Health lasts one year centrally, with year-end discounting and a small independent attempt burden of 0.00001 healthy years per recipient-equivalent. Longer clinical persistence does not repeat resource payments for free.

Twenty-five percent of gift-supported recipient-equivalents are assumed to incur $20 of additional actual travel expense and $10 of actual lost disposable pay. These costs can persist despite equivalent free care or no clinical response; waiting leisure is not converted to lost earnings. Central recovery pay is zero because the cited nutrition evidence supplies no measured wage effect. Positive and negative $100 work-response stresses among a judged 20% of diet-cohort workers are common-alive hypothetical effects, not baseline lifetime earnings from saved lives.

Free, substitution and diet cohorts are crossed with burden and worker states before logarithms. The signed resource bridge uses a $25,000 annual household baseline and half-year receipt timing. Actual cash losses are debited first, then the transfer; pay uses the cash-adjusted baseline, and lost pay is debited before any recovery pay. Negative effects remain fully counted. Positive diet-resource gains receive 50% retention for nutrition/financial-stress overlap; substitution gains receive full retention because they obtain no duplicate diet-health credit. Positive recovery pay receives 50% retention; negative pay is never attenuated. These are transparent overlap judgments, not identified utility weights.

Per $10,000, local clinical health is 0.00167693 healthy years. Consumption-and-cash resource welfare is +0.00847958 and actual-pay welfare −0.000206689, giving net resources +0.00827289 and combined +0.00994982 equivalent years. The resulting donor price is $10,050,431 per ten equivalents; health alone is $59,632,681. Raw net consumption-equivalent resources plus actual cash costs are +$593.36—not cash handed to households. Actual cash outlay is separately −$20.77 and actual lost-pay present value −$10.39. Restricted food and freed food budget are counted once.

The donor-support boundary is full $2,965,205 recipient accrual expense, not cashflow or a verified marginal quote. Recognized donated delivery food of $226,550 is already included and is not added again or subtracted to manufacture physical productivity. A gross companion adds $56,400 from 2,256 reported volunteer hours at a judged $25/hour, yielding $3,021,605 annually and $10,241,597 per ten combined equivalents. That opportunity-cost allowance is not actual lost volunteer wages or donor cash. The three-year expense mean remains $2,151,781; historical cost is not paired with larger current output to manufacture a cheaper ratio.

Both health and household-resource locality are independently 98% for the specified LA/Orange shopper pathway, not farmer locations or headquarters. The fixed $25,000 gift ceiling is a comparison domain, not verified delivery capacity. Forty unweighted cases test funding, health, restricted valuation, burdens, actual work, overlap, local shares, incidence, units, duration, cost and genuine unknowns. Whole-portfolio health and combined value remain unknown centrally.

Historical comparison and financial appendix. The prior clinical-only central was $9,772,603.75 per better life, with C=2,965,205, R=1,224,579, u=240, q=0.005, a=0.5, b=0.25, g=0.98 and d=0.03. All thirteen historical cases remain frozen under historicalModel. Those u/q/a/b assumptions are historical, not the current model. The numerical proximity of the current combined price is not preserved health or an organizational trend: a lower independently reconsidered clinical prior and a new signed food-resource ledger generate it. The following financial analysis is historical; source financial facts remain useful.

Original whole-recipient expenses are [2022 $1,511,795](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202343189349316339/IRS990), [2023 $1,978,343](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202443199349317814/IRS990) and [2024 $2,965,205](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349320717/IRS990). The central cost numerator retains all programs, administration and fundraising. No separately netted activity cost was identified. The three-year mean is $2,151,781, but it is not paired with larger 2024 output to manufacture a cheaper ratio.

The 2022 return reports an audit and Schedule D reconciles the same expense; the signed opinion was not located. FY2023–24 report compilation/review, not independent audit. [2024 Schedule M](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349320717/IRS990ScheduleM) confirms $226,550 donated food is already recognized. Do not add it again. The reported pounds times stated unit valuation differs by $95,998.10; retain filed expense pending ledger clarification, not an arbitrary correction. The Market Match grant subtotal exceeds separately stated incentive/coupon totals by $189,596; do not turn this into extra outcomes.

The 2,256 reported delivery volunteer hours valued at an assumed $25/hour raise an augmented recipient cost envelope to $3,021,605. This is a sensitivity, not full measured societal cost; shopper time and outside administration remain unmeasured. Central conditional health remains 3.0342 LA QALYs at $9.77 million per 10, or $9.96 million with that volunteer allowance. The lower health prior gives $48.86 million per 10. These are assumption-driven component ratios, not measured marginal returns or confidence bounds.
sections.funding:
In 2024, $805,512 of Market Match incentives flowed through Ecology Center invoices and $419,067 through county ARPA via Food Access LA. [Food Access LA's 2025 report](https://foodaccessla.org/fala-2025-impact-video) says that county ARP program concluded and names HALA among partners. Thus the county channel cannot be presumed ongoing. Conversely, [CDFA's current award list](https://cafarmtofork.cdfa.ca.gov/farm_to_fork/grants/cnip.html) confirms renewed Ecology Center funding and a $394,271 Food Access LA WIC/Senior expansion award involving HALA. Statewide and partner awards are not all HALA revenue, and no net HALA shortfall is established.

The [2026 CNIP RFP](https://cafarmtofork.cdfa.ca.gov/farm_to_fork/grants/docs/2026/cnip_2026_rfp_calfresh.pdf) anticipates $13.5 million statewide with one-year awards within a February 2027–June 2028 window. Match is not mandatory; cost sharing is scored but no automatic donation multiplier exists. Incentive and indirect-cost restrictions might leave some costs uncovered, but a current HALA budget is needed to quantify that. No anti-supplant rule was located. Published deadline details conflict; this report is not application advice.

At year-end 2024 cash was $81,479, about 0.33 months of annual expense, while grants receivable were $312,495, 79% of assets. Unrestricted net assets were $86,037 versus restricted $184,912. These are dated liquidity indicators, not available-cash or insolvency conclusions. [Schedule L](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349320717/IRS990ScheduleL) discloses an outstanding $10,000 officer loan without indicated board approval or written agreement; diligence is warranted, not a misconduct inference.

Donor readiness remains on hold. Obtain current contracts and reimbursement aging, unrestricted cash, replaced ARPA allocations, an unfunded eligible demand queue, and a priced marginal plan showing what changes with versus without a gift. Historical scale is a normalization, not a verified funding tranche. The central 25% funding response remains judgment; replacement can make it zero. No donation, outreach or application was made.

Current comparison: funding=.25 is a conditional proportional-response judgment, not verified extra slots or an identified expected return. Otherwise-equivalent free incentives are separately partitioned at .30 of gift-supported redemption. Current CDFA awards involving HALA do not disclose its complete allocation; the expired county program and public replacement baseline remain unresolved. No automatic private match, outreach or donation is claimed.

model.costScope: Whole recipient accrual support proxy, no subtraction of recognized donated food; derived volunteer gross companion. Neither is a marginal cash quote or capacity promise.
model.geographicAttribution: Separate health/resource resident shares .98 for LA/Orange shopper pathway; no farmer/headquarters attribution.
model.formula: Gift-supported redemption=gift/supportCost*redeemedScale*funding. Disjoint free/substitution/diet cohorts precede health and household-state ledgers. Signed cash loss, restricted transfer, actual lost pay and recovery pay use sequential shared log-resource baselines; positive overlap applies only to positives. Price10=10*gift/(known positive local health+signed resources).
model.counterfactual: Existing qualifying food spending, other free incentives, public reimbursement and alternative food programs continue; no automatic gift match. Net qualifying-cost stress is separate from travel.
model.attribution: Restricted food or freed food budget counts once; no transaction/household/member multiplication, donated foodstock cash, farmer revenue or charity payroll addition.
model.uncertainty: Conditional finite planning comparison; no identified whole-portfolio expected return, probability intervals or verified marginal tranche.

reports.program: Integrated housing, recuperative care and supportive health services

what: Illumination Health + Home, formerly Illumination Foundation, combines housing with recuperative care and supportive services.
The conditional estimate prices a substantial medical-respite component against the full recipient budget.
Housing, family services and other health pathways remain unpriced, so this is not a complete portfolio ranking.
strengths: Post-hospital recuperative care has a concrete clinical mechanism and external randomized evidence.
Current reported respite volume anchors scale without treating all clients as marginal beneficiaries.
The cost reconstruction includes recognized donated resources and separately netted event costs.
reservations: External randomized QALY differences were small and statistically uncertain.
CalAIM, hospital payments and public contracts can substitute for donations.
LA/Orange residence and current marginal capacity are unmeasured; Inland Empire activity is outside the edition.

sections.what: The [current organization](https://illuminationhealthhome.org/) confirms the name change from Illumination Foundation. The same EIN, 71-1047686, is the recipient; housing and integrated services are included rather than treating respite as a separately restricted charity. [Healthcare services](https://illuminationhealthhome.org/service/healthcare-services/) include post-hospital recovery and behavioral support. The older [service overview](https://www.ifhomeless.org/) describes Orange County, Los Angeles County and Inland Empire operations. Riverside and San Bernardino benefits are outside this LA–Orange MSA; headquarters is not beneficiary geography.
sections.monitoring: The [FY2024–25 impact report](https://illuminationhealthhome.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Illumination_2024-25_Impact-Report.pdf) reports 2,329 recuperative-care clients, 6,826 clients overall and 1,719 housed. These are outputs, not additional health gains, and categories can overlap. The model uses respite volume only, with no extra housing QALYs added for the same clients. Track unique admissions, comparable discharge alternatives, symptom and EQ-5D trajectories, completion, readmission and resident county. The latest throughput is paired with FY2024 audited cost as a prospective scale approximation, not a matched-year observed cost per outcome.
sections.qualitative:
A [Danish randomized respite study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12913-020-05358-4) compared a two-week recovery stay with usual discharge arrangements. It found lower subsequent costs, but the between-group QALY difference was small and not statistically significant. The first six participants were assigned to intervention rather than randomized, and quality-of-life follow-up was incomplete. Different insurance, housing and clinical needs limit transfer. Hospital savings are not QALYs, and a negative cost-utility ratio does not establish a large health effect.

The central q=0.005 QALY is an explicit modest health-area judgment per otherwise additional respite episode, not the trial's measured coefficient. It represents about 1.8 quality-adjusted days over no more than one year. Zero or adverse health is possible. No avoided-death lifetime term, housing effect, or repeated annual cohort is added.
sections.cost:
FY2024 gross recognized recipient cost is $55,822,486: $55,426,178 audited expense plus $396,308 netted event costs. The audit includes donated services/materials/facilities and depreciation. [Original audit](https://illuminationhealthhome.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/The-Illumination-Foundation-06.30.2024.pdf) The FY2023 original return reconciles $47,541,549 to $47,992,708 audited expense through $451,159 donated services/facilities; adding $321,001 event costs gives $48,313,709. FY2022 return expense plus events is $39,155,013, but its donated-resource reconciliation is not verified, so that year is noncomparable and no synthetic three-year mean is supplied.

At full recipient cost, 2,329 respite clients × 0.5 net service additionality × 0.25 funding responsiveness × 0.005 QALY × 0.8 LA/Orange share / 1.03 gives 1.130583 LA QALYs, or $493.75 million per 10. These fractions are judgments, not observed conversion rates. The wide positive cases, zero and adverse stress retain uncertainty. Outside hospital, clinical and partner resources require separate societal costing; savings are not subtracted from this recipient denominator.
sections.funding: The [FY2024 audit](https://illuminationhealthhome.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/The-Illumination-Foundation-06.30.2024.pdf) reports $35.90m program fees and $16.23m federal/state contracts and grants. Net assets were $22.93m, including $1.27m restricted, but much of the balance sheet is property rather than spendable cash. These figures do not prove a current funding gap. CalAIM and hospital alternatives make funding response distinct from clinical effectiveness. The [current impact report](https://illuminationhealthhome.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Illumination_2024-25_Impact-Report.pdf) identifies CalOptima partnership; financed expansion is baseline, not automatically caused by a new gift.

reports.program: Independent living, home access, community transition and disability support

what: Dayle McIntosh Center supports independent living for people with disabilities and older adults in Orange County.
Its services include home access, community transitions, assistive technology and peer support.
The estimate prices a home-access health component at full recipient cost while leaving other portfolio outcomes unpriced.
strengths: The current home-access page identifies a concrete role for donations above funder limits.
Original returns reconcile annual expenses to reported audited totals without an identified netted event or inventory addback.
Home modifications have a plausible functional-health pathway supported by external randomized multicomponent evidence.
reservations: No current annual modification count, marginal allocation or unit cost was found; the central bridge explicitly uses judgments.
Most revenue is public funding, and equivalent services or funder reimbursement may replace donor spending.
DMC is not the tested CAPABLE clinical team, and functional independence is not automatically a measured QALY.

sections.what: DMC is a nonresidential, peer-based independent-living organization, EIN 95-3313707. Its [current identity page](https://daylemc.org/about-us-2/) describes Orange County services and public/private financing. The [service portfolio](https://daylemc.org/services/) includes assistive technology, independent-living skills, housing, transitions and personal-assistance navigation. An ordinary gift supports this whole recipient, not a separately designated modification program. The estimate includes only the home-access health component; rights, autonomy and other services are not assigned a fabricated health uplift.
sections.monitoring:
The [Home Access page](https://daylemc.org/home-access/) describes ramps, bathroom access and other modifications, including CalOptima eligibility and limited Laguna Niguel funding. Work can depend on available funding; costs above a funder's lifetime budget may require a donation or another resource. This establishes a mechanism, not a verified queue or price. Measure completed unique homes, actual resource cost, resident county, alternative insurance/municipal funding, functional health before and after installation and adverse events.

The [community-transition program](https://daylemc.org/services/transition-services/community-transitions/) coordinates housing and support after institutional care, typically following consumers for 90 days. Its beneficiaries can overlap with Home Access. Transition stories are not annual throughput or controlled outcomes; no separate transition QALYs are added here.
sections.qualitative:
The [2019 CAPABLE randomized trial](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/2720136) found a 30% reduction in ADL disability scores at five months in low-income older adults. Its intervention combined occupational therapy, nursing and home repairs; delivery cost was $2,825 per person in that historical trial. At 12 months the same trial no longer found a statistically significant ADL advantage (adjusted relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.68–1.18). A disability-score reduction is not a health-utility change, and DMC's modification service is not verified to reproduce the clinical package.

Importantly, a [2025 randomized post-hospital CAPABLE trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40990312/) did not improve its primary ADL outcome overall, although mobility and a high-comorbidity subgroup improved. This argues against applying a universal treatment effect to every modified home. The central 0.01 QALY is a deliberately modest, explicit first-year health-area judgment—about 3.65 quality-adjusted days—not an empirical QALY coefficient. There is no assumption that disabled life is intrinsically less valuable, no mortality credit, and no health gain after year one. Autonomy gains may matter outside this health metric.
sections.cost:
The original accrual returns report $3,919,818 in FY2023, $3,857,305 in FY2024 and $3,729,186 in FY2025, years ending September 30; mean $3,835,436.33. Each Schedule D reconciles to the same reported audited expense, with no donated-service adjustment. Part VIII shows no event, gaming or inventory expenses to restore. This establishes recognized recipient cost, not absence of unrecognized donated equipment or volunteer effort. [FY2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/953313707/202620869349300547/full)

The conditional model allocates an assumed 20% of the full budget to representative home-access packages costing an assumed $5,000 each, including installation and coordination. That implies 149.17 packages before additionality, not observed output. A 50% no-equivalent-service fraction and 25% funding response imply 18.65 additional packages before geography. At 0.01 first-year QALY, 98% LA/Orange share and 3% discount, the result is 0.177408 LA QALYs, or $210.20 million per 10. The $5,000 is a current planning prior, not an inflation-adjusted trial price or a quoted DMC charge.

All recipient cost remains in the numerator, and the home-access allocation limits credited output. Positive joint cases are broad judgments, with zero and net-harm alternatives. Outside clinical care, public implementation and unrecognized donated resources would add social cost; they are not treated as free. This is not a complete portfolio return.
sections.funding: The [FY2025 original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/953313707/202620869349300547/full) reports $3,156,228 government grants, $296,327 other contributions and $508,062 service fees. Total revenue was $3,961,771, with net assets of $1,031,209. Neither a surplus nor a named public funder determines next-dollar effectiveness. DMC's [funding description](https://daylemc.org/about-us-2/) identifies government, CalOptima and aging-system partners. b=.25 is an explicit assumption about extra recipient capacity after replacement funding, separate from a=.5, which concerns whether recipients would otherwise obtain equivalent home access. A costed current list of unmet projects would materially improve this estimate.

sections.what:
This report covers the entire Didi Hirsch Psychiatric Service recipient, EIN 95-1816023, operating as Didi Hirsch Mental Health Services. Its ordinary donation route does not guarantee that the next gift supports only its strongest suicide-prevention activity. [Ordinary donation route](https://didihirsch.org/get-involved/donate/)

Current services include 988, counseling, hospital referrals and support groups. Attempt-survivor groups are for California residents, while bereavement groups are available nationwide. Broad health care and substance-use work also belong in the recipient scope. [Current suicide prevention, follow-up and support services](https://didihirsch.org/suicide-prevention/)

The 2025 annual report records 246,098 988 calls, chats and texts; 97% were resolved without emergency services and 69% of contacts with suicidal intent improved by the interaction's end. These are contact-level reported outcomes, not distinct lives saved. Teen Line receives international contacts, so headquarters location does not establish the geographic impact numerator. [2025 Annual Report, including current services and financial summary](https://didihirsch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/2025-Annual-Report.pdf)
sections.monitoring:
A direct study of the UCLA–Didi Hirsch partnership describes outreach within 24–72 hours after discharge, safety planning, emotional support and linkage to care. It involved focus groups with 18 providers/counselors, not a controlled patient-outcome comparison. Participants identified referral and communication gaps, making successful engagement—not referrals sent—the meaningful delivery metric. [Qualitative evaluation of UCLA–Didi Hirsch post-discharge follow-up partnership](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10655296/)

The organization's SOSA research enrolled 92 attempt survivors in an eight-week group and assessed pre/post self-reported symptoms and resilience. Without a comparison group, improvement can reflect treatment elsewhere, natural recovery and selective completion; it does not identify mortality effects. [Open-label evaluation of Survivors of Suicide Attempts groups](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30080086/)

ED-SAFE provides stronger external evidence for a bundle of ED resources and follow-up calls. In sequential phases, one-year attempt risk was 23% with usual care versus 18% with the intervention; screening alone did not show the same improvement. This was not random assignment to Didi Hirsch, and reduced attempts must not be relabeled an equal proportional reduction in deaths. [ED-SAFE sequential-phase suicide prevention trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28456130/)

Request unique-patient engagement, repeat contacts, alternative care received, symptoms over time, attempted self-harm and mortality linkage with an appropriate comparison. Include uncontactable referrals and dropout. A same-person repeated crisis should not receive a fresh lifetime survival credit each time.

The outpatient branch separately uses 5,498 reported clients and a 32% depression share in the adult narrative. Adult-compatible share and clinical eligibility remain assumptions; ask for unique adult depression patients and therapy offered rather than treating all outpatient clients alike.
sections.qualitative:
The [CoBalT randomized trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24824481/) enrolled 469 UK adults with depression despite antidepressants. It compared an offer of 12–18 CBT sessions plus usual care with usual care, yielding an estimated 0.057 additional QALY over 12 months. This is an intention-to-treat offer effect, not an effect per completed session. The [economic methods](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK261987/) use baseline-adjusted EQ-5D area under the curve; the model does not multiply it by another year or transplant the UK treatment price.

Transport is limited: the trial excluded psychosis, bipolar disorder, major substance misuse and patients already receiving psychotherapy or secondary depression care. Didi Hirsch treats a more complex population. A separate eligibility factor and 50% effect-transfer factor are explicit judgments, not empirically fitted adjustments. The clinical bridge is useful for a subset, but cannot establish a portfolio average.

For suicide prevention, [ED-SAFE](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28456130/) supports a bundled emergency-department and follow-up intervention, with a roughly five-percentage-point difference in one-year attempt risk. It does not identify deaths prevented by Didi Hirsch alone. Hotline relief, severe-illness care, child development, substance-use treatment and avoided coercive responses may have substantial value, but no unsupported lifetime or per-call credit is added.

California scope is evaluated independently of the LA report. The [current clinical locations](https://didihirsch.org/locations/) are in California, so g_CA=.99 is a high but not certain resident-share judgment for this outpatient component; .95–1 is tested. It is not the geographic share of national 988 or international Teen Line benefit.
sections.cost:
Full recognized recipient resources for FY2025 are $80,043,834: $79,340,574 Form 990 expense, plus $482,866 of donated services excluded from that return total, plus $220,394 of event costs netted against revenue. The corresponding totals are $90,068,699 for FY2024 and $78,394,883 for FY2023; their mean is $82,835,805.33. Original Schedule D reconciles the annual report's $79,823,440 FY2025 expense to Form 990 before restoring event costs. The audit download was blocked; this is a filed reconciliation, not an independently reopened audit. [FY2025 return and schedules](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/951816023/202610899349301251/full)

Excluding donated services, gross Form 990 expenses are $79,560,968, $89,400,520 and $77,256,644 respectively. These are accrual expenses, not cash flows. No rental, gaming or inventory expense addback was shown in the original returns. [FY2024](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/951816023/202520839349300422/full) [FY2023](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/951816023/202431369349311023/full)

The conditional depression component yields 3.614588 California QALYs, or $221.45 million per 10, at full recognized recipient cost. Only California clinical benefit is counted. Positive joint cases are sensitivity judgments, not confidence bounds; zero and adverse outcomes remain possible. Major crisis, severe-illness and youth pathways are unpriced, not zero-valued. Outside clinical and patient resources add societal cost.
sections.funding:
The corrected recognized-resource series and event/donated-service reconciliation are disclosed in the cost section.

For 2025, the return assigns $65,368,624 to programs, $12,236,469 to administration and $1,735,481 to fundraising. Revenue includes $67,042,157 government grants and $8,829,632 contract fees. Net assets are $40,203,725, of which $3,180,468 is restricted. These data demonstrate a large contracted provider, not an identified unrestricted funding gap. The revised cost model restores those direct event costs and recognized donated services. [Original Form 990 for fiscal year ending June 2025](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/951816023/202610899349301251/full)

The annual report separately presents $79,823,440 FY2024–25 expense, now reconciled through original Schedule D and restored event costs in the revised resource series. It identifies existing government crisis-service funders and a two-year $1 million Red Cross disaster-care award; neither confirms that every useful activity is funded. [2025 Annual Report, including current services and financial summary](https://didihirsch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/2025-Annual-Report.pdf)

The May 2026 Assembly review documents rising demand, an 85.5% in-state call answer rate in early 2026 and substantially weaker text/chat response. It also describes public appropriations and funding requests. These are dated system findings, not a verified current Didi Hirsch cash gap. Contacts flowing to national backup are not necessarily unanswered, and local service may add coordination quality rather than create all of the call's benefit. [May 2026 AB 988 implementation outcomes review](https://ahea.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-05/background-paper-ab-988-outcomes-review_0.pdf)

September 2026 HHS announcements include $252 million for crisis and suicide-prevention services nationally. This review did not establish what portion, if any, reaches this recipient. Neither a national announcement nor an earlier shortage statement establishes today's marginal opportunity. [September 2026 federal behavioral-health and crisis-service awards](https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/hhs-awards-380-million-988-suicide-prevention-behavioral-health.html)

what: Breathe Southern California combines asthma support with education, equipment and air-quality advocacy.
BEAM serves eligible residents of Los Angeles and San Bernardino counties, both within California.
The estimate prices only the BEAM health component at full recipient cost; other portfolio health remains unpriced.
strengths: A current insured asthma pathway and original accounts establish real operations and recipient-scale costs.
Home-asthma randomized evidence supplies a finite symptom-day bridge instead of equating visits with health.
Named LA purifier distribution locations and public-agency response documents make geography and substitution questions concrete.
reservations: Insurer-covered asthma and a separate public purifier program may replace services credited to private gifts.
The priced BEAM pathway omits potentially important purifier and policy effects, so it is not a complete portfolio ranking.
Annual marginal patients, county mix, effective purifier use and health-relevant exposure reductions are unknown; past matching claims are not current offers.

sections.what:
Breathe Southern California, EIN 95-1641451, is distinct from similarly named Northern California organizations. The [current BEAM eligibility](https://www.breathesocal.org/beam) requires residence in Los Angeles or San Bernardino County. Both are inside the California edition. Accordingly, g_CA=1 applies to the modeled eligible BEAM branch, conditional on eligibility being followed; it is not the whole portfolio's geographic share. The [current homepage](https://www.breathesocal.org/) reports 300-plus BEAM patients during 2024–2026, not annual or gift-induced throughput.

The recipient also operates purifier response, education and policy work. Those pathways may matter substantially but require separate exposure and implementation models; devices, maps and workshop counts are not QALYs.
sections.monitoring:
A randomized King County study of 373 Medicaid-enrolled children found an additional 2.10 symptom-free days per two weeks (95% CI 1.17–3.05) and 1.31 fewer urgent-care events over 12 months. Its structured multi-contact intervention differs from a visit with optional follow-up. Outcomes included self-report, and caregiver questionnaire points are not preference-based QALYs. [Randomized Medicaid childhood-asthma home-visit outcomes and costs](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4605150/)

The adult HomeBASE trial similarly improved symptom-free days and asthma-related quality of life but did not improve unscheduled health-care use. This supports a morbidity pathway while cautioning against automatically assigning hospitalization savings or childhood effects to every adult. [HomeBASE randomized adult asthma trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25419871/)

For BEAM, request unique-patient baseline severity, completed visits and supplies, symptom days or validated utility at follow-up, hospital claims, retention and alternative-provider availability. Compare against contemporaneous usual care and avoid selecting only high-utilization patients at a temporary peak. The public workshop page describes instruction, not controlled follow-up demonstrating fewer exacerbations. [Lung Power education workshops](https://www.breathesocal.org/lungpower)
sections.qualitative:
The clinical and environmental pathways are plausible, but their marginal funding mechanisms differ. A new gift might support navigation for otherwise unserved patients, effective filter use or people outside a public program's footprint. That hypothesis needs a costed queue and comparison against services already available.

The [public Palos response](https://www.aqmd.gov/palos) distinguishes the June smoke episode from ongoing cleanup monitoring and odors. It reports up to $5 million additional purifier funding, direct shipment and three years of replacement filters for eligible residents. This is an alternative-provider counterfactual—not funding received by Breathe. It makes gross distribution counts a particularly weak proxy for private-donation impact.

The [organization's LinkedIn account](https://www.linkedin.com/company/breathesocal) reports thousands of purifiers and a matching appeal ending September 4; the exact post date and subsequent fulfillment are unverified. That deadline has passed, so no active match or remaining donor gap is assumed. [AAFA's partner account](https://asthmaandallergyfriendly.com/USA/aafas-2026-asthma-capitals-report-highlights-certified-partners-driving-community-impact/) documents an order of 300 upgraded Rabbit Air units, not that the entire shipment was donated. The policy portfolio needs its own finite exposure and coalition-attribution model.
sections.cost:
The conditional BEAM estimate is $214.15 million per 10 California QALYs, charging $2,923,727 full recipient FY2025 expense. It is partial health, not a whole-portfolio expected return. The model posits 100 annual courses, 25% funding responsiveness, half the external trial symptom-day effect, 75% within-year timing and 0.10 utility per additional symptom-free day. At one year and 3% discount it yields 0.136529 California QALYs. All eligibility counties are in California; no observed geographic population weighting is claimed.

The current cumulative count does not establish annual throughput or a funding gap. The clinical bridge gives .005461165049 QALY per additional course, with no mortality, permanent cure or duplicate hospitalization effect. Joint positive scenarios, zero and adverse stress retain uncertainty. Original FY2023–25 returns have now been reopened in the shared LA evidence and no separately netted direct costs were identified; the three comparable expense amounts remain $2,075,948, $2,305,383 and $2,923,727. Outside medical, insurer and partner resources are separate societal costs.
sections.funding:
Original accrual returns for fiscal years ending June report expenses of $2,075,948 in 2023, $2,305,383 in 2024 and $2,923,727 in 2025: a three-year mean of $2,435,019.33. The 2024 return supplies the 2023 comparative. Its $4,719,274 revenue included $2,441,575 miscellaneous income; that unusually large category should not be assumed recurring clinical revenue. [Original Form 990, fiscal year ending June 2024 with 2023 comparative totals](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/951641451/202501359349311575/full)

For 2025, revenue was $2,573,083, including $1,527,260 contributions and $814,003 rent. The return classifies every expense as program, with zero management/fundraising allocation; this does not establish zero overhead. It reports no independent financial-statement audit. Net assets were $10,700,896, including $4,612,972 restricted; Schedule O labels a $1,092,063 reconciliation addition only as a book/tax difference. Those facts merit clarification rather than interpreting the $350,644 revenue-expense deficit as proof that every gift funds additional care. [Original Form 990, fiscal year ending June 2025](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/951641451/202611359349315411/full)

Government-grant and program-fee rows on that historical return do not negate the current contracts on the BEAM page. Detailed payer receipts, current BEAM cost centers and contract reimbursement margins are needed before allocating ordinary donations. [BEAM services, eligibility, counties and managed-care contracts](https://www.breathesocal.org/beam)

DHCS's finalized update removes assessment and self-management education from the Asthma Remediation Community Support beginning January 2026 because the Asthma Preventive Services benefit covers them; physical supplies and modifications remain complementary remediation services. This is a separation to avoid duplication, not elimination of all asthma support. The old all-in-one description should not be used to infer a new donor gap or a flat payment received for each patient. [Final asthma-remediation definitions and January 2026 benefit separation](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/Documents/MCQMD/Community-Supports-February-2025-Service-Definition-Updates.pdf)

Current DHCS resources describe a provider enrollment pathway for community organizations delivering asthma preventive services. A gift might improve access, pay unreimbursed navigation or serve people otherwise excluded, but a costed unmet queue and the alternative plan/provider response were not found. [Current CHW and asthma provider enrollment resources](https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/community-health-workers/)

model.geographicAttribution: Both named BEAM eligibility counties are in California; g_CA=1 conditional on compliance. A .95 sensitivity allows eligibility/movement leakage. This is independently scoped, not a copy of the LA model's .5 county-share judgment.
