what: Essential Access Health supports sexual and reproductive health services, training and public-program administration.
Its California partner-treatment program supplies medication for eligible partners unlikely to obtain timely clinical care.
The conditional estimate prices only repeat-infection prevention against all recipient costs; the larger reproductive-health portfolio remains unpriced.
strengths: Partner STI treatment has randomized evidence of reducing persistent or recurrent infections.
The organization operates a concrete medication distribution pathway with site logs and expired-dose reporting.
Current public funding announcements and original returns allow scrutiny of pass-through funding and substitution.
reservations: No verified ordinary-gift allocation, incremental medication yield or currently unfunded treatment queue was found.
Large restricted public grants and reimbursements are not equivalent to private-donation-sensitive additional care.
Sex, pathogen, treatment timing and recurrent-infection risks materially change the QALY conversion.

sections.what:
This is the entire Essential Access Health recipient, EIN 95-2564024, rather than a restricted medication project. Its activities include provider funding, training, clinical research and policy. The official site links the ordinary donation route, but no gift or endorsement was made. [Current programs and ordinary donation link](https://www.essentialaccess.org/programs-and-services)

One inspectable clinical pathway is California expedited partner therapy: eligible providers obtain free medication for partners unlikely to receive prompt treatment. This is a delivery mechanism, not evidence that every distributed dose is taken or prevents infection. [California free partner-treatment program](https://orders.essentialaccess.org/about)
sections.monitoring:
The medication system requires site-specific logs and reporting of expired stock, with a licensed repackager shipping on the organization's request. The index patient's own treatment matters because a partner pack can otherwise be diverted to that patient. Useful marginal monitoring would add unique index patients offered treatment, partner uptake, alternative access, repeat infection and the funding source of each additional offer. [Partner medication distribution and accountability FAQ](https://orders.essentialaccess.org/faq)

In a 2005 randomized trial, persistent or recurrent infection at 3–19 weeks occurred in 121/931 standard-referral patients versus 92/929 expedited-treatment patients: relative risk 0.76 (95% CI 0.59–0.98). Effects differed by pathogen; the composite absolute reduction cannot simply be paired with the highest sex-specific disease burden. [Randomized expedited partner treatment trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15716561/)

A later Washington stepped-wedge community trial increased EPT receipt but its adjusted population outcomes were uncertain: chlamydia positivity prevalence ratio 0.89 (0.77–1.04) and gonorrhea incidence ratio 0.91 (0.71–1.16). Clinic efficacy therefore does not establish the population return on a statewide implementation dollar. [Washington community randomized EPT implementation trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25590331/)
sections.qualitative:
Access, privacy and reproductive autonomy can matter independently of measured health. This report does not convert avoided births or the monetary value of care into QALYs. Training attendance, grant awards and reimbursed visits likewise are not themselves health outcomes.

EPT supplements rather than universally replaces clinical evaluation. Current CDC guidance describes its role when partners are unlikely to access timely care; trial transfer must respect current eligibility and treatment practice. [Current clinical treatment of gonorrhea](https://www.cdc.gov/gonorrhea/hcp/clinical-care/index.html)

The strongest next diligence request is a costed, currently unfunded California delivery margin: how many additional eligible patients would receive and use partner treatment, compared with Medi-Cal, Family PACT, ordinary partner referral and other free sources? Existing payment alternatives are explicitly described on the patient page. [Partner medication and existing payment options](https://www.essentialaccess.org/partner_meds)
sections.cost:
The conditional EPT repeat-infection prevention price is $543.57 million per ten California QALYs, charging all $46,675,922 of gross recognized recipient spending. This narrow component must not be presented as a complete reproductive-health return. A 5% EPT allocation and $100 full delivery-resource cost per eligible index-patient offer are judgments, not observed marginal program costs or medication quotes. The resource allowance includes drug, logistics, counseling and partner delivery; an additional partner-resource sensitivity is retained.

The trial's absolute repeat-infection difference is 121/931 minus 92/929, about 3.094 percentage points among followed participants. A 50% transfer factor discounts current patient mix, follow-up selection, treatment practice and the uncertain community implementation evidence. A separate 25% funding-response factor discounts payer replacement and existing free supply. We use a judgmental 0.01 discounted QALY per repeat infection avoided, not the largest female infection burden paired indiscriminately with a pooled effect. A 98% California resident share gives 0.858685 California QALYs.

No partner or downstream transmission benefit is added, no new lifetime is assigned to recurrences, and no extra adherence factor duplicates the trial strategy effect. The underlying disease model uses finite sequela duration; an additional 3% one-year timing discount only moves the avoided infection to the delivery date. Routine medication harms and missed clinical evaluations could offset benefits; zero and adverse stress cases remain.
sections.funding:
Original accrual returns and Schedule D yield gross expenses of $31,893,649 in 2022, $52,995,581 in 2023 and $46,675,922 in 2024, averaging $43,855,050.67. The earlier comparative comes from the 2023 return. [Original 2023 Form 990 with 2022 comparative totals](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/952564024/202403209349311455/full)

In 2024, $40,147,199 was classified as program expense and $6,525,628 as administration. Revenue was $37,119,151, including $32,635,022 government grants. Despite the revenue-expense deficit, unrestricted net assets rose from $7,995,747 to $8,641,940 while restricted net assets fell from $15,543,653 to $5,998,097. This is consistent with restricted-fund spending timing and does not establish an unrestricted cash crisis. Neither balances nor functional ratios identify marginal cost-effectiveness. [Original 2024 Form 990](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/952564024/202543179349311349/full)

April 2026's announcement says California and Hawaii Title X received one year of level funding; describing the prior withholding as still unresolved would be stale. [2026 Title X award received](https://www.essentialaccess.org/about/press-room/essential-access-health-receives-title-x-funding-amid-ongoing-federal-uncertainty)

June 2025's final-award announcement described $36.5 million cumulatively awarded for uncompensated care, including reimbursement of earlier services. Those patients cannot all be attributed to a new gift. [June 2025 uncompensated-care awards](https://www.essentialaccess.org/about/press-room/essential-access-health-announces-final-awards-californias-uncompensated-care)

Current HCAI information now describes a new $30 million uncompensated-care allocation within broader 2026–27 reproductive-health appropriations, with administrator procurement expected in September 2026. Essential Access administered prior funds, but the new award is not yet established as its revenue. State appropriations do not prove all needs are met; they do require avoiding duplicate private-donor credit. [Current reproductive-health appropriations and administrator procurement](https://hcai.ca.gov/workforce/initiatives/reproductive-health-and-gender-affirming-care-programs/)

Fresh original three-year reconciliations restore inventory costs of $17,637, $2,695 and $1,635, plus $1,460 of donated services in 2024. Investment expenses of $57,667, $45,699 and $40,332 already included in return expense are retained, not added twice. No separately netted event cost is reported.

reports.program: Housing-policy research, education, coalition support and Metropolitan Abundance Project

what: California YIMBY Education Fund produces housing research and implementation analysis and supports the national Metropolitan Abundance Project.
It is legally distinct from California YIMBY's advocacy and political entities.
The conditional estimate prices a California housing-health component against all recipient spending; other geographic and policy benefits remain unpriced.
strengths: A plausible high-leverage pathway runs from better implementation rules to additional homes, lower housing costs and improved living conditions.
Original research discusses financial feasibility and local implementation, not merely legal zoning capacity.
Independent empirical supply research supports an affordability mechanism, while the report keeps that distinct from health outcomes.
reservations: No reviewed source identifies the marginal extra completed homes caused by an ordinary Education Fund donation.
California benefit allocation is not the same as its Sacramento address: MAP explicitly works nationally and the c4 shares employees.
The accounts change from cash in 2022–23 to accrual in 2024, and housing or financial gains cannot automatically be priced as QALYs.

sections.what: The [recipient's research catalogue](https://cayimby.org/reports/) covers ADU implementation, housing impact fees, underproduction and local approval processes. Its [national MAP project](https://www.metroabundance.org/about-us/) works on housing, transportation and governance; MAP's [giving page](https://www.metroabundance.org/donate/) identifies the Education Fund as its recipient. The main [giving instructions](https://cayimby.org/waystogive/) distinguish this c3 from California YIMBY's c4 and PAC. Shared branding does not justify assigning every affiliate policy win to this charitable gift.
sections.monitoring: The [ADU retrospective](https://cayimby.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/CAY-ADU_Report-2024-v4.pdf) documents a substantial permitting expansion but is a historical, uncontrolled policy account, not a marginal donor evaluation. Its chart separates permits from completions; footnotes note changing data collection and unverified affordability classifications. No new gift receives credit for all past ADUs. A useful next evaluation would link a specific Education Fund analysis or implementation intervention to changed rules, actual net completions, occupancy, resident outcomes and a credible no-intervention comparison.
sections.qualitative: [Research on large new apartments](https://research.upjohn.org/up_workingpapers/316/) supports rent reductions nearby rather than inevitable rent inflation, but is not a health trial and may not transfer to small ADUs or every neighborhood. [Terner's early SB9 review](https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/sb-9-turns-one-applications/) shows why legal or modeled feasible capacity is not production: financing, local restrictions and construction constraints matter. [HCD's current SB79 guidance](https://www.hcd.ca.gov/planning-and-research/sb79-tod) confirms the law is already operative and public agencies have implementation duties; future gifts need to improve on that funded baseline. Housing can affect health through stability, crowding, location and pollution, but [MTO](https://www.nber.org/papers/w18772) concerns a different low-income mobility intervention with heterogeneous effects. The [recent income trial](https://www.nber.org/papers/w32711) also cautions against treating financial relief as an automatic lasting clinical gain.
sections.cost:
The conditional California housing-health price is $454.77 million per ten California QALYs. It charges three years of all recipient spending, $9,141,486, including national and unpriced activities. It is not a complete portfolio or societal return. We posit 1,000 net additional occupied California homes conditional on an implementation change over that support window; this is an explicit scale judgment, not permitted capacity, a project pipeline or a forecast from the ADU report.

A 10% incremental coalition implementation probability, 10% Education Fund contribution and 25% ordinary-funding response imply 2.5 net additional home-equivalents. The c3 contribution excludes credit assigned to its c4 and public agencies. Ten years of benefit at years 3–12 gives 8.040534 discounted home-years per added home. A judgmental 0.01 QALY per home-year across affected residents yields 0.201013 California QALYs, without multiplying again by household occupancy. The utility prior is not inferred from rent dollars, the MTO trial or a housing unit count.

Net homes exclude displacement of construction elsewhere in California. Health may arise through less harmful crowding or instability, but some residents simply move from other adequate housing, and transportation or pollution effects can offset gains. Current SB79 duties and already permitted development are baseline. A construction-resource sensitivity adds $500,000 per attributable net home; this is a judgmental resource proxy, not a current local unit quote or net fiscal cost.
sections.funding:
The [2024 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/851438188/202523219349314572/full) reports $3,047,162 expenses and $1,628,879 revenue, with $4,318,400 unrestricted and $845,879 restricted net assets. Spending is $2,833,521 program, $150,595 management and $63,046 fundraising. [Schedule R](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349314572/IRS990ScheduleR) identifies shared employees with the c4; [Schedule D](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349314572/IRS990ScheduleD) records $386,898 due to a related party. Original [2022](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/851438188/202410339349301631/full) and [2023](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/851438188/202403189349309890/full) returns check cash accounting, while 2024 checks accrual. The displayed historical series is therefore not a clean three-year mean. A deficit supports asking about future capacity, but neither it nor reserves establishes the effect of a marginal gift. Construction capital, public infrastructure and costs to other advocates are outside the recipient denominator and must be disclosed in any future societal comparison.

Fresh checks of all three original returns confirm no separately netted event or inventory costs. The 2024 accrual versus 2022–23 cash distinction remains; no synthetic comparable mean is produced. The 2024 and 2023 Schedule D expense-reconciliation sections are blank, not evidence of zero donated services; the 2022 Schedule D endpoint was unavailable. Unrecognized shared or volunteer resources remain a cost limitation. The c3-specific source perimeter is retained.

what: Transportation Alternatives organizes for safer walking, cycling and transit across New York City.
This report includes its entire recipient, including Families for Safe Streets, research, membership and events.
Safer streets could avert serious injuries, but this review cannot establish the health return from an additional unrestricted gift.
strengths: Current campaigns organize around identifiable street-design decisions.
Original audits and tax reconciliations recover separately netted event costs.
The injury mechanism is more direct than assigning health value to petitions or cycling counts.

sections.what: Transportation Alternatives Inc., EIN 51-0186015, combines advocacy, organizing, research, membership and events. Families for Safe Streets is inside this recipient, not a second charity credited independently. Current work includes Central Harlem protected lanes, connected Brooklyn and Queens networks, speed-limit implementation and transit access. An ordinary gift supports this mixed portfolio, not a guaranteed lane project. [Current campaigns](https://transalt.org/citywide-campaigns) [Central Harlem proposal](https://transalt.org/citywide-campaigns/central-harlem-bikeway)
sections.monitoring:
Measure additional or accelerated implementation, collision risk and finite health, rather than campaign participation. NYC DOT's 2005–2018 evaluation reports an 18.1% before/after reduction in killed-or-severely-injured road users across 146 protected-bike-lane treatments and 36.7 centerline miles. Selection of dangerous corridors, regression to the mean and concurrent changes matter; the association is not a randomized causal contrast or an estimate of TA's contribution. A historical scenario halves the association, but this does not establish donation-driven implementation. The 31st Street proposal reports 26 people killed or severely injured during 2021–2025, giving 5.2 annual events as a selected high-risk corridor anchor, not a representative mean for TA's campaigns. [DOT evaluation](https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/downloads/pdf/safety-treatment-evaluation-2005-2018.pdf) [31st Street proposal](https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/html/pr2026/nyc-dot-redesign-of-31st-st-in-astoria-queens.shtml)

A useful recipient disclosure would list proposed, unsuccessful and implemented campaigns, prior city commitments, implementation dates, funding constraints and matched safety trends. Citywide improvements or income-group trends cannot identify TA's contribution. [DOT equity analysis](https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/html/pr2025/vision-zero-report-street-redesign.shtml)
sections.qualitative:
Protected street design has a plausible injury pathway, while public agencies retain legal, engineering and spending authority. Existing city projects, elected officials, other advocates and community demand remain in the counterfactual. Current Central Harlem organizing demonstrates an active opportunity, not a measured probability of success. The model represents four corridor-equivalent opportunities over an annual portfolio cycle, not four observed additional projects or credit for 31st Street itself.

The denominator includes only residents of the official 22-county New York–Newark–Jersey City MSA. A 95% resident share of the modeled injury benefit is an explicit judgment: city streets also serve tourists and commuters from outside this MSA. All five city boroughs are within scope; headquarters location alone is not the allocation method.
sections.cost:
The current cost per ten additional MSA-resident QALYs from an unrestricted gift is not established. Transportation Alternatives campaigns for safety improvements, but no source identifies how many additional corridor changes a gift causes, its share of a coalition's contribution, or the health effects of those changes.

The earlier $71.4 million per ten QALYs calculation remains below as a historical conditional diagnostic, not a measured central estimate or donor recommendation. It charged the full $5,186,682 annual recognized recipient expense to one street-injury pathway and assumed four corridor equivalents, 5.2 serious/fatal events per year from one selected street, 18.1% before/after injury association, 50% transfer, 25% incremental coalition effect, 30% TA share and 50% donation response. The implementation and attribution terms are not calibrated by those sources. Multiplying uncertain factors produces reproducible arithmetic, not a reliable unrestricted-gift estimate.

The historical exercise assigns finite health gains to avoided fatal and serious injuries, with explicit duration, utility and discounting choices; it does not value physical activity, air quality, accessibility, crash-family support, travel changes or harms. A separate illustrative public-cost case is not a construction quote. Zero implementation, donor substitution and adverse effects remain possible. A new central estimate would require a gift-responsive project pipeline, matched safety outcomes, defensible MSA residency and complete resource costs.
sections.funding:
March-ending audited expenses are $4,447,542 in FY2023, $5,135,283 in FY2024 and $5,186,682 in FY2025. Each reconciles to the original Form 990 expense plus separately netted fundraising costs of $67,853, $141,953 and $83,095 respectively. FY2024 expense includes a $206,481 employee-retention credit that reduced payroll-tax expense, so the three-year accounting mean is not an unadjusted recurring resource-cost baseline. No additional donated-service adjustment is reported in Schedule D; unrecognized volunteer opportunity costs remain outside this series. [FY2025 audit, Note 15](https://transalt.org/s/FY25-Transportation-Alternatives-Inc-Financial-Statement-FINAL-1.pdf) [FY2024/2023 audit](https://transalt.org/s/Transportation-Alternatives-Inc-24-AUD-FINAL.pdf)

FY2025 support and revenue were $4,335,312 and ending net assets $3,270,676, of which $523,106 were restricted. The unrestricted decline was $426,460; the full $851,370 decline is not an unrestricted cash need. The board designated $1 million as a stability reserve. Two donors supplied about one-quarter of FY2025 support and revenue. These facts support asking about funding resilience but do not identify gift additionality. The directory's displayed FY2025 period conflicts with the original audit: the report uses the year ended March 31, 2025, not March 2026. [Financial directory](https://transalt.org/financials) [Donation route](https://transalt.org/donate)

Expense appendix: FY2025 recognized costs comprise $4,317,855 program services, $371,200 management/general and $497,627 fundraising. The three-year recognized accounting mean is $4,923,169; reversing the one-off FY2024 payroll-tax credit for a sensitivity would make the mean $4,991,996, not change audited expense. Neither series includes all public or volunteer opportunity cost. Schedule D establishes the tax-return reconciliations.

what: OnPoint NYC provides supervised overdose-prevention spaces in East Harlem and Washington Heights.

sections.what:
OnPoint NYC formed from New York Harm Reduction Educators and Washington Heights Corner Project in 2022. This report uses On Point NYC Inc., EIN 20-8672015, and its entire reported resource envelope. It includes overdose prevention, clinical and mental-health care, syringe services, outreach and basic-needs support. The current service page explicitly includes Bronx outreach alongside the two Manhattan centers. Families or predecessor names do not receive separate overlapping credit. [History](https://onpointnyc.org/history/) [Services](https://onpointnyc.org/)

The ordinary donation route does not promise an exclusive OPC purchase. The model therefore retains all recipient costs and quantifies only a clinically meaningful overdose-survival component. [Donate](https://onpointnyc.org/donate/)
sections.monitoring:
The third-year report covers November 30,2023 to November 29,2024, despite its 2025 navigation label. It lists 434 purported fatal overdoses prevented; this review treats these as reported intervention events, not independently demonstrated deaths averted. The model assumes that annual event scale remains a usable planning anchor with FY 2025 costs; a cumulative 2,000-event milestone in May 2026 is not annualized. [Third-year report](https://onpointnyc.org/year-three-impact-report/) [Current milestone](https://onpointnyc.org/2000-overdose-interventions/)

The original first-two-month evaluation distinguishes naloxone, oxygen, monitoring and stimulant-related supportive interventions, and has no untreated comparison group. These categories have different untreated lethality. Ask for distinct intervention recipients, repeat events, severity, alternative rescue, out-of-site deaths and longitudinal survival. [Initial evaluation](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2794323)

The newly retrieved original PDF locates enrollment/utilization on printed pages 14–15, wraparound 16–17, buprenorphine 18, wound care 19, interventions 22–24 and EMS 30–31. Activity counts do not establish counterfactual treatment success. Unique OPC users are not unique overdose-intervention recipients. The PDF's EMS percentage is per OPC visit, unlike the website highlight's intervention denominator. [Original report](https://onpointnyc.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/OnPoint-NYC-Impact-Report-Year-3-web.pdf)
sections.qualitative:
A Vancouver model estimated 8.4–50.9 potentially averted deaths among 1,004 recorded overdose events, depending strongly on assumed community nonfatal overdose incidence. Of those events, 453 met its potentially fatal definition, based on naloxone, emergency calling or ambulance use. The 8.4–50.9 estimate is modeled deaths across the 1,004-event program, not measured deaths or the fatality rate of its 453 severe events. That historical, pre-fentanyl model is context for our 2% untreated-lethality judgment, not a modern New York causal rate. A further 50% transfer/alternative-rescue factor reflects contemporary community naloxone, emergency response and differences in severity. [Original mortality model](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18839040/)

A later Vancouver cohort found lower adjusted all-cause mortality among frequent users, but residual confounding and nonrandom selection limit causal transfer. Ontario's controlled interrupted time-series did not identify a statistically significant aggregate mortality improvement. Neither result warrants assigning all city overdose trends to OnPoint. Local difference-in-differences crime research provides reassurance against a simple crime-increase claim, not QALYs or proof that every possible adverse effect is absent. [Cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31770391/) [Ontario study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39104058/) [NYC crime study](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2811766)

Alternative access includes city naloxone, drug checking and vending machines, and SSPs such as Housing Works, Harlem United, VOCAL and Alliance for Positive Change. These establish that alternative services exist, not that any particular participant receives them. Clinical, infection, wound care, treatment, warmth/respite and mental-health pathways remain unpriced pending attributable health coefficients; no overlapping mortality award is added. Possible precipitated withdrawal, delayed emergency escalation, increased risky consumption or displacement, and participant cash/time burdens remain unresolved. Ontario's aggregate null cannot establish zero individual benefit; population dilution and possible slowing of mortality increase matter. [Alternative access](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/alcohol-and-drug-use-services.page)
sections.cost:
The beta conditional reference keeps the alpha health assumptions and adds an explicitly hypothetical signed household consumption branch: 4.204 health QALYs plus 1.301 income-equivalent healthy years equals 5.505 welfare-equivalent healthy years. At $16,203,740 annual recognized expense, cost is about $29.4 million per 10 combined equivalent years. Health-only remains $38.5 million per 10 QALYs. The Coefficient Giving-inspired log crosswalk is a welfare comparison, not measured clinical QALYs or an observed OnPoint return.

The 434 annual intervention events are assigned to 217 distinct people by judgment, or two events each. A 2% lethal-risk input and 50% contemporary transfer factor imply a 0.02 annual hazard reduction during one funded year. Counterfactual mortality hazard is 0.08 and intervention hazard 0.06 during that year. Both groups subsequently face 0.08, so later overdose and competing mortality erode the survival difference. We integrate their survival difference for at most ten years at utility 0.7 and a 3% discount rate. Each person has one survival trajectory: repeated rescue cannot create multiple lifetime awards.

Only 25% of this proportional continuation-scale benefit is attributed to an ordinary gift after public support, reserves and replacement donors; that is an explicit funding-response prior, not an observed budget elasticity. A 98% MSA-resident share is also judgment, acknowledging nonlocal users without assuming city-site location proves residency. The boundary is the official 22-county MSA, not the wider CSA.

Broad alternatives change severity, unique-person clustering, funding response, competing mortality and horizon. Zero and harmful outcomes remain possible. A 10% extra-resource stress tests unrecognized volunteer and partner resources; it is not a measured add-on. Recognized donated medication is already in the financial envelope and is not added twice. Future medical spending and broader social opportunity costs are unpriced.

Household reference: two disjoint common-alive cohorts, 100 additional households gaining $300 annual net purchasing power and 100 other households bearing $30 annual net cash burden, at $10,000 baseline annual household consumption/resources. All last one year, with 98% MSA allocation and 3% discounting. The gain count assumes 400 eligible exposures times 25% donor response, a prior not calibrated from activity counts. These are expected common-alive household person-year exposures, excluding income obtained only because someone survives. For a household with both gains and costs, net them before applying the log; the two modeled cohorts are disjoint. No earnings multiplier, extra-survivor consumption credit or positive-overlap haircut is used.

Food/hygiene services can release purchasing power when they replace paid purchases, but replacing another free provider releases none. Benefits case management can increase resources, but no verified net awards, household baseline or persistence was found, so earnings and benefit awards remain unpriced. Beneficiary gains are net of their own cash burdens; the disjoint burden-only cohort includes households with no gain. The positive gain and negative burden stay unchanged at clinical null. A separate complete funding-replacement case has no additional service exposure and no induced burden. Negative losses have full causal and independent weight.

Taxpayer EMS savings are neither household consumption nor returned donor cash. The PDF's $13 million claim applies an assumed $30,000 per avoided emergency response, not a measured counterfactual saving; no savings are subtracted from the cost envelope.10% additional partner-resource stress adds cost. Cash-only operating expense and participant-time opportunity cost remain unknown. Alpha health low/high alternatives remain intact in the embedded historical diagnostic. New clinical-null, financial-only, adverse, unknown, burden-only, delay, consumption and residence cases are conditional sensitivity cases, not confidence bounds.

Independent share=1 is a conditional structural choice because the health branch values only finite survival and does not also assign mental-health or stability utility. Common-alive basic-needs households are a service cohort, not selected rescue survivors. No measured absence of overlap is claimed. Low/high donor-response cases jointly scale clinical capacity and household exposure to 10%/50%; per-exposed-household negative cash loss retains full weight. Clinical-null switches lethality only, preserving service exposure and signed consumption.
sections.funding:
Original June-ending accrual returns and Schedule D reconciliations report $11,980,572 in FY 2023, $15,432,498 in FY 2024 and $16,203,740 in FY 2025. The FY 2023 amended return supersedes its earlier filing and explicitly aligns with completed audited statements. The three returns report no separately netted fundraising, gaming or inventory expense, and no donated-service addback in Schedule D. FY 2025 Schedule M reports $336,016 in donated drugs/medical supplies, already recognized as property rather than an additional service addback. We flag FY 2023 as noncomparable pending confirmation of the exact merger-period perimeter rather than display an artificial three-year mean. [FY 2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202621359349304162/IRS990) [FY 2023 amendment](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202423619349300202/IRS990 ScheduleO)

FY 2025 revenue was $19,268,609, including $18,181,362 government grants, and ending net assets were $18,520,698; cash was $6,815,648 and grants receivable $9,424,280. Net assets are not all spendable cash. Current city reporting explicitly funds sustained/expanded wraparound hours and services and names OnPoint in infrastructure investments. An ordinary donor cannot receive credit for all these appropriated services. [Current settlement report](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/basas/opioid-settlement-funds-report-06032026.pdf)

The official financial directory still emphasizes older documents, so this review uses more recent original IRS filings. No verified current unfunded opening or dollar-specific capacity promise was assumed. [Financial directory](https://onpointnyc.org/financials/)

Expense appendix: FY 2025 Form 990 functional costs are $14,411,565 program services, $1,664,638 management/general and $127,537 fundraising, totaling $16,203,740. The earlier amended original amount is retained, but no comparable three-year average is accepted until the merger-period perimeter is resolved.

October 5 beta verification: the IRS-derived directory still identifies On Point NYC Inc., EIN 20-8672015, and corroborates FY 2025 expense $16,203,740, revenue $19,268,609 and net assets $18,520,698. Original Form 990, schedules and XML returned security blocks. Detailed government grants, cash, receivable, functional expenses and donated-property reconciliation above remain inherited from the September 14 alpha primary checks, not freshly reverified. Own financial directory still links 2022 WHCP and 2020–21 audits. [Current extraction](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/208672015)

Recognized accrual cost is a starting full-recipient resource envelope, not measured cash outlay. The $336,016 noncash-property value cannot simply be subtracted to establish cash expense without inventory and expense matching. Volunteer services, outside clinical resources and participant time could increase total cost; only the explicit 10% resource case prices omitted partner resources. FY 26 city quarterly participants overlap, so they are not summed into unique annual reach. Unfunded hours, incremental staffing and ordinary-gift response remain unverified.

model.costScope: Whole merged recipient annual recognized cost; overdose-survival component only. Unpriced clinical, infection, psychosocial and public effects prevent a whole-portfolio claim. Household signed consumption is separately in the welfare denominator; editionQalys is health-only.
model.geographicAttribution: g=.98 is a subjective share of modeled unique participants who reside in the official22-county MSA. All sites/known outreach are within the MSA but residence records were unavailable.
model.formula: d=ln(1.03); delta=(E/U)*l*a; lambda1=m-delta>=0; F(k,t)=(1-exp(-k*t))/k. H=U*u*[F(lambda1+d,1)-F(m+d,1)+(exp(-lambda1)-exp(-m))*exp(-d)*F(m+d,T-1)]; Qall=b*H-h; QNYC=g*Qall; Price10=10*C/QNYC if positive. The event-level risk input is converted to an annual hazard decrement by the explicit linear approximation delta=(E/U)*l*a, not asserted to be an exact probability-to-hazard identity.; I=.5*sum_j[N_j*g_j*sum_t((1+r)^(-delay-t))*ln(1+netConsumptionChange_j/baselineConsumption_j)]; W=editionQalys+I. Every net change is household-specific before log; disjoint cohorts only.
model.counterfactual: Public grants, opioid settlement support, ordinary community naloxone/EMS and existing staffing continue. The intervention changes one year's mortality hazard, not all subsequent risk; equal post-year-one hazards impose recurrence and competing mortality.
model.attribution: l is a historical-context-informed lethality prior, a a contemporary transfer/rescue factor, b financial additionality. No separate lives-saved multiplier, rescue-lifetime sum, or additional portfolio mortality claim.
model.uncertainty: Weak-confidence partial-health best estimate. report.program: Integrated harm reduction, overdose prevention and low-barrier health support

what: OnPoint NYC combines overdose prevention with low-barrier clinical, harm-reduction and basic-needs services.
We assess the merged recipient rather than treating its overdose rooms as the whole organization.
Our weak-confidence estimate is about $38.5 million per 10 MSA-resident QALYs for a finite overdose-survival component, with other health pathways unpriced.
strengths: Immediate monitored care addresses an acute and preventable risk.
Current city records confirm continued local delivery and public support.
Original returns expose whole-recipient costs and donated medical property.
reservations: Intervention counts are not observed lives saved.
The unique-person distribution, counterfactual lethality and marginal funding response are judgment-based.
Substantial public funding and other services make a single-component price an incomplete portfolio assessment.

sections.what:
OnPoint NYC formed from New York Harm Reduction Educators and Washington Heights Corner Project in 2022. This report uses On Point NYC Inc., EIN 20-8672015, and its entire reported resource envelope. It includes overdose prevention, clinical and mental-health care, syringe services, outreach and basic-needs support. The current service page explicitly includes Bronx outreach alongside the two Manhattan centers. Families or predecessor names do not receive separate overlapping credit. [History](https://onpointnyc.org/history/) [Services](https://onpointnyc.org/)

The ordinary donation route does not promise an exclusive OPC purchase. The model therefore retains all recipient costs and quantifies only a clinically meaningful overdose-survival component. [Donate](https://onpointnyc.org/donate/)
sections.monitoring:
The third-year report covers November 30,2023 to November 29,2024, despite its 2025 navigation label. It lists 434 purported fatal overdoses prevented; this review treats these as reported intervention events, not independently demonstrated deaths averted. The model assumes that annual event scale remains a usable planning anchor with FY2025 costs; a cumulative 2,000-event milestone in May 2026 is not annualized. [Third-year report](https://onpointnyc.org/year-three-impact-report/) [Current milestone](https://onpointnyc.org/2000-overdose-interventions/)

The original first-two-month evaluation distinguishes naloxone, oxygen, monitoring and stimulant-related supportive interventions, and has no untreated comparison group. These categories have different untreated lethality. Ask for distinct intervention recipients, repeat events, severity, alternative rescue, out-of-site deaths and longitudinal survival. [Initial evaluation](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2794323)
sections.qualitative:
A Vancouver model estimated 8.4–50.9 potentially averted deaths among 1,004 recorded overdose events, depending strongly on assumed community nonfatal overdose incidence. Of those events, 453 met its potentially fatal definition, based on naloxone, emergency calling or ambulance use. The 8.4–50.9 estimate is modeled deaths across the 1,004-event program, not measured deaths or the fatality rate of its 453 severe events. That historical, pre-fentanyl model is context for our 2% untreated-lethality judgment, not a modern New York causal rate. A further 50% transfer/alternative-rescue factor reflects contemporary community naloxone, emergency response and differences in severity. [Original mortality model](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18839040/)

A later Vancouver cohort found lower adjusted all-cause mortality among frequent users, but residual confounding and nonrandom selection limit causal transfer. Ontario's controlled interrupted time-series did not identify a statistically significant aggregate mortality improvement. Neither result warrants assigning all city overdose trends to OnPoint. Local difference-in-differences crime research provides reassurance against a simple crime-increase claim, not QALYs or proof that every possible adverse effect is absent. [Cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31770391/) [Ontario study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39104058/) [NYC crime study](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2811766)
sections.cost:
The conditional best estimate is $38.5 million per 10 official-MSA QALYs: about 4.204 QALYs against $16,203,740 annual recipient cost. This is an overdose-survival price with other health pathways left unpriced, not a measured whole-portfolio return or a proven lower bound.

The 434 annual intervention events are assigned to 217 distinct people by judgment, or two events each. A 2% lethal-risk input and 50% contemporary transfer factor imply a 0.02 annual hazard reduction during one funded year. Counterfactual mortality hazard is 0.08 and intervention hazard 0.06 during that year. Both groups subsequently face 0.08, so later overdose and competing mortality erode the survival difference. We integrate their survival difference for at most ten years at utility 0.7 and a 3% discount rate. Each person has one survival trajectory: repeated rescue cannot create multiple lifetime awards.

Only 25% of this proportional continuation-scale benefit is attributed to an ordinary gift after public support, reserves and replacement donors; that is an explicit funding-response prior, not an observed budget elasticity. A 98% MSA-resident share is also judgment, acknowledging nonlocal users without assuming city-site location proves residency. The boundary is the official 22-county MSA, not the wider CSA.

Broad alternatives change severity, unique-person clustering, funding response, competing mortality and horizon. Zero and harmful outcomes remain possible. A 10% extra-resource stress tests unrecognized volunteer and partner resources; it is not a measured add-on. Recognized donated medication is already in the financial envelope and is not added twice. Future medical spending and broader social opportunity costs are unpriced.
sections.funding:
Original June-ending accrual returns and Schedule D reconciliations report $11,980,572 in FY2023, $15,432,498 in FY2024 and $16,203,740 in FY2025. The FY2023 amended return supersedes its earlier filing and explicitly aligns with completed audited statements. The three returns report no separately netted fundraising, gaming or inventory expense, and no donated-service addback in Schedule D. FY2025 Schedule M reports $336,016 in donated drugs/medical supplies, already recognized as property rather than an additional service addback. We flag FY2023 as noncomparable pending confirmation of the exact merger-period perimeter rather than display an artificial three-year mean. [FY2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202621359349304162/IRS990) [FY2023 amendment](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202423619349300202/IRS990ScheduleO)

FY2025 revenue was $19,268,609, including $18,181,362 government grants, and ending net assets were $18,520,698; cash was $6,815,648 and grants receivable $9,424,280. Net assets are not all spendable cash. Current city reporting explicitly funds sustained/expanded wraparound hours and services and names OnPoint in infrastructure investments. An ordinary donor cannot receive credit for all these appropriated services. [Current settlement report](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/basas/opioid-settlement-funds-report-06032026.pdf)

The official financial directory still emphasizes older documents, so this review uses more recent original IRS filings. No verified current unfunded opening or dollar-specific capacity promise was assumed. [Financial directory](https://onpointnyc.org/financials/)

Expense appendix: FY2025 Form 990 functional costs are $14,411,565 program services, $1,664,638 management/general and $127,537 fundraising, totaling $16,203,740. The earlier amended original amount is retained, but no comparable three-year average is accepted until the merger-period perimeter is resolved.

reports.program: Free primary and specialty care for working uninsured Bergen County adults

acceptance.evidence: docs/geography-discovery/bvmi-nyc-independent-acceptance-2026-10-02.md — corrected finite conditional model accepted; no verified marginal donation capacity.

what: BVMI provides free primary, chronic-condition and mental-health care to uninsured adults in working households in Bergen County, within the NYC metropolitan area.
Clinicians offer consultations, testing, treatment and referrals, with a dedicated counseling service.
Its Garfield center opened in June 2026, extending access alongside its existing services.
strengths: Free care can improve symptoms and functioning for people without equivalent timely treatment.
Working-household eligibility and annual Bergen residency checks define whom the program serves more clearly than visit counts alone.
Three years of original audited accounts and an identifiable counseling cohort support an inspectable health-and-income comparison.
reservations: The conditional estimate is about $29.4M per better life; patient response, otherwise-paid care and recovery earnings are judgments, not measured local causal effects.
The 2025 patient and spending baseline predates the new center; committed funding, volunteers and recruitment may constrain what another donation adds.
Household costs can offset savings and earnings, while long-term prevention, outside care and current donor-sensitive capacity remain incompletely known.

sections.what:
Bergen Volunteer Medical Initiative Inc., EIN 20-2633437, is the entire recipient in scope. It provides primary, chronic and urgent care, mental-health support and outside specialist/diagnostic referrals. [Eligibility](https://www.bvmi.org/services/) requires an uninsured adult living in Bergen County, a working household and income up to 250% of the federal poverty level; residency and income documentation are checked annually. Bergen County belongs to the official New York–Newark–Jersey City MSA. This supports a central local patient-health share of one, with a 98% sensitivity for exceptions or subsequent moves; indirect benefits do not automatically inherit that allocation.

The [June 2026 newsletter](https://www.bvmi.org/june-2026-pulse/) dates Garfield’s first patients to June 17, 2026. The current site lists Wednesday and Thursday clinic hours. Earlier campaign plans for a 2025 opening and later three-to-five-day service are not observed capacity. The 2025 annual patient/cost baseline therefore predates Garfield operations. The model is a continuation-scale normalization, not a verified 2026 operating budget or a claim that another donor opens the clinic.
sections.monitoring:
The [2025 impact report](https://www.bvmi.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/BVMI-Impact-Report-2025.pdf) reports 1,026 patients and 9,725 visits, with 25% of visits by telehealth. The patient count, not repeated visits, anchors the main model. Diabetes and hypertension control rates of 60% and 65% are compared with unmatched national benchmarks, not an untreated local group; condition denominators, baseline severity and follow-up retention are not supplied. The comparison of 12 ER visits per 100 patients with 35 among uninsured people nationally does not identify prevented visits. The claimed hospital savings are not subtracted from cost.

The [June update](https://www.bvmi.org/june-2026-pulse/) also reports 156 counseling patients in 2025 after mental-health visits grew following a 2023 practitioner hire. This cohort overlaps the total 1,026 and may overlap diabetes/chronic care. It is not added as a new population. No local PHQ-9 trajectory, utility, completion or treatment-free comparator was found. Needed measures are baseline severity, retained effective care, unsuccessful referrals, alternative care received and voluntary patient-health follow-up. Accepting new patients is not proof of an unfunded waitlist.

The October recheck distinguishes 1,026 unique reported patients from 9,725 visits and 156 counseling patients. Counseling is modeled as a subset, not another cohort; a patient-level join was unavailable. Blood-pressure/diabetes control benchmarks and claimed ER savings are not causal effects or household cash. Useful monitoring would link unique patients and households to completion, other available care, symptoms, actual payments, net earnings and incremental staffing.
sections.qualitative:
There is a plausible route from continuous free care to symptom relief and prevention. But the [Oregon randomized insurance experiment](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23635051/) found depression and financial-protection improvements without significant measured blood-pressure or glycated-hemoglobin improvement over two years. Insurance access differs from BVMI’s care, so it is a mechanism check, not its causal yield.

A closer [free-clinic randomized study](https://ijic.org/articles/5421/files/submission/proof/5421-1-20945-1-10-20201124.pdf) tested enhanced integrated behavioral care against usual care in uninsured low-income Texas patients. It found an adjusted 1.67-point PHQ-9 advantage at 12 months but no significant physical-health endpoint advantage. Of 585 randomized participants, 370 completed that follow-up. Baseline depression imbalance, attrition, provider overlap and the different service setting limit transfer. PHQ-9 points are not QALYs, and the trial does not establish BVMI’s treatment quality, persistence or gift response.

The aggregate central prior remains explicitly subjective: 25% of genuinely additional patient-equivalents improve by 0.1 utility for six months, minus 0.0005 QALYs per patient-equivalent for care burdens. The health area is finite, within one year, and includes within-period fade and competing-risk effects in the judgment; no lifelong prevention award is made. A separate mental-health-only case uses the 156 counseling patients with an assumed mean 0.02 utility gain for six months. It replaces rather than adds to the aggregate prior. Neither utility choice is a measured trial conversion. Zero and adverse effects remain possible; longer-term preventive and financial-security effects remain unknown rather than worthless.

The recalibration treats financial protection and symptom improvement as different pathways. The trial and insurance evidence motivate a credible but uncertain mechanism, not a local causal coefficient. Household savings require otherwise-paid care; newly incurred access and prescription costs are retained. Finite health and common-alive earnings are separately timed, and absent benefits are distinguished from missing measurements.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter estimates about **$29.4 million per better life** for this conditional comparison of BVMI support, including health and signed household resources. The program is promising because it makes primary and mental-health care accessible without clinic charges, but its local effect and next-dollar capacity are not measured. The estimate describes selected pathways, not a priced donation opportunity or a complete portfolio return.

**What does support buy?** A $10,000 normalization corresponds to **1.15 offered patient-equivalents**, **0.92 completed care-equivalents**, and **0.46 people receiving additional effective care** in this model. That is approximately $21,671 of support per additional care-equivalent, not the observed price of a patient slot. Annual patients, 1,026, are observed; funding response 40%, completion 80%, and the counterfactual mix are judgments. We assume 20% would otherwise buy equivalent care, 30% obtain equivalent free care, and 50% lack timely equivalent care. Purchasers and other-free-care patients do not receive another clinical benefit from identical treatment. Independent acquisition costs can still occur.

**Cost boundary.** Original 2025 functional expenses are $4,513,270, including $688,451 recognized donated services, $267,377 donated goods and $119,967 event direct-benefit costs. The activities statement reports $4,393,303 after netting event costs; these are not two additive expense totals. Removing recognized donated inputs gives a **$3,557,442 cash-like accrual support proxy**. It still includes depreciation and is not cash flow or a marginal quote. We retain a separate gross institutional allocation, including those complements and a judged $100 outside-resource allowance per offer. This companion costs $12,802 per $10,000 normalization and yields about **$37.6M per better life**. Donated goods’ wholesale value and specialized clinicians’ market-hourly value are not automatically household savings, and unrecognized volunteer hours are not added again.

**From care to health.** The 156 counseling patients are assumed to be a subset of the 1,026 annual patients. We assign them only a mental-health pathway and the remaining 870 only a physical-health pathway; physical needs of counseling patients remain unquantified rather than double credited. Among additional completions, 20% of the physical group gain 0.05 utility for nine months; 50% of the counseling group gain 0.035 for one year. These are finite symptom/function judgments, not measured BVMI QALYs or a conversion from depression-score points. Treatment harm of 0.0007 healthy years per additional completion and offer harm of 0.00002 per offer are separately charged, with a half-year discount convention. The result is **0.003760 healthy years per $10,000**, or **$26.6M per ten health years** without household resources. No mortality or permanent life-extension stream is inserted.

The original integrated-care trial compared enhanced care with usual free care, with attrition, baseline imbalance and a predominantly unemployed population. It supports a counseling mechanism but does not identify BVMI utility, response, wages or donation coefficients. The Oregon insurance experiment found reduced depression and financial strain but no significant two-year blood-pressure/HbA1c improvement; its authors also report no significant employment or earnings effect. Insurance differs from direct free-clinic care. Neither result is transplanted as a local coefficient; smaller, null and adverse pathways remain in the scenarios.

**Household money and earnings.** We use the [published income-to-health comparison](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/): one-half the logarithm of the household-resource ratio. This is welfare equivalence, not clinical QALYs. A $30,000 annual disposable household baseline is a judgment, not an eligibility threshold or measured distribution. Only otherwise-purchasing patients who complete equivalent care receive a judged $350 avoided actual payment; they receive no additional clinical access credit. Patients who otherwise obtain free care receive no purchase saving.

All induced offers incur a judged $15 incremental travel, acquisition or missed-pay cost. Completed purchasers and other-free-care patients incur another $20 relative to their alternatives; unmet-care completions incur $90. Forty percent of that latter group fill a newly obtained prescription costing $150 net of assistance. These are amounts added relative to no gift, not all observed travel or nominal medical bills. Recognized donated supplies do not establish that every prescription would be free. Prescription-filled and unfilled states are valued separately before applying the logarithm, rather than logging an average cash amount.

Clinical responders alive in both worlds may recover net earnings: worker share 60%, $600 annual gain for half a year, first receipt at one year. Working-household eligibility does not mean each patient works, and these quantities remain uncertain. Positive earnings receive a 50% independence adjustment for overlap with function/utility; negative pay is charged in full. No saved-life lifetime wages, employer revenue, volunteer leisure or public-payer ER savings are added. Cash changes are applied first and pay valued against the resulting household baseline. A 0.9 household-per-patient approximation preserves aggregate dollars while reducing duplicate household baselines; it does not recover family covariance.

Net cash is **−$30.69 present value per $10,000** and common-alive net pay **+$19.81**, before the welfare-overlap adjustment. Cash-equivalent welfare is −0.000522 years and earnings-equivalent welfare +0.000164: signed resources total **−0.000358 years**. Together with clinical health, that gives **0.003403 combined years**, producing the $29.4M headline. Household costs remain in the denominator as welfare losses, not as another donor cash charge. No-pay, negative-pay, high-cost, failed-offer and matched-free-alternative cases test the conclusion. A high household-cost case is net adverse despite positive clinical health; it has no favorable dollar-per-life ratio.

**Why the estimate changed.** The preceding clinical-only estimate was **$15.10M** using the full $4,513,270 gross annual expense and a broad patient-response formula. Its complete fifteen scenarios are preserved. On a like gross-resource clinical boundary, the revised estimate is **$34.04M**; the donor-support clinical comparison is $26.59M after separating donated inputs. Disjoint counterfactual cohorts and separately reconsidered finite clinical pathways reduce the modeled health effect; net household burdens then increase the donor-support figure to $29.39M. This is changed modeling, not evidence of organizational deterioration.

**Financial appendix.** Comparable gross annual expenses are $3,817,656 (2023), $4,089,961 (2024), and $4,513,270 (2025). Cash-like accrual proxies after removing recognized donated services and goods are $2,772,431, $3,180,003 and $3,557,442. Audited net assets and restricted grants may support existing plans, but are neither a funding gap nor proof of no need. The patient baseline predates Garfield’s opening. Current gift-sensitive staffing, unique household outcomes and a costed incremental plan are the most important missing inputs.
sections.funding:
Original [2024/2023](https://www.bvmi.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/BVMI-2024-Audited-Financial-Statements.pdf) and [2025/2024](https://www.bvmi.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/BVMI-2025-Audited-Financial-Statements-2025-24.pdf) audits give gross expenses of $3,817,656, $4,089,961 and $4,513,270. Functional totals restore the event direct-benefit amounts netted in the activities statements. The [2024 return](https://www.bvmi.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/2024-BVMI-990-Public.pdf) reconciles its $3,215,204 expense plus $738,382 donated services to audited net expense, then $136,375 event costs produces gross $4,089,961. The cheaper tax figure is not the resource denominator. The latest audit is unmodified, signed April 15, 2026; its control report is not a guarantee of effective controls.

At December 2025, the audit reports $2,126,434 cash and $2,196,966 financial assets available for general expenditure after restrictions, approximately 5.8 months of gross annual expense. Availability includes receivables, not just immediate cash. Restricted net assets are $2,623,487; two donors generated 53% of contributions/private grants, and three supplied 80% of receivables. This is substantial existing support with concentration risk, not proof of either no need or imminent service loss.

The [Russell Berrie Foundation](https://www.russellberriefoundation.org/news/2025/12/15/legacy-grant-fuels-bergen-voluntary-medical-initiatives-expansion-sustainability) announced $1.5 million for expansion and sustainability with a target exceeding 2,000 annual patients by 2029. This is committed support and a target, not another donor’s achievement or current volume. Its scope differs from the older $1.75 million campaign, so subtraction does not reveal a verified $250,000 gap. The [enacted FY2027 state scoresheet](https://pub.njleg.state.nj.us/publications/budget/FY%202027%20Appropriations%20Act%20Scoresheet.pdf), section F page 19, includes $400,000 for BVMI despite a zero governor proposal. Appropriation is not receipt, and contract terms remain needed. Calendar-year 2025 government revenue includes $469,215 federal ARPA and $656,511 state expenditures; the $250,006 FY2026 grant entry is spending-to-date, not its total award.

Donor readiness remains on hold pending current restrictions, available staffing/volunteer capacity, demand and recruitment constraints, a priced marginal plan, and a with/without-gift counterfactual. The Patient Emergency Fund is a possible designated route for procedures or basic access needs, but no current case queue, gap or outcome evidence establishes a recommended tranche. No outreach, application or donation was made.

The 2025 audit and June 2026 opening update confirm an active recipient and existing funded expansion. Restricted assets, donor concentration, grants, accepting patients and volunteer availability do not establish a currently purchasable extra slot. The cash-like accrual allocation is a support comparison, not actual cash expenditure or verified marginal capacity.

model.costScope: Whole-recipient cash-like accrual support excluding recognized donated inputs; donor numerator retained, gross institutional complements separately allocated. Not cash flow, marginal capacity or complete societal cost.
model.geographicAttribution: Bergen residency supports NYC metropolitan attribution1, not city-proper impact. Locality applies once to clinical and signed household flows.
model.formula: Offers=gift/cashLikeCost*patients*funding; completions=offers*completion; new care=completions*(1-purchasers-otherFree). Disjoint mental/physical finite responder utility minus clinical harm; signed household cash states then common-alive pay use the shared logarithmic bridge. Price=10*gift/(health+resources) for known positive total.
model.counterfactual: Otherwise equivalent purchased care, equivalent free/public care and unmet timely care partition recipients. Buyers gain only actual payment savings; identical clinical treatment benefits/harms cancel. No repeated visit outcomes or saved-life lifetime wages.
model.attribution: Funding response and effective completion are separate judgments; observed annual patient cohort is not marginal throughput. Counseling subset receives only its assigned clinical stream; household grouping is approximate, not measured deduplication.
model.uncertainty: Clinical response, utility, duration, capacity, household income/payment/Rx/wage quantities are explicit unmeasured judgments. Unknown placeholders do not imply no effect. Positive-overlap zero welfare does not establish raw pay; negative earnings remain signed. Long-term prevention and wider portfolio effects remain unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: Per10K:1.1536 offers,0.9229 completions,0.4615 additional care,0.0783 physical and0.0351 mental responders;0.003760 health plus−0.000358 resources=0.003403 combined equivalents.

historicalModel.costScope: Full audited gross recognized recipient cost, including donated services/goods and netted event direct-benefit costs. Outside care and other social resources incompletely measured. Annual cost is a normalization, not a requested gift or verified funding tranche.
historicalModel.geographicAttribution: Bergen County residency verified annually by recipient eligibility; central g=1 for modeled patients within official22-county MSA, with .98 sensitivity. No headquarters or population-share shortcut.
historicalModel.formula: Q=N*a*b*(c*u*t-h)*g/(1+d), with N=1026,a=.5,b=.5,c=.25,u=.1,t=.5,h=.0005,g=1,d=.03. One annual cohort only. Price10=10*C/Q only when Q>0. Mental-health-only scenario replaces aggregate N and utility assumptions; it is not added. The denominator (1+d) applies a year-end discount convention to the finite benefit area; it does not imply benefits persist for a full year.
historicalModel.counterfactual: Other free/sliding-scale providers, emergency care, future insurance, volunteer availability, current grants and committed Garfield expansion continue. a removes care replacement; b removes funding replacement; they represent distinct constraints and appear once each.
historicalModel.attribution: Annual patient cohort, not repeated visits. a discounts alternative effective care; b discounts replacement funding and capacity constraints. All clinical priors are finite and uncalibrated. Mental-health cohort overlaps total care and is evaluated separately.
historicalModel.uncertainty: No controlled BVMI utility effect or ordinary-gift elasticity is identified. Source-linked judgments are contextual, not estimated from those sources. Zero, adverse and unknown wider-portfolio outcomes remain; scenarios are not confidence bounds.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: 1026 annual patients and9725 visits in2025;156 counseling patients overlap total. Neither clinical-control benchmarks nor counseling counts demonstrate incremental health.

sections.what: NYLPI, EIN 13-2860703, is the entire recipient. Its FY 2025 return describes disability justice, environmental justice, health justice and pro bono programs. The latter three cannot be removed from costs to make a Health Justice price appear cheaper. Current work includes care access for immigrants, accessibility, crisis-response alternatives and environmental implementation. [Health Justice](https://www.nylpi.org/our-work/health-justice/) [Current portfolio proposals](https://www.nylpi.org/nylpi-offers-proposals-to-advance-disability-and-environmental-justice-in-nyc-via-the-mayors-commission-on-government-efficiency/)
sections.monitoring:
March 2026 testimony reports 85 people receiving comprehensive immigration/health screenings and 60 direct immigration cases in FY 2025. A separate medical-provider count is 44 screenings; these groups may overlap and are not summed. The described release and treatment examples show a plausible mechanism but do not identify average incremental health. We anchor only to 85 screened people, then explicitly model a probability of changed effective care. [Original testimony](https://www.nylpi.org/resource/camilla-samuelsson-testimony-to-the-committees-on-mental-health-and-substance-use-joint-with-the-committee-on-health-and-the-committee-on-disabilities-march-19-2026/)

Request a deduplicated case record linking advocacy to effective care, alternative representation, health trajectory and residence. Clinical evaluations can inform a legal proceeding without changing treatment; representation can protect rights with value outside QALYs. Neither is automatically a clinical success.
sections.qualitative:
The work addresses credible medical barriers, and current training recruits clinicians to identify deficiencies and prepare individualized advocacy. Oregon's randomized coverage experiment illustrates that access can improve mental health without detectable near-term physical-health gains. It is a mechanism check, not a direct NYLPI effect estimate. [Current medical training](https://www.nylpi.org/event-recap-medical-providers-network-training-medical-records-review-2/) [Clinical access evidence](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23635051/)

Commercial waste zones, climate enforcement, accessible transit and disability rights could dominate total health value. Existing laws, city appropriations and other coalition members remain the policy counterfactual. Current submissions establish a role but do not quantify its effect on implementation or resident exposure, so they are described rather than assigned invented emissions or treatment counts. [Current waste implementation work](https://www.nylpi.org/resource/justin-wood-comments-regarding-dsny-proposed-commercial-waste-zones-implementation-rule/)
sections.cost:
The conditional partial-health price is about $409 million per 10 MSA QALYs.

This conditional calculation prices only a medical-legal health component against the entire recipient's annual gross cost. It is not a best estimate of complete portfolio return, a lower bound, or a basis for concluding that NYLPI ranks below direct-service charities. Other policy and disability health is unpriced.

The model starts from 85 annual people screened, assumes 25% obtain a consequential effective-care change, 50% of that work is additional to alternatives, and 50% of proportional capacity responds to an ordinary gift. Conditional health improvement is 0.1 utility for six months, less 0.0005 QALYs of process burden per attributable screened person, discounted 3% at year end. Every clinical and attribution factor is a judgment, not an observed success rate. Benefits stop within one year; no lifelong transplant or detention-release award is inferred from a case narrative.

An 85% MSA-resident share is a weak-confidence judgment for this component only. NYC residents detained outside the boundary can still qualify by residence; nonresident statewide clients cannot. Orange County NY is outside the official 22-county MSA, so a detention facility there is not itself a local-benefit claim. The geography of the whole NYLPI portfolio remains different and unestimated.

A clinical-cost stress adds $5,000 per donor-attributable effective-care case, while a separate 25% recipient-cost stress tests unrecognized pro bono and volunteer resources. These are illustrative, not audited additions. Zero replacement, adverse burden and wide positive alternatives are retained.

what: NYC-EJA coordinates community-led environmental policy campaigns across New York City and the state.
Its work includes heat protection, cleaner transport, energy and land-use decisions.
This estimate prices a conditional heat-policy component against the whole recipient's cost, not the complete portfolio.
strengths: Current campaigns address substantial local health risks.
Original returns reconcile gross expenses to audited expense.
An explicit implementation counterfactual avoids crediting already enacted laws.
reservations: Policy and donor-response probabilities are subjective rather than measured.

sections.what: NYC-EJA is a citywide alliance, not the sum of all member organizations. Its ordinary gift supports coordinating, research and advocacy across environmental issues. Heat protection is one current pathway with a defined local population; cleaner transport, energy and land-use work remain outside this numerical component. [Current campaigns](https://nyc-eja.org/campaigns/extreme-heat-and-air-quality/)
sections.monitoring: The organization describes work on cooling access and implementation. The Council's enacted law requires covered rental sleeping rooms to have qualifying cooling by June 2030, subject to tenant elections and other conditions. Rules, affordability, uptake and enforcement therefore matter more than the existence of the law. Request a campaign-specific baseline, additional households able to use cooling, tenant costs, agency commitments and evidence of NYC-EJA's contribution. [Original law](https://legistar.council.nyc.gov/LegislationDetail.aspx?GUID=156F95BB-CA74-44F3-A07B-A0E54EA0C10F&ID=6788510) The law also has hardship extensions and a separate NYCHA cooling-plan compliance route; the model does not assume universal cooling by 2030.
sections.qualitative:
The current city report estimates approximately 500 annual heat-related deaths, mainly heat-exacerbated mortality rather than directly certified heat deaths. That is a risk envelope, not a count that advocacy can claim. Survival after preventing a heat death can be short because underlying illness is common; the model explicitly limits remaining survival. It does not add a separate pollution mortality estimate that could overlap. [City evidence](https://a816-dohbesp.nyc.gov/IndicatorPublic/data-features/heat-report/)

Congestion pricing already began in January 2025. Existing transit and cooling commitments remain in the counterfactual, while future implementation may still be improved. [Transportation work](https://nyc-eja.org/campaigns/transportation-justice/)
sections.cost:
The conditional heat-component estimate is about $80.4 million per 10 MSA QALYs. It is not an estimate of the entire environmental portfolio or a lower bound on its value.

Three years of whole-recipient expense are charged to a five-year implementation benefit beginning four years from the valuation date. Conditional additional cooling protection reduces the city mortality envelope by 1%; a 25% coalition implementation probability, 20% NYC-EJA attribution and 50% funding response produce 0.125 attributable deaths avoided per year. These are explicit priors, not observed rates. Each avoided death receives at most five years at 0.6 utility with a 20% annual competing-mortality hazard; all outcomes are discounted 3%.

The scenario is deliberately finite: no indefinite continuation, no separate morbidity bonus and no credit for already enacted policy. The higher and lower cases vary the uncertain implementation and survival bridge. Zero funding response and a net one-QALY adverse case are retained. A $1 million added-resource sensitivity represents possible induced public, landlord and household costs; it is not a verified cost estimate. Another stress adds 25% for unrecognized coalition resources. Rental burdens, electricity insecurity and policy displacement could make net effects negative.
sections.funding:
Original annual gross expense is $1,125,024 in 2022, $2,192,165 in 2023 and $2,504,216 in 2024. Each Schedule D reports audited expense equal to Form 990 expense, without donated-service additions; event, gaming, rental-expense and inventory-cost lines are blank. The latest return uses accrual accounting. Its $5,696,887 net assets include $3,429,390 restricted resources, so the full balance is not unrestricted spending capacity. No specific extra campaign commitment for a new gift was verified. [Original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349319307/IRS990)

Schedule L discloses a $120,000 annual rental transaction associated with a board member; this is a governance question, not evidence of impropriety or an additional expense. [Disclosure](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349319307/IRS990ScheduleL)

The city reports that HEAP cooling assistance closed June 5, 2026 with unmet demand. This makes affordability a concrete implementation concern, but does not prove NYC-EJA can secure more funding or that a gift does so. [Current public funding](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/about/press/pr2026/nyc-health-department-releases-report-on-heat-related-deaths.page) [Donate](https://nyc-eja.org/support-donate/)

Expense appendix: FY 2024 functional expense is $2,364,603 program, $94,580 management/general and $45,033 fundraising, totaling $2,504,216. Program expense includes $1,129,170 grants, so recipient grants and member spending must not both be added to this cost basis. The comparable 2022–24 mean is $1,940,468.33. The model projects three years at the latest annual cost, not this historical mean.
