acceptance.evidence: docs/geography-discovery/njhrc-nyc-independent-acceptance-2026-10-02.md — corrected conditional health/resources comparison accepted; not verified donation capacity.

what: NJHRC delivers free harm-reduction supplies through discreet statewide mailing, community distributors and New Brunswick outreach.
It provides overdose-response education and supports community leadership, research and policy advocacy.
Naloxone access aims to help people respond promptly when someone experiences an opioid overdose.
strengths: Peer and confidential delivery can reach people who face barriers to pharmacy or clinical access.
Its historical reporting documents supplies being used in reported reversals, beyond distribution alone.
Original financial filings and identifiable delivery routes make the cost and counterfactual assumptions inspectable.
reservations: The conditional estimate is about $19.8M per better life; unique coverage, additional rescue and local residence are planning judgments, not observed causal effects.
Public supplies and alternative responders can replace some benefits, and current cash-funded expansion capacity is unverified.
Household costs may offset savings and earnings; wider infection-prevention, care and policy effects are not yet quantified.

sections.what: The recipient is NJHRC, EIN 85-4099652, not National Harm Reduction Coalition or NEXT Distro. Ordinary support covers delivery, community education, research and advocacy. New Brunswick outreach is local to the MSA, but mail and community distribution operate statewide. [Portfolio](https://njharmreduction.org/our-work/) [Gift destination](https://actionnetwork.org/fundraising/donate-to-njhrc) The [current access page](https://njharmreduction.org/get-naloxone/) describes free, confidential statewide mailing and prioritization of likely overdose witnesses if supplies are limited. Requests by recipients, community distributors and partners do not identify unique people ultimately protected.
sections.monitoring:
In its [November 20, 2023 announcement](https://njharmreduction.org/sheilahpowell/), NJHRC reported distributing more than 10,000 naloxone doses that had been used in at least 140 overdose reversals during 2023 to that point. These are historical doses and events, not a current full-year unique-person cohort, verified deaths averted or marginal private-donation impact. The same source describes state collaboration and NEXT affiliation. Reporting completeness, repeated victims and victim residence are not disclosed. No current replacement recipient-specific series was verified.

The [state report](https://nj.gov/health/hivstdtb/documents/nj-harm-reduction-centers-biennial-report-2022-2024.pdf) covers a network, not NJHRC alone. Its statewide participant, kit, referral and treatment figures cannot be substituted for NJHRC outputs. The [FY2025 opioid-abatement report](https://www.nj.gov/opioidfunds/documents/reports/AA%20-%20State%202025%20Report.pdf?v=2026-06-04) likewise reports collective harm-reduction expansion, with grant and hiring delays; it does not identify NJHRC's incremental capacity.

The pinned 2023 MSA includes twelve New Jersey counties: Bergen, Essex, Hudson, Hunterdon, Middlesex, Monmouth, Morris, Ocean, Passaic, Somerset, Sussex and Union. New Brunswick is within Middlesex, but statewide mail recipients need not be local. Package destination can differ from the rescued person's residence. The historical g=.65 is unmeasured; neither all New Jersey nor the broader CSA is an acceptable substitute.

The October 2 recalibration rechecked the original 2022–24 returns and selected provider/state HTML. The November 2023 announcement remains a dated dose/event record, not a current full-year unique-victim or causal-death series. The current numeric comparison uses explicit planning coverage and household linkage, rather than treating those records as measured marginal production.
sections.qualitative:
Targeted community access has a plausible causal advantage when pharmacy or emergency access is too late. The Massachusetts interrupted time-series evaluation supports the mechanism but is observational and predates today's drug supply and broad naloxone availability. The contemporary HEALing cluster trial found no statistically significant primary mortality reduction from a bundled community scale-up; its rate ratio was 0.91 with a 0.76–1.09 interval. Neither study supplies NJHRC's marginal rescue rate. [Earlier evaluation](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23372174/) [Randomized counterevidence](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2401177)

Current NJHRC material addresses medetomidine and related risks, showing why naloxone supply alone is not the entire response. No separate infection-prevention or policy mortality benefit is added to this component. [Current work](https://njharmreduction.org/medetomidine/) The HEALing trial evaluated a bundle, and only 38% of selected evidence-based strategies were initiated before its comparison year. The nonsignificant result is relevant uncertainty, not proof that naloxone cannot work. Neither study calibrates this provider's current gift response.

Finite survival modeling avoids assigning a fresh lifetime to every repeated rescue, but it still requires an incremental mortality effect and a relevant surviving population. A reported reversal does not show the person would otherwise have died. Additional infection prevention, wound care, treatment linkage, mental wellbeing and policy effects may matter; referrals alone do not establish completed care. Avoid crediting both an averted death and the same person's future health twice across pathways. Unpriced effects are unknown, and a rescue-only calculation is not a lower bound on whole-recipient benefit.

The current review checked primary indexed abstracts, not full papers. A 2026 exploratory community analysis did not find a significant naloxone-distribution association, while buprenorphine and retention associations were positive. This is relevant counterevidence, not a randomized NJHRC component effect. The clinical, timing, household and geographic coefficients remain declared judgments. [Primary abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42283399/)
sections.cost:
GiveBetter estimates approximately **$19.8 million per better life** for this conditional comparison of NJHRC support, including health and signed household resources. The program is promising because free, confidential distribution can put naloxone in places where timely access matters. The calculation models selected pathways rather than an identified expected return for the whole portfolio or a verified donation offer.

**What does support buy?** A $10,000 normalization corresponds to **2.43 offered coverage opportunities**, **1.94 fulfilled opportunities** and **3.89 planning doses**. We estimate **0.78 opportunities without equivalent pre-event access** and **0.0155 additional timely rescue events**. These are modeled units, not measured purchases or a promised service tranche. The independently chosen annual baseline is 1,200 unique victim-centric coverage opportunities; funding response is 35% and fulfillment 80%. Two doses per fulfilled opportunity are a planning convention. Mailing recipients often are witnesses, not victims: linking recipient, witness, victim and household into one unit is an unmeasured simplifying assumption, not joined administrative records.

**From delivery to additional benefit.** We assume 5% would otherwise purchase equivalent protection, 55% obtain equivalent free protection and 40% lack timely equivalent pre-event access. Purchasers and other-free recipients receive no duplicate clinical benefit from matched protection. Within the unmet group, an 8% probability of at most one unique victim event and a 25% residual timely-response advantage govern additional events. The timing assumption concerns other witnesses or emergency response at the event, rather than applying the same pre-access public alternative twice. Neither the sources nor reported reversals identify these probabilities. Lower reach, higher substitution, funding-null and adverse scenarios remain available.

**From rescue to health.** At a half-year event time, a judged 12% absolute counterfactual survival advantage gives one finite ten-year survival tail, with annual hazard 8%, utility 0.7 and 3% discounting. An additional, disjoint 10% injury-avoidance state receives 0.2 utility for six months among people alive in both worlds. Each victim-centric unit contributes at most one event and one survival tail; repeated doses or reversals are not new lifetimes. Treatment harm of 0.001 healthy years per additional event and independent offer harm of 0.000005 per offer are charged. The result is **0.005161 local healthy years per $10,000**, or **$19.4M per ten health years** before resources. These are declared judgments, not locally measured QALYs or a conversion of an observed mortality association.

**Household resources.** Otherwise-purchasers save a judged $20 actual payment, not donated-stock retail value. Twenty percent of offered households incur a judged $15 incremental travel or lost disposable-pay cost relative to their alternative, including failed offers. Extra common-alive rescue events incur $60 net household medical, transport or family lost-pay costs; this is not a hospital charge or a universal EMS bill. Among common-alive injury-avoided people, 30% receive $400 annualized recovery earnings for a quarter-year. Half of positive earnings welfare is retained to avoid clinical/work overlap; negative earnings are fully debited. Ordinary lifetime wages from merely surviving longer are not added.

Discrete group, fulfillment, acquisition and outcome states are evaluated before logarithms. Cash at the event adjusts the household baseline before recovery-pay welfare is calculated. The inherited Coefficient Giving crosswalk converts signed changes against a judged $20,000 household baseline into health-equivalent welfare units; these are not clinical QALYs. Local discounted raw cash is **−$3.95** and recovery pay **+$0.03** per $10,000 normalization. Cash welfare is **−0.00009876** and earnings welfare **+0.000000368**, so resources are net negative and combined benefit is **0.005063 equivalents**. This changes the health-only $19.4M to the combined **$19.8M**. Household mapping, incidence, baseline, sign and amount remain uncertain, with positive, negative and unavailable alternatives retained.

**Cost and locality.** Original FY2024 expenses are $2,125,515, including $396,000 recognized donated medical supplies. Removing those inputs gives a **$1,729,515 cash-like accrual support proxy**, not cash flow or a marginal quote. Recognized noncash is counted once; its value never becomes household saving. The companion gross institutional allocation is $12,290 per $10,000 cash normalization and gives **$24.3M per better life**, excluding unknown unrecognized inputs. Clinical and resource residence shares are separately judged at 65% in the pinned NYC metropolitan area, not NYC city; equal shares do not identify witness or victim residence.

**What changed?** The old alpha diagnostic was **$10.46M**; the latest beta central was unknown. The new comparison replaces spending-generated reach with an independent physical coverage prior, partitions competing access, uses one event-time survival tail, and includes signed household resources. The full seven-case prior is preserved in history. It is not evidence that observed effectiveness deteriorated. Original filings, dated output reporting and primary abstract evidence constrain claims but do not identify a preferred empirical posterior or current funded capacity.
sections.funding:
The [FY2024 original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349324447/IRS990) reports $2,125,515 total expense: $1,824,131 program, $267,124 management/general and $34,260 fundraising. The $396,000 in-kind supplies are already in Part IX and must be counted once. [Schedule M](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349324447/IRS990ScheduleM) reports one contribution/item entry, not one dose, and leaves its valuation-method cell and explanatory section blank. Quantities, formulations, expiry and acquisition or replacement prices are unverified. Removing this accounting value yields $1,729,515 remaining recognized expense, not verified cash cost. Depreciation and accrual items remain.

The return's Part IV 12a and 12b answer No to separate or consolidated independent audited statements, while Part XII 2b answers Yes to an independent audit. [Schedule D](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349324447/IRS990ScheduleD) has blank audit-reconciliation sections. No original audit was located, so audited total-resource cost is not established; the conflicting answers warrant clarification without speculation about cause. Event, rental and inventory cost lines are blank. The $245,978 operating right-of-use asset and corresponding lease liability are balance-sheet amounts, not additional annual expense. [Schedule O](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523219349324447/IRS990ScheduleO) labels other professional fees but does not allocate expenses among interventions.

FY2024 revenue was $2,233,601, including $1,750,800 government grants; cash was $18,178, grants receivable $188,366 and net assets $262,236. Historical liquidity does not establish a current funding gap. The [ordinary gift route](https://actionnetwork.org/fundraising/donate-to-njhrc) supports supplies, advocacy and leadership; an offer to discuss earmarking is not evidence for a restricted purchase here. No costed additional service tranche or funding-contingent capacity ceiling was verified.

Original [FY2023](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202401809349300715/IRS990) expense is $2,128,588 versus $2,136,736 in FY2024's comparative column. Original [FY2022](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202333199349327823/IRS990) expense is $746,927; its $164,196 Schedule M medical supplies differ from $138,616 Part VIII noncash revenue. The original $171,830 closing net assets also differ from the next return's $214,718 opening balance. These differences remain unresolved; no comparable three-year average is constructed.

As of its [March 2025 announcement](https://www.nj.gov/health/news/2025/approved/20250326a.shtml), New Jersey reported 30 operating harm-reduction sites, 53 authorized sites, free naloxone at over 700 pharmacies and DIRECT distribution to more than 1,400 entities. NJHRC's older seven-center directory is not current capacity evidence. Public alternatives may displace some private-funded provision but do not prove full substitution: trust, travel, stock availability and timing can leave additional access valuable.

The October 2 conditional cost proxy subtracts FY2024 recognized noncash once. It does not resolve audit-answer, comparative-year or donated-stock valuation discrepancies, and does not establish current marginal funding room. Three original annual filings remain available below; an incomparable series is not presented as a verified three-year cash average.

model.costScope: Whole-recipient cash-like accrual support proxy; gross institutional allocation separately retained. Not cashflow, marginal capacity or all societal inputs.
model.geographicAttribution: NYC metro health and household residence shares separately judged0.65; witness/recipient/victim linkage unmeasured. Locality applied once.
model.formula: Offers=gift/cashCost*N*funding; fulfilled=offers*completion; unmet=fulfilled*(1-buyer-free); events=unmet*event*timely. One finite event-time survival/injury benefit minus harm, plus signed household cash/pay state logarithms. Price=10*gift/(local health+local resource equivalents) for known positive total.
model.counterfactual: Equivalent purchased protection, equivalent free pre-access and unmet protection are disjoint; residual event-time responders reduce rescue additionality separately. No repeated-victim lifetimes or ordinary saved-life wages.
model.attribution: Unique victim-centric coverage and one household/state mapping are unmeasured planning assumptions. Public funding response, completion and event-time response are separate judgments, not fitted production coefficients.
model.uncertainty: All nonfinancial clinical, physical reach, response, household and locality quantities are judged. Null, adverse and unknown alternatives retained; no identified whole-portfolio EV or donor capacity.

historicalModel.costScope: Full annual gross recognized recipient expense, including donated supplies once. Not a verified audited resource total or marginal unrestricted-donation cost. All material recipient health pathways are in decision scope, but the historical numerical diagnostics quantify only a conditional overdose-survival pathway.
historicalModel.geographicAttribution: Historical g=.65 is an unmeasured prior, not the beta central. The pinned NYC MSA includes Bergen, Essex, Hudson, Hunterdon, Middlesex, Monmouth, Morris, Ocean, Passaic, Somerset, Sussex and Union in New Jersey. Rescued beneficiary residence, rather than supply delivery location, is required. No whole-state or CSA attribution.
historicalModel.formula: Historical diagnostics only: U=C*f/k; delta=e*t*l; dlog=ln(1+d); F(v,t)=(1-exp(-v*t))/v; H=U*u*[F(m-delta+dlog,1)-F(m+dlog,1)+(exp(-(m-delta))-exp(-m))*exp(-dlog)*F(m+dlog,T-1)]; Qall=b*H-h; QMSA=g*Qall. Cost sensitivities change numerator only. The encounter-level mortality input l is mapped linearly into a hazard decrement delta=e*t*l as an approximation, not an exact probability-to-hazard identity. With h=0 and numeratorCostUSD=C, C cancels from price. Unobserved f/k generates the output denominator; accounting revaluation must not be interpreted as physical added reach.
historicalModel.counterfactual: State naloxone procurement, pharmacy access, other community distributors and emergency response continue. t credits only additional timely rescue beyond those alternatives. An ordinary gift does not buy all donated stock anew.
historicalModel.attribution: f allocates an assumed capacity share, k turns that share into unique risk-person years, e*t*l gives a one-year mortality hazard difference, and b applies funding response once. No separately multiplied repeat-rescue lifetime or national affiliate credit.
historicalModel.uncertainty: Whole-recipient central withdrawn. Actual unique reach, additional timely rescue, funded capacity, victim residence and material non-overdose outcomes are unidentified. Legacy priors remain explicit historical diagnostics; no calibrated uncertainty distribution or guaranteed lower bound is available.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: The provider reported more than 10,000 doses and at least 140 reversal events by November 20, 2023. These are neither a current full-year unique cohort nor causal deaths averted. Supply recipient, overdose witness, repeat event and unique survivor are distinct units.

reports.program: Whole recipient; conditional local heat-policy implementation

acceptance.evidence: Independent original financial, source, finite causal and all-scenario audit; accepted as partial-health research, not donor endorsement.

what: WE ACT combines community organizing, research, education and advocacy for environmental justice.
Its charitable recipient works locally, statewide and nationally, including on housing, heat and toxic exposures.
The numerical estimate covers only additional NYC heat-policy implementation while charging the full recipient's operating cost.
strengths: A documented coalition role connects local organizing to a real implementation opportunity.
Current heat risk is source-grounded and benefits are restricted to local residents.
Full-recipient accounting retains national work and separately netted event resources.
reservations: Campaign attribution and funding response remain subjective.
Existing laws and public programs can substantially substitute for new advocacy.
Most environmental, workforce and national outcomes are unpriced, so this is not complete portfolio return.

sections.what: The ordinary charitable recipient is West Harlem Environmental Action Inc., EIN 13-3800068, doing business as WE ACT. Its work spans Northern Manhattan, state policy and a federal office; the whole operating denominator remains in this estimate. The related WE ACT 4 Change is a separate 501(c)(4), not a second pool of charitable outcomes to append. [Recipient](https://weact.org/donate/) [Affiliate disclosure](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202513219349324771/IRS990ScheduleR)
sections.monitoring: The impact report documents coalition work on the cooling-center law and a wider city/state/federal portfolio. These establish a role, not marginal deaths prevented. The 2026 policy agenda was prepared before final enactment of the residential cooling law, and the heat webpage retains a petition to pass it. The current Council record is authoritative: the law was enacted in January 2026 with key requirements beginning in 2030. New gifts can at most improve implementation beyond this baseline, not earn the law's full historical benefit. [Impact report](https://weact.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/WE-ACTs-2024-2025-Impact-Report-Final.pdf) [Current legal status](https://legistar.council.nyc.gov/LegislationDetail.aspx?GUID=156F95BB-CA74-44F3-A07B-A0E54EA0C10F&ID=6788510) Tenant elections, hardship extensions and the separate NYCHA cooling-plan route limit the 2030 requirement; no universal cooling or additional law-passage benefit is assumed.
sections.qualitative:
WE ACT's heat coalition and energy-assistance advocacy offer a concrete pathway through affordability, uptake and enforcement. The latest city report estimates roughly 500 annual heat-related deaths, predominantly modeled heat-exacerbated mortality. This is the local risk envelope, not a campaign output. Preventing death may extend life briefly rather than restore a full healthy lifetime, which is why survival is constrained. [Campaign](https://weact.org/programs/heat-health-equity/) [Current mortality evidence](https://a816-dohbesp.nyc.gov/IndicatorPublic/data-features/heat-report/)

Healthy housing, toxic-product regulation, clean energy and workforce work may dominate total value. No sensor, workshop, bill or grant is automatically treated as a health outcome. Their unpriced value is a reason not to rank the organization using the heat component alone.
sections.cost:
The conditional local heat-component price is approximately $361.2 million per 10 MSA QALYs, not complete portfolio cost-effectiveness.

The cost numerator is three years of the entire charitable recipient's gross operating expense. The scenario assumes an additional cooling-implementation package could reduce the city's annual heat mortality envelope by 1% beyond already funded and mandated protections. A 25% coalition probability, 20% WE ACT contribution and 50% ordinary funding response yield 0.125 attributable deaths avoided annually for five cohorts starting four years from valuation. These are transparent priors, not measured effects. Each death avoided is valued at no more than five remaining years with 0.6 utility and a 20% annual competing-mortality hazard, discounted 3%.

All modeled deaths are NYC-resident deaths, so the component's MSA share is 100%; this does not assign national benefits to New York. The parallel NYC-EJA scenario shares the same coalition opportunity and is correlated, not another independent citywide reduction. A combined giving model would need to reassess joint additionality rather than add both prices or benefits mechanically.

Positive alternatives vary implementation, attribution, funding and survival. Complete replacement and a one-QALY adverse outcome are retained. Added $1 million induced household/public cost and 25% coalition-resource cases test omitted costs; neither is a measured invoice. Rent, electricity costs, grid effects and displacement can offset health gains.
sections.funding:
FY2024 gross expense is $11,254,011: Part IX $11,067,147 plus $186,864 separately netted event expense. Schedule D has no donated-service addback. FY2022 is $7,890,202: Part IX $7,618,578 plus $197,262 recognized donated services and $74,362 event expense. FY2023 original current-period gross is $13,137,650: Part IX $13,013,153 plus $124,497 event expense. Its audit reconciliation contains an additional $147,947 prior-year adjustment, not assigned to the current operating year; the next return's comparative expense also differs by $75,351. FY2023 is noncomparable pending reconciliation, not smoothed into a synthetic mean. [FY2024 original](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202513219349324771/IRS990) [FY2023 reconciliation](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202443169349303479/IRS990ScheduleD)

FY2024 reports $2,428,022 government grants and $17,182,896 net assets, including $2,714,557 restricted. Cash and savings total $11,214,924. Those balances do not establish a new-gift capacity commitment. The impact report's fundraising categories differ from return revenue, so they are not substituted for accounting totals. Current national and local work remains in the whole-recipient scope. [Donate](https://weact.org/donate/)

Expense appendix: FY2024 Part IX is $8,291,799 program, $2,360,382 management/general and $414,966 fundraising, totaling $11,067,147. Add separately netted event resources $186,864 to reach $11,254,011. FY2023 remains noncomparable; the three-year projected model cost is not a verified historical mean.

model.costScope: Three years of all charitable recipient gross operating expense, including national programs, grants and event resources; not only the local heat campaign. Capital acquisition is not added on top of recognized annual expense; a resource stress addresses omitted capacity.
model.geographicAttribution: g=1 for modeled NYC-resident heat mortality, entirely within the official 22-county MSA. No statewide campaign or climate benefit assigned by headquarters.
model.formula: v=ln(1+d)+m; q=u*(1-exp(-v*L))/v; A=sum(j=0..T-1)(1+d)^(-lag-j); Qall=D*r*p*a*b*q*A-h; QMSA=g*Qall; price10=10*C/QMSA if positive.
model.counterfactual: Enacted cooling law, existing HEAP, cooling centers, agency enforcement and other coalition members continue. Only improvement beyond that baseline is credited; no historical passage or total congestion-pricing gain.
model.attribution: The shared coalition framework assigns WE ACT a subjective 20% central contribution to additional implementation, not credit for the whole coalition. The NYC-EJA report separately assumes 20%; these correlated scenarios are not independent interventions to sum. Existing legal mandates receive no new-gift credit.
model.uncertainty: Judgment-based scenario, not a statistical forecast or complete portfolio ranking. Marginal cooling uptake, health protection and campaign additionality are not observed. Positive alternatives, zero and harm are retained.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional implementation of cooling access and affordability -> annual heat deaths avoided beyond baseline -> finite survival-adjusted QALYs.

sections.what: CGE is the full charity, EIN 22-3560158. START is its home-based perinatal program, not a separate gift recipient. Ordinary support also funds residential and outpatient treatment, childcare, housing and training. None of those costs is removed to manufacture a cheap START price. sections.monitoring: The 2024 report records 53 START clients and 118,555 session minutes, up from 39 clients in 2023. These are service outputs, not successful clinical changes. The 2025 report presents graduate recovery and anxiety improvements but does not supply an appropriate untreated comparison or complete attrition denominator; its national benchmarks are not causal controls. We do not convert the reported 65% anxiety reduction into 65% more QALYs. [2024 report](https://www.cge-nj.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Impact_Report-for-sharing.pdf) [2025 report](https://www.cge-nj.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/CGE_Impact_Report_2025.pdf)
sections.qualitative: START can overcome transportation and childcare barriers by bringing clinicians, peer recovery and doula care to the home. Its current 18-month service design does not guarantee 18 months of clinical benefit. The integrated-treatment review found benefits against no treatment, but did not show statistically significant superiority over non-integrated treatment on pooled substance-use measures. We therefore discount alternative care and refrain from translating an uncontrolled before/after change directly into effect. [Current program](https://www.cge-nj.org/programs/start/) [Clinical evidence and limitations](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20809957/)
sections.cost:
The conditional START maternal-health component costs approximately $147.6 million per 10 MSA QALYs against the entire charity's annual cost. This is not complete portfolio return, a lower bound or a direct-service ranking.

The model carries the observed 2024 scale of 53 clients forward, then assumes 60% meaningful improvement, 50% additional treatment beyond alternatives and 50% funding response. For those improved, utility rises 0.1 initially, waning at a 50% annual hazard for no more than one year, with 3% discounting. A small 0.001-QALY treatment burden per additional client is subtracted. Every clinical and response parameter is a judgment; no overdose death or lifelong recovery is added.

START's listed counties—Essex, Hudson, Hunterdon, Middlesex, Morris, Passaic, Somerset and Union—are all within the official MSA. The wider charity reports clients from 13 New Jersey counties, so this geography does not generalize to its whole portfolio. Child development, custody, housing, other treatment and training effects remain unpriced. Positive, zero and adverse alternatives are shown. Additional clinical partner costs of $5,000 per donor-attributable improvement and a separate 25% resource stress test costs omitted from the recipient accounts.

sections.what: The recipient is New York Legal Assistance Group, EIN 13-3505428. LegalHealth is a division, not a separate charity. Its health-related legal work sits alongside a much larger housing, immigration, benefits and family-law portfolio, all retained in the cost denominator. [Division](https://legalhealth.org/) [Current access routes](https://nylag.org/gethelp/)
sections.monitoring:
The original February 2025 testimony reports that LegalHealth helped 250 undocumented immigrants establish Medicaid eligibility during 2024. That is the model's native output. It is not proof of 250 new treatments or lives saved. Case examples establish that consequential treatment is possible but do not identify its frequency. Current LegalHealth pages show inconsistent counts of partner sites and an undated 7,000-client headline; we do not combine those with the historical eligibility cohort. [Original testimony](https://nylag.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/NYLAG-FY-25-26-Budget-Testimony-Joint-Legislative-Health-Hearing-Final.pdf)

The next evidence upgrade needs coverage status, treatment obtained, alternative assistance, residence and health trajectory. Current Medicaid implementation work addresses real administrative barriers, but its total policy effect is not inferred from the number of published guidance pages. [Current implementation guidance, updated September 2026](https://nyhealthaccess.org/entry/257/)
sections.qualitative:
Coverage can enable care that legal status or insurance disputes previously blocked, but emergency and safety-net care may already exist. Oregon's randomized coverage experiment found some mental-health benefits without clear short-term improvements in several physical-health measures. It supports a cautious access mechanism, not direct calibration for these medically complex patients. [Randomized access evidence](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23635051/)

Other legal services can protect health through stable housing, income or safety, while also producing valuable rights-based outcomes that QALYs omit. These pathways are not assumed to have zero value; they are outside this partial calculation.
sections.cost:
The conditional coverage-access component is approximately $881.8 million per 10 MSA QALYs. This is not complete portfolio return or a valid standalone ranking of NYLAG against clinical charities.

The model begins with 250 historical eligibility gains, retains half for uncertain current transfer, and assumes half are additional to other representation. A 25% ordinary funding response then applies. Half of those cases obtain consequential effective care, producing 0.2 initial utility improvement with a 50% annual waning hazard for at most one year. A 0.001-QALY process burden per additional case is subtracted; discounting is 3%. These are transparent priors, not measured legal success-to-health conversion rates.

A 95% MSA residence share reflects the regional hospital pathway but is not observed. The official MSA includes Long Island and Westchester; it does not include all New York State. No national or statewide headcount is assigned wholesale to local benefit.

High and low cases vary transfer, clinical benefit, funding and duration. Zero replacement and adverse process burden remain possible. Additional medical resources of $20,000 per attributable effective-care case and a 25% higher valuation of donated legal services stress full costs. A separate case excludes the accounting credit loss. None changes beneficiary volume merely because the cost numerator changes.
sections.funding:
Gross annual recognized resources are $87,686,413 in FY2023, $99,702,741 in FY2024 and $100,312,616 in FY2025. These June-ending accrual amounts equal Part IX plus donated services ($40,861,954/$47,464,896/$42,371,761), uncollectible-account losses ($104,961/$551,204/$342,670), and separately netted event expense ($244,808/$211,189/$187,979). The audit reconciliation does not include event expense in its addbacks, so event resources are added once after that reconciliation. Credit losses are retained conservatively but are not described as new treatment resources. [FY2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202641329349300449/IRS990) [Audit reconciliation](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202641329349300449/IRS990ScheduleD)

FY2025 government grants were $46,123,020; net assets were $25,176,283, including $692,750 restricted. Cash and savings were $2,335,335 while grants receivable were $24,308,323, so net assets are not all liquid cash.

On August 11, 2026, NYC Health + Hospitals announced a $23.7 million seven-year LegalHealth contract and reported nearly 4,000 patients served in 2025. Additional city funding also supports the partnership. This is a substantial existing commitment, not a new-gift funding gap, and materially limits marginality assumptions. [Current public contract](https://www.nychealthandhospitals.org/pressrelease/nyc-health-hospitals-commits-23-7-million-to-new-york-legal-assistance-groups-legalhealth-unit-for-free-legal-services-for-patients/) [Donate](https://nylag.org/donate-now/)

These additions are not reassigned across functional categories without the audit allocation. The comparable three-year recognized mean is $95,900,590.

reports.program: Whole recipient; conditional integrated harm reduction, clinical care and net household resources

acceptance.evidence: docs/geography-discovery/nyc-sachr-independent-20261005.md; original-source and independent twenty-case/281-check challenge accepted.

what: St. Ann's Corner of Harm Reduction provides a South Bronx health hub with overdose prevention, sterile supplies, buprenorphine access and ongoing care coordination.
Meals, hygiene, outreach and a current workforce initiative support many of the same participants, so their health and economic effects need a shared cohort and clear accounting.
We examine additional integrated engagement supported by an ordinary gift, with the whole recipient's costs and net household resources rather than the retail value of free supplies.
strengths: Current clinical, outreach and LUCHA workforce pages identify concrete services and current enrollment, rather than only a historical mission statement.
Three original annual returns reconcile the full recipient's operating and event costs and reveal its reliance on government grants.
One unique-person survival comparison and signed household-resource ledger avoid assigning every rescue another lifetime or treating every free item as a cash saving.
reservations: No current unique clinical cohort, retained-treatment series, net employment outcomes or gift-funded engagement queue was found; outcome and capacity priors remain judgments.
NYC supplies free naloxone and other providers continue care, so extra distribution or a referral does not prove an incremental health benefit.
The conditional estimate is about $22.3 million per better life; net household-resource effects are slightly negative centrally, and low-benefit or adverse scenarios have no positive finite price.

sections.what:
The ordinary charitable recipient is St. Ann's Corner of Harm Reduction Inc., EIN 13-3724008, as its [donation page](https://www.sachr.org/donate) confirms. Its South Bronx hub offers overdose prevention, sterile supplies, HIV/HCV testing and treatment linkage, buprenorphine and wound care. The [current programs](https://www.sachr.org/program) also describe meals, hygiene and behavioral care; these are overlapping services for the same people, not separate additive patient populations. The site includes nonstandard holistic modalities; this model does not assign acupuncture, Reiki or every social activity a clinical effect.

The [LUCHA workforce page](https://www.sachr.org/workforce-development), retrieved directly when the browser wrapper failed, advertises eight weekly sessions, job readiness, financial/computer literacy, interview and resume support, coaching and summer/fall 2026 and winter 2027 enrollment options. It identifies Hispanic Federation and Fund for the City of New York support. That establishes advertised services and a possible employment mechanism, not measured placements or wage gains. This is a whole-recipient gift comparison, not a newly invented restricted clinical/workforce fund.
sections.monitoring:
The [annual-impact page](https://www.sachr.org/annual-impact) still ties 2,816 unique participants, 851,689 services and 24,851 meals to its 2023 report. These are historical reach/output totals. Repeat services, meals, tests and medical contacts are not completed treatments or unique lives saved. The image-only annual-report interpretation from the alpha review is preserved as earlier evidence; it was not freshly visually audited in this revision. Current [drop-in](https://www.sachr.org/drop-in) and workforce pages confirm ongoing offers but do not supply a fresh annual unique cohort.

Useful monitoring would link a privacy-preserving unique cohort to engagement intensity, buprenorphine initiation and retention, alternative-provider access, repeat overdose outcomes, wound/infection outcomes, quality of life, household costs and actual disposable pay. Address-based MSA residency, repeat households, food purchase versus unmet consumption and failed applicants need measurement. A dated additional-staff/slots workplan and covered versus uncovered grant commitments would identify marginal capacity. This review makes no contact or enrollment and treats current scale transfer as a judgment.
sections.qualitative:
The clinical case is strongest for maintaining access to effective opioid treatment and timely overdose response. The [Sordo primary synthesis](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC5421454/fullTextXML) associates treatment with lower mortality, but in/out-treatment contrasts are observational and include treatment selection, cycling and older drug markets. Its buprenorphine rates cannot simply become a local hub effect. A [British Columbia fentanyl-era cohort](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC7190018/fullTextXML) supports retention relevance while remaining an observational comparison in a different health system.

Contemporary implementation evidence constrains optimism. The original HEALing Communities mortality trial, retained from alpha, found no statistically significant mortality reduction; the newly read [2025 secondary randomized analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12302724/) found no improvement in MOUD receipt, 180-day retention or linkage after relevant acute-care encounters. Community-wide implementation differs from SACHR's selected participants, but a promising bundle does not guarantee causal uptake. We therefore use modest explicitly judged mortality/utility differences and retain zero and adverse alternatives.

The central utility change represents residual clinical/function benefit among people alive in both worlds. It is not an independently measured generic utility effect or a claim that every social service improves health. Food, consumption and workforce channels are separately signed; half of positive economic welfare is retained to limit overlap with generic wellbeing, while negative cash burdens remain fully charged. Survival benefits do not receive extra ordinary lifetime earnings. Dignity, HIV/HCV transmission, housing navigation and broader employment/community effects remain unpriced, rather than assumed literally absent. This is a partial conditional research model, not a complete expected-value estimate or donor-ready recommendation.
sections.cost:
Our conditional estimate is about **$22.3 million per better life**: ten combined healthy-year and household-resource equivalents for NYC metro residents. The initial health-only estimate was $13.5 million. The revision changes clinical assumptions, survival accounting, delay and harms as well as adding net household resources; it does not mean measured performance deteriorated.

**What additional money could provide.** The latest full-recipient annual cost is $5.27 million. Applying a judgment about current scale to historical unique reach implies roughly $2,338 in average organizational support per annual engagement equivalent. With an assumed 25% funding response, that becomes about $9,353 in donor funding per additional engagement. These are conditional calculations, not verified marginal prices, additional treatment completions or available slots. Shared administration, fundraising and event expenses enter the denominator once.

**Health benefits.** The central case assumes a modest one-year reduction in mortality among a high-risk subgroup, plus a small improvement in clinical functioning among people alive in both worlds. Treatment starts after three months; the survival comparison is capped at ten years, with no permanent mortality reduction or separate lifetime credit for each overdose rescue. High- and lower-risk groups have different baseline hazards, replacing the initial uniform 8% annual hazard. A small independent health burden remains even when clinical benefits disappear. These are explicit judgments, not locally measured treatment effects.

**Net household resources.** The model distinguishes households whose meals and hygiene supplies replace purchases from households receiving otherwise unmet consumption. It subtracts additional travel costs, actually lost disposable pay and medicine or copay costs after assistance and alternative care. A small workforce-response scenario adds net disposable earnings after taxes, benefits, work expenses and other-provider substitution. SACHR's workforce page establishes an offered program, not a measured placement or wage effect. Free naloxone receives no automatic retail purchase-saving credit.

Following [Coefficient Giving's logarithmic comparison](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/), the economic calculation uses a judged $20,000 annual household-resource baseline and converts dated net resource changes into healthy-year equivalents. Baseline survival, NYC attribution and discounting apply once. Half of positive economic welfare is retained to limit overlap with generic wellbeing; negative resource burdens remain fully charged. Newly surviving participants receive no additional credit for ordinary baseline earnings. Actual purchases, unmet consumption and nested medical payments use a shared cash ledger to avoid duplicate benefits or inconsistent logarithms.

At a $10,000 mathematical normalization—not a gift recommendation—the central model produces about 0.00461 health years and −0.00013 income-equivalent years, or 0.00448 combined years. Scaling costs and engagement together leaves the price unchanged. Every assumption and signed pathway is recorded in the appendix.

**Uncertainty and scope.** A favorable bundled scenario is approximately $1.57 million per better life; a weak-response, higher-burden scenario is net negative. Zero expansion gives zero effects. Clinical-null and complete clinical-substitution cases retain costs and harms. A selected external-resource companion adds $2,000 per additional engagement for unrecognized clinical, public-stock and volunteer inputs, giving approximately $27.1 million at the same welfare result; this is not a complete net societal-cost estimate. No duplicate procurement expense or public-stock saving is added. Unmeasured other-program effects and actual funding response could dominate this partial model.
sections.funding:
The three original returns were freshly retrieved directly; the browser wrapper failed. Fiscal periods are July 2022–June 2023, July 2023–June 2024 and July 2024–June 2025. Full-recipient gross expense is **$4,348,379/$5,106,419/$5,267,469**, adding direct fundraising-event costs $73,846/$115,347/$95,881 to Part IX totals $4,274,533/$4,991,072/$5,171,588. The comparable annual mean is $4,907,422.33. The 2025 functional amounts $4,384,865 program, $602,749 management and $183,974 fundraising reconcile to Part IX, with direct events added once. [2023 original](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202421369349307717/IRS990) [2024 original](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202531299349302658/IRS990) [2025 original](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202630649349300233/IRS990)

Recognized noncash gifts $94,661/$95,182/$109,444 are not added again to reported expense merely because they are noncash. Latest [Schedule D](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202630649349300233/IRS990 ScheduleD) reconciles audit expense to Part IX without extra donated-service adjustment. Actual audit opinion/control findings were not newly reviewed; a Form 990 statement that an audit exists is not a fresh independent-audit acceptance. Latest government grants $4,469,690 dominate support; revenue $4,828,637 is net of event expense while the chosen gross cost denominator adds that expense back. The $342,951 deficit is unchanged when gross revenue/cost are treated consistently.

The 2025 balance sheet reports $291,414 cash, $1,940,700 pledges/grants receivable and $2,113,536 net assets without donor restrictions. Receivables, lease right-of-use assets/liabilities and equipment mean unrestricted net assets are not cash runway or proof of spare operating capacity. Grant timing, renewals, current restricted commitments, actual staffing/clinical slots and replacement funding are missing. A deficit suggests continuity questions, not a verified next-dollar treatment opportunity.

NYC's [current provider route](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/naloxone.page) provides free naloxone and fentanyl strips to registered OOPPs. Its [May 2026 mail campaign](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/about/press/pr 2026/free-naloxone-by-mail-campaign.page) reports285,000 kits distributed citywide in 2025 and free mail/community routes. Supplies alone cannot identify SACHR's unique engagement or donor return. The workforce page names existing funders without grant amounts; no additional support package or available capacity is verified. No donation, contact, form submission or new restricted-gift arrangement was made.

model.formula: k=ln(1+r); F(v,t)=(1-exp(-v*t))/v; E=G*b*N*f/C; B=u*(F(mH-delta+k,1)-F(mH+k,1)+(exp(-(mH-delta))-exp(-mH))*exp(-k)*F(mH+k,T-1)); H=E*a*(z*exp(-(mH+k)*L)*B+p*v*(z*exp(-(mH+k)*L)*F(mH+k,1)+(1-z)*exp(-(mL+k)*L)*F(mL+k,1)))-E*h*S0(L)*exp(-k*L); S0(t)=z*exp(-mH*t)+(1-z)*exp(-mL*t). Economic paths: .5*people*ln(1+gain/base)*S0(receipt)*g*independentShare/(1+r)^receipt for each one-off/year receipt. Joint-stratum bases follow burden then receipt then medicine; negative effects independence1. Price10=10*(G+E*external)/(g*H+sum economic paths), null if combined<=0.
model.counterfactual: Current grants, other hub/medical care, public naloxone, food/benefit routes and job support continue. b controls gift-induced engagement, a clinical equivalence only; economic incidence is separately net incremental, not multiplied by a again. Financial additionality is not applied twice.
model.attribution: One unique overlapping cohort, no additive rescued lifetimes; only first-year high-risk mortality improvement. Morbidity/economic gains use baseline-alive cohort, no extra survival earnings. Buyer and unmet consumption strata disjoint; no public procurement/retail savings. Shared negative burden counted once, positive overlap reduces welfare rather than changing actual receipts.
model.uncertainty: Partial unweighted judgment scenarios, not a measured donor effect, confidence interval, source-vetted donor recommendation or complete EV. Current reach, generic utility, local hazard, gift capacity, funding replacement and net resource incidence unknown; observed inputs limited to filings and older page counts.

historicalAlphaModel.costScope: All recipient gross annual operating expense, including recognized noncash and separately netted events; external medical and volunteer resource sensitivities retained.
historicalAlphaModel.geographicAttribution: g=.98 is a subjective local-residence share for a South Bronx/neighboring-borough cohort. NYC lies entirely within the official 22-county MSA; no headquarters-based statewide benefit assignment.
historicalAlphaModel.formula: k=ln(1+d); F(v,t)=(1-exp(-v*t))/v; B=u*[F(m-delta+k,1)-F(m+k,1)+(exp(-(m-delta))-exp(-m))*exp(-k)*F(m+k,T-1)]; M=p*v*[z*F(m-delta+k,1)+(1-z)*F(m+k,1)]; Qall=N*f*a*b*(z*B+M)-h; QMSA=g*Qall; price10=10*C/QMSA when positive.
historicalAlphaModel.counterfactual: Existing public grants, other harm-reduction services and medical care continue. a discounts replacement by alternative services; b separately discounts whether unrestricted funding changes the supported scale. Neither is reapplied per mechanism.
historicalAlphaModel.attribution: One unique cohort and a combined mortality effect prevent repeat-rescue and overlapping-service lifetime double counting. Mortality and short-lived utility changes are distinct terms on the same survival curve.
historicalAlphaModel.uncertainty: Reasoned integrated clinical scenario, not a measured program effect or comprehensive social return. No source-calibrated probability is claimed; broad alternatives, complete substitution and adverse outcomes are explicit.
historicalAlphaModel.nativeOutcomes: Unique participants -> additional integrated harm-reduction/clinical engagement -> one-year mortality-hazard and utility changes -> finite survival-adjusted QALYs. Central annual normalization transfers 2,816 older participants to 2,252.8 current-equivalent participants; after care and funding additionality, 281.6 integrated-engagement equivalents remain, including 168.96 higher-risk equivalents. Whole-recipient cost per additional engagement is $18705.50 and per local equivalent $19087.25. These are judgment-based native units, not observed retained buprenorphine patients or additional rescues. Mortality and morbidity components contribute 1.9876 and 2.0022 all-population QALYs.

acceptance.evidence: Independent Medium source, original-financial and all-scenario audit with scope/counterfactual/native-unit corrections. Accepted as a conditional alpha estimate, not donor endorsement.

what: NJEJA organizes and advocates on cumulative pollution, port operations, energy policy and environmental justice across New Jersey.
Its most plausible material health benefit is a reduction in residents' pollution exposure beyond existing protections.
The estimate models that major policy pathway with full recipient costs, explicit campaign priors and a separate NYC-MSA beneficiary share.
strengths: State permitting and port decisions provide concrete routes from advocacy to exposure change.
Recent comments show ongoing attention to local pollution, affordability and reliability.
The model prices a major portfolio mechanism rather than workshop or tree-planting counts.
reservations: No campaign-specific population-weighted exposure reduction is measured.
Large reserves and already funded regulation may reduce ordinary-gift additionality.
Energy substitution, relocation and reliability effects can make net health impact negative.

sections.what: NJEJA is a separate New Jersey charitable recipient, EIN 81-4338010, not NYC Environmental Justice Alliance or Ironbound Community Corporation. Its portfolio spans cumulative-impact permitting, port pollution, energy policy, organizing and youth development, with statewide and national engagement. All these activities remain in the cost denominator. [Portfolio](https://njeja.org/what-we-do/) [Recent policy submission](https://njeja.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/NJEJA-Comments-BPU-ResourceAdequacy.pdf)
sections.monitoring:
The portfolio webpage contains substantial historical material, including a pre-enactment cumulative-impact bill and 2018 projects; these are not new donation opportunities. NJDEP's current environmental-justice program and March 2026 data update establish an active regulatory baseline. The model asks whether organizing improves enforcement, design or deployment beyond that baseline, not whether it deserves the entire law's benefit. [Current agency program](https://dep.nj.gov/ej/)

NJEJA opposed the PVSC standby-power permit in September 2024. A February 2026 EPA order denies a different petitioner's request for a permit objection; that is neither an NJEJA victory nor proof that its campaign caused a defeat. The clean-ports selection already anticipated $344,138,135 for the Port Authority's proposed zero-emission package. Neither all permitted emissions nor the full funded package is attributed to a new donation. [NJEJA comments](https://njeja.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/NJEJA-Opposes-PVSC-Fourth-Power-Plant-1.pdf) [EPA order](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2026-02/passaic-valley-sewerage-order_02-03-2026.pdf) [Public funding baseline](https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/epa-announces-historic-400m-clean-ports-investment-new-jersey) The EPA Clean Ports announcement is a 2024 selection baseline, not independently verified September 2026 disbursement or achieved emissions reduction. Current [NJDEP rules](https://dep.nj.gov/ej/law/) remain an existing permitting baseline; a new gift is not credited for reenacting that law.
sections.qualitative:
The selected pathway is cumulative particulate-exposure reduction across the industrial, port and energy-policy portfolio. It is potentially material because modest changes can affect many residents; it is not claimed to be observed. The exposure scenario is deliberately independent of activity counts and of any one permit's maximum emissions. A large Medicare cohort supports an association between fine particles and mortality, but transfer to the modeled adult population, confounding and the timing of health response remain uncertain. [Clinical evidence](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1702747)

NJEJA's 2025 energy comments favor a narrow renewable definition and oppose nuclear and several other technologies. These positions are not automatically counted as health benefits. The counterfactual must include replacement generation, grid reliability and affordability: preventing one local project could shift pollution or delay cleaner capacity. The adverse scenario explicitly allows net particulate exposure to rise. Climate, toxic pollutants, flooding, empowerment and income effects are not separately priced; the estimate is a major local-health pathway, not complete social return. [Energy comments](https://njeja.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/NJEJA-Comments-BPU-ResourceAdequacy.pdf)
sections.cost:
The conditional major air-policy pathway price is approximately $72.26 million per 10 MSA QALYs, not a measured complete portfolio return.

The central judgment scenario assumes an additional policy package produces a net 0.1 microgram/m³ reduction in annual PM2.5 exposure for 500,000 adults for five years, beginning after a two-year implementation delay. Neither number is an observed campaign forecast. The population is a hypothetical affected cohort, much smaller than the state's historical 4.5-million-person overburdened-community envelope, not a claim that all such residents benefit. A 50% epidemiological transfer factor, 25% incremental coalition probability, 20% NJEJA contribution and 25% ordinary funding response are each explicit priors. [Population envelope](https://dep.nj.gov/newsrel/21_0028/)

A single cohort survival comparison, capped at fifteen years from exposure onset, replaces repeated 'deaths saved times lifetime' arithmetic. Eighty percent of the modeled cohort's gains are assigned to the MSA as a subjective residence/exposure share reflecting northern urban work; Camden, Trenton and other non-MSA residents are not automatically local. This geography prior is not calibrated by NJEJA's headquarters.

Three years of the entire recipient's latest operating cost are charged. The main estimate excludes separately induced compliance investment because it is unmeasured, so a $10 million additional-resource case is prominent. A 25% unrecognized-resource case tests donated coalition inputs. The positive range is wide, complete funding replacement gives zero, and energy displacement can produce net harm. This is not a claim that regulation is costless or that the portfolio always lowers pollution.

The physical bridge is 250,000 conditional concentration-person-years, reduced to 2,500 additional local concentration-person-years by the policy, contribution, funding and geography factors, before epidemiological transfer. That is $1,613.75 of whole-recipient cost per additional local concentration-person-year. N refers to adults alive when exposure reduction starts; using today’s fixed cohort instead would reduce the health term by exp(-0.01 × 2), about 2%. The three-year expense numerator is a constant-scale projection charged upfront, not an observed future budget or three completed financial years.
sections.funding:
The original FY2024 return reports $1,344,794 total expense, with no netted rental, event or inventory costs and no noncash-contribution amount. Its Schedule D audit reconciliation is blank and its accounting checkbox is cash, unlike the accrual FY2023 return. The current-period figure is a usable disclosed resource proxy, not a verified full accrual audit. FY2023 reports $975,780 and its Schedule D audit expense agrees. FY2022 reports only $28,867; Schedule O identifies a $900,451 receivable for sponsor-held funds from activity before September 1, 2022. That transition-year perimeter is not a mature annual cost. FY2022 and FY2024 are marked noncomparable to prevent a synthetic three-year mean. [FY2024 original](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202533029349302233/IRS990) [Transition explanation](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202323189349314617/IRS990ScheduleO)

FY2024 reports $4,123,595 cash and $4,553,002 net assets, including $726,845 restricted, against $1,288,707 revenue. The government-grant line is blank, which does not rule out public-origin pass-through grants. These balances weaken any claim of an immediate funding bottleneck; the central funding response is only 25%. A new ordinary gift may support reserves, organizing, staff continuity or projects elsewhere rather than the modeled exposure package. [Donate](https://njeja.org/donate/)

FY2024 Part IX allocates $1,201,749 to programs and $143,045 to management, with zero reported fundraising. Schedule O says no board return review was or would be conducted and that documents were not publicly available through the organization; the original IRS filing is nonetheless publicly accessible. These disclosures are governance/information limitations, not proof of misuse. No three-year average is displayed because the sponsor transition and accounting-method change remain unresolved.

model.costScope: Three years of latest whole-recipient reported gross expense; FY2024 cash-basis proxy, not a verified accrual audit. No program-only denominator; induced compliance and unrecognized-resource sensitivities explicit.
model.geographicAttribution: g=.8 is an explicit prior for the modeled exposure cohort, not an observed share of statewide beneficiaries. Only official 22-county MSA residents' gains enter the local denominator.
model.formula: k=ln(1+d); delta=m*(1-exp(-beta*pm))*c; F(v,t)=(1-exp(-v*t))/v; Qall=N*u*p*a*b*exp(-k*lag)*[F(m-delta+k,T)-F(m+k,T)+(exp(-(m-delta)*T)-exp(-m*T))*exp(-k*T)*F(m+k,L-T)]-h; QMSA=g*Qall; price10=10*C/QMSA if positive. N is the hypothetical cohort alive at exposure onset after lag, not a fixed group counted today. Thus pre-onset survival is not applied again; if N instead denotes today’s fixed cohort, multiply the positive survival term by exp(-m*lag). No benefit occurs before exposure onset.
model.counterfactual: Existing EJ law, permitting staff, funded clean-port projects and other advocates continue. pm is net incremental exposure after relocation and replacement generation, not total regulated emissions. b captures ordinary-donation response once.
model.attribution: One correlated policy portfolio opportunity, with separate coalition additionality p, NJEJA contribution a and funding response b. Do not add full policy benefits from each coalition member or duplicate grants flowing between them.
model.uncertainty: All campaign-scale, exposure and attribution figures are explicit judgment. The exposure hypothesis is not empirically calibrated. A major potential portfolio pathway is priced, but climate, toxics, social benefits and non-PM harms remain incomplete.
model.nativeOutcomes: Policy implementation beyond baseline -> net population-weighted PM2.5 concentration change -> finite cohort survival -> local QALYs. Central exposure before attribution is 500,000 adults × 0.1 microgram/m³ × 5 years = 250,000 concentration-person-years. Policy incrementality, coalition contribution, funding response and local share yield 2,500 additional local concentration-person-years; the epidemiological transfer factor affects health, not this physical unit. Cost is $1,613.75 per modeled additional local concentration-person-year. This is a scenario diagnostic, not measured avoided emissions or an observed permit effect.
