what: Parker Family Health Center provides free medical care to uninsured Monmouth County residents.
Its services include primary care, chronic-disease management, mental-health support and connections to specialty care.
Its new dental clinic is designed to provide preventive and restorative care for people without affordable dental access.
strengths: Free, scheduled care can address symptoms and chronic conditions that otherwise go untreated.
Volunteer clinicians and community partners contribute services alongside donated cash.
Original returns and audited accounts allow a more transparent comparison of cash-like costs and gross resources.
reservations: The conditional estimate is about $10.2M per better life; patient reach, clinical response and household effects are planning judgments rather than measured causal effects.
The dental clinic’s annual treatment volume, costs and additional donation-funded capacity are not yet verified.
Purchased or other free care can replace some benefits; household burdens and broader unmeasured portfolio effects remain important.

sections.what: Parker Family Health Center Inc., EIN 22-3619518, provides primary, chronic-disease, women's, pediatric and specialist-linked care. Medical eligibility requires Monmouth residence, income below 300% of the federal poverty level and no insurance or qualifying public coverage; dental eligibility concerns dental insurance and can include medically insured seniors. [Current medical eligibility](https://www.parkerfamilyhealthcenter.org/patients) Brookdale confirms a June 17, 2026 ribbon-cutting for the free dental clinic, supported by volunteer clinicians and public/private partners. Its services include preventive care, fillings, X-rays and simple extractions. This updates the older prospective opening language. [Opening](https://www.brookdalecc.edu/parker-family-health-center-brookdale-community-college-and-monmouth-county-celebrate-opening-of-new-free-dental-clinic/)
sections.monitoring:
The 2024 return reports 342 diabetes patients and says diabetes affects approximately a quarter of patients; 1,368 is therefore an inferred cohort, not a deduplicated count. Women's, pediatric, screening, nutrition and medication-service counts overlap and are not added. The hospital partner reports 246 Parker hypertension-nutrition patients/contacts in 2024 and 109 in the first half of 2025; these establish shared service delivery rather than clinical improvement. [Partner report, printed p212](https://www.rwjbh.org/documents/community-health-needs-assessment/MMC-CHNA-2025.pdf) Brookdale reports over 20,000 prior-year visits, not unique patients. Dental plans forecast 1,000–1,500 annual patients, but actual post-opening volume and outcomes were not found. [Dental proposal](https://impact100jerseycoast.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/2025-Grantee-Parker-Health-Summary.pdf) Request unique medical/dental IDs, referral completion, baseline and follow-up blood pressure/HbA1c, depression and pain/function measures, adverse effects, and comparable untreated or later-treated patients. Also request appointment queues and capacity added by a specified unrestricted grant. Parker's June23 announcement says patients would begin during summer; the ceremony itself is not proof of completed treatment. [Current announcement](https://www.parkerfamilyhealthcenter.org/news-events/2026/6/23/parker-expands-access-to-care-with-new-free-dental-clinic)

Parker's March2025 volunteer report says over18,000 visits in the preceding year; the June2026 partner figure of over20,000 is also visits, not deduplicated patients. Neither threshold supports an exact growth rate or an appointments-per-gift slope. The Summer2026 newsletter still anticipated first dental patients; no September completed-volume, staffing-hours or wait-list count was found. Twelve physical positions do not establish twelve concurrently staffed treatment chairs. [Visit report](https://www.parkerfamilyhealthcenter.org/news-events/volunteerrecognition) [Summer newsletter](https://mailchi.mp/8817aefb6a34/parker-newsletter-summer2026-17245064) County FY2026 draft action plan printedpp45–46 estimates over1,100 low-income residents in a proposed nursing-cost application, not observed deduplicated throughput; it does not replace the1,368 inference. [County draft](https://www.co.monmouth.nj.us/documents/24/FY2026_AAP_Draft.pdf)

The October 2 recalibration freshly rechecked selected original returns, audit pages, patient eligibility and the dental announcement. Inferred medical reach and forecast dental demand remain distinct from observed unique patients. Current model quantities describe conditional opportunities and completed courses, not measured additional appointments or patient outcomes. A patient-to-household mapping and the residual medical/dental family overlap remain unmeasured.
sections.qualitative:
The plausible mechanism is continued access to medications and coordinated clinical care, producing symptom/function improvement and, potentially, prevention of later disease. Oregon's randomized Medicaid experiment reduced depression and financial strain but did not detect significant two-year improvements in selected physical-health measures. Wide intervals permit clinically meaningful effects; the result does not prove physical care is ineffective. Insurance differs from Parker's clinic, and SF-8 scores are not QALYs. [Original trial](https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2022-08/nejmsa1212321.pdf) A 2024 Noor free-clinic paper estimates health value by attaching lifetime preventive-service coefficients to annual service records; it does not observe causal QALYs. We do not transfer its 146-QALY or ROI claim. [Original study](https://d-nb.info/1352896346/34) Parker-specific controlled outcomes remain missing. The historical model consequently retained a finite one-year clinical utility prior and no separate mortality award. Dental pain relief is plausible; the explicit prospective dental scenario is a feasibility illustration, not observed benefit or a second full-health award to overlapping patients.

Alternative bridge: the Oregon2018 follow-up is the same experiment, not an independent replication. Its9.15-percentage-point depression-screen reduction is a prevalence difference, not a QALY or general clinical response rate. A deliberately conditional depression-only stress substitutes .0915 for the broad .25 response prior and interprets a=.5 as combined clinic-transfer/care-additionality discount. With the remaining utility, duration and funding priors, this gives1.043752 QALYs and $23.26m per10. It replaces rather than adds to central health gains. No validated PHQ-to-utility mapping or Parker depression cohort supports this conversion; it is a plausibility stress, not a Parker causal estimate or confidence interval. [Original follow-up](https://www.milbank.org/wp-content/uploads/mq/volume-96/march-2018/BAICKER_et_al-March-2018.pdf)

The current recalibration separately reassesses medical and dental finite symptom/function effects and signed household resources. The original insurance paper was read only in targeted tables/results; the labor evidence is the investigators’ summary, not the blocked full paper, and dental evidence is a primary indexed observational abstract. None supplies a measured Parker QALY or earnings coefficient. The numeric inputs remain declared planning judgments, with adverse, zero and unknown alternatives.
sections.cost:
GiveBetter estimates approximately **$10.2 million per better life** for this conditional comparison of Parker’s medical and dental work, including health and household resources. Free care is promising because it can improve symptoms and functioning while protecting household budgets. This calculation tests explicit selected pathways; it is not an identified expected return or a verified package of additional appointments.

**What does support buy?** Under a $10,000 normalization, 90% of the budget goes to medical care and 10% to dental care. The model estimates **1.95 medical opportunities**, **1.66 completed courses**, **0.83 otherwise-unmet care equivalents** and **0.12 responders**. Dental contributes **0.27 distinct opportunities**, **0.19 completed courses**, **0.094 otherwise-unmet equivalents** and **0.038 responders**. Fractional figures are expected planning units, not clinic prices or promised patients. Dental spending displaces medical dollars; the full gift stays in the numerator.

Annual medical reach of 1,368 remains an inference from 342 diabetes patients and an approximate quarter-patient share, not a verified deduplicated cohort. Dental reach of 500 is half a first-year forecast, with a further 75% distinct-benefit factor. These are independent physical priors, not patient counts generated from spending. The overlap factor does not identify unique households: remaining repeat-patient and family overlap are unmeasured. Funding response is 25%, medical completion 85% and dental completion 70%, each a declared judgment.

**From care to health.** We partition completed recipients into 30% who would purchase equivalent care, 20% who would obtain equivalent free care and 50% who would otherwise lack it. Purchasers and equivalent-free recipients receive no duplicate clinical credit. Among otherwise-unmet patients, medical response is judged at 15%, with 0.08 utility improvement for a finite year, annual waning 0.5, a quarter-year delay and 3% discounting. Dental response is 40%, with 0.05 utility for six months. Medical and dental harms of 0.001 and 0.002 healthy years per additional completed unmet course, plus 0.00001 independent harm per offered attempt, are fully charged. The result is **0.007561 local healthy years per $10,000**, or approximately **$13.2M per ten health years**. No mortality, permanent screening-prevention or lifetime benefit is inserted.

These symptom and function assumptions are independently reconsidered, not measured Parker effects or converted SF-8 scores. The Oregon insurance experiment found mental-health and financial-protection improvements but no significant short-run measured physical-health effect. Insurance differs from a free clinic. Observational dental evidence supports symptom-relief plausibility, not a Parker response coefficient. Lower-benefit, zero-response and adverse alternatives are substantive stresses, not confidence intervals.

**Household savings, costs and earnings.** Otherwise-purchasers save a judged $300 for medical care or $200 for dental care in actual counterfactual household payments. These are not donated-retail values, provider costs or insurance payments; forgone care does not create a purchase saving. Thirty percent of all offered households incur $60 medical or $40 dental incremental travel or actual lost disposable pay, including failed completion. Twenty percent of newly treated unmet households incur $100 medical or $50 dental maintenance costs relative to their without-gift route. Leisure time is not treated as lost wages.

Only unmet completed responders receive the recovery-pay pathway: 40% are affected workers, with $400 annualized medical recovery pay for one year or $200 dental recovery pay for six months. These are judgments about people alive in both worlds, not baseline wages credited because someone survives. Half the positive earnings welfare is retained to avoid overlap with clinical function; negative earnings are fully debited. The investigators’ employment null makes no-pay and negative-pay cases important.

Purchaser, access, completion, acquisition and maintenance states are evaluated separately before logarithms. Cash adjusts a judged $25,000 household resource baseline before recovery pay is valued. The inherited Coefficient Giving crosswalk expresses these signed changes in health-equivalent welfare units, not clinical QALYs. Discounted raw household cash is approximately **+$103** and recovery pay **+$21** per $10,000 normalization. Their welfare equivalents are **+0.002047** and **+0.000208**, respectively. Adding resources to health yields **0.009816 equivalents** and the combined **$10.2M** price. Patient-to-household mapping, baseline, payment incidence and worker response remain unmeasured.

**Cash-like costs, gross resources and locality.** The FY2024 audit reports $1,954,936 operating expense. Restoring $22,722 netted fiduciary fees once gives $1,977,658 gross expense. Removing $401,902 expensed donated services and supplies gives a **$1,575,756 cash-like accrual proxy**, which still includes depreciation and accruals: it is neither cash flow nor marginal capacity. Capitalized donated equipment is not wrongly removed from annual expense. The return’s different noncash total remains unreconciled.

Dental annual cash and gross budgets of $350,000 and $500,000 are explicit planning judgments, not audited current costs. The matched gross institutional envelope is approximately $12,724 per $10,000 normalization and gives **$13.0M per better life**. It is incomplete where additional external medicines, nursing and partner space remain unmeasured; the old augmented resource envelope remains a diagnostic. Health and household residence shares are independently parameterized at 100% for the Monmouth/NYC metropolitan scope, not NYC city. Eligibility supports this scope but is not a joined address dataset.

**What changed?** The previous **$7.71M** estimate used an augmented annual resource numerator and inherited broad clinical assumptions. The new model separately considers cash-like and gross boundaries, revised finite clinical response, dental budget displacement, alternative care and signed household resources. The old thirteen-case model is preserved in history. This is a change in the comparison and judgments, not evidence of observed organizational deterioration or a measured donation return.
sections.funding:
The newly read signed audit confirms FY2024 gross operating expense $1,954,936 and FY2023 $2,155,804. FY2024 equals return expense $1,917,459 plus $37,477 netted event expense. Audit note3 separately nets fiduciary fees $9,129+$13,593=$22,722 against investment return; these are restored in the whole-recipient model, while securities principal and unrealized gains are not costs. Note10 identifies $3,316,303 available for general expenditure at December 2024 after restrictions and designations—1.70 times annual gross operating expense, not a current cash runway. The $1,164,941 board-designated endowment can be appropriated by board vote; $458,482 moved to operations in 2024. [Signed audit, notes3/9/10](https://www.parkerfamilyhealthcenter.org/s/Signed-Audit-2024.pdf)

Note13 recognizes services $357,328, supplies $44,574 and capital equipment $40,000; Schedule M reports different service/equipment categories ($433,394/$15,000). The category discrepancy remains unresolved although total expense reconciles. Nursing time is unrecognized. The historical model retained transparent external medication/nursing allowances and does not add either in-kind disclosure again. Note14 provides donated dental space from May2025 at nominal $1 rent, with Parker funding buildout; current fair-value operating cost is unknown.

A July2026 state allocation awards $438,215 for Parker oral-health/diabetes/hypertension initiatives; this is announced funding, not verified disbursement or recurring revenue. [State allocation, p6](https://nj.gov/rural-health-transformation/documents/njrht-funding-allocations-2026.pdf) The grantmaker also confirms a 2025 $100,000 dental award. [Grant confirmation](https://impact100jerseycoast.org/impact-100-jersey-coast-opens-applications-for-2026-100k-grants/) Existing grants, endowment support, volunteer labor and partners remain in the counterfactual. No current costed residual funding gap was verified. Coverage changes may raise adult demand after September30, while income-eligible child coverage continues; demand alone does not show donation-sensitive capacity. [NJ guidance](https://nj.gov/humanservices/dmahs/obbba/non-citizen/) [Child coverage](https://www.nj.gov/coverallkids/faqs/)

The applicable state RFA specifies monthly cost reimbursement, conditional performance/payment, no supplanting of existing or anticipated funding, and no new construction. The published initial project period runs February–October2026; Parker's signed contract/amendments were not obtained. Thus the award is not unrestricted current cash, and cannot automatically be subtracted dollar-for-dollar from an unspecified new-gift opportunity. Request the approved activity budget, payments, unreimbursed costs and excluded operating needs. [RFA pp16–22,30](https://nj.gov/rural-health-transformation/documents/njrht-2026-rfa-advancing-technology-prevention-workforce-capacity.pdf)

Provident lists $20,000/year for2025–27 outreach/diabetes work; Monmouth Park Charity Fund confirms a2025 $20,000 dental award. These are committed baseline resources, not a measured residual gap or evidence of present balances. No aggregate annual grant total is inferred across differently timed awards. [Provident](https://www.theprovidentbankfoundation.org/our-grants/2025-empowerment) [Dental grant](https://www.mpcharityfund.org/parker-family-health-center-receives-20000-grant-for-dental-clinic-in-monmouth-county/)

The October 2 audit check separates $401,902 expensed noncash services/supplies from $40,000 capitalized equipment. Cash-like accrual support is $1,575,756 and gross expense with restored fees is $1,977,658; neither establishes current cash flow or marginal appointment capacity. Return/audit noncash differences and the old external medicine/nursing allowances remain unresolved. The conditional dental allocation and standalone budgets are judgments, not grant quotes. Original annual expenses below remain accounting figures, separate from these modeling boundaries.

model.costScope: Entire donor budget with separate medical/dental cash-like accrual support proxies; matched gross institutional allocation separately retained. Not cashflow, capacity quote or all societal inputs.
model.geographicAttribution: NYC metro health and resource residence separately parameterized1 for Monmouth eligibility; not NYC-city or whole-USA effect. Patient/household overlap and addresses unmeasured.
model.formula: MedicalOffers=gift*(1-dentalAllocation)/medicalCash*medicalN*funding; dental analogous with dedup. Completed=offers*completion; unmet=completed*(1-buyer-free); responders=unmet*response. Finite utility minus declared harms, plus signed cash-first household state logarithms. Price=10*gift/(local health+local resource equivalents) when known positive.
model.counterfactual: Purchased equivalent care, equivalent free care and unmet care are disjoint planning groups; matching clinical effects cancel for equivalent-care groups. Actual induced expenses and finite common-alive earnings remain separate.
model.attribution: Medical/dental budget allocation displaces dollars rather than adding free output. Reach, family mapping, alternative care, funding response and clinical/earnings effects are separate declared judgments.
model.uncertainty: No identified expected donation return, empirical posterior, current capacity or full-portfolio lower bound. Clinical/resource/native unknowns and adverse alternatives remain distinct.
model.nativeOutcomes: Per10K:1.95 medical offers/1.66 completed/0.83 unmet/0.12 responders;0.27 dental offers/0.19 completed/0.094 unmet/0.038 responders. Health0.007561 plus resources0.002255.

historicalModel.costScope: Augmented recipient expense envelope: 2024 gross operating expense plus netted fiduciary fees and judgmental external medication/nursing allowances. Not a measured complete resource cost or a verified marginal cash-gift price. External medication allowance may overlap recognized prescription/supply expense; no arbitrary subtraction is made without reconciliation.
historicalModel.geographicAttribution: Medical Monmouth residency criterion supports g=1 for the modeled medical cohort; sensitivity g=.95 allows leakage. Proposed dental service and state grant areas Monmouth/Ocean are within the official 22-county NYC MSA. Service eligibility is not a measured match of every beneficiary address.
historicalModel.formula: C=C0+I+M*w+H*s*k+Cd; N=(D/share)*f; v=rho+ln(1+d); A=(1-exp(-v*T))/v; Qmedical=N*a*b*(p*u*A-h); Qdental=Nd*rd*ad*b*(pd*ud*Td-hd)*od; Qall=Qmedical+Qdental; QMSA=g*Qall; price10=10*C/QMSA if positive, otherwise null. Dental term is scenario-only, half-year undiscounted approximation; it is not included in central.
historicalModel.counterfactual: Existing clinic operations, accumulated reserves, appropriated public/private funding, free medicines, other safety-net care and volunteer supply continue. a reflects treatment substituted from alternatives; b is the unknown proportional output response to new unrestricted funding beyond that baseline. Keeping b=.25 is an explicit prior, not inferred from a funding request or asset ratio; 0,.1,.15 and .5 sensitivities expose this uncertainty.
historicalModel.attribution: One inferred medical cohort, with aggregate net clinical response, prevents additive counting of overlapping chronic disease, mental health, nutrition and screenings. Central dental and policy gains are unpriced, not proven zero; prospective dental scenario applies additionality and residual-overlap factors and adds an illustrative annual resource allowance.
historicalModel.uncertainty: A deeper evidence review, not evidence of causal health effectiveness. Prices are conditional estimates without a calibrated posterior or confidence interval. Current marginal medical and dental output/cost curves are missing; financial solvency does not prove funding irrelevance, and an opening does not prove new gifts caused it. Sources attached to judgment inputs provide context only, not estimates of the numerical coefficients. High two-year gains assume persistence after one funded year; high-recurring-cost explicitly charges a second identical annual envelope.
historicalModel.nativeOutcomes: Inferred 1,368 medical people become 171 additional clinical-access equivalents under a=.5 and b=.25; 42.75 modeled responders receive finite utility gain. These are conditional equivalents, not measured successes. Central QALYs are 3.147996.

reports.program: Whole recipient; maternal, infant and early-childhood health scenario

acceptance.evidence: Independent fifth-three audit 2026-09-14; conditional alpha model accepted with listed precise clarifications. Not an endorsement or verified marginal funding offer.

what: NMPP supports families through perinatal case management, home visiting, doula care, clinical partnerships and early-childhood education.
The modeled health pathways include maternal well-being, nonfatal infant morbidity, rare infant deaths and modest early-childhood health gains.
All recipient operating costs remain in the denominator, with explicit overlap, public-funding and geographic adjustments.
strengths: Primary reports document substantial ongoing perinatal and early-childhood services.
Independent research supports several mechanisms, while current city audit evidence identifies delivery barriers.
The model addresses material family-health pathways without converting every referral or birth into an outcome.
reservations: Cohort overlap and the number of births actually exposed to intensive care are not directly measured.
Rare-event, utility and donor-response inputs are explicit judgments.
FY2024 is available only as a later-return comparative, not independently verified gross accounts.

sections.what: NMPP, EIN 13-3782555, is the whole charitable recipient, including Head Start/Pre-K, Healthy Families, PICHC, Healthy Journey, doula care, pediatric and obstetric community-health workers, workforce and advocacy activities. Healthy Journey focuses on Harlem ZIP codes and also serves displaced families. Hospital partnerships may serve residents beyond those ZIP codes. [Current program scope](https://nmppcares.org/services/ghhs)
sections.monitoring:
The original 2024 report's charts show 210 PICHC clients and 93 births, 242 Healthy Journey clients and 83 Healthy Families families. It separately reports 90 postpartum-doula enrollments, 117 obstetric-CHW enrollments and 185 Head Start students. These are not disjoint unique people. The model applies an explicit overlap adjustment to the five maternal/family program counts and uses a separate assumed annual birth cohort; it does not sum every referral, visit or doula trainee. [Original report](https://nmppcares.org/sites/default/files/Years%20in%20review/NMPP%202024%20Year%20In%20Review%20Final.pdf)

The city's 2025 doula audit found favorable aggregate comparisons but no randomized local effect, fragmented data and inconsistent shelter access. Those limitations matter for precisely the families NMPP aims to reach. The sepsis partnership paper describes community-centered research, not demonstrated deaths prevented. Neither historical paid-leave enactment nor all future sepsis gains is awarded to a new gift. [City audit](https://comptroller.nyc.gov/reports/audit-report-on-the-new-york-city-department-of-health-and-mental-hygienes-oversight-of-doula-programs-in-underserved-neighborhoods/) [Sepsis research](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11568907/)
sections.qualitative:
Maternal and infant health is the most plausible severe-outcome pathway, but the estimate also recognizes Head Start's substantial recipient cost and potential short-term child health contribution. A New York randomized home-visiting study found low-birth-weight rates of 5.1% versus 9.8%; it was an older selected prenatal subgroup, not an NMPP evaluation. Labor-support trials support some delivery outcomes but do not establish a large infant-mortality effect. Low birth weight is a risk marker, not itself a QALY count. [Home-visiting trial](https://www.healthyfamiliesnewyork.org/Research/Publications/HFNY_low_birth_weight_article.pdf) [Labor-support review](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003766_continuous-support-women-during-childbirth)

The numerical model therefore uses much smaller explicit net clinical priors rather than importing the trial's full birth-weight difference. Early-childhood benefits are modest and short-lived in the central case; long-run educational, income, parenting, community and policy effects remain unpriced. Head Start evidence does not justify assigning each student a lifetime health gain. [Head Start follow-up](https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/opre/head_start_executive_summary.pdf)
sections.cost:
The conditional family-health price is approximately $65.51 million per 10 MSA QALYs.

The whole-recipient annual cost is $7,445,700. The five overlapping maternal/family program counts sum to 742 service slots; a subjective 60% unique-person factor produces 445.2 modeled family-care participants. A separately assumed 250 births spans the multiple prenatal programs without counting all family-service recipients as current births. This is not an observed unique birth total.

The central clinical priors are: 0.01 fewer nonfatal infant-morbidity cases per supported birth, with 0.1 utility gain waning at 0.2 annually for at most three years; 0.0001 fewer infant deaths per birth, valued with a 30-year cap, 0.9 utility and 0.005 competing mortality; a 0.04 maternal symptom-response probability with 0.2 utility gain for at most one year; and a 0.005 average child-health utility gain for 185 Head Start students for at most one year. These are judgment-based native health outcomes, not observed program effects or a claim that birth-weight improvement causes all these gains.

Infant nonfatal morbidity and infant survival terms are mutually exclusive outcome channels; the morbidity term has no additional mortality value. Maternal and preschool benefits concern different people. A 50% alternative-service adjustment and 50% ordinary funding response are applied once to the combined health total. The local share is 98%, with lower shares tested for hospital referrals and displacement outside the MSA. Complete replacement and a net-harm case are retained. Added clinical/partner costs and unrecognized volunteer resources are explicit sensitivities. This is a broad conditional family-health scenario, not measured total portfolio return.
sections.funding:
The original return ending June 30, 2025 and the current original audit agree on $7,445,700 total expense, including all programs and administration, with no separately netted event cost. The audit recognizes $146,554 in-kind revenue within its accounts; it is not added again. A $152,615 prior-period adjustment reduces net assets and is not classified as new annual operating expense. FY2023 original full-year expense is $6,974,520. FY2024's $7,162,212 appears only as the FY2025 return's comparative: it is marked noncomparable pending its original gross reconciliation. The older FY2022 return covers only January–June and is not annualized into this comparison. [FY2025 audit](https://nmppcares.org/sites/default/files/2516_001.pdf) [FY2025 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202601339349301115/IRS990) [FY2023 original](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202432819349300908/IRS990)

FY2025 reports $5,019,578 government grants, $532,503 cash, $2,058,352 grants receivable and negative total net assets of $270,747. These indicate funding and working-capital vulnerability, not proof that a private gift creates new clinical capacity. Existing publicly financed childcare, home-visiting, Medicaid-related doula care and hospital support remain in the baseline. The audit and return differ in presentation of restricted balances, so the negative total—not a claim about freely spendable restricted resources—is used here.

reports.program: Serious-violence diversion, survivor recovery and justice-system change

acceptance.evidence: Independent fifth-three audit 2026-09-14; conditional alpha model accepted with listed precise clarifications. Not an endorsement or verified marginal funding offer.

what: Common Justice offers restorative alternatives to incarceration for serious violent felonies and support for survivors in Brooklyn, Manhattan and the Bronx.
It also funds advocacy, national partnerships, training and narrative work, so an ordinary gift is not restricted to local diversion.

The conditional price covers violence, trauma and incarceration-related health effects of its core direct-service pathway using the entire recipient’s cost; it is not a complete valuation of its wider portfolio.
strengths: Current original accounts permit a three-year gross-cost reconciliation.
Randomized evidence supports a restorative-conferencing mechanism, although not this exact replacement-for-prison program.
The model prices several material direct-service health pathways and explicitly tests worse violence outcomes.
reservations: Annual unique cases and episode costs are not disclosed in the current sources inspected; the capacity denominator is a judgment.
Very low reconviction among selected graduates is not a causal estimate and does not identify harm among all referrals.
National replication and advocacy may dominate the true return, but their incremental local effects remain unpriced.

sections.what: Common Justice’s [2025 impact report](https://e1.nmcdn.io/assets/commonjustice/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/CJ-Impact-Report-2025.pdf) describes work with people aged 16–28 accused of violent crimes and those they harmed. Participation depends on survivor agreement and cooperation from the legal system. Its principal direct-service pathways are accountability, prevention of repeat violence, survivor recovery and avoidance of damaging incarceration. The full recipient also works on victim compensation, civic engagement, replication and public narratives.
sections.monitoring: The report describes agreements in all completed circles, 8% terminated for a new crime since inception, and one new violent-felony conviction in a study of graduates enrolled during 2012–2022. These are selected, differently timed observations, not annual treatment effects: graduates exclude failures, convictions miss unreported harm, and no matched counterfactual is supplied. The developing healing scale is not yet a QALY measure. Unique entrants, completion, victim outcomes, alternative sentences and all-referral follow-up would materially improve the estimate.
sections.qualitative: A randomized-evidence [Campbell review](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.4073/csr.2013.12) supports the possibility that consensual restorative conferences reduce subsequent offending and victim distress. Those trials often supplemented normal justice and are not a direct experiment in Common Justice’s diversion model. The central estimate therefore uses explicit priors, not the review’s standardized effect as an injury rate. Consent, survivor autonomy, new victimization and loss of incarceration’s incapacitation effect matter. The adverse scenario permits increased violence and net health deterioration.
sections.cost:
FY2025 gross recipient expense is $8,027,684: Form 990 Part IX $7,972,026 plus Schedule D donated services $19,475 plus separately netted event expense $36,183. FY2024 is $8,472,083 ($8,441,733 plus $30,350 donated services); FY2023 is $6,770,078 ($6,758,628 plus $11,450). All are July–June accrual periods. The model retains the whole recipient cost. Direct-service spending of $2,973,529 divided by an assumed $60,000 per complete case episode gives a steady-state annual equivalent of 49.56 case pairs, not an observed enrollment count. National programs are not removed from the numerator.

The conditional central price is approximately $140.68 million per ten NYC MSA QALYs. The $60,000 complete-case cost is a capacity judgment, not an observed fee or funding offer. Effects are approximated at cohort onset; delayed prevention would lower positive present value. No-prison-health and adverse cases expose dependence on the largest health assumption.
sections.funding: The [ordinary donation page](https://commonjustice.org/donate) confirms Common Justice, Inc., EIN 82-0993366. FY2025 reported revenue is $7,405,997, government grants $1,985,121 and net assets $15,357,301. Its impact report appeals for help amid dwindling resources, but neither a deficit nor that appeal proves that the next gift opens a case. The model discounts alternative services and prosecutions once and funding response once; existing government commitments and enacted compensation reform belong in the baseline. It deducts no prison-budget savings and includes an induced-resource sensitivity.

model.geographicAttribution: Only health accruing within the official 22-county NYC MSA is priced. Three-borough delivery motivates a 98% central share; no national chapter or expenditure-share proxy.
model.formula: N=D/c. F(r,T)=(1-exp(-(r+ln(1+d))*T))/(r+ln(1+d)). Q_all=N*a*b*[v*((1-z)*ui*F(ri,Ti)+z*ud*F(md,Td))+ps*us*F(rs,Ts)+up*F(0,Tp)-h]. Q_NYC=g*Q_all. Price=10*C/Q_NYC when positive, otherwise null. Violence effects over two years are valued at onset for simplicity; a delay sensitivity can only reduce their positive value. Fatal and nonfatal victimization are mutually exclusive; survival is counted once per victim.
model.counterfactual: Existing courts, alternative diversion, survivor services and government-funded work continue. v is the signed net violence difference versus that baseline, including incapacitation; a addresses replacement delivery, b addresses marginal funding response, each once.
model.attribution: No credit for every graduate avoiding reconviction, previously enacted laws or nationwide media reach. Direct service is a central operational mechanism but only about half of program spending; wider institutional change remains a material omitted pathway.
model.uncertainty: Scenario ranges are subjective alternatives, not confidence intervals. Capacity and all clinical coefficients are unobserved priors. The central is donor-useful only as an explicitly partial-health estimate, not a complete portfolio ranking.
model.nativeOutcomes: Complete restorative case-pair episodes, inferred from program expenditure and assumed episode cost. Net violent victimizations prevented, split into fatal and nonfatal outcomes. Incremental trauma recovery among existing survivors and health-only effects of avoiding incarceration.

reports.program: Community violence intervention, trauma recovery and overdose response

acceptance.evidence: Independent fifth-three audit 2026-09-14; conditional alpha model accepted with listed precise clarifications. Not an endorsement or verified marginal funding offer.

what: Newark Community Street Team responds to high-risk conflicts, supports injured people and survivors, and provides trauma care and overdose response.
Its ordinary recipient portfolio also includes school safety, crisis response, community organizing and public-safety partnerships.
The conditional estimate prices several central clinical pathways against the full recipient cost, while leaving wider neighborhood, educational and institutional effects unpriced.
strengths: Current original accounts and a detailed 2025 evaluation identify a substantial local service portfolio.
The model includes prevention of new violent injury, trauma recovery and unique-person overdose survival rather than equating contacts with lives saved.
The latest audit documents corrective actions and the separate fiscal-sponsorship perimeter.
reservations: The local evaluation explicitly lacks a control group and cannot establish a causal reduction in violence.
Return narratives repeat some counts across years and mix clients, participants and cumulative totals, so effective annual reach remains uncertain.
Public contracts, emergency responders and other providers can substitute for donations; long-term neighborhood effects may be much larger or smaller than the priced component.

sections.what: [NCST’s current programs](https://www.newarkcommunitystreetteam.org/what-we-do/) combine outreach and high-risk intervention with hospital-based violence intervention, victim services, a trauma recovery center, school Safe Passage and crisis response. The 2024 original return also identifies an active overdose response team. These are linked parts of a local safety system, not independent beneficiary lists. The estimate covers the most directly defensible material health pathways across that system; it is not merely a price for naloxone and it is not a full social-return estimate.
sections.monitoring: The [November 2025 UCLA evaluation](https://www.newarkcommunitystreetteam.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/NCST-Evaluation-and-Proof-of-Concept-2025-FINAL-.pdf) uses qualitative work through July 2025 and quantitative data from January 2022 to March 2024. It explicitly states that no control group permits causal identification. Positive contemporaneous correlations between interventions and crime principally document reactive deployment, not crimes prevented; nearby stronger causal language is not supported by that design. The 2024 return reports 119 mediations, 137 hospital-program consents, 265 trauma-program participants and 30 naloxone reversals. Some counts repeat older narratives or conflict with cumulative client descriptions. The model therefore applies explicit current-annual and overlap adjustments, and does not sum 15,185 event participants as unique beneficiaries.
sections.qualitative: The [2026 EAST review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42611686/) conditionally supports hospital violence programs, but rates its heterogeneous evidence low quality. The odds ratio is transferred through an assumed baseline injury risk and a further local-effect attenuation, not called an NCST trial. The local evaluation supports trust, immediate response and survivor-service mechanisms. Overdose response can be valuable, but arriving before EMS is not equivalent to preventing a death; unique people, otherwise-timely rescue and competing mortality are modeled separately. School safety, institutional legitimacy, housing assistance and broader community spillovers could be important and remain outside the modeled health numerator; their recipient costs remain in the full-cost denominator.
sections.cost: FY2024 original audited expense is $6,286,421: Form 990 Part IX $6,263,321 plus $23,100 donated use of premises (rent). No separately netted event or inventory costs were reported. Its expense total includes a $157,019 recovery of previously uncollectible receivables; the central forward resource cost adds that credit back, giving $6,443,440, with the audited-total alternative shown separately. FY2023 audited expense is $8,131,996. FY2022 gross expense is $6,362,857 ($6,333,008 plus $29,849 donated services), but is not comparable because it included a CBPSC fiscal-sponsorship perimeter that phased out in early 2023. No synthetic three-year mean is used. Full recipient cost includes administration and unpriced programs; external clinical and emergency resources receive a separate sensitivity.
sections.funding: The ordinary [NCST donation route](https://www.newarkcommunitystreetteam.org/donate/) must not be confused with an optional CBPS Collective designation. The 2024 audit reports $1,288,345 due to CBPSC, remitted in 2025; this liability is not newly purchased NCST service. The FY2024 return reports $3,593,335 government grants and $688,476 Safe Passage revenue; the audit presents program-service revenue as $688,475, a one-dollar filing difference not used to alter cost; $1,487,559 of $3,681,801 net assets was donor restricted. The 2023 audit reported misappropriation connected to weak bank-reconciliation review. The latest audit reports these controls corrected and no new significant financial-reporting deficiencies, while retaining a repeated late-filing finding. The model does not assume a current unfunded gap: only 25% of proportionate delivery is attributed to marginal funding in the central case, and a zero-response case remains.

model.costScope: Full recipient annual forward resource cost, including donated services and unpriced programs. Partial multi-pathway clinical denominator; not all portfolio value.
model.geographicAttribution: Newark is in Essex County within the official 22-county NYC MSA. g=0.98 is a direct-beneficiary retention prior, not a headquarters-based share of national CBPSC work.
model.formula: F(r,T)=(1-exp(-(r+ln(1+d))*T))/(r+ln(1+d)). V=oV*[M*fM*pM+H*fH*l*(r0-OR*r0/(1-r0+OR*r0))]. QV=V*[(1-z)*ui*F(ri,Ti)+z*ud*F(md,Td)]. QT=T*fT*pT*uT*F(rT,TT). QR=R*oR*tR*deltaR*uR*F(mR,TR). Q_all=a*b*(QV+QT+QR-h); Q_NYC=g*Q_all; price=10*C/Q_NYC if positive, else null. V counts unique newly prevented violent injuries, QT existing-survivor recovery, QR unique overdose survival. Effects are valued at onset; one-year delay multiplies Q by 1/1.03.
model.counterfactual: Emergency medical response, ordinary hospital/mental-health care, funded local safety programs and natural recovery continue. External HVIP evidence is attenuated before assigning NCST’s contribution; overdose timely-rescue substitution is modeled explicitly. Funding response b applies once, not again per program.
model.attribution: No causal credit for city crime trends, public meeting attendance or historical program existence. The priced pathways span the central clinical mission, while Safe Passage’s broader safety, community organizing, housing and national learning effects are explicitly unpriced. a is contribution within delivered care, not another donor multiplier. Existing-trauma utility gains must be additional on person-time alive in both arms and exclude utility already included in newly added survival years. The overdose unique-person adjustment must also remove repeat rescues and any survivor already credited a prevented violent death. These are modeling assumptions, not observed linked-person exclusions.
model.uncertainty: Clinical conversion, native event risks, current annual reach, overlap and funding response are judgments. The range is not a statistical interval; pooled OR confidence limits are only ingredients in broader scenarios. Negative effects and zero are possible.
model.nativeOutcomes: Distinct high-risk mediation opportunities and current hospital enrollments translated to net new violent injuries prevented. Existing-survivor clinical episodes translated to incremental finite trauma recovery. Naloxone reversals deduplicated to people with incremental timely rescue and finite survival.

inputs.name: M
inputs.rationale: Part III reported 119; not the evaluation’s differently defined and much larger logged HRI event count.

inputs.name: fM
inputs.unit: fraction representing distinct current-year effective mediation opportunities
inputs.rationale: 60% prior handles repeat conflicts, unique opportunities and current capacity; no claim of audited reach.

inputs.name: pM
inputs.unit: net violent injury probability reduction per effective mediation
inputs.rationale: 3 percentage points net difference for one-year mediation opportunity, not 3% of all city crime.

inputs.name: H
inputs.rationale: Part III says 137 consents; the same number occurs in an older return narrative, so treat temporal accuracy as uncertain.

inputs.name: fH
inputs.unit: fraction representing effective current annual hospital enrollments
inputs.rationale: 80% current-effective fraction; original reported consents are not verified unique current completions.

inputs.name: r0
inputs.unit: two-year violent reinjury risk without HVIP
inputs.rationale: 10% two-year untreated reinjury risk is a local prior, not supplied by the external pooled odds ratio.

inputs.name: OR
inputs.unit: odds ratio of violent reinjury, external review
inputs.rationale: 0.60 (95% CI 0.38–0.94), 10-study meta-analysis; low quality and heterogeneous, not NCST causal evidence.

inputs.name: l
inputs.unit: local transfer fraction of external risk difference
inputs.rationale: Half the external risk difference retained for local delivery and population transfer.

inputs.name: oV
inputs.unit: non-overlapping fraction of combined violence prevention
inputs.rationale: 20% deducted for overlap between mediation and hospital pathways; also avoids separately adding Safe Passage injuries.

inputs.name: z
inputs.unit: fatal share of prevented violent injuries
inputs.rationale: 5% fatality mix prior for prevented serious violent injuries; not a measured NCST outcome.

inputs.name: ui
inputs.unit: utility burden of nonfatal violent injury
inputs.rationale: Physical and trauma burden of a new nonfatal injury; not a fiscal crime-cost conversion.

inputs.name: ri
inputs.rationale: Recovery 0.5 annually; avoids permanent disability assumptions.

inputs.name: Ti
inputs.rationale: Finite three years.

inputs.name: ud
inputs.unit: survivor utility after prevented violent death
inputs.rationale: 0.8 health-adjusted survival rather than full-quality life.

inputs.name: md
inputs.rationale: 2% competing annual mortality; unique victims counted once.

inputs.name: Td
inputs.rationale: Finite 20-year horizon.

inputs.name: T
inputs.rationale: Return reports 265 participants alongside 202 clients described cumulatively; cannot interpret both as annual distinct totals.

inputs.name: fT
inputs.unit: fraction representing unique effective annual trauma episodes
inputs.rationale: 50% prior for annual unique completed clinical episodes, removing ambiguous reach and attendance duplication.

inputs.name: pT
inputs.rationale: 15% extra recovery beyond natural recovery and ordinary care; not observed locally.

inputs.name: uT
inputs.rationale: 0.15 utility gain among extra responders, not a validated scale conversion.

inputs.name: rT
inputs.rationale: Effect decays at 0.5 annually.

inputs.name: TT
inputs.rationale: Finite two-year trauma benefit; existing injuries only, distinct from prevented new injuries.

inputs.name: R
inputs.rationale: 30 reported reversals in 2024; neither 30 deaths prevented nor 30 necessarily unique people.

inputs.name: oR
inputs.rationale: 70% unique-person prior to prevent repeat-rescue lifetime double counting.

inputs.name: tR
inputs.unit: fraction without otherwise timely effective rescue
inputs.rationale: 20% would lack timely alternative rescue; 27 arrivals before EMS does not identify this parameter.

inputs.name: deltaR
inputs.unit: mortality risk reduction in that rescue subset
inputs.rationale: 20% absolute mortality difference within the otherwise untimely-rescue subset, not among all contacts.

inputs.name: uR
inputs.rationale: 0.65 utility, reflecting morbidity in a high-risk rescued cohort.

inputs.name: mR
inputs.unit: annual competing mortality hazard after rescue
inputs.rationale: 10% annual competing mortality includes subsequent fatal overdose and other causes.

inputs.name: TR
inputs.rationale: Finite 10-year survival; no automatic lifetime credit or extra post-rescue SUD benefit.

inputs.name: a
inputs.unit: NCST attributable service share within the delivery ecosystem
inputs.rationale: 50% recipient contribution within hospital, emergency and clinical partnerships; no credit for the whole local coalition.

inputs.name: b
inputs.rationale: 25% marginal response to an ordinary gift; public contracts, reserve substitution and referral limits persist.

inputs.name: g
inputs.unit: NYC MSA fraction of priced health
inputs.rationale: 98% because modeled direct pathways serve Newark, allowing migration outside official 22-county MSA. National CBPSC benefits excluded.

inputs.name: h
inputs.unit: additional QALY harm before attribution/funding multipliers
inputs.rationale: Zero central; one additional QALY of harm in adverse scenario beyond increased violent injury.

inputs.name: d
inputs.rationale: 3% annually; continuous-equivalent log(1+d).

Survival is finite and discounted with competing mortality; no rescued person receives multiple lives.
The adverse case permits net escalation, worse reinjury and separate harm.

Attribution and funding response each apply once; zero funding elasticity eliminates all marginal health.

what: CIDNY helps people with disabilities obtain benefits, navigate care and move into community living.
It also provides peer mental-health support and advocates for accessibility and disability rights.
Our very uncertain, conditional estimate is $59.5 million per 10 NYC-MSA QALYs for the quantified pathways within whole-recipient costs.
strengths: Program-level reporting makes a conservative, unsummed transition cohort identifiable.
Disability-led service delivery addresses practical barriers to using publicly financed care.
Original returns and annual summaries provide a traceable financial baseline.
reservations: Transition totals conflict and program overlap is unresolved.
Health utility, counterfactual success and marginal funding responsiveness are subjective priors.
Public contracts dominate funding, and broader advocacy outcomes remain unpriced.

sections.what: The charitable recipient is Center for Independence of the Disabled in New York, Inc., EIN 13-2984549, distinct from CIDNY Independent Living Services. Its mix includes navigation, transition coordination, ombudsman work, peer support and policy advocacy. The model retains all functions in the expense denominator. [Official program and financial index](https://www.cidny.org/annual-reports/)
sections.monitoring: The supplied primary-source audit records 132 Open Doors transitions, 225 Housing Services transitions and a conflicting 387 president's aggregate. We use only 132; none of the others are added. CBT has 27 unique participants, but reported survey improvement is uncontrolled and response-selected. The 65,000 reach claim and assistance contacts are not clinical beneficiaries. The model requests unique IDs across programs, baseline status, actual additional care, six- and twelve-month health measurement, and unsuccessful cases. [FY25 report](https://www.cidny.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/CIDNY-2024-25-Annual-Report.pdf)
sections.qualitative: Moving to a preferred community setting can improve autonomy, while navigation can make existing health benefits usable. The national MFP evaluation follows 803 survey completers before and one year after transition; it supports plausibility, but neither a randomized CIDNY effect nor an EQ-5D utility increment. Our 0.05 transition utility is therefore a judgment, not that study's measurement. No disability cure, survival gain or lifetime credit is assumed. [Original evaluator description](https://www.mathematica.org/publications/money-follows-the-person-change-in-participant-experience-during-the-first-year-of-community-living)
sections.cost: The central conditional estimate is $59.5 million per 10 NYC-MSA QALYs (0.00016808 QALYs per $1,000). For a $1,000 unrestricted gift, annual output-to-whole-expense ratios are scaled by a 0.5 capacity elasticity, then counterfactual success and finite health gains. Central annual-equivalent inputs are 132 transitions, 708 care-navigation consumers and 27 CBT participants; success fractions 0.3/.2/.3, annual utilities 0.05/.02/.05, and durations 1.5/.5/.5 years. Navigation and CBT receive 0.8 and 0.5 residual-overlap multipliers. Mortality is an assumed 5% annually for transitions, 2% navigation and 1% CBT; benefits start after 0.25 years and discount 3%. Additional community time ends when alternatives catch up. Other portfolio net health is zero as a provisional accounting convention, not proof of no benefit or a lower bound. The formula and every scenario override are serialized.
sections.funding: Annual-summary FY2023/2024/2025 expenses are $8,937,955/$9,831,086/$11,736,265, a descriptive mean of $10,168,435.33. Latest expense includes program $10,283,988, management $1,349,456 and fundraising $102,821. Original FY2023 Form 990 confirms $8,937,955; FY2022 original shows $8,292,256. The website's '2024' return is an image PDF not successfully read here: three original comparable recent returns are NOT verified. FY2023's annual-summary stale footnote is superseded for that amount by its original return. FY24/25 remain annual-report financial approximations. FY25 government contracts $9,643,944 and veterans revenue $1,656,969 make full gift additionality implausible without a staffing constraint; 0.5 elasticity is deliberately contestable. Public care and housing costs are outside donor costs. [FY2023 original return](https://www.cidny.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/CIDNY-06_30_23-990-V1-Public-Disclosure-Copy-CENTER-FOR-INDEP.-OF-THE-DISBLED-IN-NY.pdf)

model.costScope: $1000 unrestricted donor cost; whole-recipient FY25 annual expense calibrates output scaling. Public treatment/housing expenditures and unrecognized volunteer resources excluded; not full social cost-effectiveness.
model.geographicAttribution: g=1 for these modeled five-borough pathways within OMB23-01 NYC MSA; statewide advocacy excluded. This is not all-recipient benefit allocation.
model.formula: For pathway j: k=ln(1+d)-ln(1-m_j); F_j=exp(-k*lag_j)*(1-exp(-k*T_j))/k (T if k=0). Qall=(D/C)*b*sum(N_j*r_j*u_j*F_j*o_j)-h; Qedition=(D/C)*b*sum(N_j*r_j*u_j*F_j*o_j*g_j)-h*gH. Price10=10*D/Qedition if positive.
model.counterfactual: Existing contracts, transition subsidies, other navigators and clinical providers continue. r is the fraction whose meaningful outcome is changed versus those alternatives; duration is only time gained before convergence. b removes grant replacement and capacity constraints.
model.attribution: b=.5 is marginal output elasticity relative to historical average productivity, not a claimed unrestricted program allocation. Whole-recipient expenditure stays in C. No policy credit added.
model.uncertainty: Very weak confidence. Source-observed service counts are anchors, not causal effects; r,u,T,b,o and mortality are subjective. Null and negative outcomes are plausible.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional transitions accelerated, actual care access improved, and CBT response beyond alternatives; these map to finite incremental health utility.

reports.program: Counseling, legal assistance, shelter and economic empowerment for survivors

acceptance.evidence: docs/geography-discovery/nyc-sanctuary-independent-20261005.md: original-source challenge, independent signed welfare arithmetic and exact historical-model preservation accepted. Conditional reference, not empirical expected value or gift guarantee.

reports.priceScope: Conditional marginal unrestricted-gift judgment reference; 10 healthy-year equivalents combining health and signed net-consumption welfare

what: Sanctuary provides counseling and crisis support to survivors of gender violence and their children.
Its lawyers help clients with protection, immigration, housing, public benefits and family matters.
It also provides shelter, career training, job placement and practical financial support.
strengths: An integrated service portfolio addresses safety, mental health and financial barriers.
Original financial statements distinguish donated legal services from paid resources.
Career support includes childcare access, transportation and other practical assistance.
reservations: The $207.1M reference per 10 healthy-year equivalents depends on unmeasured health and financial effects.
Service reach, placements and salaries do not establish additional benefit beyond other providers.
Marginal expansion, survivor-controlled resources, harms and client overlap remain unknown.

sections.what: Sanctuary for Families, Inc., EIN 13-3193119, operates with New Beginnings Housing Development Fund Corporation in the consolidated portfolio. We assess unrestricted support across its services. Training, internships and placement may improve economic resources; legal work may secure benefits, housing and support. [EEP](https://sanctuaryforfamilies.org/our-approach/client-services/economic-empowerment-services/) [Legal services](https://sanctuaryforfamilies.org/our-approach/client-services/legal-services/)
sections.monitoring: FY24–25 reports 9,230 adults and children served, more than 2,600 clinical/crisis clients, more than 7,000 legal clients, 428 shelter residents and more than 450 broad economic-support clients. These are people, not sessions; cross-program uniqueness and therapy completion are undisclosed, so do not sum them. The impact page says 65% find work within one year; EEP reports $41k average salaries without a current annual cohort or comparison group. Neither establishes causal earnings or survivor-controlled net consumption. Feedback and progress forms support monitoring. Needed: deduplicated adults/households, all-entrant follow-up, exposure, retention, baseline/comparison consumption, taxes, benefit withdrawal, work costs and resource control. [Annual report](https://sanctuaryforfamilies.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Sanctuary-for-Families-Annual-Report-FY24-25.pdf) [Impact](https://sanctuaryforfamilies.org/impact/impact-and-results/) [Evaluation](https://sanctuaryforfamilies.org/impact/evaluation/)
sections.qualitative: PATH randomized normal advocacy against advocacy plus eight psychological sessions and two follow-ups in 260 UK women; 64% had twelve-month follow-up. Depression and distress improved, but physical health and further abuse did not differ; missing-data imputation reduced effects. This supports a mental-health mechanism, not Sanctuary's utility, response or injury prevention. The new reference removes uncalibrated shelter-injury credit and halves the prior response (.10 to .05), utility (.08 to .04) and duration (one year to half a year). These choices test mixed crisis/referral/therapy exposure, transfer and persistence uncertainty; they are judgments, not fitted trial coefficients. Shelter can still provide safety and housing value. Retaliation, stress and retraumatization are possible harms; adverse-event imbalance does not prove a causal harm rate. [PATH](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0205485)
sections.cost: Conditional reference: $207,106,666 per 10 NYC-MSA healthy-year equivalents, separating health QALYs from signed independent consumption welfare. This is not an empirical expected value. Annual average non-donated spending is about $3,677 per reported client, or 0.000272 reported client-years of reach per budget dollar; additional reach from an actual gift is unknown. The assumed half-capacity expansion produces 0.000001915 additional clinical responders per dollar. Financial pathways use distinct adult resource recipients, not visits, gross wages or household multipliers. Judgment priors: 67.5 workforce adults (15% of a 450-person broad-support anchor) and 200 disjoint legal/benefits adults; $20,000 baseline consumption; net gains $1,500/$1,000; .25 additional-resource shares; one finite year and one/.5-year delays. A 3% time discount plus .005 ordinary mortality attrition applies; no survival benefit or ordinary extra survivor income is credited. Half positive financial welfare remains after health overlap; negative costs receive full weight across all 450 exposed workforce adults and 200 legal adults without a success multiplier. Positive, negative, clinical-null, neutral, zero-expansion and unknown cases are explicit. The old $34,644,592.51237719 alpha health-only price rises because clinical assumptions shrink and injury credit is removed, partly offset by conditional financial welfare; the full original model remains diagnostic. Full donated-resource burden gives $626,309,186 per 10 combined healthy-year equivalents with unchanged annual outcomes and capacity; donated labor/goods are an economic resource cost, not the gift's marginal cash requirement.
sections.funding: FY25 operating expense $102,237,655 plus $387,934 donor event benefits gives $102,625,589 gross; removing $68,528,009 donated legal services and $161,556 goods gives $33,936,024 non-donated accrual cost. FY24 comparable cost is $31,917,251. All programs, overhead and event costs remain in scope; this is not cash outflow. The 990 reports $33,654,637: Schedule D subtracts pro bono services and $55,009 indirect fundraising from operating expense. Annual-summary $33,539,090 is $9,000 below comparable net non-donated operating expense; this residual remains unreconciled. Only two comparable original years are verified, so no three-year average is claimed. Public, fee and volunteer support stay baseline; no gift-funded expansion bottleneck is documented. The official donation route is live. [Audit](https://sanctuaryforfamilies.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Sanctuary-for-Families-FY25-Audit.pdf) [990](https://sanctuaryforfamilies.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Sanctuary-for-Families-990-FY25.pdf) [Donate](https://sanctuaryforfamilies.org/support-us/ways-to-donate/)

sources.title: FY25 original return Part I and Schedule D

model.costScope: Full consolidated non-donated gross accrual cost C=$33,936,024. D=1 is arithmetic normalization, not a gift suggestion. b maps annual-recipient output to conditional marginal output; actual gift expansion unknown. Existing pro bono labor remains baseline. The reference is cash-like non-donated accrual, not cash flow. Full-resource sensitivity uses $102,625,589 including donated-resource valuation with identical annual outcomes and capacity assumptions.
model.geographicAttribution: .95 NYC MSA share based on local operations is a judgment, not measured residence. Half-share scenario tests leakage; policy benefits unpriced.
model.formula: Health=D/C*b*N*r*u*exp(-k*lag)*(1-exp(-k*T))/k; k=ln(1+d)-ln(1-m). Income=.5*people*discounted receipt-years*ln(1+net gain/baseline consumption)*causalShare*editionShare*independentShare; people=D/C*b*N. Income effective discount=(1+.03)/(1-.005)-1 includes common-alive attrition. .5 is the repository $50k/$100k welfare conversion. Health fields are health-only. Price10=10*D/(editionHealth+signedIncomeEquivalent) if total positive and known.
model.counterfactual: Existing public services, other workforce/clinical providers, legal aid, benefits and self-found jobs continue. Positive causalShare is an additional-resource fraction, not placement success. b is donor expansion separately. Negative scenarios charge exposed cohort costs with causalShare1.
model.attribution: Legal/benefits adults exclude workforce adults; no child or household multiplier. Positive financial independentShare.5 removes possible mental-health overlap; negative burdens retain1. No new shelter-injury or legal-to-health credit.
model.uncertainty: Explicit conditional judgment reference, not empirical expected value. Effects, consumption baseline, resource control, donor capacity and geography lack calibrated data; signed adverse, unknown and null cases remain.
model.nativeOutcomes: Reported annual people, additional clinical responders and distinct adults with retained consumption changes; gross wages, visits, jobs and case wins are not automatic QALYs.

incomeDecomposition.basis: Hypothetical judgment; not measured wage arithmetic
incomeDecomposition.negative: All450 broad-support adults are exposed in workforce-cost stress tests; no placement/causal-success dilution. Net losses -1500/-1000 at full causal/independent weight. Positive .25 resource attribution remains separate from assumed number exposed.
incomeDecomposition.baseline: $20k adult controlled annual consumption includes earnings, transfers and in-kind support; not zero earnings. No redistribution credited merely because survivor status changes.

historicalAlphaModel.costScope: $1000 unrestricted gift scaled by all-recipient non-donated accrual cost including all support/event costs; current donated legal labor is baseline. Not social cost-effectiveness.
historicalAlphaModel.geographicAttribution: g=.95 prior for service beneficiaries within NYC MSA, not measured residence allocation. National precedent benefits unpriced; sensitivity .5–1.
historicalAlphaModel.formula: For pathway j: k=ln(1+d)-ln(1-m_j); F_j=exp(-k*lag_j)*(1-exp(-k*T_j))/k (T if k=0). Qall=(D/C)*b*sum(N_j*r_j*u_j*F_j*o_j)-h; Qedition=(D/C)*b*sum(N_j*r_j*u_j*F_j*o_j*g_j)-h*gH. Price10=10*D/Qedition if positive. For uniformly timed injury events over W years multiply F by (1-exp(-k*W))/(k*W). The full episode T follows each event, so horizon is lag+W+T.
historicalAlphaModel.counterfactual: Public survivor services, existing clinicians and pro-bono support continue. r counts extra response or absolute injury probability reduction. No full volunteer network credit.
historicalAlphaModel.attribution: b=.5 marginal output elasticity is a prior. Physical injury excludes mental-health sequelae and uses .75 residual-overlap factor. No restricted clinical allocation assumed.
historicalAlphaModel.uncertainty: Very weak. Clinical transfer, gift additionality and injury effects dominate. Zero or negative net health remains plausible.
historicalAlphaModel.nativeOutcomes: Additional clinical responders and physical injury episodes prevented; not summed service contacts or legal wins.

what: HWCLI helps Long Island residents enroll in benefits and coordinates the HEALI social-care network.
The health model covers additional insurance access and a narrowly discounted nutrition-services pathway in Nassau and Suffolk counties.
The central model implies about $50.2 million per10 NYC-MSA QALYs.
strengths: Clear Nassau/Suffolk service footprint inside the MSA.
An operating public-benefits and social-care infrastructure can connect otherwise missed residents to services.
The model separates recipient coordination credit, alternative help and marginal funding.
reservations: The 2025 report reproduces a financial activity statement labeled 2024, so forward cost is uncertain.
Network service counts are not unique improved-health beneficiaries.
No measured unrestricted-gift elasticity or recipient-specific utility effect establishes the central judgments.

sections.what:
HWCLI provides benefits navigation and leads HEALI. HEALI contracts with providers and coordinates services; eligible care is Medicaid-covered. Nassau and Suffolk are both in the defined MSA. [Network structure](https://healiny.org/about/)

The report records 4,891 insurance enrollments and 7,000 network nutrition services in 2025. These are distinct model inputs, not health outcomes. [2025 report](https://hwcli.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/06/FINAL-2025-HWCLI-ANNUAL-REPORT.pdf)
sections.monitoring: Track completed coverage, genuinely otherwise-uninsured months, distinct nutrition recipients and completed service intensity, plus pre/post utility with comparison groups. Do not count screenings, benefit dollars or referrals as QALYs. Oregon randomized evidence found improved mental health but no significant measured physical-health improvements at two years; our 0.01 annual utility assumption is an explicit transfer judgment, not a trial coefficient. [Original trial](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsa1212321)
sections.qualitative: Coordination may reduce language and administrative barriers, but providers, public insurers and other navigators remain active without a new gift. The network's own description confirms multiple independent partners and Medicaid financing; HWCLI cannot receive all network health credit. Unmodeled housing, maternal-health and advocacy outcomes are set net zero, not established absent. [HEALI](https://healiny.org/about/)
sections.cost: Central cost is $10,313,844: twice $5,156,922 historical whole-recipient expense for forward SCN ramp-up. Health=.25×[4,891×.3×.01×.5 +7,000×.25×.5×.02×.5×.2×.5]=2.0528750000000002 MSA QALYs, or $50,240,974 per 10. The final 0.5 nutrition factor removes potential overlap with coverage utility. All causal conversion factors are judgments. For an illustrative $1,000 gift, whole-portfolio scaling corresponds to 0.474 historical enrollments and 0.679 network nutrition units before additionality/attribution adjustments; these are normalized activity equivalents, not promises or measured unit costs. No mortality benefit, perpetual benefit or public treatment savings is added. Partner and public medical costs are outside recipient cost.
sections.funding:
The original annual report lists $5,156,922 expenses, including $2,472,321 personnel/fringe and $2,684,601 nonpersonnel, in its activity statement labeled 2024 despite a 2025-financials heading. We preserve the statement year and do not treat this as an audited 2025 cost. Its balance-sheet/net-asset figures conflict internally and are not used for a reserve estimate. No three-year mean is established. [Financial page](https://hwcli.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/06/FINAL-2025-HWCLI-ANNUAL-REPORT.pdf)

An unrestricted gift is modeled as following the whole portfolio, with only 25% incremental capacity after substitute grants, public funding and reserves. Neither that fraction nor the forward multiplier is observed. The website has a donation link, but there is no verified restricted marginal offer. [Official site](https://hwcli.com/)

what: CBWCHC delivers multilingual primary, dental and mental-health care in Manhattan and Queens.
Its clinical teams provide prevention, chronic disease management, therapy and coordinated specialty referrals.
Language access, insurance enrollment help and sliding fees support patients facing barriers to affordable care.
strengths: Direct clinical services provide a tangible health mechanism.
Language access and reduced fees address barriers even among insured patients.
Current original financial and patient reporting supports an explicit whole-recipient model.
reservations: Clinical utility, persistence, patient residence and gift additionality remain unmeasured.
Public/insurance reimbursements and other providers make substitution material; an annual deficit does not establish marginal capacity.
Household medical/travel costs and disposable-pay gains could move combined welfare in either direction.

sections.what: The center offers medical, dental, mental-health, social-work and support services at clinical sites in Manhattan and Queens. Its multilingual staffing can improve access and continuity. Services span prevention and chronic disease management; a visit is not equivalent to an additional healthy year. [Services and history](https://www.cbwchc.org/about-us) [Locations](https://www.cbwchc.org/locations)
sections.monitoring:
Request patient-level residence, treatment completion, baseline severity and quality-of-life change, with alternative-provider comparison and durable follow-up. HRSA quality awards and screening performance demonstrate delivery quality, not donor causation. Oregon insurance randomization supplies a cautionary analogy: access can improve mental health while short-term measured physical effects remain undetected. It does not validate our clinic utility coefficient. [Original randomized evidence](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsa1212321)

The IMPACT depression trial supports a clinical pathway in depressed older adults, but its 0–10 quality-of-life scale is not a QALY and its protocol/population is not this recipient. Hepatitis-B antiviral trial evidence demonstrates disease-specific benefit but cannot identify incremental CBWCHC treatment starts or deaths avoided. Survival remains 0 centrally. [IMPACT original trial](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/195599) [Original antiviral trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15470215/)
sections.qualitative:
Language-concordant care may prevent misunderstandings and help people navigate specialist referrals. The counterfactual includes other community centers, hospitals and insured physician care; an uninsured-only screen would also miss real language barriers. Conversely, treating every existing patient as dependent on a donation greatly overstates marginal impact. [Provider context](https://www.cbwchc.org/about-us)

2025 reported 8% uninsured does not imply that 8% alone receive additional benefit:70%+ best served in non-English languages may face barriers despite insurance. Nor does it justify 20% as measured. The old 0.20/0.02/0.5/0.30 clinical anchor survives only as an explicit conditional judgment; new evidence does not identify a better numerical point. Effective-care and financing substitution are different: the first asks what care adds versus another provider; the second asks what a gift adds versus public reimbursement/reserves/other donors. Both can be 0. Screening quality and awards identify delivery rather than causal outcomes. A claim of cost effectiveness for a marginal unrestricted gift requires a specific capacity plan.

The current insurance page reports a 2026 coverage change. The 2025 uninsured share is not a measured current rate; its consequences for actual donor-funded access and net household costs remain uncertain.
sections.cost: Latest original recipient annual expense $97,126,149 is retained. The conditional clinical reference is 70,000 patients × 0.20 effective care beyond alternatives × 0.02 mean utility × 0.5 years × 0.30 gift additionality × 0.95 MSA residence = 39.9 MSA QALYs. Signed consumption is included at 0 as an unresolved neutral placeholder, not a finding of no effect; combined reference price is $24,342,393 per 10 healthy-year equivalents. Utility includes any mental, dental, chronic-care and symptom gains; these pathways are not separately stacked. Residual common-alive wellbeing, mortality and clinical harms are provisionally 0 and tested separately. No benefit continues beyond its finite duration. The full cost and scaled historical outputs are a recipient portfolio allocation, not an observed marginal gift production function. A $1,000 gift corresponds to 0.721 historical patient equivalents before adjustments or 0.043 additional effective-care equivalents under the conditional allocation, not promised extra appointments.
sections.funding:
The 2025 annual report's financial page reports $82,219,650 program expenses plus $14,906,499 general/administrative expense, totaling $97,126,149. Revenue is $89,787,848, of which $61,388,351 is patient services; the reported decrease in net assets is $7,338,301. Audit status, precise period dates and consolidation detail are not provided on that page, so no audited three-year mean is claimed. [Original report, printed page 11](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/65525600ad11f5d8bc8c3450/6a21d66b1ec4b680b9058e9a_2025%20CBWCHC%20Annual%20Report_ForWeb.pdf)

Giving is directed to the operating health center; the official page identifies programs exceeding conventional reimbursement. A budget deficit does not prove a 30% gift elasticity; unrestricted gifts may replace funds or maintain existing care. Our model follows the recipient-wide mix without claiming a restricted offer. [Official donation page](https://www.cbwchc.org/give)

Deep review retains the latest original full expense. Original 2024/2023 annual summaries give $96,968,903/$86,144,763; their three-year mean $93,413,271.67 is tested, not called an audited mean. The 2023 audit includes Healthview and eliminates internal rent: consolidated functional expense $86,144,763 versus operating-center standalone $86,810,288.2024/2025 audit downloads returned 403; current consolidation/audit detail is still missing. [Original 2023 audit](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/download-audit?download=true&filename=2023-12-GSAFAC-0000036363)
sections.income: Household welfare uses the shared signed logarithmic crosswalk in lib/income-health-equivalence.mjs:0.5 × people × discounted years × log(after/before). Baseline $25,000 annual consumption and half-year exposure are judgments used only for scenarios, not measured patient income. Costs comprise incremental medical spending, transport and lost disposable pay; positive resources comprise actual medical savings and common-alive net disposable-pay gains after taxes, benefits withdrawn and work costs. All negative costs count fully; only positive log gains receive 0.5 independent share to limit overlap with clinical utility. The positive log uses baseline consumption after costs, preventing costs being erased by overlap adjustment. No gross wages, ordinary earnings of additional survivors, public-budget savings, fee discounts versus posted charges, or duplicate value for already-counted free/purchased medical treatment is added. Financial-upside and financial-downside cases are hypothetical balances; unknown-financial has no combined price. [Current payment/sliding-fee route](https://www.cbwchc.org/health-insurance) Income uses household equivalents, not visits or every patient as a separate household. The 0.5 households-per-patient deduplication factor is a judgment; scenarios must supply actual unique affected households before claiming measured consumption impact. Clinical and residual utility exclude the hypothetical additional survivors; ordinary additional-survivor income receives no credit. The survival scenario begins at the shared benefit delay and ends after five years. The resource-effect cohort is independent of additional clinical care: annual patients × resourceShare × gift-financing share × common-alive share × household deduplication. The 0.2 resource share is a conditional scenario judgment, not measured. Financial relief can occur even where another provider would deliver equivalent clinical care; the financial-only case checks this distinction.
