sections.what: VOCAL-NY, EIN 13-4094385, is Voices of Community Activists & Leaders–VOCAL-NY Inc. It combines organizing with harm reduction; the related VOCAL-NY Action Fund is not the donation recipient modeled here. [Original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202543219349328569/IRS990) The charity's current overdose-prevention page offers training and care coordination at 300 Douglass Street, Brooklyn. [Service](https://www.vocal-ny.org/service/overdose-prevention/) Its2024 report gives 14 reversal events, 645 Narcan kits and 5,438 syringe-program transactions. These are different measures and are not added together as independent lives saved. [Annual report, p1](https://www.vocal-ny.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/2024-VOCAL-Annual-Report.pdf)
sections.monitoring: Request incident-level rescue records, repeat-person identifiers, emergency-service response, likely severity without intervention, kit source, participant residence and subsequent mortality. Current reporting establishes activity but cannot identify counterfactual deaths. Track the effect of additional unrestricted dollars on service hours and distinct high-risk clients. Emergency rescue must be followed by effective treatment and care; this model does not claim such treatment gains.
sections.qualitative: The causal pathway is staff/peer availability -> timely opioid-overdose response -> a subset of deaths prevented -> finite quality-adjusted survival. The original Massachusetts interrupted time-series study found lower overdose mortality where overdose education and naloxone were implemented, but its ecological design and older drug environment do not establish VOCAL's effect size. [Study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23372174/) An original Medicaid cohort found high mortality after nonfatal overdose; this motivates substantial competing-mortality discounting, not a promise of 20 healthy years. [Cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29926090/) No separate HIV, housing, syringe, kit-distribution or policy health benefit is added, preventing overlapping claims.
sections.cost: Central cost is $9,186,268 per annual recipient-equivalent. Fourteen reported events imply $656,162 per event at whole-recipient cost, not the operating price of a rescue. The model discounts recurrence, counterfactual fatality, alternative rescue, partner credit and donation response. This gives 0.224 additional deaths prevented before geography and 0.2128 locally, or 0.0000232 local deaths prevented per $1,000. A survivor receives 0.7 quality weight, 0.08/year continuous mortality hazard (7.69% one-year mortality), 3% discounting and a 20-year horizon; the resulting local benefit is 1.1427 QALYs. Thus price is $80.4 million per 10 local QALYs. Scenario prices span $4.66 million to $9.10bn; these are conditional stress tests, not statistical intervals. Zero additional capacity produces no finite positive price. Unmeasured external public and volunteer costs could increase social cost.
sections.funding: FY2024 Form 990 expense is $8,876,913, revenue $13,060,599 and ending net assets $11,325,497. Part VIII reports $5,310 direct event expense. Schedule D reports $9,567,593 consolidated audited expense: remove $386,635 net Action Fund/consolidation adjustment and retain $304,045 donated services/use relative to the return; then add netted event expense. Central denominator is $9,186,268. The audit-plus-event sensitivity is $9,572,903. [Return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202543219349328569/IRS990), [Schedule D](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202543219349328569/IRS990ScheduleD) Assets are not all available cash. No costed current unrestricted funding gap was verified. The50% gift-response factor is a judgment. The [official donation link](https://give.vocal-ny.org/donate) redirects to a checkout; processor payee/tax standing needs final donor diligence. The $304,045 in-kind add-back comes from the consolidated reconciliation; its allocation to the c3 alone is not separately demonstrated here. Retaining it is a conservative cost assumption. Only two years of return-reported expense are available in this packet, not three separately verified annual returns.

sections.what: DuPage Health Coalition, EIN 36-4448208, serves DuPage County within the Chicago metro. Access DuPage links uninsured residents to low-cost care rather than insurance. Silver Access supports ACA premiums, while pharmacy, education, pantry and navigation programs serve additional needs. The official giving page links a Give Lively route; no checkout transaction was tested.
sections.monitoring: FY2025 audit note 8 identifies 5,871 enrollees, not completed treatments, responders or unique households. The model treats this as an enrolled-cohort proxy; enrollmentFraction=1 is a judgment about annual exposure, with a half-cohort sensitivity. One enrollee per resource household is explicitly judged, not observed. A two-enrollees-per-household sensitivity aggregates both participants' full burdens before the single household log. Annual renewal and treatment uptake are distinct. Track additional completed care, residence, unique households, actual spending, copayments, missed work and alternatives. Cumulative people served since 2001 are not annual outcomes.
sections.qualitative: The previously reviewed Oregon randomized insurance experiment supports access and financial protection as mechanisms but found no significant changes in measured physical endpoints over two years. It is not this coalition's coordinated care or a calibration of its clinical utility, response or spending. Alpha k=.75, a=.25, u=.05 and T=.5 remain explicit unsupported local priors, not an empirically calibrated EV. One finite morbidity area avoids adding referral, prescription and mortality benefits again. A quarter-year delay is now explicit. Other programs retain costs but are unpriced in central clinical benefit because completion, effect and overlap are unknown, not zero or a lower bound.

Current Access eligibility excludes people eligible for Medicaid, Medicare, ACA or employer insurance; county residence and low income are required. CareLink is Cook-resident restricted and is not assumed available to ordinary DuPage residents. DuPage sliding-fee services, FQHCs, hospital charity care, medication assistance and changing insurance eligibility are relevant alternatives. Silver Access 2026 terms retain tax credits, member premium obligations, copays and deductibles. No priced unfunded capacity, provider expansion commitment or marginal funding replacement was verified. The full portfolio and next-dollar response remain unknown.

model.formula: annual=N*enrollmentFraction; exposed=annual*b; clinical=exposed*k*a; otherExposed=otherHouseholds*b; union=exposed+otherExposed. Q_all=clinical*u*discounted finite years−union*harm/discount(delay); Q_MSA=Q_all*g. Household count=exposed*householdsPerEnrollee; all participant costs aggregate per household before one CG log. Price10=10*(C+partnerCost)/(clinical+signed resources); unknown partner cost gives unknown price.
model.counterfactual: Existing DuPage sliding-fee/FQHC/hospital charity care and insurance alternatives, not Cook-only assistance; some patients otherwise forgo care.
model.attribution: Enrollment exposure, annual funded response, clinical uptake/response and actual resource success are distinct judgments; partner annual costs stay full regardless of clinical success.
model.uncertainty: Conditional reference, not calibrated EV or complete portfolio. Partner opportunity costs, households, local utility, net savings and marginal funding unresolved.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional completed coordinated care, finite morbidity utility and signed actual otherwise-paid medical/premium resources; no debt face value or retail-care income.

historicalAlphaModel.formula: Q_all=N*k*a*u*T*b; Q_MSA=Q_all*g; cost=(C+R)*f; price10=10*cost/Q_MSA
historicalAlphaModel.costScope: Full DHC recipient expense, including recorded pantry in-kind; excludes partner care reported above $50m. This is a recipient-budget perspective, not full economic resource cost. The $50m sensitivity is a rounded reported-value floor illustration, not an upper bound or measured opportunity cost.
historicalAlphaModel.counterfactual: a removes equivalent care elsewhere and ineffective care; b separately removes replacement financing/volunteer capacity. One morbidity pathway avoids double counting.
historicalAlphaModel.geographicAttribution: DuPage residence required; .99 allows mobility/errors within the pinned MSA framework.
historicalAlphaModel.uncertainty: Central illustrative scenario and favorable/poor bounds are judgments, not calibrated EV or confidence interval. Cross-recipient results cannot be summed without deduplication. These costs are whole-portfolio equivalents, not marginal gift purchase guarantees. Cost numerators use different accounting recognition of donated care; central prices must not be interpreted as a comparable economic-efficiency ranking. Favorable and poor scenarios are illustrative cases, not exhaustive bounds.

reports.program: Uninsured adult primary, dental, behavioral and navigation care in McHenry County

what: Family Health Partnership Clinic provides primary, dental and behavioral care to uninsured adults in McHenry County.
Its onsite dispensary and referral coordination can make treatment and chronic-disease management more accessible.
The narrow conditional reference is $30.969 million per ten combined healthy-year welfare equivalents; it is not a calibrated estimate of the whole clinic or a marginal donation.
strengths: Local continuity of care, medication dispensing and coordinated referrals address practical access barriers.
The current report separates visits, therapy and prescriptions from health outcomes; cohort deduplication still needs verification.
The original audit now reconciles full recognized resources, including thrift inventory and donated services.
reservations: No local causal utility, event reduction, household savings or donor-expansion response was verified.
Hypertension control is not a symptom improvement, and diabetes and hypertension cohorts can overlap.
Unrecognized volunteer opportunity costs, other program outcomes and the government-funding claim need further reconciliation.

sections.what: Family Health Partnership Clinic, EIN 36-4277029, is the Crystal Lake recipient serving uninsured McHenry County adults within the Chicago metro. It provides medical, dental, pharmacy and behavioral care, with specialty referrals when available. Its official site links the existing Network for Good giving route; an actual checkout was not verified. Patients face sliding fees but are not turned away for inability to pay. Medicaid, Medicare and private insurance are not accepted.
sections.monitoring: FY2025 reports 6,093 visits, 321 new-patient visits, 626 therapy sessions, 12,437 prescriptions and 509 medical/dental volunteer hours. These are outputs, not unique annual people or additional health. January–June graphs visibly report 67% diabetes and 84% hypertension control. Comparator case mix differs, so these do not establish causal improvement. Text extraction from the original PDF third page contains '245 Patients' and '409 Patients', but these counts are NOT visible in the rendered page. They may be obsolete or hidden design text and are not verified observed cohorts. N=409 is therefore retained only as an unsupported narrow chronic-care population hypothesis, not a source-established count. The 245 sensitivity is another hypothetical cohort, not measured diabetes exposure. Unique patients, dose, households and condition overlap remain unknown. Other clinical, dental, therapy and navigation benefits and burdens remain unknown, not zero; the annual denominator is broader than the priced channel.
sections.qualitative: Hypertension is often asymptomatic; good control mainly prevents future cardiovascular events, rather than automatically delivering .05 immediate utility. The retained .30 additional response, .05 utility and half-year duration are weak explicit reference priors, not calibrated local evidence. No control percentage is used as a response rate. A separate finite cardiovascular hypothesis replaces, rather than adds to, the short morbidity area. SPRINT randomized intensive versus standard blood-pressure targets among older high-risk adults without diabetes or stroke. Its initial annual composite event rates were 1.65% versus 2.19%, but serious hypotension, syncope, electrolyte abnormalities and kidney events were higher with intensive therapy. The clinic is not that intervention or population. Event sensitivity uses the observed .0054 annual difference, a judged .25 transfer, three finite years and an unsupported one-equivalent loss per composite event; no separately recurring mortality or survivor earnings are credited. An additional harm stress covers the whole exposed cohort. This illustrates uncertainty, not a recommended local efficacy estimate.
sections.cost:
The original FY2025 audit reports $2,538,482 expenses. It already includes $54,077 direct donor benefits and recognized professional services, so neither is added again. Pink Door sales separately net $100,874 inventory cost, producing full gross recognized resources of $2,639,356. The 990 reconciliation reaches the same audit amount through $2,393,158 functional expenses + $86,349 donated services + $58,975 event expense. The different audit event classification is not an extra cost. Note 9 recognizes $73,999 professional services and $12,350 other services; unpaid volunteer time is not reflected. The central recognized-resource boundary therefore does not establish complete economic cost. $25,000/$100,000 additional nonoverlapping volunteer opportunity budgets and unknown-cost cases are separate. Current official financial links yielded FY2025 only; comparable prior full-cost years were not verified in this bounded review.

Full annual costs remain in the denominator. b=.35 is an unsupported annual funded-work response beyond replacement funding, alternative care and volunteer capacity, not an extra haircut on already demonstrated incremental outcomes. b=1 is shown. A marginal gift has no verified capacity price. The judged 409-person narrow cohort × .35 exposes 143.15 patient units; .30 clinical response gives 42.945 people. Half-year .05 utility, quarter-year delay, 3% discount and .98 metro share give 1.044406 clinical QALYs. The old 6,093 × .25 episode prior and $6.735524 million health-only price are frozen diagnostically; narrowing is a scope correction, not proof that all other benefits are absent.

Signed household resources are counted separately and once. A .30 resource-success prior among the same exposure means 42.945 households avoid $300 actually otherwise-paid medical spending within one year, net of alternative insurance/charity, forgone care, taxes, benefits and replacement. This is not retail service value or face-value debt, and these households are not assumed identical to clinical responders. Work gain is unknown-neutral at $0, not measured zero. Each positive component retains .5 for health overlap; each negative remains full. All exposed patients incur a judged $100 incremental annual total for repeated-visit travel, missed work, copays and added care versus alternatives, including unsuccessful or clinically untreated patients. Success households net $50; 100.205 others lose $100. One patient per household and one welfare-equivalent person per household are reference judgments, not observed family size. A two-patients-per-household case aggregates both patients' costs before one log; it does not count visits as households. Baseline annual household resources are judged $20,000. .5 × people × discounted years × log(1 + net/baseline) gives −.192151 resource equivalents and .852255 combined equivalents, implying $30.969081 million per ten combined equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs.

Clinical-null preserves all resource exposure and burdens. Financial-only, adverse, true-zero, no savings, no expansion and complete unknown are distinct. Clinical people are a subset of resource exposure; harms cover the full union. Provider/payer net-margin loss and additional own-resource cost stresses are distinct household incidence, excluding clinical input costs already in the denominator. Central external incidence is unknown-neutral and may include positive or negative offsets; the headline is a partial boundary, not complete world net benefit. Ordinary survivor wages, prescription retail prices, food pounds and thrift retail multipliers are not income benefits.
sections.funding: The audit records $1,387,765 grants, $336,676 program fees, $5,575,072 net assets and $3,758,041 financial assets available within twelve months; the 990 classifies $1,387,765 government grants. The annual report's no-government-reliance wording does not reconcile with whole-entity government receipts. The official program page separately identifies county Mental Health Board navigation funding, but this does not prove it explains all receipts. Ask for the clinical/navigation funding split and whether restricted funding can expand the priced cohort. Note 8 describes $4,210,376 held by a community foundation with redirection power, excluded from the clinic balance sheet, not immediately available clinic cash. Reserves do not prove zero useful expansion. Sliding-fee/FQHC care, hospital charity, changing insurance eligibility and forgone treatment are relevant alternatives; no same retail treatment purchase is assumed. No priced unfunded volunteer capacity or next-gift treatment commitment was verified.

model.costScope: Full annual recognized recipient resources across clinic, navigation and thrift; unrecognized volunteers and complete economic cost unknown.
model.geographicAttribution: McHenry County Chicago metro; .98 residence prior; source geography not measured beneficiary residence.
model.formula: Health=N*b*treatedFraction*a*u*discountedYears(T)−N*b*harm, then local share. Alternate event health replaces utility with .0054*eventTransfer*eventQ*discountedYears(3). Income=.5*HH*discountedYears(1)*log1p(joint signed net/HH baseline); positives overlap individually, negatives/costs full. Headline=10*(C+volunteerBudget)/(clinical+income).
model.counterfactual: Existing sliding-fee/FQHC, hospital charity, insurance eligibility, substitute funding and forgone care; no retail-price assumption.
model.attribution: No causal increment demonstrated. Annual response .35 is a conditional reference, not measured donor elasticity.
model.uncertainty: Whole portfolio, unrecognized resource cost and marginal gift remain unknown. Central is an unsupported narrow reference, not calibrated EV or lower bound.
model.nativeOutcomes: Visible visits, sessions, prescriptions and tests are outputs, not incremental outcomes. Control percentages are noncausal. Hidden PDF text contains 245/409 patient labels not visible in the rendered original, so neither is a verified cohort. N=409 is an unsupported population hypothesis.

historicalAlphaModel.formula: Q_all=N*k*a*u*T*b; Q_MSA=Q_all*g; cost=(C+E+I+S+R)*f; price10=10*cost/Q_MSA
historicalAlphaModel.costScope: Full filed expense plus netted events/inventory and donated services from original Schedule D; external-care sensitivity adds assumed $1m, not an observed estimate.
historicalAlphaModel.counterfactual: a removes equivalent care elsewhere and ineffective care; b separately removes replacement financing/volunteer capacity. One morbidity pathway avoids double counting.
historicalAlphaModel.geographicAttribution: McHenry uninsured adult mission; .98 allows unmeasured mobility/residency leakage; excludes Kenosha and other non-MSA counties.
historicalAlphaModel.uncertainty: Central illustrative scenario and favorable/poor bounds are judgments, not calibrated EV or confidence interval. Cross-recipient results cannot be summed without deduplication. These costs are whole-portfolio equivalents, not marginal gift purchase guarantees. Cost numerators use different accounting recognition of donated care; central prices must not be interpreted as a comparable economic-efficiency ranking. Favorable and poor scenarios are illustrative cases, not exhaustive bounds.

what: Old Irving Park Community Clinic provides free primary and behavioral health care to uninsured adults in Chicago.
Volunteer clinicians and institutional partners support medication access, testing, counseling and specialist referrals.
The clinic offers continuity of care for people facing financial and practical access barriers.
strengths: Current medical and behavioral services establish an operating care mechanism.
Audits recognize much donated care and retain support costs.
Medication assistance and accessible care may protect health and household resources.
reservations: The undated patient panel is not a verified annual unique cohort.
Additional clinical response and actual otherwise-paid savings are unmeasured.
Volunteer capacity, alternative providers and marginal funding remain unresolved.

sections.what: Old Irving Park Community Clinic, EIN 33-1164946, is the whole recipient at 5425 W. Addison Street, Chicago. It offers primary and behavioral care, donated medications, medication assistance, testing and referrals through volunteers and partners. Current intake requires uninsured adults aged at least 18, Illinois residence, proof of income and income at or below 250% of the federal poverty level. It is appointment-based, not urgent care. The official donation page identifies the recipient and links its donation form; no transaction or fulfillment was tested.
sections.monitoring: The current page says more than 2,500 patients and over 150 volunteers, without a dated annual denominator. N=2,500 remains a rounded panel proxy and k=.5 a judged annual treated fraction, not an observed 1,250 annual cohort. One patient per distinct household is another explicit judgment, not verified household deduplication. Request annual unique patients, residence, completed treatments, symptoms/function, actual spending and alternative care. Historical visit counts and the $6 retail-service claim per donated dollar do not establish current health or cash productivity. The FY 2024 cost and current undated panel are unmatched in period.
sections.qualitative: The randomized Oregon Medicaid experiment supports access and financial-protection mechanisms but found no significant changes in measured blood pressure, cholesterol or glycated hemoglobin over two years. Depression and financial strain improved. Insurance coverage is not this clinic's care package; those results do not calibrate OIPCC's response fraction, utility, avoided medical spending or mortality. The retained alpha .30 incremental responder share, .05 utility and half-year relief are explicitly unsupported local priors, not an empirically calibrated expected value. Behavioral and physical symptom relief form one bounded clinical area; referrals, prescriptions and mortality are not stacked. Current Illinois HBIA coverage for adults ended June 2025, but Cook County CareLink and other clinics remain alternatives. Need is not proof of full clinic attribution.
sections.cost:
Original FY 2024 audited whole-clinic expense is $1,060,786, including management and fundraising. Its $660,816 nonfinancial contribution is already matched by expense, not an addback. Note 3 says $660,815 and retains a mislabeled 2023 heading: a $1 discrepancy and drafting error, not silently corrected. The note excludes volunteer services failing recognition criteria. FY 2023 and FY 2022 audited expenses are $1,181,581 and $1,436,262; comparable recognized accrual mean $1,226,209.67. The latest current financial index lists 2024, not a verified 2025 audit. Recognized fair value is not demonstrated economic opportunity cost. Central factor 1 retains the recognized value as a conditional resource-cost reference; .5/1.5 donor-resource valuation and $50,000 extra unrecognized recipient-resource stresses are explicit judgments. They are not next-dollar cash budgets. Depreciation is retained; capital assets are not all recurring marginal expenses.

The full annual denominator is paired with 2,500 panel proxy × .5 annual activity × .4 additional annual funded-work response =500 exposed households. Clinical .30 additional responders gives 150 residents within that union; .05 utility × .5 year after a quarter-year delay at 3% gives 3.647943 Chicago clinical QALYs with judged residence share .98. b=.4 is the conditional fraction of annual work additional after replacement funding and binding capacity, not a second donor haircut on observed incremental outcomes. b=1 is separately shown. The ordinary gift response is unpriced.

A separate .30 resource-success hypothesis gives 150 households $300 of medical spending they would actually otherwise pay within one year, net of insurance/assistance, forgone care, replacement and taxes/benefits. It is not a $300 retail care value or an inference that all uninsured people buy treatment. Each positive component retains .5 for health overlap, then full $100 incremental time, travel, childcare and additional care burden versus alternative care is subtracted. These 150 households gain $50;350 other exposed households lose $100. Resource responders need not be clinical responders; overlap is handled at the positive resource component. One welfare-equivalent person per household, $20,000 annual resources and one joint log give −.671152 equivalents after residence and delay. Extra family welfare is unpriced. Central workGain 0 is unknown-neutral, not measured zero; a positive net-work hypothesis models nonfatal missed paid work avoided after taxes, benefit withdrawal and new costs, not ordinary survivor wages.

Clinical plus resource 2.976791 implies $3.563522 million per ten combined healthy-year welfare equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs. The initial $2.886493 million health-only price is preserved. The increase reflects finite delay and explicit signed household burdens, not new demonstrated efficacy or forced favorable change. Clinical-null retains resource exposure and all costs; zero savings, full unknown, adverse and zero expansion are distinct controls. Full union clinical harm is not shrunk by resource success. Positive-only overlap never attenuates negative resource components. Payer/provider margin loss, outside care costs and unrecognized recipient costs are separate stresses. Central outside incidence is unknown-neutral and incomplete, not complete world benefit; nonlocal household resources and public opportunity costs remain unpriced.
sections.funding: FY 2024 audit revenue is $1,304,302, government grant $263,484 and net assets $1,107,740. The current donation-form statement of no government funding and older audited grant receipts concern different periods and need reconciliation; they do not establish current falsehood or misconduct. Note 3's matching donated expense shows why cash cost alone cannot rank economic efficiency. Institutional referrals and donated capacity are constraints, not costless infinite expansion. CareLink offers eligible uninsured Cook County residents discounted care at county facilities regardless of immigration status, with application and renewal requirements; its former presumptive HBIA eligibility window ended June 2026 and is not assumed currently automatic. Prescriptions and transport have separate limitations. Other free/sliding-fee clinics, insurance eligibility and medication assistance continue in the counterfactual. No priced unfunded expansion, staff bottleneck or funding replacement rate was verified. Complete annual portfolio and marginal donor EV remain unknown.

model.geographicAttribution: Patient g=.98 judged MSA residence applies to health and resources; local counterparty stress g=1. Nonlocal resources unpriced.
model.formula: annual=N*k; exposed=annual*b; clinical=exposed*a; Q_all=clinical*u*discounted(T)−exposed*harm/discount(delay); Q_MSA=Q_all*g. Separate resourceSuccess partitions households; positive-only signed medical/work components jointly net full costs before .5*persons*discounted years*log(1+net/baseline). Effective C=C−donatedUSD+factor*donatedUSD+unrecognizedCostUSD. Price10=10*effective C/(clinical+resource equivalents).
model.counterfactual: Cook County CareLink, insurance eligibility, other clinics, medication assistance and partner capacity continue; some patients otherwise forgo rather than buy care.
model.attribution: Annual activity, incremental annual capacity, clinical response, resource success and residence are distinct judgments, not independent measured probabilities. Clinical/resource responder equality is not assumed.
model.uncertainty: Conditional reference, not calibrated expected value. Unmatched panel/year, causal utility, actual spending and marginal donation response unresolved.
model.nativeOutcomes: Additional completed symptom-relieving care, finite morbidity utility and signed actual otherwise-paid medical spending/work resources; no retail care value or survivor wages.

historicalAlphaModel.formula: Q_all=N*k*a*u*T*b; Q_MSA=Q_all*g; cost=C; price10=10*C/Q_MSA
historicalAlphaModel.counterfactual: a is the share with meaningful morbidity relief beyond equivalent alternative care; b separately discounts replacement funding and constrained volunteer capacity. No mortality benefit is credited.
historicalAlphaModel.attribution: One morbidity pathway only. Other health pathways are provisionally assigned zero net benefit, not demonstrated zero or a lower bound. Visits, prescriptions and retail care values are not added as QALYs. Cross-recipient benefits cannot be summed without person-level deduplication.
historicalAlphaModel.uncertainty: All utility, causal response, duration, funding additionality and residence parameters are illustrative judgments, not measured causal effects, calibrated expected values, confidence intervals or marginal gift purchase prices. Different accounting treatment of donated care prevents comparative economic-efficiency rankings.
sensitivity: Poor and favorable scenarios vary several uncalibrated assumptions together; they are not exhaustive bounds.
Zero additionality produces zero QALYs and no finite price.
Changing cost alone scales price proportionally; changing any multiplicative benefit factor inversely scales price.
At otherwise central assumptions, k=.25/.5/1 yields half/base/double benefit. Current panel and FY2024 expenses are unmatched in time.
missingInputs: Recipient causal morbidity and health-utility outcomes with follow-up and alternative-care comparison.
Additional unrestricted dollars, priced unfunded expansion and binding staff/volunteer constraints.
Patient residence, overlap across services and clinics, and incremental economic cost of donated resources.
Dated annual unique-patient count and matched cost/activity year.
historicalAlphaModel.costScope: Full FY2024 audited recipient expense, including recognized nonfinancial resources and support costs. Unrecognized volunteer time and external partner costs remain outside accounting expense; accounting value is not opportunity cost.
historicalAlphaModel.geographicAttribution: Clinic at 5425 W Addison Street, Chicago, anchors service in Cook County within the pinned 13-county Chicago MSA. g=.98 is judged residence share, not measured; Kenosha is excluded.

what: Tri City provides free medical and dental services to uninsured Central Kane residents. Original 2024 Form 990 identifies EIN 36-4475369, resolving the malformed number previously displayed on its site without inventing a digit.
Illustrative central annual Chicago-MSA QALYs: 1.731300; model assumptions are uncalibrated.
Illustrative cost per 10 MSA QALYs: $8,003,558; not a marginal donation price.
strengths: Original annual unique medical-patient denominator.
Original reconciliation restores donated services.
Central Kane mission provides a direct local-service anchor.
reservations: No measured causal health-utility outcome.
Complete audit and in-kind valuation remain uninspected.
Volunteer supply and replacement financing affect gift impact.

sections.what: Tri City provides free medical and dental services to uninsured Central Kane residents. Original 2024 Form 990 identifies EIN 36-4475369, resolving the malformed number previously displayed on its site without inventing a digit.
sections.monitoring: Original FY2024 return reports 580 unique medical patients, 3,390 medical visits, 3,546 medications and 607 dental visits. Only the unique medical patient count enters the benefit model; dental, tests and prescriptions are not added as separate people. No causal change in patient health utility is reported.
sections.qualitative: Medical and dental access may improve pain, function and disease management. The central pathway models medical morbidity relief and assigns unmodeled dental or other health provisionally zero net QALYs, not a proven lower bound. The full cost numerator retains dental and other programs. Volunteer capacity and other care options may reduce additionality.
sections.cost: Schedule D reconciles audited expense $1,379,104 to Form 990 expense $938,094 through $441,010 of donated services/use of facilities. Central gross cost restores $6,552 direct event expense netted from revenue: $1,385,656. This addback is a modeling boundary choice; no-addback sensitivity uses $1,379,104. Noncash goods already recognized in the return are not added again.
sections.funding: Original FY2024 return reports revenue $1,128,821 and net assets $1,317,382. Schedule D audited revenue is $1,589,022. An audit-expense reconciliation is available, but the complete audit and resource valuation methods were not inspected. No priced marginal expansion plan establishes what another gift buys.

model.formula: Q_all=N*k*a*u*T*b; Q_MSA=Q_all*g; cost=C; price10=10*C/Q_MSA
model.counterfactual: a is the share with meaningful morbidity relief beyond equivalent alternative care; b separately discounts replacement funding and constrained volunteer capacity. No mortality benefit is credited.
model.attribution: One morbidity pathway only. Other health pathways are provisionally assigned zero net benefit, not demonstrated zero or a lower bound. Visits, prescriptions and retail care values are not added as QALYs. Cross-recipient benefits cannot be summed without person-level deduplication.
model.uncertainty: All utility, causal response, duration, funding additionality and residence parameters are illustrative judgments, not measured causal effects, calibrated expected values, confidence intervals or marginal gift purchase prices. Different accounting treatment of donated care prevents comparative economic-efficiency rankings.
sensitivity: Poor and favorable scenarios vary several uncalibrated assumptions together; they are not exhaustive bounds.
Zero additionality produces zero QALYs and no finite price.
Changing cost alone scales price proportionally; changing any multiplicative benefit factor inversely scales price.
No event addback lowers cost by $6,552. Do not add dental patients without deduplication.
missingInputs: Recipient causal morbidity and health-utility outcomes with follow-up and alternative-care comparison.
Additional unrestricted dollars, priced unfunded expansion and binding staff/volunteer constraints.
Patient residence, overlap across services and clinics, and incremental economic cost of donated resources.
Direct complete audit and in-kind valuation methods.
model.costScope: Whole recipient gross accounting cost: audited expense including recognized donated services plus netted direct event expense. Not medical-program expense alone. Unrecognized resources and true opportunity costs are unresolved.
model.geographicAttribution: Primary mission limits care to Central Kane County; St Charles clinic is within Kane and the pinned 13-county Chicago MSA. g=.995 is a judged residence share allowing exceptions, not a patient-level measurement.
model.nativeOutcomes: FY2024: 580 unique medical patients, 3,390 medical visits and 607 dental visits; only the first is modeled as persons.

sections.what: WGMC combines healthcare with homelessness support and care coordination across Will, Grundy and Kendall counties. Ordinary recipient costs include housing, administration and fundraising as well as clinic care.
sections.monitoring: The FY2025 report counts over 1,000 individuals served and 1,707 patient visits. N=1,000 is a rounded floor of all individuals, not unique medical patients; k=.5 is an assumed clinical share. Disease-control trends are uncontrolled and are not causal QALY calibration. Activity in FY2025 is paired with FY2024 audited costs, an explicit cross-year limitation.
sections.qualitative: Integrated medical and housing support plausibly improves access and continuity. Model only bounded morbidity relief in the assumed clinical subset; housing and other health benefits are provisionally zero net QALYs. Do not add contacts, prescriptions or procedures to people. The annual report's $6.8M+ care valuation is a resource claim, not health benefit.
sections.cost: Full FY2024 audited expense is $1,857,494, including the housing program and all support costs. It already includes $182,874 recognized in-kind equipment, supplies and prescriptions. Over 10,000 volunteer hours are unrecognized in those accounts. A separate resource sensitivity values 10,000 hours at judged $50/hour and adds $500,000; this is neither a measured opportunity cost nor a complete partner-resource estimate.
sections.funding: Audit revenue is $2,488,509, including $2,090,709 grants/contracts; net assets are $1,953,389. Finding 2024-001 reports multiple auditor adjustments needed, repeating the prior year; the audit still gives an unmodified financial opinion. Supporting documentation for all contributed services was unavailable. Prior-year net assets were restated, so tax-return values should not be treated as comparable audit totals. No priced unfunded expansion was established.

what: Legal Council for Health Justice provides free legal help to people facing disability, HIV, homelessness and barriers to care.
Attorneys and advocates embedded in health and social-service settings help clients obtain benefits, resolve insurance disputes and secure educational supports.
The program aims to make essential care and basic income more accessible to people whose health needs create legal and financial barriers.
strengths: Medical-legal partnerships reach people who may not independently find legal assistance.
Disability benefits advocacy has a concrete income-security mechanism and documented historical awards.
Current individual-client reporting and original returns support recipient identity and annual cost checks.
reservations: Current benefits awarded, unique households and counterfactual success were not reported quantitatively.
Clinical utility remains a weak prior; external randomized MLP findings are mixed.
Federal transfers and fixed-budget displacement are not free social income; central outside incidence is incomplete.

sections.what: Legal Council for Health Justice, EIN 36-3563802, provides free civil legal assistance through Chicago-area medical and social-service partnerships. Its direct programs serve people with HIV, children with chronic conditions and disabilities, and unhoused people with severe health conditions. Statewide advocacy and IL Pride Connect are additional channels, not all attributed to Chicago. The official donation page embeds a Little Green Light form; the route is current but no checkout transaction was tested.
sections.monitoring: The new 2025 annual report states over 1,600 individual clients. N=1600 is a conservative numerical reference, not a precise count or deduplicated household cohort. The older 2024 report identifies 1,610 clients and a 17.7% Homeless Outreach Program share. The new report spans fiscal finance, calendar-year supporters and events after June 2025, including December legislation; it is not one clean fiscal outcome cohort. A .177 HOP share is explicitly judged transfer of the older mix. Current 47% zero income is not zero household consumption. Resource baseline must include support, benefits and usable in-kind resources, not divide by zero cash income. Cases, web visits, hotline hours and class-action coverage are not additional clinical outcomes.
sections.qualitative: The Houston randomized medical-legal partnership study reported lower stress and fewer emergency visits but higher anxiety and hospital visits. It does not provide a direct QALY estimate or establish this recipient's clinical effect. The initial .20 response, .04 utility and one-year morbidity area remain weak conditional priors, not calibrated expected value. One aggregate health area avoids adding stress, housing, insurance access and HIV mortality again. No ordinary survivor earnings are credited. Full exposed-cohort harm and negative utility cases allow adverse results. Statewide policy efforts involve coalitions, implementation and existing funding; historical wins and broad covered populations are not priced as fresh annual donor outcomes.
sections.cost:
Original FY 2025 Form 990 expense is $3,646,350. Schedule D restores $139,067 donated services; $15,151 direct event costs are separately netted, giving full gross recognized resources $3,800,568. The Schedule D audited expense reference $3,780,384 excludes $5,033 investment expense already in the tax expense; keeping tax expense restores investment once, not twice. FY 2024 gross resources are $3,829,595 and FY 2023 $3,690,934, using the same tax + donated services + netted event convention; mean $3,773,699. These are whole recipient costs, including advocacy and support, not a program-only denominator. Current full audit was not obtained from the official page in this bounded review; original return reconciliation is observed, not a substitute claim of fresh audit verification. Unrecognized pro bono/provider opportunity resources remain unknown, with additional nonoverlapping $100,000 stress and unknown-cost cases.

b=.4 is a judged annual funded-work response beyond substitute funding/capacity, not another donor haircut on demonstrated incremental outcomes. The full annual denominator is retained and b=1 is shown. N 1600 × .4 gives 640 exposed client units, with .2 clinical response yielding 128 people. .04 utility for one finite year, quarter-year delay, 3% discount and .95 metro share yield 4.828189 clinical QALYs. Clinical responders are a subset of the resource-exposed clients; full harms and process costs cover all 640. No verified next-gift capacity price exists.

A distinct benefits pathway uses 2015 native evidence: 74 successful awards among 115 represented HOP clients. This is historical uncontrolled approval, not current causal success. A judged .5 current-transfer factor and .5 incremental-versus-alternative-advocate factor yield .16087 additional awards among HOP exposure. 640 × .177 =113.28 HOP clients, giving 18.2233 additional award hypotheses. The observed 2026 SSI individual maximum $994/month is a ceiling, not this cohort's average; .8 payable/net-retention is judged for reductions, taxes, lost benefits, support replacement and actual usable resources. No SSDI average or backpayment is invented. One finite benefit year after .75-year delay is modeled; recurring annual costs in the two-year sensitivity are conservative assumptions, not observed application charges.

Successful households receive $9,542.40 net annual benefit; positive welfare overlap .5 and full incremental time/travel/process costs $100 produce $4,671.20 net. Each other HOP household loses $100 against a judged $6,000 consumption baseline; other program households lose $100 against $15,000. One client per distinct household and one welfare-equivalent person are reference judgments. Two-client aggregation halves households and jointly doubles both awards and burdens before one household log, assuming similarly situated clients share households; family welfare is not automatically added. Work and otherwise-paid medical gains default unknown-neutral at 0, not observed zero. Positive components are individually discounted for overlap; every negative component and cost stays full. .5 × households × discounted years × log(1 + joint net/baseline) produces 2.495719 resource equivalents, combining to 7.323908 and $5.189262 million per ten combined equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs.

Clinical-null preserves income and all client costs. Financial-only, no incremental awards, no resource gains, adverse, full unknown and true-zero controls are distinct. Federal benefit transfers are recipient resource gains, not net new national income. Matched full gross-transfer incidence allocates the same $11,928 gross annual award per additional recipient across 1000 distinct payer households at $60,000 resources, without positive-overlap attenuation. A fixed-budget displacement stress uses $6,000 counterparty resources instead; these are alternative incidence hypotheses, not verified taxpayer geography. These pathways use the same finite benefit horizon and timing. Clinical care/provider own-resource loss stress excludes clinical input costs already in annual cost. Central payer, provider and displacement incidence is unknown-neutral: the local partial headline is not complete world net benefit or a lower bound. Retail legal or medical prices and gross class-action benefits are excluded.
sections.funding: FY 2025 return reports government grants $1,861,127 and net assets $4,011,092; program service revenue $373,026 supports substantial existing partnerships. Government, foundation and provider funding may replace donations or constrain scope, but reserves and grant mix do not prove zero expansion. Free assistance, SSA self-application, SOAR/social-service advocates, other legal-aid organizations, healthcare navigation and existing insurance/public-benefit eligibility are relevant counterfactuals. Ask for current HOP unique applicants, decisions, award amounts, delays, replacement assistance, household consumption and process burdens. Also request restricted/unrestricted resources, a full current audit and a priced unfunded advocacy capacity proposal. Statewide laws, historical grants and already-funded public benefits do not establish next-dollar causality.

what: Metropolitan Tenants Organization helps renters understand their rights and resolve housing problems.
Its hotline, tenant organizing and advocacy support safer housing and more stable tenancies.
In Evanston, MTO also provides advice, referrals and training under a public-service contract.
strengths: Free advice and organizing can address housing problems before they escalate.
Original city records identify current services and distinguish MTO from its legal-service partner.
Housing stability offers plausible health and household-resource benefits.
reservations: Reported issues are not unique tenants or measured successful housing outcomes.
Clinical utility, net resource gains and additional funding response remain judgment inputs.
The reference charges all recipient expense to one narrow channel and is not an organization-wide efficiency ranking.

sections.what: MTO is the Chicago-based charitable recipient, EIN 36-3351193. It provides tenant-rights advice, organizing, advocacy and referrals; legal representation is not automatically MTO-only output. The current official About page describes these services and links the donation route; no transaction was made. [Program](https://www.tenants-rights.org/about/)
sections.monitoring: The newer City renewal memorandum reports 365 MTO issues between January 1 and October 1,2025, plus approximately 21 text cases with unknown overlap. These are not 365 unique households, successful tenancies or annual completions. The FY 2025 CAPER reports approximately 464 calls jointly handled by MTO and LCBH; those cannot be added as MTO-only outcomes. The return describes a generic 8,000–10,000 annual hotline range, not a deduplicated FY 2025 success cohort. These current records establish activity, not causal clinical utility or net earnings.
sections.qualitative: The reference retains the initial health mechanism but updates the dated cost and narrow activity proxy. All issue-to-tenant, unique-household, response and utility conversions remain transparent judgments. Advice may avert housing stress, avoid moving costs or help recover deposits, but the same household cash flow is modeled jointly; overlapping positives are discounted and negative burdens are retained. No gross wages, legal claims, deposits and landlord losses are counted as independent free gains. Broader organizing, policy and job-access effects remain unquantified, not demonstrated zero. The model is a conditional limited-channel reference, not a calibrated probability-weighted expected value.
sections.cost:
Original FY 2025 Form 990 reports$980,346 recipient annual expenses, including administration and fundraising. ScheduleD reconciles the same recognized cost; blank addbacks do not prove absence of volunteer, partner or full economic costs. Charging all annual expense to a January–October narrow Evanston channel deliberately leaves broader recipient benefits unpriced and partly mismatches periods. We do not annualize the 365 issues or use the$91,600 joint public-contract ceiling as whole-recipient cost. The reference uses judged unique tenant households and incremental service response, with a finite stress-health improvement and one-off net household savings. Clinical and signed income components are shown separately below; equivalent income welfare years are not measured QALYs. Initial$21.815 M is retained as a diagnostic, not the current price. Updated cost/activity and explicit household burdens—not stronger causal evidence—explain the change.

The conditional reference is about $18.2 million per better life: 0.417 clinical QALYs plus 0.120 signed household-resource equivalents. The proxy is roughly $2,686 of whole-recipient annual expense per documented issue—not a marginal price for one successful tenant case. Judged household resource successes receive $600 net one-off resources; other exposed households lose $50 in process costs. The latter are retained even when there is no clinical or resource success.
sections.funding: FY 2025 original revenue$944,614 and ending net assets$601,222 do not establish liquid reserves or a next-donation gap. The City 2026 renewal request has a$91,600 not-to-exceed joint ceiling; the$46,800 base is split$36,800 MTO/$10,000 LCBH. Additional services are billed as incurred; prior under-spending means a ceiling is not a realized capacity expansion. Unrestricted-donor response is judged, and zero additionality is tested. Updated public funding and broader services matter to the counterfactual; no priced marginal commitment was verified.

what: Healthcare for the Homeless - Houston provides primary, dental, behavioral and street-based care for people experiencing homelessness.
It reports clinics and outreach across Houston, including dental services.
Its annual report and federal service return use different patient and visit definitions that need reconciliation.
strengths: An established local clinical delivery route addresses unmet care needs.
Original annual reports, federal service data and audited accounts permit an explicit, if partial, cost and activity model.
Finite dental-pain scenarios preserve counterfactual care, possible harm and funding-response uncertainty.
reservations: The annual report and federal data disagree on dental visits; completed symptomatic episodes and causal relief remain unmeasured.
The reported 659 depression screening/follow-up cases are not 659 patients treated for depression, so that pathway receives no modeled credit.
A funded county dental project was terminated for staffing and priority reasons; current gift-created capacity is unverified.

sections.what: HHH provides integrated primary, dental, behavioral health and outreach care. Its 2025 annual report lists 6,433 people and 19,166 visits, while the federal UDS return lists 2,965 patients and 15,986 clinic visits plus 59 virtual visits under different, unreconciled reporting scopes. The UDS identifies 1,499 dental clinic visits and 595 dental patients. This partial model quantifies finite dental-pain relief only; other clinical benefits are unestimated, not assumed absent.
sections.monitoring: The 2025 UDS measure counts 659 patients screened for depression with follow-up documented as appropriate. That measure can include negative screens and does not establish 659 depressed people treated. Its separate remission cohort includes 55 eligible patients, with the outcome numerator suppressed; it is not a substitute denominator. The annual report lists 3,219 dental visits versus 1,499 UDS dental clinic visits, so completed symptomatic episodes and reporting scope require reconciliation. [Federal UDS workbook](https://data.hrsa.gov/DataDownload/StaticDocuments/H80-2025.xlsx) [Annual report](https://www.homeless-healthcare.org/s/FINAL-2025-Impact-Report.pdf)
sections.qualitative: Local integrated care plausibly meets substantial need, but visits do not prove incremental health gains. [Harris County file 26-5142](https://harriscountytx.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8167289&GUID=9F12FC50-645B-4A78-B668-6049CC4D835E&FullText=1), passed August 17, 2026, terminated a $70,000 dental project that HHH could not implement because of changing priorities and staffing challenges. The [original agreement](https://harriscountytx.legistar.com/View.ashx?M=F&ID=15756863&GUID=E060471F-2059-41E2-8A54-E101BF76C76E) records no reimbursement as of May 31, 2026. This does not mean all dental care ceased; it does show that money alone did not resolve that project’s implementation constraint. The 2024 audit also raises liquidity and staffing-contract concerns.
sections.cost: The model retains the whole organization’s unaudited 2025 expense of $7,844,806, but quantifies only a narrower dental-pain benefit pathway. Using the clearly defined federal UDS series of 1,499 dental clinic visits, the central conditional illustration is $55.6 million per 10 Houston QALYs; the weighted signed scenario mixture is $30.3 million. Neither is a current marginal-donation price. Dental completion, alternative care, symptom relief, utility, duration and cash response are judgment priors rather than measured HHH effects. The depression pathway is unestimated pending a valid treated-patient denominator. [UDS workbook](https://data.hrsa.gov/DataDownload/StaticDocuments/H80-2025.xlsx) [Annual report](https://www.homeless-healthcare.org/s/FINAL-2025-Impact-Report.pdf)
sections.funding: Donor recommendation: HOLD. A city street-medicine agreement described a $700,000 two-year envelope with an initial term ending August 31, 2026; renewal is unverified. The separate $70,000 county dental project was terminated because HHH could not implement it, not because its gift gap was filled. The 2024 audit disclosed a $525,000 credit line due March 17, 2026; renewal and current liabilities are unverified. A current staffed care plan, grant restrictions and a priced incremental giving path are needed before recommending a gift. [City agreement](https://houston.novusagenda.com/agendapublic/CoverSheet.aspx?ItemID=35206&MeetingID=750) [County termination](https://harriscountytx.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?ID=8167289&GUID=9F12FC50-645B-4A78-B668-6049CC4D835E&FullText=1)

model.costScope: Whole 2025 unaudited organizational expense divided by a narrower UDS dental-only benefit pathway. Historical exploratory whole-cost/partial-benefit proxy, not current marginal gift price. Annual report 3219 dental visits versus UDS1499 remains unresolved; UDS selected as the narrower clearly defined series. Cross-pathway overlap multiplier removed because there is only one quantified benefit pathway.
model.geographicAttribution: Care sites and patient ZIP rows support local delivery, but 449 of 2,965 UDS patients are grouped as Other ZIP Codes and some small cells are suppressed. The modeled 95–100% Houston-metro benefit share is a judgment, not measured residence.
model.formula: dentalQalys = dentalVisits / visitsPerEpisode * symptomCompletion * incrementalRelief * dentalUtility * dentalYears; allPopulationQalys = (dentalQalys - harmQalys) * cashResponse; editionQalys = allPopulationQalys * houstonShare; pricePer10 = 10 * costUSD / positive editionQalys
model.counterfactual: Other providers, including Harris Health, may supply some care. Visits count only to the extent they yield additional symptomatic relief versus that alternative; completion and alternative-care shares are unverified judgments.
model.attribution: Whole-recipient expense is retained. Only dental-pain relief is quantified; depression, primary care, behavioral care and outreach benefits remain unestimated. No benefit from the terminated county project is credited.
model.uncertainty: Very low confidence, partial-health model. UDS/annual-report activity scopes are unreconciled. Scenario weights are subjective, not calibrated probabilities; the favorable case drives most weighted positive benefit. Marginal gift impact and staffing response are unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: UDS dental clinic visits divided by assumed visits per symptomatic episode, then assumed completion, incremental relief, finite utility and duration; not observed cured patients.

what: HRAC provides naloxone, safer-use supplies and a low-barrier Denver drop-in space.
Visitors can obtain overdose-response training, hygiene items, phone and mail access, snacks, testing and service referrals.
The project also undertakes outreach and advocacy with local partners.
strengths: Audited project schedules identify full accounting expense without adding sponsor totals again.
Original community naloxone research supports the mortality mechanism, while current recipient sources establish actual services.
The model jointly assesses health and signed household resources and retains full exposure burdens when clinical benefits fail.
reservations: Unique annual opioid-risk participants, incremental efficacy, survival and local residence remain judgments.
Whole annual cost against selected pathways leaves other benefits unknown and does not establish marginal donation capacity.
Donor HOLD: the exact official donation endpoint returned 404; a domain-only login redirect is not a verified checkout.

sections.what: HRAC provides naloxone, safer-use supplies and a low-barrier Denver drop-in space. Visitors can obtain overdose-response training, hygiene items, phone and mail access, snacks, testing and service referrals. The project also undertakes outreach and advocacy with local partners. Current morning attendance and cumulative signups are not unique annual outcomes.
sections.monitoring: Original DDPHE 2023 SAP needs assessment PDF pp13-16 describes 946 respondents, 923 retained, convenience recruitment at HRAC and Access Point, uneven recruitment protocols and a 25-dollar incentive. It pools sites and records housing status rather than county residence. Thus it cannot supply HRAC annual unique reach, a representative HRAC opioid exposure fraction, or MSA attribution. Its drug-use factsheet explicitly does not account for concurrent drugs. August 2026 contract exhibit p8 contains targets, not completed outputs. ARPA period runs January 2024 through September 2026, OAF January through December 2026. Do not annualize the ARPA target, add overlapping people across funding streams, or turn kits into deaths averted. Both streams include third-party kit recipients. Current service page describes over 12,000 signups over ten years and 125–180 visits per morning, neither a matched annual unique opioid-risk cohort. Report annual people, repeat visits, opioid-risk subgroup, reversals and residence separately; none demonstrates deaths prevented.
sections.qualitative: Walley’s original ecological interrupted time-series of 19 Massachusetts communities found lower overdose mortality with community overdose education and naloxone distribution, but does not identify HRAC-specific causal efficacy. Doe-Simkins found no overall change in heroin-use frequency in 325 repeat respondents, not proof of zero harm. The retained 10% incremental mortality reduction remains judgment beyond public supply and alternative services. The alpha model additionally multiplied by .4 marginal-gift funding additionality despite using full annual cost; that extra donor factor is removed for the annual-work reference. Its ten already-discounted healthy years are retained without discounting them twice. Explicit timing reinterpretations and strong public-alternative cases show uncertainty, not confidence intervals.
sections.cost: FY2024 HRAC whole sponsored-project accounting expense is $2,017,429, including $266,735 intercompany support, recorded in-kind program resources, personal assistance and event costs. The audited combining schedule supplies project-specific detail. No additional sponsor gross-up or current fee is added. This is observed accounting cost, not a verified complete economic opportunity-cost denominator. Medical in-kind wholesale valuation, unrecorded volunteer work and external partner inputs retain uncertainty. FY2025 project expense is $1,884,959 and is used only as cost sensitivity because matched 2025 reach is unverified. Contract service location is City and County of Denver. Service eligibility/location is not client residence. Retain g=.95 only as judgment within OMB-23-01 Denver-Aurora-Centennial MSA, excluding Boulder, Greeley and Colorado Springs. Direct personal assistance of $87,517 anchors a judged 10% otherwise-paid consumption fraction, 25% benefit withdrawal and 25% household recipient share. Positive resource gains receive a .5 overlap factor; full $10 participation/access burdens do not. Resources are jointly logged within each household-year, without retail supply values or ordinary survivor salaries. Central health is 56.62 healthy years and signed income is -1.137200581 equivalent years, giving $363,613 per better life versus the original $884,837 clinical-only reference. The change mainly repairs annual-versus-marginal attribution; it is not measured improvement. Recognized in-kind and intercompany costs are already included; outside resource and full transfer-counterparty sensitivities are separate, not automatic second additions.
sections.funding: Organization says gifts support service expansion, naloxone and supplies and its drop-in site. It does not give a priced incremental staff shift, unique cohort, stockout, or match opportunity. Denver adopted resolution 26-1273 on August 31, 2026. The third amendment changes ARPA scope to operations and retains OAF building-purchase language in the legislative title; no agreement capacity or term increase. The attached exhibit mixes procurement-of-facility labeling with operating services. It cannot be used as a clean whole-project annual budget. Exhibit A-03 p7 prints ARPA 489376 and OAF 239345 (sum 728721), while the earlier amended agreement total was 968127 and April's increase was 239375. Preserve this discrepancy; do not silently correct the exhibit or sum its numbers as the current full agreement amount. These are HRAC project columns, unlike sponsor-wide reserves. Restricted net assets may include ordinary project-purpose restrictions and are not necessarily locked capital; the schedules do not split individual donor restrictions. Neither cash nor a 149-dollar unrestricted balance alone establishes liquidity crisis, spare capacity, or additionality. The original b=.4 remains a marginal-funding diagnostic, not an extra annual-work multiplier. Public naloxone support, other local providers and the new operating grant use create substitution questions; state June 2025 award maintained free naloxone through June 2026 but does not establish September 2026 availability at HRAC. Official donation page links https://acefzmsz.donorsupport.co/-/XCYYADTX; direct audit retrieval returned HTTP 404, so checkout success is unverified. Fresh direct GET and HEAD of the exact linked /-/XCYYADTX endpoint returned 404; root’s separate domain-only redirect to login does not contradict this or establish checkout. June 2025 state support was explicitly through June 2026; no extension or current stock capacity is assumed.

model.costScope: FY2024 HRAC whole sponsored-project accounting expense is $2,017,429, including $266,735 intercompany support, recorded in-kind program resources, personal assistance and event costs. The audited combining schedule supplies project-specific detail. No additional sponsor gross-up or current fee is added. This is observed accounting cost, not a verified complete economic opportunity-cost denominator. Medical in-kind wholesale valuation, unrecorded volunteer work and external partner inputs retain uncertainty. FY2025 project expense is $1,884,959 and is used only as cost sensitivity because matched 2025 reach is unverified.
model.geographicAttribution: HRAC explicitly serves Denver people who inject drugs, with Denver fixed/mobile services. g=.95 is a judged recipient residence share within OMB-23-01 Denver-Aurora-Centennial MSA, not a measured address distribution. Boulder, Greeley and Colorado Springs are excluded from the local numerator.
model.formula: Clinical=(N*k*p*netReduction*L_effective - N*harm*discount(delay))*g; resources=sum .5*households*log(after/before)*discount*localShare; price10=10*C/(clinical+signed resources).
model.counterfactual: Public naloxone, other syringe programs, EMS and otherwise-paid household consumption. Annual program efficacy is separate from marginal-gift funding; current supply capacity unverified.
model.attribution: Walley’s original ecological interrupted time-series of 19 Massachusetts communities found lower overdose mortality with community overdose education and naloxone distribution, but does not identify HRAC-specific causal efficacy. Doe-Simkins found no overall change in heroin-use frequency in 325 repeat respondents, not proof of zero harm. The retained 10% incremental mortality reduction remains judgment beyond public supply and alternative services. The alpha model additionally multiplied by .4 marginal-gift funding additionality despite using full annual cost; that extra donor factor is removed for the annual-work reference. Its ten already-discounted healthy years are retained without discounting them twice. Explicit timing reinterpretations and strong public-alternative cases show uncertainty, not confidence intervals.
model.uncertainty: All causal, survival, resource-conversion and residence coefficients are judgments. Source-anchored cost/service envelopes do not establish calibrated EV. Null, negative, unknown, counterparty and cost-scope scenarios are explicit.
model.nativeOutcomes: Original council presentation p29 describes over 4,000 individuals annually. N=4,000 is a rounded annual service proxy, not an audited matched cohort or measured annual opioid-risk population. Original PDF retrieval succeeded. Monthly 797-client and convenience-sample survey observations are not annualized. Exact cost/cohort matching remains unverified.

reports.program: Coordinated child-abuse response, trauma treatment, prevention and survivor support
reports.priceScope: Conditional whole-recipient recognized-resource scenario; child therapy quantified, other portfolio net health unknown

what: Chicago Children’s Advocacy Center coordinates responses to child abuse across investigators, clinicians and family-support staff.
Its Family Hope Center offers trauma-focused therapies and caregiver support for children and families.
The organization also runs prevention and education work and has added services for adult survivors.
strengths: A named evidence-based therapy offers a plausible route from funded care to better child mental health.
Original returns permit a full recipient expense and donated-resource reconciliation.
Coordinated services and a central referral network can address practical barriers to care.
reservations: Reported child reach is not the number completing effective treatment or benefiting because of a gift.
The QALY conversion, program mix, local geography and funding elasticity remain judgments.
New program scope and unquantified other-portfolio net health could substantially change the result.

sections.what:
This report covers an ordinary unrestricted gift to the entire Chicago Children's Advocacy Center (EIN 36-4251865), not a restricted therapy purchase. The recipient coordinates abuse investigations, advocacy and family support, clinical care, trafficking responses, prevention and education. Family Hope Center uses several modalities, including TF-CBT, CFTSI, ARC and ITCT; it also supports caregivers and children with problematic sexual behavior. [Clinical services](https://www.chicagocac.org/what-we-do/family-hope-center/)

The portfolio has expanded since the financial reference year: Imagination Theater entered the education department in July 2025, and CAN Hope launched in November 2025 to coordinate adult survivor services. These activities belong in the ordinary-gift scope even though the quantitative channel below is child PTSD treatment. Retaining their costs while provisionally assigning their net health zero is an explicit incomplete-portfolio assumption, not evidence they have no value. [Program integration](https://www.chicagocac.org/imagination-theater-joins-chicagocac/) [CAN Hope](https://www.chicagocac.org/canhope/)

The edition counts health accruing to residents of the Chicago-Naperville-Elgin metropolitan area under OMB bulletin 23-01. Chicago location alone does not establish residence for every client or statewide training beneficiary.
sections.monitoring:
FY25's annual report lists 585 children and 154 caregivers receiving 7,035 therapy hours. These are reach and service measures; neither hours nor people establish distinct completed evidence-based courses, PTSD remission, or QALYs. The later return reports 7,034 hours, and also differs from the annual report on some investigative counts. The model uses the explicitly labeled annual-report child count, with a half-reach sensitivity, and does not combine the conflicting counts. [Annual report, p. 5](https://www.chicagocac.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/FY25-Annual-Report-Web-12.22.pdf) [FY25 return, Part III](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202631349349313328/IRS990)

The primary randomized trial compared TF-CBT with active child-centered therapy in 229 sexually abused children aged 8–14. Among complete posttreatment PTSD assessments, 19/89 TF-CBT children and 42/91 controls still met PTSD criteria: a 0.248055 difference in probability, calculated from counts. That is not a Chicago recipient estimate or a general-population prevention effect. [Cohen et al., 2004](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1201422/) The follow-up abstract describes persistent symptom differences at six and twelve months; it does not supply Chicago utility gains or demonstrate lifetime protection. [Deblinger et al., 2006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17135993/)

Request linked, deidentified counts by residence, baseline diagnosis/severity, treatment modality, adequate dose, completion, wait time and repeated health outcomes; include non-completers and reasons for missing follow-up. Compare outcomes with realistic alternative services and track adverse events and repeat exposure. Privacy-preserving aggregate evidence is sufficient; identifiable abuse records are neither needed nor requested.
sections.qualitative:
A coordinated site can reduce navigation burden and link children to care after disclosure. The PATHH network maintains a central waitlist, considers slots at multiple providers, and supports families during the wait. This supports a credible access mechanism but also identifies alternative providers that remain in the no-gift counterfactual. A referral or an investigation is not automatically an averted abuse episode. [PATHH](https://www.chicagocac.org/education-outreach-prevention/community-partnerships/pathh-collaboration/)

Clinical evidence is stronger for one named treatment than for the effect of an unrestricted donation to the combined organization. We therefore separate trial-like eligibility, course completion, transfer to this setting, access to equivalent alternative treatment and funding additionality. All local proportions remain judgments. These parameters can be correlated; multiplying them does not produce a validated probability distribution.

Important unpriced pathways include caregiver mental health, family safety, medical linkage, investigation quality, prevention, trafficking response, adult survivor services and theater education. Benefits can overlap with the same child's therapy or with partner organizations. Possible burdens include distress from the process, disrupted families, ineffective referrals and displaced care; the report does not claim these harms occurred. Their net QALYs may have either sign, and the model explicitly tests negative as well as positive other-portfolio effects. Rights, safety and dignity also matter beyond QALYs.

An original four-site quasi-experimental CAC evaluation found more coordination and referrals, yet no observed difference in mental-health service receipt in the caregiver-interview subset. It also could not determine whether higher child-removal rates represented better protection or inappropriate decisions. This supports measuring follow-through and net safety outcomes instead of assigning QALYs to investigation volume. The older study did not evaluate ChicagoCAC or an incremental gift. [OJJDP original evaluation, pp. 5–8](https://www.ojp.gov/pdffiles1/ojjdp/218530.pdf)
sections.cost:
The conditional central scenario is about $131 million of gross recognized recipient resources per 10 incremental Chicago-MSA QALYs, with very weak confidence. It retains $11,750,254 across the whole recipient and produces 0.895902 modeled local QALYs. This is a transparent scenario for an ordinary gift's proportional capacity response, not a measured marginal return, a priced donation tranche, or a claim that spending $131 million would scale this program linearly. Donor recommendation: HOLD.

The child-therapy channel is N × s × c × e × t × a × u × D. Inputs are 585 reported child recipients, 0.5 trial-like treatment eligibility, 0.7 adequate-course completion, e = 42/91 − 19/89, 0.5 local transfer, 0.5 lacking equivalent timely TF-CBT elsewhere, and a judgment of 0.1 QALY per additional PTSD-free person-year. D = 1 + 0.5/1.03: one first year and half the effect in year two, then zero. Multiply the channel plus signed other-portfolio health H by financial response b = 0.5, then local share g = 0.95. H = 0 and unrecognized resource cost K = 0 are conditional omissions. All local causal proportions and the utility/duration conversion are assumptions, not observed effects.

The 0.1 utility difference is intentionally labeled a judgment: an Australian analysis used 0.61 for PTSD and a 0.87 general-population/no-abuse comparator, applying the latter to recovered patients; this is not an observed within-person recovery gain. A small UK early-treatment economic model reports annual health-state QALYs of 0.7725 and 0.7386 (difference 0.0339). Our 0.032 stress test approximates its rounded quarterly values, rather than reproducing that annual difference exactly. Different populations, measurements and comparators prevent either from validating Chicago's value. The sensitivity cases use both values rather than importing either published intervention cost-effectiveness ratio. [Australian primary economic analysis](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1753-2000-6-15) [UK trial-based economic analysis](https://research-management.mq.edu.au/ws/portalfiles/portal/104362189/104200376.pdf)

Funding response b means a small increment in unrestricted resources yields half as much extra usable capacity as proportional historic output scaling would suggest. This is a hypothetical local derivative, conditional on hiring/capacity, stable program mix and no binding restriction. The model gives no health credit when grants/reserves replace the gift (b = 0), when equivalent care is available (a = 0), or when clinical benefit is zero. It does not claim additionality merely from historic service volume. The CCT-like comparator is retained for people receiving credit; their lack of equivalent TF-CBT is not treated as absence of every service.

The favorable joint case is about $3.76 million per 10 QALYs; the poor joint case about $75.9 billion. These are stress tests, not confidence bounds. One-year persistence alone raises the central figure to about $194.8 million; the 0.032 utility case to about $409.9 million. A negative other-portfolio case produces net harm and therefore has no finite positive price. Full parameter sets and arithmetic are provided below.
sections.funding:
The FY23, FY24 and FY25 Form 990 Part IX totals are $8,897,281, $8,862,999 and $10,486,537 (three-year descriptive mean $9,415,605.67). They share the return-expense boundary, excluding donated services and fundraising event direct costs reported outside Part IX; this mean is not a future budget. [FY23 return](https://www.chicagocac.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/ChicagoCAC-FY2023-Form-990.pdf) [FY24 return](https://www.chicagocac.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/ChicagoCAC-FY2024-Form-990.pdf) [FY25 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202631349349313328/IRS990)

For the model, FY25 Part IX $10,486,537 plus direct event costs $341,452 plus recognized donated-service/facility expense $922,265 equals $11,750,254. Schedule D reports audited expenses $11,389,882, subtracts $922,265 and adds $18,920 of fundraising expense to reach the return total; the gross model then adds event costs separately. The $922,265 is not cash donated, and $98,765 depreciation remains in the accrual expense total. Neither this boundary nor its $10,827,989 version excluding donated services is a verified marginal cash price. Additional public investigator, hospital, partner and volunteer resources remain unvalued; the 25% add-on case is illustrative, not a resource valuation.
