sections.what: PHRA reports 2025 totals of 66,838 encounters, 98,382 naloxone doses, 1,254,550 syringes, 137,906 injection-alternative kits and 21,914 fentanyl-test strips. Counts include statewide mail and Kitsap; they are supplies or encounters, not unique Seattle residents. Services include outreach, facilitated medication treatment and HCV care.
sections.monitoring: Original 2024 Form 990 functional expense is $2,726,245; adding separately netted inventory cost $1,212 gives $2,727,457 gross reported expense. Program $2,602,235, management $101,278 and fundraising $22,732 already sum to functional expense. Part XII says no independent financial-statement audit; Schedule D audited reconciliations are blank. Schedule M $1.5 million fair-value donated receipts and Schedule I $1,587,687 cost-valued distributions are different boundaries. Inventory $5,242 to $4,050 does not bridge donated receipts to consumption. DOH September 2025 report p. 19 explicitly says mail recipients do not report overdose responses; no mail reversal count is available. One order may contain one nasal kit or two injectable kits; monthly ordering is allowed.
sections.qualitative: Seattle–Tacoma–Bellevue benefits cover King, Pierce and Snohomish counties; local shares are analyst judgments. Naloxone efficacy does not establish incremental local rescue. Metro share .50, six kits per network person, .50 network conversion, treatment starts and budget response are judgments. Seattle delivery locations do not establish beneficiary residence. Public supply, alternatives, clinical partners and overlap limit attribution. Several health benefits and external resource costs are unvalued, so this is incomplete valuation in both directions. The follow-on independently checks finance/state sources and arithmetic; not every clinical source was reopened.
sections.cost:
## Inspectable finite model

Central naloxone coverage is 98,382 doses ÷ 2 doses/kit ÷ 6 kits/annual network person × .5 relevant-network conversion × .5 local share = 2,049.625 synthetic local people. This is not a finding that PHRA served exactly that many unique high-risk people. Kit recipients may be rescuers rather than patients, and multiple rescuers can cover the same patient; the divisor and conversion jointly address this unresolved mapping. A person faces one prospective overdose opportunity annually with otherwise-fatal probability .1, baseline rescue .75 and an additional .03 rescue probability. The constructed baseline mortality hazard is .025 other causes + .1 × (1 − .75) = .05, avoiding addition of overdose to an already all-cause hazard.

For one support year, survival is exp(−hazard×time), followed by common .05 mortality in both counterfactual arms. Integrating their difference over 10 years, utility .65 and 3% discount yields finite health. Repeated events do not restart lifetime benefits. The buprenorphine subcohort is embedded within the same opioid cohort: only the incremental joint-survival difference beyond rescue is added. Treatment exposure is represented as full-year person equivalents, an approximation to the timing of shorter courses, not observed one-year retention. All mortality and utility horizons are priors; no life is assigned perpetual perfect health.

Infection benefits use full-coverage equivalents derived from syringe counts, low annual infection risks and finite 10-year morbidity only. Susceptible people whose infection is prevented and already-infected people whose HCV is cured are conceptually disjoint; no HIV/HCV mortality or downstream transmission is credited. Incremental buprenorphine quality and short wound-care gains are separate from survival but remain weakly supported local priors.

Finally, a .5 whole-budget response discounts proportional activity for the ability of cash to expand or preserve publicly supported services. It is conceptually different from alternative rescue at an overdose and alternative treatment for a patient, but these uncertainties may be correlated; the full-response diagnostic makes that potential overlapping conservatism visible. It gives a central price of $1,015,329. Halving the rescue increment gives $3,889,301; a five-year survival horizon gives $3,471,836. Raising whole expense 25% for unmatched cost/service years gives weighted $997,078. No coefficients were changed after observing the first result.


Central: 13.431401 local QALYs and $2,030,657 per 10. Signed mixture: 34.193124 QALYs and $797,662 per 10. Favorable contributes 82.43% of net signed weighted modeled QALYs; excluding and renormalizing it gives $4,085,160. Subjective weights are not measured probabilities. Gross 2024 expense versus 2025 activity is a year mismatch. Expense less donated receipts is an unreconciled sensitivity, not cash spending, and is excluded from the headline. The central and signed-mixture figures are conditional calculations, not measured ordinary-gift returns.
sections.funding: Donor decision HOLD. No concrete priced additional Seattle service offer was verified. January 2026 HCA funding table declines from $26,622,530 over FY 2024–25 to $15,482,489 over FY 2026–27 (41.84%; slide text says nearly 45%). Dated caps are 100 nasal kits monthly for most partners and 3,000 mail orders including 2,000 nasal kits. These do not prove September availability or gift-funded capacity. Current cash/in-kind consumption, resident/overlap counts, partner retention and cures, and a concrete incremental plan remain needed.

reports.program: School-based WOW and BAM counseling, education and family support

what: Youth Guidance places counselors and mentors in schools to support young people facing trauma and other barriers to success.
WOW provides group-based support for girls, while BAM helps young men reflect on decisions and strengthen school engagement.
Family assistance and community programs complement this work by addressing immediate needs and connecting students with supportive adults.
strengths: WOW has randomized evidence for reduced depression and post-traumatic stress symptoms, with a transparent utility model.
BAM has multiple randomized studies and a measured early graduation contrast, alongside important scaling cautions.
Current local program counts, direct family cash assistance and original audited costs provide concrete implementation anchors.
reservations: Annual reach is not verified completed trial-equivalent care or unique households; sibling and cash-recipient overlap is unknown.
BAM graduation-to-net-resources and current transfer remain judgments, not measured earnings.
The whole annual denominator covers national and unpriced programs; school resources, public funding replacement and marginal capacity remain uncertain.

sections.what: Youth Guidance, EIN 36-2167032, provides school-based counseling, mentoring, career readiness and family support. Its official giving page identifies the legal recipient and links national and regional routes, including Chicago; no transaction or donor restriction was tested. WOW serves girls in grades 6–12, while BAM works with young men in grades 6–12 across Chicagoland, including Waukegan and the south suburbs. Geographic reach is not precise beneficiary residence within the pinned metro.
sections.monitoring: The FY2025 annual report gives national WOW reach 4,331 and BAM reach 8,679. Its Illinois pages report WOW 3,649 and BAM 7,243 participants, not unique completed trial-equivalent courses or households. Community Connections assisted more than 400 families with approximately $150,000 direct cash. The 400 figure includes broader crisis assistance; it does not establish 400 paid recipients. The reference assumes 400 equally paid household units, with concentrated 100/20-recipient Jensen sensitivities at the same aggregate cash. Current symptom-improvement and satisfaction percentages are noncausal monitoring, not fresh randomized effects. Obtain attendance, counselor dose, retention, unique household IDs, grade mix, actual cash allocations and residence.
sections.qualitative:
The original WOW randomized evaluation maps depression and PTSD scales to literature utilities, taking each student's minimum condition utility rather than adding comorbid gains. Anxiety is omitted from its cost-utility model. Table 5 assumes a full year of benefit and estimates $58,025/QALY for combined depression/PTSD. The study's $2,300 actual-participant cost is converted using .6525 uptake for its ITT analysis. Recovering 2,300/58,025=.039638 participant-equivalent utility therefore does NOT require applying uptake again. This is modeled utility, not directly measured local clinical QALYs. Current transfer .5 reflects grade mix, dose, counselors and population; half a year is a finite duration judgment, with quarter-year onset and 3% discount. No lifetime protection, arrest-to-injury conversion or extra mortality credit is added.

For BAM, original first-trial Table VI reports on-time graduation ITT .0297 and participant IV .0714, both p<.10, n=2,740. These are probability differences, not 19 percentage points: the headline 19% is relative. Later scaling trials did not detect significant outcomes in new populations. Pooled school engagement projected up to five graduation points is not observed pooled diploma completion or earnings. The reference uses .0714 participant IV with .25 current transfer, explicitly weak across current grades/dose/settings. It is not automatically applied as current causal graduation. WOW's study did not establish academic gains. BAM violence, other counseling, afterschool, career and national income effects remain unpriced and unknown, including harms.
sections.cost:
FY2025 audited expense $54,652,685 plus $204,922 direct event benefits netted against revenue gives full gross recognized resources $54,857,607. Recorded donated services and in-kind inputs are already included; no duplicate addback. FY2024 uses $56,011,499 + $276,981 = $56,288,480; FY2023 $46,884,765 + $195,100 = $47,079,865. Comparable mean is $52,741,984. These are whole national-recipient resources, not a Chicago-only or WOW-only budget. Unrecognized school space/staff and partner opportunity costs are unknown, not free; K=0 is only a recognized-boundary reference, with 25%-of-C additional budget stress and full unknown. The original FY2025 audit opinion is dated December 10, 2025; publication date is not inferred.

b=.5 denotes a conditional annual funded-work response beyond replacement funding, school capacity and counselor constraints, not a second donor haircut on measured incremental outcomes. Full annual cost stays in the denominator; b=1 is separate. WOW local 3,649 × .5 funding × .039638 utility × .5 transfer × .5 years × .95 residence, discounted after .25-year onset, yields 17.049469 clinical QALYs. The initial undiscounted conditional health-only price is preserved. All-population clinical fields retain national WOW reach; they are health-only, not complete national welfare.

BAM local 7,243 × .5 funding gives 3,621.5 exposed participant units. Judged current graduation probability .0714 × .25 gives 64.643775 additional-graduate hypotheses. A separate unsupported $1,000 net annual household-resource gain lasts only three years after four years' delay. It must be net of taxes, benefit withdrawal, commuting, childcare, college/training opportunity costs, displaced earnings and other employment; no gross salary or lifetime diploma premium is treated as observed. Positive BAM resource overlap defaults 1 because no BAM health is priced centrally; half-overlap is shown, and negative earnings or graduation changes are retained fully. This is not ordinary survivor earnings.

Current direct cash gives an additional resource anchor, not a social-income claim. $150,000 divided among judged 400 paid households, .5 additional versus other assistance and .9 net usable resources gives $168.75 per recipient. Positive WOW overlap .5 and full incremental family-process burden $20 give $64.375 net. Other WOW families lose $20, and BAM families lose $20. These burden priors concern actual incremental usable household resources versus alternatives, not retail counseling prices or monetized ordinary school hours. Cash gains and signed benefit withdrawal are netted with burden BEFORE one log. Household baseline is judged $30,000/year; future graduate baseline is $20,000/year. One welfare-equivalent person per household is explicit; family members are not automatically added.

Central WOW and BAM households are assumed disjoint, although students may be siblings. Joint-family cases combine both $20 burdens in a single household-year log. Cash recipients are assumed a subset of WOW-only households, not separate welfare people; this allocation is unverified. Two-participants-per-household aggregation preserves both participants' full costs and earning gains before the joint log, assuming similarly situated co-resident participants. Current burden/cash year and delayed earnings years 4–6 are distinct time slices, so future resource logs do not double count same-year resources. Full health harms cover the distinct WOW+BAM individual union even when households overlap.

The production .5 × households × discounted years × log(1 + joint net/baseline) bridge gives 2.419906 signed resource equivalents, combining with health to 19.469375, or $28.176358 million per ten combined equivalents, not ten clinical QALYs. Clinical-null keeps cash, earnings hypotheses and all burdens. No cash additionality, no earnings, no graduation, zero-expansion, true-zero, unknown and adverse controls differ. Complete portfolio and world-net effects remain unknown, not zero or a lower bound.

The cash transfer is already an expense in C: do not add it to resource cost again or charge the same donating households twice. Counterparty stress represents a separate displaced-beneficiary/public-budget alternative from incremental assistance, not the donor cost already in C. It allocates full pre-overlap additional cash to distinct households, with low-baseline fixed-budget displacement separate. Outside school/provider own-resource stress excludes staff/input costs already priced in C or K. Central payer incidence is unknown-neutral, not observed zero. No complete global-benefit claim follows from recipient cash gains.
sections.funding: FY2025 audit reports government grants $28,749,724, revenue $46,408,813 and an $8,243,872 net-asset decline. Net assets total $40,156,046, but $19,197,138 is donor restricted and $17,003,852 board designated; $5,273,375 financial assets are available for general expenditure within one year. $800,000 was drawn against the $10 million callable line of credit. These figures indicate funding and cash-flow constraints but do not establish a priced marginal expansion. The current Bright Futures campaign seeks a $30 million impact fund and $50 million endowment; campaign scale is not immediate clinical capacity. Existing school counseling, mentoring, public contracts and other family assistance are relevant alternatives. Ask for a funded counselor/caseload tranche, its grade/dose/Chicago share, substitution, school resource costs and cash targeting. No next-gift price or complete annual portfolio EV is verified.

what: TOMAGWA provides medical, dental, vision, pharmacy and related care for people with limited resources around Tomball and greater Houston.
It became a federally qualified health center look-alike in 2024 and serves uninsured patients alongside Medicare and Medicaid patients.
Federal reporting identifies 118 oral-surgery patients in 2024; other services are not included in this narrow health illustration.
strengths: Original filings and federal data identify the recipient, whole recognized spending and a defined surgery cohort.
Patient ZIP data and the recipient's needs assessment document substantial Houston-metro reach.
An official one-time and recurring donation route exists.
reservations: A gift-created surgery and measurable additional pain relief are unverified; existing dental grants may replace ordinary gifts.
2024 accounts are unaudited and unrecognized volunteer-service costs are unknown.
The QALY bridge is judgment-based and partial; it does not demonstrate whole-organization cost effectiveness.

sections.what: TOMAGWA provides comprehensive primary and dental care, pharmacy, vision, laboratory and case-management services. Current locations include Tomball and Champions in Houston, with mobile delivery across Greater Houston and Harris County. Its 2024 Form 990 identifies TOMAGWA Ministries Inc DBA TOMAGWA HealthCare Ministries, EIN 76-0280324, and February 2024 FQHC Look-Alike designation. Look-Alike status is not proof of federal Section 330 funding. [Recipient site](https://www.tomagwa.org/) [Original filing](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202503219349321450/IRS990)
sections.monitoring: The 2024 HRSA return counts 1,965 patients overall and 118 oral-surgery patients with 131 surgery visits (Table6A DJ97 and DI97). In 2025 the corresponding surgery counts are 135 patients and 240 visits. These are reported treatment-category patients, not observed incremental cures. Restorative and examination patients can overlap and receive no added modeled credit. The 2024 tax filing repeats a 2023 narrative of 18,326 dental services; that is neither 2024 activity nor a unique-patient count. [2024 UDS](https://data.hrsa.gov/DataDownload/StaticDocuments/LAL-2024.xlsx) [2025 UDS](https://data.hrsa.gov/DataDownload/StaticDocuments/LAL-2025.xlsx)
sections.qualitative: Care reaches a population with limited resources and plausible unmet need. The 2024 federal ZIP rows place 1,758 patients in named Houston-metro ZIP areas; 28 are in Plantersville/Grimes, 156 in other ZIPs, and some small cells are suppressed. This is overall patient residence, not surgery-specific health attribution. A Swedish prospective cohort compared root canals with extraction and found no significant intergroup QALY difference; it does not identify the benefit of TOMAGWA surgery over alternative care. The model therefore labels utility, relief and duration as priors. [Needs assessment](https://www.tomagwa.org/_files/ugd/a79649_a42ddabd7ed84d0ca420cfde6c9a8ff0.pdf) [Clinical study](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cre2.759)
sections.cost:
Whole FY2024 recognized expenses were $2,471,560, including program, administration, fundraising and $113,318 reported medical-supplies expense; the matching donated supplies must not be added again. The filing reports no audit, and 2024 volunteer-service valuation is unknown. Dividing this whole expense by only a hypothetical surgery-pain benefit produces a central $43.8 million per 10 Houston QALYs, with null and harm cases retained. Other clinical benefits remain unestimated. This is a historical partial-health illustration, not a marginal gift price or complete organizational ranking. [Original filing](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202503219349321450/IRS990) [Schedule M](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202503219349321450/IRS990ScheduleM)

An explicit missing-resource case adds a hypothetical $476,624 of volunteer/service costs (the prior year's adjustment, not an observed 2024 value), raising the conditional price to about $52.2 million per ten QALYs. An isolated zero-funding-response case preserves the other central clinical assumptions but yields zero gift-created health. Unmeasured other-portfolio benefits may be positive or negative; this narrow illustration is not a proven lower bound.
sections.funding: Donor HOLD. TRHF approved $595,000 of 2024 dental funding and described a $400,000 February–December 2025 contract; these are existing funding, not open gift gaps. UDS also reports local government and private grants. Current clinician capacity, 2026 grant renewal, restrictions and the response to a new gift need verification. The official giving form permits ordinary gifts but prices no additional surgery. [2024 funding approval](https://trhfoundation.org/images/pdfs/financials/minutes/20231129_THA_Board_Minutes_Signed.pdf) [2025 contract minutes](https://trhfoundation.org/2025-board-minutes/158-february-19-2025-1) [Give](https://www.tomagwa.org/donate)

model.costScope: Whole FY2024 recognized organizational expenses; includes medical supplies already recognized. Unrecognized volunteer costs remain unknown. Narrow surgery-only health illustration, not full portfolio or marginal gift price.
model.geographicAttribution: 2024 ZIP rows and CHNA county mapping establish actual Houston reach. Central 93% benefit share is a judgment; surgical cohort geography is unknown and some ZIP areas cross counties.
model.formula: benefit = patients * symptomaticSuccessfulShare * incrementalRelief * utility * years; allPopulationQalys = (benefit - harmQalys) * fundingResponse; editionQalys = allPopulationQalys * houstonShare; pricePer10 = 10 * costUSD / positive editionQalys
model.counterfactual: Other dental providers, public/payer coverage and existing TRHF contracts can substitute for ordinary-gift support. Symptom success, additional relief and funding response are separately explicit priors.
model.attribution: Whole-recipient expense retained; one annual surgery-patient cohort only. No double credit for exams/restorations or partners. Other programs remain unestimated.
model.uncertainty: Very low confidence in health and donation attribution. Scenarios are illustrative, not confidence intervals; no calibrated probabilities or expected-value estimate. Null and adverse are viable.
model.nativeOutcomes: Reported oral-surgery patients, discounted for symptomatic successful treatment and relief beyond alternative care, with finite utility duration and harm.

inputs.name: symptomaticSuccessfulShare
inputs.rationale: Share with a symptomatic problem and successful treatment; not an observed local completion or outcome rate.

inputs.name: incrementalRelief
inputs.rationale: Relief remaining after alternative care and spontaneous symptom change; unmeasured.

inputs.name: utility

inputs.name: years

inputs.name: harmQalys
inputs.rationale: Aggregate treatment/complication/functional loss allowance; adverse case permits net harm.

inputs.name: fundingResponse
inputs.rationale: Proxy response after funding substitution and capacity limits; not observed gift elasticity.

inputs.name: houstonShare
inputs.rationale: All-patient residence supports local care but not a measured surgery-specific health share.

Funding response of zero yields no incremental health regardless of service counts.

The hypothetical central benefit cannot establish the overall value of a broad clinical recipient whose other health pathways remain unestimated.

what: Community Servings delivers medically tailored meals and groceries to people with serious illness across Massachusetts and Rhode Island.
Registered dietitians tailor food to clients’ medical needs and provide nutrition counseling and education.
The organization also supports clients’ families and runs workforce training and food-policy programs.
strengths: The intervention has a randomized trial conducted with the actual provider, plus a larger recent Medicaid evaluation.
Original tax returns and a consolidating audit permit recipient-level cost and financing review.
County-level service counts establish substantial metro reach; a reported waitlist supports unmet demand.
reservations: Mental-health days are not QALYs: the utility-day bridge remains an explicit prior.
Current meals include family support and varying duration, not thousands of independent completed trial courses.

Waitlist size, geographic service counts and historical outcomes do not identify what an additional unrestricted gift buys. The approximately $314 million per 10 Boston-metro QALYs figure is a very weak-confidence partial-pathway scenario, not a whole-portfolio or incremental-gift price.

sections.what: Community Servings, Inc., EIN 22-3154028, is the recipient, not merely its meal program. It also provides groceries, nutrition counseling, workforce development and policy work. Its service area includes Massachusetts and Rhode Island, so all health cannot be assigned to Boston. [Who we serve](https://www.servings.org/who-we-serve/)
sections.monitoring: A 44-person randomized crossover diabetes trial compared 12 weeks of 10 meals/week against usual care plus a healthy-eating brochure. The secondary endpoint was days when mental health interfered with quality of life: 5.65 versus 9.59 days per 30 days during the 12-week on/off periods. This is not direct preference-based utility. [Trial](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11606-018-4716-z) The 2026 Medicaid evaluation compared 1,866 recipients with 1,372 eligible nonrecipients; adjusted hospitalization and ED rates were lower during a mean 6.7 months of enrollment. It is observational and does not establish mortality or QALY gains; no savings offset is used. [Study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04407-5)
sections.qualitative: Tailored food can relieve food insecurity and treatment-related dietary burden. The current population differs from the historical trial's food-insecure adults with poorly controlled diabetes. The FAME-F trial found no meaningful mental-health or utility differences between delivery/dose variants, but every arm received meals; it cannot estimate meals versus no meals. [FAME-F](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13045650/) CDC utility crosswalks require more than a single group-average mental-health-days contrast. We therefore expose, rather than disguise, a .20 utility-day prior. [CDC methods](https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/burden-toolkit/docs/technical_documentation.pdf)
sections.cost: The central partial-pathway model retains $22,289,498 whole-recipient FY 2025 gross expense. It uses 610.875 realized 12-week diabetes course-equivalents, not meals as independent people. With the observed 3.94-day mental-health contrast, .20 utility-day prior, .5 transfer, .5 financing additionality and 6139/7973 geographic share, it yields 0.710333 metro QALYs, or $313.789 million per 10. Benefits stop after 12 weeks; no avoided hospitalization, mortality, hypoglycemia, caregiver or policy credit is added. All other portfolio net health is provisionally zero, not a lower-bound claim. This is a very weak-confidence analytical scenario accepted only as a conditional alpha scenario, not a precise causal estimate.
sections.funding: FY 2025 Part IX expense 21,894,207 plus netted direct event 395,291 gives 22,289,498; FY 2024 similarly 19,432,858+379,657=19,812,515. These retain the legal recipient's whole cost, including capital planning and transfers; consolidated affiliate spending is not added again. [FY 25 return](https://www.servings.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/2024-Form-990-for-CS-Public-Copy.pdf) [FY 24 return](https://www.servings.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/2023-Form-990-for-CS-Public-Copy.pdf) The audit reports $8.195 million consolidated financial assets available within one year and an increased credit line; net assets are not all liquid. [Audit](https://www.servings.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/FY25-Financials.pdf) A 2025 management update reported 215+ waitlisted people, critical/end-stage-only enrollment and an expected $500,000 local-food grant canceled. It does not establish today's waitlist or a priced unfunded tranche. [Funding update](https://www.servings.org/blog/update-growing-demand-amid-funding-challenges/) Donor recommendation HOLD until capacity, replacement and local beneficiary response are verified. Official donation page exists; checkout was not transacted.

model.costScope: Entire legal recipient gross FY 2025 Form 990 expense; noncash/depreciation retained. Does not subtract healthcare savings; not full social cost including unrecognized volunteer opportunity cost.
model.geographicAttribution: Boston-Cambridge-Newton MA-NH CBSA 14460 under OMB 23-01. Numerator county clients: Middlesex 1294+ Essex 1102+ Suffolk 2468+ Norfolk 828+ Plymouth 447=6139. Denominator 7973 total individuals; mapped counties sum 7893, leaving 80 unresolved. No assumed New Hampshire benefit. Applying client share to diabetes meal health is a transfer judgment. Rockingham and Strafford are the two New Hampshire counties in the MSA; no verified clients there are credited.
model.formula: N=min(M*primaryMealShare*diabetesShare/(mealsPerWeek*weeks),people*diabetesShare)*courseRealization; Q_all=financialAdditionality*(N*mentalDaysDifference/30*utilityPerAffectedDay*(benefitWeeks*7/365.25)*transfer+otherQalys); Q_metro=g*Q_all; price10=10*C/Q_metro only for positive net health. benefitWeeks=12 centrally.
model.counterfactual: RCT contrast already includes usual care and brochure; do not apply a second ordinary-care subtraction. Transfer covers current population/trial uncertainty. Financing additionality separately discounts replacement by insurance/contracts/donors. Courses are annual-flow equivalents; no lifetime or repeated-year credit.
model.attribution: Primary-patient allocation, disease-dose allocation and course realization are unverified; count-based geography is not directly health-weighted. Utility-day prior is not an observed utility gain. Central other portfolio 0 is neither total-health estimate nor proven lower bound.
model.uncertainty: Very weak-confidence deterministic scenarios, not probability-weighted expectation or confidence limits. Source evidence supports native outcomes more strongly than the QALY price. Independent review accepts conditional alpha publication with these scope limits; donor status remains HOLD.
model.nativeOutcomes: FY 25: 1,221,750 meals; 7,973 individuals; 15% primary diabetes diagnosis. Trial: 3.94 fewer days when mental health interfered with quality of life per 30 days during 12-week on/off periods. These populations and denominators are not interchangeable.

inputs.name: C
inputs.rationale: Whole legal-recipient FY 2025 Part IX 21,894,207 plus 395,291 direct event expense. Includes capital planning and affiliate transfer; no meal-program cost carveout.

inputs.name: M
inputs.rationale: FY 2025 meals prepared/delivered, not people or a disease-specific dose count.

inputs.name: people
inputs.rationale: Reported total individuals; not assumed all primary diabetes patients.

inputs.name: primaryMealShare
inputs.rationale: Half of meals assigned to primary patients. Family delivery share does not identify this fraction; leaves caregiver/dependent and ambiguous meal allocation uncredited.

inputs.name: diabetesShare
inputs.rationale: 15% primary-diagnosis diabetes observed; applying the person mix to meal exposure is a separate unverified allocation assumption.

inputs.name: mealsPerWeek
inputs.rationale: Trial intervention dose, not evidence of dose completion by current clients.

inputs.name: weeks
inputs.rationale: Trial intervention duration; model credits at most 12 weeks and no residual benefit.

inputs.name: courseRealization
inputs.rationale: 80% of dose-equivalent capacity assumed to represent adequate continuous trial-like courses; no current patient-duration distribution.

inputs.name: mentalDaysDifference
inputs.rationale: 9.59 minus 5.65 days when mental health interfered with quality of life per 30 days in the 12-week randomized crossover on/off periods; secondary self-report endpoint, not generic mentally unhealthy days.

inputs.name: utilityPerAffectedDay
inputs.rationale: Explicit .20 prior: a day no longer experiencing mental-health interference with quality of life gains .20 of a full-health day. Not measured EQ-5 D or a validated application of a CDC crosswalk; test 0,.05,.4.

inputs.name: transfer
inputs.rationale: 50% replication/current-severity transfer, including secondary-outcome uncertainty, small historical trial and different current diabetes severity/food insecurity.

inputs.name: financialAdditionality
inputs.rationale: 50% effective activity survives replacement by insurance, contracts, other donors and reserves. Waitlist indicates demand but does not identify this elasticity.

inputs.name: g
inputs.rationale: 6139/7973 client-count anchor: five Boston MSA MA counties; unallocated 80 and NH counties get no credit. Assumes diabetes exposure and health yield have same residence mix; actual health share unknown.

inputs.name: otherQalys
inputs.rationale: All other portfolio net health set to 0 for a partial pathway, not a claim of no benefit or a proven lower bound.

sensitivity: Utility prior .05 quadruples price versus .20; .4 halves it. Zero utility or no gift response eliminates a finite positive price.
A reversal to two additional affected days/month yields negative health; negative results are retained.
Halving metro health share does not halve expense. Unknown 80 residents and unequal diabetes/meal distribution create additional geographic uncertainty.
One 12-week course maximum is credited per modeled person; dose-equivalent caps prevent treating meals or recurring courses as independent beneficiaries.
A 5-QALY other-portfolio harm before financing reverses the central sign. Uncredited clinical benefits could substantially increase value; the central pathway cannot rank the whole portfolio.
Four-week duration credits only a third of central health; 25% additional resource costs raises price 25%. No long-term persistence is assumed.
missingInputs: Current primary diabetes patient count, meals delivered/consumed, continuous 12-week course completion and county-linked dose.
Preference-based utility measurements or valid patient-level crosswalk inputs, replication and adverse outcomes.
Current dated waiting list, costed unfunded capacity plan, financing replacement, and uptake per incremental gift.
Whole-portfolio health and harms, volunteer opportunity costs and metro-specific disease/utility shares.

reports.priceScope: Conditional whole-recipient resource cost per 10 Atlanta-metro QALYs; not an expected gift price; donor HOLD

what: Georgia Lions Lighthouse Foundation provides eye examinations, prescription glasses and coordination of eye surgery for Georgians with limited access to care.
Its Atlanta Public Schools partnership delivers exams and glasses at school, removing travel and payment barriers.
It also serves people statewide and sends recycled glasses overseas; those activities receive no benefit credit in this narrow local model.
strengths: The original report identifies 1,114 Atlanta Public Schools examination recipients and says all students needing corrective eyewear received it.
Original tax returns permit a three-year full-resource cost reconciliation including donated services and direct event costs.
Prescription correction has a direct vision-to-quality-of-life mechanism, supported by clinical evidence but not locally quantified.
reservations: The share needing glasses, local utility change, sustained wear and alternative-glasses counterfactual are not measured.
The conditional price is driven by explicit subjective assumptions and is not a prediction of health purchased by a gift.
Current unmet funding capacity is unverified, and inconsistencies in reported screening figures require clarification.

sections.what: The recipient is Georgia Lions Lighthouse Foundation, Inc., EIN58-0548732. It operates the Harrell Vision Clinic in Chamblee, mobile and tele-optometry clinics, prescription-glasses services and a statewide surgical referral network. Eligibility targets uninsured or underinsured people in financial need; some optical services carry low fees. Current service listings and2026 school-glasses news support continuing delivery. [Services](https://lionslighthouse.org/services/) [Current news](https://lionslighthouse.org/news-events/)
sections.monitoring:
The original FY 2025 report's Atlanta Public Schools page identifies 1,114 students receiving complete eye examinations and says prescription glasses were distributed with full fulfillment for students needing corrective eyewear. This does not unambiguously establish that all 1,114 received glasses. The model therefore starts with examination recipients and explicitly assumes a prescription-needed share. No screenings are converted to restored sight. [Original report, pages 5–6](https://lionslighthouse.aflip.in/fy 25 impactreport)

The same report describes 207 surgery patients receiving 421 procedures across several diseases; those are not 421 people or 207 cataract patients. The original Form 990 corroborates the surgery counts. No surgery, statewide optical or overseas recycling benefit is added. The school page's screening count and claimed 64.28% growth require reconciliation with prior-year reporting. Neither year's screenings are added to the examination cohort. Deduplication, prescription severity, actual wear and outcomes lack independent audit.
sections.qualitative:
School delivery can remove transport and financial barriers, but provision does not guarantee sustained use or an incremental improvement over glasses that families or other charities would supply. A randomized Indian school study observed roughly three-quarter wear at short follow-up in both ready-made and custom-glasses groups; it did not compare glasses with no glasses or measure Atlanta utility. [Primary wear trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5847082/)

A Singapore cross-sectional study of699 myopic teenagers found time-tradeoff utility about0.94 in corrected versus0.92 in uncorrected students after race/sex adjustment. This association is neither a causal treatment effect nor a transferable estimate for younger Atlanta children. The model's0.01 utility increment is explicitly an analyst judgment, not the study result divided by two as a validated estimator. [Primary utility study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1771541/)

First-eye cataract surgery has randomized evidence of improved vision and health status, but the foundation's local cataract cohort and disease mix are unknown. One family testimonial cannot identify aggregate local impact; it names the sister's Paulding residence, not conclusively the patient's residence. That pathway is left unmodeled. [Primary cataract trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1772474/)

The wear trial measured use at 3–4 months among followed participants, with about 21% lost to follow-up; it cannot establish six-month sustained wear in Atlanta. The utility study elicited willingness to trade life for removal of myopia, not a randomized glasses-induced change in generic health utility. Its standard-gamble result did not show the same correction association. Thus 0.01 is a scenario choice, with zero also plausible. Prescription share, alternative access and funding response have no calibrated local priors; their product and independence are unvalidated.
sections.cost:
The conditional central is approximately $106.29 million per 10 Atlanta-metro QALYs: $3,700,076 of FY 2025 recipient resources divided by 0.348125 modeled metro QALY and multiplied by 10. This is a weak-confidence assumption exercise, not measured cost-effectiveness, a posterior expected value or an expected marginal gift price.

The bridge is 1,114 examined students × 50% needing and receiving prescription glasses × 50% effective wear × 50% incremental correction beyond alternative access × 50% funding response × 0.01 utility × 0.5 year × 100% metro attribution. The prescription share is an explicit uncalibrated assumption: full fulfillment among those needing glasses does not establish the fraction needing them. Only examination count and accounting inputs are observed. Metro attribution is inferred from school enrollment, not verified addresses. No lifetime, mortality or learning-income credit is used. Other portfolio net health is provisionally zero, not proven harmless.

The weak and favorable combinations produce about $44.75 billion and $2.95 million per 10 metro QALYs; these are not confidence limits. Zero prescription need, wear, additionality or funding response yields zero modeled health and no finite price. Net harm is also considered. The three-year reconstructed resource mean is $3,474,317.67; FY 2025 cost matches the activity period.
sections.funding:
FY 2025 Form 990 functional expense is $2,617,279. Add $892,628 donated services from Schedule D and $190,169 direct fundraising-event costs netted against revenue in PartVIII to obtain $3,700,076. This retains program, administration, fundraising and investment-management costs. It does not add the separate $650,000 surgical donated-value claim again. The Schedule D audited-expense figure $3,374,979 reconciles by subtracting donated services and adding $134,928 investment expenses to reach the tax figure; it is not the same resource scope. [Original return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202621349349310557/IRS 990) [Schedule D](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202621349349310557/IRS 990 Schedule D)

The same tax-expense-plus-donated-services-plus-direct-event-cost basis is $3,484,633 in FY 2023 and $3,238,244 in FY 2024. These are reconstructed resource costs, not a claim that standalone audit reports were retrieved. FY 2023's audited reconciliation already includes direct event costs; the reconstruction adds them only to the tax expense base, avoiding duplication. Original source files are retained for audit.

FY 2025 reports $22.42 million net assets, of which $15.61 million is donor restricted. A large balance is not proof of unrestricted cash or no funding need. The annual appeal seeks a full-time optometrist, but an appeal and historic matching offer do not verify today's unmet capacity. The official website links a live campaign whose HTML identifies this foundation as recipient; payment flow and any Atlanta restriction were not verified, and no payment was made. [Official campaign](https://www.classy.org/campaign/give-the-gift-of-clear-sight-2025/c 650490) Donor decision: HOLD pending an additional-capacity budget and gift allocation.

model.costScope: FY 2025 entire recipient reconstructed resources: tax functional expenses+recognized donated services+direct event costs excluded from PartIX. Includes investment management; not societal partner costs outside these accounts.
model.geographicAttribution: Modeled cohort is Atlanta Public Schools;100%metro is an explicit enrollment-based inference, not patient residence audit. Statewide and overseas services receive zero positive credit.
model.formula: C=2617279+892628+190169=3700076; Q_all=N*p*w*a*f*u*T-H; Q_metro=N*p*w*a*f*u*T*g-H; price=10*C/Q_metro only if positive. Central N=1114,p=.5,w=.5,a=.5,f=.5,u=.01,T=.5,g=1,H=0.
model.counterfactual: a discounts corrective eyewear obtained anyway from families, insurance, schools or alternative charities. f separately discounts capacity that would persist despite changed donor funding; neither is estimated.
model.attribution: Whole recipient costs retained without allocation to schools. KIA and school partners contribute to observed provision; alternative delivery and funding replacement remain possible. No independent claim to all partnership benefit.
model.uncertainty: Accepted only as a weak-confidence conditional alpha. No empirical posterior or expected marginal gift estimate. All bridge factors, including prescription share, are uncalibrated judgments. Donor HOLD; not a top-pick endorsement.
model.nativeOutcomes: FY2025 APS examination cohort: 1,114 students. Glasses reportedly fulfilled for those needing them; prescription-needed share is unknown. Statewide 207 surgical patients / 421 procedures excluded. Screenings and recycled shipments are not health outcomes.

inputs.name: C: full-recipient resources
inputs.rationale: Calculated from original tax functional expenses2617279+donated services892628+direct event expenses190169.

inputs.name: N: APS examination cohort
inputs.rationale: Original report p5 identifies examination recipients; it does not unambiguously identify the number needing glasses.

inputs.name: p: prescription-needed and fulfilled share
inputs.rationale: Unknown locally. One-half is an uncalibrated conditional scenario, not inferred from 100% fulfillment among those needing correction. Sensitivity spans zero to one.

inputs.name: w: effective wear fraction
inputs.rationale: Allows nonwear, poor fit, breakage and lack of sustained use; external short-term wear trial does not estimate this local rate.

inputs.name: a: incremental correction versus alternatives
inputs.rationale: Half the correction is assumed not to occur as soon via family or other providers; no local control group.

inputs.name: f: funding-response prior
inputs.rationale: Hypothetical responsiveness, not verified marginal room. Existing sponsor funding and partner capacity could fully replace new gifts.

inputs.name: u: utility improvement while effectively corrected
inputs.rationale: Explicit small utility judgment. Singapore cross-sectional association is context, not a causal calibration.

inputs.name: T: effective benefit horizon
inputs.rationale: No credit beyond six months, allowing prescription change, replacement and alternative access. No lifetime or mortality benefit.

inputs.name: g: metro attribution
inputs.rationale: Enrollment in Atlanta Public Schools strongly anchors metro delivery; beneficiary addresses not audited.

what: GHRC provides naloxone, syringe services, infectious-disease and substance-use care, linkage and basic-needs assistance.
Its five direct-service sites are in metro Atlanta, while mail and telehealth services extend statewide.
The modeled pathway is limited to conditional survival benefit from reported collaborative naloxone reversals.
strengths: The original 2024 report records 4,000 Narcan reversals in a collaborative statewide effort.
Original Form 990 and Schedule D identify the recipient and reconcile $9.323 million of annual expenses.
Community naloxone distribution has mortality evidence, although it does not identify this recipient's incremental effect.
reservations: Reported reversals are neither unique people nor deaths prevented; no county breakdown or deduplication method was found.
Partner attribution, metro share, incremental rescue, repeat-event adjustment and gift response are judgmental.
Funding room is unknown. This is a conditional initial report, not a donor recommendation.

sections.what: Georgia Harm Reduction Coalition, Inc., EIN 58-2227958, is the current legal recipient; the original 2024 return names its current website. Its own site lists two Atlanta locations plus Stone Mountain, Woodstock and Norcross, and statewide mail-based naloxone. These establish local service presence, not the fraction of rescued people residing in the pinned 29-county Atlanta-Sandy Springs-Roswell MSA. [Current programs](https://georgiaharmreduction.org/programs-services/) [Original tax return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202501629349300235/IRS990)
sections.monitoring: The original 2024 annual report, pages 5 and 12, records 32,000 Narcan units and 4,000 reversals, jointly crediting GHRC, Georgia DBHDD, Georgia Overdose Prevention and NEXT Distro. Page 12 also reports 25,000 individuals received and 6,355 engagements; the CEO narrative describes distribution to 6,355 persons. These denominators are not reconciled, so neither is used as a unique-person count. The model starts with reported reversal events only and gives no underreporting uplift. The report's lives-saved language is not adopted. Page 13 maps service presence across Georgia without county-level reversal or distribution volumes. [Original 2024 report](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ffSOvVIq0DW_0ycWq1X64t0LBecxTYXE/view)
sections.qualitative:
A Massachusetts interrupted time-series study found lower overdose mortality where overdose education and naloxone distribution were implemented; adjusted rate ratios were 0.73 and 0.54 for lower and higher implementation. This nonrandomized, older study supports the mechanism, not a GHRC effect size or a death-per-kit conversion. [Primary study](https://www.bmj.com/content/346/bmj.f174)

A linked Massachusetts cohort found 5.5% one-year mortality among 11,557 people discharged after nonfatal opioid overdose. This supports retaining competing mortality and a finite horizon; it does not calibrate present-day Georgia survival. [Primary survival study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31229387/)

The model assigns only one year, a 0.9 survival-area factor and 0.6 health utility after a genuinely incremental rescue. All three are judgments, not observed GHRC outcomes. A 0.5 effective unique-benefit factor reduces duplicate and overlapping follow-up from repeat rescues. A separate 0.05 incremental-rescue factor allows spontaneous recovery, rescue breathing, EMS and other naloxone to avert death anyway. Neither factor is empirically calibrated. Acute withdrawal, delayed care and other adverse health enter the adverse sensitivity; no such net harm is asserted as observed. Infectious-disease care, meals, counseling, screenings, trainings and syringes receive no additional modeled health credit.
sections.cost:
The latest original return located is calendar 2024: $9,322,976 total expenses, including $7,578,168 programs and $1,744,808 management/general; revenue was $9,124,535. Schedule D reconciles audited and tax expenses at the same $9,322,976 with no reported donated-service or other expense reconciling additions. Schedule M reports $542,712 of donated drugs/medical supplies as noncash contributions; this is not added again as though necessarily absent from expenses. Unrecognized volunteer time, partner resources and downstream health-care costs remain unpriced. [Return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202501629349300235/IRS990) [Schedule D](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202501629349300235/IRS990ScheduleD) [Schedule M](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202501629349300235/IRS990ScheduleM)

The annual report's page 23 expense-like table totals $9,368,880.18, $45,904.18 above the filed/audited reconciliation; its adjacent label says year-end balance. This discrepancy is unresolved. The model uses the original return and separately tests the annual-report amount. It charges the entire legal recipient, not just naloxone or substance-use program expenses. The illustrative central result is 0.84375 metro QALYs, approximately $110.50 million per 10, conditional on the assumptions below. This is neither the measured cost of rescuing a person nor a price for an additional donation.
sections.funding: GHRC's current own-site Donate Now link routes to Stripe. Payment was not executed, and script-dependent checkout completion and any enforceable local restriction were not verified. No quantified current unfunded capacity, marginal service budget or additional gift-created rescues were found. The 0.25 funding-response factor is an explicit scenario prior, with zero allowed; historical expense or a deficit does not establish funding room. Keep donor HOLD until current need, recipient-specific deduplicated outcomes, geographic attribution and additionality are verified. [Official route context](https://georgiaharmreduction.org/media/)

model.formula: Q_gross=R*d*a*r*T*s*u*f; Q_all=Q_gross-H; Q_metro=Q_gross*g-H; H is a metro harm and is included once in both net population totals; price_per_10=10*C/Q_metro only if Q_metro>0
model.counterfactual: r accounts for survival through alternative rescue/spontaneous recovery; f accounts for substitution or no service response to an additional unrestricted gift. No lifetime survival extrapolation.
model.attribution: a discounts joint GHRC/DBHDD/GOP/NEXT outcomes; d discounts repeat-event overlap. Four partners do not establish equal causal credit: a=0.25 is judgment, not division as an attribution estimator.
model.uncertainty: Weak confidence. Every bridge beyond the reported reversal count and legal-recipient cost is judgmental. Scenarios are conditional, not probability-weighted expected values or confidence intervals. Zero benefit remains plausible.
model.nativeOutcomes: 4,000 reported Narcan reversal events in the 2024 collaborative statewide report; not independently verified unique people or prevented deaths. 32,000 Narcan units are distribution outputs, not rescues.

what: FernCare Free Clinic provides no-cost non-emergency primary care to uninsured adults in Ferndale, Michigan.
Volunteer clinicians offer medications, basic laboratory testing and help applying for insurance.
Its current clinic schedule runs monthly, and its 2025 fundraising appeal reports more than 1,988 patient visits.
strengths: Volunteer clinicians provide uninsured adults with primary care, medicines and testing. Appropriate treatment can improve symptoms and reduce preventable disease.
Three latest accessible original IRS returns support the whole-recipient recorded-cost boundary.
The model distinguishes visits from people, current activity from old residence evidence, and average from marginal benefit.
reservations: The verified current output is visits, not unique patients or completed treatment episodes. Current residence, clinical improvement, donated-resource valuation and added capacity per dollar remain unresolved.

Obtain a current completed-care cohort and cost reconciliation, then a specific expansion or preservation budget with staffing, volunteer capacity, alternative funding and metro-resident reach. A randomized clinic-specific outcome study is not required to reopen an alpha.
Recorded costs exclude unreconciled donated resources; even the volunteer sensitivity is incomplete economic cost.

sections.what:
FernCare operates in Ferndale and offers no-cost non-emergency care, generic medications, basic laboratory testing and insurance-enrollment assistance. Its current patient page includes a 2026 clinic schedule. The current dinner appeal reports eight clinic sessions monthly; the undated About page still says six, so the newer dated activity disclosure takes precedence.

Detroit-Warren-Dearborn MSA, OMB July 2023 boundary: Wayne, Oakland, Macomb, Livingston, Lapeer and St. Clair. Ferndale is within Oakland County. Current local beneficiary share is not known; the clinic also advertises statewide access. Ann Arbor/Washtenaw, Flint/Genesee, Monroe and Windsor are outside.
sections.monitoring:
Current official service and fundraising pages; IRS BMF row; Givebutter recipient match: Current clinic schedule and active fundraising identify the recipient at 751 E Nine Mile Road, Ferndale. Establishes current operations and recipient, not effectiveness or funding room.

Three original IRS e-file renders and Schedule O: 2024 revenue $187,710, line17 expense $206,882, net assets $46,345; 2023 $147,698/$185,319/$65,517; July2021–June2022 $177,538/$209,195/$107,674. Includes a fiscal-year transition and prior-period adjustments; not three directly comparable calendar years. Gross fundraising costs netted against revenue are $254/$8,736/$6,737 respectively.

2019 original clinic review: Distinct patient and appointment denominators are explicitly separated. Residence was overwhelmingly Oakland, Wayne and Macomb. Useful historical evidence; does not establish 2025 completed-care counts or present local share.

Ettehad et al. randomized-trial meta-analysis: A 10 mm Hg systolic blood-pressure reduction was associated with major cardiovascular-event RR 0.80 in included trials. Supports treatment plausibility. FernCare's achieved BP change, baseline risk, treatment duration and adherence are unknown. It does not supply q = 0.003.

Oregon randomized Medicaid lottery study: Coverage increased access and reduced depression, while several measured physical-health outcomes did not significantly improve. Insurance coverage differs from a free clinic. More contacts alone are not a validated QALY conversion; null outcomes remain credible.
sections.qualitative:
Volunteer clinicians provide uninsured adults with primary care, medicines and testing. Appropriate treatment can improve symptoms and reduce preventable disease.

Current completed unique-patient courses, condition mix and outcome follow-up were not primary-verified. 2024 expense and 2025 visits/hours are different periods; the alpha openly uses a normalization assumption. FY2023 Schedule O includes $14,998 prior-period adjustment; FY2022 has -$4,273 bookkeeper in-kind adjustment. No smooth financial trend or simple in-kind addback is justified. Original filings are primary IRS data rendered by ProPublica, not audited financial statements. Latest three accessible filings were inspected; no recent independent audit was located. Website pages differ about clinic frequency and eligible age/underinsurance. Use current patient instructions operationally; reconcile historical tax prose before describing broad eligibility.

No numerical coefficient is empirically identified. Calling it conservative describes author intent, not an established lower bound.
sections.cost:
The scenario combines the latest inspected original spending year (2024) with verified 2025 visits. It assumes that these approximately describe one operating year; a 0.9–1.5 cost multiplier tests the mismatch but does not reconcile it. The visit coefficient is an explicit conservative judgment prior informed by clinical plausibility, not a study estimate. We do not invent a unique-patient count or infer complete courses from visits.

Q = V × a × m × q − H; recorded-spending cost per 10 = 10C / Q, if Q > 0. V = 1,988; C = $207,136; a = 0.50; m = 0.90; q = 0.003 net QALY per visit-equivalent; H = 0 in the illustrative base. Q = 2.6838. Total resource C* = C + unbooked volunteer time + unbooked medicines/labs/facilities + induced care costs, without double counting. Marginal donor Q(G) is a separate unknown function.

~$771,801 per 10 local QALYs on recorded spending; ~$1,423,862 with 3,500 volunteer hours at an illustrative $50/hour, before other omitted costs. The base is conditional, not calibrated expected value.

Whole-recipient historical expenses are verified, but reported volunteer hours and historically donated drugs show that cash spending understates total inputs. Current medicine/lab donations and their accounting treatment are unpriced. Historical 2019 or 2020 in-kind values must not simply be added to 2024 expense. The $300 patient sponsorship and $3,000 clinic sponsorship include event benefits and are fundraising descriptions, not marginal contracts.
sections.funding:
Positive scenarios are not probabilities, confidence intervals or proof of marginal donor value. There is no primary-verified current annual unique completed-care cohort in this review. A secondary social mirror says 841 unique patients in 2025; it is not used in the model. Donor recommendation and quantified funding room stay HOLD/null.

Obtain a current completed-care cohort and cost reconciliation, then a specific expansion or preservation budget with staffing, volunteer capacity, alternative funding and metro-resident reach. A randomized clinic-specific outcome study is not required to reopen an alpha.

The donation page uses $250/$2,500 examples; the newer event appeal uses $300/$3,000 and event tickets. Neither establishes marginal delivery. No causal benefits are assigned to the other community-resource activities, and no claim of whole-portfolio lower bound is made.

inputs.name: V: completed patient visits
inputs.rationale: 2026 annual-dinner letter reports patient visits. No inference that these are unique people, fully completed chronic-care courses or visits added by a new donor. Range: Official claim exceeds 1,988

inputs.rationale: 2019 clinic review reports 45.1% Oakland, 35.4% Wayne and 17.2% Macomb residence (97.7% sum; rounded). This is not a current share. inputs.name: q: overlap-adjusted health per visit-equivalent
inputs.rationale: About 1.1 quality-adjusted days per visit-equivalent, averaged across useful treatment and low-benefit follow-up. Interpret as total net course benefit allocated across its visits, never repeated lifetime credit per visit. This small prior reflects symptom relief and prevention plausibility; trials support some clinical pathways but do not identify this coefficient. No extra QALYs are added for labs, prescriptions or referrals. Range: 0.0005–0.010 in positive scenarios; zero and negative possible

inputs.name: Unbooked volunteer resource value
inputs.rationale: Official appeal reports more than 3,500 hours in 2025. Rate, role mix, overlap with booked costs and opportunity cost require reconciliation. These scenarios use the reported hour floor, not a measured full economic cost. Range: $105,000–$350,000 at $30–$100/hour

inputs.name: Additional capacity purchased by next gift
inputs.rationale: An appeal and past deficits establish fundraising, not a staffed marginal expansion or preservation counterfactual. Do not extrapolate the annual-average model linearly to a large gift. Range: May be zero

scenarios.label: Conditional recorded-spending illustration
scenarios.assumptions: 1988 × 0.50 × 0.003 all-population QALYs; multiply 0.90 local share. 2024 cost normalized to 2025 activity; all clinical factors assumed.

scenarios.label: Illustrative volunteer-inclusive cost
scenarios.assumptions: Add 3500 hours × assumed $50, subject to overlap reconciliation. Remaining omitted resources unpriced.

scenarios.label: Favorable positive stress case
scenarios.assumptions: C × .9, a .8, m .98, q .010; not a probability interval.

scenarios.label: Unfavorable positive stress case
scenarios.assumptions: C × 1.5, a .2, m .7, q .0005; not a probability interval.

scenarios.label: Null health
scenarios.assumptions: Zero effective treatment benefit or care additionality. Separately, donor funding displacement can imply zero marginal benefit.

scenarios.label: Additional harm stress test
scenarios.assumptions: Additional H=4 QALYs wholly local subtracted from gross base all-population 2.982 and local 2.6838; purely illustrative harm test. Ordinary expected harms already belong in q. Display loss, no negative price.

sensitivity: Illustrative base: ~$770,000 per 10 local QALYs on recorded spending. V 1,988; C $207,136; a 0.50; m 0.90; q 0.003; no separately modeled harm. Health is a prior-based scenario, not observed.
Favorable positive scenario: ~$120,000 per 10. 0.9 × recorded cost, a 0.80, m 0.98, q 0.010. This combines favorable assumptions and excludes omitted resources; it is not a confidence bound.
Unfavorable positive scenario: ~$22.3 million per 10. 1.5 × recorded cost, a 0.20, m 0.70, q 0.0005. The broad range shows how little the clinical conversion is identified.

Volunteer resource sensitivity: ~$1.16m–$2.08m per 10 at base health. Add 3,500 hours at $30–$100/hour to recorded spending, subject to overlap reconciliation. Medicines, discounted laboratories and induced downstream costs remain additional unknowns.

Null: No finite cost per 10. If effective care additionality or health improvement is zero, Q = 0. Independently, a gift replacing other funding may produce zero marginal benefit even when current services help.

Adverse: Net health loss is possible. If adverse events/displaced care exceed gross benefit, Q < 0. Report harm rather than a negative cost-effectiveness ratio. Base q should already deduct ordinary expected treatment harms; H is a stress test for additional unaccounted harm.

what: Kids In Need of Dentistry provides dental care for children from low-income families in Colorado.
Its Commerce City clinic offers preventive, restorative and specialized care, while Chopper Topper brings screening and preventive services to Denver-area schools.
Community outreach helps families access oral-health support.
strengths: Three original IRS filings establish whole-recipient expenses.
Original 2023 report identifies 9,337 sealants and separates clinic and outreach activity.
Randomized evidence supports permanent-molar sealants; an external US school-program model supplies a transparent health bridge.
reservations: DALY-to-QALY conversion, four-molar-equivalent scaling, residence share and benefit transport are analyst assumptions.

sections.what: KIND provides pediatric clinical dentistry in Commerce City and school prevention through Chopper Topper. Its current clinical page lists prevention, restorative and specialized care, including general anesthesia, and accepts Medicaid, Delta Dental and CHP+. Its school page describes Denver-area schools with at least half their students eligible for subsidized lunch.
sections.monitoring: The original 2023 report PDF page 3, printed pages 4–5, reports 5,302 school children, 9,337 preventive sealants, 705 clinic patients and 3,449 outreach recipients. The original 2023 990 reports 6,007 dental-service children, consistent with school plus clinic counts, but cross-program deduplication is unverified. The 2024 filing reports 7,213 dental-service children and 5,735 kit recipients without a sealant count. Do not treat all overall reach as treated children or 2023 output as current 2026 output.
sections.qualitative: Cochrane randomized evidence supports permanent-molar sealants but primary-tooth evidence is uncertain. Griffin et al. model 1.59 DALYs averted per 1,000 children receiving four first-molar sealants over four years. Dividing KIND's sealants by four creates modeled equivalents, not unique children. Transport, substitution, local residence and DALY-to-QALY conversion remain judgmental. No clinic, anxiety, kit, education or caregiver benefits are added. Excluded benefits are unquantified rather than proven zero; this is not a lower bound.
sections.cost: Use 2023 whole-recipient Form 990 expenses of $1,536,905 to match the 2023 output. This includes $1,124,202 program, $237,562 management and $175,141 fundraising. Original 2024 expense is $1,879,713 and 2022 gross resource expense is $1,559,737: Part IX $1,419,662 plus $140,075 of Part VIII line 8b direct event costs. In 2023 and 2024, relevant Part VIII netted direct-expense lines are blank; no addback is needed. The comparable three-year gross-resource mean is $1,658,785. No revenue, insurance reimbursement or external societal savings are subtracted, and no unverified in-kind gross-up is added. Unrecorded opportunity costs are outside this accounting perspective. Annual-report 2023 expense $1,531,508 differs from the IRS total; use the latter and preserve the discrepancy.
sections.funding: The official home page links a general Classy donation route redirected to give.kindsmiles.org. Redirect observed; checkout fields and receipt identity unreadable, no transaction submitted. A historical 2023–24 appeal mentioned 30 waiting schools but does not prove current funding room. Local service location is established; beneficiary residence is not. The local-share prior excludes Boulder, Greeley and Colorado Springs under the edition boundary. Average recipient spending cannot price a marginal gift without current capacity, demand, reimbursement and replacement-funding evidence.

sections.what:
Children's Research Triangle (CRT), EIN 36-4236142, provides child behavioral-health assessment and therapy, family support, professional training, research, and Camp SOAR. An ordinary gift supports this whole recipient. The official donation page names this EIN and links a donation form; no transaction was made. [Donate](https://childrensresearchtriangle.org/donate/)

Community therapists work at schools and social-service sites in Chicago, Evanston and Dolton, as well as the Loop clinic and telehealth. These are actual service anchors in Cook County, not merely headquarters evidence. The edition uses the Chicago-Naperville-Elgin MSA under OMB-23-01 (21 July 2023); residence-level attribution remains unverified. [Sites](https://childrensresearchtriangle.org/clinical-services/community-partners/)

Retain all assessment, clinical, camp, training, research, administration and fundraising costs. The audit identifies a separate for-profit affiliate, CRT Medical PC, with shared office/subcontract arrangements; this report does not merge that entity or attribute its services automatically.
sections.monitoring:
The 2024 annual report gives 1,368 children and families served, 786 people trained and 23 partners. Its 87% trauma-symptom improvement and 85% behavioral/emotional improvement figures lack denominators, attrition, timing, effect sizes and a comparison group. They are recipient monitoring claims, not causal recovery rates. [2024 report, printed p. 2](https://childrensresearchtriangle.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/CRT-2024-Annual-Report-1.pdf)

The report titled Impact Report 2025 gives 1,365 children/families, 805 trainees and 15 partners, alongside 86% trauma-symptom and 84% functioning improvement. Its camp section reports 96 campers and 130+ volunteer counselors/staff. The later HHS award narrative instead calls 1,166 people clients in 2025. Definitions are unreconciled; none is verified unique trauma-treatment starts or completions. Projected grant treatment of 70 children/caregivers annually is a target, not observed delivery. [2025 impact](https://childrensresearchtriangle.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/2026-Impact-Report-8.5-x-11-in-1.pdf) [Award](https://taggs.hhs.gov/Detail/AwardDetail?arg_AwardNum=H79SM091564&arg_ProgOfficeCode=80)

Request deidentified annual cohorts by residence, diagnosis, modality, first start, adequate dose, completion, follow-up and alternative treatment. Include missing outcomes and harms.
sections.qualitative:
School/community delivery and no-cost partner-site care offer a plausible way to reduce access barriers. CRT lists TF-CBT, CPP, SPARCS, PCIT, Theraplay, EMDR and parenting interventions; the mix is not quantified. [Therapy](https://childrensresearchtriangle.org/clinical-services/therapy/)

A CRT-affiliated randomized trial compared 40 treated with 38 control children with FAS/ARND and found improvements in executive functioning and emotional problem solving. That supports one historical intervention, not contemporary trauma-care QALYs or the ordinary gift. Its registry distinguishes standard referrals in controls; planned follow-up is not evidence of observed persistence. [Wells et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22251828/) [Registration](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00164346)

External therapy evidence supports plausible benefit but weakens any automatic symptom-to-QALY bridge. A Norwegian TF-CBT randomized economic evaluation found no significant QALY difference versus usual therapy, despite a favorable cost-effectiveness probability. [Aas et al.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29877724/)

Caregiver welfare, evaluations, research, training, crisis services, school violence prevention and camp respite may help or harm. Their net health H is unmeasured; H=0 is a modeling omission, not no value. Avoid double counting child, parent and partner gains. Family time, volunteer labor and space also consume resources.
sections.cost:
The illustrative central scenario uses $3,523,321 of whole-recipient FY2024 gross recognized resources. Its short-horizon therapy-only pathway gives approximately 0.039 Chicago-MSA QALYs, implying about $913 million per 10 QALYs. This is not an observed return, expected-value recommendation, restricted therapy price or scalable donation tranche. Donor readiness: HOLD.

Q_all = b × (N × s × q × t × a + H); Q_MSA = g × Q_all; price10 = 10 × (C+K)/Q_MSA only for positive Q_MSA. N=1,368 is mixed reported reach; s=.1 is the assumed number of eligible distinct trauma-treatment starts per reported reach unit. It combines deduplication, child-only scope, diagnosis, age and modality alignment. It is not observed 10% eligibility. t=.25 transports the external trial pathway, including local fidelity/completion differences; a=.5 removes equivalent timely alternative care; b=.25 is a hypothetical proportional gift-to-capacity response; g=.95 is a resident-health judgment. Unknown K and signed H are conditionally zero.

The external q=.0095 is the adjusted, imputed difference in QALYs over an 11-week UK trial of 29 children aged 8–17 with PTSD after a recent single event. It used SDQ mapped to CHU-9D. This is CT-PTSD, not CRT's complete modality mix; chronic trauma and younger children make transfer especially uncertain. The trial already includes noncompletion through imputation: no second completion multiplier is applied. We credit nothing after 11 weeks in the central scenario; this deliberately excludes possible later benefit. A separate sensitivity uses the paper's three-year modeled gain .0577 (about $150 million per 10 QALYs under other central assumptions); this is not observed long-term follow-up and is excluded from the central estimate. [Shearer et al., Table 4](https://acamh.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jcpp.12851)

The historical mixed denominator and current gifts are linked only by a stable-productivity assumption. Cases vary that assumption, zero finance/clinical effect/eligible reach, equivalent alternative treatment, geography, resource costs and signed other-portfolio health. Values are judgment stress tests, not confidence bounds or a posterior distribution.
sections.funding:
Original FY2022–24 Form 990 Part IX expense is $2,957,499, $3,303,788 and $3,415,329. Adding direct event expense of $78,325, $136,556 and $107,992 yields comparable gross recorded resources of $3,035,824, $3,440,344 and $3,523,321 (mean $3,333,163). In 2024, audited expense is $3,521,499; Schedule D adds $1,822 investment expense netted in the audit and removes direct events to reach Part IX. Thus the model keeps that investment resource cost; it does not confuse the audit total with Part IX. [2022 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202312939349301511/IRS990) [2023 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202403129349303570/IRS990) [2024 return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202543169349304119/IRS990) [Schedule D](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202543169349304119/IRS990ScheduleD)

All three original audits were inspected. FY2024 cash was $614,925 and net assets $776,629, including a $125,000 board reserve. The $709,579 lease liability explains most liabilities; it is not an ordinary cash borrowing. The audit's financial assets available within one year were $630,484 and the undrawn credit line $100,000. These are dated balances, not present liquidity. Opinion was unmodified; no current audit findings were listed. Volunteer/partner resources are not fully valued. [2024 audit](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/display_audit/2024-12-GSAFAC-0000381225)

The 2025 impact appeal projects a 2026 gap above $300,000 and federal support reaching zero by end-2026. Subsequent evidence prevents treating that appeal as current room: HHS records a new $499,896 action on 31 August 2026, performance period 30 September 2026–29 September 2031; Impact Grants Chicago confirms a 2026 $100,000 award, and Invest for Kids lists CRT among current beneficiaries. Award periods/restrictions differ; do not simply subtract awards from the old gap or assume five years are fully funded. [HHS](https://taggs.hhs.gov/Detail/AwardDetail?arg_AwardNum=H79SM091564&arg_ProgOfficeCode=80) [Impact Grants](https://www.impactgrantschicago.org/all-grant-recipients/) [Invest for Kids](https://investforkidschicago.org/beneficiary-category/current-year/)

Before a recommendation, reconcile current cash, grant restrictions/renewals, remaining commitments and staffing capacity to a priced incremental plan, alongside unique local outcomes and a validated utility/duration bridge. The $3,000-per-child implication of the old appeal is not used as a marginal cost.

model.costScope: Full legal recipient FY2024 gross recorded resources C; all programs, admin, direct event and investment expenses retained. Add unknown net unrecognized K. Separate for-profit CRT Medical PC not consolidated.
model.geographicAttribution: Chicago-Naperville-Elgin MSA, OMB-23-01-2023-07-21; actual Cook County sites observed. g=.95 is an unverified resident-health fraction.
model.formula: Q_all=b*(N*s*q*t*a+H); Q_MSA=g*Q_all; price10=10*(C+K)/Q_MSA only if Q_MSA>0. q is 11-week trial QALY gain; no additional duration or completion multiplier.
model.counterfactual: Without the extra ordinary gift, current grants, existing clinical services, reserves and other providers remain. Capacity response b captures replacement or expansion; a removes equivalent timely care. Waitlist/usual services remain for credited patients, as in external trial.
model.attribution: s converts mixed reach into distinct aligned child course starts; t transports clinical pathway including fidelity/completion. b financial additionality and a alternative treatment differ but are correlated. No measured recipient causal health is claimed.
model.uncertainty: Very weak confidence; hypothetical scenarios, not expected value, confidence intervals or donor-ready estimates. Unknown K and H conditionally zero; no proof of linear scalability. Short horizon excludes possible lasting benefit.
model.nativeOutcomes: Unique client starts and adequate therapy dose/completion, symptoms and functioning, family stress, evaluation follow-through, camp respite; reported reach and percentages cannot establish these causal outcomes.
