inputs.rationale: Part IX 3,415,329 plus 107,992 direct events. Equals audit expense 3,521,499 plus 1,822 investment fee netted there; includes all programs/admin/fundraising, not a current marginal price.

inputs.name: N
inputs.rationale: Not known unique children, treatment starts or completions. No automatic assignment of one unit to one treated child.

inputs.name: s
inputs.unit: eligible distinct trial-like child course starts per reported reach unit
inputs.rationale: Assumes 10 per 100 heterogeneous reach units become aligned starts after deduplication, child-only scope, age/diagnosis/modality filters. Actual fraction unknown; 2.5–30% stress tests. Clinical mix and broad evaluation/training portfolio motivate a small fraction, not empirical calibration.

inputs.name: q
inputs.unit: incremental QALY per child assigned over 11 weeks in external trial
inputs.rationale: Adjusted imputed Table 4 estimate in 29-person UK CT-PTSD study; mapped SDQ utility. This is a noisy external effect, not a CRT observation. No persistence after trial is credited.

inputs.name: t
inputs.rationale: Quarter external effect for different modality, chronic/repeated trauma, age/severity, fidelity and local completion. Trial imputation already includes missing follow-up; no extra completion factor. Zero and negative clinical cases retained.

inputs.name: a
inputs.unit: fraction lacking equally effective timely alternative care
inputs.rationale: Half would obtain equivalent care otherwise; waitlist/usual services remain for credited half. Actual alternatives unobserved.

inputs.name: b
inputs.unit: capacity response to small proportional unrestricted-resource increase
inputs.rationale: Quarter proportional response; not fraction of a gift earmarked for therapy. Current grants, reserves and staff constraints make response unknown. New award invalidates reliance on old gap alone. Zero case essential.

inputs.name: g
inputs.unit: fraction of modeled net health in pinned Chicago MSA
inputs.rationale: Actual Chicago/Evanston/Dolton service sites and audit primary metro service support high share; no client residence roster. Applied to health, not headquarters allocation.

inputs.name: K
inputs.unit: USD net unrecognized partner/volunteer resource cost
inputs.rationale: Conditional zero; partner space and camp volunteer labor unvalued. 25% add-on is illustrative, not measured. Do not double count paid labor/leases already in C.

inputs.name: H
inputs.unit: signed non-modeled portfolio QALYs before b and g
inputs.rationale: Conditional zero for caregiver, camp, evaluation, research, training, crisis and prevention net outcomes. Signed +/-1 are stress tests, not observations; remove overlaps before adding.

reports.priceScope: Annual-cost health-and-income welfare comparison; causal effects are judgment-based scenarios, not measured donation returns

what: Institute for Progress researches and helps implement U.S. innovation policy across science, biotechnology, immigration, infrastructure and emerging technology.
It publishes reform proposals, convenes experts and supplies technical assistance to policymakers; NSF independently confirms an agency partnership.
Donations support its researchers, expert convenings and practical assistance on policy design and implementation.
strengths: A formal NSF partnership and concrete clinical-trial proposals establish substantive work beyond general advocacy.
Public original IRS returns support three years of spending and a functional cost breakdown, while current publications establish continued operations.
Institutional reforms could benefit large future patient populations and produce valuable scientific, immigration and infrastructure gains beyond the pathway priced here.
reservations: The health-and-income estimate depends on hypothetical causal scale and incidence; no study identifies the combined organization-specific return.
A $10.5M July 2026 general-support grant and incomplete current financial information make marginal funding additionality uncertain.
Policy overlap is not causal attribution, and faster first-in-human trials can yield no patient benefit or harm if implementation weakens reliable evidence.

sections.what:
IFP is a Washington-based nonprofit think tank rather than a clinical care provider. Its [current organizational page](https://ifp.org/about/) identifies five research areas and lists Alec Stapp as CEO. Co-founder Caleb Watney moved to [Coefficient Giving’s public-policy leadership](https://coefficientgiving.org/team/caleb-watney/) in 2026 and remains an external IFP board member. This review evaluates an ordinary donation to the operating charity, EIN 87-2449729, rather than a newly invented restricted clinical-trial fund.

**What money buys.** Researchers develop technically specific proposals, brief policymakers, convene specialists and assist implementation. For example, IFP’s [Clinical Trial Abundance series](https://ifp.org/the-case-for-clinical-trial-abundance/) addresses recruitment, monitoring, participant compensation and regulatory information. It is a collaborative project supported by Renaissance Philanthropy, with contributors beyond IFP; the whole agenda cannot be assigned exclusively to one organization. Its [September 2026 biotechnology analysis](https://ifp.org/why-biotech-companies-go-to-australia-to-test-new-drugs/) argues for clearer, proportionate first-in-human requirements using Australia as a comparison.

**Why this could help.** Removing a consequential bottleneck could allow more useful studies, stop ineffective development sooner, or bring effective treatment to patients earlier. The chain is donation → additional policy capacity → a changed institutional decision → changed research or development → effective care actually received → incremental patient health. Each arrow can fail. Research production and policy access establish capacity, but do not establish the final health effect.

The organization also pursues talent retention, science-funding improvements and easier construction. Those pathways could dominate total value. We discuss them as unpriced benefits and risks because this review did not establish a donor-attributable bridge to household income or U.S. healthy life-years.
sections.monitoring:
**Evidence of implementation capacity.** [NSF’s September 2023 announcement](https://www.nsf.gov/news/nsf-partners-institute-progress-test-new-mechanisms-funding) independently confirms an agreement for IFP and its Metascience Working Group to design and execute experiments on research-funding mechanisms. The agency identifies tests of high-risk/high-reward funding and analyses of funding outputs. This is stronger evidence of a defined agency role than counting publications. The page is now archived; it does not establish that the agreement continues in 2026, that experiments succeeded, or that breakthroughs resulted.

**Policy overlap, with attribution limits.** The 2024 clinical agenda included publishing redacted complete response letters. [FDA independently announced publication of more than 200 such letters in July 2025](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-embraces-radical-transparency-publishing-complete-response-letters). This establishes a concrete institutional change consistent with a proposal. It does not establish that IFP caused it, that the recommendation was unique, or that the change improved patient outcomes.

The [FDA Expedited IND pilot](https://www.fda.gov/industry/fda-actions-accelerate-and-modernize-early-and-late-stage-clinical-development/fda-expedited-investigational-new-drug-ind-pilot-program) tests rolling review and qualified research institutions to accelerate first-in-human trial initiation while retaining FDA oversight. We found no reviewed evidence assigning its creation to IFP. An earlier Phase I start is distinct from an earlier final approval, dissemination and effective treatment. IFP’s September 2026 analysis engages with an existing initiative; its publication date cannot establish responsibility for the initiative’s earlier adoption.

**What we would track.** A credible evaluation would record the proposed text or operational change; IFP’s specific assistance and timing; implementers’ independent assessment of contribution; adoption and actual use; enrollment and trial completion; reliable evidence produced; and treatment use relative to a counterfactual. It should also track failed projects, participant harms and lost evidential quality. An agency announcement is an intermediate outcome, not a QALY measurement.

Our evidence confidence is higher for finances and identified activities than for effectiveness, causal contribution and marginal donor return. No reviewed public evaluation supplied an independently estimated donation-to-QALY effect. This is a statement about the evidence reviewed, not proof that useful impact has never occurred.
sections.qualitative:
**The case for support.** A specialist policy team can improve decisions affecting much larger research and infrastructure systems. The NSF agreement supports a plausible route into implementation. IFP’s [July 2026 metascience proposal](https://ifp.org/science-agencies-need-metascience-units/) explicitly argues for experiments and administrative-data analysis before scaling funding reforms. That willingness to test mechanisms is attractive, although a proposed experiment is not a demonstrated successful intervention.

There is an additional infrastructure case. [Giving Green’s grantee spotlight](https://www.givinggreen.earth/research/institute-for-progress-grantee-spotlight-2026) describes intended funding for permitting and transmission policy research, coalition-building and technical drafting. It credits IFP with contributions to protecting tax credits and convening a permitting coalition. These are the evaluator’s assessments, not independently estimated marginal climate or health outcomes. Although the page title says 2026, the substantive text says last updated November 2025, so it cannot settle funding room after July 2026. We add no climate QALYs.

**The main concerns.** Policy change depends on governments, other advocates, industry and implementation capacity. IFP may contribute substantially while a particular extra gift adds little; conversely, timely specialist support might matter at a narrow policy window. Neither outcome follows from organizational prominence. IFP and 1Day Sooner participate in overlapping clinical-reform ecosystems, so their modeled benefits must not be added as independent versions of the same win.

Faster evidence production can be beneficial when it preserves participant safety and identifies effective treatments. Reforms that weaken evidence, concentrate access among affluent patients, or improve commercial throughput without net clinical benefit can be neutral or harmful. Infrastructure and technology choices also have distributional and externality effects. The health scenario below does not capture the full portfolio’s downside.

**Funding and governance.** Coefficient Giving’s [fund listing](https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/abundance-and-growth/) records $10.5M in July 2026 general support. Its public-policy head is an IFP co-founder and external board member. That connection should be disclosed when using funder endorsement as evidence; it does not establish improper grantmaking. IFP’s [2024 Schedule O](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523119349304152/IRS990ScheduleO) reports annual conflict-policy review and board approval of compensation, but does not verify the procedures for the later grant. We would request updated decision and recusal processes alongside the next unfunded work package.

Our judgment is that IFP is a substantive, plausible institutional-reform opportunity with unusually weak measurability at the donor-to-health endpoint. Beta denotes a fuller review, not a GiveWell endorsement or measured effectiveness finding.
sections.cost:
Our central **health-and-income estimate is $325K per better life**, using ten healthy-year welfare equivalents. The previous health-only review was $88.3M; the original alpha comparison was $3.6M. These are different model versions, not measurements showing that impact changed by those ratios. Income-equivalent years are wellbeing comparisons, not observed QALYs or DALYs.

**Correcting the cost boundary.** We charge the latest inspected annual charity expense, $3,597,698, once. The previous review also multiplied the denominator by an arbitrary new-donation additionality factor based partly on grant receipts. That mixes annual-work cost-effectiveness with a marginal-gift model. We remove that factor from the annual-cost central case; implementation probabilities and the organization's contribution still apply. Receiving a grant does not prove the year's work has low value. The old funding haircut remains a sensitivity, and current room for more funding still needs a costed work package. This is not a promise that any gift size scales linearly.

**Income pathway: retaining internationally trained talent.** IFP works on immigration rules and guidance as well as clinical trials. Its [STEM workforce analysis](https://ifp.org/meeting-u-s-defense-science-and-engineering-workforce-needs-a-progress-report/) describes sizeable talent pools and practical retention obstacles. The cited annual doctorate flow, postdoc stock and visa approvals overlap; we do not sum them as new beneficiaries. Our central hypothesis is one additional useful reform affecting 5,000 people who otherwise would leave or never enter, with five years of real disposable income $20,000 higher than a $40,000 outside option. These are judgment inputs, not 5,000 documented IFP successes or a measured wage increase.

The income comparison must be against work in another country, not zero earnings. The [Clemens visa-lottery study](https://www.cgdev.org/sites/default/files/1424188_file_Clemens_wage_gaps_FINAL.pdf) supports the possibility of location-related earnings gains, but its single-firm setting does not identify our $20,000 gain. We define that gain after tax, housing, relocation and private visa costs, not a nominal U.S. salary premium. A 25% implementation probability and 10% IFP causal contribution leave 2.5% of the conditional benefit credited. We subtract an illustrative income loss of $1,000/year for 500 existing workers at a $75,000 baseline; this is a downside allowance, not a measured displacement effect. Benefits begin after three years and each annual flow is discounted at 3%.

Only gains occurring while people are U.S. residents enter this edition. Switching visa categories while staying and earning the same amount is not a gain. We do not add patents, GDP, clinical-trial savings, security or downstream innovation on top of this worker-income channel. Public-service costs and origin-country losses could change the wider assessment; an actual cohort study and a costed policy package are the next evidence priorities.

**Health component.** The earlier review's clinical chain is retained except for the mismatched donor haircut: 100,000 potential recipients × 0.1 annual QALY gain × three months of acceleration × 25% useful-reform probability × 7.9% approval likelihood × 50% conditional incremental usefulness × organizational contribution × U.S. share, discounted for 10.5 years at 3%. The [BIO historical approval benchmark](https://go.bio.org/rs/490-EHZ-999/images/ClinicalDevelopmentSuccessRates2011_2020.pdf) informs approval and delay, not the other judgment inputs. The [FDA pilot](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-launches-expedited-ind-pilot-begins-accepting-applications) is intermediate evidence, not measured earlier treatment. The 0.1 gain is conditional on a useful product, so approval and usefulness are not already folded into it. One candidate-equivalent is a narrow health pathway, not the organization's entire portfolio. Clinical failures, participant harms, care uptake and collaboration still matter.

**Combined arithmetic.** The health component is 1.629029 U.S. QALYs; signed income benefit is 109.032668 U.S. income-equivalent healthy years. Using [Coefficient Giving's comparison](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/), income welfare is 0.5 × affected people × ln(1 + real income gain/baseline income) × the explicit causal/local/non-overlap shares, summed over individually discounted benefit years. Divide ten times $3,597,698 by 110.661697 combined years to get $325K. The report, research list and shortlist all use that same calculation.

**How much confidence?** Every organization-specific cohort, probability, gain and incidence assumption here is a transparent hypothesis. Primary sources identify the workstreams and economic mechanisms, not this central return. Our joint low/high cases give Conservative joint case: $441.8M. Not a confidence limit. Favorable joint case: $7K. Not a confidence limit. Zero implementation gives zero benefit, and net harms can eliminate a positive price. The range is not a statistical confidence interval. Inspect the exact vectors below rather than treating a precise-looking price as verified.

**Costs, coverage and next evidence.** Retain full annual charity cost once for portfolio comparator; do not allocate a fictional cheap immigration team. Five benefit years are not five funded years. If work requires several annual budgets, charge them. Visa, agency, sponsor and migration costs must be netted from income or added to cost; central gain asserts net worker costs but lacks measured government/employer incremental costs. Annual-work headline removes donor funding haircut; prior factors preserved only as unknown marginal-funding sensitivity. Annual scale and causal reform probability are judgments requiring workstream evidence. Only workers who otherwise leave/never enter count; people merely changing visa class while staying do not. Alternative Canada/UK earnings can sharply reduce income gain. No new donation credit for historic USCIS reforms. Direct migrant income excludes innovations, patents, GDP and clinical benefits. Income gains among the same persons can coexist with health gains only if no QALY valuation already incorporates income. Do not add IFP clinical-trial savings also assigned to 1Day. Five years of household gains do not automatically require five annual charity budgets, nor prove that one year's work is sufficient; the three-budget stress case tests that mismatch. Other organizational channels remain unquantified rather than assumed worthless or counted as a generic growth multiplier. Before a major funding decision, ask for current project budgets, specific counterfactual effects and recipient-level outcomes. The strongest model is the one that replaces these priors with evidence, not the one with the smallest headline price.
sections.funding:
**Three years of actual spending.** Original IRS returns report [2022 expenses of $1,201,769](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872449729/202323199349321627/full), [2023 expenses of $3,079,238](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872449729/202433209349321923/full), and [2024 expenses of $3,597,698](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872449729/202523119349304152/full). These are calendar-year totals, not current budgets. Their mean is **$2,626,235**. We replace the earlier startup-year series; 2021 is not used to depress the comparison. Spending rose 16.8% from 2023 to 2024.

**Spending breakdown.** The 2024 return allocates $2,868,554 to programs (79.7%), $538,935 to management/general (15.0%) and $190,209 to fundraising (5.3%). Compensation, other wages, pensions, benefits and payroll taxes total $2,341,538 (65.1% of expense). These are functional and personnel categories, not a clinical-policy team budget. The [supplemental return](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202523119349304152/IRS990ScheduleO) itemizes $453,725 of other consultants and $37,254 of technology/web consultants. The operating mix is consistent with a labor-intensive research organization, but overhead ratios do not demonstrate effectiveness.

**Reserves are not cash runway.** At year-end 2024, the return reports $3,658,868 net assets, including $2,726,376 with donor restrictions and $932,492 without restrictions, and $2.6M pledges/grants receivable. It also reports $102,969 non-interest-bearing cash and $779,305 other investments. Total assets were $3,943,124 and liabilities $284,256. These accrual figures do not show how much unrestricted cash is available today. Dividing total net assets by expenses would overstate usable runway; even an unrestricted-net-assets ratio is not a cash forecast.

**Room for more funding.** Coefficient Giving lists July 2026 general support of $10.5M. Its duration, payment schedule, remaining balance and allocation are unverified, so it cannot be treated as one year’s expenditure or immediate available cash. The 2024 deficit likewise cannot establish a September 2026 gap after later grants. Giving Green describes a separate planned infrastructure grant, but its spotlight does not disclose a current remaining funding need.

For a large donation, request the 2026 operating budget; restricted and unrestricted cash forecast; receivable collection and grant-payment schedules; committed funding by workstream; and a costed additional project with hiring/implementation constraints and explicit actions if the gift is not made. Existing support may finance growth or leave a narrow unfunded opportunity, but neither has been verified. The [individual giving page](https://givebutter.com/ifp) is a donation route, not evidence that the next dollar buys the modeled effect.

what: 1Day Sooner combines clinical-trial policy, participant representation and support for infectious-disease research.
Its U.S. work develops FDA evidence and trial-policy proposals; its international work includes challenge models and vaccine access.
Donations support its policy researchers, participant-representation work and clinical-data projects.
strengths: CPO study collaborations, a participant council and clinical-data infrastructure give the organization concrete operations beyond general advocacy.
Original 2022–2024 returns and current cumulative-funding disclosures make spending and entity distinctions inspectable.
Better clinical evidence could affect many development programs, and participant representation addresses a neglected incentive problem.
reservations: The health-and-income estimate depends on hypothetical causal scale and incidence; no study identifies the combined organization-specific return.
International beneficiaries, clinical risks and shared work with other advocates sharply limit simple attribution.
Recent large gifts and an affiliate grant-label mismatch leave current charity funding room unverified.

sections.what:
1Day Sooner works on the people and institutions that produce medical evidence. Its [Cooperative Participant Organization (CPO)](https://www.1daysooner.org/cpo-investigator-services/) places staff scientists alongside study teams to support recruitment, representation and communications. The [CPO FAQ](https://www.1daysooner.org/cpo-investigator-services/frequently-asked-questions/) clarifies that these are collaborations, that 1Day does not conduct day-to-day trial research, and that most CPO work relies on grants with collaborators; philanthropy may subsidize some services. A donor therefore supports complementary study capacity rather than directly buying a vaccine trial.

Its U.S. [clinical-trial policy agenda](https://www.1daysooner.org/clinical-trial-abundance/) includes FDA data transparency, wider use of real-world evidence, participant compensation and IRB transparency. Policy proposals, convening and agency submissions are outputs, not enacted reforms or patient benefits. The ten-year aspiration to produce far more evidence at much lower cost is a stretch goal, not the expected result of a marginal donation.

Other work is international. [Challenge-model development](https://www.1daysooner.org/challenge-model-development/) concerns hepatitis C, Australian strep A studies and TB research in Malawi. [Vaccine-policy research](https://www.1daysooner.org/briefs-and-reports/) includes African malaria-vaccine rollout. These may have considerable global value, but people vaccinated abroad are not U.S. beneficiaries. We quantify only a hypothetical clinical-policy pathway and leave other benefits unpriced rather than assigning them invented health outcomes.
sections.monitoring:
The strongest observable evidence concerns operations. The [Participant Council](https://www.1daysooner.org/council/) has 15 members from eight countries, including four U.S. members; it meets three to four times annually and compensates attendance. Its work on representation, ethics and fair compensation is a real participant-governance output. Council composition is not an estimate of the organization's U.S. spending or patient share. For CPO, useful monitoring would count funded collaborations, eligible volunteers enrolled and retained, recruitment time compared with similar studies, and whether participant recommendations change protocols.

[CTD Commons](https://www.ctdcommons.org/home) aims to acquire and share regulatory dossiers from failed biotechnology companies, combining legal acquisition with data engineering. The [January 2026 launch](https://www.1daysooner.org/press-releases/jan-26-ctd-commons-launches-to-unlock-biotechs-lost-archive-and-accelerate-medical-innovation/) identifies both 1Day and Renaissance Philanthropy as backers. Dossiers acquired, properly redacted and reused would be stronger metrics than launch announcements. We found no public causal estimate of development time saved or additional effective treatments from its archive.

Independent evidence helps distinguish proposed from active research. [Oxford's July 2026 HIT update](https://oxfordbrc.nihr.ac.uk/recruitment-under-way-in-ground-breaking-hepatitis-c-study/) describes first-stage recruitment of people already infected with hepatitis C to donate blood for inoculum development. It does not demonstrate a successful vaccine or completed infection of healthy volunteers. 1Day's older Hep C page still anticipates recruitment in 2024, so that forecast cannot verify today's milestone. The linked ISRCTN record redirected to a holding page during review.

The [FDA's September 15, 2026 Expedited IND pilot](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-launches-expedited-ind-pilot-begins-accepting-applications) accepts applications until October 30 and tests whether rolling pre-IND preparation makes early trials more predictable. It is a relevant policy development, but no completed pilot evaluation yet establishes acceleration through later trials, approval and treatment use. A review should follow those stages and adverse outcomes, not award QALYs at the announcement.
sections.qualitative:
The case is institutional leverage with substantial causal uncertainty. A good research model or reusable archive can benefit several projects, and timely removal of avoidable trial friction can matter. Earlier evidence can also correctly stop an ineffective candidate, which is valuable without producing the model's earlier-treatment benefit. Reliable evidence and patient access matter more than the number of trials started.

Participant advocacy is a distinctive strength: study sponsors do not necessarily internalize volunteer welfare or the value of transparent results. The [informed-consent guide](https://www.1daysooner.org/guidance-for-informed-consent-procedure/) discusses quarantine, withdrawal and uncertain long-term effects. An [affiliated systematic review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9938741/) covered 15,046 challenged participants in 308 studies, found 24 reported serious adverse events and no reported deaths or permanent damage, but emphasized incomplete reporting. These historical observations are neither zero-risk evidence nor a safety forecast for a novel pathogen. The authors disclose 1Day affiliations; this is useful research, not an independent assessment of the charity.

Risks include participant morbidity and inconvenience, rare or unrecognized long-term harms, exclusion of less healthy people, and premature conclusions from surrogate endpoints or nonrepresentative samples. Compensation may improve access and fairness while requiring careful consent and risk review. Regulatory reform can save time, but weakening valid safeguards or encouraging use of ineffective products could produce negative health value. Ethical representation and scientific validity therefore belong in monitoring alongside speed.

Attribution is shared. The [briefs page](https://www.1daysooner.org/briefs-and-reports/) identifies policy papers prepared for an IFP–Renaissance project, and the symposium includes multiple organizations. FDA, investigators, other advocates and existing funders can advance the same work. We would not sum IFP and 1Day health estimates for the same reform without allocating their joint contribution. This beta review supports continued investigation of a speculative opportunity; it is not a demonstrated cost-effective U.S. health intervention.
sections.cost:
Our central **health-and-income estimate is $9.0M per better life**, using ten healthy-year welfare equivalents. The previous health-only review was $63.8M; the original alpha comparison was $3.2M. These are different model versions, not measurements showing that impact changed by those ratios. Income-equivalent years are wellbeing comparisons, not observed QALYs or DALYs.

**Correcting the cost boundary.** We charge the latest inspected annual charity expense, $2,424,138, once. The previous review also multiplied the denominator by an arbitrary new-donation additionality factor based partly on grant receipts. That mixes annual-work cost-effectiveness with a marginal-gift model. We remove that factor from the annual-cost central case; implementation probabilities and the organization's contribution still apply. Receiving a grant does not prove the year's work has low value. The old funding haircut remains a sensitivity, and current room for more funding still needs a costed work package. This is not a promise that any gift size scales linearly.

**Income pathway: cheaper reliable medical evidence.** [1Day Sooner's trial-abundance program](https://www.1daysooner.org/clinical-trial-abundance/) explicitly aims to reduce evidence-generation costs and make better use of existing data. Efficient trials can save resources even when a product fails. We therefore do not multiply this income channel by the 7.9% drug-approval probability or the separate clinical-usefulness factor used for patient health.

The central hypothesis is 20 affected trial-equivalents at $20M each, with 10% avoidable resource cost: $40M gross savings, less $2M of extra implementation, regulator, dossier, challenge-agent and participant-resource costs. [HHS's historical operational model](https://aspe.hhs.gov/reports/examination-clinical-trial-costs-barriers-drug-development) demonstrates the order of magnitude of possible trial-operation savings, not this organization's achieved saving. Twenty affected trials and a 10% saving are judgments; they are not the entire trial industry and do not imply that every trial is changed by 1Day Sooner. Before/after trial-cost and dossier-reuse data would replace these assumptions.

Of the $38M conditional net resource saving, we assign half to U.S. incidence and half of that to independent net disposable-income benefit: $9.5M. The second adjustment excludes reinvestment already represented by health, offsetting labor/provider losses and savings not reaching household consumption. Spread over 10,000 owners or payers with $100,000 income, that is a one-year $950 gain. This relatively affluent baseline avoids valuing pharmaceutical profits as if received by poor households. The 25% useful-reform probability and 15% organizational contribution apply once, giving a 3.75% causal share; realization is three years away, discounted at 3%.

Lower staff compensation is not automatically a social efficiency gain. Resources must be productively redeployed, or lost earnings and implementation burdens subtracted. The low case makes the extra implementation cost exceed savings. We do not count drug sales, participant compensation transfers or gross pharmaceutical revenue as new welfare. This channel overlaps IFP's collaborative trial work: the economic win is not separately assigned to both organizations, and gifts to 1Day Sooner are not treated as funding its separate advocacy affiliate.

**Health component.** The earlier review's clinical chain is retained except for the mismatched donor haircut: 100,000 potential recipients × 0.1 annual QALY gain × three months of acceleration × 25% useful-reform probability × 7.9% approval likelihood × 50% conditional incremental usefulness × organizational contribution × U.S. share, discounted for 10.5 years at 3%. The [BIO historical approval benchmark](https://go.bio.org/rs/490-EHZ-999/images/ClinicalDevelopmentSuccessRates2011_2020.pdf) informs approval and delay, not the other judgment inputs. The [FDA pilot](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-launches-expedited-ind-pilot-begins-accepting-applications) is intermediate evidence, not measured earlier treatment. The 0.1 gain is conditional on a useful product, so approval and usefulness are not already folded into it. One candidate-equivalent is a narrow health pathway, not the organization's entire portfolio. Clinical failures, participant harms, care uptake and collaboration still matter.

**Combined arithmetic.** The health component is 1.086019 U.S. QALYs; signed income benefit is 1.622402 U.S. income-equivalent healthy years. Using [Coefficient Giving's comparison](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/), income welfare is 0.5 × affected people × ln(1 + real income gain/baseline income) × the explicit causal/local/non-overlap shares, summed over individually discounted benefit years. Divide ten times $2,424,138 by 2.708421 combined years to get $9.0M. The report, research list and shortlist all use that same calculation.

**How much confidence?** Every organization-specific cohort, probability, gain and incidence assumption here is a transparent hypothesis. Primary sources identify the workstreams and economic mechanisms, not this central return. Our joint low/high cases give Conservative joint case: $107.04B. Not a confidence limit. Favorable joint case: $53K. Not a confidence limit. Zero implementation gives zero benefit, and net harms can eliminate a positive price. The range is not a statistical confidence interval. Inspect the exact vectors below rather than treating a precise-looking price as verified.

**Costs, coverage and next evidence.** Annual charity cost once. External added resource costs explicitly subtracted from native savings. Net resource saving cannot simultaneously be counted as reduced numerator AND added denominator. Need actual dossier reuse, trial-count, before/after cost and U.S. owner/payer incidence evidence. Annual-work headline removes donor funding haircut; prior factors preserved only as unknown marginal-funding sensitivity. Annual scale and causal reform probability are judgments requiring workstream evidence. Trials must change because of the reform/work package, not all trials in the industry. Include failed products that avoid resource use. Adoption and cost saving already conditional on reform; adding approvalProbability would double-discount the wrong endpoint. Existing grants and policy actors can deliver the same saving. Same CTA reform ecosystem as IFP. Attribute economic savings once across collaborators; do not present the two charities as independent wins. Exclude health benefits of reinvested R&D and drug revenue/sales from this savings channel. Five years of household gains do not automatically require five annual charity budgets, nor prove that one year's work is sufficient; the three-budget stress case tests that mismatch. Other organizational channels remain unquantified rather than assumed worthless or counted as a generic growth multiplier. Before a major funding decision, ask for current project budgets, specific counterfactual effects and recipient-level outcomes. The strongest model is the one that replaces these priors with evidence, not the one with the smallest headline price.
sections.funding:
We inspected original IRS-derived rendered Form 990s for [2022](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/851103820/202313189349300501/full), [2023](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/851103820/202443189349300824/full) and [2024](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/851103820/202533209349300073/full). Total expenses were **$1,554,943; $2,832,663; and $2,424,138**, a three-year mean of **$2,270,581**. The 2023 total includes a separately disclosed $394,096 settlement expense; removing only that one-off gives a descriptive mean of $2,139,216. We retain gross totals and do not call this adjusted figure an audited recurring budget.

**2024 spending.** Part IX assigns $2,262,397 (93.3%) to programs, $150,212 (6.2%) to management/general and $11,529 (0.5%) to fundraising. Staff compensation, benefits and payroll taxes total $1,153,259 (47.6%). Nonemployee services total $819,238 (33.8%); [Schedule O](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/full_text/202533209349300073/IRS990ScheduleO) itemizes $455,638 contractors, $344,784 payroll fees, $10,965 honoraria and $7,851 payroll-management fees. Payroll fees are the filing's category, not proof of an additional equivalent salary amount or external research expenditure. Travel is $176,298, conferences $77,131 and grants $86,450. These are organizational classifications; no public allocation ties them to U.S. CTA, CPO, vaccine work or the modeled reform.

2024 revenue was $1,417,665 and net assets without donor restrictions ended at $2,015,836. Cash and savings totaled $2,048,188; liabilities were $51,644. Net assets equal roughly ten months of 2024 expenses, a historical ratio rather than current runway. The filing reports no independent financial audit/review and no written conflict, whistleblower or retention policies in that year. Ask for updated governance and accounting documents before treating these historical disclosures as current practices.

The [July 2026 financial disclosure](https://www.1daysooner.org/finances-transparency/) reports $12.819M cumulative charity funding, including $4.6M from Coefficient Giving in its embedded chart. It separately reports $2.9M for the affiliated 501(c)(4) 1Day Action. [Action's own disclosure](https://1dayaction.org/finances-transparency/) itemizes $1M received in November 2023 and $1.9M in April 2026. Coefficient's [fund listing](https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/abundance-and-growth/) instead labels a $1.9M clinical-policy grant “1Day Sooner,” May 2026. The matching amount suggests an affiliate/date-label difference, but recipient metadata is unresolved; **we do not add this grant to charity cash or count it twice**. The charity also discloses a distinct $650,000 individual donation in April 2026. Cumulative receipts are not unrestricted money available today.

**Room for more funding remains unverified.** Historical deficits, a live donation page and worthwhile proposals do not establish a current marginal gap after later grants. Request the current charity cash forecast, restrictions and grant-payment schedule, CPO collaborator income, program/country budget, and the next work that would be delayed without an additional gift. Donor additionality is stronger if a defined participant-support or archive milestone is currently unfunded and not replaceable by partner grants. It is weaker if ordinary gifts release an existing funder's money or finance work already committed. The model's 50% factor remains an explicit assumption until such evidence is supplied.

model.costScope: Latest original 2024 annual charitable-entity expense, charged once as an annual-work comparator, not a current marginal gift offer. Income resource savings net modeled implementation/production costs; unmeasured external health-system and public costs remain limitations.
model.geographicAttribution: 40% of conditional patient benefit attributed to U.S. residents; not a measured geography share. Income uses only net gains during U.S. residence or U.S. consumer/owner incidence; geography adjustments in native savings and recipient cohorts are not applied twice.
model.formula: patients*annualQalyGain*earlierYears*reformProbability*approvalProbability*incrementalBenefitProbability*organizationAttribution*fundingAdditionality*usShare/(1+discountRate)^delayYears; dollars per better life = 10 × annual cost / discounted U.S. QALYs; annual-cost fundingAdditionality=1; combined price=10*annualCostUSD/(U.S. health QALYs + sum .5*people*ln(1+gain/baseline)*causalShare*editionShare*independentShare*sum annual discount weights).
model.counterfactual: Other advocates and regulators may enact the same reform; existing funders may support the same work and many affected drug candidates fail.
model.attribution: Annual-work causal contribution and implementation probability apply once to each pathway. FundingAdditionality=1 for the annual-cost central comparison; old marginal-funding factors remain sensitivities only. Do not credit future gifts with past achievements or count collaborative wins twice.
model.uncertainty: Central/low/high are transparent joint hypotheses, not posterior estimates or confidence intervals. Distinct conditionals are logically meaningful but no source identifies their product. Show undiscounted conditional benefits and total causal share so compounded skepticism is visible. Do not multiply portfolio scale by an invented count. No universal GDP-to-income conversion. Low stress case has implementation cost exceeding saved research resources. Staff/CRO wages lost are not automatically social savings; require labor reassigned productively or subtract lost income. Avoid lower compensation framed as efficiency. Quality losses, privacy and participant harm belong in signed health/economic harm scenarios.
model.nativeOutcomes: Policy work and data reuse could reduce the resources needed for reliable trials, including failed products, alongside earlier useful treatment. The affected trials and savings are hypotheses, not measured program returns.

what: FAI funds policy research, technical tools, convening and implementation advice intended to accelerate American innovation and infrastructure.
Its energy team develops federal and state permitting reforms; independently confirmed New Jersey changes are intermediate policy outcomes.
Donations to its public charity support researchers, tools, events and educational work; affiliated FAI Action handles advocacy as a separate entity.
strengths: Published playbooks and named researchers make the proposed policy mechanism inspectable.
New Jersey enacted nuclear-permitting reform and launched a permitting-dashboard pilot in 2026; these provide concrete follow-up targets.
Original tax returns identify the charitable entity and spending; specialist funders support energy-permitting work.
reservations: The health-and-income estimate depends on hypothetical causal scale and incidence; no study identifies the combined organization-specific return.
Permitting can accelerate fossil generation or new demand; health, climate and household benefits can be null or harmful.
Rapid reported fundraising growth makes 2024 expenses a stale numerator, while a current energy budget and remaining funding gap are unavailable.

sections.what:
FAI is a U.S. technology think tank that produces research, technical tools, educational engagement and talent programs. Its [about page](https://www.thefai.org/about-us) identifies a 501(c)(3), founded as Lincoln Labs/Lincoln Network and refounded as FAI in 2023. This review follows EIN **47-2239840**, whose 2022 return names Lincoln Network Inc.; it is not a new legal entity whose earlier expenses should disappear. The affiliated FAI Action is a separate 501(c)(4) for legislative advocacy. This report evaluates charitable gifts to FAI, rather than assuming an unrestricted donation finances the sister organization's lobbying.

Energy and infrastructure is one part of a broader innovation portfolio. [Building Baseload](https://www.thefai.org/posts/building-baseload-reforming-permitting-for-ai-energy-infrastructure) examines barriers facing nuclear, geothermal, solar, gas and transmission serving AI infrastructure. The [2025 second State Permitting Playbook](https://www.thefai.org/posts/state-permitting-playbook-part-ii) expands coverage to 49 states; the [campus-power supplement](https://www.thefai.org/posts/the-state-permitting-playbook-behind-the-meter-power-supplement) addresses behind-the-meter and colocated generation and ratepayer costs. These are identifiable policy products. They do not themselves establish extra electricity, a cheaper household bill or higher earnings.

The intended chain is donor-funded capacity → useful proposals and implementation assistance → additional, durable rule changes → earlier or less costly infrastructure → reliable energy, productive activity and household welfare. Each arrow needs evidence. A dashboard can improve transparency without reducing processing time; permission for a nuclear plant can remain unused because financing, licensing, supply chains or grid constraints still bind.
sections.monitoring:
The evidence is stronger for policy engagement and enacted changes than for final welfare outcomes. FAI's [Q2 2026 update](https://www.thefai.org/posts/quarterly-update-q2-2026) credits Samuel Roland with testimony, work with the governor's office and information for legislators in the New Jersey nuclear effort, and with contributing to permitting dashboards. These are the organization's own contribution claims, not independently estimated causal shares.

Two primary state sources verify the intermediate outcomes. On [April 8, 2026](https://www.nj.gov/governor/news/2026/approved/20260408a.shtml), New Jersey signed S3870/A4528, allowing nuclear-facility permitting based on compliant waste storage rather than requiring a disposal solution that had blocked approval. On [June 18](https://www.nj.gov/governor/news/2026/20260618b.shtml), it launched the dashboard pilot with ten selected projects spanning energy, housing and commercial development. Neither source establishes how much of the result required FAI. Nor do these events show a completed new reactor, generation advanced by a measured number of years or a measured reduction in pollution.

A useful monitoring package would pair an adopted-text comparison and dated account of FAI's role with interviews of officials and other participants; then track each affected project's baseline schedule, permitting milestones, capacity, technology and financing. Dashboard evaluation should compare application times, withdrawals and completed projects with a credible counterfactual, rather than count tracked projects as completed investment. For health, identify the displaced generators and exposed population. EPA's [AVERT and COBRA tools](https://www.epa.gov/statelocalenergy/benefit-evaluation-tools-energy-efficiency-and-renewable-energy-policies) provide a route from generation changes to emissions and health. We have not run them, and our deaths-per-TWh assumption is not an EPA result. No reviewed source supplies donor-caused household-income growth.
sections.qualitative:
FAI's potential value is broader than a pollution intervention. Better energy reliability and faster infrastructure may support manufacturing, compute, scientific work and economy-wide productivity. Research and technical translation can be useful where policymakers lack specialized capacity. Its products also provide observable implementation milestones rather than only broad statements about growth.

There is external support for the mechanism, although it does not validate our QALY estimate. [Coefficient Giving](https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/abundance-and-growth/) lists a **$2.714M April 2026** grant for energy-permitting reforms. [Giving Green's spotlight](https://www.givinggreen.earth/research/foundation-for-american-innovation-grantee-spotlight-2026), labeled 2026 but last updated October 2025, describes support for personnel, convenings, publications, outreach and overhead in federal permitting research and education. That review cites prior contributions to energy-policy changes; we treat this as a funder's assessment, not independent identification of FAI's marginal impact. Its planned award is not proof of a disbursed amount or an unmet funding gap.

Benefits depend on which projects and rules change. Accelerating clean replacement generation can reduce emissions; accelerating gas, supplying additional electricity demand or weakening protections can increase pollution and climate damage. Ratepayer cost shifting, local environmental burdens and distribution of gains matter. Faster AI deployment also has effects outside energy that are not priced here. Sponsor interests deserve scrutiny: FAI discloses industry support, but support is not proof that donors dictate findings. Donors should inspect research independence, funding restrictions and net public outcomes. We do not count corporate revenue, total investment or regulatory time saved as household welfare without a bridge.
sections.cost:
Our central **health-and-income estimate is $52.6M per better life**, using ten healthy-year welfare equivalents. The previous health-only review was $1.93B; the original alpha comparison was $49.6M. These are different model versions, not measurements showing that impact changed by those ratios. Income-equivalent years are wellbeing comparisons, not observed QALYs or DALYs.

**Correcting the cost boundary.** We charge the latest inspected annual charity expense, $3,719,664, once. The previous review also multiplied the denominator by an arbitrary new-donation additionality factor based partly on grant receipts. That mixes annual-work cost-effectiveness with a marginal-gift model. We remove that factor from the annual-cost central case; implementation probabilities and the organization's contribution still apply. Receiving a grant does not prove the year's work has low value. The old funding haircut remains a sensitivity, and current room for more funding still needs a costed work package. This is not a promise that any gift size scales linearly.

**Income pathway: net energy affordability.** [FAI's permitting work](https://www.thefai.org/posts/building-baseload-reforming-permitting-for-ai-energy-infrastructure) could improve energy availability, but a permitting change is not itself a cheaper completed plant. We use the same hypothetical 1-GW reactor-equivalent as the health model: 90% capacity gives 7.884M MWh/year, and six months of acceleration gives 3.942M MWh. A central judgment of a $10/MWh all-in resource advantage gives $39.42M conditional savings. No source establishes that positive cost differential for an FAI-linked project.

The comparison must deliver the same reliability and service as the counterfactual supply. The $10 advantage is defined after annualized construction capital, fuel, operations, transmission, decommissioning and regulatory/public costs. It is not a comparison of nuclear operating cost against the full cost of alternative electricity. [DOE's commercialization analysis](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/commercializing-advanced-nuclear-reactors-explained-five-charts) stresses the importance of construction cost and execution; it does not demonstrate that new nuclear power always costs less. Our zero-saving and negative-cost-advantage cases remain plausible.

We assign half the resource gain to consumers/owners and half of that as net disposable pass-through after provider losses and transfers: $9.855M across 100,000 residents, or $98.55 each against a $75,000 income baseline. These incidence assumptions are judgments, not documented bill reductions. The same 50% useful-reform probability, 25% conditional completion probability and 10% FAI contribution apply once to health and affordability. Economic gains start after ten years with a 3% discount. The 25% fossil-displacement share affects pollution health, not the value of all useful supply.

The explicit adverse case replaces +$10/MWh with -$20/MWh: cost overruns or displacement of cheaper power can outweigh positive pollution-health benefits. We exclude carbon/health damages from the cost differential when health is separately counted, and do not add gross jobs, salaries, company revenue or interest transfers. Benefits concentrated in wealthy data-center shareholders warrant a higher income baseline and lower welfare weight. AI, security, climate and other institutional channels remain unquantified, not presumed beneficial. A named financed project, an all-in alternative-cost comparison and actual incidence data are needed to substantiate the central hypothesis.

**Health component.** The earlier review's physical chain is retained except for the mismatched donor haircut: 7.884 TWh/year × half a year earlier × 25% fossil displacement × 0.7 historical gas-pollution deaths/TWh × 15 QALYs/death × 50% useful-reform probability × 25% conditional build probability × 10% FAI causal contribution, discounted ten years at 3%. The [primary gas-pollution study](https://depts.washington.edu/airqual/Marshall_116.pdf) and [EIA generation data](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_03_01_a.html) support a historical analogue, not a current local marginal rate. This is not an observed plant or a full net-health assessment. A past moratorium repeal cannot be attributed to a future donation.

**Combined arithmetic.** The health component is 0.096246 U.S. QALYs; signed income benefit is 0.610686 U.S. income-equivalent healthy years. Using [Coefficient Giving's comparison](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/), income welfare is 0.5 × affected people × ln(1 + real income gain/baseline income) × the explicit causal/local/non-overlap shares, summed over individually discounted benefit years. Divide ten times $3,719,664 by 0.706932 combined years to get $52.6M. The report, research list and shortlist all use that same calculation.

**How much confidence?** Every organization-specific cohort, probability, gain and incidence assumption here is a transparent hypothesis. Primary sources identify the workstreams and economic mechanisms, not this central return. Our joint low/high cases give Conservative joint case: $735.05B. Not a confidence limit. Favorable joint case: $348K. Not a confidence limit. Zero implementation gives zero benefit, and net harms can eliminate a positive price. The range is not a statistical confidence interval. Inspect the exact vectors below rather than treating a precise-looking price as verified.

**Costs, coverage and next evidence.** Full annual charity cost once. $/MWh net advantage must include all external production/implementation costs; it is currently a judgment requiring a project comparison. Financial interest savings are transfers, not automatically real welfare; new jobs are not added as gross salaries. Omitted FAI technology/AI/security pathways can be harmful or beneficial and cannot be inferred from energy alone. Annual-work headline removes donor funding haircut; prior factors preserved only as unknown marginal-funding sensitivity. Annual scale and causal reform probability are judgments requiring workstream evidence. Compare same service and reliability against otherwise supplied power, not nuclear bill vs no bill. Moratorium repeal may never produce reactor. Federal licensing, financing, supply chains and other advocates are dependencies; one extra gift cannot claim completed 2026 repeal. Income affordability uses full central accelerated MWh, not netDisplacement=.25, which only governs pollution-displacing generation. Shared reform/build/attribution/funding causal factors apply once to both pathways; no additional health-to-income factor. Carbon/social health damages excluded from $/MWh differential when health is separately counted. Five years of household gains do not automatically require five annual charity budgets, nor prove that one year's work is sufficient; the three-budget stress case tests that mismatch. Other organizational channels remain unquantified rather than assumed worthless or counted as a generic growth multiplier. Before a major funding decision, ask for current project budgets, specific counterfactual effects and recipient-level outcomes. The strongest model is the one that replaces these priors with evidence, not the one with the smallest headline price.
sections.funding:
We directly inspected the rendered original **2022, 2023 and 2024 Form 990s**, including Part IX, rather than relying only on summary extracts. They are the three latest returns listed on FAI's [financials page](https://www.thefai.org/financials-and-reports) at review. The 2022 return names Lincoln Network Inc.; the later returns name FAI, all under EIN 47-2239840. All cover calendar years and report the charitable organization's expenses, excluding an invented combined budget with FAI Action.

| Calendar year | Revenue | Total expenses | Program services | Management/general | Fundraising |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| [2022](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/472239840/202322689349300977/full) | $3,932,822 | $4,347,192 | $3,437,329 | $553,832 | $356,031 |
| [2023](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/472239840/202432919349300028/full) | $3,679,704 | $3,360,231 | $2,588,861 | $469,528 | $301,842 |
| [2024](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/472239840/202503169349305405/full) | $5,149,927 | $3,719,664 | $2,876,107 | $545,134 | $298,423 |

The three-year expense mean is **$3,809,029**. In 2024, program services were 77.3%, management/general 14.7% and fundraising 8.0%. Part III reports $1,496,345 for Policy, $707,254 for Labs and $672,508 for Events/Network. These broad classifications do not isolate the energy team and do not measure impact or spending quality. The return answered no to the lobbying-activities/501(h) question for 2024; that historical answer does not establish the allocation of 2026 legislative work across FAI and FAI Action.

Historical finances substantially understate the scale implied by recent fundraising. The search-indexed text of its [January 6, 2026 growth account](https://www.thefai.org/posts/fai-2025-growth) reports around **$20M of 2025 revenue**, more than 30 full-time employees and further hiring. It explicitly labels 2025 figures preliminary and unaudited. It reports funding of 56% foundations/nonprofits, 31% industry/venture capital and 13% individuals. These are organization-reported fundraising composition and scale, not audited expense allocations. The original article returned 404 during direct review; the live [Q1 update](https://www.thefai.org/posts/quarterly-update-q1-2026) still links to that URL and corroborates substantial growth without repeating the amounts. Treat the cached figures as provisional historical disclosure requiring reconfirmation. The 2024 net assets of $3,427,251 and annual surplus of $1,430,263 also predate this expansion; they cannot establish September 2026 runway.

**Room for more funding is unverified.** The Coefficient grant and rapid revenue growth do not prove that the next useful energy project is fully funded, but they make a generic shortage assumption weak. Before a substantial grant, request the current expense budget and actuals, restricted versus available balances, energy-team staffing and costs, grant durations and commitments, plus a ranked list of additional work that would not happen under existing funding. Specify the charitable entity, funding term, deliverables and any research-independence safeguards. Without this, the initial 20% donor additionality remains a judgment rather than a demonstrated marginal opportunity.

model.costScope: Latest original 2024 annual charitable-entity expense, charged once as an annual-work comparator, not a current marginal gift offer. Income resource savings net modeled implementation/production costs; unmeasured external health-system and public costs remain limitations.
model.geographicAttribution: 100% of this domestic modeled pollution-health pathway is attributed to U.S. residents. Income uses only net gains during U.S. residence or U.S. consumer/owner incidence; geography adjustments in native savings and recipient cohorts are not applied twice.
model.formula: (capacityGW*capacityFactor*8760/1000)*earlierYears*netDisplacement*deathsPerTWh*qalyPerDeath*reformProbability*buildProbability*organizationAttribution*fundingAdditionality*usShare/(1+discountRate)^delayYears; dollars per better life = 10 × annual cost / discounted U.S. QALYs; annual-cost fundingAdditionality=1; combined price=10*annualCostUSD/(U.S. health QALYs + sum .5*people*ln(1+gain/baseline)*causalShare*editionShare*independentShare*sum annual discount weights).
model.counterfactual: Other advocates or existing funders may produce the same reform; power may supply new demand.
model.attribution: Annual-work causal contribution and implementation probability apply once to each pathway. FundingAdditionality=1 for the annual-cost central comparison; old marginal-funding factors remain sensitivities only. Do not credit future gifts with past achievements or count collaborative wins twice.
model.uncertainty: Central/low/high are transparent joint hypotheses, not posterior estimates or confidence intervals. Distinct conditionals are logically meaningful but no source identifies their product. Show undiscounted conditional benefits and total causal share so compounded skepticism is visible. Do not multiply portfolio scale by an invented count. No universal GDP-to-income conversion. For explicit adverse sensitivity replace central +$10/MWh with -$20/MWh while retaining incidence and build probability: cost overruns/taxpayer subsidy can make affordability negative even if pollution-health positive. Nuclear construction can displace cheaper firm power. Fossil/data-center expansion can increase pollution, prices or catastrophic-risk exposure.
model.nativeOutcomes: Permitting work could accelerate reliable electricity supply and lower its all-in resource cost, alongside reduced pollution. No named FAI-linked project yet establishes the modeled generation or savings.

inputs.name: capacityGW
inputs.rationale: One 1-GW nuclear reactor equivalent, within the scale of existing U.S. reactors. Conditional analogue, not an identified FAI-caused project.

inputs.name: capacityFactor
inputs.rationale: 90% operating capacity factor, a round analogue informed by the EIA fleet record; not a future project forecast.

inputs.name: earlierYears
inputs.rationale: Effective-care or generation acceleration relative to the counterfactual, not time saved on an administrative step. Revised timing judgment; no measured org-specific lead.

inputs.name: netDisplacement
inputs.rationale: Share of additional generation replacing fossil output rather than meeting new demand. Revised 25% central judgment; a generation counterfactual is not measured.

inputs.name: deathsPerTWh
inputs.rationale: Historical gas PM2.5 analogue: approximately 800 modeled deaths / 1126.635 TWh of 2014 U.S. gas generation = 0.710, rounded to 0.7. Judgment transfer, not current marginal New Jersey emissions modeling.

inputs.name: qalyPerDeath
inputs.rationale: Fifteen quality-adjusted remaining years per avoided premature death; judgment, not a measured age or mortality profile.

inputs.name: reformProbability
inputs.rationale: Probability of an additional useful operational policy change from the modeled work. Does not credit a new gift with already enacted reforms; judgment, not measured causal probability.

inputs.name: buildProbability
inputs.rationale: 25% probability of an operating project conditional on enabling reform. Financing, federal licensing and construction can still fail; explicit judgment, not evidence that a plant has been built.

inputs.name: organizationAttribution
inputs.rationale: Incremental organizational contribution within a collaborative policy ecosystem, conditional on useful reform. Judgment; overlapping advocates are not separate independent wins.

inputs.name: fundingAdditionality
inputs.rationale: Annual-work comparator: no extra donor haircut on full annual expense. Prior factor remains sensitivity, not a measured marginal offer.

inputs.name: usShare
inputs.rationale: Residence share of modeled health beneficiaries, not headquarters or spending share. Judgment; no global benefit is relabeled as U.S. benefit.

inputs.name: delayYears
inputs.rationale: Time to realization, not duration of the benefit. Clinical central uses the BIO historical 10.5-year Phase-I-to-approval average as a proxy; energy uses an explicit ten-year construction/rollout judgment.

inputs.name: discountRate
inputs.rationale: 3% annual discount convention; judgment, not an observed organizational performance parameter.

inputs.name: costUSD
inputs.rationale: Latest inspected original 2024 charity expense, used as an annual accounting comparator; not a current marginal funding offer.

inputs.name: Annual-cost versus marginal-gift boundary
inputs.rationale: Full annual expenses estimate annual-work contribution, not return from an extra donation. Unknown marginal funding capacity remains a reservation; old haircuts retained only as sensitivities.

inputs.name: Income pathway central

reports.program: Youth suicide-risk therapy funding and insurance navigation
reports.priceScope: Conditional full annual recipient cost against an explicitly judged finite therapy-access channel; not whole-portfolio expected value or a marginal donation offer.

what: Second Wind Fund pays for therapy for eligible Colorado youth at risk of suicide and helps insured families navigate care.
The conditional initial reference combines finite symptom-health benefits with signed caregiver household resources, not deaths prevented or future child salaries.
Full FY2025 expenses are $1.94M; the annual recipient cohort and Denver share remain explicit hypotheses.
strengths: The legal recipient and current direct donation route are clear.
Funded therapy and insurance navigation address different practical barriers to treatment.
Null, adverse, payer-cost and cohort sensitivities expose the assumptions behind the reference.
reservations: The reported 10,000 youth served since 2002 is cumulative, not an annual completed cohort.
Insurance, Medicaid, I Matter and other providers can reduce additionality.
Local utility, sustained outcomes, caregiver net earnings and marginal donation capacity are unmeasured.

sections.what: Second Wind Fund Inc, EIN 73-1701536, funds eligible youth therapy and navigates insurance access. Current family information offers 12 funded sessions; the FY2025 return describes 12–20 sessions. These are dated service descriptions, not measured completed treatment or causal recovery.
sections.monitoring: Request annual unique youth, completed sessions, Denver county residence, repeated/sibling households, sustained symptom outcomes and referral alternatives. The cumulative 10,000 youth and 70,000 sessions since 2002 cannot supply an annual denominator.
sections.qualitative: Fast referral targets and private therapy access are promising mechanisms, but are not proof of incremental QALYs. I Matter offers another public free-session route. The model uses N500 annual youth and Denver share .6 as judgments, not observations; clinical response .4, utility .05 and half-year persistence are hypotheses.
sections.cost: Full FYending June2025 expenses are $1,915,520 plus $24,200 netted direct event costs. The conditional center yields 1.346 health QALYs and 0.09782 signed income-equivalent years, approximately $13.43M per better life. One adult caregiver household proxy per youth is adjusted in deduplication sensitivities. A $1,000 net disposable work/resource gain for 20% of attributed households is already after taxes, benefit withdrawal, commuting and work costs; it is not measured, and is halved for positive overlap. Full $30 access/time cost and health burden apply to every exposed household even with no benefit. Delay .1 is the assumed engagement onset for health and access/resource costs, not immediate costs capitalized into later gains.
sections.funding: FY2023–2025 full annual costs are $1.155M, $1.447M and $1.940M. Government grants and insurance routes form part of the counterfactual. Fundraising claims of $100 per session or $1,250 to save a life do not establish marginal impact; annual program cost $1.491M is only a recognized-cost sensitivity excluding other costs and volunteer resources.

model.costScope: Full statewide FY2025 recognized annual cost; partial finite therapy and caregiver channel, unmeasured navigation/prevention effects are unknown rather than zero. Not allocated Denver spend or a next-gift forecast.
model.geographicAttribution: Pinned ten-county Denver CBSA19740; .6 beneficiary share is judgment because no county-resident distribution was found. Office location is not beneficiary geography.
model.formula: Exposed=N×unique; incremental union=exposed×b; health=(union×response×q×discounted finite duration − exposed×harm×onset discount)×Denver share. Income=0.5×joint household log net resources with positive-only overlap and full access costs, plus distinct payer losses localized once. Better-life price=10×cost/(health+signed income equivalent).
model.counterfactual: Medicaid, private insurance, I Matter free youth therapy, other providers and household support without recipient-funded access.
model.attribution: N500, .5 additionality and .4 clinical response are explicit initial hypotheses; cumulative service reach and referral targets do not identify them.
model.uncertainty: Clinical utility/duration, annual unique youth, sibling overlap, caregiver net resources, volunteer economic costs, alternative care and gift expansion remain unmeasured.
model.nativeOutcomes: Current cumulative reach 10,000 youth since2002 and 12-session funding cap; original FY2025 return 12–20 sessions. No verified annual completed cohort.

what: Maria Droste Services of Colorado, EIN 84-1182130, provides counseling, community care and clinical training.
Its 2025 report identifies 675 unique outpatient clients, distinct from the broader session totals used in earlier reporting.
The conditional initial reference includes symptom-health benefits and signed household resources, with an explicit FY2024 cost/FY2025 output mismatch.
strengths: Current primary reporting distinguishes outpatient clients from therapy sessions.
Sliding fees, insurance billing and community delivery provide practical access routes.
Full access burdens, alternatives and negative income effects are retained rather than assumed away.
reservations: County residence, household overlap and causal clinical outcomes remain unmeasured.
FY2025 income shares do not establish full current expenses, so the cost/output vintages differ.
Training and community benefits are unpriced; whole recipient cost against outpatient benefits is not portfolio expected value.

sections.what: The Denver-based charity provides outpatient counseling, school/community care and supervised clinician training. Its own intake page offers statewide telehealth and in-person services, Medicaid/private insurance, and sliding fees for uninsured clients below 200% FPL. These establish services and alternatives, not clinical effects.
sections.monitoring: The 2025 primary PDF reports 830 clients: 675 outpatient and 155 community, alongside 10,619 sessions. The outpatient section explicitly calls its 675 clients unique. Do not add Children First, SMHP, training hours and all sessions as unique people. Request deduplicated households, county residence, completed doses, sustained symptom outcomes and fee/time/work burden.
sections.qualitative: The model confines its center to the outpatient cohort with .9 household deduplication and .8 Denver share judgments. Additionality .35, clinical response .5, utility .04 and half-year persistence are unmeasured hypotheses. Insurance/public clinics and spontaneous recovery reduce incremental benefit; no gross child future wages, mortality or donated-hour retail value are counted.
sections.cost: Full FY2024 recognized cost is $3,487,726, paired explicitly with FY2025 outpatient output because a reviewed FY2025 full expense amount was not found. Center: 1.45370 health QALYs plus −0.320963 signed income-equivalent years, approximately $30.79M per better life. The .118 resource-response fraction is a judgment informed by roughly 59% adult share × .2 possible adult/caregiver response. A $500 net disposable gain is after tax, benefit withdrawal and work costs; only positives are halved for overlap. Every exposed household retains $50 net access/fee/time costs and clinical burden even if treatment fails. Delay .1 is engagement onset for both costs and benefits, not capitalized earlier losses.
sections.funding: Original event-inclusive full expenses: FY2022 $2,527,157; FY2023 $2,843,028; FY2024 $3,487,726. FY2024 functional program cost $2,378,708 is a broad recognized-cost sensitivity, not allocated outpatient cost. Current 2025 reporting describes financial pressures and a grant/earned-revenue mix; this is not evidence of marginal donor expansion or verified capacity. Unpaid trainee/provider resources and insurer/taxpayer incidence require deeper investigation.

model.costScope: Whole recipient FY2024 full recognized annual cost against FY2025 outpatient unique-client reference; deliberately unmatched vintage and partial benefit scope. Other training/community benefits unknown, not zero; no marginal gift claim.
model.geographicAttribution: Pinned ten-county CBSA19740; statewide telehealth means .8 Denver share is a judgment, not office-based attribution. .9 household deduplication is also judged.
model.formula: Exposed=N×unique; incremental union=exposed×b; health=(union×response×q×discounted finite duration − exposed×harm×onset discount)×Denver share. Income=0.5×joint household log net resources with positive-only overlap and full access costs, plus distinct payer losses localized once. Better-life price=10×cost/(health+signed income equivalent).
model.counterfactual: Medicaid/private insurance, public behavioral-health clinics, other counseling providers and household support without this recipient.
model.attribution: .35 incremental uptake and .5 clinical response are unmeasured initial hypotheses, not satisfaction rates or causal recovery measurements.
model.uncertainty: Cost/output vintage mismatch, no county distribution, untreated comparison, actual fees/time, sustained utility or after-tax household work changes. All are explicit hypotheses with null/adverse sensitivities.
model.nativeOutcomes: 2025 primary report: 675 unique outpatient clients, 155 community clients and 10,619 sessions; 2024 session statistics are not unique completed outpatient clients.
