reports.program: Energy bill assistance, home efficiency and public energy-affordability access
reports.priceScope: Conditional whole annual recipient cost against partial bill-assistance health and household-resource benefits; not whole-portfolio expected value or marginal gift price.

what: Energy Outreach Colorado helps income-qualified households pay utility bills and improves home energy efficiency and safety.
Its statewide 2025 household total covers several programs, so a bill-assistance subset and Denver share are explicit judgments.
The initial reference includes health and signed net household resources, including a distinct public or tariff-payer loss.
strengths: Current service, legal recipient and direct donation route are verified.
Original annual finances expose public and utility funding alongside cash assistance.
Clinical-null, financial-only, payer and cost-scope scenarios keep redistribution and health separate.
reservations: Reported households are not a deduplicated annual bill-assistance cohort.
LEAP, WAP and utility obligations are important alternatives rather than entirely donor-created benefits.
Clinical utility, net cash displacement, county residence and marginal gift expansion are unmeasured.

sections.what: Energy Outreach Colorado, EIN 74-2543881, provides bill payment, emergency furnace repairs, efficiency upgrades and advocacy statewide. Current 2026 outreach awards are supported by mandatory utility-customer charges and promote access to LEAP, WAP and EOC programs, not new household income equal to the grant amount.
sections.monitoring: The current homepage reports 40,789 households and 120,328 individuals served in 2025 across programs. These are not added together. Request unique bill-assistance households, repeated payments, county residence, disconnections avoided, indoor temperatures and net recipient/payer resource changes. The cumulative $410 M invested since 1989 is not an annual denominator.
sections.qualitative: The center assigns half of the reported household envelope to bill assistance, with .9 deduplication and .45 Denver share as judgments. Incremental benefit share .25 reflects public/utility alternatives; .2 clinical response, .01 utility and half-year persistence are hypotheses about temperature/security, not measured recipient QALYs. Furnace, efficiency, institutional and policy benefits outside this channel are unknown rather than zero.
sections.cost: Whole FYending September 2025 recognized cost is $76,988,385, including $79,557 netted direct event costs. Bill-program cost $21,873,982 is a cost-aligned recognized-channel sensitivity, excluding allocated overhead and volunteer costs. Net household resource gain $500 is judged after benefit withdrawal and otherwise-paid bills, halved for positive overlap; $15 participation burden is charged to all exposed households. A distinct $150 payer loss per attributed household tests tariff/public incidence. No gross grant, retail energy value or ordinary survivor wages are treated as net welfare.
sections.funding: Original full expenses are FY 2023 $65,890,165, FY 2024 $83,135,058, FY 2025 $76,988,385. Original period headers confirm these fiscal years. FY 2025 government grants $14,090,961 and restricted efficiency/furnace programs mean general donations do not automatically expand all observed services. The current donation page redirects to an owned donor-support payment route; actual next-gift capacity requires recipient confirmation.

model.costScope: Whole statewide annual recipient cost against partial bill-assistance benefit reference; recognized bill-program sensitivity is not full social cost or marginal gift.
model.geographicAttribution: Pinned ten-county Denver CBSA 19740; .45 household share judged given statewide service and no county output distribution.
model.formula: Exposed=N×channel×unique; incremental union=exposed×b; clinical people=union×response. Health=(clinical people×q×discounted finite duration−exposed×harm)×Denver share. Household joint-log net resources preserve full costs; distinct payer losses apply to the attributed union and local allocation once. Price=10 C/(health+signed income equivalent).
model.counterfactual: LEAP, WAP, utility payment plans, mandated utility-charge assistance, other community providers and household support without added recipient work.
model.attribution: .25 incremental share, .5 bill-channel share and .9 deduplication are separate transparent judgments, not measured causal success.
model.uncertainty: Native program overlap, public replacement funding, actual disposable resources, clinical response/duration, payer incidence and local capacity remain uncertain.
model.nativeOutcomes: 2025 primary homepage: 40,789 households and 120,328 individuals across programs. FY 2025 original cash-assistance program cost 21,873,982; no matched unique bill-cohort result.

what: Cultivando supports Latino community leadership, emotional wellness and environmental-health advocacy in North Denver and Commerce City.
Its 2025 report describes coalition participation in air-toxics rulemaking, not measured emissions or clinical health improvements.
The conditional initial reference tests a finite local policy channel with health and signed household, participant and payer effects.
strengths: Current native activities and legal recipient are verified from original reporting.
Coalition participation has a concrete rulemaking mechanism beyond monitoring alone.
Separate participant and downstream-beneficiary cohorts avoid charging every hypothetical resident advocacy costs.
reservations: Monitoring and adopted standards do not establish implemented abatement or recipient causal share.
The 10,000 potential residents and utility/resource coefficients are explicit hypotheses.
Whole annual cost includes direct programs and fiscal sponsorship whose benefits are unpriced here.

sections.what: Cultivando, EIN 84-1499624, combines promotoras, community education, family/emotional wellness and environmental advocacy. Current 2025 reporting includes formal COCA coalition participation in Regulation 30, community testimony and tours near Suncor. National training in San Antonio is outside the Denver reference. Donation page links an owned Pay Pal hosted button, with no transaction performed.
sections.monitoring: The 2025 PDF reports 20+coalition leaders and 30+testimonies, five priority air-toxics standards and Hydrogen Sulfide inclusion. These are participation and rulemaking claims, not reduced exposure, completed abatement, cancer prevention or sole-recipient impact. Planned 2026 health survey is not an existing controlled outcome. Other 50 women,313 workshop participants,14 FFNgraduates and 20 homevisits are not added as unique clinical beneficiaries. The official AQCC 2024–2025 report independently confirms priority-air-toxic benchmarks adopted in September 2025 under the legislative mandate; it does not establish Cultivando's causal contribution or implemented exposure reduction.
sections.qualitative: The policy reference hypothesizes 10,000 local residents, .3 implementation and .15 incremental recipient attribution, .003 healthyyear/resident/year over 3 years after 2 years delay. All are unmeasured judgments, not conversions from cancer-risk thresholds. Existing regulation, public enforcement and other coalition members are alternatives. .5 household resource proxy is judged;30 engaged household-equivalent advocates are distinct from the hypothetical downstream population.
sections.cost: Full FY 2025 cost is $1,508,452. Center yields 3.704403 health QALYs and .486624 signed income-equivalent years, about $3.60 M per better life. $100 net household resources after tax/benefits/compliance effects are halved only if positive. All 30 engaged participants retain $10 current effort cost and health stress even if policy fails; implemented-policy payer compliance $20,000 and 20 worker households losing $1,000 are distinct judged incidence, gated by incremental implementation. Current-year effort and delayed gain are not capitalized together; same-year participant gains/costs are joint logs. These are hypotheses, not measured pollution-driven work returns.
sections.funding: Original full costs: FY 2023$1,603,171, FY 2024$1,653,391, FY 2025$1,508,452. FY 2025$333,654 Fortaleza Familiar fiscal sponsorship ended after its independent charity recognition. Full numerator includes that program, whose benefits are unknown here; excluding this transfer is a boundary sensitivity, not an adjusted whole-portfolio evaluation. Environmental-program recognized cost $432,384 is another partial-scope sensitivity excluding overhead, direct programs and unpaid resources. Annual report revenue $1,132,325 is not an expense estimate; actual next-dollar capacity requires confirmation.

model.costScope: Whole FY 2025 recognized recipient cost including sponsorship, against one policy benefit channel. Environmental cost 432384 and excluding 333654 sponsorship are scope diagnostics, not complete marginal cost.
model.geographicAttribution: Potential residents are explicitly local North Denver/Commerce City CBSA 19740 hypothesis; g 1 represents that chosen local channel, not all organizational work. Texas and other nonlocal program benefits excluded as unknown.
model.formula: Policy b=implementation×recipient incremental attribution. Health=(N×b×q×finite delayed duration−engaged×current harm)×Denver share. Delayed household resources and current participant costs are separate actual-year logs; same-year overlapping participants use joint gain minus cost. Distinct compliance/worker losses are implementation-gated and localized once. Price=10 C/(health+signed income).
model.counterfactual: Existing regulatory enforcement, baseline industry obligations, other COCA coalition members and public services absent added recipient advocacy.
model.attribution: Separate .3 implementation probability and .15 incremental recipient share, both judgment; benchmark adoption is not proof of implemented emission reduction.
model.uncertainty: No measured emissions attributable to recipient, local population/dose, clinical utility, work/resource or compliance incidence; finite delayed and failed-policy regimes tested.
model.nativeOutcomes: 2025 coalition participation 20+leaders/30+testimonies, standards/rulemaking claims and community programs. No delivered causal emission-health cohort.

inputs.rationale: Original FY2025 full functional expenses plus any separately netted direct event expenses; observed recognized recipient cost, not a causal coefficient.

inputs.name: N
inputs.rationale: 10,000 potential local residents is a conditionalhypothesis, notobservedannualservicebeneficiaries.

inputs.name: householdShare
inputs.rationale: .5 household resource units per potentialresident, judgeddedup.

inputs.name: engaged
inputs.rationale: 30 engaged household-equivalent advocates is judged within reported participation envelope, notall 10 kresidents.

inputs.name: implementation
inputs.rationale: .3 deliveredabatement probability beyond benchmark adoption, hypothesis.

inputs.name: attribution
inputs.rationale: .15 incremental recipient contribution versuscoalition/enforcement, hypothesis.

reports.program: Bicycle and pedestrian safety policy, education and Denver Streets Partnership
reports.priceScope: Conditional whole annual recipient cost against partial transport-policy health and net resource benefits; not portfolio expected value or a marginal donation offer.

what: Bicycle Colorado advocates for safe bicycling and walking, provides education and houses Denver Streets Partnership within the same legal recipient.
Current legislative priorities describe proposed law and infrastructure changes, not completed construction or measured injuries avoided.
The conditional reference combines finite safety-health benefits with signed commute, participation and public-resource effects.
strengths: Original legal DBA and current annual expenses are verified.
Policy, public infrastructure and education mechanisms are distinguishable.
Separate engaged and downstream populations prevent charging every hypothetical road user advocacy costs.
reservations: Road-user beneficiaries, implementation and incremental attribution remain unmeasured.
Public agencies and other advocates can deliver part of the same safety improvements.
The homepage donation link is currently broken; no validated transaction route or marginal capacity is established.

sections.what: Bicycle Colorado, EIN 84-1201078, includes Denver Streets Partnership as an IRS-listed DBA, not a second charity. Whole annual work includes infrastructure/law advocacy, Share the Road, education and Safe Routes to School. No separate DSP expenses are added.
sections.monitoring: The October2025 priorities explicitly state no target date for implementation. Municipal vehicle-fee permissions, trail funding proposals and traffic-law reforms are intermediate mechanisms, not built facilities, avoided crashes or household disposable gains. Request implemented local projects, agency/coalition roles, before/after injury exposure, county residence and net mode-change costs.
sections.qualitative: The center hypothesizes 5,000 potentially affected statewide road users, .7 Denver share, .4 implementation and .2 incremental recipient contribution. Utility .002 per person-year for three years after two-year delay is an injury-health hypothesis, not a measured program coefficient. Public plans, baseline road funding and other advocates are alternatives; exercise benefits and direct education/event welfare remain unpriced rather than zero.
sections.cost: Full FYending June2025 cost is $1,545,869. Center: 1.534386 health QALYs and .278952 signed income-equivalent years, about $8.52M per better life. A $100 annual net commute/resource gain after tax, benefits, equipment and time costs is judged and halved for positive overlap. Fifty engaged household proxies retain $10 immediate effort costs and stress even if policy fails. Distinct public implementation cost $50,000 and ten displaced-worker households losing $1,000 are judged, incremental-implementation gated. Actual-year effort and delayed resources remain separate; same-year participant gain/cost is joint.
sections.funding: Original full expenses FY2023 $2,089,992, FY2024 $1,785,914 and FY2025 $1,545,869; FY2023 adds $5,460 netted merchandise costs. The $962,129 FY2025 DSP/Share the Road/other program cost is not a narrowly allocated policy budget; all-program $1,282,839 is another recognized-cost sensitivity. Both exclude allocated full social costs. DonationUrl is null because the linked /donate-2/ route returns explicit404 on both hosts; no payment attempted. Fresh restricted marginal use and current capacity require confirmation.

model.costScope: Whole statewide recipient annual cost against partial finite safety-policy channel; direct education/event benefits unknown. Recognized DSP/other and all-program costs are scope sensitivities, not full policy or marginal costs.
model.geographicAttribution: Pinned ten-county Denver CBSA19740. Potential statewide road users and .7 local share are hypotheses; headquarters and DSP branding do not establish county-resident outputs.
model.formula: b=implementation×incremental attribution. Health=(potential road users×b×injury utility×finite delayed duration−engaged participants×current harm)×Denver share. Household resources jointly logged by actual year; full current effort independent of policy benefit, distinct public/worker losses implementation-gated and geography applied once. Price=10C/(health+signed income).
model.counterfactual: Existing transport agency plans, public funding, other coalitions, route choices and baseline road safety absent added recipient advocacy.
model.attribution: Separate .4 implementation and .2 recipient incremental attribution judgments; priorities and legal proposals are not delivered safety outcomes.
model.uncertainty: Unknown traffic exposure, projects/implementation, causal injury utility, mode-change resources, public payer incidence and next-gift capacity.
model.nativeOutcomes: FY2025 original program descriptions and current legislative priorities; no verified annual unique causal policy-beneficiary count.

what: Thriving Families provides MotherWise, La Luz postpartum groups and WiseWellness family counseling in Colorado.
The reference tests postpartum-depression prevention in a hypothetical eligible subgroup, not measured effects across every enrolled family.
Both health and signed net caregiver resources are assessed; the conditional estimate is about $57.9M per better life.
strengths: The La Luz curriculum has a relevant original randomized prevention study against usual care.
Current programs provide childcare and transport, which may reduce participation burdens.
Original three-year full annual expenses and the separate legal recipient were verified.
reservations: Historical enrolled participants are not current unique completed treatments or measured Denver households.
The prenatal ROSE trial does not directly establish local postpartum-program utility, dose or earnings.
Full recipient expenses cover broader work than the modeled prevention subset; other effects remain unknown.

sections.what: The independent legal recipient operates MotherWise, La Luz, WiseWellness and parenting programs. It separated from the University of Denver in 2019. The current official holiday page links the verified recipient ColoradoGives intake; no transaction was made.
sections.monitoring: Request unique annual households by program and ten-county CBSA19740 residence, prenatal versus postpartum eligibility, completed La Luz dose, depression episodes and usual-care referrals. Deduplicate participants, meetings and counseling appointments before tracking work or childcare outcomes.
sections.qualitative: The original ROSE randomized trial enrolled 205 at-risk pregnant adults on public assistance. At six months, depression incidence was 16% versus 31% under usual care. That 15-point difference informs a transferred prevention hypothesis, not an empirical recipient coefficient or measured QALY. Current La Luz is a four-week/six-hour postpartum group. The local eligible share, completion, utility loss and alternative access remain judgments. Marketing claims about preterm birth are not imported without the original study.
sections.cost: FY2024 full annual expenses are $1,929,744, including $30,675 netted direct event costs. The reference pairs these costs with historical FY2023 enrollment of 567 participants, not current unique households. A 0.9 household deduplication factor, 0.25 eligible share, 0.7 completion, 0.5 additionality, 0.15 transferred risk difference, 0.2 utility decrement and half-year episode duration are explicit hypotheses. Denver share 0.9 is judged. Recognized program-cost sensitivity excludes overhead and is not a priced marginal gift.
sections.funding: Usual prenatal/postpartum care, public or insured mental-health services and other charities are alternatives. Net $500 caregiver work resources are after taxes, benefit withdrawal and work expenses, not gross wages; only a judged fraction improves. Full $30 time/access costs and stress remain for all exposed households even when benefits fail. Provided transport/childcare do not prove zero burden. Distinct public payer and provider losses are tested separately, without counting capital grants as household income. A $1M state grant financed the May2024 building, not measured clinical benefits or new donor capacity.

model.costScope: Whole FY2024 legal-recipient annual cost, partial prevention benefit hypothesis; recognized program-only cost scenario is not fully allocated or marginal.
model.geographicAttribution: Ten-county CBSA19740, boundary OMB-23-01-2023-07-21. Beneficiary local share 0.9 is judgment, not headquarters attribution; broader Colorado clients excluded proportionally once.
model.formula: Clinical years = N × unique × b × eligible × completion × response × q × finite discounted T × g minus full exposed harm. Combined years add signed joint household net consumption welfare using 0.5 × log(1 + net resources / baseline), localized once; price = 10C / positive combined years.
model.counterfactual: Usual prenatal/postpartum care, covered therapy, other parenting groups and household support without this recipient. Trial controls received usual care; recipient additionality and local transfer remain uncertain.
model.attribution: Provider additionality 0.5 is separate from eligible program coverage, completed dose and transferred trial risk difference. No current local causal outcomes observed.
model.uncertainty: Conditional numerical partial-channel reference, not calibrated whole-portfolio expected value. Current completed unique cohort, matching FY2024 outputs, local trial transportability, utility, net resources and marginal capacity unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: FY2023 original filing reports 567 enrolled participants; 572 intakes, 644 family support meetings and 1,720 counseling appointments are overlapping service counts, not additional unique households. Current more-than-700 family growth claim has unspecified vintage. Preterm, other counseling and parenting effects omitted as unknown rather than zero.

reports.program: Critical home repairs, accessibility and emergency housing safety
reports.priceScope: Conditional annual full-recipient cost against limited repair health/resource benefits; not a whole-portfolio or marginal-gift expected value.

what: Rebuilding Together Colorado provides free critical repairs and modifications for vulnerable low-income homeowners.
The current recipient is the former Metro Denver affiliate, not the national organization.
A conditional health-plus-net-resource reference is about $5.86M per better life.
strengths: The original FY2024 filing identifies 72 homeowners and actual repair types.
Current eligibility, regional footprint and alternative repair providers are explicit.
The model keeps full time costs, possible harms and volunteer-resource sensitivities.
reservations: Homeowners, repair types and demographic categories overlap; they are not additional independent outcomes.
Local causal health and actual household savings remain unmeasured judgments.
The footprint includes El Paso County outside Denver's ten-county CBSA; donor-funded additional capacity is unknown.

sections.what: This legal recipient, EIN84-1514642, is Rebuilding Together Metro Denver Inc DBA Rebuilding Together Colorado. Services include larger Rebuilding Days projects, smaller Safe@Home repairs and urgent furnaces/water heaters. Some emergency work uses paid licensed trades, not only volunteers. Own donation page contains a FundraiseUp intake trigger; no transaction was made.
sections.monitoring: The original FY2024 filing reports72 low-income homeowners. The10 veterans,67 seniors,60 disabled and5 households with children overlap; repair categories can occur in the same home. Request distinct homes, residents, completed repairs, local county, sustained hazards resolved, falls/function and actual avoided household spending. Earlier2016 emergency-family figures are not substituted as current output.
sections.qualitative: Heating, water, plumbing and accessibility repairs can improve safety/function and prevent displacement, but the recipient does not report a local causal utility coefficient. Half of households incremental to alternatives, .5 clinical response, .02 utility gain for3years and.85 local share are explicit judgments. County/municipal programs, Brothers Redevelopment and family or private repair are counterfactuals. Completed repairs are not automatically causal health gains.
sections.cost: FY2024 full expenses $492,736; netted event/gaming/COGS fields blank. The$14,458 special event line is already functional expense and not added twice. FY2023 $321,790; FY2022 $483,389. The matched72 homeowners constrain the annual scope, not a next-gift price. Recognized program-cost sensitivity $370,902 omits allocated overhead; 2050 reported volunteer hours × judged$25/h adds$51,250 as a social-resource sensitivity, not measured payroll.
sections.funding: Free repairs do not mean zero household time/access cost. Full judged$50 costs and possible stress apply to every exposed household even if benefits fail. Judged$500 resources are actual avoided otherwise-paid energy/access/repair spending net of offsets, not retail repair value or appreciated property capital. Positive overlap with health/security is discounted; negative costs are not. Public/utility and volunteer resource losses are distinct sensitivities, without counting grants as new household income. Current owner-occupied eligibility excludes mortgage/tax delinquency and some renters, limiting reach.

sources.title: Current eligibility, repair programs and alternatives

model.costScope: Whole FY2024 recipient annual functional cost with netted-expense audit, not marginal donation; partial repair benefit model with program-cost and full-resource sensitivities.
model.geographicAttribution: Adams, Arapahoe, Denver, Douglas and Jefferson plus El Paso service counties; g.85 judged share within fixed ten-county CBSA19740, not measured headquarters share.
model.formula: Health = N × unique × b × eligible × completion × response × q × discounted finite T × g minus full exposed harm. Signed net household resources are joint logged once using 0.5 log(after/before); price =10C/(health + income equivalents) when positive.
model.counterfactual: Municipal/county repair programs, Brothers Redevelopment, household funds and other providers may supply repairs without this recipient.
model.attribution: b.5 additionality separate from clinical response; unique homes and local share hypotheses explicit; full exposed harms/access costs retained at b0.
model.uncertainty: No local controlled utility, actual savings, repair persistence or marginal capacity measured. Numerical reference conditional, broader displacement/community effects unknown not zero.
model.nativeOutcomes: FY2024 72 homeowners and overlapping repair/demographic counts;2050 volunteer hours; not national nearly100,000 volunteers or cumulative thousands local beneficiaries.

reports.priceScope: Historical full annual recipient cost against conditional current navigation benefits; not a matched current whole-portfolio or marginal-gift EV.

what: Benefits in Action assists with SNAP, health insurance, disability and other public-benefit applications.
Its food-delivery program ended April30,2026; current navigation continues statewide.
A conditional health-plus-net-transfer reference is about $14.3M per better life.
strengths: Current recipient sources identify free application assistance and dated food-program closure.
Original filings and legal donor identity were independently checked.
The calculation includes recipient resources, full participation burdens and distinct public-payer losses.
reservations: Individuals and families are mixed units; applications are not unique approvals or causal outcomes.
Historical expenses include discontinued food delivery and are not a current navigation budget.
Incremental enrollment, household benefit amounts, health utility and local share remain hypotheses.

sections.what: Benefits in Action, EIN87-3774775, offers free application assistance, benefit literacy and referral support. SNAP, Medicare, Medicaid, Connect for Health Colorado, Social Security and LEAP are mechanisms, not measured new income. Official donation page names the legal payee/check route and links ColoradoGives; no transaction made. Food delivery ended April30,2026, despite stale donor-profile food wording.
sections.monitoring: The homepage2025 envelope is16000 individuals and families and28000 applications. These are mixed units and overlapping applications, not unique households or approvals. Its87% Medicaid enrollment/fewer-emergency-visits statement is descriptive, not a controlled causal coefficient. Request distinct current households, approvals versus alternative application, benefit duration, service county, after-tax/other-benefit-withdrawal resources and payer costs. Cumulative75000 since2015 is not annual output.
sections.qualitative: Enrollment may improve access to care and constrained household consumption, but self-application, county agencies, insurers and other navigators are alternatives. Model16000 mixed units times.5 household conversion; .2 incremental access, .2 health-compatible share, .3 clinical response and .01 utility for one year are explicit judgments. No ER reduction or avoided-death coefficient is imported. Current statewide navigation differs from the former four-county food service.
sections.cost: Original full FY2024 expenses $4,368,504 include $8,972 netted direct event costs. FY2023 full $2,525,910; two comparable full-year mean $3,447,207. FY2022 covered only July–December: $770,665 including $13,412 direct events, excluded from annual mean and not annualized. FY2024 $3,853,488 recognized program cost combines navigation and then-food work; it is only a historical mixed-program sensitivity, not allocated current navigation or a marginal donation price. Cost/output/program vintages do not match, so this is a conditional partial reference.
sections.funding: Judged$2400 annual resources for half of incremental households are actual disposable food/cash/utility benefits net of taxes, offsets and other benefit withdrawal, not insurance retail spending or gross wages. Positive gain is overlap-adjusted. Full$25 time/access costs and stress apply to all exposed households even failed applications. Same household benefit and costs share one log. Distinct taxpayer households lose full$2400 per changed household, without positive-overlap discount; local incidence applied once. Taxpayer baseline/group size and net benefit amounts are judgments. Insurance clinical access and consumption savings are not duplicated; additional public treatment/provider costs are adverse sensitivities. Next-gift capacity after food closure unknown.

model.costScope: Historical whole FY2024 annual entity expense with current navigation-only benefit hypothesis; no claim current budget, all-portfolio EV or next-gift offer.
model.geographicAttribution: Statewide navigation and Colorado Springs co-locations; g.6 judged beneficiary share in ten-county Denver CBSA19740. Former Jefferson/Denver/Adams/Arapahoe food footprint is not current navigation share.
model.formula: Health = N × unique × b × eligible × completion × response × q × finite discounted T × g minus full exposed harms. Same-household net resources including access costs are joint logged; distinct government payer loses full transferred resources localized once. Price=10C/(health + signed income equivalents) when positive.
model.counterfactual: Public self-application, county eligibility offices, insurer assistance and other navigators without this recipient; approved benefit may have arrived anyway.
model.attribution: Incremental benefit access b.2 is distinct from health eligibility/clinical response and resource recipient fraction. Enrollment and submitted applications are not additionality.
model.uncertainty: Finite one-year conditional reference, no local controlled health or disposable-income effect. Current unique cohort/budget and approval additionality unknown; food closure breaks portfolio comparability.
model.nativeOutcomes: 2025 mixed16000 individuals/families and28000 applications;87% Medicaid descriptive statement; current fooddelivery ceased2026. No counts converted to deaths prevented, completed treatments or net income automatically.

what: Hunger Free Colorado connects households to food resources through a multilingual hotline, outreach and statewide partners.
It also organizes and advocates on school meals and food policy, whose benefits are not automatically counted as its own.
A conditional health-plus-net-transfer service reference is about $4.72M per better life.
strengths: The latest original filing identifies a matched annual application-household envelope.
Current service routes and local-versus-statewide boundaries are explicit.
Full public-payer transfer losses and applicant burdens are retained alongside household benefits.
reservations: HFC and partners submitted applications; these are not unique new approvals or recipient-only causal effects.
Local utility, net food resources, eligibility and additionality remain judgments.
Full recipient expenses cover policy and organizing beyond the limited service reference.

sections.what: Hunger Free Colorado, EIN 68-0551464, operates a multilingual food hotline, bilingual mobile outreach and partner network, alongside school-food advocacy. It is not the distinct Food Justice for All entity. Own donation page embeds an EveryAction form; its endpoint returned HTTP200, with no transaction made.
sections.monitoring: The original FY June2025 filing reports online SNAP applications for more than17,357 households submitted by HFC and partners. Thirty thousand individual connections are not added to this household count. Request unique approvals, continued receipt, HFC versus partner contribution, Denver residence, alternative application access and actual net resources. Current eligibility changes can alter reachable capacity; descriptive applications are not proof of treatment or improved nutrition.
sections.qualitative: Food assistance may improve food security and health, but neither submitted applications nor school-meal access establishes local causal utility. The reference uses .15 combined recipient/partner versus alternative-provider additionality, .6 resource receipt, .3 health-compatible share, .2 response and .01 utility for one year as judgments. County self-application and other navigators are alternatives. School-food, farmer and cafeteria-worker effects remain unknown, not zero; no gross wages or statewide population multiplied by a slogan.
sections.cost: FY June2025 full annual cost is $5,030,480: $5,007,591 functional expenses plus $22,889 netted fundraising expenses. Comparable FY2024 $5,550,876 and FY2023 $6,295,996 give mean $5,625,784. Recognized client-services expense $3,008,512 is an annual channel sensitivity without fully allocated overhead, not a marginal gift. Whole annual cost against a limited SNAP service channel is conservative on omitted benefits but not whole-portfolio EV. The59.6MB2025 annual report exceeded web retrieval limits and was not reviewed; matched original IRS native narrative was read.
sections.funding: Judged $2,000 net annual constrained food-consumption resources are after other-benefit withdrawal and offsets, not retail charity value or healthcare billing. Positive gains are overlap-adjusted to .6; full $10 applicant time/access costs and stress remain even failed applications. Same-household gains and costs share a joint log. Distinct taxpayer households lose the full $2,000 per changed household without positive-overlap discount; local incidence is applied once. Lower-income recipient and payer consumption baselines are judgments. Public implementation, coalition attribution, finite policy delay and job/displacement effects need separate review before wider policy benefits are added. Current donor-dependent capacity is unmeasured.

model.costScope: Whole annual FY2025 recipient cost against conditional limited SNAP-navigation benefits; recognized client-services and full-year mean sensitivities, no marginal capacity price.
model.geographicAttribution: Statewide network; g .45 judged beneficiary share in Denver's ten-county CBSA19740, not headquarters or all-Colorado attribution. Recipient and payer incidence localized once.
model.formula: Health = N × unique × b × eligible × completion × response × q × finite discounted T × g minus full exposed harm. Joint net household food resources minus access costs logged once; distinct public payer loses full transfer resources localized once. Price=10C/(health + signed resource equivalents).
model.counterfactual: County self-application, public agencies, statewide partners and other navigators may obtain benefits without Hunger Free Colorado.
model.attribution: b .15 jointly represents recipient contribution within the partner network and additional access versus alternatives, not observed successful attribution. Resource receipt distinct from health response.
model.uncertainty: Conditional initial reference, not measured causal EV. Unique current approvals, local consumption/utility, partner attribution, public payer cost and gift capacity unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: FY2025 original filing more than17,357 application households across HFC plus partners and30,000 food-resource individual connections; not completed clinical outcomes. Organizing participants and statewide school benefits not added.

what: Doctors Care provides primary and behavioral health care plus insurance and resource navigation in Littleton.
It accepts insured and uninsured patients with sliding fees, rather than providing uniformly free care.
A conditional clinical-plus-net-resource reference is about $9.78M per better life.
strengths: The original FY2025 filing provides matched clinic-client and visit counts.
Current fees, insured/public alternatives and expanded age eligibility were checked.
The model includes negative patient costs and tests outside payer and volunteer resources.
reservations: Clinic clients, coverage clients and outreach touchpoints overlap and are not additional unique cohorts.
Incremental health utility and work-resource changes remain judgments, not local causal measurements.
Whole annual cost includes coverage/navigation beyond the limited modeled clinic channel.

sections.what: Doctors Care, EIN 84-1150815, combines primary care, behavioral health, care coordination and coverage assistance. Current new-patient eligibility is newborn through age64; older filings describe up to50. Medicaid, CHP+, private insurance and uninsured patients are accepted. The correct donor route is own get-involved page with a ColoradoGives iframe; its linked endpoint returned HTTP200, no transaction made. The unavailable /donate path is not used.
sections.monitoring: Original FY2025 clinic served2,569 clients through7,920 visits. Coverage assistance served898 clients through1,228 appointments, which may overlap clinic patients. More than6,000 ambassador touchpoints are not unique health outcomes. Request deduplicated households, program overlap, Denver county, completed care, clinical change, treatment alternatives, fees/time and actual net work resources. Placeholder homepage patient stories are not causal evidence.
sections.qualitative: Primary care and behavioral health can improve function and access, but no recipient-specific utility or mortality coefficient was found. The model uses .8 client-to-household/primary-affected-person conversion, .3 incremental care versus alternatives, .4 health response and .03 utility for one year, all judgments. One household's primary clinical benefit is represented, not summing every family member automatically. Other primary-care/FQHC providers, public/insured care and counseling are alternatives. Coverage-only, vaccine and other portfolio benefits remain unmeasured, not zero.
sections.cost: FY2025 full functional expenses $3,393,823 with blank netted fundraising/gaming/COGS. FY2024 $3,231,491 and FY2023 $2,989,134 give mean $3,204,816. Recognized program expense $2,790,718 combines clinical and client services, not an allocated clinic-only cost. Whole annual cost against a clinical subset is a partial-channel reference, not a complete portfolio estimate or next-donation price. A $4M full-social-resource sensitivity allows for donated provider time and uncounted outside resources; not an observed wage bill.
sections.funding: June2026 fees range $20–$160 for all visits, with additional lab/implant costs; inability to pay does not remove time burdens. The observed average3.08 visits/client is not uniform dose. Judged $75 annual net copay/time cost and .0005 stress apply to every exposed household, even failed benefits. Judged $500 net work resources for a fraction of incremental households exclude taxes, benefit withdrawal and commuting/work costs; not salaries of survivors. Positive gains receive .5 overlap adjustment, all losses remain full, and work/access costs are joint logged. Central medical cash savings are zero as an explicit unmeasured conservative hypothesis, with positive and adverse cases—not proof of no benefit. Separate public/insurer/provider losses include only additional outside resources, avoiding duplication of recipient expenses already in C. Next-gift capacity and volunteer hours are unknown.

model.costScope: Whole FY2025 annual recipient functional cost against limited clinical partial benefits; combined-program recognized costs and social-resource sensitivities are not marginal gift prices.
model.geographicAttribution: Littleton clinic serves beyond its location; g .95 judged beneficiary share within fixed ten-county Denver CBSA19740, not observed residence or all-Colorado share.
model.formula: Health = N × unique × b × eligible × completion × response × q × finite discounted T × g minus full exposed harm. Joint signed net household work/medical resources less full access costs logged once; distinct outside payer resources localized once. Price=10C/(health + income equivalents) when positive.
model.counterfactual: Other primary-care/FQHC providers, public or insurance-covered care, covered counseling and other enrollment assistance without Doctors Care.
model.attribution: b .3 incremental access separate from clinical response; .8 conversion explicitly judged because unique clients are not household counts. All exposed negative harms/costs retained at b0.
model.uncertainty: No empirical local causal utility or disposable-income calibration. Coverage clients may overlap; outside costs, geographic residence and gift capacity missing.
model.nativeOutcomes: Matched FY2025 2,569 clinic clients/7,920 visits;898 coverage clients/1,228 appointments;6,000 ambassador touchpoints not added. Counts are delivery, not successful incremental clinical outcomes.

reports.program: Medical-bill navigation and consumer health policy
reports.priceScope: Historical matched FY2023 full annual recipient cost against a partial assistance channel; current productivity and policy benefits unknown, not zero, and not a marginal-gift offer.

what: Free Consumer Assistance Program helps people contest bills, denied coverage and eligibility barriers; it does not pay their medical bills.
The charity also advocates for consumer protection and implementation of Colorado health policy with agencies and coalitions.
This historical numerical reference pairs FY2023 costs with 777 annual clients; it is not current productivity, cumulative bills saved or whole-policy expected value.
strengths: Current recipient, free-service route and linked donation intake are identified.
Original three-year IRS costs are checked, including netted fundraising costs.
Actual cash avoidance and full provider/insurer incidence are distinguished from nominal charges written off.
reservations: The observed 777 annual clients are historical and not unique households or causal outcomes; current cohort, local share and utility remain uncertain.
Bills saved are not necessarily otherwise-paid consumption, and the counterparty can lose the same collectible cash.
Whole annual costs fund policy and organizing too; their implemented health and resource effects remain unmeasured rather than assumed zero.

sections.what:
CAP supports billing appeals and applications while policy work addresses affordability, coverage and consumer protections.

Current cumulative counters differ across the same page; neither is used as annual delivered cases.
sections.monitoring:
Seek annual unique clients, actual collected cash avoided, completed appeals and recipients inside the ten-county Denver boundary.

Measure implemented policy changes against agency obligations and alternatives, not only legislation or coalition participation.
sections.qualitative:
Self-appeals, legally required hospital assistance, insurers and other advocates form the counterfactual. Staffing limits can delay responses.

Historical Axis work in southwest Colorado is outside this edition; headquarters do not establish beneficiary geography.
sections.cost:
Matched FY2023 full annual cost is $1,536,690: functional expenses $1,523,080 plus $13,610 netted event costs. Latest FY2024 full cost is $1,801,425 and is a mismatched-vintage sensitivity.

The historical 2023 model uses 777 observed clients, judged 90% unique households, 50% Denver share and 40% additionality. A $2,000 nominal bill reduction × 25% otherwise-paid collection fraction implies $500 cash avoided, not medical retail value.

Positive gains receive a 50% overlap adjustment; $25 access costs and process harms apply to all exposed households. A full $500 provider/insurer loss per changed household is retained without overlap discount.

Policy implementation, attribution, finite duration and delay are missing causal inputs; they are not assigned statewide population benefits. Latest-cost and annual-mean scenarios are sensitivities, not CAP allocations or marginal costs.
sections.funding:
Own donation page links a working EveryAction intake; no transaction was made. Free CAP access is not conditional on giving.

Current grants or appeals do not prove capacity to convert the next unrestricted dollar into incremental completed assistance.

model.costScope: Matched historical FY2023 full annual recipient cost against observed 777 assistance clients; latest FY2024 costs shown as mismatched-vintage sensitivity, not current productivity.
model.geographicAttribution: Judged 0.5 Denver beneficiary share within CBSA19740; statewide work and southwest Colorado pilot are not all local.
model.formula: Health = (N × unique × b × eligible × completion × response × q × finite discounted duration − all-exposed process harm) × Denver share. Signed resources jointly log changed and other exposed households, with full distinct provider/insurer loss and geography once; price = 10 × C / combined equivalents.
model.counterfactual: Mandated hospital assistance, public eligibility, insurers, self-appeals, other navigators and agency implementation would continue without CCHI.
model.attribution: b=.4 and successful cash recovery=.6 are conditional judgments, not local trial estimates. Wider policy implementation and causal contribution remain unknown.
model.uncertainty: Annual unique cohort, collectibility, utility, local share and policy effects are not empirically calibrated; null, adverse, payer and cost-boundary scenarios expose this.
model.nativeOutcomes: Original 2023 annual report states 777 clients and more than $2M nominal bill savings that year across 48 counties. Annual clients are not deduplicated households or incremental successes. Current and IRS cumulative counters are not annual outcomes.

reports.program: Volunteer mental health access and community service
reports.priceScope: Conditional FY2024 full annual cost against a current partial counseling channel; not measured whole-portfolio or marginal-gift effectiveness.

what: Spark connects Colorado residents facing care barriers to volunteer counseling and partner referrals, with up to ten free sessions.
It retains independent EIN84-0782124 as a Project Helping subsidiary and also operates other volunteer and senior/community programs.
The numerical reference uses an observed connection envelope, not verified unique completed therapy or parent-wide outcomes.
strengths: Current mental health access, licensed volunteers and recipient-specific giving route are identified.
Original three-year full annual recipient costs exclude parent-wide totals and avoid adding netted costs twice.
Health and signed resources include participation, alternative care and volunteer opportunity costs instead of free-service retail value.
reservations: Six thousand annual connections can include referrals; household uniqueness, clinical completion and causal effects remain judgments.
Current undated service counters are paired with FY2024 expense only as a conditional capacity reference, not measured FY2024 productivity.
Full costs cover senior, disaster and other work whose benefits remain unknown; neither community-support expense nor $75 session promotion is counseling marginal cost.

sections.what: The current program offers individual, couples and family counseling, host-site services and support groups. Up to ten sessions is a ceiling, not completed dose; the roughly three-week wait and partner referrals limit direct service assumptions. It does not provide crisis, inpatient or medication treatment.
sections.monitoring: Request unique annual direct patients, completed session distributions, referral-only clients, Denver beneficiary counts and controlled outcomes. Track current volunteer capacity and whether added gifts change access rather than replacing insurance or other providers.
sections.qualitative: Statewide staff and partner coverage do not establish Denver share. Medicaid, insurance, public clinics and other community providers remain alternatives. Parent Project Helping impact is excluded; clinical and household additionality are not established by testimonials.
sections.cost: FY2024 full annual cost is $2,111,453; netted event, gaming and inventory expenses are blank. Current 6,000+ annual connections are conservatively entered as 6,000, with judged 90% household uniqueness, 40% suitable completion, 40% additionality, 30% clinical response, .02 utility for half a year and 50% Denver share. These are not observed QALY coefficients. Changed households receive judged $100 after-tax/benefit/work-cost resources and $30 actual otherwise-paid copay avoidance, not retail therapy value; positive gains receive a 50% overlap adjustment. Full $10 access cost and process harm apply to every connected household. Distinct providers lose the full $30 actual copay per changed household. Volunteer opportunity loss is separately judged $30 per completed-service recipient, borne by volunteers rather than patients or providers, independent of benefit success. This does not duplicate the copay counterparty. Community-support $1,722,291 is only a mixed-program cost sensitivity; unmeasured other-program benefits are unknown, not zero. Household work/copay gains and provider cash losses are gated by eligibility and completed service. They become zero at completion=0 or eligibility=0, while all-connected access burdens remain; clinical response is a separate health-only hypothesis.
sections.funding: Own homepage directs donors to this recipient’s ColoradoGives profile, which identifies the independent legal subsidiary. No transaction was made. The $75 session illustration and current high demand are not verified incremental capacity or full marginal cost; parent management and transfer scope remain uncertain.

model.costScope: Observed FY2024 independent-recipient full annual expense against a partial current counseling access channel. Parent totals not added; no allocated therapy or next-gift cost is claimed.
model.geographicAttribution: Judged .5 share inside ten-county Denver CBSA19740; statewide coverage and other Colorado staff prevent an all-Denver assumption.
model.formula: Clinical health = (N × unique × b × eligible × completion × response × q × finite discounted duration − all-connected process harm) × Denver share. Household gains and full access costs are jointly logged; distinct provider loss and completed-service volunteer opportunity loss are retained with geography once. Price = 10 × C / combined equivalents.
model.counterfactual: Insurance, Medicaid, public and partner providers, other volunteer counselors and untreated care barriers without Spark. Completion and additionality are distinct hypotheses.
model.attribution: b=.4 causal additionality, completion=.4 and response=.3 are independent judgments, not a local trial or all connected clients receiving therapy. Resource gains and provider losses require suitable eligibility and completed direct service; no separate referral-income effect is assumed.
model.uncertainty: Current unique clinical dose, effect utility/duration, donor capacity, geography, household resources, volunteer displacement and parent support are not measured. Finite, null, adverse and cost-boundary cases expose uncertainty.
model.nativeOutcomes: Current own mental wellness page states 6,000+ people connected annually, including partner referrals, and up to ten free sessions. Neither is a unique completed-patient outcome. Whole Spark volunteers/hours/projects and parent impact are excluded from clinical N.

reports.program: Child trauma therapy, coordinated response and prevention
reports.priceScope: Matched FY2025 consolidated annual cost against partial trauma-treatment benefits; not whole-portfolio or marginal-gift effectiveness.

what: DCAC provides trauma treatment for children and non-offending families alongside forensic response and prevention.
Its 2025 treatment cohort contains 624 clients, including 50 adults, rather than thousands of outreach or advocacy contacts.
The historical annual reference includes clinical health and signed caregiver household resources; it does not assign child lifetime wages.
strengths: Newest treatment table and audited full consolidated costs are matched to 2025.
Named trauma treatments, licensed clinicians and coordinated family services provide a concrete mechanism.
Internal foundation transactions, repeated sessions and recognized donated services are not added again.
reservations: Clients are not unique completed households; dose, clinical response, utility and local share remain judgments.
Full annual costs cover forensic and prevention work whose benefits are unknown in this partial treatment model.
New Justice Center funding is future capital capacity, not demonstrated current incremental care or marginal donation impact.

sections.what: Current therapy addresses trauma with family engagement and named evidence-based approaches. Assessment and acceptance precede treatment. The treatment cohort is not a claim that every forensic interview prevents harm.
sections.monitoring: Request unique treated people and households, completed therapy dose, measured clinical outcomes, caregiver disposable resources and local patient share. Separate prevention and forensic additionality from mandated public-agency work.
sections.qualitative: Insurance, public victim support and other trauma clinicians form the baseline. Sessions, interviews, trainings and repeat family contacts are overlapping outputs, not independently added successes. Statewide/international training is not automatically Denver benefit.
sections.cost: FY2025 consolidated full functional cost is $3,354,733, including netted event costs and recognized donated services; these are not added twice. It is paired with the observed 624 treatment clients. Household/treated-person uniqueness .75, completion .7, causal additionality .4, clinical response .4, utility .03 for one year and Denver share .9 are explicit judgments. Resource gains of $150 are caregiver household disposable resources after taxes, benefits withdrawn, childcare and work costs, not child wages. They require completed eligible care and a separate .5 resource-success hypothesis. Positive gains receive .5 overlap adjustment; full $40 access/time costs and process harms apply to every exposed household, including unsuccessful care. Central actual copay avoidance and external payer loss are zero judgments, not proof of no economic effect; sensitivities assess them. Already recognized donated services remain in C; external opportunity-cost sensitivity refers only to unrecognized volunteer resources. A reported treatment expense sensitivity excludes shared overhead and is not verified marginal cost.
sections.funding: Own giving page links the current Hope Starts Here campaign; no payment was made. Consolidation includes the inactive supporting Advocacy Center Foundation with intercompany elimination, not another additive charity. Public bond approval for a future Justice Center does not establish completed incremental capacity; household public-payer incidence remains a sensitivity rather than a gross grant benefit.

model.costScope: Full audited FY2025 consolidated functional expenses, including event costs and recognized donated services; inactive foundation eliminated internally. Partial treatment benefits, not whole-portfolio EV.
model.geographicAttribution: Judged .9 share inside ten-county Denver CBSA19740. Denver/Adams service anchors do not measure residence; nonlocal training excluded from treatment benefits.
model.formula: Health = (N × unique × b × eligible × completion × response × q × finite discounted duration − all-exposed harm) × local share. Completed eligible changed households jointly log net caregiver resources and full access costs; full negatives and distinct payer incidence retained. Price = 10 × C / combined equivalents.
model.counterfactual: Other trauma clinicians, insurance, public child-protection and victim advocacy without DCAC; lower coordination or untreated barriers may remain.
model.attribution: b=.4 additionality, completion=.7 and clinical response=.4 are hypotheses; observed sessions are not causal outcomes. Caregiver resources require eligible completed treatment, not referrals alone.
model.uncertainty: Utility, duration, family overlap, clinical completion, alternative providers, caregiver gains, local share and next-gift capacity remain unmeasured. Other prevention/forensic channels are unknown, not zero.
model.nativeOutcomes: 2025 annual report treatment table:624 clients (574under18,50adults) and4,796sessions. The clients are not proven unique completed households. Outreach and forensic contacts are not added to the therapy denominator.

reports.program: Sexual assault trauma therapy, advocacy and prevention
reports.priceScope: Matched FY2024 full recipient annual cost against partial individual-therapy benefits, not whole-portfolio or marginal-gift effectiveness.

what: The Blue Bench provides free trauma-specific therapy and advocacy for survivors of sexual assault.
The matched 2024 reference uses 212 individual-therapy clients, not 2,295 mixed service contacts.
Health and signed household resources are assessed together without interpreting uncontrolled symptom improvement as causal QALYs.
strengths: Annual therapy count and full IRS costs are matched to 2024.
Free, time-limited specialist care offers a concrete access mechanism.
Calls, repeated advocacy and overlapping group clients are not added as unique therapy beneficiaries.
reservations: Completion, response, utility, household deduplication and local share remain judgments.
The observed PTSD pre/post comparison lacks a control and does not measure QALYs.
Full recipient costs fund other unquantified channels; current donor capacity is uncertain.

sections.what: Current services include individual and group trauma therapy, crisis support, hospital advocacy, case management and prevention. Therapy does not bill insurance and is usually time-limited to six months. Advocacy or compensation applications do not establish increased disposable income.
sections.monitoring: Request unique therapy clients and households, completed sessions, comparative symptom and utility outcomes, residence inside the pinned ten-county CBSA, actual otherwise-paid copays and after-cost work resources. Separate crisis contacts, advocacy and prevention outcomes from overlapping therapy clients.
sections.qualitative: The annual table sums individual therapy 212, group 40, case management 252, post-conviction advocacy 166, resource navigation 425 and 1,200 calls to a mixed-unit total of 2,295. Only the individual-therapy envelope is used. The reported 76.2% to 25% PTSD symptom criterion comparison is uncontrolled and has unclear sample and attrition; it cannot identify causal utility.
sections.cost: Matched calendar FY2024 full cost is $2,589,919: functional $2,585,426 plus netted direct event $4,493. The observed individual-therapy envelope is 212. Household conversion .9, completion .8, additionality .4, response .4, utility .03 for half a year and local share .95 are judgments. A $200 net household work/resource gain is after tax, benefit withdrawal and work/childcare costs, requires completed eligible care and separate .5 success, and is not survivor gross wages. Positive gains receive .5 overlap adjustment. All exposed households retain full $20 access/time loss and .0002 process harm even with failed benefits. Actual otherwise-paid copay saving and payer loss are central zero judgments, not measured absence. Sensitivities assess full provider/payer losses and unrecognized volunteer opportunity resources. The $1,396,328 therapy/advocacy program cost is a mixed-channel recognized-cost sensitivity, not allocated therapy-only or marginal gift cost.
sections.funding: Own current donation page identifies EIN 84-0905184; no transaction was made. Public victim support, insurance and alternative trauma providers remain in the counterfactual. Current funding disruption and the available newer impact report do not prove funded incremental clinical capacity. Government compensation transfers require recipient and payer incidence, not gross awards as income.

model.costScope: FY2024 full IRS functional cost plus netted direct event expense. Partial individual-therapy benefits; crisis, advocacy, prevention and other benefits unknown, not zero.
model.geographicAttribution: Judged .95 Denver CBSA19740 resident share; nine service counties include Lincoln outside the ten-county pinned boundary. Service catchment does not measure recipient residence.
model.formula: Health = (N × unique × b × eligible × completion × response × q × finite discounted duration − full exposed harm) × local share. Eligible completed changed households jointly log net resources and full access costs; other exposed households retain costs. Distinct payer incidence is localized once. Price = 10 × C / combined health and income equivalents.
model.counterfactual: Other trauma clinicians, public victim support, insurance and natural recovery without this free specialist therapy; untreated access barriers remain plausible.
model.attribution: Additionality .4, completion .8 and response .4 are judgments. Uncontrolled local pre/post symptoms do not identify incremental causal success.
model.uncertainty: Current donor capacity, therapy completion, utility, duration, household overlap, net work gains, provider losses and local residence are unmeasured. Other channels are unknown.
model.nativeOutcomes: 2024 annual table reports 212 individual-therapy clients. Group 40 can overlap; mixed total 2,295 includes 1,200 calls and is not unique people or completed households.

reports.program: In-home youth and family therapy, foster care and parent recovery support
reports.priceScope: Matched FY2025 full annual recipient cost against partial MST family-treatment benefits; other channels unknown, not whole-portfolio or marginal-gift EV.

what: Savio provides home-based youth and family therapy with public-service funding and coordination.
The matched 2025 reference uses 520 MST clients, not a sum of overlapping statewide programs.
It assesses clinical health and signed caregiver resources without assigning children's future wages.
strengths: Newest IRS native MST count and full annual expenses are matched to 2025.
Home-based family work offers a concrete clinical and access mechanism.
Multiple program counts, broad annual reach and public-funded savings are not added as independent benefits.
reservations: Causal completion, utility, alternative-provider additionality and local residence remain hypotheses.
Full recipient cost covers foster care, early childhood, trauma and grant administration whose effects are unknown.
Near-free family care is not equivalent to cash savings or donor-funded marginal capacity.

sections.what: Current home-based services include adolescent family treatment, trauma care, early-childhood caregiver work, foster care and parent substance recovery. Historical residential care closed in 2020 and is not counted as current adolescent capacity. New Bluestem family recovery is a separate current mechanism, not a reason to revive the old adolescent residential program.
sections.monitoring: Request deduplicated MST households, completed treatment and fidelity, comparable outcomes against contracted alternatives, caregiver disposable resources, Denver resident share and demonstrable unrestricted-donation capacity. Separate program substitution from treatment received and outcomes gained.
sections.qualitative: FY2025 original reports 520 MST clients plus FFT, sexual-behavior, trauma, family-wellness and foster cohorts; cross-program overlap is unknown, so they are not summed. The annual 1,800 Colorado families reached is not completed unique therapy. Public Medicaid/CYMHTA/county funding and other clinicians form the counterfactual. Broad success narratives do not identify causal QALYs.
sections.cost: FY2025 full IRS cost $14,274,461 is paired with 520 MST clients. The annual report's $13,906,047 expense differs; no unexplained blending is used. Household conversion .9, completed dose .8, incremental additionality .25, response .4, utility .04 for one year and CBSA share .55 are judgments, not observed causal coefficients. Caregiver $250 net resources are after taxes, benefits withdrawn, childcare and work costs, require completed care and separate .5 resource success, and are not child wages. Positive resource gains receive .5 overlap discount; all exposed families retain $30 time/access cost and .0002 process harm regardless of benefit. Actual otherwise-paid copay and external payer losses are central zero judgments with full-incidence sensitivity. The $7,093,017 adolescent mixed-program cost tests the recognized cost boundary; it is not allocated MST-only or marginal-gift cost. Clinical health and patient process harm use all 520 patients; .9 household conversion applies to caregiver resources only. Original randomized START/START II comparisons against active public services did not establish superior placements or QALYs. The positive access-gap reference is not trial-calibrated: .04 utility is a judged 14.6 healthy-day-equivalent annual improvement among responders, not measured Savio utility. The strong-public-alternative clinical/resource-null scenario is explicit.
sections.funding: Current giving page identifies Savio House Inc. DBA Savio, EIN 84-0570279, Stripe processing and greatest-need giving unless restricted. No transaction was made. Statewide contracts and Medicaid support can substitute for donated funding; government expenditure or retail free therapy value is not automatically net family consumption. New program needs indicate possible uses, not measured next-dollar impact.

model.costScope: Full calendar FY2025 IRS functional expense; netted event expenses blank. Only partial MST benefit reference; other channels unknown.
model.geographicAttribution: Judged .55 share of MST client households inside ten-county Denver CBSA19740. Statewide programs and Colorado Springs/Western Slope reach prevent assigning all beneficiaries to Denver.
model.formula: Health = (N patients × b × eligible × completion × response × q × finite discounted duration − full exposed patient harm) × local share. Completed eligible households jointly log net caregiver resources and full home-session costs; all negatives and distinct payer incidence retained. Price = 10 × C / combined health and income equivalents.
model.counterfactual: County/Medicaid contracted care, other family treatment and justice services without Savio; home access and fidelity may differ.
model.attribution: Judged .25 incremental additionality against publicly funded substitute providers, completion .8 and response .4. Native enrollment is not causal outcome.
model.uncertainty: Clinical utility, duration, completion, family overlap, actual substitute provision, caregiver gain, local share and next-gift capacity unmeasured. Other programs unknown, not zero.
model.nativeOutcomes: Original FY2025 reports 520 MST clients, not completed households; other native program categories are not added.

reports.program: Vaccination access partnerships, education and policy
reports.priceScope: Matched FY2025 full coalition annual cost against partial supported vaccination-channel benefits; not whole-portfolio or marginal-gift EV.

what: Immunize Colorado supports partner vaccination access, provider education and policy.
The matched 2025 reference uses 440 supported Shots for Tots and Teens patients, not 1,355 vaccines or all partner activity.
Health and signed household resources are assessed without treating outreach as changed uptake or children as immediate wage earners.
strengths: Newest full IRS cost and supported vaccination patient envelope are matched to 2025.
Current clinics and public alternatives identify a concrete access mechanism.
Partner doses, VISTA contacts and statewide education are not summed as unique coalition-caused beneficiaries.
reservations: Vaccine mix, completed protection, residence and coalition additionality remain judgments.
Full coalition costs cover other policy and education channels whose effects are unknown.
The nonprofit's annual cost omits potentially material partner delivery and public vaccine resources.

sections.what: Current support helps partners offer no- or low-cost vaccinations alongside education, VISTA and policy work. The program serves children and some adults; caregiver time is relevant without assigning children's earnings. Coalition-supported delivery is not ownership of every clinical dose.
sections.monitoring: Request unique patient households, age and vaccine mix, completed protective series, doses truly additional to public VFC/insurance access, resident share and partner resource cost. For policy distinguish supported legislation from implemented access, changed uptake and recipient attribution.
sections.qualitative: The 2025 supported Shots for Tots and Teens envelope is 440 patients. Multiple doses do not constitute multiple independent people, and other partner, messenger and VISTA populations may overlap. National/statewide education contacts and policy support are not measured uptake. Those other mechanisms remain unknown rather than zero.
sections.cost: FY2025 full cost $571,433 includes $569,413 functional expense plus $2,020 netted direct event costs. It is paired with 440 supported patients. Unique household conversion .8, completed indicated dose .9, coalition additionality .3, efficacy-response .8 and expected morbidity-equivalent .003 for one year are judgments; no measured recipient QALY conversion or uniform lifetime vaccine benefit is claimed. Denver share .75 is judged from clinic locations, not observed residence. Resource gain comprises $40 net caregiver/adult sick-time/work resources and $10 actually-paid illness cost avoidance after taxes/benefit changes/work costs. Separate .2 resource incidence limits the gained subgroup; this is not a measured adult proportion or child wages. Positive gains receive .5 overlap adjustment. All exposed households retain full $5 travel/time loss and .00002 vaccine/process harm, including failed incremental benefits. Central external partner/public loss zero is a limitation; sensitivities assess provider/payer/volunteer resources without importing hospital or partner budgets. The $222,806 outreach cost is mixed education, not clinical allocation; a recognized-cost sensitivity cannot establish marginal vaccination price. Health and patient process harms use all 440 patients, without household deduplication. Resources alone use a judged post-dedup household allocation: pediatric caregivers (388/440), adult patients (49/440), and three age-unknown patients whose household units retain burdens but no gains. Caregiver and adult resource incidence can be independently null. The distinct household allocation is a hypothesis, not observed deduplication. Original seasonal placebo-controlled influenza evidence establishes efficacy and dose dependence, not this vaccine mixture's QALYs. Central .003 represents a judged 1.095 expected healthy-day-equivalent per patient before vaccine efficacy for one year. A separate flu-risk illustration uses hypothesized .05 annual infection risk, seven days at .5 utility loss and trial .5098 efficacy; it is not a measured clinic coefficient.
sections.funding: Current own donor page identifies EIN 84-1479975 and links its Neon route; destination could not be rendered by the browser tool and no transaction occurred. Hospital office/email affiliation does not mean its budget is this recipient's. Public VFC, insurance, health departments and other clinics are alternatives. Coalition policy support may change implemented uptake, but the initial reference does not assign an unmeasured statewide policy coefficient.

model.costScope: Full calendar FY2025 coalition IRS expense including netted direct event costs, against partial supported patient benefit. Partner delivery costs and other channels unmeasured; not full social portfolio EV.
model.geographicAttribution: Judged .75 share in pinned ten-county Denver CBSA19740, based on metro clinic anchors but without recipient residence data; statewide activities not fully assigned to Denver. New detailed county counts describe clinic locations (including Boulder), not residence; .75 remains judged.
model.formula: Health = (N patients × b × eligible × completion × response × q × finite discounted duration − full exposed patient harm) × local share. Completed eligible changed households jointly log net caregiver/adult resources and full access costs. Positive-only overlap and distinct payer/provider loss are retained. Price = 10 × C / combined equivalents.
model.counterfactual: VFC, Medicaid/private insurance, local public health and other clinical providers without coalition support; access and trust barriers may leave additional patients.
model.attribution: Judged .3 coalition contribution after alternative access, .9 complete protection and .8 response. Supported patients and doses do not establish changed uptake or causal disease reduction.
model.uncertainty: Vaccine mix, incidence, age, protection duration, household overlap, local residence, attribution and delivery costs unmeasured. Policy/education/VISTA benefits are unknown, not zero.
model.nativeOutcomes: Original 2025 patient report: 440 patients, including 388 children, 49 adults and three age-missing. Clinic county totals are location, not resident geography; doses and other partner channels not added.

what: CHN supports Coloradans living with or at risk of HIV through treatment access, prevention and social support.
The matched FY2025 reference uses 557 PrEP navigations, not the sum of tests or all statewide clients.
Clinical patients and resource households are distinct; other channels remain unquantified.
strengths: Matched fiscal 2025 native navigation envelope and original full annual cost.
An original randomized PrEP trial anchors the prevention mechanism, not recipient attribution.
Public alternatives, household costs and external medication-resource incidence are explicit.
reservations: Navigation is not verified adherence or unique successful prevention.
Clinical utility, risk, additionality and Denver share are judgments.
Whole recipient costs cover substantial HIV care, nutrition and harm reduction outside this partial reference.

sections.what: Current statewide HIV client services, dental and mental health care, insurance assistance, nutrition, harm reduction and sexual-health prevention are not independent additive cohorts. HeyDenver and Hey719 report 557 PrEP navigations in FY2025; Colorado Springs is outside the Denver CBSA.
sections.monitoring: Request deduplicated PrEP starts, adherence and persistence, baseline infection risk, alternative provider access, residence, participant costs and restricted marginal capacity. Track HIV treatment continuity and overdose outcomes separately; reported reversals are not automatically deaths averted.
sections.qualitative: IPERGAY randomized high-risk MSM to on-demand medication or placebo with common counseling/testing: 2 versus 14 infections and 86% relative reduction over median 9.3 months. CHN serves different populations and navigation is a different intervention. Eligibility .8, adherence .6 and navigation additionality .2 remain hypotheses. Medication gastrointestinal and renal adverse events were more common; privacy and access harm are unmeasured.
sections.cost: FY2025 full cost $36,416,135 includes $99,264 netted direct event costs. The 557 navigation envelope is observed, not a causal patient count. Untreated infection risk .02 per year and utility decrement .2 for ten finite years are judgments: q=.004 is risk times annual illness burden, biological efficacy .86 applied once, not ten repeated years of infection risk. Judged Denver share .6 and household grouping .9 affect geography and income respectively; health retains all patients. Prevented-infection households gain $1,000 net work resources plus $200 otherwise-paid illness costs after tax, benefit and work-cost netting, with .5 positive overlap; no lifetime wages or retail medication value. Every navigation household retains $5 access/time costs even if prevention fails. Process/privacy harm .00002 per navigator is judged. Public medication delivery resources are unknown centrally and tested at $500 per eligible completed household, independent of navigation additionality. The $3,905,246 mixed education/prevention program-cost sensitivity is not allocated PrEP cost or marginal-gift efficiency.
sections.funding: Current own giving page identifies Colorado Health Network Inc., EIN 84-0961159, and region-designated support. No transaction was made. Federal prevention funding uncertainty can affect delivery but is not evidence every donation creates otherwise absent PrEP. Existing public clinics, insurance and medication assistance are counterfactual providers.
